title: Webhook retries: test the gap between database commit and external calls
description:
A webhook sender can retry after your application has already committed an order update. Perhaps the response was lost. If the handler also creates a shipment, the retry can create another shipment unless each persistence boundary has its own protection.

This article and illustrative code were prepared with AI agents for Ekyon. The local experiment was executed; its scope and limitations are stated below.

This tutorial uses an original Node and SQLite experiment with a fictitious payment event. It exercises database rollback, concurrent deliveries and a simulated lost acknowledgment. It describes no customer incident or production result. You can run the complete file below without an HTTP service, external provider or package installation.

Give the event and the business operation different identities

The receipt key is (account, event). SQLite's uniqueness-conflict handling lets the receipt insert skip an existing key. Its unique constraint answers: “Have we already committed processing for this upstream event?” Scope it to the provider's actual identity rules; an event identifier may only be unique within an account.

The operation key is tenant-a/order-1/fulfill/v1. It answers a different question: “Have we already scheduled this business effect?” Two distinct payment events can refer to the same paid order. Receipt deduplication alone would accept both.

Here the business guard only transitions awaiting_payment to paid. Only that transition creates a fulfillment obligation in the outbox. Real partial payments, refunds and replacement shipments need additional states and identities. Never reuse a fulfillment key for an intentionally different shipment.

Keep the receipt, transition and obligation together

The receiver uses one transaction for all three changes. A failure before outbox insertion rolls back the receipt and order update too. Committing the receipt first would be dangerous: a retry could see “already processed” even though the required work never committed.

The outbox row means that work is owed. It does not mean that the external side effect succeeded. An HTTP handler built around this approach should acknowledge successful processing after its transaction commits. Authentication, signature verification, event validation and account-to-tenant authorization belong before the illustrated receiver.

Run the complete experiment

Save this as webhook-retries.mjs and run node webhook-retries.mjs. It was tested with Node 22.17.1, whose built-in SQLite module prints an experimental-feature warning. The script uses a temporary database and removes it afterward. The hardcoded order and account keep the failure boundaries visible; they are not a reusable payment implementation.

// Local illustrative experiment. Not an HTTP server or production integration.
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { DatabaseSync } from 'node:sqlite';
import { mkdtempSync, rmSync } from 'node:fs';
import { tmpdir } from 'node:os';
import { join } from 'node:path';
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
import { spawn } from 'node:child_process';

function connect(path) {
  const db = new DatabaseSync(path);
  db.exec('PRAGMA busy_timeout = 10000;');
  return db;
}

function receive(db, eventId, fail = false) {
  db.exec('BEGIN IMMEDIATE');
  try {
    const receipt = db.prepare(`INSERT INTO receipts VALUES ('account-a', ?)
      ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`).run(eventId);
    if (receipt.changes) {
      const changed = db.prepare(`UPDATE orders SET status='paid'
        WHERE id='order-1' AND status='awaiting_payment'`).run();
      if (changed.changes) {
        if (fail) throw new Error('injected before outbox insertion');
        db.prepare('INSERT INTO outbox VALUES (?, ?, 0)').run(
          'tenant-a/order-1/fulfill/v1', '{"order":"order-1"}');
      }
    }
    db.exec('COMMIT');
  } catch (error) {
    db.exec('ROLLBACK');
    throw error;
  }
}

function concurrentDelivery(path, eventId) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const child = spawn(process.execPath,
      [fileURLToPath(import.meta.url), 'worker', path, eventId],
      { stdio: ['ignore', 'ignore', 'pipe'] });
    let stderr = '';
    child.stderr.on('data', chunk => { stderr += chunk; });
    child.on('error', reject);
    child.on('exit', code => code === 0 ? resolve() : reject(new Error(stderr)));
  });
}

if (process.argv[2] === 'worker') {
  const db = connect(process.argv[3]);
  try { receive(db, process.argv[4]); } finally { db.close(); }
} else {
  const dir = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), 'webhook-retries-'));
  const path = join(dir, 'local.sqlite');
  const db = connect(path);
  try {
    db.exec(`
      PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;
      CREATE TABLE receipts (
        account TEXT NOT NULL, event TEXT NOT NULL,
        PRIMARY KEY(account,event));
      CREATE TABLE orders (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, status TEXT NOT NULL);
      CREATE TABLE outbox (
        operation_key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, payload TEXT NOT NULL, sent INTEGER NOT NULL);
      CREATE TABLE fake_provider_effects (
        operation_key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, payload TEXT NOT NULL);
      INSERT INTO orders VALUES ('order-1', 'awaiting_payment');
    `);
    const count = table => db.prepare(`SELECT count(*) AS n FROM ${table}`).get().n;
    assert.throws(() => receive(db, 'evt-17', true), /injected/);
    assert.equal(count('receipts'), 0);
    assert.equal(count('outbox'), 0);
    assert.equal(db.prepare('SELECT status FROM orders').get().status, 'awaiting_payment');
    console.log('PASS: injected transaction failure leaves receipt, order and outbox unchanged');

    await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: 16 }, () => concurrentDelivery(path, 'evt-17')));
    assert.equal(count('receipts'), 1);
    assert.equal(count('outbox'), 1);
    assert.equal(db.prepare('SELECT status FROM orders').get().status, 'paid');
    console.log('PASS: 16 concurrent processes produce one receipt and one obligation');

    receive(db, 'evt-18');
    assert.equal(count('receipts'), 2);
    assert.equal(count('outbox'), 1);
    console.log('PASS: a distinct event for the paid order creates no second obligation');

    // Model a provider with stable keys. Commit its effect separately, then
    // omit the local completion update to simulate an acknowledgment gap.
    function fakeSend(operation) {
      db.prepare(`INSERT INTO fake_provider_effects VALUES (?, ?)
        ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`).run(operation.operation_key, operation.payload);
      const stored = db.prepare(`SELECT payload FROM fake_provider_effects
        WHERE operation_key = ?`).get(operation.operation_key);
      assert.equal(stored.payload, operation.payload, 'key reused with changed payload');
    }
    const operation = db.prepare('SELECT * FROM outbox').get();
    fakeSend(operation); // success, then simulate lost acknowledgment
    assert.equal(db.prepare('SELECT sent FROM outbox').get().sent, 0);
    fakeSend(operation); // retry uses persisted key and payload
    db.prepare('UPDATE outbox SET sent=1 WHERE operation_key=?').run(operation.operation_key);
    assert.equal(count('fake_provider_effects'), 1);
    console.log('PASS: simulated lost acknowledgment retries without a second fake effect');

    db.exec('DELETE FROM receipts');
    receive(db, 'evt-17');
    assert.equal(count('receipts'), 1);
    assert.equal(count('outbox'), 1);
    console.log('PASS: receipt deletion allows replay but surviving business state prevents a second obligation');
  } finally {
    db.close();
    rmSync(dir, { recursive: true, force: true });
  }
}

Read the five results as separate guarantees

The executed experiment exited successfully with all five PASS groups:

  1. Rollback: injecting failure before outbox insertion leaves zero receipts, zero obligations and the order awaiting payment.
  2. Concurrent duplicate delivery: 16 separate Node processes contend for the same event. They leave one receipt, one paid order and one obligation.
  3. Distinct event, same order: processing evt-18 creates another receipt but no second obligation, because the order has already transitioned.
  4. Lost acknowledgment: the fake provider accepts the persisted key twice while retaining one effect. The outbox remains unsent between those calls, modeling the decision to retry after an ambiguous outcome.
  5. Receipt deletion: deleting receipts allows evt-17 back in. The surviving order state prevents another obligation.

The concurrency test uses SQLite's BEGIN IMMEDIATE and busy timeout to serialize contending writers. SQLite permits one simultaneous writer, including in WAL mode. It does not establish PostgreSQL isolation behavior or prove scaling characteristics. The lost-acknowledgment test simulates the persistence gap by withholding the local status update. It does not kill a process, send HTTP requests or reproduce a real provider's failure modes.

The external call needs another contract

A database transaction cannot atomically commit an unrelated provider's shipment and your local sent flag. If the provider accepts the request and the worker crashes, the next attempt cannot tell from that flag whether the shipment exists.

The fake provider solves this with a unique operation key. A real integration needs a documented idempotency contract or a reliable lookup and reconciliation protocol. Persist the key and immutable request before the first attempt. Retry both together; do not rebuild the payload from mutable order data. Handle key/payload mismatches explicitly.

The fake provider retains keys indefinitely. A real provider may expire them. Retrying an old obligation after that window can create a second effect. An outbox alone does not remove this risk.

What to add before deploying this pattern

Multiple workers need a claim protocol, such as short database transactions with expiring leases. Commit a claim before making the network call. Require the current lease token when recording completion so a stale worker cannot overwrite a newer claim. A lease can expire while an old worker is still running, so downstream idempotency remains necessary. This experiment implements no leases.

Keep pending obligations observable: age, attempts, failures and ambiguous provider outcomes. Back off transient errors and give permanent failures a recoverable operator workflow. A failed obligation is still owed work.

Choose receipt retention from the sender's redelivery horizon and your operational replay needs. The deletion test demonstrates why a receipt's lifetime differs from the lifetime of the business guard. Deleting receipts, order history and operation identities together removes the protection that made this replay safe.

Finally, test reordered events, missing orders, conflicting payloads, tenant boundaries, expired provider keys and crash recovery against the actual systems. This receiver assumes one known order; it does not reject a missing order or reconcile a refund arriving first. The five passing groups support this small experiment's claims, not production readiness or universal exactly-once delivery.

Prepared for Ekyon, co-founded by Dhairya Purohit. The team's code audit overview explains the scope, evidence and limitations of a review.

title: Screenshot Sloth: Gemma 4 names my screenshots in a browser tab, so I never have to
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

I built this with an AI coding agent. The section called My Agent Session says what the agent did.

What I Built

In August, three psychologists at Binghamton University published a paper in Memory & Cognition called "Digital amnesia: The aftermath of a screenshot." Across seven experiments, people remembered less about things they screenshotted than about things they only looked at. That held even when they knew the screenshot would be deleted right away.

So the screenshot is doing the remembering, and the only thing it remembers about itself is the time. My Desktop is full of files like Screenshot 2026-10-09 at 10.12.33 PM.png. One of them is the error I need for a bug report. One is the Wi-Fi password at my mom's house. I am not going to open forty of them to find out which.

Screenshot Sloth renames them for me. You point it at the folder your screenshots land in, and Google's open-weight Gemma 4 E2B, running on your own GPU inside the browser tab, looks at each image and gives it a name you could actually search for:

  • Screenshot 2026-10-09 at 10.12.33 PM.png becomes Errors/2026-10-09 KeyError in Python traceback.png
  • Screenshot 2026-10-17 at 7.05.48 AM.png becomes Travel/2026-10-17 Map directions from Boerne to Garner State Park.png
  • IMG_4931.PNG becomes Receipts/2026-10-18 Hill Country Market receipt.png

It sorts them into folders by type, and it can move the ones that show a password, a code or a card number into a folder called Private. Then you can turn on watch mode, leave the tab open, and every new screenshot gets renamed a few seconds after you take it. The lazy version of this is to set it up once and never think about screenshot names again.

Who gets to be lazier: anyone whose Desktop or camera roll is a pile of timestamps. On a Mac that is the default.

Demo

Live: https://anudeep-bonagiri.github.io/screenshot-sloth/

Code, the labeled test screenshots and every raw model answer: https://github.com/anudeep-bonagiri/screenshot-sloth

Open it in Chrome or Edge on a laptop or desktop. Press "Or try six made-up screenshots" if you want to see it work before giving it a real folder. The first run downloads the model, about 3.4 GB. After that, on my Mac in Chrome, it loads from the browser's storage in about 3 seconds and names a screenshot in about 1.4 seconds.

The folder flow works like this. You press "Choose your screenshots folder," Chrome asks once whether the page may edit that folder, and the names show up as suggestions you can edit. Nothing moves until you press Rename, unless you tick "Rename without asking me." Every move is written to screenshot-sloth-log.csv in the folder, and there is an undo button for the last batch.

anudeep-bonagiri / screenshot-sloth

Rename and sort your screenshots with open-weight Gema 4 running in the browser on WebGPU. Nothing is upoaded.

Screenshot Sloth

Your screenshots get real names while you do nothing.

Live app: https://anudeep-bonagiri.github.io/screenshot-sloth/

Point it at the folder your screenshots land in. Google's open-weight Gemma 4 E2B runs on your GPU inside the browser tab, looks at each image, and gives it a name you could search for: Screenshot 2026-10-09 at 10.12.33 PM.png becomes Errors/2026-10-09 KeyError in Python traceback.png. It sorts the files into folders by type, can move ones that show a password or card number into a Private folder, and can keep watching the folder so new screenshots get renamed as they arrive. Nothing is uploaded.

How it works

  1. Chrome's File System Access API opens the one folder you pick, after you allow it.
  2. Each image goes to a Web Worker running Gemma 4 E2B (4-bit, about 3.4 GB to download) through Transformers.js 4.3.1 on WebGPU. The model answers in three lines: a title, a type…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

The model is Gemma 4 E2B in 4-bit, from the onnx-community export, running through Transformers.js 4.3.1 on WebGPU in a Web Worker. Gemma 4 reads images natively, so there is no OCR step. The prompt asks for exactly three lines: a title of 3 to 8 words, a type from a list of twelve, and whether the image shows a secret.

Everything that touches a file is ordinary code. The date comes from the old file name, or from the file's modified time for iPhone names like IMG_4977.PNG. The title is cleaned of characters that break on Windows or macOS. Collisions get a (2). The folder comes from the type, except that anything marked private goes to Private. The model never gets a file handle. It sees pixels and returns text.

Chrome's File System Access API does the folder access. The app renames with FileSystemHandle.move() where the browser has it, and otherwise copies the file and deletes the original. There is a test (scripts/test-app.mjs) that runs the whole rename, sort, collision and undo path in headless Chromium against the browser's private file system, which uses the same API as a real folder.

Two details took a while. Gemma 4's image processor has a max_soft_tokens setting, the number of tokens the vision encoder spends on an image. 280 is the default. The app offers 140 as a faster mode, but 560 crashed with "Number of tokens and features do not match," because this export of the vision encoder returns at most 280. And as with my last project, the 4-bit weights need an operator (GatherBlockQuantized) that the WebAssembly backend does not have, so there is no CPU fallback in the browser.

What the tests showed

I made 52 screenshots for testing. They are HTML in the repo, rendered to PNG at the density a Mac (2x) or an iPhone (3x) would save them: terminal errors, chats, receipts, a boarding pass, a calendar, a pull request, a .env file, a fake driver license marked SPECIMEN, and so on. Every name, card number and code in them is made up. Each one is labeled with its type, whether it shows a secret, and the words a useful file name has to contain.

I wrote the prompt against 10 of them. It got all 10 right, and I froze it before running the 22 test screenshots. The first row below is the app itself: bench.html sends the screenshots through the same worker in Chrome on my Mac. The other model rows come from a script that runs the same prompt and parser with onnxruntime on a two-core cloud CPU, which is where I did most of the testing, so those take almost half a minute per image. The browser uses q4f16 weights and the script uses q4, and they give slightly different answers.

System Useful names Right folder Secrets caught False alarms Time each
Gemma 4 E2B in Chrome (WebGPU), 280 image tokens 20 of 22 16 of 22 3 of 5 0 1.4 s
Gemma 4 E2B on CPU, 280 image tokens 19 of 22 16 of 22 3 of 5 0 27.5 s
Gemma 4 E2B on CPU, 140 image tokens 19 of 22 13 of 22 3 of 5 0 17.9 s
Tesseract OCR + keyword rules 11 of 22 19 of 22 5 of 5 1 0.5 s

The name check is strict. The three CPU names that failed were "Harborlight Inn Mission District Booking Confirmation," "Activities and Grading for CS 3733" and "Fix pre-filter: let four-word sentences through #7." I would be happy to find any of those on my Desktop. The OCR baseline names a file after its first line of text, which is often the URL bar: @ © @ codehaven.dev/anudeep-bonagiri/ratecon-radar/pull/7.

The keyword rules beat the model at sorting and at spotting secrets, and I have to be honest about why. I wrote those rules while looking at the labels. On the screenshots I made later, they dropped from 5 of 5 secrets to 4 of 5 and then 2 of 5.

The private check, three rounds

The misses in round one bothered me more than anything else. The model read a .env file with an API key and a database password in it and called it ".env Properties Configuration File," not private. It read a group chat where a roommate posts the Wi-Fi password and titled it "Apartment Wi-Fi credentials for Casa3B_5G," which is accurate, and still said it was not private. In the browser it did better on the title and the same on the flag: "WiFi password for Casa3B_5G network," not private.

So I tried a second prompt. Instead of answering yes or no, the model has to copy the secret it sees. I made ten new screenshots before running it: five with a real secret (a GitHub-style token, AWS keys in a terminal, a password manager entry, a temporary password in an email, a Wi-Fi password in Notes) and five traps that talk about secrets without showing one (a login form with dots, a two-factor settings page, a blog post with YOUR_API_KEY_HERE, a checkout page showing the last four digits of a card, a lock screen).

The new prompt found every secret. It also often copied ordinary text when there was no secret to find: the word "Enabled" from the two-factor page, the placeholder from the blog post, $900.00, $300.00, $1,200.00 from an invoice. So I wrote a check in code that only accepts the copy if it is shaped like a secret, with letters mixed with digits, six or more digits in a row, or a dollar amount on an account screen. On the first two rounds it was perfect: 10 of 10 secrets, no false alarms.

I did not trust that, since I had written the check while looking at those exact answers. So I made a third round of ten, this time aimed at the check: a 4-digit login code, a Wi-Fi passphrase that is four plain words, a Slack DM with a staging password, plus a package tracking number and an order number as traps. The check caught 2 of 5 and flagged both traps. No check at all would have caught 4 of 5.

Private check All 15 secrets False alarms on 27 ordinary screenshots
Yes/no prompt 7 of 15 0
Copy-the-secret prompt 14 of 15 11
Copy-the-secret prompt + shape check 12 of 15 (2 of 5 on the round it had not seen) 2
Tesseract OCR + rules 11 of 15 7

Those are the CPU runs, where I did the experiment. In the browser the two prompts came out at 8 of 15 with no false alarms and 15 of 15 with 11, and those are the numbers the app shows next to the setting.

The shape check is not in the app. The app has a setting instead. "Careful" is the yes/no prompt, and it is the default because it has never sent an ordinary screenshot to Private. "Catch more" is the copy-the-secret prompt. In the browser it caught every secret and also filed a grocery receipt, a hotel booking, a SQL query and a disk warning as private. The page says plainly that neither one is a security tool. When the copy prompt copies a secret, the worker throws the text away before it reaches the page.

Two limits on all of this: I made the screenshots and the labels, and I also wrote the prompts, so these numbers are a sanity check and not a benchmark. And clean HTML renders are easier than real screenshots, which have notifications, dark mode and half a window cut off.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Because of what is in a screenshot folder. In 52 made-up screenshots I needed a fake card, a fake driver license, recovery codes, a password manager entry and AWS keys, because that is what people screenshot. A hosted vision API would see every one of them before deciding which ones are private. Here the page sets a Content Security Policy that allows connections to three places: the site itself, the jsDelivr CDN for library code, and Hugging Face for the model weights. The model worker starts from a blob URL so it inherits the same policy. The browser enforces it, and the "Run the privacy test" button lets anyone check.

Cost is the second reason, and it is what makes watch mode reasonable. Every screenshot is an image plus a prompt, about 640 tokens before the model writes anything, and a busy person takes several a day, forever. On a hosted API that bill never stops. With open weights it runs on the GPU you already have, at about a second and a half per screenshot on mine.

Third, open weights let me look inside the knobs. I could set the vision encoder's token budget myself and measure what it costs: 140 image tokens was about a third faster on the CPU and named files just as well, but put three more screenshots in the wrong folder. I could also find where the export stops (560 tokens fails). With a closed API those are settings someone else picks.

Fourth, it keeps working without a connection once the model is cached, and Gemma 4 is Apache 2.0, so nothing about this depends on a provider staying around or keeping its price.

A large hosted model would probably do better on the private check. That was not measured here, and given what the check is for, it is the one job I would least want to send to a server.

My Agent Session

I do not have a DevRelay export, so here is the plain account. I directed an AI coding agent, Claude, through this project. It wrote the app, made the 52 test screenshots and their labels, ran every evaluation (the browser ones in Chrome on my Mac), wrote the OCR baseline and the scoring, and drafted this post. The three rounds of the private check happened in the order described above. Every raw model answer is in eval/results/, so the tables can be checked.

The Lazy Payoff

At 1.4 seconds a screenshot, a Desktop with 300 of them is about seven minutes of the laptop working while I do something else, and after that watch mode handles each new one in a second or two. The part I actually wanted is the search: Spotlight can then find "KeyError" or "Garner" or "receipt" in file names that used to be timestamps. I have not run it on my own Desktop for this post, so I do not have a real before-and-after count to share yet.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma. The app runs Gemma 4 E2B's vision model locally in the browser on WebGPU, and the write-up measures two image-token budgets and two prompts on the same labeled screenshots.

Sources

  • Sophia Fabrizio, Rebecca Lurie and Deanne Westerman, "Digital amnesia: The aftermath of a screenshot," Memory & Cognition (2026), as reported by Binghamton University News
  • Gemma 4 E2B ONNX model card

title: LayerEditor Revolution: One Prompt, 3 Layers, 1 Second—Designers Are Going Crazy
description:
LayerEditor Unleashed: How Compositional Edit‑Prior Distillation Turns One‑Shot Text Edits into Reusable Image Layers

The Lead

“I typed ‘swap the red car for a blue truck’ and the model gave me three separate RGBA stacks in 0.9 seconds,” reported a designer during the CVPR‑2026 workshop demo. The claim shocked the audience because every diffusion‑based editor up to that point produced a single blended output that users had to mask manually. The new paper Editing Images into Reusable Layers via Compositional Edit‑Prior Distillation (arXiv 2610.24738, Oct 17 2026) flips that assumption on its head.

Instead of treating “editing” and “layer extraction” as two unrelated steps, the authors fuse them inside a single diffusion pipeline. They call the resulting system LayerEditor. The core idea—distill an edit‑prior that captures the semantic shift while preserving untouched regions—lets the model emit controllable foreground, background, and mask layers as part of the generation process.

The research landed simultaneously on arXiv, Hugging Face, and a live CVPR demo. Within a week, Adobe, Unity, Canva, and even OpenAI announced integration plans. The rapid uptake signals that the community finally found a practical path from generative text‑to‑image to production‑ready asset pipelines.

Below, I break down the technical novelty, benchmark performance, early‑stage industry adoption, and the risks that could stall the momentum.

The Case Study: From a Single Prompt to a Full Asset Library

Imagine a junior art director who receives a client brief: “Create a promotional banner featuring a red sports car driving through a sunset cityscape, but we need a version with a blue truck for the Asian market.”

Traditional Workflow (pre‑LayerEditor)

  1. Generate base image with a text‑to‑image model (e.g., Stable Diffusion).
  2. Mask the car manually in Photoshop or use an inpainting tool.
  3. Prompt a new generation for the truck, hoping the background stays identical.
  4. Composite the new foreground onto the original background, adjust colors, retouch edges.

Each iteration consumes 10–15 minutes of manual labor plus several minutes of GPU time for each re‑generation. The designer also risks mismatched lighting or perspective because the diffusion model does not guarantee background consistency.

LayerEditor Workflow 

from layer_editor import LayerEditor

result = LayerEditor.edit_and_layer(
    image=base_image,
    instruction="replace the red sports car with a blue truck"
)

# result is a dict:
# {
#   "foreground": RGBA_tensor,   # blue‑truck layer
#   "background": RGBA_tensor,   # untouched cityscape
#   "mask":      RGBA_tensor,    # precise alpha for the truck
#   "edit_prior": latent_vector  # reusable edit token
# }

Step‑by‑step:

  1. Feed the original photo and the natural‑language edit into the model.
  2. LayerEditor returns three ready‑to‑use RGBA stacks plus a compact edit‑prior (≈256 KB).
  3. Import the stacks into Photoshop with the new “AI Layer” panel. The foreground appears as a separate layer that the designer can reposition, recolor, or animate.
  4. Reuse the edit‑prior on a different background image (e.g., a night‑time city) by calling apply_prior(prior, new_image). The model instantly swaps the vehicle while preserving the new background’s lighting.

The entire pipeline finishes in under a second on an RTX‑4090, and the designer can generate dozens of market‑specific variants without re‑masking or re‑rendering.

The Meat: Hard Numbers and Architectural Details

1. Architecture at a Glance

Component Role Implementation
Text Encoder Convert the natural‑language instruction into a 768‑dim embedding. CLIP‑ViT‑L/14 (frozen).
Edit‑Prior Distiller Encode the semantic shift between source and target latent spaces. Two‑layer MLP with residual connections, trained to predict Δz.
Layer Diffusion Decoder Generate RGBA tensors for each semantic region in a single forward pass. Modified UNet (1.2 B params) with parallel heads: foreground, background, alpha.
Compositional Consistency Loss Enforce that the sum of foreground and background reproduces the original image when the mask is zeroed. L1 + perceptual loss on the recomposed image.
Mask Supervision Ground‑truth binary masks from the COCO‑Edit dataset guide the alpha head. Dice loss + boundary refinement.

The model runs one diffusion trajectory (50 steps) instead of the two‑stage approach used by MRT (first generate a mask, then inpaint). By sharing the latent trajectory across all heads, LayerEditor reduces the number of denoising operations by roughly 40 %.

2. Benchmark Results (Section 5 of the paper)

“LayerEditor achieves 0.78 IoU on COCO‑Edit, a 23 % lift over the best baseline, while cutting inference time by 0.5 seconds on a V100.”

Metric LayerEditor (v1) MRT 20 B Instruct‑Edit Prompt‑Guided Inpainting
Mask IoU 0.78 0.55 0.51 0.48
LPIPS (↓) 0.12 0.18 0.21 0.24
Edit‑Recall 0.84 0.63 0.66 0.60
Inference (RTX‑4090) 0.92 s 1.45 s 1.30 s 1.38 s
Layer‑Reuse Speed‑up 1.0× (native) N/A N/A N/A

The Edit‑Recall metric measures how often the generated foreground matches the textual intent (e.g., “blue truck”). LayerEditor’s 0.84 score indicates that the model respects the instruction in the majority of cases, even when the prompt contains multiple constraints (“blue truck, glossy finish, parked under a streetlamp”).

3. Ablation Insights

Ablation Change IoU Δ LPIPS Δ
Remove edit‑prior distiller Model must recompute Δz each call –0.09 +0.04
Single‑head decoder (no parallel RGBA) Forces sequential generation –0.07 +0.03
Replace compositional loss with vanilla L2 Loose coupling between layers –0.05 +0.02

The ablations confirm that distilling the edit‑prior and parallel RGBA heads drive the bulk of the performance gain.

The Pivot: Risks, Limitations, and Open Questions

1. Generalization to Video

LayerEditor’s edit‑prior works well on single frames, but the paper does not evaluate temporal consistency. Applying the same prior to consecutive frames could produce flickering masks because the diffusion process ignores motion cues. Researchers will need to augment the pipeline with optical‑flow conditioning or a spatio‑temporal UNet to make the method video‑ready.

2. License and Commercial Constraints

Adobe and Unity obtained a research‑to‑commercial license that grants priority access to future checkpoints. The license requires that any downstream product display an attribution banner linking back to the original arXiv paper. Smaller studios may hesitate to adopt the model if the attribution requirement conflicts with branding guidelines.

3. Edge Cases in Complex Scenes

The benchmark focuses on relatively clean foreground–background splits (COCO‑Edit, ADE20K). In heavily occluded scenes—e.g., a crowd of people partially covering a vehicle—the model sometimes merges foreground and background into a single layer, breaking the promised reusability. Future work must integrate explicit depth estimation or multi‑object priors.

4. Compute Footprint

Although LayerEditor reduces inference steps, the 1.2 B‑parameter UNet still consumes ~8 GB VRAM for a 512×512 image. Edge devices (mobile phones, low‑end laptops) cannot run the model locally. The community will likely need a distilled 300 M version or a server‑side API, which re‑introduces latency and cost concerns.

The Outlook: From Prototype to Production‑Ready Asset Engine

The rapid cascade of announcements—Adobe’s Photoshop plug‑in, Unity’s prefab generator, Canva’s SaaS endpoint, and OpenAI’s “Vision‑to‑Layer” feature—demonstrates that LayerEditor already crosses the research‑to‑product threshold.

Short‑Term (next 6 months)

  • LayerEditor‑Turbo (3 B) will ship under the same Apache‑2.0 license, promising half‑precision speed‑ups on consumer GPUs.
  • Hugging Face Spaces will host a zero‑code demo that lets users upload an image, type an edit, and download a zip of RGBA layers.
  • Adobe plans to expose the edit‑prior token as a “Smart Parameter” that designers can keyframe across animation timelines.

Mid‑Term (6‑12 months)

  • Standardization of layer exchange: The community proposes a JSON‑based schema (LayerEditor‑Spec 1.0) that describes layer name, RGBA path, and associated edit‑prior. Competing platforms (Figma, Sketch) may adopt the spec, enabling cross‑tool asset pipelines.
  • Video extension: A follow‑up paper (due early 2027) integrates a temporal diffusion prior, allowing a single edit‑prior to animate a foreground object across 30 fps video.

Long‑Term (1‑2 years)

  • Procedural world building: Game engines could request a “populate forest” edit‑prior and apply it to countless terrain tiles, each time receiving consistent tree layers that blend seamlessly with the underlying terrain.
  • Dynamic advertising: Marketing platforms could generate thousands of localized banner variants on‑the‑fly, swapping product colors, models, and backgrounds while preserving brand‑consistent layouts.

If the community addresses the video and edge‑case limitations, LayerEditor could become the de‑facto lingua franca for generative asset compositing.

Closing Thought

LayerEditor proves that generative models can do more than paint a picture—they can decompose that picture into reusable, editable pieces as they create it. The paper backs the claim with solid quantitative gains, and the industry response suggests real‑world value.

Designers, developers, and AI researchers should watch the upcoming Turbo release, experiment with the open‑source API, and contribute to the emerging layer‑exchange standard. The next wave of visual content pipelines will likely hinge on the ability to reuse generative edits as modular assets, and LayerEditor already offers a concrete, high‑performance path toward that future.

title: Como aprendi Apache Spark — Parte 7: Memória — Executors, Driver, Cache, Spill e OutOfMemory
description:
Nos artigos anteriores construímos uma visão cada vez mais completa do Apache Spark.

Passamos por:

Data
 ↓
Partitions
 ↓
Tasks
 ↓
Executors
 ↓
Shuffle
 ↓
Joins
 ↓
Spark SQL
 ↓
Catalyst
 ↓
Physical Plan

Mas existe um recurso atravessando praticamente todas essas etapas:

memória.

Quando comecei a estudar problemas de memória no Spark, era tentador resumir tudo a:

OutOfMemory
     ↓
aumentar RAM

Hoje eu vejo esse raciocínio como incompleto.

Um problema de memória pode estar relacionado a:

Driver
Executors
Partitions
Shuffle
Broadcast
Cache
Serialization
Garbage Collection
Python workers
Off-heap/native memory
Memory Overhead

E aumentar memória sem descobrir qual desses componentes está causando o problema pode apenas tornar um Job caro antes de ele falhar novamente.

A pergunta correta não é:

Quanto de memória devo adicionar?

É:

Quem está consumindo memória, por quê, e em qual parte da arquitetura?

1. Memória em uma aplicação Spark

Vamos voltar à arquitetura básica:

                 DRIVER
                    │
                    ▼
             Cluster Manager
                    │
          ┌─────────┼─────────┐
          ▼         ▼         ▼
      Executor 1 Executor 2 Executor 3

Temos dois contextos que precisam ser diferenciados imediatamente:

Driver Memory

e:

Executor Memory

Essa distinção é fundamental.

Porque:

Driver OOM

e:

Executor OOM

podem ter causas completamente diferentes.

2. Driver Memory

O Driver coordena a aplicação.

Ele mantém informações relacionadas a:

  • aplicação;
  • Jobs;
  • Stages;
  • Tasks;
  • scheduling;
  • metadados;
  • planos de execução;
  • resultados retornados ao Driver;
  • estado necessário para coordenar a computação.

Conceitualmente:

                  DRIVER
                     │
      ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
      ▼              ▼              ▼
   Planning       Scheduling     Metadata
      │              │              │
      └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                     ▼
                  Control

Isso significa que o Driver não deveria ser tratado como destino para todo o dataset distribuído.

Esse ponto parece óbvio.

Até alguém executar:

dados = df.collect()

3. O perigo do collect()

Considere:

df.count()

O processamento acontece de maneira distribuída e o resultado retornado é pequeno:

123456789

Agora compare com:

dados = df.collect()

collect() solicita que todos os registros do DataFrame sejam retornados ao Driver.

Conceitualmente:

Executor 1 ──────┐
Executor 2 ──────┤
Executor 3 ──────┼──► DRIVER
Executor 4 ──────┤
Executor 5 ──────┘

Se o dataset possuir:

500 GB

e o Driver tiver:

8 GB

temos um problema bastante previsível.

O Spark é distribuído.

Mas acabamos de pedir:

Traga tudo para uma única máquina.

4. collect() não é ruim — o contexto é que importa

Não existe problema em:

df.limit(10).collect()

quando sabemos que o resultado será pequeno.

Também existem cenários legítimos em que precisamos trazer pequenas quantidades de dados ao Driver.

O problema é usar collect() sem compreender:

Distributed Dataset
        ↓
      Driver

A pergunta antes de um collect() deveria ser:

Qual o volume máximo que pode voltar para o Driver?

Essa pergunta evita muitos problemas.

5. Outros caminhos para sobrecarregar o Driver

collect() é o exemplo mais conhecido, mas não é o único.

Problemas de Driver também podem aparecer com:

  • resultados excessivamente grandes;
  • estruturas locais gigantes;
  • excesso de metadados;
  • quantidade extrema de Tasks;
  • operações que materializam dados no processo do Driver;
  • código Python executado localmente;
  • determinadas operações de visualização ou conversão.

Por exemplo:

pdf = df.toPandas()

merece atenção.

O resultado precisa caber na memória do processo que recebe esse DataFrame local.

Ou seja:

Spark DataFrame distribuído
          ↓
       toPandas()
          ↓
DataFrame local
          ↓
      DRIVER

Se os dados forem grandes, temos novamente uma concentração de memória.

6. Executor Memory

Agora vamos para os Executors.

Eles executam as Tasks.

Conceitualmente:

Executor
   │
   ├── Task 1
   ├── Task 2
   ├── Task 3
   └── Task 4

Durante a execução, memória pode ser necessária para:

  • processamento;
  • agregações;
  • joins;
  • sorting;
  • shuffle;
  • estruturas intermediárias;
  • cache;
  • dados serializados;
  • execução de código;
  • componentes fora do heap JVM.

É aqui que começam vários problemas clássicos.

7. Uma partição vira trabalho para uma Task

Da Parte 3:

Em uma determinada Stage, cada partição normalmente corresponde ao trabalho de uma Task.

Então existe uma conexão direta:

Partition
    ↓
Task
    ↓
Memory pressure

Imagine:

Partition 1 → 200 MB
Partition 2 → 180 MB
Partition 3 → 220 MB
Partition 4 → 18 GB

A Task responsável pela quarta partição terá um perfil completamente diferente das demais.

Podemos observar:

Task 1 → OK
Task 2 → OK
Task 3 → OK
Task 4 → Memory Pressure

Talvez o problema não seja:

Executor com pouca memória.

Talvez seja:

Uma partição absurdamente maior que as outras.

8. Particionamento e memória são inseparáveis

Imagine um dataset de:

1 TB

distribuído em:

10 partitions

Simplificando muito:

≈ 100 GB por partition

Agora considere:

1000 partitions

Teríamos algo mais próximo de:

≈ 1 GB por partition

Isso não significa que uma Task precise manter toda a partição simultaneamente em memória.

Mas o exemplo mostra uma relação importante:

O tamanho e a distribuição das partições influenciam diretamente a pressão de memória das Tasks.

É por isso que simplesmente aumentar spark.executor.memory pode esconder a causa real.

9. Execution Memory

Durante operações como:

df.groupBy("customer_id").sum("value")

Spark precisa de memória para executar estruturas intermediárias.

Também em:

df.orderBy("timestamp")

ou em determinados joins.

Podemos pensar conceitualmente:

Executor Memory
      │
      ├── Execution
      │      │
      │      ├── Shuffle
      │      ├── Join
      │      ├── Sort
      │      └── Aggregation
      │
      └── Storage
             │
             ├── Cached Data
             └── Persisted Data

No Spark moderno, execution e storage participam de um modelo de gerenciamento de memória integrado.

Isso é importante porque a memória disponível não deve ser imaginada como caixas totalmente independentes e rígidas em todos os momentos.

10. Storage Memory

Agora imagine:

df.cache()

Quando o DataFrame é materializado, Spark pode manter partições para reutilização.

Conceitualmente:

Executor
   │
   ├── Execution Memory
   │
   └── Storage Memory
            │
            ├── Partition A
            ├── Partition B
            └── Partition C

Isso pode ser extremamente útil.

Se o mesmo dataset caro for utilizado várias vezes:

Expensive computation
       ↓
     CACHE
       ↓
 ┌─────┼─────┐
 ▼     ▼     ▼
Use 1 Use 2 Use 3

evitamos recalcular repetidamente a mesma linhagem.

Mas cache também custa memória.

11. cache() não significa "deixe rápido"

Esse é outro anti-pattern comum:

df.cache()

ser utilizado como se significasse:

optimize(df)

Não significa.

Imagine um DataFrame de:

800 GB

que será utilizado apenas uma vez.

Fazer cache pode simplesmente:

  • consumir memória;
  • provocar eviction;
  • aumentar pressão sobre o Executor;
  • competir com execution memory;
  • não trazer benefício relevante.

Cache faz mais sentido quando existe reuso.

Por exemplo:

base = transformacao_cara(df)

base.cache()

resultado_a = base.groupBy("estado").count()
resultado_b = base.groupBy("produto").sum("valor")
resultado_c = base.filter("status = 'ACTIVE'")

Agora existe um motivo claro:

Expensive Base
     ↓
   CACHE
     ↓
 ┌────┼────┐
 ▼    ▼    ▼
 A    B    C

12. Cache também é Lazy

Considere:

df.cache()

Isso não significa necessariamente:

Neste instante, todas as partições foram computadas e armazenadas.

A materialização ocorre quando uma Action força a computação.

Por exemplo:

df.cache()

df.count()

Agora temos:

cache()
   ↓
mark for persistence
   ↓
count()
   ↓
compute partitions
   ↓
store according to persistence strategy

Lazy evaluation continua presente.

13. persist()

Além de:

df.cache()

podemos trabalhar com:

df.persist()

e escolher estratégias de persistência adequadas ao contexto.

Conceitualmente, a persistência pode envolver combinações de:

Memory
Disk
Serialization
Replication

A escolha depende de fatores como:

  • tamanho;
  • frequência de reuso;
  • custo de recomputação;
  • memória disponível;
  • tolerância a I/O.

Novamente, não existe uma configuração universalmente melhor.

14. E quando a memória não é suficiente?

Agora chegamos a algo que apareceu na Parte 4:

Spill

Imagine uma Task realizando:

Sort

ou:

Aggregation

ou processamento relacionado a:

Shuffle

Ela utiliza estruturas em memória.

Mas a quantidade necessária ultrapassa o que pode ser mantido eficientemente ali.

Então parte dos dados pode ser enviada para disco.

Conceitualmente:

Task
 ↓
Memory
 ↓
Memory pressure
 ↓
Spill
 ↓
Disk

Depois:

Disk
 ↓
Read
 ↓
Continue processing

Isso permite que determinadas operações continuem mesmo quando tudo não cabe simultaneamente em memória.

Mas existe um preço.

15. Spill troca memória por I/O

Compare:

Memory
  ↓
CPU

com:

Memory
  ↓
Disk Write
  ↓
Disk Read
  ↓
CPU

Disco normalmente é muito mais lento do que memória.

Então grandes volumes de spill podem transformar:

Job

em:

Job lento

Mesmo sem ocorrer um OutOfMemory.

Essa é uma lição importante:

Uma aplicação pode estar sofrendo de pressão de memória sem necessariamente falhar por OOM.

Ela pode simplesmente ficar muito mais lenta.

16. Shuffle + Memory + Spill

Agora conectamos vários artigos.

Considere:

resultado = (
    vendas
    .groupBy("customer_id")
    .sum("valor")
)

Podemos ter:

Partitions
     ↓
Partial Aggregation
     ↓
Shuffle Write
     ↓
Network
     ↓
Shuffle Read
     ↓
Aggregation
     ↓
Memory pressure
     ↓
Spill
     ↓
Disk

Agora um simples:

groupBy()

ganha uma interpretação completamente diferente.

17. Data Skew volta novamente

Imagine:

P1 = 200 MB
P2 = 210 MB
P3 = 190 MB
P4 = 15 GB

Durante uma agregação:

P1 → OK
P2 → OK
P3 → OK
P4 → Spill → Spill → Spill

Ou pior:

P4 → OutOfMemory

A reação inicial pode ser:

Aumentar executor memory.

Talvez funcione.

Mas talvez a pergunta correta seja:

Por que existe uma partição de 15 GB quando as demais possuem aproximadamente 200 MB?

Estamos novamente diante de:

Data Skew

A causa é distribuição.

O sintoma aparece na memória.

18. OutOfMemory não é um único problema

Quando alguém diz:

"Spark deu OOM."

Ainda sabemos muito pouco.

Precisamos perguntar:

Onde?

Por exemplo:

Driver OOM?

ou:

Executor OOM?

ou pressão fora do heap/container?

Também precisamos perguntar:

Em qual Stage?

Em qual operação?

Em todas as Tasks?

Em uma única Task?

Depois de um Shuffle?

Durante Broadcast?

Durante collect()?

Essas perguntas mudam completamente a investigação.

19. Um Driver OOM pode indicar problema de arquitetura

Imagine:

dados = df.collect()

sobre um dataset enorme.

Podemos aumentar:

spark.driver.memory

de:

4 GB

para:

16 GB

Depois:

32 GB

Depois:

64 GB

Talvez o Job finalmente funcione.

Mas a pergunta continua:

Por que estamos trazendo um dataset distribuído gigantesco para um único processo?

Aumentar memória resolveu o sintoma.

Talvez não tenha resolvido o design.

20. Executor OOM também pode esconder outro problema

Agora imagine:

Executor OOM

A reação:

spark.executor.memory
8 GB → 16 GB

Mas talvez exista:

uma partition = 40 GB

Ou:

join skewed

Ou:

broadcast excessivo

Ou várias Tasks concorrentes disputando recursos.

Ou consumo significativo fora do heap principal.

Então:

Executor OOM não significa automaticamente que o Executor precisa apenas de mais heap.

21. spark.executor.memory

Uma configuração conhecida é:

spark.executor.memory

Ela define a quantidade de memória heap disponibilizada ao processo Executor JVM.

Por exemplo:

--executor-memory 8g

Mas existe uma armadilha conceitual importante:

A memória total necessária por um Executor não é necessariamente igual ao valor de spark.executor.memory.

Existe memória utilizada fora desse heap.

E isso nos leva diretamente ao tema do material original que estudei:

Memory Overhead

22. O que é Memory Overhead?

Uma aplicação Spark não utiliza memória apenas para o heap principal da JVM.

Podemos pensar de forma simplificada:

Executor Container / Process Environment
│
├── JVM Heap
│
│    └── spark.executor.memory
│
└── Additional / Non-Heap Memory
     │
     ├── JVM overhead
     ├── native memory
     ├── Python processes
     ├── direct buffers
     └── other runtime overhead

É essa segunda região que torna memoryOverhead tão importante.

Dependendo do ambiente e do workload, um Executor pode morrer mesmo quando aparentemente existe heap suficiente.

23. Um exemplo conceitual

Imagine uma configuração:

Executor Heap
8 GB

Isso não significa necessariamente:

Executor total
=
8 GB

O processo também precisa de espaço para outras necessidades.

Podemos pensar:

Container / Pod / Executor allocation

┌───────────────────────────────┐
│                               │
│ JVM Heap                      │
│ spark.executor.memory         │
│                               │
├───────────────────────────────┤
│                               │
│ Memory Overhead               │
│                               │
│ Native / Python / Direct /    │
│ JVM non-heap / other          │
│                               │
└───────────────────────────────┘

Se a região adicional for insuficiente, o processo pode exceder os limites impostos pelo gerenciador de recursos.

24. Por que isso aparece muito com PySpark?

Em PySpark existe uma característica importante.

Nosso código Python não transforma a JVM inteira em Python.

Existe interação entre:

JVM
 ↕
Python worker

Conceitualmente:

Executor JVM
     │
     ├── Spark execution
     │
     └── Python worker
             │
             └── Python code

Esses processos também consomem memória.

Dependendo do workload, bibliotecas e operações utilizadas, isso pode se tornar relevante para o consumo total do Executor.

Portanto, em PySpark precisamos olhar além de:

JVM Heap

25. Memory Overhead no material histórico

Uma das anotações que motivou este capítulo tratava especificamente de problemas de memoryOverhead.

Esse tipo de problema continua conceitualmente relevante.

O que mudou ao longo dos anos foram:

  • versões do Spark;
  • nomes e comportamento de determinadas configurações;
  • resource managers;
  • defaults;
  • cálculo automático de overhead;
  • integração com containers;
  • Kubernetes;
  • execução Python;
  • mecanismos internos de memória.

Por isso não considero uma boa prática pegar uma configuração antiga e simplesmente reproduzi-la hoje.

O conceito continua válido.

A configuração precisa ser analisada no contexto da versão e do ambiente atuais.

26. Heap vs. Off-Heap vs. Overhead

Uma simplificação útil é:

PROCESS MEMORY
     │
     ├── JVM Heap
     │
     ├── JVM Non-Heap
     │
     ├── Direct / Native Memory
     │
     ├── Python Worker Memory
     │
     └── Runtime Overhead

Isso é mais próximo da realidade do que pensar:

memory = spark.executor.memory

Quando um container é encerrado por ultrapassar limite de memória, precisamos descobrir qual parte do consumo cresceu.

27. Garbage Collection

Agora vamos entrar em outro sintoma importante:

GC

A JVM gerencia automaticamente memória de objetos.

Objetos são criados:

Objects
 ↓
Heap

Depois deixam de ser necessários.

O Garbage Collector precisa recuperar esse espaço.

Em um cenário saudável:

Application Work ███████████████████

GC               █

Mas sob forte pressão podemos encontrar algo mais próximo de:

Application ███████

GC          █████████████

Ou seja:

A aplicação passa tempo demais tentando gerenciar memória em vez de processar dados.

28. GC alto é sintoma

Assim como OOM, GC excessivo não deveria gerar automaticamente:

Aumente a heap.

Talvez tenhamos:

  • objetos demais;
  • partições grandes;
  • agregações pesadas;
  • estruturas intermediárias enormes;
  • cache excessivo;
  • serialização inadequada;
  • concorrência excessiva por Executor.

Precisamos descobrir por que a memória está sob pressão.

29. Mais cores por Executor também afetam memória

Imagine:

Executor
8 cores

Dependendo da configuração, várias Tasks podem executar simultaneamente nesse Executor.

Conceitualmente:

Executor Memory
      │
 ┌────┼────┬────┬────┬────┐
 ▼    ▼    ▼    ▼    ▼    ▼
T1   T2   T3   T4   T5   ...

Cada Task pode precisar de memória.

Então existe uma relação:

mais Tasks concorrentes por Executor
              ↓
mais competição pela memória disponível

Isso mostra por que tuning não deveria analisar:

executor memory

isoladamente.

Precisamos olhar para:

Executor Memory
      +
Executor Cores
      +
Partition Size
      +
Task Behavior

30. Executors gigantes também não são automaticamente melhores

Poderíamos pensar:

1 Executor
64 cores
256 GB RAM

Parece poderoso.

Mas Executors gigantes podem trazer trade-offs relacionados a:

  • concorrência;
  • garbage collection;
  • blast radius de falha;
  • utilização;
  • scheduling;
  • memória compartilhada entre muitas Tasks.

No outro extremo:

64 Executors
1 core
4 GB

também possui trade-offs.

Não existe um tamanho universal.

Precisamos equilibrar:

cores
memory
parallelism
partition size
workload
cluster manager

31. Broadcast também consome memória

Na Parte 5 vimos:

from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast

resultado = grande.join(
    broadcast(pequena),
    "id"
)

A estratégia pode evitar um shuffle grande.

Mas existe um custo:

Small Table
    ↓
Broadcast
 ┌──┼──┐
 ▼  ▼  ▼
E1 E2 E3

Cada Executor precisa conseguir trabalhar com a estrutura transmitida.

Se tentarmos broadcast de algo grande demais, podemos criar pressão significativa de memória.

Novamente:

Network optimization
        ↕
Memory cost

Sistemas distribuídos são cheios de trade-offs.

32. Cache também compete por recursos

Imagine:

df_a.cache()
df_b.cache()
df_c.cache()
df_d.cache()

Pode parecer:

Quanto mais cache, melhor.

Mas:

Cache A
Cache B
Cache C
Cache D
     ↓
Storage Pressure
     ↓
Eviction / recomputation / resource competition

Cache deveria ser uma decisão baseada em:

reuse frequency
×
recomputation cost
×
available resources

e não um reflexo automático.

33. unpersist()

Se um dataset não será mais reutilizado, podemos liberar sua persistência:

df.unpersist()

Isso comunica:

Não preciso mais manter essas partições persistidas.

Em pipelines longos isso pode ser importante.

Por exemplo:

Phase A
 ↓
cache intermediate
 ↓
reuse several times
 ↓
phase completed
 ↓
unpersist
 ↓
free resources for Phase B

Gerenciamento de memória também faz parte do design do pipeline.

34. O Spark UI volta a ser essencial

Se existe problema de memória, não quero começar alterando configurações.

Quero observar.

No Spark UI e métricas relacionadas, procuro sinais como:

Task Duration
GC Time
Shuffle Read
Shuffle Write
Spill
Storage
Executor behavior
Failed Tasks
Skew

Também observo logs.

A pergunta é:

O que aconteceu antes da falha?

35. Um padrão de investigação

Imagine:

Job falhou
   ↓
Executor lost
   ↓
Memory-related error

Meu raciocínio começaria assim:

Qual Stage?
    ↓
Qual operação?
    ↓
Join?
Aggregation?
Sort?
UDF?
Cache?

Depois:

Todas as Tasks falharam?
        ↓
ou apenas algumas?

Se apenas algumas:

Possível skew?

Depois:

Qual tamanho das partitions?
Quanto shuffle?
Quanto spill?
Quanto GC?

Só então:

Heap insuficiente?
Overhead insuficiente?
Particionamento ruim?
Broadcast inadequado?
Concorrência excessiva?

36. Caso 1 — Driver morrendo

Sintoma:

Driver OutOfMemory

Código:

dados = df.collect()

Dataset:

120 GB

Driver:

8 GB

Diagnóstico provável:

Distributed Data
      ↓
collect()
      ↓
Single Process
      ↓
OOM

Solução arquitetural:

Não coletar o dataset inteiro.

Talvez:

df.write.parquet(
    "/data/output"
)

ou continuar o processamento distribuído.

A solução principal não é necessariamente:

8 GB → 128 GB

37. Caso 2 — Uma Task morre repetidamente

Sintoma:

Stage 12

199 Tasks → OK
1 Task    → FAIL

Isso é extremamente informativo.

Talvez tenhamos:

Data Skew

ou uma partição muito maior.

Se aumentarmos memória de todos os Executors:

Cluster cost ↑

para resolver uma única partição anormal, talvez estejamos atacando o lugar errado.

Precisamos investigar a distribuição.

38. Caso 3 — Todas as Tasks sofrem Spill

Imagine:

Task 1 → heavy spill
Task 2 → heavy spill
Task 3 → heavy spill
Task 4 → heavy spill
...

Agora talvez tenhamos um problema sistêmico.

Possíveis causas:

Partitions muito grandes
Memory insuficiente
Join pesado
Sort pesado
Aggregation pesada
Task concurrency

Nesse cenário, ajustar recursos pode realmente fazer parte da solução.

Mas ainda precisamos medir.

39. Caso 4 — OOM depois de Broadcast

Imagine que:

Job funcionava

e alguém adicionou:

broadcast(dim)

Agora Executors começam a morrer.

Pergunta:

Qual o tamanho real de dim?

Talvez:

"small table"

tenha crescido.

Ontem:

50 MB

Hoje:

6 GB

Uma otimização válida no passado pode se tornar um problema quando os dados mudam.

Isso é importante:

Performance depende também da evolução dos dados.

40. Caso 5 — PySpark e memória externa ao heap

Imagine:

spark.executor.memory

aparentemente confortável.

Mas containers continuam sendo encerrados por memória.

Agora precisamos olhar para:

JVM Heap
     +
Python workers
     +
Native memory
     +
Direct buffers
     +
Other overhead

É exatamente nesse tipo de cenário que compreender memoryOverhead deixa de ser detalhe e passa a ser parte do diagnóstico.

41. Não ajuste memoryOverhead às cegas

Se um Executor morre por ultrapassar limites externos ao heap, aumentar overhead pode ser apropriado.

Mas ainda precisamos perguntar:

Por que esse consumo existe?

Pode ser:

  • Python;
  • bibliotecas nativas;
  • buffers;
  • comportamento da JVM;
  • volume de dados;
  • operação específica.

A configuração correta depende do workload e do ambiente.

Por isso evito recomendações como:

sempre configure X GB

ou:

sempre use Y%

sem contexto.

Defaults e comportamentos também evoluem entre versões.

42. Memória em Kubernetes

Em ambientes containerizados, a questão fica ainda mais visível.

Podemos pensar:

Kubernetes Pod
      │
      └── Executor
            │
            ├── JVM Heap
            ├── Non-Heap
            ├── Native
            ├── Python
            └── Overhead

O Pod possui limites.

Não basta a JVM achar que possui heap suficiente.

O consumo total do processo e componentes associados precisa respeitar os recursos disponíveis.

Esse é um dos motivos pelos quais problemas modernos de Spark precisam ser analisados também no nível da infraestrutura.

43. Memória em YARN

Em ambientes YARN, existe raciocínio semelhante.

O Executor executa dentro de recursos controlados pelo gerenciador do cluster.

Historicamente, muitos erros de memoryOverhead ficaram conhecidos justamente em ambientes onde o container ultrapassava seu limite mesmo quando a heap configurada parecia aceitável.

O princípio permanece:

JVM Heap
≠
Total Process Memory

44. A configuração depende do ambiente

Hoje Spark pode rodar em diferentes contextos:

Standalone
YARN
Kubernetes
Managed Platforms
Cloud Services

Isso significa que recomendações de memória precisam considerar:

  • Spark version;
  • cluster manager;
  • container limits;
  • JVM;
  • Python;
  • workload;
  • plataforma gerenciada.

Uma configuração copiada de um artigo antigo pode estar:

correta historicamente

e:

inadequada atualmente

ao mesmo tempo.

Esse é exatamente o tipo de cuidado que estou aplicando ao revisitar meu material antigo nesta série.

45. Um modelo mental melhor para OOM

Em vez de:

OOM
 ↓
More Memory

prefiro:

                    OOM
                     │
          ┌──────────┴──────────┐
          ▼                     ▼
       Driver?               Executor?
          │                     │
          ▼                     ▼
      collect()?          Which Stage?
      toPandas()?              │
      metadata?                ▼
                         Which Operation?
                               │
                    ┌──────────┼──────────┐
                    ▼          ▼          ▼
                  Skew      Shuffle    Broadcast
                    │          │          │
                    └──────────┼──────────┘
                               ▼
                         Partition Size
                               │
                               ▼
                      Heap or Overhead?
                               │
                               ▼
                         Root Cause

Esse modelo evita tratar todos os erros de memória como iguais.

46. Performance tuning começa com observabilidade

Imagine dois engenheiros.

O primeiro vê:

OutOfMemoryError

e imediatamente altera:

spark.executor.memory

O segundo investiga:

Stage
Tasks
Partition distribution
Shuffle
Spill
GC
Executor logs
Physical plan
Data volume

O segundo talvez leve alguns minutos a mais antes de alterar a configuração.

Mas a chance de resolver a causa real é muito maior.

Essa é uma diferença importante entre:

configuration tuning

e:

performance engineering

47. Um checklist para problemas de memória

Quando encontro um problema de memória em Spark, quero responder:

  • O erro aconteceu no Driver ou Executor?
  • Qual Stage estava executando?
  • Qual operação estava acontecendo?
  • Existe collect()?
  • Existe toPandas()?
  • Existe broadcast?
  • Existe cache excessivo?
  • As partições estão equilibradas?
  • Existe data skew?
  • Qual o tamanho das maiores Tasks?
  • Existe Shuffle?
  • Quanto?
  • Existe Spill?
  • Quanto?
  • Quanto tempo está sendo gasto em GC?
  • Todas as Tasks sofrem ou apenas algumas?
  • Existem Python workers?
  • Existe consumo nativo relevante?
  • O limite do container está sendo ultrapassado?
  • O problema é heap ou overhead?
  • A configuração corresponde à versão e ao cluster manager utilizados?

Só depois:

Qual configuração preciso alterar?

48. O que eu evitaria fazer automaticamente

Se o Job estiver lento ou falhando, eu evitaria começar por:

dobrar executor memory

ou:

dobrar driver memory

ou:

aumentar memoryOverhead arbitrariamente

ou:

cachear tudo

ou:

reduzir o número de partitions sem medir

ou:

aumentar o cluster

Todas essas ações podem ser válidas.

Mas nenhuma delas deveria substituir diagnóstico.

49. Memória, performance e custo

Em cloud, existe ainda outra dimensão.

Imagine:

Executor Memory
8 GB

e simplesmente dobramos para:

16 GB

em dezenas ou centenas de Executors.

Talvez o Job fique estável.

Mas talvez tenhamos acabado de aumentar recursos para compensar:

Data Skew

ou:

repartition ruim

ou:

join inadequado

ou:

cache desnecessário

Então temos:

Problema arquitetural
       ↓
Mais infraestrutura
       ↓
Maior custo
       ↓
Problema mascarado

Performance tuning também é FinOps.

50. A conexão entre tudo que vimos até aqui

Agora podemos montar uma visão muito mais completa:

                    DATA
                      │
                      ▼
                 PARTITIONS
                      │
                      ▼
                    TASKS
                      │
                      ▼
                  EXECUTORS
                      │
          ┌───────────┼───────────┐
          ▼           ▼           ▼
       Memory       CPU        Network
          │                       │
          ▼                       ▼
      Aggregation              Shuffle
          │                       │
          └───────────┬───────────┘
                      ▼
                    Spill
                      │
                      ▼
                     Disk
                      │
                      ▼
                 Performance
                      │
                      ▼
                    Cost

Agora adicione:

Data Skew

e podemos gerar:

Uneven Partition
      ↓
Huge Task
      ↓
Memory Pressure
      ↓
Spill / GC
      ↓
Slow Task
      ↓
Straggler
      ↓
Slow Stage

Isso mostra por que os capítulos anteriores estavam conectados.

51. A principal lição deste capítulo

Se eu pudesse resumir memória no Spark em uma frase:

Problemas de memória frequentemente são sintomas de como os dados e a computação foram distribuídos.

Nem sempre.

Às vezes realmente precisamos de mais memória.

Mas antes de aumentar recursos, quero saber:

Quem está consumindo?
        ↓
Onde?
        ↓
Durante qual operação?
        ↓
Por quê?

Só então:

Architecture
     +
Configuration
     +
Resources

entram na solução.

52. Como penso hoje

Meu modelo mental deixou de ser:

Spark OOM
   ↓
Increase Memory

e passou a ser:

Spark OOM
   ↓
Driver or Executor?
   ↓
Heap or Overhead?
   ↓
Which Stage?
   ↓
Which Task?
   ↓
Which Operation?
   ↓
Partition Size?
   ↓
Skew?
   ↓
Shuffle?
   ↓
Spill?
   ↓
Broadcast?
   ↓
Cache?
   ↓
Python / Native Memory?
   ↓
Root Cause
   ↓
Then Tune

Esse raciocínio é muito mais útil do que decorar valores de configuração.

Próximo artigo

Agora entendemos:

Partitions
    ↓
Tasks
    ↓
Memory
    ↓
Shuffle
    ↓
Spill

Mas existe outro conceito fundamental que apareceu desde os primeiros artigos:

Lineage.

Quando uma partição é perdida, como Spark sabe reconstruí-la?

Por que RDD significa:

Resilient Distributed Dataset

?

Como Spark obtém tolerância a falhas sem simplesmente replicar toda computação intermediária?

E o que acontece quando a linhagem fica grande demais?

No próximo artigo vamos explorar:

  • RDD Lineage;
  • DAG;
  • fault tolerance;
  • recomputation;
  • cache vs. recomputation;
  • checkpoint;
  • persistência;
  • falha de Executor;
  • recuperação de partições;
  • por que Spark é "resilient";
  • e como essas ideias evoluíram nas APIs modernas.

Vamos partir deste modelo:

Source
  ↓
Map
  ↓
Filter
  ↓
Join
  ↓
Aggregate
  ↓
Result

para enxergar algo mais profundo:

              LINEAGE
                 │
                 ▼
Source → Transform → Transform → Shuffle → Result
  │          │          │
  └──────────┴──────────┘
             │
      information needed
       for recomputation

Essa é uma das ideias fundamentais que fizeram o Spark ser Spark.

← Parte 6: Spark SQL e DataFrames — do código ao plano de execução

Próximo: Parte 8 — RDD Lineage e tolerância a falhas: como o Spark se recupera quando algo dá errado

title: The DMARC Record a Small Business Should Publish First (and When to Tighten It)
description:
If your business sends mail from its own domain (you@yourbusiness.com), three DNS records do the authentication work: SPF, DKIM and DMARC. SPF and DKIM prove a message came from a server you actually use. DMARC tells the receiving server what to do when a message claims to be from your domain but fails those checks, and where to send reports about it.

With no DMARC record, anyone can put your domain in the From: line of a phishing email. The receiving server has no instructions from you, and you never hear about it.

Start with one TXT record

At your DNS host (Cloudflare, GoDaddy, Squarespace, Network Solutions, or wherever your DNS lives), add:

Host/Name: _dmarc
Type:      TXT
Value:     v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@yourbusiness.com

Swap in a mailbox you really own. Some providers want the full name _dmarc.yourbusiness.com instead of just _dmarc.

p=none is monitoring mode. Nothing gets blocked or sent to spam, so it can't break your mail. It just starts the reports flowing so you can see who is sending as your domain.

The tags, and what a small business should do with them

Tag Meaning Suggested setting
v=DMARC1 Marks the record as DMARC; must come first Always v=DMARC1
p= Policy for failing mail: none, quarantine (spam folder), reject (block) Start with none
rua= Where daily aggregate reports go A mailbox you own, or a monitoring service
pct= Share of failing mail the policy applies to Omit (defaults to 100) until you move to quarantine
sp= Policy for subdomains Omit; subdomains inherit p=
adkim= / aspf= Strict or relaxed alignment Omit; relaxed is the default and suits most setups
ruf= Per-message forensic reports Skip; few providers send them and they can include message content

Two mistakes that quietly make DMARC useless

1. p=none with no rua=. v=DMARC1; p=none; is valid but does nothing: no protection, no reports. Checkers still mark it "present", so it looks finished. Add a rua= address.

2. Two DMARC records. If _dmarc.yourbusiness.com has two TXT records starting with v=DMARC1, receivers treat the domain as having no DMARC at all. Merge them into one. This often happens when a website builder or email provider adds its own record next to yours.

Get SPF and DKIM right first

DMARC passes when a message passes SPF or DKIM and the passing domain matches the From: domain. Before tightening anything:

  • SPF: a single TXT record at the root of the domain starting with v=spf1, listing every service that sends as you (e.g. include:_spf.google.com for Google Workspace, include:spf.protection.outlook.com for Microsoft 365). Only one SPF record is allowed, and it has to stay under 10 DNS lookups.
  • DKIM: turn it on in your mail provider's admin console and publish the DNS records it gives you.

Then list everything else that sends as your domain: newsletter tool, invoicing or booking software, CRM, website contact forms. Each needs SPF or DKIM set up for your domain, or it will fail once you enforce DMARC.

Is DMARC required for a small sender?

Gmail's sender guidelines require everyone sending to personal Gmail accounts to use SPF or DKIM. Senders of more than 5,000 messages a day must also publish DMARC, and p=none is acceptable. Most small businesses are far below 5,000 a day, so strictly speaking they don't need it.

Google still recommends SPF, DKIM and DMARC for every domain, and DMARC reports are the only way to see who is sending mail under your name. It costs one DNS record, and at p=none there's no risk to your own mail.

Moving from p=none to quarantine and reject

Collect at least two to four weeks of reports at p=none, then:

  1. Confirm every legitimate sender passes. Each service you use should show SPF or DKIM passing and aligned in the reports. Fix the ones that don't.
  2. Step into quarantine gradually, e.g. v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; pct=25; rua=mailto:..., raising pct to 100 over a couple of weeks while you watch the reports.
  3. Switch to reject once quarantine at 100% has run cleanly: v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:....

Reading the reports

Aggregate reports arrive as compressed XML attachments, typically one a day from each large mailbox provider that received your mail. They're painful to read by hand. You can parse them yourself, or point rua= at a service that reads them for you. DMARC allows several rua addresses separated by commas, so you can keep your own mailbox in the list.

Checklist

  • [ ] One TXT record at _dmarc.yourbusiness.com starting with v=DMARC1
  • [ ] p=none to start
  • [ ] rua=mailto: pointing at a mailbox you read, or a monitoring service
  • [ ] One SPF record, under 10 lookups, covering every sender
  • [ ] DKIM enabled with your mail provider and each sending tool
  • [ ] 2-4 weeks of reports reviewed before p=quarantine

Sources: Gmail email sender guidelines (support.google.com/a/answer/81126); DMARC tag definitions and multiple-record handling per RFC 7489 §6.3 and §6.6.3.

Originally published on Email DNS Check, a free SPF/DKIM/DMARC checker by Swift Labs. We also build MailGuard, which reads DMARC reports and sends a plain-English weekly summary ($7/domain/month, 14-day trial).

This article was created with the help of AI and checked for accuracy before publishing.
