title: Add long-term memory to a Mastra agent (input/output processors, per-user recall)
description:
Disclosure: I'm Mohammed, founder of MemorySync. I drafted this article with AI assistance and reviewed it for accuracy against the official MemorySync and Mastra docs. The code is adapted from the docs and I haven't run it.

Mastra agents already have memory. Give an agent a Memory from @mastra/memory and pass memory: { resource, thread } on each call: resource is a stable id for the user and thread isolates one conversation (Mastra memory docs). Mastra also has working memory and semantic recall, stored in whichever storage provider you configure.

If that's working for you, keep it. This post is for when you want durable facts about each user extracted and recalled by a hosted service, wired in through Mastra's own processor pipeline. It uses MemorySync's Mastra integration, memorysync-mastra. MemorySync is a hosted memory layer, and I'm building it. Mastra behaviour comes from its docs on memory and processors. Everything about MemorySync comes from its Mastra Memory guide. The code is adapted from those docs. I haven't run it for this post, so check it against your versions.

What you'll set up

  1. An input processor that injects recalled facts before the model call, and an output processor that sends the user's message for fact extraction after it.
  2. Per-call user identity, so one agent can serve many users.
  3. Optional: recall modes, five memory tools and standalone helpers.

Install 

npm install memorysync-mastra

Per the guide it supports @mastra/core 1.42+ (Node 20+ for the package; current @mastra/core itself requires Node 22+). npm currently lists 1.1.0 with peer @mastra/core >=1.42.0 <2.0.0. Set MEMORYSYNC_API_KEY in the environment, or pass apiKey, and keep it server-side.

Step 1: Add the processors

Mastra processors are hooks in the agent pipeline: inputProcessors run before messages reach the model, outputProcessors run after the model responds and before the result is returned (processors docs). MemorySync uses one of each:

import { Agent } from "@mastra/core/agent";
import { openai } from "@ai-sdk/openai";
import { createMemorySyncProcessors } from "memorysync-mastra";

const { inputProcessor, outputProcessor } = createMemorySyncProcessors({
  userId: "customer-7",     // scopes memory to one end user
  sessionId: "thread-42",   // groups the stored facts by thread
});

const agent = new Agent({
  id: "assistant",
  name: "Assistant",
  instructions: "You are a helpful assistant.",
  model: openai("your-model"),
  inputProcessors: [inputProcessor],
  outputProcessors: [outputProcessor],
});

await agent.generate("I'm vegetarian and I fly aisle.");

// Later, same user, any thread
const { text } = await agent.generate("Book my trip: flight plus a dinner spot.");

Per the guide:

  • Recall is injected once per generate/stream call (it uses processInput, not the per-step hook), so multi-step tool loops don't add the block twice. Your instructions stay first; the memory block is appended after them.
  • Only the user's message is sent; MemorySync stores just the durable facts in it. Assistant replies aren't stored.
  • If recall fails, the call proceeds without context. If persisting fails, it's reported through onError (a console warning by default) and never thrown.

Prefer less wiring? withMemorySync(config, { userId }) wraps your agent config and merges both processors in, keeping any processors you already have (MemorySync's run after yours).

Step 2: Resolve the user per call

A Mastra server agent serves many users, so identity is resolved per call, in this priority order:

import { RequestContext } from "@mastra/core/request-context";
import {
  createMemorySyncProcessors,
  MASTRA_RESOURCE_ID_KEY,
  MASTRA_THREAD_ID_KEY,
} from "memorysync-mastra";

// 1. Your own resolver wins over everything
createMemorySyncProcessors({
  resolveIdentity: (requestContext) => ({
    userId: currentSession.userId,
    sessionId: currentSession.threadId,
  }),
});

// 2. Static ids (scripts, workers)
createMemorySyncProcessors({ userId: "customer-7", sessionId: "thread-42" });

// 3. Mastra's RequestContext, set by your server middleware
const ctx = new RequestContext();
ctx.set(MASTRA_RESOURCE_ID_KEY, "customer-7");
ctx.set(MASTRA_THREAD_ID_KEY, "thread-42");
await agent.generate(messages, { requestContext: ctx });

// 4. Mastra's own memory ids on the call
await agent.generate("I moved to Lisbon.", {
  memory: { resource: "customer-7", thread: "thread-42" },
});

Option 4 is handy if you already use Mastra memory: the same resource id becomes the MemorySync user. If no source yields a user id, recall is skipped and the write is refused (reported through onError), never sent to a default scope. Take the id from your auth session, not from the request body.

Step 3: Streaming 

const stream = await agent.stream("Plan a dinner for my team.", {
  memory: { resource: "customer-7", thread: "thread-42" },
});
for await (const chunk of stream.textStream) process.stdout.write(chunk);

The user's message is sent once, after the full stream. Per the guide, a stream that errors mid-flight (finishReason: "error") sends nothing, so the retry sends the message once.

Step 4 (optional): Recall modes and switches 

createMemorySyncProcessors({ userId, mode: "query" });   // relevant to the latest message (default)
createMemorySyncProcessors({ userId, mode: "profile" }); // stable overview of the user
createMemorySyncProcessors({ userId, mode: "full" });    // both

createMemorySyncProcessors({ userId, persist: false });  // read-only
createMemorySyncProcessors({ userId, recall: false });   // write-only

createMemorySyncProcessors({
  userId,
  k: 12,
  template: "What you know about this user:\n{context}",
});

Step 5 (optional): Tools and helpers 

import { createMemorySyncTools } from "memorysync-mastra";

const agent = new Agent({
  id: "assistant",
  name: "Assistant",
  instructions: "Use the memory tools to remember durable facts.",
  model: openai("your-model"),
  tools: { ...createMemorySyncTools({ userId: "customer-7" }) },
});

// For agents you don't fully trust: search and list only
createMemorySyncTools({ userId: "customer-7", readOnly: true });

The five tools are add_memory, search_memory, list_memories, update_memory (tags and importance only) and delete_memory; they return readable error strings instead of throwing. For workflows there are getMemoryContext, searchMemories and saveTurn. saveTurn sends only the user's message and throws on failure. The guide says a turn sent by both the processors and saveTurn is recognised server-side and extracted once.

Troubleshooting

  • Nothing is remembered. Check onError output; a call with no resolvable user writes nothing by design.
  • A new thread knows nothing. The user id (or resource) must match across calls. The thread can differ.
  • Version errors. The package targets @mastra/core 1.x from 1.42, and current core needs Node 22+.

Common questions

Does a Mastra agent remember previous conversations?
Yes, if you give it a Memory from @mastra/memory and pass memory: { resource, thread } on each call. To recall earlier messages, call the agent with the same resource and thread values. lastMessages controls how many recent messages are included (Mastra memory docs).

Where does Mastra store memory?
In the storage provider you configure. Memory needs a storage provider to persist message history; the quickstart uses @mastra/libsql (Mastra memory docs).

What's the difference between resource and thread in Mastra memory?
resource is a stable id for the user or entity, and thread isolates one conversation. Each thread's owner can't be changed after creation, so don't reuse a thread id across owners. Working memory and semantic recall are resource-scoped by default, so they carry across that user's threads (Mastra memory docs).

Can I use Mastra's Memory and the MemorySync processors together?
Yes. MemorySync's guide recommends running both: Mastra's Memory for the conversation history, and the MemorySync processors for durable per-user facts across threads. The processors can also read the user and thread from the same memory: { resource, thread } option (MemorySync Mastra guide).

Sources

  • MemorySync Mastra Memory guide: docs.memorysync.io/guides/mastra
  • Mastra docs: mastra.ai/docs/memory/overview and mastra.ai/docs/agents/processors
  • npm: memorysync-mastra 1.1.0

Try it

If you want to see the save, reload and recall loop before wiring up an agent, the MemorySync playground runs it in your browser: memorysync.io/try.

title: Add long-term memory to a Pydantic AI agent (one capability, per-user recall across runs)
description:
Disclosure: I'm Mohammed, founder of MemorySync. I drafted this article with AI assistance and reviewed it for accuracy against the official MemorySync and Pydantic AI docs. The code is adapted from the docs and I haven't run it.

Pydantic AI keeps context across runs through message history: you pass message_history= (or the previous result's conversation) into the next Agent.run, and result.all_messages() / new_messages() give you the messages back (Pydantic AI message history docs). Storing and reloading that list is up to you, and it only covers one conversation. Start a new thread and the agent knows nothing about the user it talked to yesterday.

This post adds per-user long-term memory with MemorySync's Pydantic AI integration, pydantic-ai-memorysync. MemorySync is a hosted memory layer, and I'm building it. Pydantic AI behaviour comes from its official docs on message history and capabilities. Everything about MemorySync comes from its Pydantic AI Memory guide. The code is adapted from those docs. I haven't run it for this post, so check it against your versions.

What you'll set up

  1. One MemorySyncCapability in the Agent constructor that recalls relevant facts before every run and sends the user's prompt for fact extraction after a successful run.
  2. User identity taken from your deps, so one agent can serve many users.
  3. Optional: five memory tools, a typed search tool and async helpers.

Install 

pip install pydantic-ai-memorysync

Per the guide it needs pydantic-ai (or pydantic-ai-slim) 2.0+ and Python 3.10+. PyPI currently lists 1.1.0 with pydantic-ai-slim>=2,<3. Set MEMORYSYNC_API_KEY in the environment, or pass api_key, and keep it server-side. This is Python only; the guide points TypeScript users to the Vercel AI SDK or Mastra integrations.

Step 1: Add the capability

In Pydantic AI, a capability is a reusable unit of agent behaviour that you pass to the Agent constructor instead of wiring instructions, tools and hooks separately (capabilities docs). MemorySync ships memory as one:

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai_memorysync import MemorySyncCapability

agent = Agent(
    "openai:your-model",
    instructions="You are a helpful assistant.",
    capabilities=[MemorySyncCapability(user_id="customer-7")],
)

# First run
await agent.run("I'm vegetarian and I fly aisle.")

# A later run, new conversation, same user
result = await agent.run("What should I cook tonight?")

What happens, per the guide:

  • Recall goes through the instructions channel, not into the message list. The model sees a "Relevant memories about this user" block after your instructions, but it is never a conversation part. So if you replay result.all_messages() into the next run, old memory blocks don't pile up in the transcript.
  • Capture happens in after_run, which Pydantic AI fires only when a run succeeds. A failed run leaves no half-remembered turn.
  • Only the user's prompt is sent. MemorySync extracts the durable facts in it and stores those; filler like "ok" or "thanks" yields none. The model's reply, tool calls, retry prompts and thinking parts aren't sent. Streaming runs send the prompt once the stream completes.
  • Prompts are grouped by the run's conversation_id (sent as session_id). Pass session_id="..." to pin it yourself. persist=False gives read-only memory.

Failure handling: if recall fails, the agent runs with its base instructions; if the send fails, the run result is untouched. Both report through on_error (a logging warning by default).

Step 2: Take the user from your deps

One agent usually serves many users, so don't hard-code user_id:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai_memorysync import MemorySyncCapability

@dataclass
class MyDeps:
    user_id: str

agent = Agent(
    "openai:your-model",
    deps_type=MyDeps,
    capabilities=[MemorySyncCapability()],  # reads ctx.deps.user_id
)

await agent.run("hi", deps=MyDeps(user_id="customer-7"))

# Or resolve it from anything on your deps:
MemorySyncCapability(user_id_resolver=lambda ctx: ctx.deps.user_id)

The resolution order is user_id_resolver(ctx), then a static user_id, then ctx.deps.user_id. If none is found, the run goes ahead without memory and the miss is reported through on_error; it never falls back to a shared namespace. My advice: fill user_id from your authenticated user record, not from the request body.

Keep using message_history for the current conversation. The capability adds what Pydantic AI doesn't do on its own: facts about the user that carry over to new threads.

Step 3 (optional): Memory tools

If you want the model to decide what to save:

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai_memorysync import create_memorysync_tools

agent = Agent(
    "openai:your-model",
    instructions="Use the memory tools to remember durable facts.",
    tools=create_memorysync_tools(user_id="customer-7"),
)

# For agents you don't fully trust: search and list only
create_memorysync_tools(user_id="customer-7", read_only=True)

The tools are add_memory, search_memory, list_memories, update_memory (tags and importance only; memory text can't be changed) and delete_memory. In Pydantic AI a tool exception fails the whole run, so these return short readable error strings instead of raising.

Step 4 (optional): Typed search and helpers

When downstream code consumes tool output structurally, use the typed search tool. It returns list[MemoryResult] (Pydantic models with id, text, score), and on failure returns [] and reports through on_error:

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai_memorysync import create_memory_search_tool

agent = Agent(
    "openai:your-model",
    tools=[create_memory_search_tool(user_id="customer-7")],
)

For hand-wired setups there are async helpers:

from pydantic_ai_memorysync import get_memory_context, save_turn, search_memories

context = await get_memory_context("what should I cook?", user_id="customer-7")  # "" for a new user
hits = await search_memories("dietary preferences", user_id="customer-7")

# Explicit persistence. This one raises on failure.
await save_turn(user_id="customer-7", user="I'm vegetarian",
                assistant="Noted!", session_id="thread-42")

save_turn sends only the user message. API errors raise MemorySyncAPIError, which carries the HTTP status and server detail.

Troubleshooting

  • Nothing is remembered. Check on_error output. A run with no resolvable user proceeds memoryless; so does a failed run, because capture only happens after success.
  • A new thread knows nothing. The user_id must be identical across runs. session_id / conversation_id can differ.
  • Duplicate memory text in the transcript. It shouldn't happen with the capability, since recall rides the instructions channel. If you see it, check you're not also pasting get_memory_context output into your prompt.
  • Version errors. The package targets pydantic-ai 2.x.

Common questions

Does Pydantic AI keep memory between runs?
Not on its own. Each Agent.run only sees the messages you pass in. To continue a conversation, pass the earlier messages back with message_history=, using result.all_messages() (everything, including prior runs) or result.new_messages() (only the current run) (Pydantic AI message history docs).

How do I persist message_history to a database?
The docs' intended route is a TypeAdapter: ModelMessagesTypeAdapter serializes messages to JSON and back. For a conversation you plan to continue, they suggest storing its Conversation (via ConversationTypeAdapter) rather than the messages alone. Where those bytes live and when to reload them is left to your application; conversation_id is the key to store them under, and the resolved value is on the result as AgentRunResult.conversation_id (message history docs).

How do I stop message history from growing too large?
Use the ProcessHistory capability. It lets you change the history before each model request, for example to keep only recent messages or summarize old ones (message history docs).

How do I make an agent remember a user across new conversations?
A stored history only covers the conversation it belongs to. For facts that should follow a user into new threads, you need a separate memory store. The setup in this post uses MemorySync's MemorySyncCapability: it adds recalled facts through the instructions channel, so nothing is added to your message history, and it sends the user's prompt for fact extraction only after a run succeeds (MemorySync Pydantic AI guide).

Sources

  • MemorySync Pydantic AI Memory guide: docs.memorysync.io/guides/pydantic-ai
  • Pydantic AI docs: ai.pydantic.dev/message-history/ and ai.pydantic.dev/capabilities/
  • PyPI: pydantic-ai-memorysync 1.1.0

Try it

If you want to see the save, reload and recall loop before wiring up an agent, the MemorySync playground runs it in your browser: memorysync.io/try.

title: Block has unveiled a new artificial intelligence system that speaks with a strikingly human voice.
description:
Block research has announced Dessa, a full-duplex voice AI model trained directly on human speech rather than text pipelines.

Running locally on consumer hardware with an NVIDIA GPU, it supports simultaneous speaking and listening while incorporating natural vocal expressions.

How the new system works

The system's key difference is that it was trained exclusively on recordings of human speech, rather than text that is later converted to voice. According to the company, this allows it to sound unusually natural, including features such as pauses, laughter and crying.

The model has the ability to speak and listen simultaneously, meaning that the conversation can flow just like a normal conversation between two people. It was trained using only human speech and an NVIDIA graphics card, and its technical specifications allow it to run locally on high-performance everyday computers, such as systems with Apple M4 Max processors or newer.

Who has access?

The model is not currently available to the general public. Block has asked security experts to test it first to examine its capabilities and implications.

READ ALSO

OpenAI cuts off direct access to artificial intelligence models on the internet

Jack Dorsey and team member Ragavan Thurairatnam shared details and examples on social media. Block is in the financial services business and sells solutions to small businesses, with its Square service already using voice technology for ordering.

title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF): When Your Browser Becomes the Attacker
description:
Imagine logging into your banking application, then opening another website in a different tab.

Without your knowledge, that website triggers a request to your banking application to perform an action you never authorized.

You didn't initiate the action, but your browser may still send your authentication cookies with the request.

That's the idea behind Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF).

What Is CSRF?

Cross-Site Request Forgery is a web security vulnerability that tricks a user's browser into performing unwanted actions on a website where the user is already authenticated.

The attacker doesn't necessarily need to steal your password or session cookie.

Instead, they exploit the trust between your browser and the application.

The problem isn't that the application doesn't recognize the user. It's that the application cannot determine whether the user intended the request.

How Does CSRF Work?

Consider an application where users can change their email addresses.

  1. A user logs into bank.example and receives an authentication cookie.
  2. The user visits an attacker-controlled website.
  3. The malicious website attempts to submit a request to bank.example to change the user's email address.
  4. If the browser includes the session cookie and the application lacks CSRF protection, the server may process the request.

The server sees a valid authenticated session, but the action originated from an untrusted website.

Modern cookie restrictions such as SameSite=Lax can block many cross-site requests, but vulnerable configurations and application behaviors can still expose CSRF risks.

How Can Developers Prevent CSRF?

1. Use anti-CSRF tokens

Generate an unpredictable token and require it on state-changing requests. The server validates the token before processing the action.

An attacker-controlled website shouldn't be able to obtain a valid token from the protected application.

2. Configure SameSite cookies

Use SameSite=Lax or SameSite=Strict where appropriate to restrict when browsers include cookies in cross-site requests.

Treat this as an additional defense rather than assuming it covers every scenario.

3. Validate request origins

Use the Origin header, with carefully configured fallback checks, or Fetch Metadata headers to reject unexpected cross-site requests.

4. Protect state-changing endpoints

Operations such as changing passwords, updating account details, or transferring funds should require appropriate CSRF protection.

Never use GET requests for operations that modify application state.

CSRF Protection in ASP.NET Core

ASP.NET Core provides built-in antiforgery support.

For MVC applications, developers can use [ValidateAntiForgeryToken] on protected actions or configure [AutoValidateAntiforgeryToken] to validate unsafe HTTP methods automatically.

Razor Pages also provides built-in antiforgery support for forms.

For APIs using cookie-based authentication, ensure the relevant endpoints have an appropriate CSRF defense.

APIs authenticated exclusively with bearer tokens explicitly supplied through authorization headers are generally not susceptible to traditional cookie-based CSRF.

Key Takeaway

Authentication verifies who is making a request.

CSRF protection helps verify that the request came through an intended, trusted interaction.

A valid session doesn't automatically mean a request is legitimate.

Secure applications must validate not just the user's identity, but also the trustworthiness of state-changing requests.

title: Refresh tokens in a .NET 10 Minimal API: rotation, reuse detection and revocation
description:
In the previous posts of this series I've been building a free .NET 10 Minimal API starter: JWT authentication, per-user ownership, rate limiting and health checks.

Until now, login returned a single JWT that lasted 60 minutes. That has two problems:

  • It can't be revoked. If a token leaks, whoever has it keeps access for up to an hour, and "log out" only means the client forgets the token.
  • Shortening it hurts users. A 15-minute token without a way to renew it means logging in again every 15 minutes.

Refresh tokens solve both. In this post I'll go through the design I chose, the code, how I tested expiry without waiting a week, and a couple of mistakes I made on the way.

The code is in the repo: Fmaes2/dotnet-minimal-api-starter.

The design in one table

Login now returns two tokens:

Access token Refresh token
Format JWT (signed, self-contained) Opaque random string
Lifetime 15 minutes 7 days
Sent to Every protected endpoint Only /api/auth/refresh and /api/auth/logout
Stored on the server No Yes, as a hash
Can be revoked No (it just expires) Yes 
{
  "accessToken": "eyJhbGciOi...",
  "accessTokenExpiresAt": "2026-10-24T15:45:00Z",
  "refreshToken": "q3Zx...",
  "refreshTokenExpiresAt": "2026-10-31T15:30:00Z"
}

The access token stays stateless, so protected endpoints don't hit the database to validate it. The refresh token is the stateful part, and it's only checked once every 15 minutes.

Three rules on top of that:

  1. Rotation: each refresh token can be used only once. Using it returns a new pair and invalidates the old token.
  2. Reuse detection: if an already used token shows up again, assume it was stolen and revoke the whole session.
  3. Revocation: logout revokes the session; logout-all revokes every session of the user.

I return the refresh token in the response body. For browser SPAs an HttpOnly cookie is the usual recommendation, but it brings CSRF and CORS into the picture, so I left it for a future post.

Storage: hash it, like a password (but not quite) 

public class RefreshToken
{
    public Guid Id { get; set; }
    public required string UserId { get; set; }
    public required string TokenHash { get; set; }
    public Guid FamilyId { get; set; }
    public DateTime CreatedAt { get; set; }
    public DateTime ExpiresAt { get; set; }
    public DateTime? RevokedAt { get; set; }
    public Guid? ReplacedByTokenId { get; set; }

    public bool IsActive(DateTime utcNow) => RevokedAt is null && ExpiresAt > utcNow;
}

A few decisions worth explaining:

Only the hash is stored. A refresh token is a credential. If the database leaks, plain tokens would let an attacker log in as any user for a week. With hashes, the leak is useless.

SHA-256, not bcrypt. Password hashes are slow on purpose because passwords have little entropy and can be brute-forced. A refresh token is 64 random bytes (512 bits), so there's nothing to guess, and a fast hash is enough. It also has a nice side effect: SHA-256 is deterministic, so the lookup is just WHERE TokenHash = @hash on a unique index.

var plain = Base64Url.EncodeToString(RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(64));
var hash = Convert.ToHexString(SHA256.HashData(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(plain)));

FamilyId groups the tokens of one login. Every token issued by rotating inherits it. That's what makes "revoke the whole session" a single UPDATE.

DateTime, not DateTimeOffset. My integration tests use in-memory SQLite, and the EF Core SQLite provider can't translate DateTimeOffset comparisons to SQL. DateTime in UTC works on both SQLite and PostgreSQL (timestamptz), and Npgsql throws if a non-UTC DateTime sneaks in, so mistakes surface early.

Rotation and reuse detection

This is the core of the feature:

public async Task<IssuedRefreshToken?> RotateAsync(string token, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var now = time.GetUtcNow().UtcDateTime;
    var hash = Hash(token);

    var stored = await db.RefreshTokens.AsNoTracking()
        .SingleOrDefaultAsync(t => t.TokenHash == hash, ct);

    if (stored is null)
        return null;

    if (stored.RevokedAt is not null)
    {
        // Someone is using a token that was already consumed: treat it as theft.
        await RevokeFamilyAsync(stored.FamilyId, now, ct);
        return null;
    }

    if (stored.ExpiresAt <= now)
        return null;

    var (plain, replacement) = NewToken(stored.UserId, stored.FamilyId, now);

    await using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);

    // Conditional update: only one concurrent request can claim the old token.
    var claimed = await db.RefreshTokens
        .Where(t => t.Id == stored.Id && t.RevokedAt == null)
        .ExecuteUpdateAsync(s => s
            .SetProperty(t => t.RevokedAt, now)
            .SetProperty(t => t.ReplacedByTokenId, replacement.Id), ct);

    if (claimed == 0)
        return null;

    db.RefreshTokens.Add(replacement);
    await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
    await tx.CommitAsync(ct);

    return new IssuedRefreshToken(stored.UserId, plain, replacement.ExpiresAt);
}

Why reuse detection works. Imagine an attacker steals a refresh token. Now two parties have it: the real client and the attacker. Whoever uses it first gets a new pair. When the other one tries, the token is already revoked. The server can't tell which of the two is the attacker, so it revokes the whole family and both have to log in again. The real user is annoyed once; the attacker is locked out.

Why the conditional update. Reading the token and then marking it as used is a classic race: two requests can both read it as active and both get a new pair. WHERE Id = @id AND RevokedAt IS NULL lets the database decide: only one UPDATE affects a row, the other gets 0 and returns 401. It needs no row version column, so it behaves the same on PostgreSQL and SQLite.

Why the transaction. Revoking the old token and inserting the new one must happen together. Without it, a failure on the insert would leave the user with a revoked token and no replacement.

Why AsNoTracking. ExecuteUpdateAsync runs SQL directly and bypasses the change tracker, so a tracked copy of the token would be stale. Not tracking it avoids that trap.

The endpoints 

group.MapPost("/refresh", Refresh)
    .AddEndpointFilter<ValidationFilter<RefreshTokenRequest>>()
    .RequireRateLimiting(RateLimitingExtensions.AuthPolicy);

group.MapPost("/logout", Logout)
    .AddEndpointFilter<ValidationFilter<RefreshTokenRequest>>();

group.MapPost("/logout-all", LogoutAll).RequireAuthorization();

private static async Task<Results<Ok<AuthResponse>, UnauthorizedHttpResult>> Refresh(
    RefreshTokenRequest req, UserManager<IdentityUser> users, TokenService tokens,
    RefreshTokenService refreshTokens, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var rotated = await refreshTokens.RotateAsync(req.RefreshToken, ct);
    if (rotated is null)
        return TypedResults.Unauthorized();

    var user = await users.FindByIdAsync(rotated.UserId);
    if (user is null)
        return TypedResults.Unauthorized();

    var (access, accessExpires) = tokens.CreateToken(user);
    return TypedResults.Ok(new AuthResponse(access, accessExpires, rotated.Token, rotated.ExpiresAt));
}

Some details:

  • /refresh and /logout are anonymous: by the time the client calls them, the access token has probably expired. The refresh token itself identifies the session.
  • /refresh reloads the user instead of copying claims from the old token, so a changed email (or, later, roles) is picked up.
  • /logout always returns 204, even for unknown tokens. Different answers would let someone probe which tokens are valid.
  • /refresh reuses the existing auth rate limiting policy. Logout doesn't need it: brute-forcing a logout gains nothing.
  • The validator caps the token at 200 characters (a real one is 86), so nobody can make the server hash megabytes of input.

Don't forget ClockSkew

TokenValidationParameters.ClockSkew defaults to 5 minutes: a JWT is still accepted up to 5 minutes after it expires, to tolerate clock differences between servers. With a 60-minute token nobody notices. With a 15-minute token, it's 33% of extra lifetime for a token you can't revoke.

ClockSkew = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)

Testing expiry without waiting 7 days

The service gets the time from an injected TimeProvider instead of DateTime.UtcNow:

builder.Services.TryAddSingleton(TimeProvider.System);

TryAdd only registers it if nothing else did, which leaves room for the tests to swap it. With the Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing package, the expiry test moves the clock forward instead of waiting:

[Fact]
public async Task Refresh_WithExpiredToken_Returns401()
{
    var clock = new FakeTimeProvider(DateTimeOffset.UtcNow);
    using var app = factory.WithWebHostBuilder(b =>
        b.ConfigureTestServices(s => s.AddSingleton<TimeProvider>(clock)));
    var client = app.CreateClient();
    var login = await RegisterAndLoginAsync(client);

    clock.Advance(TimeSpan.FromDays(8));
    var response = await RefreshAsync(client, login.RefreshToken);

    Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.Unauthorized, response.StatusCode);
}

ConfigureTestServices runs after Program.cs, and when a service is registered twice the container resolves the last one, so the fake clock wins.

The other tests cover rotation, reuse revoking the whole family, unknown and empty tokens, logout and logout-all.

One case I deliberately didn't test: two concurrent refreshes with the same token. The test factory shares a single in-memory SQLite connection, and SqliteConnection isn't meant to be used from several threads at once. The test could fail because of the connection rather than my code, which is the definition of a flaky test. Testing it properly needs a real PostgreSQL instance, for example with Testcontainers.

Mistakes I made along the way

1. A table called RefreshToken instead of RefreshTokens. I configured the entity in OnModelCreating but forgot the DbSet. The code that used db.RefreshTokens didn't compile, and when I looked at the migration I'd already generated, the table name was singular. EF Core names a table after the DbSet property; without one, it uses the class name. Since the branch wasn't pushed yet, I added the DbSet, removed the migration, generated it again and amended the commit.

2. A 500 on login. The new code was running, but the migration was still pending in my local database because MigrateOnStartup is off in Development. The response only said "An unexpected error occurred" (on purpose, the global handler doesn't leak details), and the real cause was in the Serilog output. dotnet ef migrations list showed the migration as (Pending), and dotnet ef database update fixed it. I added this to the README's troubleshooting section.

Breaking change

The login response changed from { token, expiresAt } to { accessToken, accessTokenExpiresAt, refreshToken, refreshTokenExpiresAt }, and the default access token lifetime went from 60 to 15 minutes. In Conventional Commits that's a feat!: with a BREAKING CHANGE: footer.

Known limitations

  • Access tokens can't be revoked: after logout they stay valid until they expire (15 minutes at most).
  • If a client fires two refreshes at once with the same token, one gets 401. Clients should keep a single refresh in flight.
  • Expired and revoked tokens aren't cleaned up from the database yet.

What's next

Roles and policies. One thing I already know will bite: with MapInboundClaims = false (see part 2), IsInRole won't find the roles unless RoleClaimType is set in TokenValidationParameters.

If you have ideas or questions, open a Discussion in the repo or leave a comment here.
