If CPU utilization is low, I/O wait is low, and the system is not swapping, slow requests may instead be caused by locks, network latency, application-level delays, or connection-pool exhaustion.

Remember that vmstat reports system-wide statistics, not PostgreSQL-only statistics. Confirm the suspected bottleneck with another signal before making changes.

Interpreting common performance patterns

What you observe Likely interpretation First action
Database host has almost no idle CPU and a run queue larger than the CPU count. CPU saturation. Find expensive queries using tools such as pg_stat_statements; reduce unnecessary concurrency or add CPU capacity.
Database host has low CPU utilization, high I/O wait, and blocked tasks. Possible storage bottleneck. Check query plans, cache hit rates, checkpoint activity, indexes, and storage latency.
Sustained si or so activity. Memory pressure and swapping. Review work_mem, connection counts, parallel-query usage, and available RAM.
Low CPU and I/O wait, but many sessions waiting on locks. Lock contention. Identify blockers and shorten transactions.
Many sessions are idle in transaction. Applications are holding transactions open unnecessarily. Fix transaction handling and consider idle_in_transaction_session_timeout.
One application CPU core is near 100%, with high event loop delay. CPU-intensive JavaScript is blocking the event loop. Offload computation, chunk work, or use additional application processes.
Database appears healthy, but application connection-pool wait time is high. Connection exhaustion or poor concurrency management. Inspect pool sizing, transaction duration, and unbounded parallel queries.
High context-switch rates alongside a large run queue. Potentially excessive runnable concurrency. Confirm CPU contention and reduce unnecessary concurrency or increase CPU capacity.

These are diagnostic starting points, not definitive conclusions. Correlate multiple measurements before changing configuration.

Asking PostgreSQL what its sessions are waiting for

PostgreSQL can report what active sessions are waiting on through pg_stat_activity.

SELECT wait_event_type, wait_event, count(*) AS sessions
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'active'
GROUP BY wait_event_type, wait_event
ORDER BY sessions DESC;

This query groups active sessions by their reported wait event.

Common categories include:

  • Lock: Waiting for a heavyweight lock.

  • IO: Waiting for certain I/O operations.

  • LWLock: Waiting for an internal lightweight lock.

  • Client: Waiting for client-related communication events.

An active session with a NULL wait event is not currently reporting a wait event. It may be executing on the CPU, but a single snapshot cannot establish how much CPU it is consuming or whether CPU saturation is the system-wide bottleneck.

For that reason, take multiple snapshots and correlate them with CPU, storage, and application metrics. A snapshot dominated by lock waits points toward contention; one dominated by I/O waits suggests investigating storage. Many active sessions with no reported wait events, combined with high CPU utilization, make CPU saturation more plausible.

10. One Request, End to End

The following table brings the pieces together by tracing a request from the application to PostgreSQL and back. It shows which resource is involved at each stage, where the request might wait, and what commonly goes wrong.

Step What happens Main resource Can it wait? Typical problem
1 An HTTP request arrives and the operating system delivers it to Node.js. Network and kernel Yes, before delivery. Network or load-balancer overload.
2 The event loop executes the request handler. JavaScript thread and CPU Yes, if the event loop is busy. CPU-heavy JavaScript blocks other requests.
3 The application requests a database connection from its pool. Application resources Yes, if all connections are occupied. Pool exhaustion.
4 The driver sends SQL through a network socket. Kernel network stack Yes, depending on network buffering and connection state. Network delays or connection setup overhead.
5 SQL travels to the database host. Network Yes, for the round trip. Latency, packet loss, or network congestion.
6 The PostgreSQL backend becomes runnable and is scheduled. CPU and operating-system scheduler Yes, if CPU cores are busy. CPU saturation.
7 PostgreSQL parses and plans the query. CPU Usually little explicit waiting. Poor query plan or expensive planning.
8 PostgreSQL reads table and index pages. Memory and storage Yes, on cache misses or slow I/O. Storage-bound workload.
9 PostgreSQL acquires required locks. Lock-management structures Yes, if conflicting locks exist. Lock contention or a lock queue convoy.
10 A modifying transaction writes WAL records and commits. Storage Yes, when waiting for durable WAL flush. Slow storage or commit latency.
11 Results travel back and the application processes the response. Network and JavaScript thread Yes, if the network or event loop is delayed. Large result sets or event loop blocking.
12 The application serializes and sends the HTTP response. JavaScript thread and network Yes, if computation or network delivery is delayed. Expensive serialization or slow clients.

Not every request passes through every stage. For example, a read-only query does not normally require the same WAL commit flush as a transaction that modifies data.

Read this table as a diagnostic checklist. End-to-end latency is the result of the work performed and the waits encountered across these stages. Optimizing a stage that contributes little to the total delay will have limited impact, which is why measuring first matters.

11. Practical Rules Derived From This Mental Model

These practices follow directly from how Node.js, connection pools, and PostgreSQL interact.

  • Bound database concurrency. Keep the number of simultaneously active queries within a level the database can handle efficiently. Extra concurrency can increase queueing, context switching, and memory usage without increasing throughput. The right limit depends on query cost, CPU capacity, storage performance, and parallel-query usage.

  • Keep transactions short. Transactions occupy connections and can hold locks while waiting. Long transactions contribute to pool exhaustion, lock queues, and delayed cleanup of obsolete row versions.

  • Never block the event loop with expensive synchronous work. A single JavaScript thread handles callbacks for many requests. Move CPU-heavy work to worker threads or separate processes, or divide it into smaller chunks.

  • Use concurrency deliberately. Promise.all() can reduce latency by running independent operations concurrently, but it also increases simultaneous resource demand. Use bounded concurrency when processing large collections.

  • Configure server-side timeouts. A client timing out does not necessarily stop the database query or release its locks immediately. Consider statement_timeout, lock_timeout, and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout as safeguards appropriate to your workload.

  • Treat schema changes as potential lock events. Use a suitable lock_timeout, check for long-running transactions, and prefer lower-impact operations where possible.

  • Scale the layer that is actually constrained. CPU-heavy JavaScript may benefit from more application processes. A saturated database may need query optimization or additional database resources. Lock contention requires transaction and locking changes, not simply more servers.

  • Measure each layer independently. Use event loop delay for Node.js, CPU and I/O metrics for the operating system, and pg_stat_activity and blocking-session diagnostics for PostgreSQL. This lets you identify the actual bottleneck instead of guessing.

12. Common Misconceptions

Misconception Reality
“More threads or connections always mean more speed.” Concurrency helps only while the system has spare capacity. Beyond that point, additional concurrency can increase queueing, context switching, and memory consumption.
“Asynchronous means parallel.” Async code lets a thread manage multiple pending operations. JavaScript computation remains single-threaded unless you use workers or additional processes.
“Waiting uses CPU.” A blocked task generally consumes no CPU while it sleeps, but it can still hold a connection, transaction, or lock.
“Low CPU means the system is healthy.” A system waiting on storage, locks, or the network can have low CPU utilization and still be very slow.
“A query locks the whole database.” Most statements use specific table and row-level locking mechanisms. Only certain operations require highly restrictive locks.
“Reads and writes block each other in PostgreSQL.” Under ordinary MVCC behavior, plain reads and writes generally proceed concurrently, although locking reads and certain DDL operations can block other work.
“A single-threaded program cannot have race conditions.” Operations can interleave across await points, allowing check-then-act logic to race even on one JavaScript thread.
“The database is slow, so we need a bigger connection pool.” If the database is already saturated, increasing the pool size can make performance worse. Diagnose the bottleneck first.

Conclusion

A database request is a relay race.

Your application hands work to the operating system, the network carries it to PostgreSQL, a backend process executes the query, and the results travel back to your application. Along the way, work may wait for CPU time, memory access, storage, locks, network delivery, or a free database connection.

Three principles explain most of the performance problems covered in this article.

First, different bottlenecks produce different symptoms. CPU saturation creates runnable queues, memory pressure can cause swapping, storage delays increase I/O waits, and lock contention leaves sessions waiting for other transactions.

Second, concurrency has a cost. Async functions, thread pools, connection pools, and parallel queries help systems handle work efficiently, but they all place demands on finite resources. Increasing concurrency beyond the system's capacity can increase latency rather than reduce it.

Third, waiting can be measured and investigated. Event loop delay, Linux tools such as vmstat, PostgreSQL's pg_stat_activity, and pg_blocking_pids() help answer the most useful diagnostic question: What is waiting, and what is it waiting for?

Once you can answer that question for your own system, practices such as keeping transactions short, bounding connection pools, avoiding event loop blocking, and optimizing slow queries stop being rules to memorize. They become conclusions you can derive from the system's actual behavior.

References

  1. Node.js: The event loop, timers, and process.nextTick()
  2. libuv: Design overview
  3. PostgreSQL: Explicit locking
  4. PostgreSQL: Concurrency control (MVCC)
  5. PostgreSQL: Resource consumption settings
  6. PostgreSQL: The cumulative statistics system (pg_stat_activity)
  7. Brendan Gregg: The USE Method

title: Stop Uploading Signed Contracts to SaaS: How to Build 100% Client-Side PDF Signing in TypeScript
description:
Every week, millions of developers and business owners upload sensitive non-disclosure agreements, offer letters, and vendor contracts to third-party e-sign platforms just to slap a handwritten signature on page 4.

Think about the privacy equation: to perform what is essentially a 2D composite placement of a signature glyph onto an existing document, we routinely transmit proprietary PDFs over public networks to external server farms, exposing them to server-side cache retention, worker logs, and third-party data breach vectors.

Why are we sending contracts across the wire for something modern client-side JavaScript can execute in under 30 milliseconds?

In this deep dive, we'll break down the mechanics of building a zero-upload, 100% in-browser PDF signing engine using TypeScript, pdfjs-dist, and pdf-lib. We'll solve the three biggest technical headaches along the way: PostScript coordinate inversion, Retina canvas blur, and instant client-side chroma keying for physical stamp uploads.

1. The Core Misconception: Visual Signing vs. Cryptographic PDF Bloat

Many developers assume that allowing a user to sign a document requires a heavyweight digital certificate infrastructure (PKI / X.509 cryptographic signing).

While certified digital signatures (such as eIDAS Qualified Electronic Signatures) serve regulated high-trust legal niches, the vast majority of day-to-day business documents—standard commercial contracts, invoices, rental leases, and internal acknowledgments—rely on Simple Electronic Signatures (SES). Under the US ESIGN Act and EU eIDAS regulations, an SES simply requires demonstrating intent through an applied mark or image.

The fatal architectural flaw of many in-browser PDF signers is that they take the easy route: they rasterize the entire PDF page into a giant JPEG, paste the signature on top, and stitch it back together.

Doing that destroys all vector sharpness, wipes out searchable text streams, and blows up a 400KB contract into a 15MB file.

A production-grade signer must preserve the underlying document's vector integrity, embedding the signature as a transparent overlay directly into the PDF's existing content stream.

2. The Coordinate System Nightmare: Screen Space vs. PostScript

The single biggest gotcha when placing signatures on a PDF is that web browsers and PDF engines disagree on where the universe begins.

Screen Canvas Space (DOM / HTML5 Canvas)

Origin (0, 0) is at the top-left. X increments to the right, and Y increments downwards.

PDF Cartesian Point Space (PostScript standard)

Origin (0, 0) is at the bottom-left. Measurements are in typographic points (1/72 of an inch). X increments to the right, and Y increments upwards.

If you naively take the pixel position from your drag-and-drop React overlay and pass it to pdf-lib, your signature will end up upside-down or hovering in the opposite quadrant of the page.

Here is the exact mathematical conversion formula:

// Screen coordinate: element.x, element.y (measured from top-left)
// Canvas dimensions: canvasWidth, canvasHeight (rendered by PDF.js)
// Actual PDF Page dimensions: pdfPageWidth, pdfPageHeight (from PDF document spec)

const scaleFactorX = pdfPageWidth / canvasWidth;
const scaleFactorY = pdfPageHeight / canvasHeight;

const pdfWidth = element.width * scaleFactorX;
const pdfHeight = element.height * scaleFactorY;

const pdfX = element.x * scaleFactorX;

// Invert the Y-axis: subtract the element's bottom edge from the total height
const pdfY = pdfPageHeight - (element.y + element.height) * scaleFactorY;

With this mapping, regardless of whether the user views the document on a mobile screen, a 1080p monitor, or a 4K display, the signature lands on the exact millimeter of the signing line.

3. High-DPI Capture: Eliminating the "Blurry Signature" Problem

When capturing freehand signatures via HTML5 canvas, the default canvas resolution produces fuzzy, jagged strokes on Retina and high-density mobile screens.

To get fountain-pen smoothness, you must decouple the canvas's physical drawing buffer from its CSS presentation width using window.devicePixelRatio:

function setupCrispCanvas(canvas: HTMLCanvasElement) {
  const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
  if (!ctx) return;

  const dpr = window.devicePixelRatio || 1;
  const rect = canvas.getBoundingClientRect();

  // Set internal raster buffer to high-DPI resolution
  canvas.width = rect.width * dpr;
  canvas.height = rect.height * dpr;

  // Scale the rendering context so coordinate math stays in CSS pixels
  ctx.scale(dpr, dpr);

  // Smooth out drawing paths
  ctx.lineCap = 'round';
  ctx.lineJoin = 'round';
  ctx.lineWidth = 2.5;
  ctx.strokeStyle = '#0F172A';
}

When users draw with a finger or stylus, their input coordinates map directly to CSS space, while the underlying image data exports at crisp, print-ready 300+ DPI.

4. Real-Time Chroma Keying: Stripping White Backgrounds from Stamp Uploads

A common user story is signing on a piece of paper, taking a photo on a smartphone, and uploading it.

The problem? The photo has an off-white or yellowish paper background. If you drop that JPEG onto a contract, it casts an ugly opaque box over the text and signature lines underneath.

Instead of sending the image to a cloud AI background-remover, you can perform instant luminance thresholding right in an offscreen canvas:

function makeSignatureTransparent(imageSrc: string): Promise<string> {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const img = new Image();
    img.crossOrigin = 'anonymous';
    img.onload = () => {
      const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
      canvas.width = img.naturalWidth;
      canvas.height = img.naturalHeight;

      const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
      if (!ctx) return reject('Canvas context unavailable');

      ctx.drawImage(img, 0, 0);

      const imgData = ctx.getImageData(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
      const data = imgData.data;

      // Iterate through RGBA values (4 bytes per pixel)
      for (let i = 0; i < data.length; i += 4) {
        const r = data[i];
        const g = data[i + 1];
        const b = data[i + 2];

        // If the pixel is near-white paper (brightness > 225), set Alpha to 0
        if (r > 225 && g > 225 && b > 225) {
          data[i + 3] = 0;
        }
      }

      ctx.putImageData(imgData, 0, 0);
      resolve(canvas.toDataURL('image/png'));
    };
    img.onerror = reject;
    img.src = imageSrc;
  });
}

This takes under 15ms for an average mobile snapshot, transforming paper scans into clean transparent PNG stamps that blend seamlessly over contract lines.

5. The Complete Client-Side Embedding Pipeline

Once the user places their signature, typed name, or date stamp onto the document canvas, we burn the graphic into the PDF binary using pdf-lib:

import { PDFDocument } from 'pdf-lib';

interface SignatureElement {
  pageNumber: number; // 1-indexed
  pngDataUrl: string;
  x: number;
  y: number;
  width: number;
  height: number;
}

export async function signPdfDocument(
  pdfFile: File,
  elements: SignatureElement[],
  renderedCanvasWidth: number,
  renderedCanvasHeight: number
): Promise<Uint8Array> {
  const arrayBuffer = await pdfFile.arrayBuffer();
  const pdfDoc = await PDFDocument.load(arrayBuffer, { ignoreEncryption: true });

  for (const el of elements) {
    const targetPage = pdfDoc.getPage(el.pageNumber - 1);
    const { width: pageWidth, height: pageHeight } = targetPage.getSize();

    // Decode base64 PNG data into a binary buffer
    const base64Data = el.pngDataUrl.split(',')[1];
    const binaryString = atob(base64Data);
    const bytes = new Uint8Array(binaryString.length);
    for (let i = 0; i < binaryString.length; i++) {
      bytes[i] = binaryString.charCodeAt(i);
    }

    // Embed as a native PNG object inside the PDF
    const embeddedImage = await pdfDoc.embedPng(bytes);

    // Compute inverted coordinate offsets
    const scaleFactorX = pageWidth / renderedCanvasWidth;
    const scaleFactorY = pageHeight / renderedCanvasHeight;

    const pdfWidth = el.width * scaleFactorX;
    const pdfHeight = el.height * scaleFactorY;
    const pdfX = el.x * scaleFactorX;
    const pdfY = pageHeight - (el.y + el.height) * scaleFactorY;

    // Stamp directly onto the page without re-rasterizing the document
    targetPage.drawImage(embeddedImage, {
      x: Math.max(0, pdfX),
      y: Math.max(0, pdfY),
      width: pdfWidth,
      height: pdfHeight,
    });
  }

  return await pdfDoc.save();
}

Because this only modifies the target page stream and embeds a compressed PNG object, the exported PDF retains 100% of its original fonts, selectable paragraphs, and minimal file size.

6. Inspecting the Live Pipeline

If you want to test how this coordinate translation and client-side stamp thresholding behave with actual multi-page PDFs, you can try out the live implementation over at VersaPDF's Sign Tool.

You can even keep your browser's DevTools Network tab open while dropping signatures: you will see zero outbound file payloads, as the entire rendering, thresholding, and byte-compilation pipeline runs strictly inside local memory.

What's Next?

Client-side document tooling has matured to the point where browsers can handle virtually every common office workflow. Have you transitioned any document processing tasks from server-side workers to client WebAssembly/Web APIs? How are you handling PDF coordinate discrepancies in your projects? Let's discuss below!

title: Grid Lanes masonry settles on Grid syntax, and flow-tolerance is now fit-tolerance
description:
If you wrote flow-tolerance somewhere in a Grid Lanes prototype, rename it. Saleh Mubashar's walkthrough on Piccalilli, published 22 October, says the property is now fit-tolerance. The layout mode itself is display: grid-lanes, and according to the article it works in Safari 26.4 and later, while "support in other browsers is still evolving."

The smallest version is three declarations, and they're all ones you already know from Grid:

.masonry {
  display: grid-lanes;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(14rem, 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}

That reuse is deliberate, and it took a while to get here. Rachel Andrew opened a CSSWG issue asking for a native Pinterest-style layout in 2017. Two competing shapes followed: grid-template-rows: masonry on a regular grid (Mozilla's idea, later picked up by WebKit) and a separate display: masonry mode from Chromium. In January 2025 the CSS Working Group agreed to reuse Grid's track-definition syntax, and the article says the name display: grid-lanes was settled in December 2025. Spanning works the Grid way too: grid-column: span 2 on an item.

The knob that got renamed

The browser places each item in a lane, usually the shortest one. fit-tolerance decides what counts as "shortest" when lanes are close in height. Per the source, 0 favours the tightest packing. A larger value lets the browser treat near-equal lanes as equal, so items stay closer to source order, and infinite takes that all the way. The default is normal, which resolves to 1em.

.masonry {
  fit-tolerance: 0;
}

That's the one thing I'd try today. Open a card grid in Safari, flip between 0 and infinite, and watch where the cards land. The article also notes that source order stays intact even when items move around visually, so it's worth checking keyboard order on your own content.

The caveat is the support line. One engine ships it, so for now this is progressive enhancement: browsers that don't recognise grid-lanes ignore that declaration, which means your fallback layout has to come from a declaration they do understand. What I'm watching next is whether the other engines ship it under the settled name, and how subgrid cards inside a Grid Lanes container behave in practice. The article says subgrid can work alongside it, since masonry now lives inside the Grid model.

title: # From Punch Cards to the Cloud:The Evolution of DBMS (And When You Actually Don't Need One)
description:
Whenever we build an application, our first instinct is usually to connect a database. A Database Management System (DBMS) is the software that allows us to store, retrieve, and manage data efficiently and securely.

But how did databases become the backbone of modern software? And is setting up a DBMS always the right choice? Let’s dive into the history of databases and look at the specific edge cases where you should actually avoid them.

The History and Evolution of the DBMS

The history of data storage is a fascinating journey of balancing human convenience with hardware efficiency. Here is how we got to where we are today:

1. The 1960s: The Navigational Era (Hierarchical & Network Models)

Before modern databases, data was stored on magnetic tapes and punch cards. In the 1960s, the first true DBMS emerged, utilizing Hierarchical (tree-like, parent-child) and Network (graph-like) models.

  • The Catch: Data was hard-coded to physical paths on a disk. If the structure of the data changed, developers had to rewrite the entire application to find it again.

2. The 1970s & 1980s: The Relational Revolution (RDBMS)

In 1970, IBM researcher Edgar F. Codd published a paper proposing a revolutionary idea: instead of physical paths, data should be logically organized into tables (rows and columns).

  • The Impact: This birthed the Relational Database (RDBMS) and SQL (Structured Query Language). Systems like Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL are built on this model, which prioritizes strict data integrity and relationships.

3. The 1990s: Object-Oriented Databases (OODBMS)

As Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) languages like C++ and Java became popular, developers got frustrated translating their code "objects" into database "tables."

  • The Solution: Object-Oriented Databases were created to store data exactly as it was coded in the application. While they didn't replace relational databases, they paved the way for modern ORMs (Object-Relational Mappers).

4. The 2000s: The NoSQL Boom

With the rise of Web 2.0, giants like Google, Amazon, and Facebook were generating unimaginable amounts of data. Traditional relational databases running on single servers couldn't handle the massive scale.

  • The Solution: NoSQL (Not Only SQL) was born. Databases like MongoDB, Cassandra, and Redis dropped rigid tables in favor of flexible documents, key-value pairs, and graphs. They traded strict consistency for massive speed and the ability to scale horizontally across thousands of cheap servers.

5. The 2010s to Present: Cloud-Native & NewSQL

Today, developers want the best of both worlds: the massive scalability of NoSQL combined with the strict reliability and SQL querying of traditional RDBMS. This led to NewSQL and cloud-native distributed databases (like Google Cloud Spanner and CockroachDB), which can operate flawlessly on a global scale.

When NOT to Use a DBMS

A DBMS is powerful, but it introduces overhead: it requires memory, CPU cycles, network latency, and maintenance. For maximum efficiency, you should skip the DBMS in these scenarios:

1. Managing Static Application Configurations
If you have settings, feature flags, or app parameters that change very rarely, a database is overkill.

  • Alternative: Store these in flat files like .json, .yaml, or .env. They load directly into memory quickly and can be tracked easily using Git.

2. Sequential Append-Only Logging
If your application generates thousands of system errors, access logs, or event streams per minute, writing them to a standard relational database creates huge indexing bottlenecks.

  • Alternative: Simply append this data to flat text files (.log), or use specialized log-aggregation tools designed strictly for writing data at high speeds.

3. Resource-Constrained Environments (IoT)
If you are writing software for embedded systems, microcontrollers, or basic IoT sensors, the device likely does not have the RAM or processing power to run a background database daemon.

  • Alternative: Use native in-memory data structures (like arrays and structs) or write directly to flash memory.

4. Ultra-Low Latency Requirements
In systems where every microsecond counts—like high-frequency stock trading algorithms or real-time game physics—making a network call to a database to fetch data is simply too slow.

  • Alternative: Store the required data directly in the application's RAM using language-native data structures (like HashMaps).

5. Small Prototypes and Static Portfolios
If you are building a simple weekend project, a personal portfolio, or a blog that you update once a month, provisioning a database adds unnecessary cost, complexity, and security risks.

  • Alternative: Use a Static Site Generator (like Next.js or Hugo) with Markdown files to serve your content instantly for free.

The DBMS is arguably the most important software invention of the 20th century. Going from rigid magnetic tapes to globally distributed cloud databases has completely transformed how we interact with technology. However, as developers, our job isn't to use a database for everything—it's to use the right tool for the job, and sometimes, that means using no database at all.

title: OpenAI's Scheduled Agent Automations Are Not Cron Jobs: The Delivery Gap Matters
description:
A scheduled agent task sounds simple: pick a time, save an instruction, and expect the work to happen. But the moment an agent can act on a schedule, the important question is no longer just when it starts. It is what happens if the session is busy, an approval is needed, a tool call fails, or the invocation is delivered but the work never reaches a useful result.

OpenAI's new Scheduled Automations for the Agents API makes that distinction visible. An automation stores a schedule and sends a task to an agent session. Each attempt creates an invocation record. That is not the same contract as a traditional cron process that starts a command on a host and lets the command's supervisor report its exit status. The official documentation says delivery can wait while the target session is busy, a scheduled run does not interrupt an active turn, and the application still has to handle required actions.

That is the story worth paying attention to. Agent platforms are adding scheduling, but a schedule is only one link in a longer chain: trigger, delivery, session, tools, approval, side effect, and verification. If your system treats “invocation queued” as “task completed,” it can report success while useful work has not happened.

What OpenAI has actually added

The feature lets developers save a one-time or recurring automation for an agent session. A one-time run uses a future Unix timestamp. A recurring run uses a five-field cron expression and a time zone. The automation can start a new session or continue an existing one. An application can also enable an automations tool so an agent can create, list, update, pause, resume, or delete automations in its current session.

When a run is due, the Agents API creates an invocation, described as a record of an attempt to send a task to the target session. The invocation has fields such as status, session ID, source type, and scheduled time. A manual invocation can be triggered for testing, and its history can be inspected separately from scheduled runs.

Those are useful building blocks. They let an application delegate timing and scheduling state to the API rather than maintain every timer itself. But the language in the documentation matters: the service schedules and delivers work to a session. It does not promise that every scheduled task will finish successfully, that every requested tool action will be approved, or that a downstream system has accepted the result.

A schedule is not a completion guarantee

A conventional cron entry is often treated as a direct command launch: at a time, start a process. Even there, reliable operations require more than cron. The process can crash, the host can be down, and a second run can overlap the first. But the execution boundary is comparatively clear: a process began, and its exit status can be collected.

An agent automation has a different boundary. The schedule causes an invocation to be delivered to a session. The session then needs to become available, interpret instructions, decide whether to use tools, possibly request approval, and interact with external systems. The official docs explicitly note that if a session is working, delivery waits for it to become available. The scheduled run does not interrupt the active turn or provide a missing tool result or approval. The application must handle those requirements.

That means several states that sound like success are only intermediate states:

  • The schedule is saved. This proves configuration exists, not that a run was delivered.
  • The invocation is queued. This proves the attempt is waiting, not that the session acted.
  • The invocation is completed. This is a delivery-history status, not necessarily proof that the intended external side effect occurred correctly.
  • The agent produced a response. This does not establish that a database write, email, deployment, or ticket update was accepted and verified.

The practical lesson is not that the feature is unreliable. It is that the API's unit of scheduling is a task delivery to an agent, not a business outcome. Applications need to define their own completion condition.

Why the busy-session detail changes design

Suppose an agent reviews a queue every hour and updates a ticket when it finds a clear duplicate. If the same session is still handling the previous run when the next schedule fires, the new delivery waits. That may be correct for a conversation that must preserve context. It may be wrong for independent periodic checks where each run should start with a clean state.

The docs let the developer choose whether each run starts a new session or continues an existing conversation. That choice affects more than memory. A continuing session can carry prior state and context forward, but it can also accumulate stale assumptions or make diagnosis harder. A fresh session limits conversational carry-over, but it requires the task payload and application state to provide everything the run needs.

Neither option is automatically best. A report generator that runs once per day may benefit from a new session and a bounded snapshot of the day's data. A multi-step research workflow may need a continuing session because later work depends on earlier findings. In both cases, the application should identify the authoritative input for each run rather than relying on an agent's conversational memory as the only record.

The difference between “queued” and “done” belongs in your data model

When a scheduled agent affects another system, model the workflow as a state machine. For example, a task could move through scheduled, invocation_created, delivered, awaiting_approval, action_submitted, verified, or failed. The exact names are up to the application. The important part is not collapsing those states into a single boolean called success.

The Agents API invocation history can help answer whether delivery was attempted and which session received it. The application should record the business task ID, intended operation, schedule occurrence, and the external resource affected. When the agent submits a side effect, verify that effect by reading the target system back. A model's message saying “updated” is not a receipt from the database or issue tracker.

This also suggests a useful design rule: make actions idempotent where possible. If a scheduled task is retried, resumed, manually invoked, or delivered after a delay, the same logical task should not create duplicate invoices, send repeated notifications, or open multiple identical tickets. Include a stable operation key in the action layer and let the destination reject duplicate operations. The model can help decide what action to request; deterministic application code should enforce whether that action has already been applied.

Approval is a first-class workflow state

Scheduled work can create a false sense of autonomy. A task may be due at 2 a.m., but a particular operation may still need a human decision. The documentation says a schedule does not supply a missing approval. That is an important boundary, not a minor implementation detail.

Before scheduling an agent, classify its possible actions:

  • Read-only work: gather data, summarize changes, or prepare a report.
  • Reversible writes: label an item or create a draft that can be undone.
  • High-impact writes: send external messages, change access, deploy software, issue refunds, or delete data.

The first category can often run unattended if access is properly scoped. The second should have a clear audit trail and undo path. The third should usually require an explicit authorization mechanism that is separate from the model's own judgment. A notification saying that the agent wants approval is not itself an approval workflow. The application needs to store who approved what, when, and against which version of the proposed action.

Observability should follow the whole chain

The API gives invocation records and allows developers to inspect status and session ID. That is a starting point for operations, not a complete monitoring plan. For each scheduled job, a team should be able to answer:

  • Did the schedule produce the expected invocation?
  • Was it queued, delivered, delayed, or blocked?
  • Which session and configuration handled it?
  • Did the agent request a tool, and did the tool call succeed?
  • Was an approval required, and how long did the task wait?
  • Did the target system reflect the intended change?
  • Was the run duplicated, retried, paused, or manually triggered?

A randomized delay for recurring runs is another detail worth including in expectations. The docs say the service adds a small randomized delay to spread load, and a task can wait longer if its target session is busy. Therefore, a cron expression should be read as a schedule for initiating work, not as a promise that an action will happen at the exact second. If a business process has a hard deadline, implement deadline monitoring and escalation outside the agent prompt.

The same logic applies to pause, resume, and delete. Pausing or deleting an automation does not stop work already accepted by a session, and a delivery already in progress may still reach its session. An operator who needs to stop an active action must understand the separate cancellation path. “Schedule paused” and “work stopped” are not interchangeable operational states.

Where this fits, and where it does not

Scheduled Automations can be a good fit when an application already uses the Agents API and wants recurring or one-time agent work delivered into managed sessions. It offers a shared place to define a schedule, inspect invocations, and let an agent manage schedules when that tool is enabled.

It is not a drop-in replacement for every job system. If a task is deterministic and does not need reasoning, a normal scheduler and program may be simpler. If a workflow must meet a strict service-level objective, preserve durable retries, or coordinate transactions across services, those requirements still need explicit infrastructure. An agent's ability to interpret an instruction does not remove the need for queue semantics, deduplication, timeouts, access controls, and outcome verification.

The best mental model is a scheduler attached to an asynchronous agent-session delivery system. Treat the schedule as the trigger, the invocation as evidence of an attempt, and the verified external state as evidence of completion. The distinction keeps the feature useful without attributing guarantees the API does not claim.

A checklist before scheduling an agent

  • Define what counts as completion in the external system, not in the agent's final message.
  • Decide whether each run needs a fresh session or continuing context.
  • Make repeated actions safe with idempotency keys or deduplication.
  • Keep high-impact operations behind an approval process the application enforces.
  • Monitor schedule time, invocation state, session delivery, tool results, and final state separately.
  • Set a deadline and escalation path for busy sessions or missing approvals.
  • Test pause, resume, deletion, and active-run cancellation behavior.
  • Use a conventional scheduler for deterministic jobs that do not need an agent.

The feature is a meaningful step toward agents that can work without a person sending every prompt. But a saved schedule is not an autonomous worker, and a delivered instruction is not a completed task. The design question for developers is where to place the boundary between the agent's flexible reasoning and the application's deterministic guarantees.

I write about developer tools, AI systems, and backend engineering. Subscribe for more practical breakdowns of how these systems behave in production.

Have you put an agent on a schedule yet? What do you use as proof that the task actually finished?

Save the checklist before making a scheduled agent responsible for a real side effect.

Sources

  • OpenAI API documentation: Scheduled automations
  • OpenAI API reference: Create an automation
  • OpenAI Developer Community: Introducing Scheduled Automations to the Agents API

title: Webhooks on localhost: test verification callbacks without a public endpoint
description:
A public question asks how to receive webhooks while developing on localhost. A hosted provider cannot reach 127.0.0.1, so during development the callback may never arrive. We do not represent the person who asked, and we do not claim to fix any platform. For identity onboarding the adjacent decision is concrete: what should your application do while it waits for a callback that cannot reach it? This article uses only the checked local synthetic example to show one answer. Persist a pending session with a deadline, feed synthetic callbacks directly into the handler, and let a missing callback expire locally. A missing callback must never become approval.

The problem and your decision

On localhost, an unreachable callback looks the same as a slow provider: the session stays pending. The risky shortcut is to approve users manually or to treat a timeout as success so development can continue. The decision in front of you is narrower. Do you test state transitions locally, separately from network delivery? Or do you need a real tunnelled sandbox before your logic can be trusted? The fixture supports the first path. It exercises your state handling with no public URL, no credentials and no network calls. It does not test real delivery, signatures or provider retries.

What the fixture implements

The Identity class stores sessions and events in SQLite. create() requires identifiers that start with fixture- and accepts a timeout between 1 and 3600 seconds. It stores status pending and sets deadline to now plus the timeout. It returns hosted_link pointing at example.invalid, with link_executable false. event() accepts only mode synthetic_fixture and source fixture_callback. Any other mode or source raises PRODUCTION_SIGNATURE_VERIFIER_NOT_IMPLEMENTED. Event IDs must also start with fixture-. recover() marks a pending, review or unknown session as expired once deadline has passed. It returns provider_polled false. It expires the session locally and never queries a provider.

Worked hypothetical scenario

Hypothetically, a developer runs onboarding on a laptop. A session is created at now=0 with timeout 60, so deadline is 60. No callback can reach localhost. The developer does not wait for the network. Instead, they inject a synthetic event, fixture-approved with status Approved and policy true. The read returns status approved, permission_granted true, grant_count 1, policy_version 1, allow_action true and live_permission_changed false. Sending the same event again returns the identical record, so grant_count stays 1. A later Declined event returns status declined, permission_granted false, with grant_count still 1. In a second run, no callback arrives and recover is called at now=61. The result is status expired, permission_granted false, grant_count 0, next review_or_authorized_provider_refresh and provider_polled false.

Failure handling

An event for an unknown session, or for the wrong tenant or subject, raises BINDING_MISMATCH. Reading a session that does not exist raises SESSION_NOT_FOUND. An unrecognised status moves the session to unknown, never to approved. An event that arrives after the deadline produces expired. Events on sessions that are already finalised do not reopen them; the one exception is a Declined correction to an approved session. Your application should treat each of these as a reason for review, not as a retry that eventually grants access. Even a granted result is a local fixture record: live_permission_changed is always false.

Proposed application design versus fixture behavior

Everything above is implemented fixture behavior. The following is proposed design that you would have to build and verify yourself. First, expose a development route, or a tunnel you are authorized to use, only for sandbox traffic. Second, add provider-specific signature validation. Third, perform bounded, authorized status reconciliation when a deadline passes, rather than only expiring the session. Finally, decide business permissions through your own rules. The fixture's decide() and revise_policy() methods illustrate explicit, versioned approval, but synthetic permission is not live business permission. The downloadable example has four branches for phone checks plus the identity flow. It is not the same thing as the anonymous three-scenario HTTP trial.

Acceptance checklist

Run the restart and timeout tests named in the guide. Restart with the same SQLite database and confirm the pending state survives. Confirm a duplicate event leaves grant_count at 1. Confirm recover after the deadline returns expired with provider_polled false. Confirm that non-fixture sources are rejected. Confirm that no code path turns a missing callback into approved. Before any real sandbox, record what remains unproven: signature verification, real delivery and retries, reconciliation, and real user permission. Then decide whether a saved sandbox request fits your task.

Run the checked synthetic example

Download and extract https://gridzen.ai/downloads/verification-delivery.zip, enter verification_delivery, then run with Python 3.10+. This local example makes no network calls. Use a fresh database for an independent identity run.

python3 delivery.py identity --db /tmp/gridzen-article-fixture.sqlite

Sources and scope

https://gridzen.ai/guides/missing-verification-webhook/
https://gridzen.ai/guides/current-capabilities/
Based on the checked source snapshot and local fixture; proposed application rules are design advice, not proven production behavior. Written with AI assistance and reviewed independently.

curl https://gridzen.ai/console/api/quickstart/trial \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"task": "identity_onboarding", "scenario": "success"}'

This is synthetic integration testing, not identity verification or production authorization. Real payments are disabled.

Create a free sandbox account · Integration guide

Written and tested by the GridZen team with AI assistance.

title: How to pull SEC filings, insider trades and XBRL financials into your app in 5 minutes
description:
If you've ever tried to build something on top of SEC data, you know the feeling. EDGAR has everything: every 10-K, every 8-K, every Form 4 insider trade, and years of XBRL financials for U.S. public companies. It's free and public. But getting from "I want Apple's recent insider sales" to a clean JSON array takes a surprising amount of glue code.

I built a small API to skip that glue. This post shows what it does, how to call it in a few minutes, and four real use cases with copy-paste examples. All the data comes from SEC EDGAR's public data. The API isn't affiliated with the SEC, and nothing here is investment advice.

What it does

The SEC EDGAR Insider Trading & Financials API runs on Cloudflare Workers and exposes these endpoints:

Endpoint What you get
GET /v1/filings/{tickerOrCik} Company profile + filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K with item numbers, S-1, 4…) with document URLs. Filters: forms, since, until, limit
GET /v1/insider-trades/{tickerOrCik} Parsed Form 4 transactions, one row per trade, with buy/sell totals. Filters: limit, side, codes, since, includeDerivative
GET /v1/insider-buys Market-wide open-market insider purchases grouped by company, with cluster-buy detection. Filters: days, minInsiders, minValue, role, limit
GET /v1/company/{tickerOrCik}/snapshot Revenue, margins, net income, EPS, cash flow, balance sheet and debt, with YoY growth
GET /v1/company/{tickerOrCik}/facts Raw XBRL companyfacts, passed through
GET /v1/company/{tickerOrCik}/concept/{taxonomy}/{tag} History of a single XBRL tag, e.g. us-gaap/NetIncomeLoss
GET /v1/search EDGAR full-text search (q, forms, ciks, startdt, enddt, from)
GET /v1/resolve/{tickerOrCik} Ticker ↔ CIK

You can pass a ticker (AAPL, BRK.B) or a CIK (320193) anywhere an ID is expected.

Quick start

The /v1 endpoints are served through RapidAPI. Calling the Worker directly gets you a 403 that points you to the listing.

  1. Open the RapidAPI listing and subscribe to the free Basic plan.
  2. Copy your key from the RapidAPI dashboard.
  3. Make a call: 
curl "https://sec-edgar-insider-trading-financials-api.p.rapidapi.com/v1/resolve/NVDA" \
  -H "X-RapidAPI-Key: YOUR_RAPIDAPI_KEY" \
  -H "X-RapidAPI-Host: sec-edgar-insider-trading-financials-api.p.rapidapi.com"

{ "cik": "0001045810", "ticker": "NVDA", "name": "NVIDIA CORP" }

For the rest of the post I'll use this setup:

export RAPIDAPI_KEY=YOUR_RAPIDAPI_KEY
export HOST=sec-edgar-insider-trading-financials-api.p.rapidapi.com

You can check that the backend is up without a key: https://sec-edgar-api.kidriahx.workers.dev/health returns {"ok": true, ...}, and the OpenAPI spec is at /openapi.yaml.

Use case 1: Latest 10-K and 8-K filings for a company

Say you want a "recent filings" panel on a stock page.

curl "https://$HOST/v1/filings/MSFT?forms=10-K,8-K&limit=3" \
  -H "X-RapidAPI-Key: $RAPIDAPI_KEY" -H "X-RapidAPI-Host: $HOST"

Response (trimmed):

{
  "company": {
    "cik": "0000789019",
    "name": "MICROSOFT CORP",
    "tickers": ["MSFT"],
    "sicDescription": "Services-Prepackaged Software",
    "fiscalYearEnd": "0630"
  },
  "count": 3,
  "filings": [
    {
      "accessionNumber": "0001193125-26-380280",
      "form": "8-K",
      "filingDate": "2026-09-02",
      "items": "7.01,9.01",
      "documentUrl": "https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/789019/000119312526380280/d291965d8k.htm"
    },
    {
      "accessionNumber": "0001193125-26-323660",
      "form": "10-K",
      "filingDate": "2026-07-29",
      "reportDate": "2026-06-30",
      "documentUrl": "https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/789019/000119312526323660/msft-20260630.htm"
    }
  ]
}

The items field on 8-Ks is useful: 2.02 is results of operations (earnings), 5.02 is officer/director changes, and so on. You can filter on it without opening the document.

Use case 2: Insider trades for a ticker (Form 4)

Form 4s are XML documents, and every filing can hold several transactions. The API parses them into flat rows.

JavaScript (fetch, Node 18+ or browser):

const HOST = "sec-edgar-insider-trading-financials-api.p.rapidapi.com";

async function insiderTrades(ticker) {
  const res = await fetch(`https://${HOST}/v1/insider-trades/${ticker}?limit=5`, {
    headers: {
      "X-RapidAPI-Key": process.env.RAPIDAPI_KEY, // YOUR_RAPIDAPI_KEY
      "X-RapidAPI-Host": HOST,
    },
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
  return res.json();
}

const data = await insiderTrades("AAPL");
console.log(data.summary);
for (const t of data.transactions.filter((t) => t.side === "sell")) {
  console.log(t.transactionDate, t.insiderName, t.shares, t.pricePerShare, t.is10b51Plan);
}

Python (requests):

import os
import requests

HOST = "sec-edgar-insider-trading-financials-api.p.rapidapi.com"
HEADERS = {
    "X-RapidAPI-Key": os.environ["RAPIDAPI_KEY"],  # YOUR_RAPIDAPI_KEY
    "X-RapidAPI-Host": HOST,
}

r = requests.get(f"https://{HOST}/v1/insider-trades/AAPL",
                 params={"limit": 5}, headers=HEADERS, timeout=30)
r.raise_for_status()
data = r.json()
print(data["summary"])
for t in data["transactions"]:
    if t["side"] == "sell":
        print(t["transactionDate"], t["insiderName"], t["shares"], t["pricePerShare"])

Response (trimmed):

{
  "query": { "id": "AAPL", "cik": "0000320193", "ticker": "AAPL", "name": "Apple Inc." },
  "filingsParsed": 5,
  "summary": {
    "transactions": 23,
    "openMarketBuys": 0,
    "openMarketSells": 13,
    "openMarketSellShares": 9869,
    "openMarketSellValue": 3361318.27,
    "distinctInsiders": 3
  },
  "transactions": [
    {
      "insiderName": "Newstead Jennifer",
      "insiderRole": "SVP, GC and Government Affairs",
      "transactionDate": "2026-10-20",
      "transactionCode": "S",
      "transactionType": "Open-market or private sale",
      "side": "sell",
      "shares": 2399,
      "pricePerShare": 339.62,
      "totalValue": 814748.38,
      "sharesOwnedAfter": 34795,
      "is10b51Plan": true,
      "filingUrl": "https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/320193/000114036126040540/form4.xml"
    }
  ]
}

Use side=buy or side=sell to keep only open-market purchases (code P) or sales (code S). Use codes=P,S,M for finer control.

Use case 3: Market-wide cluster buys

When several insiders buy the same stock in the open market within a short window, people call it a "cluster buy." The API keeps a rolling store of recent Form 4 purchases (it scans EDGAR every 10 minutes) and groups them by company:

curl "https://$HOST/v1/insider-buys?days=7&minInsiders=2&limit=5" \
  -H "X-RapidAPI-Key: $RAPIDAPI_KEY" -H "X-RapidAPI-Host: $HOST"

r = requests.get(f"https://{HOST}/v1/insider-buys",
                 params={"days": 7, "minInsiders": 2, "limit": 5},
                 headers=HEADERS, timeout=30)
for c in r.json()["results"]:
    print(c["ticker"], c["insiderCount"], c["totalValue"])

Response (trimmed, from the morning of Oct 24, 2026):

{
  "window": { "days": 7, "from": "2026-10-17", "to": "2026-10-24" },
  "clusterBuys": 10,
  "results": [
    {
      "ticker": "RAPP",
      "issuerName": "Rapport Therapeutics, Inc.",
      "insiderCount": 6,
      "isClusterBuy": true,
      "totalShares": 61694,
      "totalValue": 1664824.35,
      "avgPrice": 26.9852,
      "firstTransactionDate": "2026-10-21",
      "lastTransactionDate": "2026-10-23",
      "insiders": [
        { "name": "PAUL STEVEN M", "role": "Director", "value": 974277.92 },
        { "name": "Ignelzi Troy A.", "role": "Chief Financial Officer", "value": 143550 }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

One caveat: this feed only covers filings since the scanner started running, so it's a recent-activity feed, not a historical database.

Use case 4: Financial snapshot from XBRL

Pulling "revenue" from XBRL sounds simple, but companies use different tags (Revenues, RevenueFromContractWithCustomerExcludingAssessedTax, …), and annual and quarterly facts are mixed together. The snapshot endpoint picks the tags and lines up the periods for you:

const snap = await fetch(`https://${HOST}/v1/company/AAPL/snapshot`, {
  headers: { "X-RapidAPI-Key": process.env.RAPIDAPI_KEY, "X-RapidAPI-Host": HOST },
}).then((r) => r.json());

const rev = snap.metrics.revenue;
console.log(rev.latestAnnual.value, rev.annualGrowthPct);

{
  "company": { "cik": "0000320193", "ticker": "AAPL", "name": "Apple Inc.", "fiscalYearEnd": "0926" },
  "metrics": {
    "revenue": {
      "tag": "us-gaap:RevenueFromContractWithCustomerExcludingAssessedTax",
      "unit": "USD",
      "latestAnnual": { "value": 416161000000, "periodEnd": "2025-09-27", "fiscalYear": 2025, "form": "10-K" },
      "priorAnnual": { "value": 391035000000, "periodEnd": "2024-09-28" },
      "annualGrowthPct": 6.43,
      "latest": { "value": 109417000000, "periodEnd": "2026-06-27", "fiscalPeriod": "Q3", "form": "10-Q" }
    }
  }
}

Each metric includes the exact XBRL tag and accession number, so you can trace any number back to the filing. If you need a metric that isn't in the snapshot, use /v1/company/AAPL/concept/us-gaap/NetIncomeLoss.

Bonus: full-text search. /v1/search?q="share repurchase"&forms=8-K wraps EDGAR full-text search. When I ran it, it reported 5,661 matching 8-Ks from the past year, returned 100 per page.

Why not just call EDGAR directly?

You can, and for a one-off script you probably should. The SEC's APIs are free. Here's what this API handles for you:

  • User-Agent rules. SEC asks every client to declare who it is (a name and contact email) in the User-Agent header. Requests without one can be blocked.
  • Rate limits. SEC's fair-access limit is 10 requests per second. Parsing insider trades means one request per Form 4, and a snapshot uses several XBRL lookups. The API spaces out its SEC calls globally and caches results.
  • CIK lookups. Most SEC endpoints want a zero-padded CIK, not a ticker.
  • Messy formats. Form 4s are XML with separate derivative and non-derivative tables. The submissions JSON stores filings as parallel arrays. companyfacts can run to megabytes per company, with duplicate facts across filings.

If you only need one company's 10-K list, go direct. If you're building a feature on top of insider trades or fundamentals, a wrapper saves you a few evenings.

Pricing

RapidAPI has four plans. Basic is free and covers every endpoint, which is enough to try things out. Paid tiers add more requests per month. Current quotas and prices are on the pricing page.

If you'd rather work in batches (pull every 8-K in a date range into a dataset, or schedule a run), the same kind of data is also available as an Apify actor: SEC EDGAR Filings & Financials on Apify. It's billed per result.

Links

  • RapidAPI listing: https://rapidapi.com/KidriahChannel/api/sec-edgar-insider-trading-financials-api
  • Apify actor: https://apify.com/monriah-studio/sec-edgar-filings
  • OpenAPI spec: https://sec-edgar-api.kidriahx.workers.dev/openapi.yaml

If you build something with it, or hit a filing it parses wrong, let me know in the comments. Edge cases in Form 4s are endless, and I'd like to fix them.

— Caleb Love

title: I Built Tenant-Scoped Memory That Erases for Real — 89 Tests, 27 Mutations, Byte-Level Verified
description:
ragleap-memory 0.1.0 + ragleap-security 0.1.0 — One SQLite File, Real Erasure, Scope Enforced in SQL

I just released two new libraries: ragleap-security 0.1.0 (101 tests) and ragleap-memory 0.1.0 (89 tests). Both v0.1.0, both first releases, both with mutation testing.

TL;DR: Tenant isolation enforced inside SQL, not in app code. And erase() actually removes bytes.

ragleap-security — stdlib only

from ragleap_security import Scope, AuditLog, SecretStr, check_size

scope = Scope.parse("org:gov-dept/region:south/branch:chennai")
print(scope.covers(Scope.parse("org:gov-dept/region:south"))) # True

child = scope.narrow("facility:factory1")

org:gov-dept/region:south/branch:chennai/facility:factory1

log = AuditLog("audit.jsonl")
log.append({"op": "add", "scope": str(scope)})
log.verify() # hash-chain check

secret = SecretStr("sk-...")
print(secret) # SecretStr(***) — never leaks in repr
check_size(data, max_bytes=1_000_000)

5 modules, no deps. You can audit it in an afternoon.

Why hash-chained JSONL? Tamper-evident. If someone edits line 10, verify() fails because hash chain breaks. Not tamper-proof (can't prevent edit), but can detect.

Verified: 101 tests, 30/30 mutations killed, reproducible build matches PyPI.

ragleap-memory — the interesting part

Problem with most memory libs: They do SELECT * FROM memories WHERE tenant_id = X in app code. But they still return different errors for "not found" vs "not allowed" — leaking existence.

Our approach: scope filtering inside SQL, same response for missing vs outside-scope.

from ragleap_memory import SQLiteStore
from ragleap_security import Scope

store = SQLiteStore("memory.db")
scope_a = Scope.parse("org:hospital/branch:chennai")
scope_b = Scope.parse("org:hospital/branch:mumbai")

store.add(text="ICU bed count changed to 12", type="fact", trust="trusted", scope=scope_a)

Same scope → found

print(store.search("ICU", scope=scope_a)) # [fact]

Different scope → looks like missing, not "access denied"

print(store.search("ICU", scope=scope_b)) # [] — same as missing

Typed entries: episode (raw events), fact (distilled), summary (compressed). All default to untrusted — you must explicitly trust.

Operations that matter for enterprise:

id1 = store.add(text="Old threshold", type="fact", scope=scope_a)
id2 = store.supersede(id1, text="New threshold is 80", scope=scope_a) # history kept

store.forget(id2, scope=scope_a) # soft delete
store.erase(id2, scope=scope_a) # hard delete + vacuum

After erase, byte-level check:

grep -a "New threshold" memory.db → not found

grep -a "New threshold" memory.db-journal → not found

We actually tested byte-level search after erase on two SQLite builds.

Other ops: export (dump for migration), sweep_expired (TTL), compact (vacuum), optional audit log without entry text (privacy).

FTS5 search: Full-text search, not vector. Why? Deterministic, no embedding cost, works offline. For Hindi, Tamil, Arabic, Chinese with spaces — whole-word tested. Without spaces (Chinese/Japanese) — not split yet, known limit.

Mutation testing

We run scripts/mutation_check.py — it mutates code (change == to !=, remove WHERE clause, etc.) and checks tests kill it.

security: 30/30 killed

memory: 27/27 killed

If a mutation survives, your tests are weak. We fixed until all killed.

Reproducible builds

Build locally before tagging, compute SHA-256, build on CI after tagging, compare. If different, fail. For these releases, local SHA matches PyPI SHA.

ragleap_memory-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl sha256 c60a1e4f91e323c04ba04d7628abb7028039206d2330921a7ca00ae053a3533e
ragleap_security-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl sha256 e3f31d3703d552cde53080e6d6c56cef733954d61deeaba586bdce48db53075d

Not verified — honest

No Windows / NFS / multi-process writes / power-loss tests
No retrieval benchmark (precision/recall unmeasured)
Tenant isolation holds inside lib, but nothing else uses it yet
No independent security review — see docs/threat-model.md

Install

pip install ragleap-security==0.1.0
pip install ragleap-memory==0.1.0

Repo: github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core

Release PRs: #907 (security), #922/#924 (memory)
Workflows: 40016023080, 40060689857

This is foundation for human digital twins and org-wide memory with real isolation. Next: integrate Scope into agents.

If you care about multi-tenant AI, try breaking the scope isolation — I'd love a failing test.

title: Your tennis CSV should not stop at last season: build an updating ATP/WTA dataset
description:
A tennis notebook can be perfectly reproducible and quietly out of date. It still loads a CSV, still draws a chart, and still answers a question about a season that ended months ago.

I wanted the same convenient workflow with a fresh source: one row per match, winner and loser columns, rankings, serve statistics and pre-match Elo. Then I wanted to do something a static season file cannot do on its own: pick an interesting match and open its point-by-point history.

This tutorial starts with the first half: an updating local match dataset. The last section shows how it connects to deeper analysis.

Disclosure: I build and maintain the CrawlPlant Actors used here. This is an independent dataset in the column layout associated with Jeff Sackmann's tennis files; it is not his dataset or an affiliated project.

Run this project: Get the code, sample data and finished outputs on GitHub. To fetch your own data, use the live recipe and follow the .env setup guide to add your APIFY_TOKEN. Actor calls can incur charges; the setup explains per-run limits.

Start with a small, inspectable batch

Install the Python API client and pandas:

pip install apify-client pandas

Set APIFY_TOKEN in your environment. The helper below starts a run, checks its status, and retrieves the dataset through the client's paginated iterator. Calling it can incur Apify charges; begin with a small date range and set a spending limit in your Apify run settings.

import os
import json
import math
from pathlib import Path

def call_actor(slug, run_input):
    from apify_client import ApifyClient

    client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
    run = client.actor(f"crawlplant/{slug}").call(run_input=run_input)
    if not run or run["status"] != "SUCCEEDED":
        raise RuntimeError(f"Actor did not succeed: {run and run['status']}")
    rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
    if len(rows) >= run_input["maxItems"]:
        raise RuntimeError("Result reached maxItems; narrow the range or increase the cap before claiming completeness.")
    return rows

Fetch a completed calendar week rather than an unfinished day. The dataset Actor uses winner_* and loser_* fields, while the other Actors generally use player1 and player2.

rows = call_actor("tennis-match-dataset", {
    "years": [],
    "dateFrom": "2026-10-12",
    "dateTo": "2026-10-18",
    "tours": ["atp", "wta"],
    "maxItems": 2000,
})

import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(df[["tourney_name", "winner_name", "loser_name", "score"]].head())

For a whole season, use years: [2025] instead of the date window and increase maxItems. A result at the cap is not proof that you downloaded the season; the helper deliberately stops you from making that assumption.

Update by identity, not by row number

An overlapping window is useful. It gives recently corrected scores or statistics another chance to reach your local copy. Appending every batch would turn those corrections into duplicate matches.

Use match_id as the key and let the new record replace the old one:

def update_dataset(old_rows, new_rows):
    # Refresh an overlap window: corrected rows replace the same match id.
    by_id = {}
    for row in [*old_rows, *new_rows]:
        key = row.get("match_id")
        if not key:
            raise ValueError("A match_id is required for an update")
        by_id[key] = row
    return list(by_id.values())

Write the result through a temporary file so an interrupted write does not overwrite your existing snapshot with half a JSON document:

def write_snapshot(path, rows):
    path = Path(path)
    temporary = path.with_suffix(path.suffix + ".tmp")
    temporary.write_text(json.dumps(rows, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    temporary.replace(path)

from pathlib import Path
import json

path = Path("tennis-matches.json")
old_rows = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")) if path.exists() else []
updated = update_dataset(old_rows, rows)
write_snapshot(path, updated)
pd.DataFrame(updated).to_csv("tennis-matches.csv", index=False)

The JSON file is the update source; the CSV is a convenient export. Schedule an overlapping fetch once a week. A seven-day overlap does not catch a correction to a match from six months ago: occasionally refresh an older season if historical revisions matter to your work.

Ask a question the table can actually answer

Here is a useful first chart: how often did the lower-ranked player win in this particular batch?

ranked = df.dropna(subset=["winner_rank", "loser_rank"]).copy()
ranked = ranked[~ranked["score"].fillna("").str.contains(r"RET|W/O|DEF")]
ranked = ranked[ranked["winner_rank"] != ranked["loser_rank"]]
ranked["lower_ranked_winner"] = ranked["winner_rank"] > ranked["loser_rank"]
summary = ranked.groupby("tour")["lower_ranked_winner"].agg(["sum", "count", "mean"])
print(summary)

The illustration uses a saved 233-row Actor result from October 22, 2026. Its tournament-week labels span October 5–19; it was not produced by the fixed calendar-week request above. It is an example batch, not an estimate for the full tour. The chart excludes missing or tied ranks and retirement, walkover and default scores. Qualifying matches remain included. A ranking upset also does not necessarily mean a market upset.

Zoom into the matches that caught your attention

The column layout becomes more useful when the row is a starting point. match_id can be passed to Tennis Point-by-Point as matchIds. winner_id and loser_id can be matched to the player objects returned by Tennis Match History.

Keep the identity convention clear: these are Flashscore identifiers. They are not interchangeable with the numeric player identifiers in Sackmann's original files. The column names are familiar; that does not make every field or tournament-level convention identical.

Start with ATP & WTA Tennis Match Dataset, inspect one batch, and only then schedule it. The useful milestone is a notebook that stays current without quietly multiplying its rows.

Watch an overlapping update replace a row

This deliberately stale local value demonstrates the update rule; it is not a claim that the source corrected this match:

stale = {**rows[0], "score": "DEMO OLD VALUE"}
refreshed = update_dataset([stale], [rows[0]])
assert len(refreshed) == 1
assert refreshed[0]["score"] == rows[0]["score"]
print(stale["match_id"], stale["score"], "->", refreshed[0]["score"])

One identity remains one row. The companion saves the before/after records in reports/update-demo.json and regenerates the exact ranking-upset chart as assets/01-rank-upsets.png and .svg.

Download and reproduce the example

Download the offline companion ZIP. Extract it, open a terminal in that folder and run:

python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python render.py

The package includes the dated sample data, calculation functions, complete chart renderers and finished reports. It generates the series' charts and reports together; no API token or paid Actor/model call is required. The live-fetch code earlier in this article is a separate option and can produce different counts.

Inspect the sources: chart renderer, AI charts, report generation, and data notes. Both PNG and SVG outputs are written to assets/; reports go to reports/.

Keep building: Browse all 48 runnable examples, including Python, JavaScript and AI workflows across the CrawlPlant Actors.

title: The HTTP Status Codes You're Probably Using Wrong (And How to Fix Them)
description:
How many times have you inspected an API response in production, only to find:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{
  "code": 403,
  "status": "error",
  "message": "User not authorized"
}

Or an endpoint returning 400 Bad Request for everything from invalid JSON syntax to failed business logic rules?

HTTP status codes are the standardized language of the web. When used correctly, they make client-side error handling trivial, improve reverse proxy caching (Cloudflare, Nginx), and save engineers hours of debugging. When misused, they turn API integrations into a guessing game.

Let's dive into the most frequently confused status codes, their real RFC definitions, and how to apply them cleanly in your APIs.

1. 401 Unauthorized vs. 403 Forbidden

This is by far the most abused pair in modern API design — largely because HTTP's original naming in RFC 9110 is somewhat misleading.

+---------------------------------------------------------+
|                  Client sends a request                 |
+---------------------------------------------------------+
                            |
             Does the server know who you are?
             (Valid token / session / API key?)
               /                               \
             NO                                 YES
             /                                   \
   401 Unauthorized                      Is the user allowed
 (Better name: Unauthenticated)          to touch this resource?
                                           /                 \
                                         NO                   YES
                                         /                     \
                                   403 Forbidden           200/201/etc.
  • 401 Unauthorized actually means Unauthenticated. The client has not provided valid credentials (missing Authorization header, expired JWT, or invalid API key). Crucially, a 401 response typically includes a WWW-Authenticate header telling the client how to authenticate.
  • 403 Forbidden means: “I know exactly who you are, but you don't have permission to do this.” Sending new authentication tokens will not change the outcome unless the user's role or permissions change.

💡 Rule of thumb: If logging in again might fix it, use 401. If logging in won't help because your account lacks admin privileges, use 403.

2. 400 Bad Request vs. 422 Unprocessable Content

Before RFC 9110 (and RFC 4918 WebDAV), teams dumped every validation failure into 400. Modern REST design prefers separating syntax from semantics:

  • 400 Bad Request: The server cannot parse the request at all. This means malformed JSON (missing closing bracket), invalid query string encoding, or invalid HTTP headers. The payload literally cannot be parsed by the deserializer.
  • 422 Unprocessable Content (formerly Unprocessable Entity): The syntax is completely valid (clean JSON, well-formed fields), but the business validation failed. 
// Example: POST /api/users
// Payload sent: {"email": "not-an-email", "age": -5}
// The JSON parsed successfully, but the fields are invalid.

HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Content
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "errors": [
    { "field": "email", "message": "Must be a valid email address" },
    { "field": "age", "message": "Must be greater than 0" }
  ]
}

Separating these two allows frontend clients to easily route 422 responses directly to UI form validation states, while treating 400 as an unexpected client-side bug.

3. The Redirect Quagmire: 301/302 vs. 307/308

Back in the early days of HTTP/1.0, browsers did something unintended: when they received a 301 Moved Permanently or 302 Found in response to a POST request, they would rewrite the follow-up request method to GET.

This behavior became de facto standard, breaking form submissions and API mutations. To resolve this without breaking legacy websites, the IETF introduced 307 and 308:

Code Name Semantic Preserves POST/PUT Method?
301 Moved Permanently Resource permanently at new URL ❌ Usually rewritten to GET
302 Found Temporary redirect ❌ Usually rewritten to GET
307 Temporary Redirect Temporary redirect ✅ Guaranteed to preserve method & body
308 Permanent Redirect Permanent redirect ✅ Guaranteed to preserve method & body

💡 In modern APIs: If you enforce HTTPS redirects or route versioning (e.g., /api/v1/checkout → /api/v2/checkout), use 308 Permanent Redirect or 307 Temporary Redirect. Using 301 or 302 on a POST payload will result in the client sending an empty GET to the new endpoint!

4. 502 Bad Gateway vs. 504 Gateway Timeout

When debugging backend infrastructure behind a reverse proxy (Nginx, Envoy, Cloudflare, AWS ALB), these two indicate completely different root causes:

  • 502 Bad Gateway: The reverse proxy contacted the upstream service (e.g., your Node/Python/Go container), and the upstream sent an invalid or abruptly closed response (e.g., upstream process crashed with an OOM error, segfaulted, or returned corrupt HTTP).
  • 504 Gateway Timeout: The reverse proxy contacted upstream, but the upstream took too long to respond (exceeded proxy_read_timeout or ALB timeout). Often caused by unindexed database locks, third-party API stalls, or CPU starvation.

5. When to Return 204 No Content

204 No Content is designed for actions that succeed but have nothing meaningful to return in the response body.

  • Good use cases:
    • DELETE /api/items/42: The item is gone; returning empty body with 204 is clean.
    • PUT /api/users/me/preferences: Saved successfully, and the client already knows what state it sent.
  • Watch out for:
    • A 204 response must never include a message body (not even {}).
    • If your frontend relies on receiving the updated object timestamp or auto-generated fields (like updated_at), return 200 OK with the entity instead.

A Handy Reference for Everyday Debugging

With over 60 standardized status codes across RFC 9110 and related extensions (from 206 Partial Content for video streaming to 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After), keeping track of exact caching semantics, headers, and troubleshooting steps is tough.

When designing APIs or debugging production logs, I frequently reference this HTTP Status Codes Directory. It has quick RFC references, cause-and-solution breakdowns, and raw response snippets for every status code without the clutter of reading through 200-page IETF specs.

Quick Summary Cheat-Sheet 

1xx -> Hold on (Protocol upgrades, Expect: 100-continue)
2xx -> Here you go (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content)
3xx -> Go over there (Use 307/308 for APIs to preserve POST/PUT)
4xx -> You (the client) messed up (401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 422 validation)
5xx -> We (the server/infra) messed up (502 crashed upstream, 504 timed out upstream)

What's your API design pet peeve?

Do you enforce 204 on deletes, or prefer returning { "success": true }? How do you structure your error response schemas? Let's discuss in the comments below!

How can I connect a Pure Peptide product with its CoA?

Some directory cards show an average purity and HPLC-UV method. A reported percentage belongs to the described sample and method. It is not by itself a measure of nominal mass, sterility, endotoxin content or suitability for a particular experiment. Inspect the full document for the measurements needed by the institution instead of supplying missing fields from another product.

A public link and an authenticated current-lot assessment are also different. Follow the report where available and ask for clarification if the expected lot, analytical scope or issuing record cannot be matched.
