The supplier’s verification explanation can orient the buyer, but the issuing laboratory’s own record is the relevant independent reference.

Compare the material name, report identifier, dates and stated results. Small discrepancies can matter if they indicate that the supplier copy and the original record are not the same document. A verified certificate must also apply to the batch being purchased. Document authenticity and batch applicability are separate checks.

If a lookup fails, first review the identifiers and the tool’s requirements. A missing result does not automatically establish fraud; it can reflect entry errors, access rules or another verification method. At the same time, the absence of independent confirmation should not be described as successful verification. Record the actual outcome and obtain clarification where necessary.

Keep the verification evidence with the procurement record if it is required by the laboratory. This can include the original report reference or an official confirmation. The goal is traceability: another reviewer should be able to understand what was checked. A promotional phrase such as verified quality is much less informative than a clear explanation of the record and the route used to confirm it.

Quick questions about this offer

Which code should I enter?

Enter plain PURE30 for the advertised up-to-30% offer. Decorative brackets identify the code visually and should not be typed into the coupon field. Inspect the actual accepted saving and complete amount before payment.

What delivery information matters?

The current FAQ describes Canada-only delivery, a 19+ purchasing requirement and a free-shipping threshold assessed after coupons. Confirm the actual post-code merchandise amount and accepted shipping line. A dispatch estimate is different from an arrival guarantee.

Does the code establish a personal benefit?

The code concerns the purchase price. The specification, analytical record and relevant paper answer their own material and scientific questions. Research products remain distinct from finished skincare products, supplements and clinical formulations.

What is the clear next step?

Review Retatrutide, Tirzepatide against the approved research requirement. Match the selected option with its relevant document, confirm the Canadian receiving details and enter plain PURE30. Review the accepted merchandise reduction separately from delivery and any other displayed charge, then approve the complete payable total.

Use promo code ⟨⦅PURE30⦆⟩ for up to 30% off at Pure Peptide. Enter plain PURE30, confirm the actual adjustment and read shipping and the final total before payment.

title: From DevTools to Code: Stop Manually Translating cURL Commands
description:
We've all been there:

  1. You open Chrome / Firefox DevTools.
  2. You inspect an API request on the Network tab that works perfectly.
  3. You right-click and hit "Copy as cURL (bash)".
  4. You paste it in your terminal — 200 OK. Magic! ✨
  5. Now you need to reproduce this exact call in your backend (Python, Node.js, Go, or PHP).

And then the tedious part begins: stripping headers, escaping double quotes, formatting JSON payloads, mapping cookies, and figuring out whether the authorization header needs Bearer or Basic auth.

Manually translating cURL into production code is not just boring — it’s error-prone. Here’s a breakdown of why this process trips developers up, what to watch out for, and how to automate it seamlessly.

The Subtle Traps of Manual cURL Conversion

A typical cURL command copied from the browser looks something like this:

curl 'https://api.example.com/v1/orders?status=active' \
  -X POST \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json;charset=UTF-8' \
  -H 'User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 ...' \
  -H 'Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.9' \
  --data-raw '{"order_id":12345,"items":[{"id":1,"qty":2}],"notes":"Don'\''t forget sauce"}' \
  --compressed

When you translate this by hand, three things usually go wrong:

1. Escaping Quotes & Multiline Strings

Notice that 'Don'\''t forget sauce'? Bash has weird string escaping rules. When you copy that directly into Python or JavaScript, string delimiters often break, causing subtle JSON parse errors that take 15 minutes of head-scratching to debug.

2. Bloated Browser Headers

DevTools exports everything — Sec-Ch-Ua, Sec-Fetch-Dest, Accept-Encoding, Cache-Control, etc.
In code, you usually only care about:

  • Content-Type
  • Authorization
  • Custom app headers (e.g., X-API-Key)

Copying 25 headers into your codebase creates technical debt and can cause unexpected CORS or cache behavior.

3. Payload Serialization Discrepancies

  • --data vs --data-raw vs --data-binary
  • application/x-www-form-urlencoded vs multipart/form-data vs application/json

In Python requests, sending a form uses data=..., while sending JSON uses json=.... If you accidentally pass a raw string to data= with a JSON header, Python won't serialize it properly, leading to mysterious 400 Bad Request responses.

The Target: What Clean Target Code Should Look Like

Let's look at how that cURL command maps cleanly to modern idioms across the most common stacks:

Modern JavaScript (Fetch API)

With Node.js 18+ having native fetch, you rarely need external dependencies for straightforward HTTP calls:

const response = await fetch('https://api.example.com/v1/orders?status=active', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    'Authorization': 'Bearer eyJhbGciOi...',
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    order_id: 12345,
    items: [{ id: 1, qty: 2 }],
    notes: "Don't forget sauce"
  }),
});

const data = await response.json();
console.log(data);

Python (Requests / HTTPX)

In Python, idiomatic code avoids manual string concatenation:

import requests

url = "https://api.example.com/v1/orders"
params = {"status": "active"}

headers = {
    "Authorization": "Bearer eyJhbGciOi...",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
}

payload = {
    "order_id": 12345,
    "items": [{"id": 1, "qty": 2}],
    "notes": "Don't forget sauce",
}

response = requests.post(url, params=params, headers=headers, json=payload)
print(response.status_code, response.json())

Go (net/http)

Go requires more boilerplate, making manual conversion especially tedious:

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "net/http"
)

func main() {
    payload := map[string]any{
        "order_id": 12345,
        "items": []map[string]any{
            {"id": 1, "qty": 2},
        },
        "notes": "Don't forget sauce",
    }
    body, _ := json.Marshal(payload)

    req, _ := http.NewRequest("POST", "https://api.example.com/v1/orders?status=active", bytes.NewBuffer(body))
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer eyJhbGciOi...")
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

    client := &http.Client{}
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
}

Automating the Workflow

Unless you are learning HTTP semantics from scratch, writing this boilerplate manually every day is a waste of engineering time.

Whenever I'm reverse-engineering an API or migrating endpoints, I keep a dedicated web utility open in a pinned tab. If you haven't found a clean one yet, check out this interactive cURL Converter.

A few things that make a converter actually good:

  • Two-way support: Not just cURL → Code, but converting code back to cURL when you need to reproduce a bug on an SSH box or share a minimal reproduction with DevOps.
  • Multiple targets: Handling Fetch, Axios, Python Requests, HTTPX, Go, and PowerShell out of the box.
  • Header filtering: Letting you inspect headers, query params, and auth tokens separately so you don't paste unwanted tracking cookies into your codebase.

Pro-Tips for Working with cURL in Dev & CI/CD

To wrap up, here are 3 quick cURL command tips that make terminal debugging much faster:

  1. Print HTTP status and response time without headers: 
   curl -o /dev/null -s -w 'Status: %{http_code} | Time: %{time_total}s\n' https://api.example.com/health
  1. Follow redirects automatically: Always add -L (or --location) if you suspect an unexpected 301/302 is swallowing your payload.
  2. Fail silently in scripts: Use -fsSL in Docker builds or CI workflows so that non-200 responses trigger a proper exit code instead of continuing silently.

What's your API debugging setup?

Do you prefer copying from browser DevTools, drafting queries in Postman / Bruno / Insomnia, or scripting directly with cURL? Drop your workflow in the comments below!

title: How to Convert PDFs to Markdown for RAG and Chatbots (and When Not To)
description:
Markdown keeps a document's headings, lists and tables in plain text that chunkers and LLMs handle well, so it's a sensible format to put between a PDF and your vector store. PDFs with a real text layer convert cleanly. Scanned PDFs need OCR first. Tables, multi-column layouts and repeated headers are where conversions usually go wrong, so check the output before you embed it.

Disclosure: this post is published by Appie.run. One of the conversion routes below is Appie's free converter and one section mentions Appie's chatbot product. The open-source routes work just as well, and for batch jobs they're the better choice.

Why Markdown before embedding

Three practical reasons:

  • Headings give you chunk boundaries. A ## Refunds heading is a natural place to split. Plain text extracted from a PDF loses that signal, and you end up splitting every N characters, often mid-sentence or mid-table.
  • Cleaner, smaller context. Markdown carries structure with very little markup. You avoid sending the model layout noise such as page furniture, odd line breaks and font artefacts.
  • Citations. If you keep the heading and page number with each chunk, your bot or RAG app can say where an answer came from. That matters for policies, contracts and manuals, where people will want to check the source.

Markdown isn't magic, though. If the PDF has no text layer or the converter scrambles the reading order, the Markdown will be just as wrong as the plain text would have been.

Step 1: check what kind of PDF you have

Before choosing a tool, find out whether the PDF has a text layer.

The manual check: open it in any PDF viewer and try to select a sentence. If the text highlights word by word, there's a text layer. If you can only draw a box around the whole page, it's an image, which usually means a scan or a photo.

The scripted check (for a folder of files) uses PyMuPDF. Since PyMuPDF 2.x the Markdown helpers that used to live in the separate pymupdf4llm package ship inside pymupdf itself (per the pymupdf4llm repo, which is now an empty compatibility package).

# pip install --upgrade pymupdf
import pymupdf

doc = pymupdf.open("policy.pdf")
for number, page in enumerate(doc, start=1):
    chars = len(page.get_text().strip())
    flag = "OK" if chars > 50 else "NO TEXT LAYER? needs OCR"
    print(f"page {number}: {chars} characters  {flag}")

The 50-character threshold is arbitrary. A page that is mostly a diagram will also come back low, so treat the result as a prompt to look, not a verdict. We ran this against a small test PDF with PyMuPDF 2.0; adapt it for your setup.

Step 2: convert

Pick the route that matches the job.

Route A: a free web converter for one-off files

If you have one policy document or one manual and want Markdown in a minute, a web converter is the fastest path. Appie's free Convert PDF to Markdown tool (ours) extracts each page to Markdown, and you copy or download the result. Its limits, as stated on the tool page on 22 Oct 2026:

  • PDFs with real text only. A photo scan needs OCR first.
  • The first 30 pages are included.
  • You complete a Cloudflare Turnstile captcha before it runs.

For anything longer than 30 pages or for a recurring job, use a library.

Route B: a Python library for batches

Four open-source options are worth a look. Descriptions below are taken from each project's own README, read on 22 Oct 2026; test them on your own documents, because results vary by layout.

  • PyMuPDF: its README lists "native Markdown output for RAG and AI pipelines" via doc.to_markdown(). Lightweight and quick to install.
  • Marker: converts PDF, images, PPTX, DOCX, XLSX, HTML and EPUB to Markdown, JSON and chunks. The README says it formats tables, equations and code blocks, removes headers and footers, and can optionally call an LLM to improve accuracy. Runs on GPU, CPU or MPS.
  • Docling: parses many formats with "advanced PDF understanding" including page layout, reading order and table structure, and exports Markdown, HTML and lossless JSON.
  • MarkItDown (Microsoft): a lightweight utility for converting PDF, Office files, HTML and more to Markdown for LLM pipelines. Its README is candid that output is meant for text analysis tools, not high-fidelity human-readable conversion. It also warns that it performs I/O with the privileges of the current process, so sanitise inputs in untrusted environments.

A minimal batch script with PyMuPDF:

import pathlib
import pymupdf

src = pathlib.Path("pdfs")
out = pathlib.Path("markdown")
out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

for pdf in src.glob("*.pdf"):
    md = pymupdf.open(pdf).to_markdown()
    (out / f"{pdf.stem}.md").write_text(md, encoding="utf-8")
    print("converted", pdf.name)

Tested with PyMuPDF 2.0 on a two-page sample; adapt for your setup.

Route C: OCR first for scans

If Step 1 flagged pages without a text layer, you need OCR before (or as part of) conversion. Marker and Docling both list scanned-document handling in their READMEs, and MarkItDown lists OCR for images. Another approach is to run an OCR tool that adds a text layer to the PDF, then use Route A or B. Whatever you pick, OCR output needs a closer review than a born-digital PDF: check numbers, names and anything in a table.

Step 3: clean up

Run through this checklist on a sample of the output before converting hundreds of files:

  1. Headers and footers. Company name, document title and "Page 4 of 37" repeated on every page will pollute every chunk. Strip them with a regex or your converter's option.
  2. Tables. Open a few tables in a Markdown preview. Merged cells and tables that span two pages are common failure points. If a table is critical (a price list, a spec sheet), consider fixing it by hand or storing it as CSV alongside the Markdown.
  3. Reading order in multi-column layouts. Read a two-column page top to bottom. If paragraphs from the left and right columns interleave, try a layout-aware converter.
  4. Hyphenation. Words split across lines ("con-\nversion") hurt search. Rejoin them.
  5. Page markers. Keep a page reference somewhere (a comment such as <!-- page 12 --> or chunk metadata) so you can cite it later.
  6. Images and charts. Most converters drop them or emit a placeholder. If a chart holds the answer to likely questions, describe it in text.

Step 4: chunk by heading and keep page numbers

Chunk on headings first, then split long sections by size. Keep the heading and page number as metadata on every chunk. Here's a small example using PyMuPDF's per-page output:

import re
import pymupdf

pages = pymupdf.open("policy.pdf").to_markdown(page_chunks=True)  # one dict per page

chunks = []
for page in pages:
    page_no = page["metadata"]["page_number"]
    # split before each H1 to H3 heading, keeping the heading with its text
    for section in re.split(r"\n(?=#{1,3} )", page["text"]):
        section = section.strip()
        if section:
            heading = section.splitlines()[0].lstrip("# ").strip()
            chunks.append({"text": section, "heading": heading, "page": page_no})

This splits per page, so a section that runs across a page break becomes two chunks. That's usually fine for retrieval, and the page numbers stay accurate. If you'd rather keep sections whole, convert the full document, split on headings, and record page numbers from the page markers you added in Step 3. Tested on a two-page sample with PyMuPDF 2.0; adapt for your setup.

A few rules of thumb (general guidance, not benchmarks):

  • Prepend the heading path to each chunk's text ("Refund policy > EU orders") so the embedding knows the context.
  • Keep tables whole inside one chunk where you can.
  • Store the source file name with the page number, so answers can link back.

Skip the pipeline: upload the PDF straight to a hosted chatbot

If your goal is a support bot or an internal Q&A assistant, rather than a custom RAG system, you may not need any of the above. Many hosted chatbot builders accept PDFs directly and handle extraction and chunking for you; check whether the one you use does.

Appie AI Chatbots (ours) accepts PDFs, DOCX, CSV and text, plus URLs, sitemaps and product feeds, as knowledge sources (appie.run/ai-chatbots). Creating a bot is free, and each conversation with the bot costs 1 credit (pricing, as of 22 Oct 2026). The Free plan includes 500 credits and needs no credit card. It's a hosted bot, so you don't control the chunking; if you need that control, build the pipeline above.

To test whether a PDF answers questions well before building anything, try Appie's free AI Chat With Your PDF tool. You upload a text-based PDF and ask for a summary or a specific fact; per the tool page, answers must come from the PDF, and if the fact isn't there it says so. If it can't find answers you know are in the document, the PDF probably has a text-layer or layout problem to fix first.

For hosted options, see best AI chatbots trained on your own website data.

FAQ

How do I convert a PDF to Markdown for free?

For a single text-based PDF, use a free web converter such as Appie's Convert PDF to Markdown (first 30 pages, text PDFs only). For batches, use an open-source library such as PyMuPDF (doc.to_markdown()), Marker, Docling or MarkItDown.

Can I convert a scanned PDF to Markdown?

Only after OCR. A scan is an image of text, so a converter has nothing to extract until OCR adds a text layer. Some libraries, such as Marker and Docling, include OCR; review OCR output carefully.

Is Markdown better than plain text for RAG?

Usually, because headings, lists and tables survive, which gives you better chunk boundaries and lets you keep section context for citations. It won't fix a bad extraction, so check the output either way.

How should I chunk Markdown from a PDF?

Split on headings first, then split long sections by size. Keep the heading path, source file and page number as metadata on each chunk, and keep tables whole where you can.

Convert a text PDF to Markdown free (first 30 pages): appie.run/tools/convert-pdf-to-markdown. Or upload the PDF straight into an Appie chatbot; the Free plan has 500 credits and needs no credit card. More free tools: appie.run/tools.

title: Musk showed Europe the kill switch. 74% of its top sites have one
description:
Originally published at tensorust.com.

Short answer: Yes, Europe's internet has a US off switch, and it is not Starlink. I scanned the 100 most-visited sites of every EU country plus the UK (2,789 sites) on Oct 24, 2026: 73.9% rely on an American company for their web hosting, their email or their DNS, and 35.5% rely on one for all three. Cloudflare and Microsoft alone touch more than half of them. You can check your own domain in about 60 seconds with the three commands further down.

TL;DR: Elon Musk's reported order to throttle Starshield for Ukraine made "the US kill switch" a real thing in European capitals this month. So I measured it. Of 2,480 top European sites with all three layers visible, 1,833 use a US company somewhere and 881 are American all the way down. Microsoft or Google runs the email of 49.7% of them. Government domains split hard: 94% of 627 UK government domains lean on a US company, against 19% of 163 French ones. And on AI, Europe's top sites carry 237 Anthropic and 159 OpenAI domain verifications, but only 8 for France's Mistral. Every row is in the CSV.

Key numbers

What Number Source, checked Oct 24 2026
Top European sites scanned (top 100 per EU27 country domain + .uk) 2,789 Tranco list 262N9 + our DNS scan
Use a US company for web, mail or DNS 73.9% (1,833 of 2,480) Our scan
US company for all three layers 35.5% (881 of 2,480) Our scan
Web served from a US company's network 56.3% (Cloudflare alone 29.0%) Our scan + iptoasn
Email (MX) run by Microsoft or Google 49.7% (724 Microsoft, 525 Google) Our scan
DNS run by a US company 53.0% (Cloudflare alone 726 sites) Our scan
UK government domains on a US company (any layer) 94.0% of 627 Our scan, .gov.uk domains in the Tranco 1M
French government domains on a US company 18.8% of 163 Our scan, .gouv.fr domains
Government front doors (29) with a US layer 18 of 29 Our scan
AI vendor domain verifications on top sites Anthropic 237, OpenAI 159, Cursor 26, Mistral 8 Our TXT-record scan

Download the data (CSV, 4,265 rows: every domain with its country, Tranco rank, web host network, mail provider, DNS provider, US or not for each layer, and which AI vendors it verified with).


Three in four of Europe's top sites have an American layer. Our public-DNS scan of the Tranco top 100 per EU27 country domain plus .uk, Oct 24 2026. Rendered with our game engine.

The switch got flipped, and Europe noticed

On Oct 14, Ukrainian units found their Starshield links, the military version of Starlink, capped. The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk personally ordered the restriction, citing US officials; the New York Times covered the fallout. Musk had first pointed at the US government, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio says there was "no foreknowledge". Who gave the order is still argued. What it did is not.

This morning Steve Blank, the Stanford adjunct professor behind the customer-development method half of Silicon Valley learned from, posted "Elon Musk Just Gave Europe a Reason to Replace American Technology". It raced up Hacker News, 254 points and 249 comments in under two hours. He has spent the month in London and quotes the question policymakers keep asking him:

"What happens if other U.S. CEOs, Microsoft, OpenAI or Anthropic, Oracle, Palantir, or Google, decide to restrict/limit or deny access to their products? What capabilities would Europe lose if enterprise software and/or AI across Europe goes dark?" (Steve Blank, Oct 24 2026)

That is a question with an answer you can measure. Not the military part. The everyday part: which European websites, inboxes and domain names stop working if a handful of American companies are told to, or decide to, switch them off. So I measured it.

How I checked: 4,265 domains, three layers, public DNS only

Every site needs three things to be reachable. A web host (the network that answers when you load the page), mail servers (the MX record: who receives the domain's email) and DNS (the nameservers that tell the internet where everything lives). If any one of them is cut, something breaks. If DNS is cut, everything breaks.

  • Top sites: the first 100 domains of each EU27 country code (.de, .fr, .it ... ) plus .uk in the Tranco top-1M research ranking (list 262N9, built by Victor Le Pochat and colleagues at KU Leuven to resist manipulation). 2,789 domains; Malta, Cyprus and Luxembourg have slightly fewer than 100 in the list.
  • Government: every domain in the same 1M list under an official government suffix (.gov.uk, .gouv.fr, .bund.de, .gov.pl, .gob.es, .gv.at, .gov.it, .europa.eu and so on): 1,446 domains. Plus each country's central government "front door" (gov.uk, info.gouv.fr, bundesregierung.de ...), 29 in all.
  • The scan: A, CNAME, MX, NS and TXT lookups through public resolvers, then each IP matched to the network that owns it with the free iptoasn table. Mail and DNS providers were matched by hostname first (outlook.com is Microsoft, awsdns is Amazon), network second. 48 seconds for the main pass, about 11 AM ET today.
  • "US company" means US-headquartered: Cloudflare, Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Akamai, Fastly, Proofpoint, Cisco and the like, even when the server sits in Frankfurt. That is the point: a US company answers to US law, including the CLOUD Act, wherever its servers are. I counted Imperva (owned by France's Thales) and Mimecast (UK) as not US, which makes the US numbers smaller, not bigger.

Want to see if you are in the 74%? Skip to check your own domain.

Three in four of Europe's top sites have an American layer

Of the 2,480 top sites where all three layers answered, 1,833 (73.9%) use a US company for at least one. 881 (35.5%) use US companies for all three: page, inbox and the DNS that would let them move. Only 26.1% are fully European or self-run.

The obvious objection: the list includes google.de, amazon.fr and youtu.be, which are American companies' own European domains. Fair. I dropped 81 of those brand domains and reran it. The answer moved from 73.9% to 73.3%. This is not Google's sites being American. This is Europe's sites.

The layer that matters most is the one people never think about. If your web host disappears, you repoint DNS to another host and you are back in hours. If your DNS provider and your web host are the same US company, you can't repoint anything, because the switch that would move you is the one that got flipped.

Cloudflare, not Musk, is Europe's biggest switch


Cloudflare and Microsoft hold the biggest switches. Our scan, Oct 24 2026.

Starlink got the headlines. Cloudflare has the reach. It serves the web traffic of 786 of Europe's top sites (29.0% of those with a web host) and runs the DNS of 726. Microsoft runs the inbox of 724. Google runs the inbox of 525. Amazon hosts 259 and does DNS for 333. Add Akamai and Fastly and six US companies hold the big switches for most of the continent's attention.

To be clear, none of these companies has threatened anything, and Cloudflare in particular has publicly pushed back on takedown demands before. My point is narrower and, I think, harder to dodge: the risk Europe just discovered is structural, not personal. Starshield was one company and one man. The web is four or five companies and a legal system. A court order, a sanctions list or a bad Tuesday at one of them reaches more Europeans than a satellite cap ever could. If you want the outage version of that, our Cloudflare status page tracks it.

It has happened before, at small scale. In May 2025, the AP reported that the International Criminal Court's chief prosecutor lost his Microsoft email after US sanctions and moved to Swiss Proton Mail. Microsoft said it never stopped serving the court itself, only the sanctioned official. Both things can be true. That is exactly how a targeted switch works.

The country ranking: Ireland and Malta are all-in, Czechia barely


Malta and Ireland are all-in, Czechia barely. Our scan, Oct 24 2026; percentages of sites where all three layers answered.

Malta (97%), Ireland (96%) and the UK (94%) top the chart: almost every big site there has an American layer. Italy (91%), Spain (89%) and the Netherlands (86%) follow. Germany, the country that talks most about digital sovereignty, lands at 67%, mid-table.

The bottom is the interesting part. Czechia (42%), Austria (55%), Poland (56%) and Slovenia (58%) have the most self-reliant big sites in the EU. Czechia has a reason: it never let Google win. Seznam, the Czech search and email company, still runs a real chunk of the Czech web, and big Czech sites sit on local hosts like VSHosting and the academic network CESNET. It is the one country in the EU where "use the local one" is already the default.

My read: dependency tracks how early a country's internet went English-first. Ireland hosts the European headquarters of half of Big Tech; of course its top sites run on them. The countries with their own search engines, mail providers and hosting scenes (Czechia, Poland) are the ones a US switch would hurt least.

Governments: the UK outsourced the state, France did its homework


The UK runs its public web on US clouds; France and Austria mostly do not. Government-suffix domains in the Tranco 1M, our scan, Oct 24 2026.

Government domains are where this stops being an IT question. Across EU government domains in the list (819), 47.7% touch a US company. Across UK ones (627), 94.0% do. That is not a typo. The UK runs most of its public web on Amazon (151 domains), Cloudflare (131), Microsoft (72) and Fastly (66), and 72.5% of UK government domains that receive mail route it to a US company, 331 of them straight to Microsoft.

France is the opposite. Only 18.8% of 163 .gouv.fr domains have a US layer and just 2.3% of their mail goes to a US provider. Most French ministries receive mail through the state's own interministerial network (RIE) or French providers. Austria is even tighter at 7.9%. Spain is the odd one: its government web and mail are mostly its own, but the shared government nameservers (ns1.age.gob.es and ns2.age.gob.es) answer from Cloudflare's network, so 89.9% of Spanish government domains have American DNS.

That Spanish detail is the whole argument in one record. Spain kept the house and rented the front door.

29 front doors: 18 have an American hinge


18 of 29 front doors have an American hinge. Our scan, Oct 24 2026.

The main government portal of each country (and europa.eu) is the page citizens hit first. 18 of 29 rely on a US company for at least one layer. Malta's gov.mt is American three times over: Cloudflare in front, Microsoft for mail, Microsoft for DNS. Italy's governo.it serves through Akamai and takes mail through Microsoft. Even France's front door, info.gouv.fr, is served through Cloudflare, while its mail and DNS stay French.

Eleven are fully home-grown on all the layers they publish: Germany, Austria, Finland, Hungary, Latvia, Luxembourg, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia and Croatia. The European Commission's europa.eu hosts itself, but receives its mail through Proofpoint, a US company. Make of that what you want.

The AI layer: Mistral is losing at home, 8 to 396


US AI labs 396, Mistral 8. Verification records are a lower bound. Our TXT scan, Oct 24 2026.

Blank's list of feared switches included OpenAI and Anthropic, so I checked that too. When a company buys a team or enterprise plan from an AI lab, it usually proves it owns its domain by publishing a TXT record like openai-domain-verification=.... Those records are public. Across Europe's 2,789 top sites I found 237 Anthropic verifications, 159 OpenAI, 26 Cursor, 8 Perplexity and 8 Mistral. 332 different top sites verified with at least one of the two big US labs; 64 verified with both.

Mistral is France's AI champion, the company French ministers hold up as proof Europe can compete. Among Europe's most-visited domains it has 8 verified customers, and 5 of them are universities. If an American switch for AI exists, Europe has already plugged into it, and it chose Anthropic first. This is a lower bound (plenty of teams use these tools with no record at all), but the ratio is the story: 396 to 8. If you want to see what an open or European model would cost you instead, our price check of 215 models has the open-weights numbers.

Microsoft 365 shows up the same way: 1,069 top sites and 565 government domains carry a Microsoft 365 tenant record (MS=ms...). That is the "enterprise software across Europe goes dark" scenario in Blank's quote, sitting in public DNS.

Check your own domain in 60 seconds

You don't need my scan. Three lookups tell you who holds your switches. Replace example.eu with your domain:

dig +short NS example.eu
dig +short MX example.eu
dig +short www.example.eu
whois -h whois.cymru.com " -v 203.0.113.10"

The first line names your DNS provider (awsdns = Amazon, cloudflare.com = Cloudflare, azure-dns = Microsoft). The second names your mail provider (outlook.com = Microsoft, google.com = Google, pphosted.com = Proofpoint). Put the IP from the third line into the fourth to see which company owns the network serving your site. On Windows, nslookup -type=NS example.eu does the same job. Or just search your domain in our CSV: if it is a top European site, it is already in there.

What to do if you are in the 35% with no exit

This is my opinion, not a compliance checklist. Moving everything to Europe tomorrow is expensive and mostly theatre. Having an exit is cheap:

  1. Split DNS from hosting. If one company runs both, add a secondary DNS provider in another jurisdiction (deSEC, a Berlin nonprofit; Gandi or OVHcloud in France; Hetzner in Germany). A second nameserver is the cheapest kill-switch insurance on the internet.
  2. Write down your mail exit. Know which provider you would move MX to, export a mailbox once to prove you can, and keep MX TTLs short.
  3. Keep one copy of the site somewhere boring. A static build on a European host (Hetzner, OVHcloud, Scaleway, IONOS) or a European CDN like Slovenia's Bunny.net that you can point DNS at in an hour.
  4. Know your AI fallback. If your product calls one US model, test it once against an open-weights model you could host yourself.

Steve Blank's bet is that AI makes cloning Office, Oracle and Salesforce cheap enough for Europe to finally do it. Maybe. My bet is less romantic: Europe doesn't need to clone Microsoft. It needs a second nameserver. Dependency is fine. Dependency with no exit is the kill switch.

What I think happens next

Some of this is speculation, so take it as that. I think the Starshield episode does for European IT what the Snowden files did for encryption: years of slow talk turn into budget lines. Denmark's digital ministry started moving to LibreOffice in 2025, and the German state of Schleswig-Holstein says almost 80% of its workstations already switched. Expect copycats in every ministry that just watched a drone feed go dark.

What I don't think happens: the UK moving. 94% is not a vendor choice, it is an operating model, and Whitehall has run a "cloud first" policy since 2013 that pushed departments onto public cloud by design.

My bet, in public: I rerun this exact scan on Oct 24, 2027. EU government domains with a US layer drop below 40% (from 47.7% today). The UK stays above 90%. Europe's top sites overall barely move, because private companies buy whatever works.

Your turn: would your company survive 24 hours if Microsoft and Cloudflare turned you off? Tell me what breaks first in the comments.

Caveats

  • This is DNS, not contracts. A US CDN in front of a site does not mean the data is stored in the US, and a US company running a layer does not mean it would ever cut it.
  • I classified the first web IP, the primary MX and the nameserver set. Sites with several providers (say, a European primary MX and a US backup) are counted by the primary.
  • Top 100 per country domain misses European companies on .com and .eu. Government suffix lists are uneven (the UK puts far more agencies under .gov.uk than Germany puts under .bund.de), so compare governments by percentage, not counts, and only where there are 20+ domains.
  • Akamai's main European network is registered in the Netherlands; I counted it as US because Akamai is a US company. Imperva and Mimecast count as non-US.
  • AI verification records are a floor. Many teams use these tools without one, and some records are left over from old trials.
  • Not legal or security advice.

The numbers so far

Item Now (Oct 24 2026) Rerun
Top European sites with a US layer 73.9% Oct 24 2027
Top sites US on all three layers 35.5% Oct 24 2027
EU government domains with a US layer 47.7% Oct 2027 (bet: below 40%)
UK government domains with a US layer 94.0% Oct 2027 (bet: above 90%)
Mistral vs OpenAI + Anthropic verifications 8 vs 396 Oct 2027

More from the same beat: the open-source dependency audit we ran this morning (1 in 4 top npm installs sits on a known hole), the open vs closed AI price check, and every policy and AI-deal story on the AI industry hub.

Find the holes before someone else does

Knowing who can switch you off is half of it. The other half is what a stranger can already reach. If you built your app with Lovable, Bolt, Cursor, Replit or Supabase, the $49 Launch Check tells you whether a stranger can read your tables, find exposed keys or open your storage buckets. Plain-English report in 48 hours. You get the holes found and the fix for each. If we missed something we checked, we write the fix at no extra cost until it is closed. Email support@tensorust.com; a real person replies within one business day. Prefer free first? Run the free landing page teardown.

Follow for one checked, data-backed answer to the fights everyone is having, every day.

Sources

  • The Wall Street Journal, reporting that Musk ordered the Starshield restrictions, Oct 2026; The New York Times, Starshield and Ukraine, Oct 21 2026
  • Tranco (Le Pochat et al., KU Leuven), top-1M list 262N9, downloaded Oct 24 2026
  • iptoasn.com IP-to-ASN table (ip2asn-v4), downloaded Oct 24 2026
  • US Department of Justice, CLOUD Act resources
  • AP via The Boston Globe, Trump's sanctions on ICC prosecutor have halted tribunal's work, May 15 2025; heise online, Microsoft denies mail blockade at the International Criminal Court
  • Computing, Denmark's Digital Ministry shifts from Microsoft to LibreOffice, 2025; Land Schleswig-Holstein, digital sovereignty update, Dec 2025

title: React JS – Complete Beginner Guide
description:
React is a JavaScript library used to build interactive user interfaces, especially for websites and web applications.

React helps you build websites using reusable pieces called components.

1. Install React
The easiest way to start a new React project is with Vite.
Open your terminal and run:

npm create vite@latest my-react-app
cd my-react-app
npm install
npm run dev

Choose React → JavaScript when prompted. Then open the local URL displayed in your terminal, usually http://localhost:5173/.

2.Your first React component
Create or replace the code in src/App.jsx:

function App() {
    return (
        <div>
            <h1>Hello, Sajin Joe!</h1>
            <p>Welcome to React.</p>
        </div>
    );
}

export default App;

Explanation:

  • function App() creates a component.
  • return describes what appears on the screen.
  • JSX lets you write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript.
  • export default App allows another file to import the component.

React component names normally start with a capital letter.

title: AI Can Find a Bug. But Can You Trust Its Fix?
description:
AI coding tools are getting better every day. They can write functions, generate tests, review pull requests, and even suggest fixes in seconds.

But there’s a problem I keep thinking about:

What if the AI identifies a real bug but gives you a fix that introduces another one?

Imagine this scenario:

  • An AI reviewer flags a security vulnerability.
  • It suggests a patch that looks convincing.
  • The developer applies it.
  • The code appears fine, but the fix is incomplete—or the tests have been changed to accommodate the bug.

Now what?

A green test suite doesn't automatically mean the bug is fixed. A confident explanation doesn't prove the patch is correct. And a suggested fix that looks good in a code diff still needs independent verification.

The problem I'm exploring

While building CodeGuard AI, I've been exploring how to evaluate AI code reviews beyond simply counting the number of issues they detect.

Some questions I'm trying to answer:

  • Can an AI reviewer distinguish real bugs from false positives?
  • Can it identify incorrect test expectations?
  • Does its suggested patch actually address the original problem?
  • Can we verify a fix without letting the patch generator simply change the goalposts?

I'm particularly interested in the gap between finding a problem and proving that the proposed solution works.

That's where I think developer tools have a lot of room to improve.

I'd love to hear from other developers

If you use AI coding assistants or AI-powered code reviewers, I'm curious about your experience:

  1. Have you ever accepted an AI-generated fix that later caused another bug?
  2. Do you trust AI-generated patches, or do you always verify them independently?
  3. What would convince you that an AI code review is reliable enough to use in a real project?

I'm building in this space, so honest criticism and real-world examples would be especially valuable.

What's the biggest thing stopping you from fully trusting AI-generated code?

discuss #ai #programming #webdev

title: I Read a 179KB Inline Chat Bundle on an AI Companion App: 4 API Bugs the UI Hid
description:
When we test AI companion apps at The Companion Lab, we normally treat them as black boxes: we send the same six standardized prompts, pay with our own bank card, record the exact credit card descriptor, and walk the cancellation screens.

Last week, the CTO of EroLove reached out and granted our test account a month of Premium so we could run our benchmark (full EroLove review and disclosure here). While inspecting the chat page in DevTools, I noticed something unusual: instead of a chunked Webpack or Vite build, the entire chat client ships as a single 179 KB inline JavaScript bundle inside the HTML document, talking to an undocumented JSON API.

Reading that 179 KB bundle—and probing the endpoints it calls—turned up four architectural bugs that a normal UI walkthrough would either misdiagnose or miss completely. Here is what the client code and network responses revealed, and why each failure mode matters if you are building an LLM-backed web application.

1. Feature Flags vs. Static SEO Copy: 30 Pages Promising an Endpoint That Returns 404

If you read EroLove's marketing pages, category landings, or even its /privacy policy, they repeatedly state that users can upload and send their own photos into the chat. Yet inside the chat UI, there is no attachment or upload button anywhere.

Looking at the 179 KB inline script explains why:

// Simplified from the inline client bundle
if (feat("userPhotos")) {
  renderUploadButton();
}

The client gates the upload button on a runtime feature flag fetched from GET /api/config. When we inspected the live response from /api/config on October 23, 2026, the enabled array was:

{
  "features": ["chatPhotos", "presence", "voice"]
}

"userPhotos" is omitted, so the UI cleanly hides the button. Meanwhile, the client bundle still contains the complete upload implementation: fileToJpegDataUrl(), sendPhoto(), the [userphoto] message parser, and all its error handlers.

To see whether the backend route was merely hidden or actually disabled, we sent a signed-in request directly to the endpoint named in sendPhoto():

POST /api/chat/upload HTTP/2
Host: erolove.ai

The server responded immediately:

HTTP 404 Not Found
{"error": "not_found"}

Why this matters

Shipping dark code behind a feature flag is normal. The bug is letting 30 static pages—including the privacy policy and machine-readable .md twins—describe data handling for a feature whose backend route returns 404. When your static SEO/GEO layer and your runtime /api/config flags have no shared source of truth, your documentation lies about your API surface.

2. Unconstrained Language Extraction in an LLM Memory Pipeline

The standout feature in EroLove—and the reason it scored well on conversation in our full API teardown and memory test—is its transparent memory panel. Unlike most companion apps that hide long-term memory in an opaque vector store, EroLove exposes GET /api/memory?companion=..., allowing users to read, edit, pin, delete, or export every extracted fact as HTML.

We tested memory extraction across three companions in an all-English session. Our account's default_language was "en", every companion metadata object had language: "en", and every prompt we sent was in English.

Then we inspected the extracted facts array returned by the memory API:

  • Companion 1 (Anna, persona set in Tallinn, Estonia): Every English fact we planted (a cat named Miso, a shellfish allergy, rent stress) was extracted and stored in Estonian.
  • Companion 2 (Rae): Extracted facts came back in French.
  • Companion 3 (Yuna): Returned facts: []—nothing extracted at all.

When we manually edited one of Anna's Estonian memory strings into English via the memory API, the next chat turn immediately reflected our edit. That isolated the bug: memory injection and editing work, but the background memory-extraction prompt does not pin the output language to the session's default_language. Instead, the extractor LLM appears to infer the output language from the character's biographical flavor text (e.g., "Tallinn" triggering Estonian) or drifts into another language entirely.

Takeaway for LLM engineers

If you run an asynchronous fact-extraction pass over chat history to populate a user-visible memory store, explicitly constrain the output language in the extraction system prompt and schema (e.g., "Write every fact in the user's session language: en"). Never assume an LLM will output English summaries just because the user's messages are in English—especially when the system prompt contains foreign proper nouns.

3. Collapsing Content-Policy Refusals and Queue Outages Into One UI String

During our image-generation test, we requested 5 photos across our session (10 Sparks per photo). Three succeeded in 16–23 seconds at 768x1024. Two failed.

In the browser UI, both failures displayed the exact same toast:

"Couldn't take a photo right now — try a bit later"

A normal user—or a black-box reviewer—reads that message as a transient server or GPU queue outage and clicks retry.

Look at the actual JSON payload returned by the polling endpoint, however, and you see something completely different:

{
  "status": "blocked",
  "charged": 0
}

And in the client bundle's switch statement, status === "blocked" (a content/moderation filter rejection) and photo_queue / timeout errors are routed to the exact same user-facing error string.

To EroLove's credit, the backend refunded the Sparks on both blocked attempts (charged: 0). But collapsing a deterministic policy refusal ("blocked") into a transient retry message ("try a bit later") trains users to keep hammering the generation queue with the same prompt.

4. Negative Caching on a Poll-Before-Ready Image CDN, Plus an "Unlimited" Cap

Two smaller findings from the same bundle inspection rounded out the audit:

  1. CDN caching 404s on newly generated media: Generated photos are served from /img/photos/{userId}/{photoId}.webp. When the client requests that URL before the worker finishes writing the WebP file, the edge returns 404. On one of our three successful renders, that initial 404 was cached, leaving the image broken until we appended a cache-busting query string. If your client polls or prefetches media URLs, never allow your CDN to cache 404 Not Found responses on deterministic asset paths without Cache-Control: no-store on the error response.
  2. "Unlimited messages" is dailyLimit: 800: While the pricing page advertises "Unlimited messages" on Premium, inspecting the authenticated user object (me.dailyLimit) shows a hard ceiling of 800 messages per day. In a 1-on-1 chat nobody will hit 800 turns, but in EroLove's multi-character rooms—where a single user prompt triggers multiple character replies—the math adds up much faster.

Summary & Reproducible Dataset

Black-box UI testing tells you whether an app feels good; reading the client bundle tells you why it broke.

We published our full October 2026 findings—covering all 10 tested AI companion apps, $136.89 in real card charges, 7 captured bank statement descriptors, and our 60-prompt benchmark—as an open CC BY 4.0 dataset:

  • AI Girlfriend & Companion App Statistics & Benchmarks (Oct 2026) — full numbers on pricing traps, token meters, memory recall, and billing descriptors.
  • EroLove Teardown: Best Memory Here, and Two Photos That Failed — full write-up with reproduced API payloads.
  • Is EroLove Safe & Legit? Billing & Privacy Audit — compliance check and operator verification.
  • All 10 Ranked AI Companion Reviews & Raw CSV/JSON Dataset on GitHub.

title: How I Built a Weekly Comfortable Region Ranking Using Weather Data
description:
How I Built a Weekly Comfortable Region Ranking Using Weather Data
I have been working on a personal project called weather2, a weather analysis platform that automatically collects weather data and generates multilingual reports.

Recently, I published a historical dataset called:

Weekly Comfortable Region Ranking Dataset

The idea behind the project is simple:

Which cities around the world have the most comfortable outdoor conditions this week?

Instead of looking only at temperature, I combine several weather indicators to calculate a custom Comfort Score.

Metrics Used
The ranking is based on:

Temperature
Humidity
Discomfort Index (DI)
Heat Index
Wet Bulb Temperature
WBGT (Wet Bulb Globe Temperature)
These indicators help estimate how comfortable or stressful outdoor conditions may feel.

Data Collection
Weather data is collected automatically and processed through SQL-based workflows.

The project currently generates:

Multilingual weather reports
Historical weather reports
Weekly Heat Stress Index
Weekly Comfortable Region Ranking
Historical CSV datasets
Dataset
I recently published the complete historical dataset as a CSV file.

Dataset page:

https://yahikoyama.github.io/weather2/comfortable_region_dataset.html

CSV download:

https://yahikoyama.github.io/weather2/CSV/all_weekly_comfortable_region.csv

Example Fields
The dataset contains:

Ranking
FromDate
ToDate
City
Country
Average Temperature
Average Humidity
Heat Index
Wet Bulb Temperature
WBGT
Discomfort Index
Comfort Score
Why I Built It
Many weather sites focus on raw temperature values.

I wanted a way to compare locations using multiple comfort-related indicators and produce an easy-to-understand ranking.

The goal is not to determine the "best" city, but to create a reproducible dataset that allows comparison between locations and climate conditions.
