title: React: estados de email accesibles y medibles
description:
Un formulario de registro puede parecer terminado cuando el usuario pulsa “Enviar”. En realidad, ahí empieza una parte delicada del producto: explicar si el correo se está enviando, si ya llegó, si caducó el enlace o si la persona debe intentarlo otra vez.

En interfaces React es común resolverlo con un isLoading y un mensaje verde para éxito. Funciona en una demo, pero se queda corto en producción. Un estado de email debe ser entendible sin color, anunciar sus cambios a un lector de pantalla y dejar una señal que el equipo pueda medir. La accesibilidad no es una capa final, es parte del contrato de la interfaz.

El problema no es enviar el email, sino explicar su estado

La entrega de un mensaje tiene varios relojes: el navegador, la API, el proveedor de correo y la acción del usuario. Si la interfaz mezcla todos esos momentos, aparecen preguntas muy humanas: “¿debo hacer clic otra vez?”, “¿se perdió mi cuenta?” o “¿por que el botón sigue desactivado?”.

Un buen diseño separa al menos estas situaciones:

  • idle: todavía no se ha solicitado el mensaje.
  • sending: la aplicación recibió la acción y espera una respuesta.
  • sent: el backend aceptó la solicitud, pero eso no garantiza que el usuario ya lo leyó.
  • verified: el enlace fue confirmado correctamente.
  • expired: el enlace ya no es válido y se necesita uno nuevo.
  • error: la aplicación no pudo completar o confirmar la operación.

Esta diferencia evita prometer “email entregado” cuando solo conocemos “solicitud aceptada”. También hace mas fácil diseñar copias, pruebas y métricas por separado.

Un modelo de estados pequeño y observable

En lugar de varios booleanos que pueden contradecirse, un estado discriminado mantiene una sola verdad visible:

type EmailState =
  | { kind: "idle" }
  | { kind: "sending" }
  | { kind: "sent"; expiresAt: string }
  | { kind: "verified" }
  | { kind: "expired" }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string };

El componente puede derivar de kind el texto, el botón y el foco. El dato expiresAt permite mostrar una fecha o un contador sin fingir que el mensaje seguirá siendo válido para siempre. Si el backend devuelve un identificador de intento, guardarlo como dato técnico ayuda a investigar reintentos duplicados.

Para flujos que necesitan contexto adicional, conviene estudiar patrones como las aprobaciones por email con contexto mínimo. La idea útil aquí no es copiar el caso, sino mantener cada transición explicable.

React y CSS para comunicar sin depender del color

Un mensaje de éxito verde y un error rojo pueden ser una señal visual secundaria, nunca la única. El texto debe decir qué pasó y cuál es el siguiente paso. Por ejemplo, “Enlace enviado. Revisa tu bandeja y solicita otro en 45 segundos” es mucho mas accionable que “Listo”.

Para anunciar cambios dinámicos, un contenedor estable puede usar role="status" para mensajes informativos y role="alert" para errores que requieren atención inmediata. No conviene montar y desmontar varios anuncios a la vez: los lectores de pantalla pueden leerlos en un orden confuso.

function EmailNotice({ state }: { state: EmailState }) {
  const urgent = state.kind === "error" || state.kind === "expired";
  const text = copyFor(state);

  return (
    <p
      className={`email-notice email-notice--${state.kind}`}
      role={urgent ? "alert" : "status"}
      aria-live={urgent ? "assertive" : "polite"}
    >
      {text}
    </p>
  );
}

En CSS, el estado debe conservar contraste, foco visible y una estructura legible con zoom. Un icono de reloj puede acompañar a sending, pero el texto “Enviando…” sigue siendo necesario. Tambien es útil reservar una altura mínima para el aviso: así el formulario no salta cada vez que cambia el mensaje, algo pequeño que mejora la percepción de calidad.

Si el correo de prueba se consulta en un buzón aislado, un enlace como validar correos después de un cambio de infraestructura recuerda otra frontera importante: el frontend solo conoce la respuesta del flujo que está observando. Para una prueba manual, un tp mail so puede servir para separar una dirección temporal del buzón personal; no debe usarse para datos sensibles ni confundirse con una confirmación de entrega.

Métricas y pruebas que respetan la accesibilidad

Medir no significa registrar el contenido del mensaje ni la dirección completa. Es suficiente con eventos acotados, por ejemplo:

  • email_verification_requested cuando el usuario inicia la solicitud.
  • email_verification_sent cuando la API acepta el envío.
  • email_verification_resend cuando se pide otro enlace.
  • email_verification_verified cuando el token es válido.
  • email_verification_expired cuando la persona vuelve tarde.

Con esos eventos se puede comparar la tasa de verificación, el tiempo hasta el éxito y la frecuencia de reenvíos. Un aumento de errores después de cambiar CSS no prueba una causa, pero sí indica dónde mirar. El dashboard debe evitar emails crudos; incluso un dato de prueba llamado “dummy e mail” merece el mismo cuidado que cualquier identificador.

Las pruebas frontend deberían cubrir teclado, foco, texto visible y anuncios. Un caso mínimo es: enviar, esperar el estado sent, comprobar que el mensaje aparece una sola vez y verificar que el foco queda en un lugar razonable. Tambien hay que probar expired y error con mensajes largos, porque muchos diseños solo funcionan con una frase corta.

Preguntas frecuentes

¿role="status" reemplaza al texto visible?

No. El rol ayuda a comunicar un cambio a tecnología asistiva, pero el mensaje visible sigue siendo necesario para personas que leen la pantalla sin usar un lector.

¿Conviene usar un contador?

Sí, si explica una restricción real, como el tiempo antes de permitir otro envío. Debe actualizarse sin anunciar cada segundo, por que eso crea ruido. Anuncia el inicio y comunica cuando el botón vuelve a estar disponible.

¿Debo decir “enviado” o “entregado”?

Di solo lo que el sistema puede demostrar. Si la API aceptó la solicitud, “solicitud enviada” o “revisa tu bandeja” es más preciso que “correo entregado”.

Checklist final

  • [ ] Existe un estado explícito para cada resultado relevante.
  • [ ] El texto explica el siguiente paso sin depender del color.
  • [ ] Los avisos dinámicos tienen una estrategia de aria-live.
  • [ ] El foco, el zoom y el teclado funcionan en éxito y error.
  • [ ] Las métricas no guardan el contenido ni la dirección completa.
  • [ ] Se prueban reenvíos, expiración, latencia y mensajes largos.

Un estado de email bien diseñado conecta React, CSS, accesibilidad y observabilidad. El resultado no es solo una pantalla mas bonita: es una interfaz que reduce dudas, evita reenvíos innecesarios y da al equipo señales claras para mejorarla.

title: I got tired of laggy timelines, so I've been using Tempis
description:
Every few months I end up needing a timeline in some app. A scheduling view, a project plan, a feed of events plotted against time. And every few months I rediscover that most timeline components fall apart once you give them real data. Fifty items, fine. A couple thousand? Scroll goes choppy, memory creeps up, and hovering over anything feels like wading through syrup.

The reason is usually the same. These libraries keep a DOM node for every single item. The browser is great at a lot of things, but keeping thousands of absolutely-positioned divs in sync while you pan around is not really one of them.

Tempis takes the other route and draws everything to a canvas. One element, no per-item nodes. So the question of "how many items can I show" stops being about your layout engine and starts being about how much you actually want on screen. It's held up fine for me past 5,000 items, and the whole thing is under 18 KB gzipped with zero dependencies, which I appreciated more than I expected to. Nothing else to audit, nothing else to break.

Here's the smallest thing that does something useful:

import { TempisTimeline } from '@tempis/timeline';

const timeline = new TempisTimeline('#canvas', {
  responsive: true,
  items: [
    { id: 1, label: 'Design',  start: '2026-01-05', end: '2026-01-15', grouping: 'Frontend' },
    { id: 2, label: 'Build',   start: '2026-01-12', end: '2026-01-28', grouping: 'Frontend' },
    { id: 3, label: 'Launch',  start: '2026-01-30', grouping: 'Frontend' },
    { id: 4, label: 'API',     start: '2026-01-08', end: '2026-01-25', grouping: 'Backend' },
  ],
  range: { start: '2026-01-01', end: '2026-02-01', position: 'bottom' }
});

An item with a start and end is a range. An item with just a start is a point in time. When they overlap, they stack themselves, so you're not doing lane-assignment math by hand. The grouping field is what splits those four items into a Frontend row and a Backend row, and you can collapse groups, sort them your own way, and let people click a legend to filter by category. That legend-plus-grouping combo is the thing I reach for most, honestly. It turns a flat wall of bars into something you can actually read.

If you're not on a build step, there's a CDN drop-in:

<script src="https://unpkg.com/@tempis/timeline/dist/tempis_timeline.min.js"></script>
<script>
  new tempis_timeline.TempisTimeline('#canvas', { /* same options */ });
</script>

Past the basics, the stuff that's saved me time: dependencies between items with the connector arrows routed automatically (and it doesn't fall over in RTL layouts), bands for drawing reference markers and lines across the whole thing, per-item styling when you need one bar to stand out, and animated focus() to glide over to a specific item or date instead of teleporting. You can export the current view to a PNG if someone wants a screenshot for a deck. And if you've already standardized on Luxon or Day.js, there's a date adapter so you don't have to fight it over date handling.

The interactivity comes through callbacks, nothing exotic:

new TempisTimeline('#canvas', {
  items,
  onItemClick: (id) => openDetails(id),
  onItemContextClick: (id, pos) => showMenu(id, pos),
  onRangeChange: (start, end) => fetchVisibleData(start, end),
});

That last one is quietly the useful one. onRangeChange fires as the visible window moves, so you can lazy-load and only pull the data that's actually in view instead of shipping everything up front. For a live feed or a big historical dataset that's the difference between snappy and not.

There's a React wrapper too, @tempis/react, if you'd rather not manage the instance lifecycle yourself:

import { TempisTimeline } from '@tempis/react';

function App() {
  return (
    <TempisTimeline
      items={items}
      options={{ responsive: true }}
      onItemClick={(id) => console.log('clicked', id)}
      height={400}
    />
  );
}

items, categories, bands, and dependencies are props that sync on their own. When you need to do something imperative, like focus an item, grab the current range, or export an image, you reach for a ref:

const ref = useRef<TempisTimelineRef>(null);
// ...
ref.current?.focus({ id: 1, animate: true });

It's all TypeScript with real declarations, and the React package re-exports the core types so you're not installing two things just to import TempisTimelineItem.

One bit of honesty before you npm install: Tempis is source-available, not MIT. It's free for personal projects, learning, and evaluation, but commercial use that makes money needs a paid licence. Worth a look at the LICENSE so there are no surprises later.

If you want to poke at it before writing any code, the examples page has live demos, and the getting started docs go deeper than this post does. If you end up building something with it, I'd genuinely like to hear what. The timeline UIs people come up with are always more interesting than the demos.

title: Update: one page got indexed in 2 days, but my core tool pages are still "never crawled" after 11 weeks
description:
A while ago I wrote about why Google ignored my React SPA tool site and what I changed. I said I'd post an update and be straight about it if things didn't improve. So here it is: it worked for one page and did nothing for the two that matter most.

Some context: PinFetcher is an independent Pinterest downloader suite (not affiliated with Pinterest). I bought the domain as an expired one in August 2026, so it isn't a blank slate. A previous owner ran a WordPress site there, and Google still remembers some of those old URLs.

What happened

  • Media Saver, a page I added in October, was indexed within 2 days of my submitting it in URL Inspection.
  • Pinterest Video Downloader and the image downloader, my two core tools, still show Last crawl: N/A in URL Inspection. That means Googlebot has not fetched them even once. I've requested indexing two or three times a month. Every time: "Indexing requested". Nothing changes.

What I verified on the stuck pages

The same checklist as before:

  • The live test says "URL is available to Google".
  • The rendered HTML has the full content (about 1,700 words), a self-referencing canonical, index, follow, and no noindex.
  • Both pages are in the sitemap and linked from the header on every page.

A quick way to check the raw HTML of any page:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://your-site.com/your-page
curl -s https://your-site.com/your-page | grep -oE '<link rel="canonical"[^>]*>|<meta name="robots"[^>]*>'

What Crawl Stats showed

  • Google is visiting: 655 requests since Aug 5, so it isn't blocked.
  • But 88% of them were "Refresh" (re-checking URLs it already knows) and only 12% were "Discovery". Google rarely finds new URLs on a young domain.
  • 38 requests were 404s on paths I never created (/pl, /he, feed URLs). They're leftovers from the previous owner's site, and Google keeps rechecking them.

The Links report gave me a lesson

I had 8 external links from directories and profiles. All 8 point to the homepage. None points to a tool page. I'd built a handful of listings, and every one sent trust to a single URL. If you want a specific page to be found, link to that page.

What I can't explain

I don't know why Media Saver was fast and the older pages weren't. It's newer, I submitted it, and it has a lot of text, but I can't prove any of that was the reason, so I won't pretend I can.

What I'm doing now

  • Adding deep links to the two tool pages in my directory listings, my YouTube channel and this article.
  • No more Request Indexing on those two pages. It hasn't helped.
  • Checking back in a week and posting the result either way.

Takeaways

  1. A clean live test doesn't guarantee a crawl. It only rules out a bug on your side.
  2. Check the Links report: do your external links point at the pages you want found?
  3. Crawl Stats shows how much of Google's visiting is discovery. If it's mostly refresh, new URLs will wait.
  4. If you bought an expired domain, expect old URLs to show up in your logs for months.

If you've been through a "never crawled" phase on specific pages while others got indexed, what finally changed it for you?

title: Why I drew my own icons for a doodle app
description:
I built Zketch for doodling, and doodles don't follow straight lines. Yet every button around its canvas was drawn with a ruler: dead-straight edges, compass-perfect arcs, corners that meet at exact angles. Replacing them took me from a pile of uneven sketches to 143 brush-drawn icons whose small imperfections are the whole point, and then to zicons, a set anyone can use.


Figure 1. A handful of the 143 zicons icons: one pen, one line, a little wobble.

A doodle app with ruler-straight buttons

Zketch is a drawing app that runs in the browser. You open it, pick a brush and scribble. For a long time, the buttons around that scribbling came from Lucide, a popular open-source icon set, plus a few extra SVGs I added in the same style so they'd match. The undo arrow, for example, used the path from Feather, the set Lucide grew out of: a perfect arc with a radius of exactly 9, ending in an arrowhead bent at a right angle. Everything matched, and that was the problem.

There's nothing wrong with Lucide or Feather. They're made for precise, neutral interfaces, and they're very good at that. But Zketch isn't a neutral interface. It exists for loose, wobbly lines. Everything on the canvas said "draw freely," and everything around it said "measure twice." The icons didn't carry the feel of the reason I was making the app. Put side by side with what replaced them, the difference is small but it's everywhere:


Figure 2. Zketch's toolbar tools in Lucide (top) and zicons (bottom), shown larger than in the app: the same tools, with softer corners and lines that aren't quite straight.

Drawing them by hand, and why it didn't work

The obvious fix was to draw new ones myself, and I had the right tool for it. I sketched icons in Zketch, with its own brushes.

They had plenty of character, and not one came out the same size as the next. Charming on paper. Less charming as a button you're trying to click.

An icon set has a job that a sketch doesn't. Every icon has to sit on the same grid, carry the same weight, and stay readable at 14 pixels as well as at 56. Drawn freehand, each icon was a one-off, and a toolbar of one-offs looks messy rather than playful. None of those files are left, but the lesson stayed: I wanted my pen's feel without my hand's inconsistency.

Imperfect on purpose

Things drawn by hand aren't perfect, and that's exactly why they feel human. A line drawn without a ruler drifts a little. A circle never quite closes the way a compass would. Corners come out soft because a pen can't make a sharp one. Those were the qualities I wanted, so the question became: how do you keep the imperfections and drop the mess?

My answer was to decide in advance exactly where the imperfection is allowed to live, and to make everything else strict. The strict part became a short set of rules:

  • Every icon is drawn on a 24 by 24 grid and stays roughly inside the middle 18 by 18.
  • One even line, 1.6 units wide, with round ends and round joins. No fills.
  • Rounded corners everywhere. Nothing ends in a sharp point.
  • Few strokes, and each stroke is a single pen movement. Most icons need two or three.

The imperfect part is small. Straight edges bow very slightly, and circles are a little out of round. That's all. But a bow that small, repeated across a whole toolbar, is enough to make the set feel drawn rather than built.

Teaching code to hold the pen

I already had a drawing pipeline in Zketch, and I needed the feel of my brush on these icons. So I split the work in two. I describe each icon as a few pen movements, and code does the actual drawing, the same way every time.

The description is a centerline: the path the middle of the pen travels, before any line width is added. For the pencil icon it's two strokes, a body with five rounded corners and the little line underneath:

packages/icons/defs/core.mjs

pencil: {
  strokes: [
    poly([[14.6, 5.1], [18.8, 9.3], [8.6, 19.2], [4.9, 19.1], [4.8, 15.4]], [1.8, 1.8, 1.3, 1.1, 1.3]),
    path("M3.5 21.5c2.5-1.4 4.4-1.6 6-2.2"),
  ],
},

The first list is where the corners go, and the second is how round each corner is. From there, a small generator takes over. It rounds the corners, bends the straight edges, walks along the result dropping a point roughly every third of a unit, and then thins those points down to the few that actually shape the line. Zketch uses the same trick to keep drawn strokes small. What comes out is one SVG path per icon, whatever the icon looks like. You can follow the pencil through it, left to right:


Figure 3. One icon through the generator: 5 corners and a curve become 135 sampled points, then 24, then a single 1.6-wide SVG path.

A wobble that never changes

The bow on each straight edge is random, and that's a problem. Randomness in an icon set means a different icon on every build: the undo arrow you shipped yesterday quietly changes shape today.

So the randomness is borrowed from the icon's name. The generator turns the name into a number with a tiny hash function and uses that number as the seed for its random choices:

packages/icons/lib/catalog.mjs

const d = sampleIcon(mod[name], hash(name)).map(toPathData).join("");

Every icon wobbles in its own way, and each one wobbles the same way forever. Here's the same square drawn with three different names. The inner red dashes are the straight square it started from (the outer ones mark the area every drawing stays inside), and the black line is where the pen went:


Figure 4. One square, three seeds: the bow changes with the name, never between builds.

Important:
Seed the randomness from the icon's name, and a wobbly line becomes as reproducible as a straight one.

Goodbye, Lucide

With the generator doing the drawing, my job changed. I was no longer fighting my own hand to make two icons the same size. I was deciding what each icon should say in two or three pen movements, and the code made sure every one of them said it in the same voice.

I worked outward from the canvas: first the tools Zketch uses most, then the rest of the app, then everyday icons and art tools for whatever comes next. Each new icon went onto a contact sheet beside all the others, at several sizes, because an icon that looks lovely at 56 pixels can turn to mush at 14. On one sheet, an icon that doesn't belong is easy to spot:


Figure 5. Twenty of the 143 icons at 14, 18, 24 and 56 px, all drawn with the same line.

Once the sheet looked like one set, I swapped them in. Every screen in Zketch moved to the brush-drawn icons, and Lucide came out of the project. The buttons around the canvas finally looked like they belonged to the drawing inside it. Zketch's project notes now carry a one-line rule: no Lucide.

Letting the lines breathe

The bow made the icons look drawn. I also wanted them to feel alive.

In old hand-drawn cartoons, every frame was traced again by hand, so the lines shimmer slightly even when nothing moves. Animators call it line boil. zicons fakes it with two SVG filters: one makes a field of noise, and the other nudges each part of the icon's line by the amount the noise says. The noise cycles through three patterns in a 0.36-second loop, so a new one arrives every 0.12 seconds:

packages/icons/runtime/render.js

export const SEEDS = [3, 11, 23];
export const BOIL_RATE = 0.36;

That's about eight new frames a second, which reads as a traced cartoon rather than smooth motion. The drawing itself never changes; only the noise over it does. Here are the three frames, with the real line in red on top:


Figure 6. Three boil frames, 0.12 s apart: the red path is the same in each, only the filter's noise moves.

The hard part was size. A shimmer that looks lively on a big icon makes a small one unreadable, so icons under 32 pixels get a gentler boil than larger ones, and within each group the wobble is scaled so it looks the same on screen at any size. You can have it on all the time, or only when someone hovers the icon or the button it sits in.

In your own project, the boil is off until you ask for it, one icon at a time, so whether it runs, and whether it follows reduced-motion settings, is your call. On the zicons site it's on for everyone, because the boil is how these icons show what they can do. If it's too much, a switch at the top of the page stops it.

From Zketch's toolbar to everyone's

For a while the icons lived only inside Zketch. But I kept thinking about other people who want what I wanted: something fun, a little unusual, with a taste of its own instead of the same neat icons as every other app. So I gave the drawings their own project and called it zicons.

zicons is now where new icons get drawn. One file holds every icon with its name, group, search words and path, and everything else is generated from it: the website, plain SVG files, a sprite, and a component package for each of the big frameworks. Importing one icon adds about 3 KB to a bundle, not all 143.

The future of zicons

The 143 icons cover a drawing app and the everyday basics. That's a start, not a finish. I don't have a target number in mind. What I want is a place where all your icon needs get covered, so you never have to mix in a ruler-straight icon from somewhere else because zicons didn't have one.

Here's what's planned:

  • A Figma file, so designers can use the icons where they design, not only where they build.
  • Contributions and icon requests. Right now every icon is coordinates I type into a file. I'd like a way for you to ask for the icon you're missing, and eventually to draw one yourself that follows the same rules.
  • More icons, steadily, wherever people keep finding gaps.
  • A playground with small mock interfaces (a toolbar, a sidebar, a card) so you can see the set working together before you use it.

A note before you go

zicons works with React, Vue, Svelte and plain HTML. Everything you need to browse, restyle, copy or install the icons is on zicons.zerro.dev, and the drawings live on GitHub. If you'd rather draw with them than read about them, they're in Zketch's toolbar.

Icons are the smallest things on a screen, so it's easy to grab them off the shelf without a second thought. But they're on every page, and they tell people what kind of place they've walked into before a single word does. Zketch is a place for loose lines, and now its buttons look like someone held a pen. Whatever you're making, it's allowed to have a hand in it too. A little wobble never hurt anyone.

Originally published on zerro.dev.

title: Two Paths to Take an Agent Runtime onto Mobile: a Remote Console and an On-Device Go SDK
description:
Project: Baize — a team-facing AI assistant runtime (Go 1.25+, MIT)

Repo: https://github.com/rebornace/baize

This is the follow-up to From a Single Agent Loop to an Auditable Runtime: Baize's Architecture. That post covered the server-side runtime; this one focuses on the two mobile paths.

Baize is a single-process Agent runtime written in Go that sits alongside your business systems, consolidating the LLM, tools, legacy HTTP APIs, and human checkpoints into auditable runs. Once the server side was stable, mobile was not built as a simple mobile web page. Instead, Baize offers two paths: one uses a Capacitor shell to remotely control the full console, so you can approve work on the go with zero development; the other compiles the Go orchestration core into an Android AAR and an iOS XCFramework via gomobile, so the conversation runs on the device and the UI is drawn entirely by your own app. This article walks through the actual code: how the two paths divide the work, the key and approval design of the on-device SDK, and how to choose.

1. There are actually two kinds of mobile demand

Before building anything for mobile, it helps to separate the requirements, because they point at two different problems.

The first kind is internal teams and operators handling things on the go. They need to read conversations, do human approvals, change settings, and deal with logins from their phone — essentially "carry the desktop console in my pocket." In this scenario the conversation engine, connectors, and approval flow are already running stably on the server; the phone only needs an entry point, not a second implementation.

The second kind is embedding Agent capabilities into your own product. These teams want a branded, native UI, with the conversation and tool loop running directly on the device and less dependence on an always-on sidecar, and they have their own requirements for UI and key management. Here the phone is not a remote control — it is where the capability lives.

The two demands differ in who owns the UI, where the code runs, and the integration cost. Forcing them into a single path would leave embedders stuck with a generic page, while operators who just wanted mobile approvals would be forced to build a native UI. Baize therefore splits them into two paths, each handling one side.

2. One diagram: the two paths

Path A is a remote-control console: the phone shell does not run a conversation engine, it loads the full remote console from the same origin. Path B is the on-device SDK: the Go orchestration core is compiled into the app, the UI is drawn by the app, and the conversation runs on the device. Let's expand each in turn.

3. Path A: a thin shell, the full console with zero development

Path A is deliberately light. You can open the reachable /ui directly in a mobile browser, or use the Capacitor project in the repository to wrap a WebView and build an Android or iOS app.

The shell loads the remote console from the same origin: once you configure the server address, the WebView simply opens the remote /ui. Conversation, settings, human approvals, connectors, MCP, messaging channels, and browser login are all identical to the desktop — nothing is lost by moving to the phone. The only things the shell handles itself are mobile nuisances: the safe area, the keyboard, and opening login pages in the system browser.

There is one deliberate choice here: the shell loads the remote /ui from the same origin by default rather than proxying another layer of HTTP inside the shell. Conversation and approval depend on server-pushed events (SSE); adding an HTTP proxy inside the shell would buffer those streaming responses and break the experience of messages arriving one by one. Loading from the same origin keeps streaming replies and approvals smooth inside the shell.

From an architecture standpoint, the shell runs no conversation engine at all — it is, quite literally, a remote control. The integration cost is close to zero: without writing any mobile code, the team gets the same operational capabilities on a phone as on desktop. The only deployment detail is that the public address must be reachable from the phone — the phone talks to the server address, not the localhost loopback on your computer.

4. Path B: compile the Go orchestration core into the app

Path B answers a different need: embedding Agent capabilities into your own product, with a native, branded UI.

Baize compiles the Go orchestration core into an Android AAR and an iOS XCFramework via gomobile, and exposes a binding-friendly public API (the binding package is mobileagent). There is a real engineering detail here: gomobile cannot bind Go internal packages, so Baize re-exports the binding-friendly interfaces from a separate top-level package, while the internal implementation stays under internal. The binding layer only surfaces the handful of methods an app actually needs.

What runs on the device is a slimmed-down, OpenAI-compatible conversation and tool loop. The division of work between the app and the SDK is clear:

  • The app owns layout, theming, the history list, the input box, and the approval card; it owns secure storage of keys and the remote-config fetch strategy; and it owns thread management (network calls must not block the main thread).

  • mobileagent owns the session, the conversation, the tool loop, and the pause/resume of approval. Every result is returned as a JSON string, and it never touches any UI.

The call surface is intentionally small:

  • Configure sets the model endpoint, key, and model name once.

  • Send runs one conversation turn and stops when it hits a tool that needs approval.

  • Approve and Deny handle the two approval decisions.

  • ChatOnce does a single-turn connectivity test without tools.

  • Reset clears the in-memory history.

  • NewAgent creates an independent session.

  • MessageCount returns the number of messages.

  • HasAPIKey reports whether a key is already held in memory.

5. Why the on-device SDK is slimmed down

The on-device SDK deliberately does not move the full server-side runtime into the phone. On the device it keeps only an in-memory session and a minimal tool surface: today there are two tools, get_time and http_get. get_time executes directly and returns the time, while http_get must pass human approval first. The full connector set, MCP bridging, messaging channels, and the operational approval product surface stay on the server Runtime.

This is a division of labor, not a capability cut. The server Runtime is aimed at "connect many systems and keep operating them as a team," which requires the full connector, audit, and operations surface. The on-device SDK is aimed at "close, light, embedded in your own product," which needs a controllable conversation loop and a minimal tool set. Keeping the two separate makes the on-device component small and controllable and leaves teams free to draw their own experience on top; when the full capability is needed, the app can always fall back to the server Runtime.

The tool loop itself has a boundary: a single turn's tool loop is capped at a fixed number of rounds (currently 8). When it reaches the cap, it ends and returns, so the model cannot loop forever on the device. The session and keys live only in memory and are never persisted in the Go binding layer — they are cleared on reset or exit.

6. Keys go to the system safe, not the Go package

There is one explicit rule in the on-device design: the Go binding layer only holds the key in memory and never writes it to disk. Anything that needs to persist is handed to the native safe provided by the app's platform.

On Android, the sample uses EncryptedSharedPreferences. The master key uses the AES256-GCM scheme, with keys encrypted with AES256-SIV and values with AES256-GCM. What gets stored includes the model endpoint, key, model name, and config endpoint, and there is a separate method to clear the key. On iOS, the equivalent is the Keychain, stored by service name and account name, and restricted to this device only and available after first unlock.

The flow is: when the app starts (or needs the key), it reads the key from the system safe, then injects it into the on-device runtime's memory via Configure; the Go binding layer never handles persistence. The reason is that a cross-platform Go binding cannot guarantee the security level of key storage, whereas EncryptedSharedPreferences and the Keychain are the security boundaries the platform actually endorses — hardware-backed or managed by the system as a whole. The binding does not overstep into storage it cannot do well; it hands security to the platform, and the app fully owns the key lifecycle.

7. Foreground human approval: a JSON status protocol

Human-in-the-loop on the device is expressed through a simple JSON status protocol. The return values of Send, Approve, and Deny are all JSON strings that the app parses to decide what to render:

  • done: the turn is finished; the UI shows the reply in the text field.

  • needs_approval: a tool is waiting for approval, carrying call_id, name, args_json, and summary. The app renders an approval card from these; approving calls Approve with the call_id, and rejecting calls Deny. Until the user makes a choice, no new Send should be issued.

  • error: execution failed; the UI shows message.

The approval summary is a single human-readable sentence. For http_get, it produces the method ("GET") plus a truncated URL, so on a phone you can see at a glance what the app is about to call.

The http_get that requires approval is a read-only tool, but even though it is read-only, Baize still requires explicit approval and adds a set of guardrails when it runs: only http and https are allowed; requests have a timeout (currently 15 seconds); redirects are capped (currently 3); the response body has a size limit (currently 256 KB, and anything larger is truncated and marked); and the result carries the final address (final_url) so you can verify where a redirect actually landed. Rejecting fires no network request at all and simply lets the conversation continue.

Narrowing what an on-device model is allowed to do is the core idea: keep tools read-only, require explicit approval for actions, and keep the network boundary clear — then on-device autonomy is contained within a safe range.

8. Remote config, multiple sessions, and desktop debugging

So the app does not have to hardcode the model endpoint and model name, the binding layer offers remote config: FetchRemoteConfig pulls JSON from a config endpoint you own, and ApplyRemoteConfigJSON merges that config into the in-memory session. The config can include the model endpoint and model name, and optionally the key. The fetch strategy is decided by the app; the SDK only applies it.

For multi-session scenarios, use NewAgent to obtain an independent instance rather than sharing the package-level default session. Each instance maintains its own history and pending-approval state.

You do not have to tether a phone during development. Baize ships a desktop debug entry point that runs the binding layer directly on your computer, and it includes a fake model so you can get the UI and approval cards working before swapping in a real model. When an Android emulator needs to reach the host machine, use the emulator's standard host address (10.0.2.2).

9. How to choose

The decision is straightforward:

  • If you want the full settings pages, connectors, and operational approval flow, and the phone is only a portable entry point, choose Path A.

  • If you want a branded native UI, the conversation running on the device, and less dependence on an always-on sidecar, choose Path B and draw your own UI using the empty shell in the repository as the calling sample.

  • The two can coexist: operators and internal teams use Path A, while the end-user-facing app uses Path B.

Closing

The two mobile paths are, at heart, separating two different problems: "the operator's portable console" and "the embedded on-device Agent." The former pursues zero development and full parity with the desktop; the latter pursues a native experience, on-device control, and a clear key boundary. The key decisions in the on-device SDK — holding keys only in memory, requiring approval even for read-only tools, giving network actions explicit guardrails, and keeping the session and tool loop minimal — all revolve around one goal: letting the capability run safely, and personally, on the device.

Baize is an open-source project under continuous development (written in Go, MIT licensed). The mobile Capacitor shell, the Android and iOS empty shells, the on-device bindings, and the corresponding build scripts are all in the repository.

Repository: https://github.com/rebornace/baize

Docs: https://rebornace.github.io/baize

If you are also putting Agents into production — especially if you are thinking about how to safely bring capabilities onto a phone — I'd like to hear how you handle mobile and key management. The full mobile getting-started guide and build steps will be covered in a follow-up post.

title: How to compare cloud GPU prices without getting misled
description:
When you shop for cloud GPUs, the headline number is rarely the whole story. Here is the checklist I use to avoid being misled.

1. Start with the provider's own pricing page

Aggregators and blog posts go stale fast. Read the price on the provider's official pricing page, and keep the link.

2. Compare per-hour price by GPU model and VRAM

"One GPU" can mean very different hardware. Compare like for like: the same model (for example an A100 vs. an H100) and the same VRAM size (40 GB vs. 80 GB), then look at price per hour.

3. Watch for storage and egress fees

Persistent disks, snapshots and outbound data transfer can add a surprising amount to the bill, especially for large datasets and model checkpoints. Check whether they are included.

4. Separate spot from on-demand pricing

Spot or preemptible instances can be much cheaper, but they can be interrupted. Record which type each price refers to, and never mix them in one comparison.

5. Date your comparison

GPU prices change often. Write down the date you checked each price so readers (and future you) know how fresh it is.

I keep a dated, source-checked comparison at AskGPU.

title: 20 of 21 agent configs just scored lower: what the Coding Agent Index v2.0 reset measures
description:
Yesterday Artificial Analysis shipped version 2.0 of its Coding Agent Index, and almost every agent on the board got worse on paper. Of the 21 configurations measured on both versions, 20 moved down. The mean index score fell from 54.8 to 47.4. No model regressed and no harness regressed. The test changed.

That distinction matters if you pick agents off leaderboards, or if you benchmark your own. Here is what actually moved, and how I read the new board.

What changed on October 23

The index now averages three benchmarks with equal weight, over 290 tasks total:

  • FrontierCode v1.1 (from Cognition): 100 software engineering tasks on real open-source repositories. New in v2.0, replacing DeepSWE v1.1.
  • Terminal-Bench 4.0 (Laude Institute): 66 terminal tasks. Carried over unchanged from v1.5.
  • SWE-Atlas-QnA-AA (Scale AI's tasks, Artificial Analysis grading): 124 repository Q&A tasks. Same tasks, reworked grading.

Each task runs three times and the attempts are averaged. The full construction is on their methodology page.

FrontierCode grades like a maintainer

This swap is where the score drop comes from. The same 21 configurations that averaged 65.6 percent on DeepSWE v1.1 average 45.1 percent on FrontierCode v1.1.

The grading explains the gap. FrontierCode scores each attempt against a rubric of blocking and non-blocking checks. Fail a blocking check and the attempt scores zero, even if the code works. Pass all the blocking checks and you land between 70 and 100 percent, depending on the non-blocking ones. The benchmark's own framing: changes to real open-source repositories, graded on whether a maintainer would merge them.

The 100 tasks come out of a 150-task set that is not publicly released, which keeps the tasks out of search results and training data. That is the point of a private split.

The row is a variant, not a model

From the methodology page: each public row is an agent variant, not a model. Settings that change behavior, including reasoning settings, get their own rows.

At the top of the new board, Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 (max) leads at 61.7, ahead of Claude Code with Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) at 59.3 and Muse Code with Muse Wonder Full (max) at 58.9. Claude Code with Claude Fable 5.1 (max with fallback) sits at 57.6. Same harness, three models, three scores. Two rows can share a model and sit several points apart on settings alone.

This is the part I keep pointing at when people ask whether agent configuration matters. The index cannot report a model's score without first fixing a harness and its settings. The model is half the measurement and the harness is the other half, and only one of those halves is under your control.

The judge got stricter too

SWE-Atlas-QnA kept its 124 tasks, but Artificial Analysis reworded 127 of the 1,306 rubric criteria and switched the judge to GPT-6 Luna (xhigh) with five votes per criterion. The dataset and judge configuration are published on Hugging Face.

The effect: across the 21 shared configurations, the Q&A mean fell 1.7 points, from 58.8 to 57.1 percent, with 14 of 21 moving down. Individual rows swung by up to 7 points. Muse Code with Muse Spark Open (xhigh) fell 7.0. Codex with GPT-6.1 Sol (max) gained 2.1.

When a judge revision moves rows by more than the gap between adjacent products, judge noise is part of the reading. A 2-point difference on a leaderboard is not a verdict.

The cost frontier survived

Four configurations sit on the cost frontier, per the launch announcement:

Configuration Index score Cost per task
Codex with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max) 47.3 $0.39
Codex with GPT-6.1 Sol (max) 54.1 $1.50
Codex with GPT-6 Astra (max) 54.7 $7.04
Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 (max) 61.7 $11.42

Those are pay-per-token API costs, not subscription prices. The leading row also averages about an hour of agent wall time per task, 3,661 seconds in the leaderboard's efficiency data. Cheapest and best are 14.4 index points and about $11 apart. Both ends of that line are rational picks, at different task volumes.

One methodology detail worth knowing before you compare these numbers against your own bills: cached input is priced separately from uncached input where the provider supports it, and cache-write charges are included. Prefix caching moves agent bills in ways a flat per-task figure hides, which I broke down with numbers here.

Cheating is scanned, not assumed

Agents get internet access on FrontierCode. A scan of each trajectory zeroes any attempt that fetched the upstream solution, meaning the source pull request, its merge commit, or a mirrored copy. Artificial Analysis runs a modified version of Cognition's rule-based scanner for this.

Terminal-Bench 4.0 adds an agent judge, Claude Code with Claude Sonnet 5, run through Harbor. It reads the full trajectory and flags the classics: editing the test files that grade the task, writing to the verifier's reward file, or fetching a reference solution from outside.

Two rules in the methodology deserve credit. Installing packages and reading library documentation count as normal work. And a search for the solution that turns up nothing is not a violation, as long as the agent works the answer out afterward. The line is whether the network supplied the answer, not whether the agent connected.

How to read the next leaderboard

What I check now, in order:

  1. The index version. v1.5 and v2.0 scores are not comparable. The 54.8 to 47.4 mean drop is what a yardstick change looks like. Treat any screenshot without a version stamp as noise.
  2. What the row actually is. A variant, with harness, model and settings fixed. "Claude Opus 5.5 scores 61.7" is a shorter sentence than the truth.
  3. The attempts behind it. Three attempts, averaged. A single benchmark run on your own repo is weather, not climate.
  4. The blocked rate. Safety refusals that block an attempt score zero, so a 2 percent blocked rate costs at most 2 points. Worth checking before you blame the model.

And if you run your own comparisons, pin the setup the way you pin dependencies:

# eval-setup.md, committed next to the results
benchmark: Coding Agent Index v2.0 (FrontierCode v1.1 / Terminal-Bench 4.0 / SWE-Atlas-QnA-AA)
agent: <name + version>
model: <name + reasoning setting>
attempts: 3, mean reported, date of run recorded

I keep making this argument for versioning agent config files, and benchmark versions deserve the same discipline. An eval you cannot reproduce is a number you cannot defend.

What I take from the reset

The drop from 54.8 to 47.4 is not bad news. FrontierCode's maintainer standard is closer to the PRs I actually review than a diff-applies-and-tests-pass check is. If the industry's headline number gets harder and more honest, that helps everyone choosing tools.

The packing is the other takeaway. On FrontierCode, 15 of the 24 configurations on the index score between 43 and 49 percent. The field is tight in raw capability. Which means the harness, the settings and the instructions you wrap around a model are not a rounding error in the outcome. They are a measurable part of it, and a leaderboard made of agent variants keeps proving it.
