title: Why Your Automatic System Might Be Hiring and Firing for the Wrong Reasons
description:
Imagine you run a small restaurant chain five branches, one shared kitchen manager watching all of them from head office. Instead of visiting each branch, the manager watches one number on a screen: "average busy-ness across all branches." When it's high, hire more chefs. When it's low, let some go.

Sounds efficient. It's also exactly how a lot of automatic systems decide when to add or remove servers and it can go wrong in the exact same way it would go wrong for our restaurant.

Lie #1: the average can hide the real picture

Say two of your five branches are completely slammed, and three are quiet. The "average busy-ness" comes out looking... totally normal. Nothing about that one number tells you two branches are drowning and need help right now.

Or the opposite happens: all five branches are only a little busy, but the way the number gets calculated say, by adding up small readings from each branch at slightly different times makes the combined number spike for no real reason. The manager sees "high," panics, and starts hiring.

The number wasn't fake. It was calculated correctly. It just wasn't measuring what the manager assumed it was measuring. This is the single most common mistake in automatic systems: trusting a summary number without ever asking how it was built and what it actually represents.

The fix is boring but effective: before you let a number drive real decisions, go check what's actually happening underneath it at least once. Does "average" here mean "typical branch," or does it mean "all branches blended together in a way nobody would recognize"? Usually it's worth looking at the raw numbers behind the average, not just the average itself, before trusting it.

Lie #2: firing chefs is instant, hiring chefs isn't

Here's the part that makes this genuinely dangerous, not just annoying.

Letting a chef go happens the moment you decide it. But hiring a new chef isn't instant they need to get trained, learn the menu, get comfortable with the kitchen. Say that takes a full day before they're actually useful.

Now picture the manager, reacting to that misleading "average" number, cutting staff aggressively one branch after another, back to back, because the number kept saying "too many chefs." A few hours later, real customers show up in numbers nobody expected, and now every branch is short-staffed at once. The manager scrambles to hire back but that takes a full day to actually help, because new hires aren't useful the moment they walk in.

This is the trap: cutting is fast and reversible-feeling, but recovering is always slower than you think. If your system can remove capacity in seconds but takes minutes (or longer) to bring it back usefully, you should always be more cautious removing than adding never the other way around. Most automatic scaling systems let you set a "give it time before reacting again" rule for exactly this reason. If you've never set one, it's worth checking whether your system has one.

Lie #3: "the limit is huge" is usually an assumption, not a fact

One more thing worth checking before you ever get burned by it: is there a hidden ceiling somewhere you've never actually tested?

Back to our restaurant maybe the gas line in the kitchen can only support so many stoves running at once, no matter how many chefs you hire. Nobody ever thought about it, because normal days never got close to that number. Then one unusually busy day arrives, and the kitchen hits a wall that has nothing to do with staff count at all.

Cloud platforms are full of these quiet defaults and ceilings you're never shown until you brush up against one. The safe habit is simple: for anything your system depends on scaling smoothly, actually go find out what the real ceiling is, on a calm day, before you need the answer on a bad one. Don't assume "it's probably big enough."

The takeaway

Automatic scaling is genuinely useful most of the time, it quietly does the right thing and you never have to think about it. But it's built on trusting a number, and reacting to that number fast. That combination means two small mistakes compound into a big one very quickly: a slightly misleading number, plus a system that reacts to it faster than it can recover, plus a hidden ceiling nobody checked and suddenly you're firefighting a problem that was actually three separate small gaps stacked on top of each other.

The habit that fixes all three: before you trust an automatic system's number, understand what it's really measuring. Before you let it react fast in one direction, make sure recovery in the other direction is at least as fast. And before you assume a limit is "big enough," go check.

title: Design Token Architecture for Scalable Theming
description:
• How I organize a token taxonomy that survives scale
  • Why Style Dictionary is table stakes — and how to extend it
  • Token versioning & publishing that won't break teams
  • Mapping tokens across web and native platforms without surprises
  • A migration checklist you can run this week

Design tokens are the single source of truth that determines whether your product family remains consistent or fragments into one-off styles across teams and platforms . When teams treat tokens as an afterthought, theming becomes a long-running maintenance tax — you trade speed today for chaos tomorrow.

The problem shows up as duplicated hex values in three repos, three different dark-mode strategies, components that look off by a pixel across platforms, and last-minute accessibility fixes that slip through. Teams waste time reconciling visual regressions; product launches stall while engineers hunt down where a color actually lives. That is a governance and tooling failure — not a design problem.

How I organize a token taxonomy that survives scale

Design tokens must do one job: make visual decisions explicit, discoverable, and changeable without touching component code. The pragmatic taxonomy I use separates tokens into three layers: raw tokens, aliases, and semantic tokens. That separation keeps intent clear and reduces blast radius when values change .

  • Raw tokens (primitives) — atomic values: hex/rgb colors, numeric spacing scales, font families, raw sizes. These change rarely and should map closely to source assets from designers.
  • Alias tokens (scales & palettes) — reusable scales and brand palette items (for example blue.500, space.3). Aliases centralize a single design decision (the scale) and let you repurpose it consistently.
  • Semantic tokens (contracts) — named for purpose, not color or size: color.button.primary.bg, radius.card.default, typography.heading.1. Components consume semantic tokens only.
Layer Example name Typical owner Change frequency Use by code
Raw (primitive) color.raw.blue.500 Design tokens team Very low Not directly by components
Alias color.alias.brand.primary Design system team Low Used to compose semantic tokens
Semantic color.button.primary.bg Component/product teams Moderate Directly consumed by components

Example token JSON (Style Dictionary / DTCG-friendly structure):

{
  "color": {
    "raw": {
      "blue": {
        "500": { "value": "#0B5FFF", "type": "color", "description": "Brand blue 500 (sRGB)" }
      },
      "white": { "value": "#FFFFFF", "type": "color" }
    },
    "alias": {
      "brand": {
        "primary": { "value": "{color.raw.blue.500.value}" }
      }
    },
    "semantic": {
      "button": {
        "primary": {
          "background": { "value": "{color.alias.brand.primary.value}" },
          "text": { "value": "{color.raw.white.value}" }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

Why this matters in practice:

  • Stability: Components reference semantic tokens only; you can retune an alias or raw value without changing component code.
  • Traceability: Each token carries description, type, and optional deprecated flags so maintainers and codemods can map change impact.
  • Theming: Build themes by swapping alias values (or semantic overrides) rather than editing component usage.

Style Dictionary (and other tools) favor a CTI (category-type-item) layout to support transforms and filters. Use that shape to make automated transforms reliable and to enrich tokens with metadata for platform-specific builds .

Important: Treat semantic tokens as the contract between design and engineering — raw values are implementation detail, not the contract.

Why Style Dictionary is table stakes — and how to extend it

Style Dictionary is the pragmatic choice for multi-platform token pipelines because it already understands transforms, formats, and common platform needs (CSS, JS, Android, iOS) and is extensible with custom transforms and formats . Use it as the build engine, not the policy system.

Typical config (excerpt):

// style-dictionary.config.js
module.exports = {
  source: ['tokens/**/*.json'],
  platforms: {
    css: {
      transformGroup: 'css',
      buildPath: 'dist/css/',
      files: [{
        destination: 'variables.css',
        format: 'css/variables',
        options: { outputReferences: true }
      }]
    },
    js: {
      transformGroup: 'js',
      buildPath: 'dist/js/',
      files: [{ destination: 'tokens.esm.js', format: 'javascript/esm' }]
    },
    android: {
      transformGroup: 'android',
      buildPath: 'dist/android/',
      files: [{ destination: 'colors.xml', format: 'android/resources' }]
    },
    ios: {
      transformGroup: 'ios',
      buildPath: 'dist/ios/',
      files: [{ destination: 'Colors.swift', format: 'ios-swift/class.swift' }]
    }
  }
};

Why you will extend Style Dictionary:

  • Built-in transforms handle name casing and unit conversions, but you will need platform-specific tweaks: px -> dp/sp for Android, rem -> pt for iOS typography, and color-space conversions for Display P3 or platform-native color types .
  • Preserve token references in outputs using options.outputReferences so generated CSS/JS produces var(--semantic-token, var(--alias-token)) fallbacks and keeps intent readable downstream .

Custom transform example (register a simple size transform):

const StyleDictionary = require('style-dictionary');

StyleDictionary.registerTransform({
  name: 'size/pxToDp',
  type: 'value',
  matcher: token => token.type === 'size',
  transformer: token => `${Math.round(parseFloat(token.value) * (160/96))}dp`
});

Operational notes:

  • Run StyleDictionary.buildAllPlatforms() inside CI to emit a deterministic set of artifacts (CSS variables, TypeScript types, Android XML, iOS Swift files).
  • Keep transforms idempotent and testable. Add unit tests for a transform that converts spacing across platforms.

Style Dictionary is not the only tool, but it is widely adopted and integrates with the newer DTCG (Design Tokens) movement to standardize JSON formats across tools .

Token versioning & publishing that won't break teams

Treat your token package like a public API. Use semantic versioning and map changes to semantic impact so downstream consumers can safely adopt updates .

Semver mapping I use:

Change type SemVer bump Example
Breaking semantics or removals Major (1.x → 2.0.0) Rename color.button.primary.bg to a different function
Additive, non-breaking tokens or new themes Minor (1.2.0) Add color.toast.info.bg
Fix metadata, typos, build fixes Patch (1.2.1) Correct description or type, rebuild artifacts

Operational policy:

  1. Add a deprecated: true flag and replacement pointer to old tokens in a minor release. Consumers get lint warnings before removal.
  2. Remove a deprecated token only in a major release; include a clear migration table in release notes.
  3. Publish per-semver release artifacts for each platform and include exact SHA/tarball links for native consumers.

Distribution patterns:

  • Publish a canonical design-tokens npm package with generated artifacts (dist/css, dist/js, dist/android, dist/ios). Shopify and others publish token packages to npm as a single distribution point .
  • For very large ecosystems, split tokens into smaller packages (per-component token packages). Fluent UI’s semantic-tokens RFC describes the per-component package approach to reduce the blast radius and to emit per-component fallback CSS variables .

Automated release pipeline (example):

  • CI: npx style-dictionary build → run token validation linters → run color-contrast checks → build artifacts → npm version {patch|minor|major} → npm publish.
  • Add changelog entries that map old→new tokens and include example replacement code snippets.

Atlassian’s token ecosystem shows how linting and codemods can be part of the rollout: they expose a token() helper, lint rules, and codemods to help replace raw values with tokens safely . Use those patterns to avoid surprise breakages.

Mapping tokens across web and native platforms without surprises

Cross-platform pitfalls are predictable: unit mismatches (px vs dp vs pt), color-space mismatches (sRGB vs Display P3), and different platform naming conventions. Plan transforms to handle those differences centrally rather than ad-hoc in product code .

Key tactics:

  • Encode type and unit metadata on tokens so transforms can make deterministic conversions (for example type: "size", unit: "rem").
  • Use Style Dictionary’s built-in transforms for common conversions (remToSp, remToDp) and color transforms for different platform color objects .
  • For color, prefer storing tokens in a modern color space and generate platform-specific representations in the build step. The DTCG spec now documents color handling and interoperable color formats; align your schema to be compatible .

Example CSS-based theming pattern (generate with Style Dictionary):

/* dist/css/variables.css (generated) */
:root {
  --color-button-primary-bg: #0B5FFF;
  --color-button-primary-text: #FFFFFF;
}

[data-theme="dark"] {
  --color-button-primary-bg: #093b9f;
}

Fallback strategy for gradual migration (generated):

/* in component CSS */
background: var(--semantic-button-primary-bg, var(--alias-brand-primary, #0B5FFF));

For native:

  • Android: emit colors.xml under res/values/ with names converted to snake_case or lowercase as required.
  • iOS: emit Colors.swift or .xcassets + color catalogs, using PascalCase or idiomatic Swift names.

Style Dictionary’s formats include a wide set of ready-made outputs for Android and iOS; use those and customize only when necessary . You can also generate TypeScript declarations to get strong typings for token consumption on the web .

Design tool sync:

  • Keep designers and engineers aligned by syncing tokens from Figma (Tokens Studio / Figma Tokens plugin) into the token repository, then run the build pipeline to produce artifacts consumers use .

A migration checklist you can run this week

This is a compact, runnable checklist. Each line is a discrete sprint chunk.

  1. Audit (1 week)
    • Extract current variables and hard-coded values across repos (grep/shell scripts, theme folders).
    • Export the design file tokens (Tokens Studio or Figma Tokens) to JSON for reference .
  2. Define taxonomy & ownership (1 week)
    • Create folders: tokens/raw/, tokens/alias/, tokens/semantic/, tokens/themes/.
    • Author token naming conventions (CTI) and a small governance doc.
  3. Seed tokens & config (1 week)
    • Put primitives under raw/; create alias scale files; define the initial semantic tokens.
    • Add style-dictionary.config.js and a package.json script: "build:tokens": "style-dictionary build".
  4. Build & validate (ongoing)
    • CI job: npm run build:tokens → run a token linter and color-contrast checks (automate with an a11y script).
    • Commit generated artifacts to an artifacts branch or publish to an internal npm registry.
  5. Pilot adoption (1 sprint)
    • Pick a single small component or page. Use the semantic tokens only in that module.
    • Add a temporary compatibility layer if needed: component reads semantic token then falls back to legacy CSS var.
  6. Codemod and scale (2–4 sprints)
    • Replace direct hex values and legacy CSS vars progressively via codemods and lint rules.
    • Publish a minor release with deprecated flags before removal.
  7. Ongoing governance
    • Enforce token usage with lint rules and CI checks.
    • Use change logs that include explicit migration paths and code snippets.

Quick example package.json tokens scripts:

{
  "scripts": {
    "build:tokens": "style-dictionary build",
    "test:tokens": "node ./scripts/validate-tokens.js",
    "release:tokens": "npm run build:tokens && standard-version"
  }
}

Short codemod pattern (conceptual) to replace var(--old-token) with semantic helper usage:

// pseudo-code for jscodeshift replacement
// find CSS-in-JS literal strings containing 'var(--old-token)' and replace with `token('color.button.primary.bg')`

Real-world reference points:

  • Atlassian publishes token linting and codemods to help teams migrate and enforce usage .
  • Shopify historically published token artifacts for multiple formats and distributed via npm .
  • Fluent UI is moving toward per-component semantic token packages and explicit fallback structures to reduce breaking changes .

Callout: Ship early, pilot wide. A single component fully migrated to semantic tokens is worth more than half a token repo left in limbo.

Adopt the taxonomy, automate builds with Style Dictionary, and treat tokens like a public API: version them, test them, and communicate changes. That approach turns theming from a constant firefight into a predictable engineering workflow and makes consistent cross-platform theming achievable at scale .

Sources:
Design Tokens Community Group - Specification and ecosystem guidance for the DTCG JSON format and community-driven best practices; used to justify token standardization and cross-tool interoperability.

Style Dictionary — Built-in formats & transforms reference - Documentation of Style Dictionary formats, transform groups, and transform registration used for platform builds and customization examples.

Using CSS custom properties (MDN) - Behavior, scoping, and @property guidance for CSS custom properties used in theming and fallback strategies.

Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 (SemVer) - The semantic versioning specification referenced for mapping token changes to version bumps and release policy.

Atlassian Design System — Use tokens in code - Concrete examples of token helper functions, linting guidance, and migration tooling recommendations used as a practical model for adoption.

Shopify Polaris Tokens (GitHub) - Example of a real-world token package and distribution approach (npm, multiple formats) illustrating multi-format distribution.

Tokens Studio for Figma (official repo) - The Figma plugin used by many teams to manage tokens in design files and sync them to code; referenced for design tooling integration.

Fluent UI RFC: Fluent Semantic Tokens (GitHub issue) - A real-world RFC discussing per-component semantic tokens, fallback structures, and reduced blast radius for token changes.

title: Model a hazmat shipping paper as ordered segments, not five columns
description:
A hazmat shipping paper becomes testable when the basic description is stored as one ordered array, the mixed-load marker as an enum, and the retention clock as a date field captured from the carrier rather than the order.

Most shipping-paper bugs are not missing data. They are data that arrived in the wrong shape. A description split across five nullable columns cannot express "these five entries, in this order, as one block, with everything else after them." A boolean named is_hazmat cannot express which of three permitted mixed-load markers the offeror chose. A retention_years integer computed from the order timestamp cannot express the rule in 49 CFR 172.201(e), because the clock starts when the initial carrier accepts the material. Reshaping the model is the whole job. Validation falls out of it.

The basic description is an ordered array, not five fields

49 CFR 172.202(a) lists what the shipping description must include: the identification number from Column (4) of the § 172.101 table, the proper shipping name from Column (2), the hazard class or division number from Column (3), the packing group in Roman numerals from Column (5), and the total quantity with its unit of measurement. The regulation treats that set as a single object called the basic description, and and 49 CFR 172.201(a)(4) constrains everything else: anything extra goes after that block, not inside it.

That ordering constraint is the reason to model the description as an array of typed segments with a position index, not as sibling columns. Each segment carries a kind drawn from a closed set, and the validator asserts that the five required kinds appear once each, in the sequence the regulation lists, with no additional-information segment at a lower index than the last required one. Packing group has its own wrinkle. 49 CFR 172.202(a)(4) excepts Class 1 materials, self-reactive substances, Division 5.2 materials, and entries not assigned a packing group from the requirement, so the assertion is conditional on the material, not unconditional. Store the exception basis alongside the segment or the validator will fire on correct papers.

Hazard class carries two separate conditionals under 49 CFR 172.202(a)(3). A subsidiary class or division number need not be entered at all when no matching subsidiary label is required. And when it is entered, it goes in parentheses immediately after the primary class or division number, except for combustible liquids.

segment := {
  position:      int,          # 1-based, dense, no gaps
  kind:          enum,         # id_number | psn | hazard_class | packing_group | quantity | additional
  value:         string,
  unit:          string|null,  # required when kind = quantity
  exception_ref: string|null   # e.g. "172.202(a)(4)" when the segment is legitimately absent
}

assert description.segments
  .filter(s => s.kind in REQUIRED_FIVE)
  .map(s => s.kind)
  == ["id_number","psn","hazard_class","packing_group","quantity"]

assert description.segments
  .filter(s => s.kind == "additional")
  .every(s => s.position > position_of("quantity"))

Quantity deserves its own note. 49 CFR 172.202(a)(5) requires the total quantity by mass or volume, or by activity for Class 7 materials, together with the applicable unit of measurement, and excepts transportation by aircraft from the requirement. A quantity segment without a unit should fail validation rather than pass as an empty string.

The mixed-load marker is an enum with three members

When a hazardous material and a non-regulated material share one shipping paper, 49 CFR 172.201(a)(1) gives the offeror three acceptable ways to distinguish the hazardous entry: enter it first, enter it in a color that clearly contrasts with the non-regulated description, or place an "X" before the basic description in a column captioned "HM." A boolean collapses those into one bit and loses the choice. Store the marker as an enum whose members are first_position, contrasting_color, and hm_column_x, then assert that exactly one is set whenever the paper carries both kinds of material.

Two smaller rules ride along. 49 CFR 172.201(a)(2) requires the shipping description and all copies used for transportation to be legible and printed in English, manually or mechanically. 49 CFR 172.201(a)(3) bars any code or abbreviation in the required description unless the subchapter specifically authorizes or requires it. The second is checkable against a maintained allowlist of authorized abbreviations, and it is worth running as a lint rather than a hard block, because the allowlist has to track the subchapter.

Page count and the total-page notation are their own fields

A multi-page shipping paper has a structural requirement that gets skipped when documents are assembled at print time. Under 49 CFR 172.201(c) a paper may run over several pages provided the pages number in sequence and page one states how many pages there are in total, the rule offering "Page 1 of 4 pages" as its own example.

Model page_number, page_total, and total_notation_present as first-class fields on the document, not as artifacts of the PDF renderer. The assertion is trivial once the fields exist: page numbers form a dense sequence from one to page_total, and total_notation_present is true on the first page whenever page_total exceeds one. A renderer that paginates after the fact cannot satisfy this, which is the point. The notation is a property of the document the offeror provides, not of the file that leaves the printer.

The emergency phone needs two checks, not one

49 CFR 172.201(d) asks for two things on the face of the paper: an emergency response telephone number, and where that number routes through a service provider, the name or contract number of whoever holds the agreement with the provider. Those are separate obligations and they fail separately.

The first check is availability: a number is present and parses as a dialable number in the expected format. The second is accountability: if a service provider is in use, a named person or contract number is recorded against that provider. A paper can pass the first and fail the second, which is exactly the case a single emergency_contact string hides. Keep the provider relationship as a reference to a record rather than free text, so the contract number can be re-verified when it changes.

Retention forks on cargo class and starts at carrier acceptance

49 CFR 172.201(e) sets two periods. Hazardous waste keeps its copy for three years past acceptance by the first carrier; everything else covered by the subpart keeps two, and the trigger event is the same in both branches. Each copy must include the date of acceptance by the initial carrier, with a stated alternative for rail, vessel, or air shipments where the date on the waybill, airbill, or bill of lading may be used instead.

The engineering consequence is that acceptance date must be an independent, immutable field. Deriving a retention deadline from an order timestamp produces a date that is wrong by however long the goods sat before handover, and the error runs in the direction that loses records early. Store carrier_accepted_on and acceptance_date_source, the latter distinguishing a direct acceptance date from a transport-document date, then compute the deadline from the cargo classification. The same section requires the copy to be accessible at or through the principal place of business and producible to an authorized official at reasonable times and locations, so the record needs a location pointer as well as a date.

The shipper's certification is stored as wording, signer and time

49 CFR 172.204(a) requires the person offering the material to certify conformity by printing on the shipping paper either the certification in 49 CFR 172.204(a)(1) or the declaration in 49 CFR 172.204(a)(2). The two texts differ, and the regulation permits a substitution in each: "herein-named" may replace "above-named" in the first, and "above" may replace "below" in the second where appropriate.

Storing a certified: true flag discards the only thing that matters later, which is which wording appeared and who put it there. Store the exact text, the variant used, the signer identity, and the signing timestamp. Rail shipments have a further permitted path under 49 CFR 172.204(a)(3), where the certification may be received verbally or with an electronic signature, so the record type should distinguish a printed certification from a captured one.

Marking and description are separate obligations with separate chapters. Nothing in the shipping-paper model above substitutes for country-of-origin marking on the article or its container.

What we can check, and what we cannot

FulfillNexa by SBT (fulfillnexa.com) operates three sites in China: Suzhou at 13,000 square meters, Dongguan at 8,000, and Shenzhen at 3,000. Our systems can validate field presence and segment order on a shipping paper. They cannot verify that a certification's content matches the goods actually in the box. The offeror signs 49 CFR 172.204, not the warehouse.

title: Model hazmat training as a per-person, per-function authorization row
description:
A warehouse can answer "can this person handle this hazmat shipment today" as a database lookup if the training record is modeled as one authorization row per person and function, with an explicit expiry predicate. The rule text already supplies every field that row needs.

The row is per person and per function, not per person

49 CFR 172.702(a) puts the duty on the employer, in one sentence: every hazmat employee it has gets trained to the standard the subpart sets. The unit of training is not the employee. It is the employee crossed with the function, because 49 CFR 172.704(a)(2)(i) ties function-specific training to the requirements and special permits that apply to the functions that person actually performs.

A single training table keyed on employee ID cannot express that. Two people trained on the same general awareness module may hold different function authorizations, and one person may hold several. Model the authorization as its own row and let the employee table hold only identity.

Five columns the record must carry, and one more the rule adds

49 CFR 172.704(d) states that the record "must include" five items, and each maps to a column rather than to a scanned PDF page.

training_record
  employee_name              -- 172.704(d)(1)
  last_completion_date       -- 172.704(d)(2)
  material_ref               -- 172.704(d)(3) description, copy, or location
  provider_name_address      -- 172.704(d)(4)
  trained_and_tested_flag    -- 172.704(d)(5) certification

authorization
  employee_id  -> training_record.employee_name
  function_code
  status                     -- active | supervised_only | blocked

The fifth item is the one engineering teams drop. 49 CFR 172.704(d)(5) wants the employer's own certification that the worker was both trained and tested. Testing is a separate duty in its own right under 49 CFR 172.702(d), which asks that each employee be tested by appropriate means on the subjects 172.704 covers. Training without a test result is an incomplete row. Store the flag as a boolean that defaults to false and cannot be flipped by the training import alone.

The material reference deserves a note. The rule accepts "a description, copy, or the location of the training materials." A pointer into a document store satisfies the third option, provided the pointer resolves. A dead link is not a location.

The predicate has two branches, and both must be evaluated

Authorization is not a single date comparison. 49 CFR 172.704(c)(2) sets the recurrent cycle: "A hazmat employee must receive the training required by this subpart at least once every three years." 49 CFR 172.704(c)(1) opens a separate window for people who are new or who changed functions. Two conditions attach: an already trained and knowledgeable hazmat employee supervises the work directly, and the training has to close within 90 days of the hire or the move.

Read together, those two lines mean a valid authorization needs a completion date inside the three-year cycle, or an open 90-day window with a named supervisor attached to the assignment. The second branch is not a pass. It is a conditional state that must carry the supervisor's identity, since an unsupervised new hire falls outside 49 CFR 172.704(c)(1) entirely.

A predicate that checks only the three-year cycle will approve a brand-new employee with no record at all. A predicate that checks only the 90-day window will approve someone whose last completion date is years stale. Both branches, every time.

Deletion policy cannot be a fixed number of days

The retention clause in 49 CFR 172.704(d) is conditional on employment, not on elapsed time: the employer must retain the record "for as long as that employee is employed by that employer as a hazmat employee and for 90 days thereafter." A cron job that deletes rows older than some constant will either destroy a live authorization or keep a stale one past its lawful life.

The retention boundary is an event, not a duration. Termination date plus 90 days. Until that event fires, the record stays regardless of age, which is why a training completion from four years ago must still be present even though it fails the currency predicate. Currency and retention are different questions and belong in different columns.

Treating departure as an immediate delete is the classic failure. The record must survive the person's last day by 90 days, and 49 CFR 172.704(d) also obliges the employer to hand that current-training record over when an authorized DOT official asks, at a reasonable time and place. A record deleted at offboarding cannot be produced on request.

Where the boundary sits for a fulfillment warehouse

Training duty rests with the hazmat employer under 49 CFR 172.702(a), and 49 CFR 172.702(c) allows that training to come from "the hazmat employer or other public or private sources." Sourcing training from a third party does not move the obligation. 49 CFR 172.704(c)(4) is blunt about it: "Each hazmat employer is responsible for compliance with the requirements of this subchapter regardless of whether the training required by this subpart has been completed."

A fulfillment warehouse is not the hazmat employer of its customers' staff and does not issue training conclusions for anyone. What a warehouse can hold is the data layer that lets the employer's own record stay resolvable. Nothing more.

FulfillNexa by SBT (fulfillnexa.com) keeps the receiving side of that data layer on three Chinese floors, the largest being 13,000 square meters at Suzhou. What lands at goods-in is an arrival timestamp, a weight and piece count per SKU, and a dated packing change. None of the three is a training record and none substitutes for one. The declared number stays the customer's.

title: One item per row: designing bulk order creation
description:
A merchant who ships forty parcels a day doesn't want to fill in a form forty times. Most of them already keep those orders somewhere else, in a spreadsheet or an export from the store they sell on. What they need is a way to bring a day's orders in at once, fix whatever is wrong before anything is created, and never end up with the same order twice.

That's the whole brief for bulk order creation. The interesting part is that the first design decision, what one row means, shapes everything after it.

Diagram: the first plan put one order on a row and hid its items in a drawer. the shipped sheet puts one item on a row, the way the file already does, and sends the orders in one bulk request. See it on maruf.ing

the need behind it

Three things matter to the merchant, in this order:

  1. Getting the orders in. Most of them arrive as a CSV, not typed by hand. If the import is fussy, people give up and go back to the one-by-one form.
  2. Fixing problems before anything is created. A wrong city or a missing phone number should be caught on the sheet, not discovered after a parcel is booked.
  3. No duplicates. Creating forty orders is a batch. If the network drops halfway, retrying must not create the first twenty again.

Every decision below is in service of one of these.

first approach: one order per row

My first sketch put one order on each row. Recipient name, phone and address on the left, then a products cell showing a summary like "2 items". Clicking it opened a side drawer with the same product and variant picker the single-order screen uses.

It looked tidy. An order is the thing the merchant is creating, so one row per order felt right.

The problem showed up as soon as I thought about the import. The files merchants already have put one item on each row, with the order reference repeated for a multi-item order. That's how most store and shipping exports work, Shopify's included. A sheet shaped differently from the file turns every import into a translation step, and every error points at a cell that doesn't exist in the merchant's own spreadsheet.

So I dropped it.

second approach: one item per row

The sheet now has the same shape as the file:

  • one row is one line item
  • adjacent rows with the same order reference are one order
  • a row with a blank order reference is its own single-item order
  • the same reference on rows that aren't next to each other is an error, not a silent merge
order ref name phone city sku qty
A-101 Rahim 017… Dhaka TSHIRT-L 1
A-102 Karim 018… Dhaka MOUSE-01 1
A-102 CABLE-1M 2

This also lines up with the backend. Each group of rows becomes exactly the payload the single-order form already sends, so the server doesn't need a second idea of what an order is.

The drawback is readability. Once an order spans rows, it's easy to lose track of where one ends and the next begins, and recipient details repeated on every row look like separate orders.

The fix:

  • Order-level cells (recipient, address, amount to collect) show only on an order's first row. The rows below stay empty, so a total never looks like it's charged twice. The order reference repeats in a muted color as the group marker.
  • A bracket in the row-number column marks each multi-item order, inset at both ends so two neighbouring orders stay visibly separate. Dividers are dashed inside an order and solid between orders.
  • No merged cells. rowSpan looks like the natural tool, but inserting rows, keeping row keys stable and sorting all get harder once cells span rows.

an import that doesn't give up

A strict importer is easy to build and miserable to use: one unexpected column header and the whole file is rejected. Since getting orders in is the first need, the import here never refuses a file. It loads what it can and marks the rest on the sheet.

  • Headers are matched ignoring case, spaces and punctuation, so Phone, phone and Phone (*) all land in the same column. Columns the sheet doesn't know are ignored.
  • Common aliases map to the same field. A product can arrive as sku or as a free-text item name, a pickup point as pickup location or store, so files exported from different tools load without editing.
  • Unknown products become custom line items named after the text. An item that isn't in the catalogue yet is still a real parcel, so it's not a reason to reject the order.
  • Locations are matched against the real list. An exact match is fine. A close match ("banani dohs" for "Banani Old DOHS") is filled in and marked yellow for review. No match is red. When the city or zone is missing, an address parser fills it in from the street address, also yellow.
  • Unknown pickup locations fall back to the merchant's default one, marked yellow until someone picks.

tip: Red blocks the submit, yellow doesn't. A "go to error" button jumps to the top-most, left-most red cell, so fixing a file walks it in reading order.

submitting the batch

Once the sheet is clean, the orders go to the server in one request. The obvious shortcut, looping over the single-order endpoint, is slow for big batches and falls apart on exactly the third need: a request that times out after the server already created the order looks like a failure, and a retry creates a duplicate.

So the batch gets its own endpoint, built on the same rules as the single one:

POST /orders/bulk

{
  "orders": [
    { "idempotency_key": "A-101", "order": { ...the single-order payload... } },
    { "idempotency_key": "A-102", "order": { ...the single-order payload... } }
  ]
}

HTTP/1.1 200 OK

{
  "results": [
    { "idempotency_key": "A-101", "status": "created", "order_id": "ord_8f2k" },
    { "idempotency_key": "A-102", "status": "failed",
      "errors": { "pickup_location": "this location is inactive" } }
  ]
}
  • Each element is the exact single-order payload, and the server runs the same create logic for each one. There's one definition of a valid order, not two.
  • Results are per order. One bad order doesn't fail the batch. The response says which ones were created and which failed, and why.
  • Each order carries an idempotency key, here the merchant's order reference. If the same key comes back, the server returns the order it already created instead of making a new one. A retry after a timeout becomes safe.
  • Field errors map back to cells. pickup_location in the response turns that cell red on the sheet, with the server's message.

On the sheet, created orders lock and failed ones stay editable, so the merchant fixes only what failed and submits again. The keys make that second submit harmless for the orders that already went through.

keeping the sheet fast

A spreadsheet that lags while you type is worse than a form. The first version re-rendered every cell on every keystroke: fine with ten orders, sluggish with sixty. Two changes fixed it. Cells type into local state and commit to the sheet on a short pause or on blur, and rows are memoized so an edit only re-renders the row it touched. Validation and the address parser then run per committed value, not per key.

what it costs

  • Order fields live on the first row. To change a recipient you edit the order's first row, not any row. That's the price of matching the file.
  • Big orders get tall. A forty-item wholesale order is forty rows. For a tool aimed at many small orders, that's acceptable.
  • Partial success needs a UI. Per-order results are more honest than all-or-nothing, but the sheet has to show a status on every order and make "fix and resubmit" obvious.

the lesson

I started by designing the sheet around what an order is what the file looks like. When most of the data arrives as a file, the file's shape is the interface. The database, the API and the validation can all adapt to it, and here they barely had to.

First published on maruf.ing. I write about boring backend systems.

title: I scanned my machine for the Brotli RCE. Three stacks were exposed — and the patched one still reports the vulnerable version.
description:
On Wednesday, Node.js disclosed CVE-2026-111497 — "Node2Shell" — an out-of-bounds write in Google's Brotli decoder that can give a remote, unauthenticated attacker code execution in any process that decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data. By Thursday it had a Python chapter. By Friday, Aikido was calling the wider thing "HTTP2Shell," because the vulnerable decoder is bundled into runtimes, HTTP clients, gateways, and half the internet's plumbing. CVSS v4.0: 9.2.

The part that got my attention wasn't the bug. It was this sentence in Aikido's write-up: as of October 23, advisory databases didn't map the CVE to either PyPI package, so pip-audit, Dependabot, and Safety wouldn't flag vulnerable versions. A critical RCE that your scanner cannot see is a specific kind of problem — the kind where "we run pip-audit in CI" and "we are patched" stop having anything to do with each other.

So I audited the machine I'm writing this on. Not a production fleet — one Linux VM, the box that runs my cron jobs and builds my projects. If it's exposed in three places, yours probably is too.

First: what's actually on this box

Brotli reaches a machine through more doors than you installed it through. I checked the three stacks I know about:

Python (pip/distro package)   Brotli 1.1.0     affected range: <= 1.2.0 (PyPI)
Node.js v24.22.1              bundled Brotli reports "1.2.0"
system libbrotli (dpkg)       1.1.0-2build2    curl 8.5.0 links brotli/1.1.0
brotlicffi                    not installed

Three stacks, three separate Brotli builds, none of them something I ever typed install brotli to get. Python's copy arrived as a distro package. Node's is compiled into the runtime. curl's is the system library. This is the defining feature of this CVE: the vulnerable code is a transitive property of other software, and each copy gets patched (or not) on its own vendor's schedule.

Two honesty caveats before the numbers. First, version strings are evidence, not proof: Linux distributions backport security fixes without bumping upstream version numbers, so a "1.1.0" distro package may or may not contain the fix — the vendor's own advisory is the tiebreaker. Second, as you'll see in the Node section, the same lie runs in the opposite direction.

The scanner experiment: the blind window is real, and it already closed

Aikido's claim was time-stamped — "as of October 23." Claims like that expire, so I ran the experiment instead of repeating it. OSV now carries PYSEC-2026-4322 (PyPI brotli) and PYSEC-2026-4323 (PyPI brotlicffi), both published October 23 and modified this morning, October 24, at 10:55 UTC. I pointed pip-audit 2.10.1 at four one-line requirements files:

Brotli==1.2.0        -> FOUND  CVE-2026-111497 / GHSA-9v8h-qqgm-4m35, fix: 1.2.1
Brotli==1.1.0        -> FOUND  CVE-2026-111497 / GHSA-9v8h-qqgm-4m35, fix: 1.2.1
Brotli==1.2.1        -> No known vulnerabilities found
brotlicffi==1.2.0.2  -> FOUND  CVE-2026-111497 / GHSA-9v8h-qqgm-4m35, fix: 1.2.1.0

So the blind window was roughly two days — disclosure on the 21st–22nd, database mapping on the 23rd — and it has closed for the PyPI ecosystem, if your scanner actually refreshes OSV data. That's the part worth internalizing: for about 48 hours, every Python shop running a scanner got a green checkmark on a critical RCE. The scanner wasn't broken. The data wasn't there yet. "Scanner says clean" always means "scanner's database says clean as of its last sync," and this week that distinction had a CVSS 9.2 inside it.

The two databases don't even agree with each other yet. OSV's PYSEC entry enumerates 10 affected brotli versions (0.5.2 through 1.2.0); the GitHub Advisory entry for the same CVE enumerates 7 (1.0.4 through 1.2.0). The fixed-version range is the same (1.2.1), so the practical answer doesn't change — but if your tooling diffs version lists rather than ranges, the lists currently differ.

One more range subtlety. Aikido's patch table lists branch fixes for the C library — 1.0.10 and 1.1.1 alongside 1.2.1. Those exist as upstream Brotli releases. There is no Brotli==1.1.1 on PyPI; for the Python package, 1.2.1 is the only fixed line OSV knows. Don't sit on 1.1.0 waiting for a 1.1.1 pip release that isn't coming.

The Node paradox: the patched runtime still reports the vulnerable version

This box runs Node v24.22.1, which is one of the fixed releases in Node's October security batch. Its changelog entry for the CVE is a cherry-pick of upstream commit 0ed4268 — the actual fix, backported. And yet:

$ node -e "console.log(process.versions.brotli)"
1.2.0

A scanner that reads process.versions.brotli — or any version-string inventory — will flag this patched runtime as vulnerable forever, because a cherry-picked fix doesn't bump the bundled library's version string. Put the two halves together and you get the week's real lesson:

  • For ~48 hours, Python scanners missed a vulnerable library that was actually there.
  • Indefinitely, version-based Node scanning invents a vulnerable library that isn't there.

The version number is a proxy for the code. This CVE breaks the proxy in both directions at once.

I diffed the fix. It's 3 files that matter.

Since the release notes for the fixed PyPI versions don't mention the CVE (Aikido notes this, and it's true of the artifacts I pulled), I downloaded both source distributions from PyPI and diffed them myself:

brotli-1.2.0.tar.gz   7,388,632 bytes
brotli-1.2.1.tar.gz   7,389,447 bytes

files differing: 5 (2 are PKG-INFO metadata)
  c/common/version.h        2 added,  2 removed   (version bump)
  c/include/brotli/decode.h 1 added,  3 removed   (error -17: "reserved" -> BLOCK_SWITCH)
  c/dec/decode.c           59 added, 30 removed   (the actual fix)

The root cause is a classic, and the diff tells it cleanly. DecodeBlockTypeAndLength() returned a boolean, and BROTLI_FALSE meant two different things: "this stream is malformed" and "I need more input." On the fast path, callers discarded the return value entirely (the CVE pairs CWE-252, unchecked return value, with CWE-787, out-of-bounds write). A crafted stream that declares a single block type and then exhausts it forces a block switch that cannot succeed, and the decoder keeps going with stale state — into memory it shouldn't touch.

The fix changes the return type from boolean to an error code, splits the two meanings apart (BROTLI_DECODER_NEEDS_MORE_INPUT vs the newly un-reserved BROTLI_DECODER_ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH, -17), and makes the three block-switch call sites actually check the status via a new BROTLI_SAFE_WITH_STATUS macro. That's the whole patch. Sixty-two net lines in one decoder file, sitting unfixed-in-released-form since February — OpenAI, who found the bug that month, says the root cause was fixed in the Brotli source back then too, but nobody recognized it as a security issue, so no release shipped it until this week. The fix existed for ~8 months. The release is what was missing.

The exposure path, verified locally

"You're exposed if a library you use decompresses Brotli" sounds abstract until you watch it happen. My local urllib3 is 2.0.7. Two facts, both measured, not quoted:

from urllib3.util.request import make_headers
make_headers(keep_alive=True, accept_encoding=True)
# {'accept-encoding': 'gzip,deflate,br', 'connection': 'keep-alive'}

When the Brotli package is importable, urllib3 advertises br on every request — which is why requests and httpx users are in scope without ever importing Brotli themselves. And the decode side doesn't care what you advertised:

local server test (urllib3 HTTPResponse, Content-Encoding: br,
client never sent Accept-Encoding: br):
  33-byte Brotli body -> decoded to the original 190 bytes, no complaint

urllib3 picks its decoder from the response's Content-Encoding header, full stop. A malicious server can send Brotli to a client that never asked for it, which is exactly why Aikido says removing br from your Accept-Encoding is not a fix. Uninstalling the package, or rejecting br at a proxy before anything decodes it, is.

What I'm doing about it, and the scope of this post

Upgrade paths (from the vendor advisories): PyPI Brotli → 1.2.1, brotlicffi → 1.2.1.0; Node → 22.23.4 / 24.22.1 / 26.12.1 or newer; Bun → 1.4.4; native libbrotli → 1.2.1 (or your distro's security update); Envoy and Istio have their own fixed trains. Rebuild container images — an image built last week stays vulnerable no matter what your lockfile says today. If you can't upgrade yet, uninstalling the Python packages genuinely removes those decode paths (gzip/deflate keep working), and a proxy rule rejecting Content-Encoding: br in both directions buys time.

What I did not do: I didn't build the crafted stream or run the ASan proof-of-concept. Everything above is version inventory, scanner behavior, a source diff, and decoder-selection behavior on my own machine — that's enough to act on, and the exploit itself adds heat, not information. The one number I can't give you is whether your box is exposed, because that was the whole point of this post: until two days ago your scanner couldn't tell you either, and on Node it still can't — in the opposite direction.

Sources: Aikido's Node2Shell/HTTP2Shell write-up (aikido.dev, updated Oct 23), Node.js October 2026 security releases, OSV entries CVE-2026-111497 / PYSEC-2026-4322 / PYSEC-2026-4323 / GHSA-9v8h-qqgm-4m35 (queried Oct 24). All version checks, pip-audit runs, the sdist diff, and the urllib3 test are my own runs on a 2 vCPU Linux VM today.

title: Claude's download page only detects your OS on a direct visit
description:
I found a small but visible UI bug on Claude's download page, claude.ai/download.

What happens

  • Direct visit: the page detects your operating system and shows the matching download options.
  • Arriving from another page (for example claude.ai/downloads, then "Download for Linux"): the OS check doesn't run. Every platform's button is shown, and the "Windows (arm64)" and "macOS" buttons render on top of each other.

Steps to reproduce

  1. Open claude.ai/downloads
  2. Click "Download for Linux"
  3. Look at the download buttons on claude.ai/download

Seen in Chrome on Fedora Linux.

Likely cause

My guess: the OS detection only runs on a full page load, so an in-app navigation renders the fallback "all platforms" layout, and that layout was never checked with all five buttons visible at once.

title: Go 1.27 Ships a uuid Package. Dropping google/uuid Takes 4 Steps and One NULL Catch
description:
• Book: The Complete Guide to Go Programming
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Open a Go service's go.mod and there's a good chance github.com/google/uuid is in it. Its latest tag, v1.6.0, dates from January 2024. Since Go 1.27 shipped on 2026-08-19, you no longer need it for the common cases. The release notes say it in one line: "The new uuid package generates and parses UUIDs."

The import path is just uuid. The swap looks like a find-and-replace on the import line. It mostly is. Two things will fail to compile, which is good, because the compiler finds them for you. One thing compiles fine and then fails at runtime on the first row with a NULL in it. That one is the reason for this post.

What the stdlib package gives you

The package docs describe a small surface, built on RFC 9562:

  • type UUID [16]byte, comparable with ==.
  • New() for general use, currently the same as NewV4().
  • NewV4() (122 random bits) and NewV7() (48-bit millisecond timestamp plus at least 62 random bits).
  • Parse, MustParse, and the functions Nil() and Max().
  • Methods: String, Compare, MarshalText, UnmarshalText, AppendText.

Parse accepts the hyphenated form, the same form in curly braces, the urn:uuid: prefix, and 32 bare hex digits, in either case. That matches the input forms google/uuid accepts, so stored strings keep parsing.

What's missing compared to google/uuid: no v1, v3, v5 or v6 constructors, no Version() or Time() methods, no MarshalBinary, and no NullUUID type. This write-up of the accepted proposal walks through why the API stayed this small; the discussion lives in golang/go#62026.

Here is the service we'll migrate. It's the shape most code has: a v7 ID generator, a nil check, and a table with a nullable foreign key.

package orders

import (
    "database/sql"

    "github.com/google/uuid"
)

type Order struct {
    ID       uuid.UUID
    ParentID uuid.UUID // uuid.Nil when no parent
}

func NewOrder() (Order, error) {
    id, err := uuid.NewV7()
    if err != nil {
        return Order{}, err
    }
    return Order{ID: id}, nil
}

func (o Order) IsRoot() bool {
    return o.ParentID == uuid.Nil
}

func Load(db *sql.DB, id uuid.UUID) (Order, error) {
    var o Order
    err := db.QueryRow(
        `SELECT id, parent_id FROM orders WHERE id = $1`,
        id,
    ).Scan(&o.ID, &o.ParentID)
    return o, err
}

Step 1: bump the go directive first

Do this before you touch an import:

go mod edit -go=1.27

The compiler won't stop you from importing uuid while go.mod still says go 1.26. Your tests will. Go 1.27 made go test run the stdversion vet check by default, and that check "reports the use of standard library symbols that are too new for the Go version in force in the referring file, as determined by go directive in go.mod and build tags on the file." Skip the bump and go build passes, then go test fails, on your machine and in CI.

Watch for files with their own //go:build go1.26 style constraints too. The check reads build tags as well as go.mod.

Step 2: swap the import and follow the compiler

Change the import to "uuid", run go build ./..., and fix what breaks. Two errors show up in almost every codebase.

NewV7 no longer returns an error. In google/uuid the signature is func NewV7() (UUID, error). In the stdlib it is func NewV7() UUID. Same story for uuid.Must(uuid.NewRandom()), which becomes uuid.NewV4().

Nil is a function now. In google/uuid, Nil and Max are variables. In the stdlib they are func Nil() UUID and func Max() UUID, so x == uuid.Nil compares a UUID against a function and fails to compile. Add the parentheses.

func NewOrder() Order {
    return Order{ID: uuid.NewV7()}
}

func (o Order) IsRoot() bool {
    return o.ParentID == uuid.Nil()
}

If your code called id.Time() or id.Version(), you have to write those yourself. Both are fixed bit positions in RFC 9562: the version is the high nibble of byte 6, and a v7 timestamp is the first 48 bits, in milliseconds.

func Version(u uuid.UUID) int {
    return int(u[6] >> 4)
}

func V7Time(u uuid.UUID) time.Time {
    ms := int64(u[0])<<40 | int64(u[1])<<32 |
        int64(u[2])<<24 | int64(u[3])<<16 |
        int64(u[4])<<8 | int64(u[5])
    return time.UnixMilli(ms)
}

Step 3: migrate package by package with a cast

In a big repo you won't flip every package in one PR. You don't have to. Both types have the same underlying type, [16]byte, so Go lets you convert between them directly. Import the old package under an alias at the seam:

import (
    guuid "github.com/google/uuid"
    "uuid"
)

func fromLegacy(id guuid.UUID) uuid.UUID {
    return uuid.UUID(id)
}

func toLegacy(id uuid.UUID) guuid.UUID {
    return guuid.UUID(id)
}

The conversion copies 16 bytes and nothing else. The JSON wire format doesn't change either: both packages implement MarshalText with the lowercase hyphenated string, so encoding/json writes the same string for both types.

While you're here, use what v7 buys you. The docs say NewV7 "always returns UUIDs which sort in increasing order, except when the system clock moves backwards", and Compare orders by big-endian bytes per RFC 9562 §6.11. A method expression drops straight into slices.SortFunc:

ids := []uuid.UUID{
    uuid.NewV7(), uuid.NewV7(), uuid.NewV7(),
}
slices.SortFunc(ids, uuid.UUID.Compare)

slices.SortFunc(orders, func(a, b Order) int {
    return a.ID.Compare(b.ID)
})

For v7 IDs, that's creation order without a separate created_at sort key, as long as the clocks behave.

Step 4: the database, and the NULL catch

The stdlib type has no Scan or Value methods. Go 1.27 doesn't need them, because database/sql itself knows about uuid.UUID:

  • Writing: the default parameter converter has a case uuid.UUID: return vr.String(), nil branch (source at go1.27.3). That's the same string google/uuid's Value() returns.
  • Reading: Rows.Scan lists *uuid.UUID as a supported destination. "The source may contain the string representation of a UUID, or a 16-byte []byte."

So Load compiles and works unchanged for rows that have a parent. Then it hits a root order with parent_id IS NULL.

google/uuid's Scan returns nil on a nil source without touching the destination (so a fresh variable stays uuid.Nil), and it does the same for an empty string. The stdlib path does neither. In convertAssignRows, the nil source branch only handles *any, *[]byte and *RawBytes. A NULL scanned into *uuid.UUID falls through to the generic "unsupported Scan" error. An empty string goes through uuid.Parse and fails there.

Your old code relied on NULL quietly becoming uuid.Nil. With the default conversion, the scan now errors on the first root order. Nothing flags it at compile time, and a test suite that only seeds child orders will pass.

The fix is the generic sql.Null[T], which has been in the stdlib since Go 1.22. Its Scan handles nil and delegates everything else to the same conversion, and its Value runs through the default converter, so a valid UUID is written as a string:

func Load(db *sql.DB, id uuid.UUID) (Order, error) {
    var o Order
    var parent sql.Null[uuid.UUID]
    err := db.QueryRow(
        `SELECT id, parent_id FROM orders WHERE id = $1`,
        id,
    ).Scan(&o.ID, &parent)
    if err != nil {
        return Order{}, err
    }
    if parent.Valid {
        o.ParentID = parent.V
    }
    return o, nil
}

If you used uuid.NullUUID, the field names change: .UUID becomes .V, .Valid stays.

One more check before you ship. The default converter only runs when your driver lets it. The driver.Value docs note that a driver implementing NamedValueChecker handles argument types itself. If yours does, read its docs for how it treats a [16]byte before you assume the string path. Reads have the same escape hatch: Go 1.27 lets a driver implement RowsColumnScanner and "scan directly into user-provided destinations", so the NULL error above is what database/sql does by default, and a driver that scans for itself may behave differently. Grep for every column you scan into a UUID, find the nullable ones, and write one test that loads a NULL. That one test covers the catch.

If this was useful

The swap is small because both types share [16]byte and database/sql already knows the new one. The Complete Guide to Go Programming covers that layer, the type system and the standard library, along with the runtime behaviour that decides whether a change like this is a cast or a rewrite. If you'd rather understand the stdlib than memorise its signatures, start with the book.

title: Re-Saving a JPEG at Quality 90 Can Make It Bigger. Measure Before You "Compress"
description:
A common bug report for image tools: "I compressed my photo and the file got bigger." It sounds impossible. It isn't, and it's worth understanding, because the same mistake shows up in build pipelines and CMS plugins.

Quality is not "percent of the original"

When you save a JPEG at quality 90, the 90 doesn't mean "90% of the file you opened". It selects a set of quantization tables, which control how much detail the encoder throws away. The encoder doesn't know or care how the input was saved before.

So take a photo that was saved at quality 75, open it, and save it at quality 90. The encoder now spends more bits per block than the original did. It carefully preserves detail, including the blocky artefacts from the first save. The result looks no better than the q75 file, and it's larger.

Measure it yourself

This Node script takes any JPEG and re-encodes it at a few qualities, then saves it ten times in a row at quality 90:

// node resave.mjs photo.jpg
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises"
import sharp from "sharp"

const original = await readFile(process.argv[2])
console.log("original".padEnd(12), (original.length / 1024).toFixed(0), "KB")

for (const quality of [95, 90, 80, 70]) {
  const out = await sharp(original).jpeg({ quality }).toBuffer()
  console.log(`q${quality}`.padEnd(12), (out.length / 1024).toFixed(0), "KB")
}

let gen = original
for (let i = 1; i <= 10; i++) gen = await sharp(gen).jpeg({ quality: 90 }).toBuffer()
console.log("10x q90".padEnd(12), (gen.length / 1024).toFixed(0), "KB")

Here's one run on a synthetic test image (random noise, 1600×1200, originally saved at quality 75). Real photos will give different numbers, so treat this as a demonstration and run it on yours:

original     613 KB
q95          918 KB
q90          770 KB
q80          639 KB
q70          584 KB
10x q90      761 KB

Three things to notice:

  • q90 and q95 made it bigger, by 26% and 50%.
  • Even q80 made it bigger. Only going below the original's quality actually saved bytes.
  • Ten saves at q90 didn't keep growing. After the first re-encode the size settles. The quality loss from repeated saves is real, but it's mostly in the first generations.

Run it on your own photos. You'll quickly learn where "compression" stops paying for that kind of image.

The rule every compressor needs

Whatever the settings, a compressor must never hand back a bigger file than it was given:

const blob = await encode(file, { type: "image/jpeg", quality })
const grew = blob.size >= file.size
const result = grew
  ? { blob: file, size: file.size, grew: true } // keep the original, say so
  : { blob, size: blob.size, grew: false }

And tell the user when it happens. "Already well compressed, kept the original" is useful information. A silent "-0%" or a larger download is a bug.

What actually reduces a JPEG

If the quality is already low, re-encoding won't save much. These do:

  1. Fewer pixels. A 4000 px photo shown at 1200 px on a page wastes most of its bytes. Resizing usually saves more than any quality setting.
  2. Strip metadata. EXIF, embedded thumbnails and colour profiles can add tens of KB, and EXIF may include GPS location.
  3. Chroma subsampling (4:2:0). Most photo encoders use it by default; check yours does for photos.
  4. A modern format where you control the delivery, like WebP or AVIF on your own site.

And keep the original. Every lossy save throws detail away for good, so compress from the master copy, not from yesterday's compressed export.

Try it on your photos

BatchSet's free JPEG compressor follows these rules: you pick a quality, it shows the size change on every file, and when a re-encode would be bigger it keeps your original and says so. It runs in the browser, so the photos aren't uploaded.

This article was drafted with an AI assistant. The script was run before publishing; the numbers shown come from a synthetic test image, as stated.

title: Stripping metadata without breaking colour: keep the ICC profile
description:
Strip EXIF, XMP and IPTC, but never drop the ICC profile unless you convert the pixels to sRGB first. A phone photo in Display P3 that loses its profile is read as sRGB, and the colour goes flat. In my test, Pillow's default save() cut average saturation from 55.3 to 49.4. sharp's default converts to sRGB before it strips, so it stays close at 54.2.

Why does dropping the profile change the colour?

An ICC profile tells the viewer what the numbers in each pixel mean. The same RGB triple is a more saturated green in Display P3 than in sRGB. When the profile goes, every browser falls back to sRGB and reads the P3 numbers as sRGB numbers. Nothing is "lost" in the bytes. The meaning is.

Phone photos often carry a Display P3 profile, like the one below. A "strip all metadata" step that treats the profile like GPS data quietly dulls every one of them.

What does each library do by default?

I took a 2250 × 4000 phone photo whose embedded profile is Apple's "Display P3" (548 bytes), resized it to 1200 px wide, and saved it as a quality-80 JPEG in several ways.

sharp first. Its output docs say all metadata is removed by default, and keepIccProfile() keeps the input profile:

import sharp from 'sharp';
import { writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises';

const src = 'p3.jpg';
const base = () => sharp(src).resize({ width: 1200 });
const variants = {
  default: base().jpeg({ quality: 80 }),
  keepIcc: base().keepIccProfile().jpeg({ quality: 80 }),
  srgbTagged: base().withIccProfile('srgb').jpeg({ quality: 80 }),
  ignore: sharp(src, { ignoreIcc: true }).resize({ width: 1200 }).jpeg({ quality: 80 }),
};
for (const [name, pipe] of Object.entries(variants)) {
  const buf = await pipe.toBuffer();
  await writeFile(`${name}.jpg`, buf);
  const m = await sharp(buf).metadata();
  console.log(name.padEnd(11), String(buf.length).padStart(7), 'bytes  icc:', m.icc ? m.icc.length + ' bytes' : 'none');
}

default      323884 bytes  icc: none
keepIcc      321937 bytes  icc: 548 bytes
srgbTagged   324382 bytes  icc: 480 bytes
ignore       321371 bytes  icc: none

Then Pillow. Its JPEG docs are plain about it: without icc_profile, the image is saved with no profile attached. Pillow does not convert the pixels either.

from PIL import Image

im = Image.open("p3.jpg")
icc = im.info.get("icc_profile")
im = im.resize((1200, round(im.height * 1200 / im.width)), Image.LANCZOS)
im.save("pil_default.jpg", quality=80)                    # profile gone
im.save("pil_keep.jpg", quality=80, icc_profile=icc)      # profile kept

pil_default.jpg 325604 bytes  icc: none
pil_keep.jpg    326170 bytes  icc: 548

How do you measure "flat"?

I rendered each file the way a colour-managed viewer does: apply its profile, land in sRGB. Then I took the mean of each channel and an average saturation (max channel minus min channel, per pixel).

import sharp from 'sharp';

async function look(input) {
  const { data } = await input.toColourspace('srgb').raw().toBuffer({ resolveWithObject: true });
  let r = 0, g = 0, b = 0, sat = 0;
  const n = data.length / 3;
  for (let i = 0; i < data.length; i += 3) {
    r += data[i]; g += data[i + 1]; b += data[i + 2];
    sat += Math.max(data[i], data[i + 1], data[i + 2]) - Math.min(data[i], data[i + 1], data[i + 2]);
  }
  return `R ${(r / n).toFixed(1)}  G ${(g / n).toFixed(1)}  B ${(b / n).toFixed(1)}  saturation ${(sat / n).toFixed(1)}`;
}

console.log('source     ', await look(sharp('p3.jpg').resize({ width: 1200 })));
for (const f of ['default', 'keepIcc', 'pil_keep', 'pil_default', 'pil_srgb', 'ignore'])
  console.log(f.padEnd(11), await look(sharp(`${f}.jpg`)));

source      R 102.5  G 123.5  B 71.5  saturation 55.3
default     R 102.5  G 123.5  B 72.7  saturation 54.2
keepIcc     R 102.5  G 123.5  B 71.6  saturation 55.3
pil_keep    R 102.6  G 123.6  B 71.7  saturation 55.4
pil_default R 107.7  G 123.1  B 77.0  saturation 49.4
pil_srgb    R 102.6  G 123.6  B 72.7  saturation 54.3
ignore      R 107.6  G 123.0  B 76.9  saturation 49.4
Pipeline Bytes Profile in file Saturation
Source, resized only 55.3
sharp keepIccProfile() 321,937 Display P3, 548 B 55.3
Pillow icc_profile=icc 326,170 Display P3, 548 B 55.4
sharp default (converts to sRGB) 323,884 none 54.2
Pillow, ImageCms to sRGB 328,215 none 54.3
Pillow save() default 325,604 none 49.4
sharp ignoreIcc: true 321,371 none 49.4

The broken files sit at 49.4, about 11% less saturated, with red and blue pushed up. The sharp default lands at 54.2, a touch below the source. Its conversion to sRGB clips the P3 greens that sRGB cannot hold. That is the honest cost of sRGB, not a bug.

Note: The profile costs 548 bytes here, about 0.2% of a 322 KB JPEG. Keeping it is never the reason a file is too big. Stripping it to "save space" is the mistake.

Which fix should you pick?

You have two correct options. Both remove EXIF, XMP and IPTC.

Keep the profile. Wide-gamut screens show the full P3 colour. In sharp, add keepIccProfile(). In Pillow, pass icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile") to save().

Convert to sRGB, then drop it. Every screen shows the same colour, and the file needs no profile. sharp's default already does this. In Pillow you do it yourself with ImageCms:

import io
from PIL import Image, ImageCms

im = Image.open("p3.jpg")
icc = im.info.get("icc_profile")
im = im.resize((1200, round(im.height * 1200 / im.width)), Image.LANCZOS)
if icc:
    src = ImageCms.ImageCmsProfile(io.BytesIO(icc))
    dst = ImageCms.createProfile("sRGB")
    im = ImageCms.profileToProfile(im, src, dst, outputMode="RGB")
im.save("pil_srgb.jpg", quality=80)  # no profile needed: the pixels are sRGB now

That file printed 328,215 bytes and saturation 54.3, level with sharp's default.

The one pipeline to avoid is the one that drops the profile and keeps the numbers. In sharp you only get there on purpose, with { ignoreIcc: true }. In Pillow it is the default.

Where does this bite in practice?

  • An upload handler in Python that re-saves every image "to strip GPS" with a bare save().
  • A sharp pipeline someone "fixed" with ignoreIcc: true to silence a colour-space warning.
  • A thumbnail job that copies EXIF by hand and forgets the profile, which lives in its own segment.

A quick check for any pipeline: read the output with sharp(buf).metadata(). If the input had icc and the output has none, the pixels must have been converted. Compare a saturation number like the one above to be sure.

I run the same kind of before-and-after check on every number Blinkimg publishes; how we measure lists the method.

How I measured

  • Machine: Apple M1 Pro, macOS, 2026-10-17.
  • Node v24.22.0, sharp 0.35.4, libvips 8.18.6, lcms 2.19.1.
  • Python 3.9.6, Pillow 11.3.0 in a fresh venv.
  • Source: a 2250 × 4000 phone JPEG from the Blinkimg image library, embedded profile "Display P3" (Apple, 548 bytes), no EXIF.
  • Every output: resized to 1200 px wide, JPEG quality 80. Saturation is computed after applying each file's profile and converting to sRGB with sharp.

What I did not test

PNG, WebP and AVIF outputs, 16-bit sources, and CMYK profiles. I did not measure how browsers on non-P3 screens render the P3 file.

I build Blinkimg, an image compressor and converter with a developer API. I wrote this article with help from an AI assistant (Claude), which ran the code on my machine; every number in it comes from those runs.
