title: How to Calculate Text Pixel-Width in JavaScript (And Why Character Count Lies)
description:
Every frontend developer has built a character counter at some point:

if (input.value.length > 60) {
  showWarning("Your title is too long!");
}

It feels clean, predictable, and logical. There’s just one problem: modern UI layout engines don’t care about character count.

When CSS applies text-overflow: ellipsis or -webkit-line-clamp: 2, the browser doesn’t count how many letters are inside your string. It calculates how many horizontal pixels those glyphs occupy inside a bounding box.

I ran into this firsthand while building a YouTube packaging utility. Every "YouTube SEO guide" on the internet repeats the same rule: Keep your video titles under 60 characters so they don't get cut off.

So I tested a 52-character title in uppercase:

WHY WE DROPPED KUBERNETES FOR BARE METAL SERVERS IN 2026 (56 chars)

On a standard mobile viewport, YouTube truncated it right after SERVERS...—hiding the year and killing the hook. Meanwhile, a 68-character title packed with narrow lowercase letters (i, l, t, r) rendered completely intact without an ellipsis in sight.

If you are building social previewers, SEO audit tools, or dynamic UI cards, relying on string.length will give your users false positives and false negatives. Here is why proportional fonts break character counters—and how to measure exact pixel width in JavaScript without rendering hidden DOM nodes.

Proportional Fonts vs. Monospace Math

Unless your app renders everything in Courier New or JetBrains Mono, your users are looking at a proportional typeface. In YouTube’s case, that’s primarily Roboto (for body and feed metadata) and YouTube Sans (for display headers).

In a proportional font, every glyph has its own advance width:

Character, Font (500 16px Roboto), Approximate Width
i or l, Lowercase narrow, ~4.4px
e or a, Lowercase standard, ~8.8px
W or M, Uppercase wide, ~14.8px
@ or %, Wide symbol, ~15.2px

Ten uppercase Ws take up 148 pixels. Ten lowercase is take up 44 pixels.

To String.prototype.length, both strings equal 10. To a mobile screen with a 340px text container, one fits comfortably while the other overflows by more than 300%.
Approach 1: The Naive DOM Measurement (And Why to Avoid It)

When developers first realize they need pixel width instead of character length, the instinct is to measure a hidden :

`// ⚠️ Anti-pattern: Causes layout thrashing
function getWidthViaDOM(text, font) {
const span = document.createElement('span');
span.style.font = font;
span.style.visibility = 'hidden';
span.style.position = 'absolute';
span.style.whiteSpace = 'nowrap';
span.textContent = text;

document.body.appendChild(span);
const width = span.getBoundingClientRect().width;
document.body.removeChild(span);

return width;
}`

While this works for a single string, calling it on every input event or running it across a batch of 20 title variations triggers synchronous layout recalculations (reflows). You are mutating the DOM tree, forcing the browser to compute styles and geometry, and immediately tearing it down.

Approach 2: Offscreen Canvas measureText() (Zero Reflows)

A much cleaner, faster method lives inside the HTML5 2D Canvas API: CanvasRenderingContext2D.measureText().

Because an unattached element exists entirely in memory, querying text metrics on its 2D context never touches the DOM tree and never triggers a browser reflow.

Here is a production-ready utility that reuses a single canvas instance via closure:

`const TextWidthMeasurer = (() => {
// Create a single offscreen canvas instance in memory
let canvas = null;

return function measureTextWidth(text, fontSpecification = '500 16px Roboto, Arial, sans-serif') {
if (!text) return 0;

if (!canvas) {
  canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
}

const context = canvas.getContext('2d');
context.font = fontSpecification;

const metrics = context.measureText(text);

// actualBoundingBoxLeft + actualBoundingBoxRight gives tighter glyph bounds,
// while metrics.width gives the layout advance width used by CSS boxes.
return Math.ceil(metrics.width);

};
})();

// Usage comparison:
const narrowTitle = "10 little tips to write cleaner typescript"; // 42 chars
const wideTitle = "WHY WWW ARCHITECTURE WORKS WITH WEBGL NOW"; // 41 chars

console.log(TextWidthMeasurer(narrowTitle)); // ~298px
console.log(TextWidthMeasurer(wideTitle)); // ~462px`

Notice that wideTitle is actually 1 character shorter than narrowTitle, yet it consumes 164 more pixels of horizontal screen real estate.

**

Handling Two-Line Clamping (-webkit-line-clamp: 2)

**

Single-line truncation is easy: if pixelWidth > containerWidth, the text truncates.

However, platforms like YouTube wrap video titles across two lines before cutting them off with an ellipsis (...). A single pixel sum won't tell you the whole story because words don't split arbitrarily mid-character—they wrap at whitespace boundaries.

If you have a long word near the end of Line 1 (like Authentication or Microservices), it gets pushed to Line 2 early, leaving empty space on Line 1 and eating up precious room on Line 2.

To simulate two-line wrapping accurately in JavaScript, we can write a greedy line-breaker using our TextWidthMeasurer:

`function checkTwoLineTruncation(text, maxLineWidthPx = 310, font = '500 16px Roboto, Arial, sans-serif') {
const words = text.trim().split(/\s+/);
const ellipsisWidth = TextWidthMeasurer('...', font);

let currentLine = 1;
let currentLineWidth = 0;
const spaceWidth = TextWidthMeasurer(' ', font);

for (let i = 0; i < words.length; i++) {
const wordWidth = TextWidthMeasurer(words[i], font);
const widthWithWord = currentLineWidth === 0
? wordWidth
: currentLineWidth + spaceWidth + wordWidth;

if (widthWithWord <= maxLineWidthPx) {
  currentLineWidth = widthWithWord;
} else {
  // Word doesn't fit on Line 1, move to Line 2
  if (currentLine === 1) {
    currentLine = 2;
    currentLineWidth = wordWidth;
  } else {
    // Overflowing Line 2! Calculate where ellipsis cuts it off
    return {
      isTruncated: true,
      linesUsed: 2,
      overflowStartsAtWord: words[i],
      safeTextPreview: words.slice(0, i).join(' ') + '...'
    };
  }
}

}

// Edge case: text fits on Line 2, but sits dangerously close to the ellipsis zone
const isDangerZone = currentLine === 2 && (currentLineWidth > maxLineWidthPx - ellipsisWidth);

return {
isTruncated: false,
isDangerZone,
linesUsed: currentLine,
finalLineWidthPx: currentLineWidth
};
}`

Why This Matters for Real-World Tooling

When creators brainstorm video titles, they usually front-load context and put the punchline at the end:

"I Tried Switching From VS Code to Neovim for 30 Days and Here Is What Broke"

Run that through a basic character counter (75 chars) and you only know it's "kind of long." Run it through checkTwoLineTruncation() against a mobile feed width, and you can immediately show the user that "and Here Is What Broke" gets sliced off into "and Here..." on an iPhone screen.

We implemented this exact pixel-width check inside our AI YouTube Title Generator so creators don't get their hooks cut off on mobile. And if you want to visually inspect how those two-line wraps interact with actual video artwork, dark mode contrast, and timestamp badges, you can drag and drop an image directly into our in-browser YouTube thumbnail tester without uploading anything to a server.

3 Gotchas When Using canvas.measureText()

If you decide to replace character counters with pixel measurements in your own project, watch out for these three browser quirks:

  1. Web Fonts Must Be Loaded First

If your CSS loads Roboto or Inter asynchronously from Google Fonts, calling measureText() before the font finishes downloading will silently fall back to measuring the system default (Times New Roman or Arial). Always await document.fonts.ready before running measurements:

await document.fonts.ready;
const accurateWidth = TextWidthMeasurer("Hello World", "500 16px Roboto");

  1. Emojis Have Platform-Specific Widths

An emoji like 🚀 or 🔥 is 2 bytes (or more via surrogate pairs) in JavaScript's UTF-16 .length, meaning "🔥🔥🔥".length evaluates to 6, not 3. Visually, however, emojis render as square glyphs roughly equal to the font's em size (~16px to 18px). measureText() handles emojis much more accurately than .length, though Apple Color Emoji (macOS/iOS) and Segoe UI Emoji (Windows) can vary by 1–2 pixels.

  1. letter-spacing Isn't Included in context.font

Historically, the shorthand context.font property only accepts font-style, font-weight, font-size, and font-family. If your target UI uses custom letter-spacing (e.g., -0.2px), modern browsers now support setting context.letterSpacing = '-0.2px' directly on the 2D canvas context before calling measureText().

Takeaway

string.length is great for database column constraints (VARCHAR(255)), SMS segment billing, and API payload validation.

But whenever your validation logic is meant to protect visual presentation, character count is a leaky abstraction. A 25-line Canvas helper gives your users real layout feedback in microseconds—without touching the DOM.

title: I Ran All 16 Code Snippets the USB Coding Expert Demo Can Generate. 8 Survived - and the Other 8 Fail Three Different Ways
description:
I ran all 16 code snippets the USB Coding Expert demo can generate. 8 survived, and the 8 that didn't fail in three different ways.

Every WorkflowAlpha product page ships a working demo, so you can test before you pay.
That is the whole pitch, and it means the demo has to hold up when you actually poke
it. I did that for USB Coding Expert ($149.99).

The generator is a keyword router over a fixed table: four prompts x four languages =
sixteen canned strings. I extracted the table from the live page and executed every
one of the sixteen. Here is the real tally.

8 of 16 snippets executed to a genuine result

These ran and returned the exact output the page promises:

Snippet Result
python / reverse Reversed: dlrow olleh
python / file Written 29 bytes to test.txt
python / http HTTP 200: <h1>Hello from USB Coding Expert!</h1>
javascript / reverse Reversed: dlrow olleh
javascript / file Written 29 bytes to test.txt
javascript / http HTTP 200: <h1>Hello from USB Coding Expert!</h1>
bash / reverse dlrow olleh
bash / file wrote the file, printed it back

So the reverse, file and HTTP presets are real, copy-pasteable code in three of the
four languages. That is the honest core of the demo and it is not nothing.

The 8 that did not survive, in three distinct failure modes

1. Wrong language entirely (python/token). The page hands you Solidity syntax on
the Python tab:

SyntaxError: invalid syntax
    pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

That is not a "does not compile" problem. Python cannot parse it at all. It is the
same complaint as the earlier teardown, and it is still true.

2. Missing dependency, not a bug (javascript/token). It loads web3, which is not
in the page's environment:

Error: Cannot find module 'web3'

The snippet is plausible; it just needs an install step the page never mentions.

3. Missing toolchain (bash/token). The script calls solc and geth:

solc: command not found
cat: build/Token.bin: No such file or directory

Neither binary is present on a stock host, and the page does not list them as
prerequisites.

And the four Solidity snippets I could not verify at all. There is no Solidity
compiler on this machine, so solidity/reverse, solidity/http, solidity/file and
solidity/token are not compile-checked. I checked brace balance and the pragma
line only. Do not read that as "they work" - it means I have no evidence either way.

The bash/http snippet is environment-dependent

One caveat worth flagging, because it is the kind of thing that makes a demo look
broken when it isn't. The bash HTTP preset pipes into nc -l -p 8080. On this host
that snippet answered HTTP 200 when I ran it once and hung on every retry - the
netcat build here is inconsistent about when it starts listening. If you test the demo
and the Bash tab looks dead, try the Python or JavaScript tab before concluding the
page is broken. It may be your netcat, not the product.

What this means if you are evaluating it

The demo is a real, runnable code table - not a fake animation. Eight snippets execute
and the output matches the copy. But it is a router over sixteen canned strings, not a
model, and the failures cluster exactly where the page's own marketing is weakest:

  • it says "generate real working code" while one tab returns a different language's syntax;
  • it lists four languages while the ERC-20 preset only makes sense in two of them;
  • it never states that solc, geth or web3 are required.

USB Coding Expert's actual claim is much bigger than the demo: a bootable, air-gapped,
self-contained coding environment on a USB stick that leaves the host byte-for-byte
identical. That is a systems claim and a security claim, and the sixteen-string demo
does not test either of them. It tests whether the page's generator returns coherent
snippets, which it does - eight times out of sixteen.

If you are deciding, test the demo yourself and treat it as a syntax sample, not as
evidence of the air-gap behaviour. Payment details and the full package breakdown are
on the page.

This is an independent look at a live demo. I have no affiliation with the vendor.

title: Optimizing Real-time Data Streams with WebSockets and Node.js: A High-Throughput Guide
description:
Introduction: The Pulse of Modern Applications

In today's interconnected digital landscape, real-time data is no longer a luxury but a fundamental expectation. From collaborative tools and live dashboards to instant messaging and online gaming, users demand immediate updates and seamless interactivity. Traditional request-response protocols like HTTP, while robust, often fall short in delivering the instantaneous, persistent communication required by these modern applications.

This is where WebSockets shine. Offering full-duplex, persistent connections between client and server, WebSockets are the backbone of efficient real-time data streaming. However, simply using WebSockets isn't enough; architecting them for high-throughput and low-latency, especially with Node.js, presents its own set of challenges. In this comprehensive guide, we'll dive deep into optimizing WebSocket data streams, covering everything from fundamental concepts and architectural considerations to practical performance strategies and robust implementation techniques that will enable you to build truly responsive and scalable real-time applications.

The Foundation: Understanding WebSockets

Before we optimize, let's briefly revisit what makes WebSockets so powerful for real-time communication.

HTTP vs. WebSockets: A Fundamental Difference

  • HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol): A stateless, request-response protocol. Each client request requires the server to process it and send a response. For real-time updates, this often necessitates techniques like long polling or server-sent events (SSE), which can be inefficient or introduce significant overhead.
  • WebSockets: After an initial HTTP handshake, a WebSocket connection upgrades to a persistent, full-duplex communication channel. This means both the client and server can send data to each other at any time, without the overhead of establishing new connections for each message. This 'always-on' connection makes it ideal for real-time, bi-directional data exchange.

Basic WebSocket Server Setup with Node.js

Node.js is an excellent choice for WebSocket servers due to its event-driven, non-blocking I/O model. The ws library is a popular and performant choice. Let's set up a basic server:

// server.js
import { WebSocketServer } from 'ws';

const wss = new WebSocketServer({ port: 8080 });

console.log('WebSocket server started on port 8080');

wss.on('connection', ws => {
  console.log('Client connected');

  ws.on('message', message => {
    console.log(`Received message: ${message}`);
    // Echo the message back to the client
    ws.send(`Server received: ${message}`);
  });

  ws.on('close', () => {
    console.log('Client disconnected');
  });

  ws.on('error', error => {
    console.error('WebSocket error:', error);
  });
});

This simple server listens for connections, logs incoming messages, and echoes them back. While functional, it's far from optimized for high-throughput scenarios.

Architectural Considerations for High-Throughput

Achieving high throughput with WebSockets in Node.js requires careful architectural planning, especially when dealing with a large number of concurrent connections and rapid data exchange.

1. Scaling Horizontally: Beyond a Single Process

Node.js applications, by default, run in a single thread. To leverage multi-core processors and handle more connections, horizontal scaling is essential.

  • Node.js Cluster Module: The built-in cluster module allows you to fork multiple Node.js processes, each acting as a worker. A master process manages these workers, distributing incoming connections. While simple, it requires careful handling for WebSocket sticky sessions.
  • Load Balancers with Sticky Sessions: When deploying multiple WebSocket server instances behind a load balancer (e.g., Nginx, HAProxy), it's crucial to ensure that a client's WebSocket connection always routes to the same server instance. This is known as 'sticky sessions' and is typically achieved by hashing the client's IP address or using a cookie. Without sticky sessions, a client's messages might be routed to a different server instance, breaking the continuous WebSocket connection state. 
// server_cluster.js (Simplified cluster example for concept)
import { WebSocketServer } from 'ws';
import cluster from 'cluster';
import os from 'os';

const numCPUs = os.cpus().length;

if (cluster.isMaster) {
  console.log(`Master ${process.pid} is running`);

  // Fork workers.
  for (let i = 0; i < numCPUs; i++) {
    cluster.fork();
  }

  cluster.on('exit', (worker, code, signal) => {
    console.log(`worker ${worker.process.pid} died`);
    // Restart the worker
    cluster.fork();
  });
} else {
  // Workers can share any TCP connection
  // In a real-world scenario, you'd use a shared port
  // and rely on a load balancer with sticky sessions.
  const wss = new WebSocketServer({ port: 8080 });
  console.log(`Worker ${process.pid} started on port 8080`);

  wss.on('connection', ws => {
    console.log(`Client connected to worker ${process.pid}`);
    ws.on('message', message => {
      // ... message handling ...
      ws.send(`Hello from worker ${process.pid}: ${message}`);
    });
    // ... other event handlers ...
  });
}

2. Message Queues for Inter-Process Communication and Reliability

When you scale horizontally, individual WebSocket server instances become isolated. If a client connects to Server A and sends a message meant for clients connected to Server B, Server A won't know about those clients. This is where message queues or Pub/Sub systems become indispensable.

  • Redis Pub/Sub: A lightweight and fast in-memory data store with powerful publish/subscribe capabilities. Each WebSocket server instance can subscribe to relevant Redis channels. When a message needs to be broadcast across all connected clients (potentially on different servers), the sending server publishes the message to a Redis channel, and all other subscribed servers receive it and then relay it to their connected clients.
  • Apache Kafka / RabbitMQ: For more robust, scalable, and durable message queuing, especially in enterprise-grade applications, systems like Kafka or RabbitMQ offer advanced features like message persistence, complex routing, and consumer groups. 
// Example: Conceptual Redis Pub/Sub integration
// This would typically involve a separate Redis client library (e.g., 'ioredis')

// In a worker process:
import Redis from 'ioredis';

const subscriber = new Redis();
const publisher = new Redis();

subscriber.subscribe('chat_channel', (err, count) => {
  if (err) {
    console.error('Failed to subscribe:', err);
  } else {
    console.log(`Subscribed to ${count} channels.`);
  }
});

subscriber.on('message', (channel, message) => {
  // When a message is received from Redis, broadcast to all local WebSocket clients
  wss.clients.forEach(client => {
    if (client.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN) {
      client.send(message);
    }
  });
});

// When a WebSocket client sends a message:
ws.on('message', message => {
  // Publish the message to Redis, so all other servers receive it
  publisher.publish('chat_channel', message);
});

This pattern ensures that messages are delivered consistently across all horizontally scaled instances, enabling seamless communication regardless of which server a client is connected to.

3. Backpressure Management

Backpressure occurs when a producer sends data faster than a consumer can process it. In WebSocket contexts, if your server is sending data faster than a client (e.g., a slow mobile device on a poor network) can receive or process it, messages can queue up, consuming server memory and potentially leading to crashes or dropped connections.

  • Buffering and Throttling: Implement buffers on the server-side to temporarily hold messages for slow clients. If the buffer exceeds a certain threshold, the server can throttle messages for that client or even disconnect them gracefully to protect overall system stability.
  • Rate Limiting: Implement rate limiting for outgoing messages per client or per channel to prevent overwhelming clients.
  • Congestion Control Mechanisms: More advanced protocols might employ congestion control, similar to TCP, where the sending rate is adjusted based on network conditions and receiver capacity.

Optimizing WebSocket Performance in Node.js

Beyond architectural patterns, granular optimizations within your Node.js application can significantly boost WebSocket performance and throughput.

1. Payload Optimization

Every byte sent over the network matters, especially in high-throughput scenarios.

  • Minimize JSON Size: Avoid sending unnecessary data. Use short, descriptive keys if possible.
  • Binary Data for Efficiency: For numerical or structured data, consider using binary formats like Protocol Buffers (Protobuf), MessagePack, or Avro. These can be significantly more compact than JSON for certain data types.
  • Compression: Enable WebSocket compression (permessage-deflate extension). Most WebSocket libraries, including ws, support this. While it adds a small CPU overhead, it can drastically reduce network traffic for larger payloads. 
// Example: Enabling permessage-deflate in ws library
const wss = new WebSocketServer({
  port: 8080,
  perMessageDeflate: {
    zlibDeflateOptions: {
      chunkSize: 1024 * 1024, // 1MB chunk size
    },
    zlibInflateOptions: {
      chunkSize: 10 * 1024 // 10KB chunk size
    },
    clientNoContextTakeover: true, // Don't reuse zlib contexts for better memory use
    serverNoContextTakeover: true,
    serverMaxWindowBits: 10,
    // Other options...
  }
});

2. Efficient Event Handling and Non-Blocking Operations

Node.js's strength lies in its non-blocking I/O. Leverage this fully.

  • Avoid Synchronous Code: Any long-running synchronous operation in a WebSocket event handler will block the entire Node.js event loop, freezing all other connections. Use asynchronous patterns (async/await, Promises, callbacks) for database calls, file I/O, or complex computations.
  • Worker Threads for Heavy Computations: For CPU-bound tasks that cannot be made asynchronous (e.g., intensive data processing, cryptographic operations), offload them to Node.js Worker Threads. This keeps the main event loop free to handle new WebSocket messages and connections. 
// Example: Offloading heavy computation to a Worker Thread (conceptual)

// worker.js (separate file)
import { parentPort } from 'worker_threads';

parentPort.on('message', async (task) => {
  if (task.type === 'heavyCompute') {
    // Simulate heavy computation
    let result = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < task.data.iterations; i++) {
      result += Math.sqrt(i) * Math.sin(i);
    }
    parentPort.postMessage({ type: 'heavyComputeResult', result });
  }
});

// server.js (main application)
import { Worker } from 'worker_threads';

const worker = new Worker('./worker.js');

worker.on('message', (msg) => {
  if (msg.type === 'heavyComputeResult') {
    console.log('Heavy computation finished:', msg.result);
    // Send result back to relevant WebSocket client
  }
});

ws.on('message', message => {
  // ... parse message ...
  if (message.type === 'performHeavyTask') {
    worker.postMessage({ type: 'heavyCompute', data: { iterations: 1e7 } });
  } else {
    // Handle other messages
    ws.send('Processed ' + message);
  }
});

3. Connection Management: Heartbeats and Graceful Disconnections

Maintaining a large number of persistent connections requires active management.

  • Heartbeats (Ping/Pong): Implement periodic ping/pong messages to detect unresponsive clients or network issues. If a client doesn't respond to a ping within a certain timeout, the server can assume the connection is dead and close it gracefully, freeing up resources. The ws library has built-in support for this.
  • Graceful Disconnection Handling: Always handle close and error events on the WebSocket. Remove disconnected clients from your active connections list, release associated resources, and update any state tracking. 
// server.js (with heartbeat mechanism)
const wss = new WebSocketServer({ port: 8080 });

function noop() {}

function heartbeat() {
  this.isAlive = true;
}

wss.on('connection', ws => {
  ws.isAlive = true;
  ws.on('pong', heartbeat);

  // ... message handling ...

  ws.on('close', () => {
    console.log('Client disconnected gracefully');
  });

  ws.on('error', error => {
    console.error('WebSocket error on client:', error);
  });
});

const interval = setInterval(function ping() {
  wss.clients.forEach(function each(ws) {
    if (ws.isAlive === false) return ws.terminate();

    ws.isAlive = false;
    ws.ping(noop);
  });
}, 30000); // Ping every 30 seconds

wss.on('close', function close() {
  clearInterval(interval);
});

4. Security Best Practices

High-throughput applications are often targets. Security cannot be an afterthought.

  • CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing): Ensure your WebSocket server only accepts connections from trusted origins. While WebSockets don't directly use CORS headers in the same way as HTTP, the Origin header in the initial handshake should be validated.
  • Authentication and Authorization: Implement robust authentication (e.g., JWT tokens passed during the handshake or via initial message) to verify client identity. Authorize clients for specific data streams or actions.
  • Input Validation: Sanitize and validate all incoming messages from clients to prevent injection attacks (XSS, SQL injection if messages are stored) and malformed data.
  • Rate Limiting: Beyond backpressure, implement rate limiting on client message frequency to prevent DoS attacks or resource exhaustion.

Practical Implementation: Building a High-Throughput Notification Service

Let's tie these concepts together by sketching out a more robust Node.js WebSocket server for a notification service, demonstrating scaling and basic message routing.

We'll simulate a scenario where different users subscribe to different 'topics' (e.g., product updates, social feeds). For simplicity in this example, we'll use a global map to track connections per topic, but in a multi-server setup, this would be replaced by a Redis Pub/Sub system as discussed earlier.

// server.js - High-Throughput Notification Service Example
import { WebSocketServer } from 'ws';
import http from 'http';

// A simple in-memory store for connected clients grouped by topic
// In a real multi-server deployment, this would be a distributed store like Redis
const topicSubscriptions = new Map(); // Map<string, Set<WebSocket>>

const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' });
  res.end('WebSocket server is running');
});

const wss = new WebSocketServer({ server });

console.log('Notification WebSocket server started on port 8080');

wss.on('connection', ws => {
  console.log('Client connected');

  // Initial handshake or first message could include authentication/topic subscription
  // For demonstration, let's assume a 'subscribe' message type
  ws.on('message', message => {
    try {
      const parsedMessage = JSON.parse(message.toString());

      switch (parsedMessage.type) {
        case 'subscribe':
          {
            const topic = parsedMessage.topic;
            if (topic) {
              if (!topicSubscriptions.has(topic)) {
                topicSubscriptions.set(topic, new Set());
              }
              topicSubscriptions.get(topic).add(ws);
              ws.send(JSON.stringify({ status: 'subscribed', topic }));
              console.log(`Client subscribed to topic: ${topic}`);
            }
          }
          break;
        case 'publish':
          {
            const { topic, payload } = parsedMessage;
            if (topic && payload) {
              console.log(`Publishing message to topic ${topic}:`, payload);
              // In a multi-server setup, this would publish to Redis Pub/Sub
              const clients = topicSubscriptions.get(topic);
              if (clients) {
                clients.forEach(client => {
                  if (client.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN) {
                    client.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'notification', topic, payload }));
                  }
                });
              }
              ws.send(JSON.stringify({ status: 'published', topic }));
            }
          }
          break;
        // Add other message types like 'unsubscribe', 'ping/pong' etc.
        default:
          ws.send(JSON.stringify({ error: 'Unknown message type' }));
          break;
      }
    } catch (error) {
      console.error('Failed to parse message or handle:', error);
      ws.send(JSON.stringify({ error: 'Invalid message format' }));
    }
  });

  ws.on('close', () => {
    console.log('Client disconnected');
    // Remove client from all topic subscriptions
    topicSubscriptions.forEach((clients, topic) => {
      if (clients.has(ws)) {
        clients.delete(ws);
        if (clients.size === 0) {
          topicSubscriptions.delete(topic);
        }
      }
    });
  });

  ws.on('error', error => {
    console.error('WebSocket error:', error);
  });
});

server.listen(8080, () => {
  console.log('HTTP server for WebSocket handshake listening on 8080');
});

Explanation:

  • The server listens for HTTP requests (for the initial WebSocket handshake) and then upgrades to WebSocket.
  • Clients send a 'subscribe' message to join a topic.
  • Clients (or other services) can send a 'publish' message to a topic, and all subscribed clients for that topic receive the notification.
  • On client disconnection, it's removed from all subscriptions.
  • This example is single-process. To scale, replace the topicSubscriptions Map with a Redis Pub/Sub model where each server instance subscribes to all relevant topics in Redis, and any server publishing a message sends it to Redis, which then broadcasts to all subscribed server instances, which in turn send to their local WebSocket clients.

Monitoring and Troubleshooting High-Throughput WebSockets

Once deployed, continuous monitoring is crucial to ensure optimal performance and quickly identify bottlenecks.

  • Key Metrics: Monitor concurrent connections, message send/receive rates (messages per second), message payload sizes, CPU usage, memory consumption, network I/O, and latency (time from message send to receive).
  • Node.js Performance Tools: Use built-in Node.js debugging tools (e.g., --inspect with Chrome DevTools), profiling tools (clinic.js), and APM (Application Performance Monitoring) solutions like New Relic, Datadog, or Prometheus/Grafana to collect and visualize these metrics.
  • WebSocket-Specific Tools: Browser developer tools offer WebSocket inspection. Specialized tools can also help analyze WebSocket frames and latency.

Conclusion: Building Resilient Real-time Systems

Optimizing real-time data streams with WebSockets and Node.js is a multifaceted challenge that goes beyond basic server setup. By embracing horizontal scaling, implementing robust message queuing, meticulously optimizing payloads, ensuring efficient event handling, and maintaining vigilant connection management, you can build highly performant, resilient, and low-latency applications that meet the demands of the modern web. The future of interactive applications is real-time, and with these strategies, you're well-equipped to engineer that future.

title: RAG vs CAG vs KAG: Choosing the Right Context Layer in NodeJS
description:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) solved a real problem: LLMs alone don't know your documents. But not every agent question is “find the right passage.” Sometimes you need stable context reused across thousands of requests. Sometimes you need structured entities, facts, and relationships with provenance. That is why HazelJS treats context as four complementary layers — RAG, CAG, KAG, and Memory — and ships first-class packages for each.

This post is a practical cross-comparison: what each layer is for, when it wins or loses, how we built @hazeljs/rag, @hazeljs/cag, and @hazeljs/kag, and real use cases you can run offline in hazeljs-meridian-ops.

Packages & Links

  • @hazeljs/rag — retrieval, loaders, vector stores, GraphRAG (docs)
  • @hazeljs/cag — Cache-Augmented Generation (docs)
  • @hazeljs/kag — Knowledge-Augmented Generation (docs)
  • @hazeljs/context — unified planner that combines them (docs)
  • @hazeljs/memory — agent/user continuity (distinct from domain knowledge)

Runnable labs (no API keys): meridian-ops/examples — example:rag · example:cag · example:kag · example:context

One Picture 

                 HazelJS Agent
                      │
                      ▼
              Context / Reasoning
                      │
        ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
        │             │             │
        ▼             ▼             ▼
       RAG           CAG           KAG
        │             │             │
        └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                      │
                    Memory
                      │
                      ▼
                     LLM
Layer Core question Typical answer shape
RAG What information should I retrieve for this query? Ranked passages + citations
CAG What context can I preload, reuse, and cache? Fingerprinted policy / schema blobs
KAG What entities, facts, and relationships do I know? Evidence path + provenance
Memory What has this agent learned or experienced with this user? Preferences, session facts

They are complementary. CAG is not a RAG wrapper. KAG is not “GraphRAG renamed.” Memory is not a knowledge graph.

What Each Layer Is

RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Idea: At request time, embed the question, search a vector (and optionally keyword) index, optionally rerank, then stuff passages into the prompt.

Request → Embedding → Vector / hybrid search → Documents → LLM

HazelJS surface: @hazeljs/rag — loaders, chunking, embeddings, vector stores, hybrid search, GraphRAG for document-derived graphs, RAGService / RAGPipeline. Meridian’s helpdesk agent uses the same mental model with an in-memory KB (no Qdrant required to learn the pattern).

Best when: answers live in a large, changing corpus and relevance depends on the query.

Lab: examples/rag-helpdesk-agent → npm run example:rag

CAG — Cache-Augmented Generation

Idea: Relatively stable knowledge is prepared once, fingerprinted, cached (memory / Redis / provider prompt-cache hints), then reused — without embedding + search on every request.

Knowledge sources → Prepare → Context cache → Request → Cached context → LLM

HazelJS surface: @hazeljs/cag — CagModule / CagService, sources, fingerprints, TTL / version invalidation, token budgets, optional compression, multi-tenant keys.

Best when: the same policies, schemas, catalogs, or tenant config are needed on almost every turn.

Lab: examples/cag-support-agent → npm run example:cag

KAG — Knowledge-Augmented Generation

Idea: Domain knowledge as typed entities, relations, and time-scoped facts — with provenance, confidence, contradictions, and traversable evidence — then optional LLM phrasing of that evidence.

Data → Extract / ingest → Knowledge graph → Traverse / plan → Evidence → LLM

HazelJS surface: @hazeljs/kag — KnowledgeGraph / KagService, in-memory tenant store, entity resolution, temporal facts, heuristic (industry-pluggable) query planner, ask({ explain: true }), GraphRAG import adapters (not a GraphRAG fork).

Best when: the question is multi-hop, causal, or “why did X change?” over structured domain state — not “which PDF page mentions X?”

Lab: examples/kag-commerce-agent → npm run example:kag

Memory — continuity (not knowledge)

Memory answers “what do we already know about this user / this run?” It is orthogonal to RAG/CAG/KAG. Promote a preference into KAG only when it becomes validated domain truth.

Cross Comparison

Capability matrix

Dimension RAG CAG KAG Memory
Unit of context Passages / chunks Assembled stable text blocks Entities, relations, facts Episodes / preferences
Hot path Embed + search every request Cache hit → assemble Graph traverse / plan Lookup by user/session
Data freshness Great for frequently updated docs Great for slowly changing knowledge Great for operational / transactional truth Great for conversational state
Latency profile Search + embed cost Near-instant on hit Traversal (cheap at small/medium scale) Near-instant
Explainability Citations to passages Source id + version / fingerprint Evidence path + provenance “You said X earlier”
Multi-tenancy Namespaces / metadata filters Cache keys include tenantId Store partitioned by tenantId Scoped by user / agent
Failure mode Wrong or missing passage Stale cache if invalidation is wrong Weak graph / low confidence Stale or over-trusted preference
Typical cost driver Embeddings + vector DB Prompt tokens (mitigated by cache) Ingestion + occasional LLM phrasing Storage + retrieval of history
Update cadence Continuous ingest Version bump / TTL / invalidate Event-driven graph writes Per turn / session
HazelJS package @hazeljs/rag @hazeljs/cag @hazeljs/kag @hazeljs/memory

Same question, four wrong tools

User asks If you only use… What goes wrong
“What’s our return policy?” RAG You pay embed+search every time for text that never changes per tenant version.
“How do I rotate staging API keys?” CAG You either miss the right runbook or stuff the entire handbook into every prompt.
“Why was settlement €1,420 short?” RAG Passages mention refunds; they don’t reconstruct merchant→order→payment→refund→settlement with sources.
“Remember I exclude VAT.” KAG You pollute the domain graph with a personal preference that isn’t operational truth.
Mix of policy + ledger + preference Any single layer Incomplete answer — needs @hazeljs/context.

Pros and cons (short)

Wins Loses when
RAG Large unstructured corpora; query-dependent relevance; mature tooling Multi-hop structured “why”; always-on policy paragraphs
CAG Latency/cost for stable tenant context; fingerprints; priority budgets Query-specific doc lookup; forgotten invalidation
KAG Causal paths, contradictions, provenance, industry profiles Free-form prose; “drop PDFs and go”
Memory Continuity and personalization Treating preferences as ledger truth

How HazelJS Built These Packages

We did not invent three parallel frameworks. We extended the Agent OS context substrate with clear boundaries and heavy reuse.

  1. Composition over duplication — CAG reuses RAG loaders for files/URLs when present; it does not reimplement vector search. KAG can import GraphRAG graphs; it does not own community detection or embeddings.
  2. Native HazelJS shape — @HazelModule, forRoot / forRootAsync, @Service(), typed XxxError + codes, Jest, peer @hazeljs/core.
  3. Multi-tenant by default where it matters — CAG cache keys and KAG store scopes always include tenantId.
  4. Agent OS ports, not hard couples — AgentRuntimeConfig takes duck-typed ragService / cagService / kagService / contextService. DNA declares intent; apps inject services.
  5. Toward a unified planner — @hazeljs/context calls the same contributor shape (contribute) so auto strategy can pick CAG / RAG / KAG / Memory per query.

Real-World Use Cases

Each scenario below maps to a Meridian lab (or live Meridian route). Run the lab after reading the section.

1) Help center / FAQ over a large handbook → RAG

Industries: SaaS support, internal IT, compliance Q&A, product docs.

Problem: Hundreds of docs, changelogs, and runbooks. The right answer depends on the question wording and may live in an obscure page updated last week.

// Pattern (production: @hazeljs/rag ingest + vector store)
const docs = await rag.search('How do I rotate API keys on staging?', { topK: 3 });

Why not CAG? You cannot sensibly preload the entire doc set into every prompt.

Why not KAG? The knowledge is narrative procedure text, not a fact graph (unless you later extract entities).

Lab / live: Offline rag-helpdesk-agent mirrors Meridian’s helpdesk KB. In the running app: POST /api/helpdesk/chat.

npm run example:rag
# ask: "What is the refund SLA?" → hits refund-sla doc, not the whole policy blob

2) Multi-merchant support: always-on return policy → CAG

Industries: Marketplaces, payment platforms, white-label SaaS, any multi-tenant agent.

Problem: Every merchant chat asks about returns, hours, and fee schedules. Running RAG every time burns embeddings and latency for text that rarely changes — and tenant A must never see tenant B’s policy.

cag.register(
  {
    id: 'return-policy',
    priority: 100,
    compressible: false,
    version: '2026-10',
    source: { type: 'text', content: loadMerchantPolicy(tenantId) },
  },
  'support'
);

const { context, hit } = await cag.getContext({
  namespace: 'support',
  tenantId: 'merchant-123',
});

Why not RAG? The answer is not “find a similar paragraph” — it is “always include this policy.”

Why not KAG? There is no multi-hop entity reasoning; it is static prose.

Lab: cag-support-agent — cold miss → warm hit, tenant isolation, version bump invalidates cache.

npm run example:cag
# firstHit: false, secondHit: true, otherTenantHit: false, afterVersionBumpHit: false

Other CAG fits: OpenAPI / tool schemas stuck in every tool-calling turn; compliance disclaimers; product catalog summaries that change weekly under a version key.

3) Ops / finance: “Why was settlement short?” → KAG

Industries: Commerce / payments, logistics (shipment→exception→claim), healthcare ops (patient→encounter→claim), ITSM (incident→change→outage).

Problem: The answer is a path through merchant → orders → payments → refunds → fees → settlement, with source systems and confidence — not a single handbook paragraph.

const knowledge = new KnowledgeGraph({
  tenantId: 'merchant-123',
  industry: COMMERCE_INDUSTRY_PROFILE, // opt-in vocabulary
});

await knowledge.relate({ from: 'payment-1', to: 'refund-1', type: 'HAS_REFUND' });
await knowledge.fact({
  subject: 'refund-1',
  predicate: 'amount',
  object: 1420,
  confidence: 0.98,
  source: { type: 'database', id: 'refund-456', authority: 90 },
});

const result = await knowledge.ask(question, { explain: true });
// result.evidence + result.sources — auditable, not hidden CoT

Why not RAG alone? Passages might mention refunds but won’t reliably reconstruct the causal path with provenance.

Why not CAG alone? The graph changes with every day’s ledger; caching a frozen narrative goes stale immediately.

Lab: kag-commerce-agent — builds the graph, asks the settlement question, prints evidence + contradiction handling.

npm run example:kag
# explanation includes merchant → order → payment → refund → settlement + sources

4) Hybrid desk: policy + ledger + handbook + preference → @hazeljs/context

Industries: Any production support desk that already has RAG and needs policy + ops truth.

Problem: “Why was settlement impacted by a refund, given our refund policy and my VAT preference?”

Slice of the question Layer
Stable refund policy CAG
Relational “why” on the ledger KAG
Optional handbook passage RAG
“exclude VAT” preference Memory 
const context = new ContextService({
  strategy: 'auto',
  sources: ['cache', 'rag', 'knowledge', 'memory'],
  cag,
  kag,
  rag,
  memory,
});

const assembled = await context.assemble({
  query,
  tenantId: 'merchant-123',
  userId: 'ops-1',
});
// assembled.plan.rationale explains which layers fired

Lab: context-auto-agent — auto-plans all four contributors and prints labeled assembly.

npm run example:context
# plan.sources: cag, rag, kag, memory — with per-layer rationale

5) Industry cheat sheet

Domain Prefer RAG Prefer CAG Prefer KAG
E‑commerce / payments Help center, shipping FAQs Merchant return/fee policy Settlement, chargeback, refund causality
SaaS / developer platforms API docs, changelogs Per-tenant feature flags / schemas in prompt Entitlement → usage → invoice disputes
Healthcare ops Clinical guidelines PDFs Facility policy snippets Encounter → claim → denial paths
Logistics Carrier manuals Lane / SLA templates Shipment → exception → claim chains
Internal IT Runbooks, wiki Org security policy always-on Asset → ticket → change → outage

When two columns apply in one utterance, reach for @hazeljs/context.

6) Quick decision matrix

If the user asks… Prefer Lab
“What’s in the docs / handbook about X?” RAG example:rag
“What is our always-on policy / schema / catalog?” CAG example:cag
“Why did entity A’s metric change given related entities?” KAG example:kag
“Remember that I prefer…” Memory (wired inside example:context)
A mix of the above @hazeljs/context auto example:context

Common Mistakes

  1. Using RAG for static policies — you pay retrieval forever for text that should be CAG.
  2. Using CAG for the whole knowledge base — prompts explode; retrieval exists for a reason.
  3. Treating GraphRAG as KAG — GraphRAG is document-extraction RAG; KAG is operational knowledge with facts, time, and contradictions.
  4. Auto-merging uncertain entities — HazelJS KAG keeps candidates below threshold; don’t turn that off casually.
  5. Skipping tenant in cache/graph keys — never acceptable for multi-merchant agents.
  6. Exposing raw model chain-of-thought as “explanation” — KAG explanations are evidence (entities, relations, sources).
  7. Putting user preferences only in Memory forever — promote to KAG when they become validated domain rules; keep Memory for soft personalization.

Where This Is Going

HazelJS is moving from “we have RAG, and also CAG, and also KAG” to a single context substrate:

Query → ContextPlanner → CAG | RAG | KAG | Memory → Assembly → LLM

@hazeljs/context is the first cut of that planner. Each package remains independently useful for teams that only need one layer. Meridian Ops is the teaching app: DNA + Skillgate + HITL in the live server, and offline context labs under examples/.

Try It 

# from hazeljs-meridian-ops/
npm run example:install
npm run example:rag      # handbook retrieval
npm run example:cag      # cached policy + tenant isolation
npm run example:kag      # settlement evidence path
npm run example:context  # auto planner over all four

Docs: RAG · CAG · KAG · Context

RAG optimizes retrieval. CAG optimizes reuse. KAG optimizes structured knowledge. Memory optimizes continuity. Together they are the context engine of HazelJS Agent OS.

title: I Built My Entire UI With the Wrong shadcn Style. Here’s How I Fixed It
description:
As you keep building projects, you discover surprising challenges you didn't even know existed. Have you ever tried changing the style of a shadcn project from base UI to radix UI or vice versa?, it was an issue an encountered a while ago, and it can be a bit challenging to do as it isn't straight forward.

For a bit of context, I was building a project with other developers for a client, my work was to build like a sub-section of the website that still belongs to the main website. So I created a brand new React project, and set up shadcn to start building the website with pre-built UI components. Now one mistake I made was not considering the reusable components that were already created from the main project like the <Header /> and <Footer />, and so, I re-invented the wheel, creating those components again. This didn't look like an issue initially until a review was done, and the team noticed that the UI for the app I was building didn't match the UI of the main website.

After doing some checks in my project, I found out the issue was the type of style I was using when I installed shadcn. When you install shadcn, you would be asked to select the style you want to use (either base UI or radix UI). At first, I didn't think this really mattered, and honestly, it doesn't, but when you are working with other devs, it can be important to ensure your style matches what is being used. It can also matter if you want to get detailed about what it is you're trying to achieve, as different styles provide different ways of customizing your components from shadcn.

The main website uses the radix UI style, but my project was using base UI, and I had already built the entire UI using base UI, so I had to change it to radix UI. In other to change the style, here are the steps I took:

Step 1: Updating the 'style' property in my components.json file 

/*
    Each style in shadcn has variants (e,g vega, nova, maia etc)

    You can discover the full list of variants each
    style has from this page on shadcn's website — https://ui.shadcn.com/create

    In my own case, the style was "base-nova", so I changed it to "radix-nova"
*/
{
  "style": "radix-nova"
}

Step 2: Reinstalled my components to ensure they match the new style

After changing the style, I re-installed all the components I had installed previously in the components/ folder using this command:

pnpm dlx add shadcn@latest component-name // e.g. pnpm dlx add shadcn@latest button

Step 3: Updated my package.json file to reflect the style I am using

I removed the base UI package, and replaced it with radix UI so as to ensure the components display properly. If you are changing from radix UI to base UI, the process is still the same

{
  ...
  "dependencies": {
    "@base-ui/react": "^1.7.0", // Removed this
    "radix-ui": "^1.4.3", // Added this
  },
}

Step 4: Update the node_modules folder

Once I edited the package.json file, I ran pnpm run update to update my node_modules folder, to install the radix UI package and remove base UI.

Conclusion

With these steps, I was able to successfully change from base UI to radix UI, and if you follow the exact step, you can do the same as well. That was kind of simple right?, it isn't that hard once you know what to do, surprisingly, even the shadcn docs doesn't provide a tutorial on how to do this. Have you ever encountered this kind of issue of having to change the style of your shadcn project before?

title: From a desk toy to a hotel room: what it took to ship a local voice assistant to real buildings
description:
A voice assistant that runs on your own machine is a nice weekend story. You talk, Whisper transcribes, a local LLM works out what you meant, a skill answers, Piper speaks. No cloud, no account, nothing leaves the room.

Then you try to put it in a hotel room and every assumption breaks.

On your desk there's one user, one microphone, one trusted network, and one person who knows what the assistant can and can't do. A hotel has a hundred rooms, a guest who checks out on Tuesday and a stranger who checks in on Wednesday, a Wi-Fi network shared with every phone in the building, staff who need to see requests instead of hearing them, and nobody who will tell the assistant to "try again" when it goes quiet.

Our last release, v0.4.0, is 29 commits and a few thousand lines of Rust and C++ that deal with that gap. This post walks through what changed and why, including the bugs we only found once real hardware sat on a real table.

The shape of a property deployment

Before v0.4.0 the system was one backend and a desktop frontend. Now a property runs three services plus one small device per room:

  • The pod is a microphone, a speaker, a 7-LED ring and three buttons. It does no speech work.
  • pod-gateway (the room bridge) turns a stream of audio into turns: it finds where speech starts and ends, cancels the pod's own echo, sends each utterance to the backend, synthesises the answer and streams it back.
  • aice-backend is the existing voice core: speech to text, LLM intent classification, skills, memory.
  • The facilitator is the property's side: a staff desk, tickets, stays, the device registry, and alerting. It ships as three "packs" with different defaults: aice-hotels, aice-care and aice-ward.

All of it runs on hardware in the building. The voice never leaves the property.

1. Lock the doors before you invite anyone in

The honest first entry in the changelog's Security section: before this release, the desk, the ticket API and the MCP endpoint were reachable without credentials, and a room's turn stream accepted whatever room the client said it was in. Fine on a laptop. Unacceptable on a hotel LAN.

So the first commits are all about trust:

  • Staff accounts. The desk now has local accounts with staff and supervisor roles, argon2-hashed passwords, HttpOnly SameSite=Strict session cookies, CSRF tokens on every form and API call, and a five-minute lockout after five bad passwords. Every ticket change goes to an append-only audit log that supervisors can read, and only a supervisor can reopen a closed ticket.
  • A service token between backend and facilitator. The pack writes service.token on first run, and the backend presents it as a bearer token.
  • TLS from a property-local CA. A new core-tls crate creates a certificate authority for the property, issues server certificates from it and builds rustls configs. On any non-loopback bind the facilitator defaults to TLS, serves its CA certificate for pods to pin, and refuses plain HTTP. The backend and bridge also refuse plaintext on a network bind unless you set allow_plaintext_lan explicitly.
  • The room comes from the token, not the client. This is the important one. A pod enrols with its id and a secret nonce. It shows up as pending on the supervisor's desk. When a supervisor assigns it to a room, the pod receives a device token, exactly once. From then on the backend verifies that token on every connection and every turn, and takes the device id and room from the verified token. A client can no longer say "I'm room 214."

Verification is cached for 30 seconds. If the facilitator is down, a recent answer is kept for ten minutes so a desk restart doesn't take every room offline.

2. Memory belongs to a stay, not to a room

Aice has long-term memory (Memory Palace, our palace-rs crate): it can recall what you told it last week. In a home that's useful. In a hotel it's a privacy incident waiting to happen. The guest in room 214 tonight must not hear about the previous guest's allergies.

The answer is the stay. Staff check guests and residents in and out on the desk (or with stay open|close|list). Each stay gets its own memory wing, and a turn from that room reads and writes only that wing: wake-up context, recall, ingestion, and knowledge-graph facts, which are namespaced per wing.

A few details that took more thought than the headline:

  • The backend checks the stay on every turn, not on connect. A pod that stays connected through a checkout moves to the next guest's stay instead of keeping the last one. If the facilitator can't be reached, the turn runs with memory off.
  • No stay, no memory. A room without an open stay, or any unauthenticated turn in a property deployment, remembers nothing. The shared journal skill is hidden from rooms entirely.
  • Consent is recorded per stay. Without consent the pod gets no memory wing at all. Hotels default to consent from booking terms; care homes and wards default to not agreed. Staff tick it at check-in, can change it during the stay, and every change is audited.
  • Retention is per property. memory_retention is keep (a returning guest can continue an old stay's memory), archive after N days, or wipe_on_close (the default for wards). A backend job deletes due wings, including their facts, and confirms each purge back to the facilitator.

One thing we learned the hard way while upgrading palace-rs: newer versions record wing names in several new tables (a wing registry, usage events, mined-file records, feedback). A purge that only deleted the memories would have left the names of past stays behind. Purges now clear all of them, so a wiped stay leaves nothing.

3. The pod: from test bed to real hardware

We started with an M5Stack ATOM Echo because it's tiny and cheap. It taught us something important: its microphone and speaker share one clock pin, so it cannot listen while it speaks. That makes it half-duplex. A guest can't interrupt it by voice, which for a voice assistant in a room is a real limitation.

So we wrote down what a room pod actually has to do (full-duplex audio, an echo reference, buttons, LEDs) and moved to the Waveshare ESP32-S3-AUDIO-Board. It has an ES8311 codec driving the speaker and an ES7210 ADC for the mics, both on one full-duplex I2S port. The best part: one ES7210 channel records what the speaker is playing. That loopback is the echo reference that makes everything in the next section possible. The codec register drivers are vendored from Espressif's Apache-2.0 esp_codec_dev.

Two bugs only appeared on the board:

  • TLS rejected the property certificate as "not yet valid". The pod had never set its clock, so as far as it knew it was 1970. It now syncs over NTP before opening any TLS connection.
  • mbedTLS checks names only, and the property hosts are .local names. The pod now resolves .local over mDNS.

Provisioning without a laptop

A fresh pod derives its id from its Wi-Fi MAC, generates a random nonce and keeps it in flash, and enrols with the facilitator over HTTPS pinned to the property CA. The LED ring pulses slow amber until a supervisor assigns a room on the desk. Then it connects to the room bridge over WSS with its new device token.

If the server replies "unauthorized", the pod clears its token and enrols again. If it lost its token, it can get a new one by proving its nonce, and the old token stops working. Holding the button at boot forgets the identity completely.

Signed updates

firmware keygen|publish|rollout signs images with a property ECDSA P-256 key and offers them to a stable percentage of the fleet. Pods download with their device token and install only an image whose signature verifies. In fairness: that flow is covered by tests, but at the time of the hardware bring-up we hadn't yet run a signed update end to end on the board.

Buttons that work when the AI doesn't

  • Long press = help. It raises an escalated help_button ticket for the room, and the bridge speaks a confirmation. No speech recognition or LLM is involved, so it still works when those are down.
  • Double tap = privacy mute. The pod stops sending microphone audio and the ring turns magenta. The help button still works while muted.

4. Letting guests talk over the answer

This was the hardest part of the release.

If the assistant starts reading a long answer and the guest says "no, stop, I meant breakfast," it should stop. To do that, the bridge has to hear the guest while the pod's own speaker is playing a few centimetres from the microphone. Without echo cancellation, the loudest thing the mic hears is the assistant itself, and it interrupts itself constantly.

A full-duplex pod now streams two signals during an answer: its microphone and its playback loopback. The bridge's echo canceller does two things.

First, it finds the lag. The echo arrives later than the reference. On our pod the lag measured one 40 ms frame plus 0.8 ms, but whether that extra frame was there changed from session to session. So the canceller runs a correlation search over up to 128 ms every quarter second and keeps the lag only when the correlation is confident.

Second, it learns the echo path with a 256-tap normalised LMS filter (16 ms at 16 kHz) and subtracts the predicted echo from the mic. The core loop is short:

let predicted: f32 = self.weights.iter().zip(window).map(|(w, x)| w * x).sum();
let error = heard - predicted;

let energy: f32 = window.iter().map(|x| x * x).sum();
if self.adapt && energy > ACTIVE_REFERENCE_ENERGY {
    let step = MU * error.clamp(-clip, clip) / (energy + EPSILON);
    for (w, x) in self.weights.iter_mut().zip(window) {
        *w += step * x;
    }
}

The interesting parts are around that loop:

  • The double-talk guard. If the filter keeps adapting while the guest talks, it learns their voice as "echo" and starts cancelling them. So every 10 ms block compares mic energy against predicted-echo energy. Echo alone sits near a ratio of 1 once the filter has converged, and a voice on top pushes it up. At a ratio of 2 adaptation stops, and it's judged again every block, so one loud syllable in the answer doesn't freeze the filter for good.
  • Robust updates. Even before the guard notices, the first milliseconds of a guest's voice are far larger than the usual residual. Updates use the error clipped to twice its running typical size, so those milliseconds barely move the filter.
  • Barge-in needs to beat the echo, not just be loud. The bridge stops the answer only on speech that is loud and clearly above the predicted echo for several frames. The new turn keeps the guest's first words.

Gain staging mattered as much as the maths. The reference input runs at 18 dB so it never clips, the mic has no digital gain, and the speaker is at -20 dB.

Measured on the Waveshare pod: 11-14 dB of echo removed, no self-interruption across 27 seconds of answers, and about 60% of normal-volume speech caught within a second. That isn't perfect, but it's the difference between "you can interrupt it" and "you can't."

One last detail: a full-duplex pod still has a little audio buffered when the answer ends. That tail was being heard as a new request. The bridge now waits until the pod's speaker is actually quiet.

5. Conversations, not commands

Several fixes in this release share one theme: people don't talk in single, clean commands.

  • The wake word used to be required on every turn, so follow-ups ("and tomorrow?"), corrections and barge-ins were dropped. Each connection now tracks a conversation: a wake phrase wakes it, and it stays awake while a turn is open, while an answer is playing, and for wake_word.cooldown_secs after playback ends. The bridge reports playback_started / playback_finished, so the window runs from when the guest stopped hearing the answer, not from when the text was generated. We first shipped 2 seconds, which was far too short for a natural follow-up. The default is now 8.
  • A pause split one request into fragments. A guest who paused after "Computer, ..." got their request cut into separate turns; one of them arrived as just "of tahini." Now, if speech continues before any answer has come back, it's sent again together with the first part as one request. The bridge also ignores answers for turns it has replaced, so a cancelled turn's empty answer can't swallow the real one.
  • Short-term context. The backend keeps the last few exchanges per session for chat replies, and drops them on a new stay or after 10 idle minutes. When a guest interrupts, a playback_interrupted event with the spoken ratio cuts the remembered answer down to what they actually heard.
  • Chat was making promises it couldn't keep. Asked for a pillow, the general chat path would happily say "I'll get you an extra pillow right away", and nothing would happen. Chat is now told explicitly that it cannot act, and must say a request couldn't be sent rather than pretend.
  • Silence is a bug. When a skill failed (a provider timed out, a place wasn't found), the pod said nothing. Most skill branches were returning their error past the apology code. Every skill now runs inside one block, so every failure is spoken.

Two classifier bugs were especially sneaky:

  • Rooms could never make hotel requests. The classifier only offered the hotel skill to clients that declared it, and pods declare nothing. A backend with a facilitator now always offers it.
  • The classifier's output was capped at 24 tokens. A hotel request with slots ("two towels to room 214 after 6pm") produced JSON that got cut off, failed to parse, and silently fell back to chat. The cap is now 64, and decoding still stops as soon as the JSON is complete.

6. Making it fast enough to feel like talking

In a voice interface, latency is the UX. A few changes made a large difference:

  • Whisper was encoding a full 30-second window for every clip, even a two-second "what time is breakfast." It now encodes only the audio plus a margin: from 4.8 s to 1.0 s per pass on CPU.

  • Ollama was reloading the model on every call, about 3 seconds each time. The classifier and memory calls asked for a different context size than the warm-up and the answers, and a different context size means a reload. Every call to a shared host now uses one size, so the model loaded at startup stays loaded.
  • STT ran every room through one Whisper context behind a mutex. It now uses a pool of stt.workers contexts.
  • Admission control. Turns and STT jobs take permits (service.max_concurrent_turns, stt.workers) and queue beyond them. A turn that waits longer than service.turn_queue_max_wait_ms gets a spoken "busy" reply instead of silence.
  • LLM failover. ollama_urls adds hosts next to the main one. Calls rotate across them, and a failing host is skipped for 30 seconds.
  • Pacing playback. The pod only buffers about 0.4 s of audio, so the bridge sends answers at playback speed with three chunks of lead rather than dumping them all at once.

A capacity test that can fail the build

room-loadtest enrols simulated pods on a facilitator, then drives them at real-time pace through the real bridge, backend and facilitator, and reports p50, p95 and max from end of speech to first answer audio. In CI it runs eight rooms against a backend with only two turn permits, and requires that every turn is answered, admission holds, and p95 stays under five seconds. If a change makes the system slower under load, CI goes red.

CI also now compiles the pod firmware with PlatformIO, and releases ship Linux x86_64 and aarch64 archives for appliance installs next to the macOS build.

7. When nobody picks up

A request that becomes a ticket nobody reads is worse than no assistant at all. Each pack now has alert tiers and per-tool acknowledgement windows:

  • A new ticket pages the first tier.
  • If it's still open when its window ends, it's marked escalated (by actor sla, audited) and paged to the next tier, and this repeats on the last tier until someone acknowledges it.
  • Channels are webhooks or a tool on the property's own MCP server, which is how you reach nurse call, DECT handsets or PMS paging. A dead channel doesn't block the others, and a first alert that reached nobody is retried every five seconds.
  • The schedule lives on the ticket rows, so a restart doesn't reset the timers.

Defaults differ by pack: care homes escalate falls and distress after 60 seconds, wards escalate "get a nurse" after 120, hotels use 15 minutes for everything (and the runbook tells you to tighten that for maintenance and complaints).

Pods are watched too. The backend reports which pods have an open stream every 30 seconds. An active pod that goes silent past device_offline_after_secs raises one escalated device_offline ticket and shows OFFLINE on the desk, because a room that can't call for help is itself something staff need to know about.

8. Finding where a slow turn went

Once real people are talking to it, "it felt slow" is the most common bug report and the least useful one. So the last big change is end-to-end timing of the guest journey.

First, an embarrassing one: every duration metric was exported as a Prometheus summary, so every dashboard panel built on histogram_quantile over _bucket series had been quietly empty. Every *_seconds metric is now a histogram with fixed buckets from 5 ms to 4 hours.

Then the tracing. The bridge times backend wait, speech synthesis, and end-of-speech to first answer audio; the desk times ticket resolution; stage, dependency and LLM durations attach to the turn's trace without touching call sites. Any turn whose wait after speech passes service.slow_turn_threshold_ms (3 seconds by default) is logged once as slow_turn, with:

  • the full stage timeline,
  • the slowest stage,
  • and the time no stage covers.

That last number turned out to be the most useful. When the slowest stage only explains half the wait, the problem is in the gaps: a queue, a lock, a reconnect. It's counted in voice_turn_unaccounted_duration_seconds, and a new "Guest Journey" Grafana dashboard puts it all on one screen.

What we'd tell ourselves at the start

  • Decide where identity comes from before anything else. Taking the room from a verified token rather than from the client made memory scoping, alerts and offline detection simple. Everything downstream trusts one thing.
  • Privacy is a data model, not a setting. Stays, consent and retention had to be first-class rows, including making sure purges reach every table a dependency adds later.
  • Test on the real board early. The clock, mDNS, the shared clock pin and the buffered audio tail were all invisible in tests.
  • Silence is always a bug. Busy, failed, muted, can't act: each one now has something spoken.
  • Measure the gaps, not just the stages. "Unaccounted time" found more than any single stage timer.
  • Write the capacity requirement as a test. "p95 under five seconds with eight rooms" is a sentence until CI enforces it.

What's next

The classifier is now the part that matters most: every request goes through the LLM, and a misclassified request is a missed towel or a missed nurse call. Next we're working on scoring candidate classifier models against a labelled dataset, and running a second model in shadow next to the live one in production to record where they disagree before we switch anything.

About Aice

Aice is an open-source (Apache-2.0), local-first voice assistant written in Rust. Speech recognition, the LLM and memory all run on hardware you own. With v0.4.0 it runs in hotels, care homes and wards: guests ask out loud in their room, and staff and property systems get the request, with no cloud for the voice.

Source: github.com/AncientiCe/aice

v0.4.0 release (macOS arm64, Linux x86_64 and aarch64): github.com/AncientiCe/aice/releases/tag/v0.4.0

If you're running a property and want to pilot it, or you've solved echo cancellation on a microcontroller better than we have, I'd love to hear from you in the comments.

title: Why Your Shopify Checkout Extension Should Be the Last Thing You Customize
description:
Why Your Shopify Checkout Extension Should Be the Last Thing You Customize

Checkout customization via Shopify's UI Extensions is powerful, and that's exactly why it tends to get reached for too early — before the more basic problems in the funnel get fixed.

🧲 The Pull Toward Checkout First

Checkout feels like the highest-leverage place to intervene — it's the last step before revenue. But a checkout extension can only improve conversion for people who actually reach checkout, and most funnels lose far more people earlier, on product pages and cart.

📋 What Usually Needs Fixing First

Product page load speed, clear shipping/return info before cart, and cart abandonment triggers typically have more total impact than anything checkout-side, because they affect a larger population of visitors earlier in the funnel.

✅ When Checkout Customization Actually Earns Its Place

Once the upstream funnel is solid, checkout extensions are genuinely valuable — post-purchase upsells, custom validation for B2B order minimums, localized payment options. Just don't let it be step one.

Originally published on the KLYX blog.

title: Iran reportedly planning attacks on undersea internet cables
description:
Reports indicate Iran has plans to target undersea internet cables in the Gulf if attacked, which researchers warn could disrupt global bandwidth, cloud computing, and financial transactions.

Undersea fiber-optic cables carry most of the world's internet traffic. The sources told Reuters that in addition to the strikes, Iran would seek to obstruct repair work to prolong the connectivity problems.

This information comes after statements by Yandollah Javani, a senior official in Iran's Revolutionary Guards, who had threatened that the country may target seven key internet cables under the Strait of Hormuz if its infrastructure is attacked.

What would be the consequences of any attacks on the cables?

Telecommunications experts estimate that such a development could slow down online services and create problems in financial transactions, online shopping and remote data storage services.

READ ALSO

Hacker breached LiteLLM and uploaded malicious software update

However, the true extent of the problems will depend on how quickly companies can shift traffic to other routes and alternative connections.

Analysts also note that the goal may be to pressure Gulf countries and big business executives, so that they in turn pressure United States President Donald Trump about the risks facing their investments.

Wider threats and previous incidents

Tensions in the region have also affected other technological infrastructure. In early 2026, attacks on data centers in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates are estimated to have caused permanent data loss, while there have also been threats against satellite internet facilities in the Middle East.

On a separate level, the UK government recently proposed new legislation to protect critical undersea infrastructure, which includes tougher penalties and immediate intervention capabilities.
