title: What Actually Happens When You `.await` in Rust: Futures, Pin, Wakers, and the Executor
description:
What Actually Happens When You .await in Rust: Futures, Pin, Wakers, and the Executor

You type .await. The code pauses. Later it resumes with a value. Magic? No. It's a precise chain of mechanical steps: a state machine gets pinned in memory, an executor calls poll, a waker gets registered, and the runtime sleeps until something wakes it up.

Most Rust developers use async daily but treat .await as syntax sugar. It's not. Understanding what actually happens changes how you debug hangs, why Pin exists, and why forgetting to wake a task is a bug that silently hangs forever.

The Big Picture

When you write:

async fn fetch_data() -> Result<Data, Error> {
    let response = http_client.get(url).await?;  // <-- What happens HERE?
    Ok(response.json().await?)
}

The compiler transforms this into a state machine — an enum where each variant represents a pause point (every .await). Calling the function doesn't run it. It returns a future: an inert value implementing Future. Nothing executes until something calls poll on that future.

The Future trait is the contract:

use std::pin::Pin;
use std::task::{Context, Poll};

pub trait Future {
    type Output;
    fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Self::Output>;
}

Three things stand out immediately:

  • Pin<&mut Self> — the future must not move in memory
  • Context — carries a Waker for scheduling
  • Poll — either Ready(value) or Pending (come back later)

Step 1: The Compiler Builds a State Machine

Every async fn or async {} block becomes an anonymous enum. Each .await becomes a state transition.

async fn example() {
    let data = vec![1, 2, 3];
    let reference = &data[0];      // borrows `data`
    some_io().await;               // <-- PAUSE POINT
    println!("{}", reference);     // uses reference AFTER await
}

The compiler generates roughly:

enum ExampleFuture {
    State0 { data: Vec<i32> },                    // before first .await
    State1 { data: Vec<i32>, reference: *const i32 },  // after .await, reference points INTO data
    Complete,
}

Notice the raw pointer *const i32? The reference &data[0] becomes a raw pointer because the state machine must store it across the .await boundary. If this enum moves in memory, that pointer dangles. This is why Pin exists.

Step 2: Pin — Preventing Moves That Break Self-References

Pin<P> is a wrapper around a pointer P that promises: the pointee will never move again.

use std::pin::Pin;

let mut future = example();           // returns the state machine (unpinned)
let pinned: Pin<&mut ExampleFuture> = Pin::new(&mut future); // NOW it's pinned

Once pinned, you cannot get a &mut T to the inner value (which would allow mem::swap or moving it). You only get &T — read-only access. The future is now frozen in place.

Why Pin<&mut Self> in poll? Because the executor must pin the future before polling it. The signature forces this: you literally cannot call poll without pinning first.

Two ways to pin in practice:

// Heap pin — future lives on heap, Box moves but heap allocation stays put
let pinned = Box::pin(async { 42 });

// Stack pin — future stays on stack, Pin<&mut> wrapper can move but underlying future doesn't
tokio::pin!(my_future);

Most types implement Unpin (they're safe to move). Compiler-generated futures from async fn are !Unpin — they must be pinned.

Step 3: The Executor Calls poll

An executor is just a loop that calls poll on futures that are ready to make progress.

// Conceptual executor loop (simplified)
fn executor_loop(tasks: &mut TaskQueue) {
    loop {
        // 1. Poll all woken tasks
        while let Some(task) = tasks.get_woken_task() {
            match task.poll() {
                Poll::Ready(result) => task.complete(result),
                Poll::Pending => { /* stays in queue, waiting for wake */ }
            }
        }
        // 2. Sleep until something wakes us (epoll_wait, io_uring, etc.)
        tasks.wait_for_events();
    }
}

When you .await a future, the surrounding async function's state machine calls poll on the inner future. This chains: outer poll → inner poll → inner-inner poll... until something returns Pending.

Step 4: Pending Means "Register My Waker and Come Back"

When poll returns Poll::Pending, the future must have registered its waker with whatever it's waiting on (a socket, a timer, a channel). If it doesn't, the task hangs forever — no one will ever wake it.

impl Future for MyTcpRead {
    fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Result<Bytes, Error>> {
        // Check if data is already available
        if let Some(data) = self.try_read() {
            return Poll::Ready(Ok(data));
        }
        // NOT ready — store the waker so the socket can wake us
        self.waker_slot = Some(cx.waker().clone());
        // Re-check after storing (race condition protection!)
        if let Some(data) = self.try_read() {
            Poll::Ready(Ok(data))
        } else {
            Poll::Pending
        }
    }
}

Critical rule: Always re-check the condition after storing the waker. The data might have arrived between your first check and storing the waker. This is the "double-check pattern" — skip it and you get a race where the task never wakes.

Step 5: The Waker — The Interrupt Mechanism

A Waker is a handle that lets an I/O source say "hey, this task can make progress now." It's the bridge between the kernel/IO system and the executor.

// Inside an I/O driver (simplified)
fn on_socket_readable(socket: &TcpSocket, waker: &Waker) {
    // Data arrived — wake the task
    waker.wake();  // signals executor: "put this task back in the ready queue"
}

The executor receives this wake notification (via a channel, eventfd, or similar) and moves the task to its ready queue. Next loop iteration, poll gets called again.

Spurious wakes are normal. A future might be polled even though its I/O isn't ready. That's why the double-check pattern matters — never assume poll being called means readiness.

Step 6: .await Desugars to a Poll Loop

The Rust Reference shows the approximate desugaring:

match operand.into_future() {
    mut pinned => loop {
        let mut pin = unsafe { Pin::new_unchecked(&mut pinned) };
        match Pin::future::poll(Pin::borrow(&mut pin), &mut current_context) {
            Poll::Ready(r) => break r,
            Poll::Pending => yield Poll::Pending,  // suspend HERE
        }
    }
}

The yield Poll::Pending is the suspension point. The outer async function returns Pending to its caller (the executor). When the executor polls it again later, execution resumes right after that yield — same state, same local variables, same pinned memory location.

The Complete Flow: What Happens When You Write .await 

1. You call an async function → returns a Future (state machine, NOT running)
2. You .await it → compiler inserts poll loop around that future
3. Executor pins the future (Pin::new_unchecked / Box::pin / tokio::pin!)
4. Executor calls poll(future, context_with_waker)
5. Future checks: "am I ready?"
   ├─ YES → returns Poll::Ready(value) → .await expression evaluates to value
   └─ NO  → stores waker from context, returns Poll::Pending
6. Executor sees Pending → parks the task, goes to sleep (epoll/io_uring)
7. I/O completes → driver calls waker.wake()
8. Executor wakes up, puts task in ready queue
9. Executor calls poll again → loop repeats from step 4
10. Eventually Ready → value propagates up through all .await chains

Common Misconceptions

Misconception Reality
".await runs the future in the background" Futures are lazy. Nothing runs until poll is called. The future is the computation.
"async fn returns a running task" It returns an inert Future. You must spawn it or await it to drive it.
"Pin prevents all moves" Pin<&mut T> prevents moving through that reference. You can still move a Box (the pointer moves, heap allocation doesn't). Unpin types ignore pinning entirely.
"Waking a task runs it immediately" wake() just schedules it. The executor decides when to actually poll.
"If I don't call wake(), the future will still be polled eventually" No. Without a wake, the executor has no reason to poll it. The task hangs forever.

Why This Matters Practically

Debugging hangs: If your async code hangs, something returned Pending but never got woken. Check: did the future register its waker? Did the I/O driver call wake()?

Pin errors: "future cannot be unpinned" means you're trying to move a !Unpin future after pinning it. Use Box::pin() for heap storage, tokio::pin!() for stack pinning in select!.

CPU starvation: An async loop with no .await points monopolizes the executor thread. Insert tokio::task::yield_now().await periodically.

Spurious wake bugs: If you assume poll means "data is ready" without re-checking, you'll read garbage or panic. Always re-check.

The Mental Model to Keep

  • Future = a state machine that knows how to advance itself when polled
  • Pin = a promise that this state machine won't move (so its internal pointers stay valid)
  • Waker = a callback handle that lets I/O say "poll me now"
  • Executor = the event loop that sleeps on epoll/io_uring, wakes tasks, and calls poll
  • .await = syntactic sugar for "poll this inner future in a loop until Ready, yielding Pending to my caller each time"

None of this is magic. It's a carefully designed system where every piece has a mechanical purpose. The next time you type .await, you'll know exactly what you're invoking.

Tags: rust, async, futures, pin, waker, executor, systems

title: A Rust primer for humans: what matters when your agent writes the code
description:
More and more code is being written in Rust, and a growing share of it by coding agents. Why software is converging on Rust goes into the reasons: agents have made rewrites cheap, and Rust's compiler catches many of their mistakes before anyone reads the code. If you write Python, TypeScript or Go, there's a fair chance you'll soon be approving pull requests full of Rust you didn't write.

Reading Rust takes much less than writing it, and most of it maps onto things you already know from Python. The parts that don't, ownership and borrowing, explain nearly every error message you'll see, and they're easier to follow with pictures than with rules.

Part 1: The basics

Most of everyday Rust looks like any other modern language once you know the syntax, and nearly every piece has a Python equivalent.

Install Rust and run your first program

Install Rust with rustup, the official installer. It gives you two tools. rustc is the compiler, and you'll almost never call it directly. cargo is the build tool and package manager, the equivalent of pip and python rolled together, and it's what you'll type all day.

Make a project and run it:

cargo new hello
cd hello
cargo run

   Compiling hello v0.1.0 (/Users/you/hello)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.68s
     Running `target/debug/hello`
Hello, world!

cargo new made two files. Cargo.toml describes the project and its dependencies, like pyproject.toml or package.json. src/main.rs holds the program:

fn main() {
    println!("Hello, world!");
}

fn main() is where every Rust program starts. println! prints a line; the ! means it's a macro rather than a function, which you can ignore for now beyond knowing that macros end in !. If you'd rather not install anything yet, the Rust Playground runs it in the browser.

Unlike Python, Rust is compiled. cargo run first turns your source into a native binary, then runs it. Most of the errors Python reports while your program is running, Rust reports before it runs at all. That's the main thing you get in exchange for Rust's stricter rules.

These are the five cargo commands worth knowing:

Command What it does
cargo run Compile and run the program
cargo check Check everything without building a binary. Much faster, and what agents run in a loop
cargo test Build and run the tests
cargo clippy Run hundreds of extra lints that catch code that compiles but is probably wrong
cargo fmt Format the code in the standard style

Variables are immutable unless you say mut

Here's the same handful of variables in both languages:

name = "Ferris"
count = 0
count += 1
price = 9.99

let name = "Ferris";
let mut count = 0;
count += 1;
let price: f64 = 9.99;

Two differences. Variables are declared with let, and they can't change unless you add mut. Try to write count += 1 without the mut and the compiler refuses. This sounds fussy, but it means when you read Rust, every mut marks a place where state changes, and everything else stays put.

Rust is statically typed, but you rarely write the types out. The compiler infers them, so let count = 0 is an integer without saying so. You add a type when you want something specific, like f64 above, or when the compiler can't work it out.

The types map onto Python's like this:

Python Rust Notes
int i32, i64, u32, usize... Fixed size. i is signed, u is unsigned, the number is bits. usize is used for lengths and indexes
float f64 (or f32)
bool bool true and false, lower case
str String and &str String owns its text, &str borrows it
list Vec<T> All elements have the same type T
dict HashMap<K, V> Imported from std::collections
None Option<T> Not a value you can forget to check

Rust also lets you reuse a name for a new variable, called shadowing. It's common when converting a value from one type to another:

let input = "42";
let input: i32 = input.parse().unwrap();

The second input is a new variable that happens to have the same name. The first one, the text, is gone from view.

Functions and control flow

A function lists its parameter types and its return type after ->:

fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
    a + b
}

There's no return on the last line. In Rust, the last expression in a block is its value, as long as it has no semicolon. You can still write return to leave a function early, and you'll see both.

The same idea makes if an expression, so it can produce a value, like Python's x if cond else y:

fn grade(score: u32) -> &'static str {
    if score >= 90 { "A" } else if score >= 75 { "B" } else { "C" }
}

(The &'static str return type means "a piece of text that lives for the whole program", which is what string literals are.)

Loops look familiar. 0..3 is a range, like Python's range(3):

for i in 0..3 {
    println!("i = {i}");
}

let words = vec!["read", "edit", "bash"];
for w in &words {
    println!("{w}");
}

let mut n = 3;
while n > 0 {
    n -= 1;
}

vec![...] makes a Vec, Rust's growable list. The & in for w in &words means "loop over the list without consuming it", which is your first glimpse of borrowing. There's also loop { }, which runs until you break.

Structs and methods instead of classes

Rust has no classes. Data goes in a struct, and methods go in a separate impl block:

class Task:
    def __init__(self, title):
        self.title = title
        self.done = False

    def finish(self):
        self.done = True

struct Task {
    title: String,
    done: bool,
}

impl Task {
    fn new(title: &str) -> Task {
        Task { title: title.to_string(), done: false }
    }

    fn finish(&mut self) {
        self.done = true;
    }

    fn label(&self) -> String {
        let mark = if self.done { "x" } else { " " };
        format!("[{mark}] {}", self.title)
    }
}

new has no self, so it's called on the type, Task::new("write the primer"). It's only a naming convention; Rust has no special constructor. The other two take self in different ways, and the difference matters. &self means the method only reads the task. &mut self means it may change it. Python's self doesn't tell you which, so you have to read the body. In Rust the signature tells you.

There's no inheritance either. Shared behaviour comes from traits.

Enums and match

Rust's enums are more capable than Python's. Each variant can carry its own data:

enum Shape {
    Circle { radius: f64 },
    Rect { w: f64, h: f64 },
    Point,
}

A Shape is exactly one of these three. You take it apart with match, which is like a switch or Python's match statement, with one important difference: it has to handle every variant.

fn area(s: &Shape) -> f64 {
    match s {
        Shape::Circle { radius } => std::f64::consts::PI * radius * radius,
        Shape::Rect { w, h } => w * h,
        Shape::Point => 0.0,
    }
}

Leave out a case and the program doesn't compile. Here's what you get with an enum of four statuses and a match that only handles three:

error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: `&Status::Failed` not covered
 --> examples/nonexhaustive.rs:9:11
  |
9 |     match s {
  |           ^ pattern `&Status::Failed` not covered
  |
help: ensure that all possible cases are being handled by adding a match arm with a wildcard pattern or an explicit pattern as shown
  |
12~         Status::Done => "finished",
13~         &Status::Failed => todo!(),

This pays off over time. When someone adds a fifth status next month, the compiler lists every match that needs updating. The one way to opt out is a wildcard arm, _ => ..., which catches everything not listed, including variants that don't exist yet. In review, a wildcard on an enum the code owns deserves a second look.

Part 2: Ownership and borrowing

Everything so far has a close cousin in Python. Ownership doesn't, and almost everything after this depends on it.

Every value has one owner

Python manages memory for you with a garbage collector. Many variables can refer to the same list, and the list is freed some time after the last reference disappears. C and C++ make you free memory yourself, which is fast but easy to get wrong: free something twice, or use it after freeing it, and you get crashes or security holes. Rust takes a third route. Every value has exactly one owner, and when the owner goes out of scope, the value is freed right there. The compiler checks the rules, so there's no garbage collector and no manual freeing.

To see what's being owned, look at what a String is in memory. The variable itself is small and fixed-size: a pointer to the text, its length and its capacity. The text lives elsewhere, in a region called the heap.

Moving a value

Now assign it to another variable:

let s1 = String::from("hello");
let s2 = s1;

In Python, s2 = s1 gives you two names for the same object. In C++, copying a string copies the text. Rust does neither. It copies the three small fields, so s2 points at the same text, and then treats s1 as no longer valid. Ownership has moved to s2. That's called a move.

The reason is the "freed when the owner goes out of scope" rule. If both s1 and s2 owned the text, it would be freed twice when they both went out of scope, which is exactly the C++ bug Rust exists to prevent.

Moves happen when you pass a value to a function, too. This is the error you'll see most often while learning, and in review:

fn summarize(text: String) -> usize {
    text.len()
}

fn main() {
    let prompt = String::from("fix the failing test");
    let n = summarize(prompt);
    println!("{n} bytes in {prompt}");
}

error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `prompt`
 --> examples/moved.rs:8:29
  |
6 |     let prompt = String::from("fix the failing test");
  |         ------ move occurs because `prompt` has type `String`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
7 |     let n = summarize(prompt);
  |                       ------ value moved here
8 |     println!("{n} bytes in {prompt}");
  |                             ^^^^^^ value borrowed here after move
  |
note: consider changing this parameter type in function `summarize` to borrow instead if owning the value isn't necessary
 --> examples/moved.rs:1:20
  |
1 | fn summarize(text: String) -> usize {
  |    ---------       ^^^^^^ this parameter takes ownership of the value
help: consider cloning the value if the performance cost is acceptable
  |
7 |     let n = summarize(prompt.clone());
  |                             ++++++++

Rust's error messages read like a short story. Line 6 is where prompt was created, line 7 is where it moved into summarize, and line 8 is where it was used after the move. Then come two suggested fixes. The note says summarize should borrow the text instead of taking it, which is the right fix, since it only reads the text. The help says to clone it, which makes a full copy of the text and hands over the copy. Cloning always works, which is why you'll see a lot of it in code written by people, and agents, who were in a hurry.

Values that copy instead of moving

Small, simple values don't move. Integers, floats, booleans and characters are Copy: assigning them copies the bits and both variables stay usable. That's why you'll never see this error on an i32. Moves apply to values that own something on the heap, like String, Vec and most structs.

Step through the whole lifecycle here, one line at a time:

There's an interactive figure here. Try it on the original post.

Borrowing with &

Most functions don't need to own their arguments. They just need to look at them, or change them and hand them back. For that, Rust has references, written with &. Creating a reference is called borrowing.

fn summarize(text: &str) -> usize {
    text.len()
}

let prompt = String::from("fix the failing test");
let n = summarize(&prompt);
println!("{n} bytes in {prompt}");

&prompt lends prompt to the function. The function can read it, and when it returns, prompt still belongs to main and is still usable. (The parameter type is &str, a borrowed piece of text, rather than &String. It accepts both string types, so it's the usual choice for functions that only read text.)

Many readers or one writer

There are two kinds of borrow, and one rule connects them:

  • &T is a shared reference. It can read the value but not change it, and you can have as many as you like at the same time.
  • &mut T is a mutable reference. It can change the value, and while it exists, nothing else can use the value at all, not even to read it.

The rule looks strict until you see what it prevents:

fn main() {
    let mut calls = vec![String::from("read"), String::from("edit")];
    let first = &calls[0];
    calls.push(String::from("bash"));
    println!("first call was {first}");
}

error[E0502]: cannot borrow `calls` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable
 --> examples/borrow.rs:4:5
  |
3 |     let first = &calls[0];
  |                  ----- immutable borrow occurs here
4 |     calls.push(String::from("bash"));
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ mutable borrow occurs here
5 |     println!("first call was {first}");
  |                               ----- immutable borrow later used here

first points into the vector's storage. When push runs out of room, it allocates a bigger block of memory, moves everything across, and frees the old one, so first would be pointing at freed memory. In C++ the equivalent code compiles and reads garbage, or worse. Python avoids the problem with its garbage collector. Rust avoids it with this rule, at compile time, at no cost when the program runs.

This, together with ownership, is what people mean by "the borrow checker". It has a reputation for being hard to please, and when you're writing Rust, it sometimes is. When you're reading Rust, it's working for you: the code in front of you has already passed it.

Lifetimes, just enough to read them

Sooner or later you'll see a signature like this:

fn first_word<'a>(text: &'a str) -> &'a str

The 'a is a lifetime, a name for how long a borrow is valid. Here it says the returned reference points into text, so it can't be used after text is gone. For a reader, that's the whole job of a lifetime annotation: it tells you which input a returned reference comes from. Most of the time the compiler works this out without annotations. This signature is simple enough that cargo clippy suggests dropping the 'a entirely, and when a lifetime is obvious you'll often see '_ instead of a name.

The one lifetime to recognise is 'static, which means "valid for the whole program". String literals are 'static, which is why grade earlier returned &'static str.

Part 3: Absence and failure

Python programmers lean on two things every day that Rust doesn't have: None, which can turn up anywhere, and exceptions. Rust replaces both with ordinary enums.

No null: Option

A value that might be missing has the type Option<T>, which is an enum with two variants: Some(value) and None.

fn find_user(id: u32) -> Option<String> {
    if id == 1 { Some(String::from("ada")) } else { None }
}

match find_user(2) {
    Some(name) => println!("found {name}"),
    None => println!("no such user"),
}

if let Some(name) = find_user(1) {
    println!("hello {name}");
}

You can't use the String inside without first checking which variant you have. match handles both; if let handles just the one you care about. In Python, forgetting the None check gives you AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute ... at runtime. In Rust it doesn't compile.

No exceptions: Result and ?

A function that can fail returns Result<T, E>, another two-variant enum: Ok(value) or Err(error).

fn parse_port(s: &str) -> Result<u16, std::num::ParseIntError> {
    let port: u16 = s.trim().parse()?;
    Ok(port)
}

The ? at the end of the second line does the work a try/except would. If parse() returned an error, ? returns that error from parse_port immediately. If it succeeded, ? takes the number out and carries on. Every place an error can leave a function is marked with one ?, which makes error paths easy to find when reading.

unwrap, and when it's a problem

You'll also see .unwrap(). It takes the value out of an Option or Result, and if there isn't one, it panics, which crashes the current thread. .expect("message") does the same with an explanation attached. They're fine in tests, in quick scripts, and where failure truly can't happen. In code that handles outside input, they're a crash waiting for the wrong input. In November 2025, a Cloudflare outage that broke a large part of the web for several hours came down to a Rust proxy calling unwrap() on a Result that, for the first time, held an error.

Part 4: Real programs

Strings, Vec and HashMap

Now the two string types make sense. String owns its text on the heap, can grow, and is freed when its owner goes away. &str is a borrowed view of text that something else owns: a String, or a literal compiled into the program. Functions that only read text take &str. Structs that need to keep text store a String.

Vec<T> is the growable list and HashMap<K, V> is the dictionary:

use std::collections::HashMap;

let scores = vec![72, 95, 88, 40];
let total: i32 = scores.iter().sum();

let mut ages: HashMap<String, u32> = HashMap::new();
ages.insert(String::from("ada"), 36);
if let Some(age) = ages.get("ada") {
    println!("ada is {age}");
}

ages.get returns an Option, because the key might not be there. Python would raise a KeyError from ages["ada"]; Rust makes you decide what happens in that case.

Iterators instead of list comprehensions

Where Python uses a list comprehension, Rust uses an iterator chain:

doubled = [s * 2 for s in scores if s >= 50]

let doubled: Vec<i32> = scores.iter().filter(|s| **s >= 50).map(|s| s * 2).collect();

Read it left to right: go through the scores, keep the ones that are at least 50, double each one, collect the results into a Vec. The |s| ... parts are closures, Rust's lambdas. (The **s is because filter hands the closure a reference to a reference; you'll get used to it.) Chains like this compile down to roughly the same machine code as a hand-written loop.

One detail to watch: .iter() borrows the collection, which stays usable afterwards. .into_iter() consumes it, moving each element out. Mixing them up is a common source of move errors.

Traits: shared behaviour without inheritance

A trait is a set of methods a type promises to provide, close to an interface in TypeScript or Java, or a protocol in Python.

trait Describe {
    fn describe(&self) -> String;
}

impl Describe for Task {
    fn describe(&self) -> String {
        format!("task '{}'", self.title)
    }
}

Any type can implement any number of traits, and that's how Rust shares behaviour instead of using inheritance. The standard library defines traits for common abilities: Display for printing with {}, Debug for printing with {:?}, Clone for .clone(), and so on. For the obvious ones, you can ask the compiler to write the implementation for you:

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
struct Point {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}

Functions can accept any type that implements a trait. These two are equivalent ways of writing "anything that can be printed with {}":

fn show(item: &impl std::fmt::Display) { println!("{item}"); }
fn show_generic<T: std::fmt::Display>(item: &T) { println!("{item}"); }

You'll also see Box<dyn Display>, which means the same thing decided at runtime rather than compile time, for when you need a list of mixed types.

Crates: using other people's code

Libraries in Rust are called crates, and they come from crates.io. cargo add adds one to Cargo.toml, like pip install plus a line in your requirements. The most common one you'll see is serde, which converts structs to and from JSON and other formats:

cargo add serde --features derive
cargo add serde_json

use serde::Deserialize;

#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
struct ToolCall {
    name: String,
    args: std::collections::HashMap<String, String>,
}

fn parse_calls(input: &str) -> Result<Vec<ToolCall>, serde_json::Error> {
    let calls: Vec<ToolCall> = serde_json::from_str(input)?;
    Ok(calls)
}

#[derive(Deserialize)] generates the parsing code from the struct definition, and parse_calls returns a Result because the JSON might be malformed. Other names you'll see often: tokio for async, anyhow and thiserror for errors, clap for command-line arguments, reqwest for HTTP.

Threads and async, enough to read them

Rust applies the ownership rules across threads too. Two built-in traits do it. A type is Send if it's safe to move to another thread, and Sync if it's safe to share between threads. The compiler works these out and checks them wherever a thread starts.

To share data between threads you'll see Arc<Mutex<T>>. Arc lets several threads own the same value; it counts the owners and frees the value when the last one is done. Mutex is a lock. In Rust the data lives inside the lock, so you can't reach it without calling .lock(), and forgetting to lock is a compile error rather than a race condition you find in production.

use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread;

let log = Arc::new(Mutex::new(Vec::new()));
let handles: Vec<_> = (0..3)
    .map(|i| {
        let log = Arc::clone(&log);
        thread::spawn(move || log.lock().unwrap().push(i))
    })
    .collect();
for h in handles {
    h.join().unwrap();
}

Arc has a single-threaded sibling, Rc, which is cheaper. If you try to send an Rc to another thread, you get a compile error:

error[E0277]: `Rc<Vec<i32>>` cannot be sent between threads safely
   --> examples/race.rs:6:32
    |
  6 |       let handle = thread::spawn(move || {
    |                    ------------- required by a bound introduced by this call
...
    = help: within `{closure@examples/race.rs:6:32: 6:39}`, the trait `Send` is not implemented for `Rc<Vec<i32>>`

async fn and .await work much like they do in JavaScript and Python, with one difference: Rust doesn't include a runtime to run them, so a library provides one. That's almost always Tokio, which is why you'll see #[tokio::main] above main.

Part 5: Reviewing Rust your agent wrote

Say an agent has opened a pull request in Rust, the tests pass, and you have to approve it or push back. Here's where to look.

Read the signature before the body

Rust signatures say a lot about what a function is allowed to do, and the compiler holds the function to it. You can learn most of what matters before reading the body:

In the signature What it tells you
x: Config Takes ownership. The caller can't use x afterwards
x: &Config Only reads x
x: &mut Config May change x. Look here for side effects
-> Result<T, E> Can fail, and callers must handle it
-> Option<T> Might return nothing
T: Send Must be safe to move to another thread
unsafe fn Some of the compiler's checks are off. The caller must uphold rules it can't verify
pub Part of the public API. Changes affect other code

A function that takes &Config can't quietly modify the config. A function that returns plain u32 instead of a Result is claiming it can't fail; if it parses input or does I/O, that usually means an unwrap() inside.

Read the compiler's errors, then the fix

When an agent fixes a compile error, look at what the compiler said before looking at the fix. Rust errors always have the same shape: an error code and summary, the file and line, labelled spans that tell the story in order, then note and help lines with suggested changes. Two habits help. Read only the first error, since later ones are often knock-on effects. And treat the help suggestion with some suspicion. It's the quickest edit that compiles, which isn't always the right one, as the .clone() suggestion for E0382 shows. rustc --explain E0382 prints a full explanation of any error code.

Agents do comparatively well with Rust for this reason. The same messages are available as JSON, with each suggested edit marked by how safe it is to apply, so an agent is told exactly what's wrong and often what to type. When GitHub ported its Copilot runtime to Rust using agents, ownership and borrowing errors were only 1.7% of the compile errors they ran into. The agents mostly get ownership right. What's left for you is the cases where they got it to compile in a way that costs something.

An agent's diff, annotated

Here's a typical agent diff. Click any highlighted part for what it means and how much it should concern you:

There's an interactive figure here. Try it on the original post.

Seven smells in agent-written Rust

Code an agent wrote can compile, pass the tests and still take shortcuts. These are the ones I look for first. All of them compile, so the compiler won't point them out:

Smell What it looks like What to ask
Clone to compile .clone() on a value that's only read afterwards Could this be a borrow?
Unwrap on input .unwrap() on parsed input, a network response or a file What happens on bad input?
Unexplained unsafe An unsafe { } block without a // SAFETY: comment Why is this sound, and who keeps it that way?
Stubs that compile todo!(), unimplemented!(), or a hard-coded default where logic should be Does a test reach this code?
Silenced lints #[allow(...)] added in the same diff What was the lint going to say?
Forever lifetimes 'static, Box::leak, or Arc everywhere to get past a lifetime error Does this really need to live forever?
Catch-all match _ => on an enum the code owns Should a new variant be a compile error here?

These come from people watching agents at scale. Niko Matsakis, a longtime lead of the Rust language team, wrote this month that agent-written async Rust tends to be clone-heavy. During Bun's move from Zig to Rust, agents stubbed out functions instead of fixing them until the reviewing agents were told to reject that. A quick habit: before reading a diff's logic, search it for clone, unwrap, unsafe, todo!, allow( and 'static. It takes seconds and shows you where the agent had trouble.

Try it on these snippets. Each one compiles; decide which you'd question:

There's an interactive figure here. Try it on the original post.

Where to go next

If you'd like to go from reading Rust to writing it, these are the resources most Rustaceans started with:

  • The Rust Programming Language, known as "the Book". It's free, the ownership diagrams above come from it, and chapter 4 covers ownership in more depth.
  • Rustlings: small exercises that fail to compile until you fix them, so you learn from the compiler directly.
  • Rust by Example, for people who'd rather read code than prose.
  • The Clippy lint list, the best catalogue of code that compiles but probably shouldn't.

For why so much Rust is about to land in your review queue, read Why software is converging on Rust in the age of AI. For what the agent is doing on the other side of the pull request, start with what an agent harness is.

I'm Dheeraj, a software engineer at Nutanix Enterprise AI working on agent
harnesses and developer tools. I write up the problems that took me too long to
work out. More at dheerajakula.dev/blog.

title: Why software is converging on Rust in the age of AI
description:
For about a decade, "rewrite it in Rust" was a joke. It was what an excitable stranger posted under every bug report in a C++ project, and the reply was some polite version of no, because rewrites took years and broke things that already worked. Dropbox spent years moving its sync engine from Python to Rust, and its own write-up warns that in many companies it would have been a terrible idea.

Over a few months in 2026, one large project after another did it anyway, and none of them took years. In February, Andreas Kling moved the JavaScript engine of the Ladybird browser from C++ to Rust in about two weeks, and it passed all 52,898 tests of the official JavaScript conformance suite with byte-for-byte identical output. In May, Bun, the JavaScript runtime, went from 535,000 lines of Zig to Rust in 11 days, with up to 64 Claude agents working through roughly 16,000 compiler errors. Meta merged a Rust version of the React Compiler in June and describes most of it as written by AI. By September, a single engineer at GitHub directing up to 22 agents had turned the TypeScript runtime behind Copilot into 832,000 lines of Rust. And in October, a solo developer named Brandon Thomas published open-source Rust clones of Photoshop, Illustrator and Premiere, built by directing Claude, and collected 70,000 GitHub stars in three weeks.

ForrestKnight's video on this has the best one-line summary I've seen: Rust didn't change this year, the cost of rewriting did. It's 25 minutes and worth it.

He's right, and it's half the answer. Cheap rewrites explain why teams are switching languages now. They don't explain why so many are switching to the same one, when Go, Zig and modern C++ were all available. The other half is about who reads the code. When an agent produces a thousand lines an hour, nobody reviews all of it, so whatever the compiler checks for free ends up carrying most of the weight. Rust's compiler checks more than any other mainstream language's, and agents turn out to be good at taking its feedback.

Rewrites used to take years

Choosing a language used to be one of the few permanent decisions in a project. You could swap a database or a cloud provider, but changing languages meant pausing feature work for a year or more while a team re-implemented everything and chased down the behaviour that shifted along the way. Jarred Sumner, who created Bun, described language choice for a project like his as having been "a one-way decision" until very recently.

The fish shell is a good picture of the old cost. Its move from C++ to Rust, finished in 2024 without AI, took almost two years and more than 200 contributors to port 57,000 lines. Compare that with this year:

Port From Size Time Who
fish shell (no AI) C++ 57K lines almost 2 years 200+ contributors
Ladybird's LibJS C++ ~25K lines of Rust ~2 weeks Andreas Kling, with Claude Code and Codex
Bun Zig 535K lines 11 days One engineer, up to 64 agents at once
Copilot runtime TypeScript ~430K lines in, ~832K lines of Rust out 14.5 weeks Mostly one engineer, up to 22 subagents
React Compiler TypeScript +123K lines merged June 2026 Meta, "majority coded by AI"

You can see the result on GitHub. A project's language bar is computed from its source files, and Bun's now looks like this:

These numbers deserve some care. Bun's port cost around $165,000 in API usage and needed one very experienced engineer watching it the whole time. Sumner's own estimate for doing it by hand was three engineers for about a year. Kling describes Ladybird's port as "human-directed, not autonomous". And Bun is owned by Anthropic, whose models did the work, so its write-up is partly a showcase. Even so, the cost of switching languages has fallen by something like two orders of magnitude.

One thing shows up in every port that worked: a test suite that doesn't care what language the code is in. Bun's tests are TypeScript that drives the runtime from outside, so the same 60,000 tests could judge the Zig version and the Rust version. Ladybird had test262, the official JavaScript conformance suite. Agents translate quickly, and the test suite is what tells you whether the translation is right.

The big players are betting on the same idea. In December 2025, Microsoft Distinguished Engineer Galen Hunt set a goal of "1 engineer, 1 month, 1 million lines of code" for AI-driven translation of C and C++ into Rust, then clarified that Windows isn't being rewritten and the work is a research project. DARPA runs a program called TRACTOR, short for Translating All C to Rust, with the same aim.

Why teams wanted to rewrite: speed and memory

Cheap rewrites only matter if someone wants one, and the usual reason is performance. Rust compiles to native machine code, like C and C++, and it has no garbage collector: memory is freed the moment its owner goes away, not in periodic sweeps. That raises throughput and keeps latency flat instead of spiking whenever a collector runs.

The published before-and-after numbers are large when the old code was garbage-collected or interpreted:

Project Compared with Result
Cloudflare's core proxy its NGINX and LuaJIT predecessor 10 ms faster median response, on under half the CPU and well under half the memory
AWS Aurora DSQL a tuned Kotlin version about 10x the throughput: roughly 30,000 transactions per second against 2,000 to 3,000
Discord's Read States service the Go version the latency spikes Go's garbage collector caused every few minutes went away
vLLM's frontend the Python frontend median time to first token from 166 ms to 50.5 ms
Vite 8's Rolldown bundler Rollup, in JavaScript Linear's production build from 46 seconds to 6
ty, Astral's Python type checker Pyright an incremental check in 4.7 ms instead of 386 ms
GitHub's Copilot runtime the Node version no more Node host taking about 100 MB per SDK client

Ports from C, C++ or Zig look different, because those languages were already fast. Bun got 2 to 5% faster after its move from Zig, and Claude Code, which runs on Bun, started about 10% quicker on Linux (517 ms to 464 ms). The bigger change was memory. Building a 60-module project 2,000 times in one process used 6,745 MB on the Zig version, which leaked about 3 MB per build, and 609 MB on the Rust one.

Part of the speedup from leaving JavaScript or Python comes from going native at all. Microsoft's Go port of the TypeScript compiler made full builds 8 to 12 times faster with no Rust involved. Where Rust pulls ahead of Go and the JVM is the missing garbage collector, which gives steady tail latency and a smaller memory footprint, and that's what Discord and the Aurora DSQL team said they were after.

The compiler became the first reviewer

Cheap rewrites move the bottleneck. GitHub's port produced 832,000 lines of production Rust and another 469,000 lines of tests in three and a half months. No one read that line by line. The checking moves to things that can keep up: the test suite, other agents set up as hostile reviewers, and the compiler.

Of those, the compiler is the one that runs on every single change, in seconds, and never gets tired or changes its mind. Bun's agents used the output of cargo check, Rust's fast type and borrow check, as their to-do list. They burned down those 16,000 errors crate by crate before running a single test. Sumner explained the choice of Rust over a stricter Zig style guide in one line: compiler errors are a better feedback loop than a style guide. A style guide depends on someone noticing the violation. A compiler error stops the build.

Here's what that loop looks like on a small change, with two real compiler errors in it. Press play, or step through it.

There's an interactive figure here. Try it on the original post.

There's research behind this now. A 2026 paper on generative compilation tested seven models on repository-sized Rust tasks. Left alone, the models wrote Rust that didn't compile 65.9% of the time on average; the paper is frank that Rust is harder to get right on the first try than permissive languages like C. Feeding the compiler's errors back after generation cut that to 20.7%, and checking partial programs while the model was still writing cut it to 13.1%. In one setup, a frontier model went from 51.7% non-compiling to zero.

What surprised me is how well agents do with Rust once that loop is in place. On SWE-bench Multilingual, a benchmark built from real GitHub issues in nine languages, the tested agent resolved Rust issues at the highest rate of any language, 58%. C and C++ came last at 29%. There are only 43 Rust tasks, so I wouldn't lean hard on the exact number, but it points the opposite way from the usual worry that agents would struggle with Rust because there's less of it to learn from. And in GitHub's Copilot port, the dreaded ownership and borrowing errors made up just 1.7% of all the compile errors the agents hit. Most were ordinary slips with names and types.

What Rust's compiler catches that others don't

Every typed language checks something. What matters is how many kinds of bug get turned into compile errors, and Rust covers several kinds that other languages leave to tests, sanitizers or luck. Pick a bug and see when each language finds it:

There's an interactive figure here. Try it on the original post.

Memory bugs

Use-after-free, double free and reading past the end of a buffer are the classic C and C++ bugs, and they're behind most serious security holes. Microsoft has said for years that about 70% of the CVEs it assigns are memory-safety bugs, and Chromium reports the same share of its high and critical bugs. In safe Rust, the ownership rules make all of these compile errors. Bun's last Zig release notes read like a catalogue of them: use-after-frees in node:zlib and node:http2, a double free in the CSS parser, leaks on error paths.

Android has the longest track record. Google has written new Android code in Rust since 2019, and reported in November 2025 that memory-safety bugs had dropped below 20% of Android's vulnerabilities for the first time, down from 76% in 2019. Android's C and C++ code runs at roughly 1,000 memory-safety vulnerabilities per million lines. Its 5 million lines of Rust have had one near miss, about 0.2 per million. Rust changes also had a 4x lower rollback rate and spent 25% less time in code review, and once agents write the code, review time is the part that doesn't shrink.

Data races

Rust tracks which types can safely move or be shared between threads, through two traits called Send and Sync, and refuses to compile code that would share something unsafely. In TypeScript, Go or C++, a data race compiles and fails now and then in production. Daniel Szoke from Sentry built a whole talk, Why Rust is the Ideal Language for Vibe-Coding, around this: the Rust compiler names the exact type that can't cross threads, which points the agent straight at the fix.

Forgotten cases

A match on an enum has to handle every variant. Add a new status, and every match that doesn't handle it becomes a compile error with its location. Agents are good at the change you asked for and worse at finding the six other places it should ripple to. Rust turns that hunt into a list.

Failure paths

Rust has no exceptions and no null. A function that can fail returns a Result, a value that might be missing is an Option, and the compiler makes the caller handle both before touching what's inside. You can tell from a function's signature whether it can fail, which is most of what a reviewer wants to know.

Error messages a model can act on

rustc errors give the exact location, explain why, and often include a suggested edit. The same output comes as JSON, with each suggestion marked by how safe it is to apply automatically, and cargo fix applies the safe ones. The Rust project built this for people years before coding agents existed. For a model in a loop, it's close to a set of instructions.

One toolchain everywhere

Every Rust project builds with cargo, tests with cargo test, lints with cargo clippy and formats with rustfmt. An agent that knows one Rust project knows how to build and check all of them. In C++, the build system alone can take a new human days to figure out.

Rust had all of these properties in 2018, and for years the effort of satisfying its compiler kept a lot of people away. That effort is exactly the part agents are happy to grind through, and the payoff, code that's been checked before anyone reads it, is exactly what you need when nobody can read it all. Niko Matsakis, a longtime lead of the Rust language team, makes a similar case: Rust's old promise that code which compiles usually works matters more when an agent is the one compiling.

Rust is spreading well past the server

The usual story about Rust is infrastructure, like Cloudflare's proxy and AWS's databases, and that's where it paid off first. But over the last two years Rust has moved into places that have nothing to do with servers. Click around:

There's an interactive figure here. Try it on the original post.

Browsers

Browsers parse untrusted input from every website on earth, so they were early adopters. Firefox has had Rust inside since its CSS engine, Stylo, shipped in 2017, and its WebGPU support is built on wgpu, a Rust graphics library. Chrome replaced the FreeType font library with a Rust font stack called Skrifa and removed FreeType from Blink entirely in Chrome 145. Chromium's JSON parser is Rust too, because that's what makes it safe to run on untrusted input at high privilege.

The most interesting browser story is Ladybird, a new engine built from scratch by a nonprofit. In 2024 it picked Swift as its future language. In February 2026 it dropped Swift, because the C++ interop "never quite got there", and moved to Rust, starting with the JavaScript engine that agents helped port in two weeks.

Operating systems

Kernels are where a single memory bug becomes a security hole, and Rust is now inside Windows, Linux and Android. Windows has shipped Rust in the kernel since 2024, starting with the code that handles GDI regions. The Linux kernel declared its Rust experiment over in December 2025, which means Rust is now a permanent part of Linux. Android's Binder driver has a Rust rewrite in mainline, and there are Rust GPU drivers for Arm Mali, Apple silicon and, still early, NVIDIA. In Android itself, new Rust code overtook new C++ in 2025.

Mark Russinovich's RustConf 2025 keynote is the best account of how this went inside Microsoft, including a bug that would have been a privilege escalation in C++ and became a clean, reproducible crash in Rust:

Above the kernel, System76 shipped COSMIC, a whole desktop environment written in Rust from the ground up, as the default in Pop!_OS 24.04.

Graphics, 3D and creative tools

This is the part I know best, because I'm building in it. The 3D editor I'm working on is Rust compiled to WebAssembly, drawing with WebGPU from a worker in a browser tab. Two years ago that would have been an odd choice. Now it's fairly ordinary.

The biggest surprise of the year was PhotoCraft. In October, Brandon Thomas published PhotoCraft, an open-source Photoshop alternative written in Rust, along with sibling projects for Illustrator, Premiere, Lightroom and other Adobe apps, built mostly by directing Claude agents. It has layers, adjustment curves, masks and 67 tools, and it re-saves Photoshop files that match the originals in 307 of 309 test cases.

It's honest about being early alpha and not yet a tool for professional work, and whether its "clean-room" process holds up legally is an open question. Adobe wasn't involved and hasn't commented. But a few years ago, a credible Photoshop alternative would have needed a funded company and years of work.

Graphite is another creative tool in the same spirit: a node-based vector and raster editor written in Rust, still in alpha, that mixes layers with procedural, generative editing:

Zed, the code editor, reached 1.0 this year on GPUI, its own GPU-rendered UI framework in Rust, with agents built in. Bevy is the most active Rust game engine, and Vello renders 2D vector graphics entirely on the GPU. Figma moved its multiplayer server to Rust back in 2018.

Developer tools

Python's tooling is now largely Rust underneath. Astral's uv, ruff and ty, whose company joined OpenAI in March, are among the most downloaded packages in the ecosystem. pydantic-core, the Rust engine inside Pydantic, was downloaded about 808 million times in a single 30-day stretch this autumn, roughly twice as often as pip itself. JavaScript went the same way: Turbopack is the default bundler in Next.js 16, and Vite 8 bundles with Rolldown, both written in Rust.

The coding agents themselves are moving too. OpenAI's Codex CLI left Node for Rust to get a dependency-free install and native sandboxing, and is now about 97% Rust. GitHub's Copilot runtime followed, xAI's Grok Build shipped in Rust from day one, and Warp, the terminal that has turned into an agent workspace, has been written in Rust and drawn on the GPU from the start.

The AI stack

The code around AI models has been picking up Rust for years. Hugging Face's tokenizers library and the safetensors file format are Rust, and almost every model download pulls in both. In May, vLLM, the most popular open-source inference server, merged an optional Rust frontend because the Python frontend had become the CPU bottleneck. The proposal argued that, with coding agents around, the old objection that contributors can't read Rust is "minimized".

Where Rust isn't winning

Rust has made little headway in three areas that matter a lot, GPU kernels, research code and games, and in a few others another language won on purpose.

GPU kernels

The code that actually runs AI models is still CUDA C++, plus more and more Python. NVIDIA's recent bets are Python-first: cuTile Python, the CuTe DSL in CUTLASS 4, and native CUDA Python. NVIDIA did announce official CUDA Rust in September, with two tracks called cuda-oxide and cutile-rs, but by its own description neither is production-ready, and it calls CUDA C++ and Python the mature toolchains. The community Rust-CUDA project came back to life in 2025 after three dormant years and is still early. If you write kernels for a living, Rust isn't on your list yet.

Research and training

Research lives in Python because researchers iterate in notebooks, and PyTorch and JAX are Python on top of C++ and CUDA. The biggest inference engines are Python or C++ as well: llama.cpp has about 132,000 GitHub stars and vLLM about 95,000, while the leading Rust ML framework, candle, has about 21,000. Hugging Face's TGI, the best-known inference server with a Rust core, is now in maintenance mode, and its own docs point people to vLLM and SGLang. So far Rust takes the always-on pieces around the model (the server frontend, the tokenizer, the file format), Python keeps the places where people experiment, and CUDA keeps the maths.

Games

Unreal is C++, Unity is C#, and Bevy is on version 0.20. LogLog Games wrote a widely shared post, Leaving Rust gamedev after 3 years, after 100,000 lines: games need fast iteration and hot reloading, and the borrow checker kept forcing refactors when they wanted to try ideas. Agents make refactors cheaper, but they don't change how much game development values trying ten things in an afternoon.

Places where another language won

The most useful counterexample is TypeScript itself. When Microsoft rewrote the TypeScript compiler for speed, it picked Go, and TypeScript 7 shipped this year with full builds 8 to 12 times faster. The team's reasons were specific: they wanted a line-by-line port, Go's style is close to the existing code, garbage collection suits a compiler, and the compiler's syntax trees are full of cycles, which Rust's ownership model makes awkward. Zig keeps strong projects like Ghostty and TigerBeetle, whose authors chose it deliberately. Go still runs cloud infrastructure, from Kubernetes to Terraform. And Armin Ronacher, who knows Rust well, argues that Go and TypeScript are better languages for agents, partly because agents struggle with Rust's macros.

Bugs the compiler can't see

Rust's checks have edges, and agents find them too. Bun's port had 19 regressions, all in code that compiled. In one, a debug_assert! wrapped a call that had a side effect, so release builds quietly skipped the call and hot reloading broke. Cloudflare's November 2025 outage was a Rust proxy calling unwrap() on an error it had never seen before, which crashes by design. Check Point found a Rust panic in the Windows kernel that blue-screened the machine. Code at the boundary with C stays unsafe, around 4% of both Bun's and Android's Rust, and the Linux kernel's first Rust CVE came from an unsafe block. Rust also compiles slowly: in the project's 2025 survey, 55% of respondents wait more than 10 seconds for a rebuild, and an agent running hundreds of builds feels that too.

A panic is a better way to fail than memory corruption, and a crash is better than a silent security hole. Reviewers still have to read for logic errors, panics and unsafe; Rust just makes the list shorter.

Where this is heading

Put together, the stack seems to be sorting itself into layers, and no single language gets all of them. Code that runs all day, handles untrusted input, and has to be both correct and fast is moving to Rust: runtimes, browser engines, kernel drivers, toolchains, agent harnesses, inference frontends, creative tools. Agents are speeding that up twice, by making the port affordable and by doing the part of Rust people found tedious. Code where people are still exploring, like research, prototypes, scripts and UI glue, stays in Python and TypeScript, where the feedback loop is a person trying things. GPU kernels stay wherever NVIDIA's tools are best, which today means C++ and Python. And the huge body of existing C and C++ shrinks slowly, as efforts like Microsoft's research project and DARPA's TRACTOR mature.

That's my bet for the next five years, and parts of it could be wrong. If NVIDIA's Rust tracks mature, kernels could follow. If agents get much better at the first draft, the compiler's job as a reviewer matters less. But the direction over the last two years has been consistent, and it sped up in the last one.

Try it on your own agent

If you run coding agents on a codebase, a few changes help in any language and help most in Rust:

  1. Put cargo check in the agent's inner loop, and cargo clippy -- -D warnings plus cargo test before it says it's done. The compiler is the cheapest reviewer you have.
  2. Turn on the Clippy lints that catch agent shortcuts: unwrap_used and expect_used outside tests, and undocumented_unsafe_blocks so every unsafe needs a // SAFETY: comment.
  3. Before porting anything, make sure the test suite runs from outside the code, in another language or as a black box. That's what made Bun's and Ladybird's ports checkable.
  4. Use a second agent with fresh context as a hostile reviewer that only sees the diff and is told to assume it's wrong. Bun ran two of them on every change.
  5. Read the diff yourself where the compiler can't help: logic, unsafe, unwrap, and anything that touches money or permissions.

That last step needs you to read Rust. If you don't yet, A Rust primer for humans goes from hello world to reviewing an agent's Rust diff, with Python alongside. For what's on the other side of the pull request, there's what an agent harness is and a walk through OpenCode's source. For the other side of the argument, Cliff Biffle's Common Pitfalls of Rewriting Things in Rust is worth an hour, and for where Linux is heading, so is Greg Kroah-Hartman's Untrusted data in Linux.

I'm Dheeraj, a software engineer at Nutanix Enterprise AI working on agent
harnesses and developer tools. I write up the problems that took me too long to
work out. More at dheerajakula.dev/blog.

title: I Copied a Live SQLite Database and the Copy Had No Tables: WAL Mode Keeps Commits in a Second File
description:
How can a byte-for-byte copy of a SQLite database file be missing a table the writer had already committed? I copied a live database with shutil.copy, opened the copy, and asked it for the table I had just created. It said there was no such table.

The writer had committed every row. The copy was a faithful duplicate of the file I pointed it at. That file was not the whole database.

Disclosure: I make an Android camera app. Nothing below uses its code or describes how it stores anything. Every script here ran on one Linux machine with Python 3.10.12 and the SQLite library it links (3.37.2), against throwaway databases the scripts create in their own folder.

What the tests showed:

  • In WAL mode, committed data can live entirely outside the main .db file. A copy of that file alone came back without the table, let alone the rows.
  • The same copy works perfectly once the app closes, which is why a backup script can pass every test you run on a quiet machine and still produce empty backups in production.
  • Forcing a checkpoint first can fail. One open read transaction in another connection kept the checkpoint from moving a single frame into the main file.
  • Python already ships the safe tools. Connection.backup() and VACUUM INTO both produced complete, single-file copies while the writer was still connected.

Why one file is not the database

By default SQLite uses a rollback journal: changes go straight into the database file, and the journal holds the old content in case of a rollback. Write-ahead logging flips that around. SQLite's WAL documentation puts it plainly: "The original content is preserved in the database file and the changes are appended into a separate WAL file."

So while any connection is open, a WAL database is a set of files: app.db, app.db-wal, and a shared-memory index called app.db-shm. A commit is a record appended to the -wal file. The main file catches up later, during a step called a checkpoint.

The documentation is explicit about what that means for copying: "The WAL file is part of the persistent state of the database and should be kept with the database if the database is copied or moved." And on what goes wrong if you do not: "If a database file is separated from its WAL file, then transactions that were previously committed to the database might be lost, or the database file might become corrupted."

Test one: copy the file while the writer is open

copy_test.py turns on WAL mode, creates a table, commits a batch of rows, and then copies the database three ways: the main file alone, the main file plus its -wal, and the main file alone again after the connection closes.

import os, shutil, sqlite3

def count(path):
    c = sqlite3.connect(path)
    try:
        return c.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM events").fetchone()[0]
    except sqlite3.Error as e:
        return "error: %s" % e
    finally:
        c.close()

def files(prefix):
    return sorted(f for f in os.listdir(".") if f.startswith(prefix))

db = sqlite3.connect("app.db")
print("journal_mode:", db.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL").fetchone()[0])
db.execute("CREATE TABLE events (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, note TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO events (note) VALUES (?)",
               [("event %d" % i,) for i in range(500)])
db.commit()
print("rows committed:", db.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM events").fetchone()[0])
print("files while open:", files("app.db"))

shutil.copy("app.db", "copy_main_only.db")
print("copy of app.db alone:", count("copy_main_only.db"))

shutil.copy("app.db", "copy_with_wal.db")
shutil.copy("app.db-wal", "copy_with_wal.db-wal")
print("copy of app.db + app.db-wal:", count("copy_with_wal.db"))

db.close()
print("files after close:", files("app.db"))
shutil.copy("app.db", "copy_after_close.db")
print("copy of app.db after close:", count("copy_after_close.db"))

Output:

journal_mode: wal
rows committed: 500
files while open: ['app.db', 'app.db-shm', 'app.db-wal']
copy of app.db alone: error: no such table: events
copy of app.db + app.db-wal: 500
files after close: ['app.db']
copy of app.db after close: 500

The first copy did not just lose recent rows. It lost the CREATE TABLE too, because the schema change was also a commit sitting in the -wal file. As far as the copied app.db knew, it was an empty database.

The second copy, with the -wal file carried alongside it, opened with every row. That is the documented behavior: SQLite reads the log when it opens the copy.

The third line is the trap. After db.close(), the -wal and -shm files were gone and a plain copy of app.db was complete. The WAL page describes exactly this: "When the last connection to a database closes, that connection does one last checkpoint and then deletes the WAL and its associated shared-memory file, to clean up the disk."

That is why this bug hides. If you test a backup script by stopping the app, running the script, and opening the result, you are testing the one moment when copying a single file is correct. The same script, run on a schedule while the app is up, copies a file that may be missing everything since the last checkpoint.

It also matters how the app stopped. The WAL page qualifies the clean-up rule: "if the last process to have the database open exits without cleanly shutting down the database connection ... then the WAL file might be retained on disk after all connections to the database have been closed." crash_test.py checks that by having a child process commit the same table and 500 rows, then exit with os._exit(0) without closing its connection.

import os, shutil, sqlite3, subprocess, sys

def count(path):
    c = sqlite3.connect(path)
    try:
        return c.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM events").fetchone()[0]
    except sqlite3.Error as e:
        return "error: %s" % e
    finally:
        c.close()

child = r'''
import os, sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect("crash.db")
db.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE events (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, note TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO events (note) VALUES (?)", [("event %d" % i,) for i in range(500)])
db.commit()
os._exit(0)   # the process ends without closing the connection
'''
subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", child], check=True)
print("files after the writer exited:", sorted(f for f in os.listdir(".") if f.startswith("crash.db")))
shutil.copy("crash.db", "crash_copy.db")
print("copy of crash.db alone:", count("crash_copy.db"))

Output:

files after the writer exited: ['crash.db', 'crash.db-shm', 'crash.db-wal']
copy of crash.db alone: error: no such table: events

Nothing had the database open, and the main-file copy still had no table. "Stop the app, then copy" is only safe if the app shut down cleanly, and a crashed, killed or force-stopped app is the case a backup is most likely to meet.

Is copying both files safe, then?

It worked above, but the two copies happen at different moments. If a write lands between them, the pair no longer describes one point in time.

SQLite's page on how to corrupt a database describes this risk for any background backup job: "The backup copy then might contain some old and some new content, and thus be corrupt." It also gives the condition under which a plain file copy is fine: "It is also safe to make a copy of an SQLite database file as long as there are no transactions in progress while the copy is taking place." A generic file-sync tool has no way to know whether that is true at the moment it reads the file.

Test two: checkpoint first, then copy

The obvious fix is to force a checkpoint right before the copy so the main file is current. checkpoint_test.py tries that with a second connection holding a read transaction open, the kind of thing a long-running report query or a forgotten cursor does.

import os, shutil, sqlite3

for f in os.listdir("."):
    if f.startswith(("ck.db", "ckcopy")):
        os.remove(f)

def count(path):
    c = sqlite3.connect(path)
    try:
        return c.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM events").fetchone()[0]
    finally:
        c.close()

w = sqlite3.connect("ck.db", isolation_level=None)
w.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL")
w.execute("CREATE TABLE events (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, note TEXT)")
w.execute("INSERT INTO events (note) VALUES ('first batch')")
w.execute("PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)")      # the table + 1 row now live in ck.db

# a second connection opens a read transaction and keeps it open
r = sqlite3.connect("ck.db", isolation_level=None)
r.execute("BEGIN")
print("reader sees:", r.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM events").fetchone()[0])

w.executemany("INSERT INTO events (note) VALUES (?)",
              [("later %d" % i,) for i in range(200)])
print("writer sees:", w.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM events").fetchone()[0])

print("checkpoint while reader open (busy, log, checkpointed):",
      w.execute("PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)").fetchone())
shutil.copy("ck.db", "ckcopy_during.db")
print("main-file copy after that checkpoint:", count("ckcopy_during.db"))

r.execute("COMMIT")
print("checkpoint after reader ends (busy, log, checkpointed):",
      w.execute("PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)").fetchone())
shutil.copy("ck.db", "ckcopy_after.db")
print("main-file copy after a clean checkpoint:", count("ckcopy_after.db"))
w.close(); r.close()

Output:

reader sees: 1
writer sees: 201
checkpoint while reader open (busy, log, checkpointed): (1, 200, 0)
main-file copy after that checkpoint: 1
checkpoint after reader ends (busy, log, checkpointed): (0, 0, 0)
main-file copy after a clean checkpoint: 201

PRAGMA wal_checkpoint returns three numbers: whether it was blocked, how many frames are in the log, and how many it moved into the database. With the reader open, it reported blocked, with every frame still waiting in the log and none copied across. The main-file copy taken right after held only the first row.

The WAL page explains why the checkpointer backs off: "the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader." Once the reader committed, the same pragma ran to completion and a plain copy had every row.

So a checkpoint-then-copy script is correct only if it checks the pragma's result and refuses to copy when the first number is not zero.

Test three: let SQLite make the copy

Both safe options are already in Python's standard library. Connection.backup() wraps SQLite's online backup API, and VACUUM INTO writes a compacted copy of the current state to a new file. SQLite's corruption page lists both as approaches that "will work even on a live database."

safe_backup.py wraps the first one, switches the copy to the default rollback journal so it is a single file with no sidecars, and runs PRAGMA integrity_check before declaring success.

import sqlite3

def safe_backup(src_path, dst_path):
    """Copy a live SQLite database into one self-contained file, then check it."""
    src = sqlite3.connect(src_path)
    dst = sqlite3.connect(dst_path)
    try:
        src.backup(dst)
        dst.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE")
        result = dst.execute("PRAGMA integrity_check").fetchone()[0]
        if result != "ok":
            raise RuntimeError("backup failed integrity_check: %s" % result)
    finally:
        dst.close()
        src.close()

live_backup_demo.py keeps a writer connected the whole time and makes one copy each way.

import os, sqlite3
from safe_backup import safe_backup

for f in os.listdir("."):
    if f.startswith(("live.db", "nightly", "vacuumed")):
        os.remove(f)

writer = sqlite3.connect("live.db")
writer.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL")
writer.execute("CREATE TABLE events (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, note TEXT)")
writer.executemany("INSERT INTO events (note) VALUES (?)",
                   [("event %d" % i,) for i in range(300)])
writer.commit()
print("live files:", sorted(f for f in os.listdir(".") if f.startswith("live.db")))

safe_backup("live.db", "nightly.db")
writer.execute("VACUUM INTO 'vacuumed.db'")

for name in ("nightly.db", "vacuumed.db"):
    c = sqlite3.connect(name)
    rows = c.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM events").fetchone()[0]
    mode = c.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode").fetchone()[0]
    c.close()
    extra = [f for f in os.listdir(".") if f.startswith(name + "-")]
    print("%s: %d rows, journal_mode=%s, side files=%s" % (name, rows, mode, extra))
writer.close()

Output:

live files: ['live.db', 'live.db-shm', 'live.db-wal']
nightly.db: 300 rows, journal_mode=delete, side files=[]
vacuumed.db: 300 rows, journal_mode=delete, side files=[]

Both copies had every row while the live database still had its -wal and -shm files on disk, and neither copy came with side files of its own. That last part matters for whatever moves the backup afterward: a single file cannot be split from its log, because it has none.

One difference: VACUUM INTO rebuilds the database, so its copy is not byte-identical to the source. Connection.backup() copies pages and accepts optional pages and progress arguments for large files.

What to do instead

  • Do not copy a SQLite file with cp, shutil.copy, or a sync tool while anything might have it open. Use Connection.backup() or VACUUM INTO and copy the result.
  • Write the backup to a new path, run PRAGMA integrity_check on it, then move it into place.
  • Count rows in one or two key tables in both the source and the copy, and fail loudly if the copy has fewer than you expect.
  • If a checkpoint-then-copy step has to stay, read the pragma's result and stop when the first value is not zero.
  • Test the backup with the app running, and once more after killing it, not only after a clean stop.

Things I did not test

  • Concurrent writers during the backup. The writer in these tests was idle while each copy ran. I did not measure how Connection.backup() behaves under steady writes, or how long it takes to finish on a busy database.
  • Other SQLite versions. Only 3.37.2 was tested. The WAL page also documents a rare corruption bug, the WAL-reset bug, present from 3.7.0 through 3.51.2 and fixed in 3.51.3. It involves two connections writing or checkpointing at the same instant, not copying, and these tests do not exercise it.
  • Android, network drives and cloud-sync folders. Everything ran on a local Linux disk. The WAL page states that WAL "does not work over a network filesystem". That is a separate problem from backups and was not tested here.
  • The sqlite3_rsync utility. SQLite's corruption page lists it as a third safe option for copying a live database over SSH. It was not available in this environment.

Sources. Quotes are from SQLite's Write-Ahead Logging page and its page on how to corrupt an SQLite database file. Test results come from the scripts above, each run once in the order shown, with the output pasted unedited.

If you want an old phone to record clips in the background so there is something on disk worth backing up, the app I make is Background Camera RemoteStream on Google Play. Nothing above depends on it.

If ls shows an app.db-wal next to app.db, a plain copy of app.db is missing whatever that log still holds.
