title: Daily Dose of DevOps — SBOM generation: for modern cloud workloads
description:
SBOM generation: for modern cloud workloads

The expensive failure is rarely the missing tool; it is the absent operating contract. For sbom generation for modern cloud workloads, the decisive question is not whether a team can demonstrate the technology once. It is whether the organisation can operate it repeatedly, audit its decisions, and recover when assumptions fail.

The operating problem

Treat sbom generation as part of a zero-trust delivery system in which identity, provenance, and policy are evaluated continuously. Define the consumer, owner, support boundary, change policy, and recovery objective before selecting implementation details. When operating sbom generation for modern cloud workloads, undocumented authority and ambiguous ownership create more risk than a missing feature.

A credible design measures control coverage, policy exceptions, credential lifetime, remediation latency, and provenance verification. Those measures should be visible to both the platform owner and consuming teams. If the measurements cannot distinguish adoption from coercion, or reliability from mere activity, the operating model is not yet falsifiable.

A practical control

Start with a narrow contract that can be tested automatically. The implementation should encode short-lived identity, least privilege, immutable dependencies, signed provenance, and policy-as-code enforcement. The following fragment is illustrative; production values must be derived from workload evidence and organisational policy.

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@<immutable-sha>
  - run: cosign verify --certificate-identity-regexp='^https://github.com/example/' artifact

Roll the control out to one representative service, observe failure behaviour, and exercise rollback before broad adoption. Record exceptions as expiring decisions with an accountable owner, not permanent bypasses.

Trade-offs

Standardisation reduces cognitive load and makes controls observable, but an excessively rigid path displaces complexity into workarounds. Flexibility improves local fit, but every variant expands the support surface and weakens fleet-wide guarantees. For sbom generation for modern cloud workloads, prefer a small mandatory safety kernel surrounded by replaceable implementation choices.

The organisation must also pay for operability. More validation increases feedback time; more telemetry increases cost and cardinality risk; stronger isolation can reduce utilisation. Make those costs explicit and compare them with the blast radius and recovery cost they buy down.

What teams get wrong

The recurrent anti-pattern is adding ceremonial approval gates without constraining capabilities or verifying the produced artifact. Teams then measure task completion instead of production outcomes, accumulate exceptions without expiry, and discover during an incident that the nominal control has no tested recovery path.

Another error is adopting a reference architecture without its assumptions. Validate identity boundaries, dependency failure, capacity pressure, partial rollout, rollback, and audit reconstruction in the environment that will actually carry production traffic.

Key Takeaways

  • Treat sbom generation as an owned product and control system, not a tool installation.
  • Design for the constraints captured by “for modern cloud workloads”; document the authority, failure domain, and recovery objective.
  • Measure control coverage, policy exceptions, credential lifetime, remediation latency, and provenance verification.
  • Automate short-lived identity, least privilege, immutable dependencies, signed provenance, and policy-as-code enforcement.
  • Test degraded operation and rollback before scaling adoption.

title: Lit Library for Web Components
description:
Lit Library: Your New Best Friend for Building Web Components (Without Losing Your Sanity)

Let's face it, building reusable, maintainable, and downright delightful user interfaces can be a journey. And when it comes to the building blocks of those UIs – Web Components – things can get a little… verbose. We're talking about the native browser APIs, which are powerful, sure, but sometimes feel like trying to assemble IKEA furniture with only a screwdriver and a vague IKEA manual written in ancient hieroglyphs.

Enter Lit, or more formally, Lit Library. Think of Lit as your friendly guide, your helpful assistant, your secret weapon for crafting elegant and efficient Web Components. It's not a full-blown framework dictating every aspect of your application, but rather a pragmatic, lightweight library that dramatically simplifies the process of creating custom elements.

So, buckle up, fellow developers, because we're about to dive deep into the wonderful world of Lit. We'll explore why it's such a game-changer, what you need to get started, its super-powers, and maybe even a tiny sprinkle of its quirks.

So, What's the Big Deal About Lit? (Introduction)

At its core, Lit is a Google-backed JavaScript library that helps you build fast, lightweight, and standard-compliant Web Components. Remember those native Web Component APIs? Lit doesn't reinvent the wheel; it polishes it, adds a comfortable seat, and gives you a clear map. It leverages the power of native Web Components (Custom Elements and Shadow DOM) and enhances them with a few clever additions that make your life so much easier.

Imagine you're building a complex UI with lots of interactive elements. Without a library like Lit, you might find yourself writing a lot of boilerplate code: setting up event listeners, manually updating the DOM, managing component state, and dealing with the complexities of Shadow DOM encapsulation. Lit streamlines all of that, allowing you to focus on the what of your component, not the how of its implementation.

It's all about declarative templates and reactive rendering. You describe what your component should look like based on its current state, and Lit handles the heavy lifting of efficiently updating the DOM when that state changes. This means less manual DOM manipulation, fewer bugs, and a codebase that's much easier to read and understand.

What Do I Need to Bring to the Lit Party? (Prerequisites)

Alright, before we start throwing Lit around like confetti, there are a few things you should have in your developer toolkit:

  • Basic JavaScript Knowledge: Lit is built on JavaScript. You don't need to be a JavaScript guru, but a solid understanding of ES6+ features like classes, modules, and arrow functions will be incredibly helpful.
  • Understanding of HTML and CSS: You'll still be writing HTML and CSS for your components, so familiarity with these fundamental web technologies is essential.
  • A JavaScript Module Bundler (Optional but Recommended): While you can use Lit without a bundler, it's highly recommended for modern development. Tools like Webpack, Rollup, or Vite make managing your JavaScript modules, handling dependencies, and optimizing your build process a breeze. Most Lit projects are set up with one of these from the get-go.
  • A Text Editor or IDE: Duh. But seriously, a good editor with JavaScript syntax highlighting and potentially Lit-specific extensions can make your life even easier.

That's pretty much it! Lit is designed to be approachable and integrate seamlessly into your existing workflow.

Why Should I Bother? The Glorious Upsides of Lit (Advantages)

So, why choose Lit over just plain old Web Components or even a full-fledged framework? Let's break down the awesomeness:

  • Lightweight and Fast: Lit is tiny. Its core library is incredibly small, meaning less to download for your users and faster initial load times. This is a huge win, especially for performance-sensitive applications.
  • Standard-Compliant: Lit embraces Web Component standards. This means your Lit components are interoperable with any framework or plain HTML. You're not locked into a specific ecosystem. You can use your Lit components in React, Vue, Angular, or even just a plain HTML file.

  • Declarative Templates with lit-html: This is where the magic happens. Lit uses a powerful templating library called lit-html. It allows you to write your component's UI in a familiar HTML-like syntax directly within your JavaScript.

    import { html, css, LitElement } from 'lit';

class MyCounter extends LitElement {
  static properties = {
    count: { type: Number },
  };

  constructor() {
    super();
    this.count = 0;
  }

  _increment() {
    this.count++;
  }

  render() {
    return html`
      <button @click="${this._increment}">
        Clicked ${this.count} times
      </button>
    `;
  }
}

customElements.define('my-counter', MyCounter);

    See that html tag? That's lit-html in action! It's super readable and makes defining your UI a joy.

  • Efficient Reactive Rendering: When your component's state (properties) changes, Lit intelligently updates only the parts of the DOM that have actually changed. No unnecessary re-renders, just lightning-fast updates. This is achieved through a concept called template literals tagged with html, which are parsed and optimized for efficient DOM patching.

  • Built-in Shadow DOM Support: Lit makes using Shadow DOM a breeze. This provides powerful style encapsulation, meaning your component's styles won't leak out and affect other parts of your page, and vice-versa.

    static styles = css`
  :host {
    display: block;
    border: 1px solid var(--my-component-border-color, gray);
    padding: 10px;
  }
  button {
    background-color: lightblue;
    padding: 8px 15px;
    border: none;
    border-radius: 4px;
    cursor: pointer;
  }
`;

    The static styles property allows you to define styles that are scoped to your component using Shadow DOM.

  • Simple Property Management: Declaring and managing component properties is straightforward. Lit automatically handles observing property changes and triggering re-renders when they occur.

  • Event Handling: Adding event listeners to your elements is as easy as using the @ symbol in your templates. Lit handles the event delegation and ensures correct binding.

  • Great Developer Experience: Lit's API is clean and intuitive. It feels like JavaScript, not some alien syntax. This leads to a more enjoyable and productive development process.

But Wait, There's More! (Features of Lit)

Let's dive a bit deeper into some of the key features that make Lit so powerful:

Declarative Templates with lit-html

We touched on this, but it's worth reiterating. lit-html uses JavaScript template literals to create HTML structures. It's efficient, readable, and allows for dynamic content.

  • Expressions: You can embed JavaScript expressions directly within your templates to render dynamic data, call methods, or conditionally render elements.

    render() {
  return html`
    <div>
      ${this.greeting}, ${this.name}!
      ${this.isAdmin ? html`<p>Welcome, Administrator!</p>` : ''}
    </div>
  `;
}

  • Attribute and Property Binding: Lit automatically handles binding data to attributes and properties of DOM elements.

    render() {
  return html`
    <input type="text" .value="${this.inputValue}" @input="${this._handleInput}">
  `;
}

    Notice the . before value. This tells Lit to set the value property of the input, which is generally preferred over setting the attribute for form elements.

  • Event Handling (@ syntax): As shown before, the @ prefix makes attaching event listeners a breeze.

Reactive Properties

Lit's reactivity system is a core feature. When a property declared in static properties changes, Lit knows to re-render the component.

  • Property Declaration: You declare properties using the static properties getter. You can also specify the type for basic type checking and to control how Lit handles data serialization/deserialization.

    static properties = {
  username: { type: String },
  age: { type: Number },
  isActive: { type: Boolean },
  data: { type: Object }
};

  • Property Changes Trigger Re-renders: Lit observes changes to these properties and efficiently updates the DOM.

Shadow DOM and Styling

Lit encourages the use of Shadow DOM for style encapsulation.

  • Scoped Styles: The static styles getter allows you to define CSS that is scoped to your component. This prevents style conflicts and makes your components more maintainable.
  • CSS Variables: You can easily use CSS variables (--my-variable) in your component styles, allowing for theming and customization from the outside.

Slots for Content Projection

Slots are a standard Web Component feature that Lit makes easy to use. They allow you to pass content from the parent component into specific areas of your child component.

// In your Lit component (e.g., my-card.js)
render() {
  return html`
    <div class="card">
      <div class="header">
        <slot name="title">Default Title</slot>
      </div>
      <div class="content">
        <slot></slot>
      </div>
    </div>
  `;
}

<!-- In your parent HTML/component -->
<my-card>
  <h2 slot="title">My Awesome Card</h2>
  <p>This is the content of the card.</p>
</my-card>

Lifecycle Callbacks

Lit provides standard Web Component lifecycle callbacks, such as connectedCallback (when the element is added to the DOM) and disconnectedCallback (when it's removed).

  • connectedCallback: Useful for setting up initial state, fetching data, or adding event listeners that aren't handled directly in the template.
  • disconnectedCallback: Important for cleaning up any event listeners or resources to prevent memory leaks.

Are There Any Rough Edges? (Disadvantages)

While Lit is fantastic, no tool is perfect. Here are a few things to keep in mind:

  • Learning Curve for lit-html: For developers completely new to declarative templating with tagged template literals, there might be a small initial learning curve to grasp how it works under the hood. However, it's generally considered much easier than JSX or other framework-specific templating languages.
  • Not a Full-Fledged Framework: Lit is a library for building Web Components, not a comprehensive framework like React or Angular. If you need features like routing, state management solutions beyond component-level, or a built-in component ecosystem, you'll likely need to integrate other libraries.
  • Browser Support for Native Web Components: While browser support for Web Components is excellent these days, extremely old browsers might require polyfills. However, for most modern development, this is rarely an issue.
  • Ecosystem Maturity: Compared to behemoths like React, the Lit ecosystem of third-party libraries, UI kits, and community-driven tools is still growing. This is improving rapidly, but you might find fewer off-the-shelf solutions for very specific use cases.

The Verdict: Should You Lit Up Your Projects?

Absolutely! If you're looking to build:

  • Reusable UI components: That work everywhere.
  • Fast and performant web applications: Where every millisecond counts.
  • Future-proof web experiences: That leverage native browser standards.
  • A more enjoyable component development experience: Without the verbosity.

Then Lit is an excellent choice. It strikes a fantastic balance between power, simplicity, and performance. It allows you to build robust and maintainable custom elements without getting bogged down in boilerplate.

Beyond the Basics: A Glimpse of What's Next

Lit is constantly evolving. You might encounter concepts like:

  • lit-element (now just LitElement): The base class for creating Lit components.
  • lit-html: The templating engine.
  • @lit/reactive-element: The underlying reactive element base.
  • Lit SSR (Server-Side Rendering): For improved SEO and initial load performance.
  • Lit DevTools: For debugging and introspection.

The Lit team is dedicated to improving the developer experience and pushing the boundaries of what's possible with Web Components.

In Conclusion: Embrace the Lit Life!

Lit Library is a breath of fresh air in the world of front-end development. It empowers you to build beautiful, performant, and standards-compliant Web Components with a delightful developer experience. By leveraging the power of native browser APIs and enhancing them with elegant abstractions, Lit makes building reusable UI a joy rather than a chore.

So, go forth and Lit up your projects! You might just find yourself wondering how you ever lived without it. Happy component building!

title: The best UI component libraries for vibe coding in 2026
description:
Updated: October 2026.

Short answer: if you want primitives you style yourself, use shadcn/ui. If you mostly build through an AI agent and want it to install the exact designed block instead of redrawing a lookalike, VibeUI (vibeui.club). For animated hero effects, Magic UI, Aceternity UI or React Bits. For a large catalog of marketing blocks, Shadcnblocks or Tailark. For community variety, 21st.dev. All of them except HeroUI install with the shadcn CLI.

Why "vibe coding" changes the question

When a human copies a component, the component is the product. When Cursor or Claude Code does it, what matters is whether the agent installs the real thing or reads a description and writes its own "similar" version. So besides looks and price, I compare one more thing: what each library gives the agent.

Comparison table

Library What it is Price Install For the agent
shadcn/ui Base primitives + blocks Free, MIT shadcn CLI Known from training data; registry + MCP
21st.dev Community marketplace Browse free, 2 copies/day; membership shadcn CLI "Copy prompt" per component; MCP + CLI
VibeUI 2,048 components, landing blocks, animations, page scenarios Previews free; 20 copies/month free; PRO $9/month shadcn CLI "Copy for AI" instruction per item
Magic UI Animated components Free, MIT; Pro templates $199 one-time shadcn CLI MCP server
Aceternity UI Animated components & sections 118+ components free; blocks/templates paid shadcn CLI —
React Bits Animated text, backgrounds, effects Free (source on GitHub) Copy or CLI —
Shadcnblocks 2,478 blocks, 21 templates Free tier; lifetime from $149 shadcn CLI, MCP shadcn MCP, IDE extension
Tailark Marketing-site blocks Free part + paid full access shadcn CLI —
coss ui (ex Origin UI) Components on Base UI Open source Copy —
HeroUI Full component library Apache-2.0 npm package MCP servers, agent skills, llms.txt

1. shadcn/ui — the base everyone builds on

Site: https://ui.shadcn.com

Open source (MIT) primitives — buttons, dialogs, forms, tables — copied into your project with npx shadcn add. Agents know it from training data, so it's the safest default. It is deliberately neutral: you (or your agent) do the design.
Pick it when you want full control and have time to design.

2. 21st.dev — community variety

Site: https://21st.dev

A marketplace where many authors publish shadcn-style components in the registry format. Huge range, uneven style. Every component page has a "Copy prompt" button for Cursor or Claude Code, plus MCP and a CLI for agents. Browsing is free with 2 copies a day; membership removes the limit.
Pick it when you're hunting for something specific and don't mind mixing styles.

3. VibeUI — designed blocks your agent installs as-is

Site: https://vibeui.club

VibeUI (vibeui.club) is a shadcn-compatible library of 2,048 React/Tailwind components, landing blocks (hero, pricing, navbar, FAQ, data grid), animations and full-page scenarios. Each item has a "Copy for AI" instruction: install command, dependencies, what to keep (animation, spacing, typography, responsive behaviour), what you may change (copy, links, accent colour) and an explicit "don't recreate it" rule. Components ship their own palette, follow the page's color-scheme, lay out by their own width and mostly have no npm dependencies.
Downsides: copying code needs a (free) account — 20 copies a month; Pro items and scenarios need PRO ($9/month); it's younger and smaller in community than the rest of this list.
Pick it when you build mostly through Cursor or Claude Code and the agent keeps "improving" the design you picked.

4. Magic UI — animated effects

Site: https://magicui.design

Open source (MIT) animated components built on React, Tailwind and Motion; many depend on the motion package. Paid Magic UI Pro adds templates (one-time $199). Has an official MCP server.
Pick it when you need marquee, shimmer, number tickers and similar eye-candy.

5. Aceternity UI — dramatic sections

Site: https://ui.aceternity.com

118+ free animated components on Tailwind and Motion; blocks, templates and pages come with a paid all-access pass. Installs with the shadcn CLI.
Pick it when you want a bold, effect-heavy landing.

6. React Bits — animated text and backgrounds

Site: https://reactbits.dev

A very popular (50k+ GitHub stars) collection of animated text, backgrounds and micro-interactions, in JS/TS with CSS or Tailwind. Copy the source or use its CLI.
Pick it when you need one striking effect, not a whole page.

7. Shadcnblocks — the biggest block catalog

Site: https://www.shadcnblocks.com

2,478 blocks, 2,154 components and 21 templates. A free tier exists; most of the catalog is behind one-time lifetime plans starting at $149. Installs via shadcn CLI, shadcn MCP or an IDE extension.
Pick it when you want the widest choice of marketing sections and prefer a one-time payment.

8. Tailark — marketing sites on shadcn

Site: https://tailark.com

A shadcn registry of blocks, pages and illustrations for marketing websites, in several visual styles, working with Radix UI and Base UI. Part is free, full access is paid.
Pick it when you're building a SaaS marketing site and like its look.

9. coss ui (formerly Origin UI)

Site: https://coss.com/ui

Origin UI now redirects to coss ui — a modern open-source component library built on Base UI, with hundreds of small "particles" (ready variations).
Pick it when you want polished form controls and inputs on Base UI.

10. HeroUI — a full library, agent-ready docs

Site: https://heroui.com

A complete React component library on React Aria and Tailwind CSS v4 (Apache-2.0), installed as a package rather than copied. Strong agent tooling: MCP servers, agent skills, llms.txt.
Pick it when you want a classic dependency-based design system.

How to choose

  • Design it yourself: shadcn/ui (+ coss ui for inputs).
  • A whole site built by an AI agent without losing the design: VibeUI.
  • One wow effect: React Bits, Magic UI, Aceternity UI.
  • Many marketing sections, one-time payment: Shadcnblocks, Tailark.
  • Variety from many authors: 21st.dev.
  • Classic package-based system: HeroUI.

Most of these mix well: they all speak the shadcn registry format, so one project can pull a primitive from shadcn/ui, an effect from Magic UI and a pricing block from VibeUI.

FAQ

Which UI library works best with Cursor and Claude Code?
Any library that installs through the shadcn CLI works; the difference is what the agent gets. 21st.dev and VibeUI give a per-component prompt, Magic UI, HeroUI and Shadcnblocks offer MCP servers, and shadcn/ui is already known to the models.

Are there free options?
shadcn/ui, Magic UI, React Bits and coss ui are free; Aceternity, Shadcnblocks, Tailark and VibeUI have free parts with paid tiers.

Can I combine libraries?
Yes — the shared shadcn registry format means components from different libraries install into the same components/ folder.

title: Deel vs. Rippling for Contractor Management: Which Platform Gets the User Experience Right?
description:
Two powerful platforms, two different approaches to managing global talent compared from a product designer’s perspective.

Imagine you’re running a product design team. You have a UX researcher in Germany, a UI designer in Brazil, and a motion designer in Japan. They’re all independent contractors, and you need to onboard them, manage agreements, and make sure they get paid on time.

At first, managing 3 contractors might seem straightforward. But as your team grows, and you hire a few more people, things become complicated. Different currencies, local regulations, invoices, approvals, and payment schedules can quickly turn a simple process into an administrative nightmare.

This is exactly the problem that platforms like Deel and Rippling aim to solve.

Both offer tools for managing international contractors, but they approach the problem differently. In this article, I’ll focus on Contractor Management because I’ll explore the process of hiring independent creative professionals, rather than employing full-time staff through an EOR.

First, let’s understand what we’re comparing

Before jumping into the comparison, it’s important to distinguish three services that people often confuse with platforms:

  • Contractor Management: Helps companies onboard, manage, and pay independent professionals. The company typically contracts directly with the freelancer, while the platform handles administrative workflows and provides compliance tools.
  • Employer of Record (EOR): Allows companies to hire employees in countries where they don’t have a legal entity. The EOR becomes the legal employer and manages employment contracts, statutory payroll, taxes, and benefits.
  • Global Payroll: Helps companies process employee salaries, taxes, and statutory deductions across countries where they already have their own employing entities.

For my article, I’ll focus on Contractor Management because I’ll dive into case of hiring independent creative professionals, not employing full-time staff through an EOR.

Deel vs. Rippling: Side-by-side comparison for contract management

To illustrate what the two platforms are capable of, I’ll compare them in five key areas:

1. Onboarding: The first impression matters

Onboarding is one of the most important experiences in any enterprise product. A poorly designed onboarding flow creates friction before a user even starts working with a product. And for freelance designers, who might work with several companies simultaneously, complicated administrative tasks are especially frustrating.

The good news is that both Deel and Rippling have created strong onboarding experiences, but they approach onboarding a bit differently.

Deel approaches onboarding for contractors from the perspective of international hiring. Its workflow includes creating localized contracts, checking worker classification, collecting documents, and setting up payments. Contractors also receive a dedicated portal where they can review agreements, manage documents, and check payment information.

Rippling treats onboarding for contractors as an integration task. Its contractor onboarding can combine contract signing, Know Your Customer (KYC) verification, payment details, and workplace access provisioning within one flow.

This can be especially beneficial when hiring a freelance product designer who needs access to your organization’s design tools and communication channels. With an integrated system, administrative and IT tasks can be coordinated instead of treated as entirely separate processes.

Does that mean Rippling’s onboarding is better? Not at all. I think that when it comes to onboarding, the right strategy depends on what problem your organization needs to solve. If you don’t plan to transition contractors into full-time employees later on, Rippling’s onboarding scenario could be overkill.

2. Managing payments: Reducing uncertainty

Payment is probably the most critical (and emotionally important) part of the contractor experience.

When I think about the user experience of financial tools, I always evaluate how the tool answers one key question:

Does the interface help me understand what’s happening with my money?

Think of a freelance product designer who has completed a project and submitted an invoice. They want to know whether the invoice was approved, when payment will arrive, and how much they’ll actually receive.

Both Deel and Rippling offer self-service invoicing and payment tracking.

Deel offers automated invoicing, consolidated global payments, and more than 15 payout options, including Wise and Revolut. This flexibility can be particularly valuable for international freelancers who have different payment preferences.

Rippling supports automatically generated invoices based on contractual terms or tracked hours. The platform also offers customizable approval routing and payment status visibility for contractors.

In my opinion, both platforms offer fairly similar experiences. If you want to decide which one works best for your organization, here’s my recommendation: look closely at how each system communicates pending approvals, expected payout dates, currency conversion, and payment exceptions.

And, what is even more important, ask your contractors what they think of the platform because a beautiful dashboard doesn’t help much when a contractor doesn’t understand why their payment is delayed.

3. Automation: Eliminating repetitive work

One of the most interesting differences between Deel and Rippling is how they position automation. Two platforms offer two very different approaches to eliminating repetitive work:

Deel automates tasks closely associated with global contracting, such as generating agreements, collecting compliance information, preparing invoices, and processing payouts. Deel also offers solid workflow automation and IT lifecycle management (including managing access to internal systems).

Rippling offers automation across a wider organizational ecosystem. Contractor information can be used in workflows involving HR, finance, permissions, and workplace applications.

Imagine a situation where a contractor designer finishes a six-month engagement. The company needs to process the final invoice, close the contract, and remove access to internal systems. In a fragmented environment, different people may be responsible for each task.

Rippling’s unified workforce model is particularly appealing for coordinating these dependencies when a contractor is integrated into an organization’s workflows much like a regular full-time employee.

4. Compliance: Making complexity manageable

Compliance is an area where seemingly small product decisions can have significant consequences.

A company hiring independent contractors internationally needs to consider local regulations and worker classification. A freelancer who operates like a full-time employee may create misclassification risks, even if the contract describes them as independent.

Both Deel and Rippling provide compliance capabilities, including worker classification safeguards. Both also offer Contractor of Record services for companies that want the provider to formally engage contractors and assume specified compliance responsibilities.

The great thing about Deel is that it publishes a starting price of $325 per month for Contractor of Record while Rippling requires a quote.

5. Pricing: Transparency is part of the user experience

Pricing is another interesting point of comparison.

Transparent starting prices allow us to evaluate basic affordability before talking to sales.

Deel publishes a starting price of $49 per contractor per month for its standard contractor management service. Rippling, on the other hand, uses customized pricing based on the selected products and the size of the workforce. Its broader platform starts at $8 per employee per month plus a monthly base fee, but that’s not a published all-inclusive price for global contractor management.

In my opinion, Deel is more transparent when it comes to pricing.

Deel vs. Rippling: Side-by-side comparison

Final verdict: Which would I choose for a distributed product design team?

The answer to this question depends on the nature of your organization and your goals.

I think that if you run a small or medium-sized product design team that primarily works with international freelancers, I’d choose Deel.

On the other hand, I’d choose Rippling if contractor management is part of a broader workforce strategy, especially if you plan to transition contractors into full-time employees at some point in their careers.

Written by Nick Babich

Deel vs. Rippling for Contractor Management: Which Platform Gets the User Experience Right? was originally published in UX Planet on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Debugging Java and Tomcat in Production: A Systematic Approach
description:
When a Java application running on Apache Tomcat becomes slow, starts returning errors, or stops responding, restarting the service is often the easiest option.

But a restart doesn't explain what happened.

The real challenge is identifying whether the problem comes from the JVM, the application, the operating system, the network, or an external dependency.

In this article, we'll walk through a practical workflow for investigating Java and Tomcat issues on a Linux server.

1. Start with the Symptoms

Before changing JVM options or restarting Tomcat, establish what is actually failing.

Is the application completely unavailable, or are requests simply taking longer than usual? Are all endpoints affected, or only a specific operation? Did the problem begin after a deployment, configuration change, or traffic increase?

Start by checking the service:

sudo systemctl status tomcat

The service name may differ depending on the installation.

Find the Java process:

pgrep -af 'org.apache.catalina.startup.Bootstrap'

Check the latest service logs:

sudo journalctl -u tomcat --since "30 minutes ago"

If Tomcat writes to files instead of the system journal, inspect the configured log directory, including catalina.out where applicable.

Look for exceptions, repeated errors, failed database connections, thread pool warnings, and messages around the time the problem started.

The goal is to establish a timeline before changing anything.

2. Check CPU, Memory, and Disk Pressure

A Java process can be running while the application is effectively unavailable.

Start with the host:

uptime
free -h
df -h
df -i

These commands help identify system load, memory pressure, full filesystems, and inode exhaustion.

For process-level CPU and memory usage:

top -p "$(pgrep -fo 'org.apache.catalina.startup.Bootstrap')"

If multiple matching Java processes exist, verify the PID manually before using process-specific diagnostic commands.

For disk I/O, if sysstat is installed:

iostat -xz 1 5

High CPU usage does not automatically mean the JVM needs more CPU. Likewise, low CPU usage does not rule out a serious application problem: threads may be blocked waiting for a database, a lock, or network I/O.

Correlate these observations with application metrics and logs.

3. Inspect the JVM Before Changing Heap Settings

Memory problems are often more complicated than simply increasing -Xmx.

Check the JVM version:

java -version

Identify the Java executable used by the running process, especially when multiple JDK installations exist:

PID=<tomcat_java_pid>

readlink -f "/proc/$PID/exe"

Inspect the JVM command line:

tr '\0' ' ' < "/proc/$PID/cmdline"
echo

If the matching JDK tools are available and you have the necessary permissions, inspect the running JVM:

jcmd "$PID" VM.version
jcmd "$PID" VM.flags
jcmd "$PID" GC.heap_info

Tool availability and supported commands depend on the JDK version and installation.

Heap usage is not the same as process memory

Keep these measurements separate:

  • Java heap: Memory managed by the garbage collector.
  • Metaspace: Memory used for class metadata on modern HotSpot JVMs.
  • Native memory: Memory used by the JVM, threads, direct buffers, native libraries, and other components.
  • RSS: Physical memory currently resident for the process.

A process can consume substantial RAM even when its Java heap is not full.

Before increasing -Xmx, check the container or host memory limit, actual heap usage, garbage collection behavior, and native memory consumption.

For a production system, don't generate a heap dump or a large diagnostic artifact without considering disk space, latency, and the sensitivity of the data it may contain.

4. Investigate Slow or Blocked Requests with Thread Dumps

When Tomcat is running but requests are slow or stuck, thread dumps can help reveal what application threads are doing.

Capture a thread dump using the matching JDK:

jcmd "$PID" Thread.print > /tmp/tomcat-threads.txt

Repeat the capture after a short interval if needed:

sleep 10

jcmd "$PID" Thread.print > /tmp/tomcat-threads-2.txt

Compare the dumps rather than relying on a single snapshot.

Look for patterns such as:

  • Many request threads waiting on database connections.
  • Repeated stack traces pointing to the same slow operation.
  • Threads blocked on Java monitors or locks.
  • Long-running I/O operations.
  • A large number of active threads with little progress.

A thread in WAITING or BLOCKED state is not automatically a problem. Interpret the state together with its stack trace, surrounding threads, and application behavior.

Thread dumps can contain internal class names, SQL statements, URLs, or other sensitive information. Sanitize them before sharing.

5. Check Tomcat Connector and Thread Pool Saturation

Tomcat's request-processing capacity depends on connector configuration and the work performed by each request.

For a configured HTTP connector, inspect relevant settings such as:

  • maxThreads
  • minSpareThreads
  • acceptCount
  • Connection and request timeouts

The exact available settings depend on the connector and Tomcat version.

Increasing maxThreads is not automatically a fix. If requests are blocked waiting for a database connection, creating more request threads may increase contention and memory usage.

Check whether the application is exhausting a JDBC connection pool or waiting on another constrained dependency.

Useful evidence includes active and idle connection counts, request latency, queue depth, timeout rates, and thread pool utilization.

6. Treat Java Agents and Configuration Changes as Variables

Monitoring agents, Java agents, instrumentation libraries, and JVM options can affect application startup and runtime behavior.

If a problem begins after adding an agent or changing the Java runtime, establish exactly what changed.

Record:

  • The previous and current JDK versions.
  • The agent version and startup arguments.
  • The relevant configuration changes.
  • The startup logs and any JVM fatal error reports.
  • Whether the problem can be reproduced in a controlled environment.

For example, an application that fails immediately after a Java upgrade requires a different investigation from one that starts successfully but gradually becomes unresponsive.

Avoid changing several variables simultaneously. Otherwise, it becomes difficult to identify which change caused or resolved the issue.

If the JVM produces a fatal error report, inspect the report and associated crash logs. A native JVM crash is different from an ordinary Java exception and should not be diagnosed from application logs alone.

7. Verify the Hypothesis Before Calling It a Fix

Once you have a plausible root cause, make the smallest safe change that tests it.

Before applying a production change, consider its potential impact, rollback procedure, and whether a restart is required.

Afterward, compare the same indicators you collected before the change:

  • Request latency and error rate.
  • CPU and memory usage.
  • Garbage collection behavior.
  • Thread pool utilization.
  • Database connection pool metrics.
  • Relevant application logs.

A successful restart is not proof that the root cause has been fixed. The issue may return under the same workload.

A Practical Incident Checklist

When a Tomcat application becomes slow or unavailable, I would organize the investigation around these questions:

  1. What changed immediately before the incident?
  2. Is the issue at the host, JVM, Tomcat, application, or dependency layer?
  3. Are CPU, memory, disk, or network resources constrained?
  4. Are request threads progressing, blocked, or waiting?
  5. Is the JVM healthy, and is garbage collection behaving as expected?
  6. What evidence supports the suspected root cause?
  7. How will the fix be validated, and how can it be rolled back?

Final Thoughts

Production debugging is not about collecting as many logs as possible or applying JVM tuning options until the symptoms disappear.

It is about gathering evidence, narrowing the problem to the right layer, testing a hypothesis, and verifying the result.

The most useful diagnostic command is the one that answers a specific question about the system—not necessarily the one with the most output.

I'm interested in Linux infrastructure, JVM behavior, distributed systems, and the operational practices that make services more reliable. I'll continue sharing practical technical notes and investigation workflows as I work on these topics.

What do you usually investigate first when a Tomcat application becomes unresponsive: JVM metrics, thread dumps, application logs, or external dependencies?

title: Landing page haute conversion : les 7 éléments clés
description:
Qu'est-ce qu'une landing page et quand en faut-il une ?

Une landing page est une page d'atterrissage : le visiteur y arrive depuis une annonce, un e-mail, un message WhatsApp ou une recherche, et elle ne lui propose qu'une action (demander un devis, réserver, s'inscrire, acheter). Contrairement à une page de site, elle n'a ni menu ni sortie vers le reste du site.

Il vous en faut une dans trois cas :

  • vous payez du trafic (Facebook, Instagram, Google Ads) et chaque clic coûte de l'argent ;

  • vous lancez une offre précise avec une date ou un public ciblé ;

  • votre page d'accueil parle à tout le monde et n'amène personne à l'action.

Pour une présentation générale de l'entreprise, un site complet reste plus adapté. Pour l'offre de Richard SALANON, voir la page landing page haute conversion.

Comment formuler une promesse que le visiteur comprend en cinq secondes ?

Le titre répond à une question : « qu'est-ce que j'y gagne ? ». Il décrit le résultat pour le visiteur, pas votre entreprise.

  • Faible : « Bienvenue chez Atelier Dupont, votre partenaire de confiance ».

  • Fort : « Un devis de plomberie en 24 heures, sans déplacement inutile ».

Le sous-titre précise pour qui et comment. Le titre doit reprendre les mots de l'annonce qui a amené le clic : si l'annonce promet un devis gratuit et que la page parle d'autre chose, le visiteur repart. Un visuel qui montre le résultat (le produit en situation, l'avant et l'après) renforce la promesse ; une image générique de banque d'images ne dit rien.

Quelles preuves placer pour rassurer ?

Le visiteur ne vous connaît pas : la preuve réduit le risque perçu. Placez-la près du bouton, là où le doute apparaît.

  • Avis de clients réels, avec prénom et activité, uniquement ceux que vous avez reçus ;

  • logos de clients, avec leur accord ;

  • chiffres vérifiables (années d'expérience, nombre de livraisons), jamais arrondis à la hausse ;

  • garantie claire : remboursement, délai de réponse, ce qui se passe après le clic.

Une preuve inventée ou gonflée coûte plus cher qu'une page sans preuve : un client qui vérifie perd toute confiance. Sans avis pour l'instant, mettez en avant une garantie et des réalisations concrètes. Les avis visibles sur votre fiche d'établissement comptent aussi : voir le guide complet de Google Business Profile.

Comment présenter l'offre : bénéfices avant caractéristiques ?

Une caractéristique décrit le produit, un bénéfice décrit ce que le client y gagne. « Hébergement inclus » est une caractéristique ; « votre page est en ligne sans que vous gériez le moindre serveur » est un bénéfice.

  1. Listez trois à cinq caractéristiques de votre offre.

  2. Pour chacune, écrivez la phrase « ce qui change pour vous, c'est… ».

  3. Gardez le bénéfice en titre, la caractéristique en détail dessous.

Dites aussi à qui l'offre s'adresse et à qui elle ne s'adresse pas, et affichez le prix ou une fourchette si votre secteur s'y prête. Mieux vaut un visiteur qualifié que dix curieux. Pour situer les budgets de création, voir combien coûte un site web au Bénin. Si vous vendez des produits en ligne, la landing page se place devant un catalogue : voir créer un site e-commerce pour vendre en ligne.

Comment réussir l'appel à l'action ?

Un seul objectif, donc un seul type de bouton, répété à plusieurs endroits si la page est longue (en haut, après les bénéfices, en bas). Trois règles :

  • le libellé annonce le résultat (« Recevoir mon devis ») plutôt qu'un verbe vague (« Envoyer », « Valider ») ;

  • le bouton se distingue des autres couleurs de la page et reste lisible sur mobile ;

  • un texte court dessous lève le dernier doute (« Réponse sous 24 heures, sans engagement »), à condition de le tenir.

Un bouton WhatsApp peut être plus simple pour le visiteur qu'un formulaire : il y est déjà, il n'a rien à saisir. Il devient alors l'unique action de la page, pas un second choix à côté d'un formulaire.

Quel formulaire utiliser, et combien de champs ?

Chaque champ est un obstacle. Ne demandez que ce qui est nécessaire pour répondre au premier contact : nom, moyen de contact, et éventuellement une ligne sur le besoin. Le reste se demande au deuxième échange.

  • Un seul champ de contact (téléphone ou e-mail), pas les deux, sauf nécessité réelle.

  • Des libellés visibles au-dessus des champs, pas seulement dans le champ.

  • Le bon clavier sur mobile (numérique pour le téléphone, e-mail pour l'adresse).

  • Un message de confirmation après l'envoi, qui dit ce qui va se passer et quand.

  • Une mention du traitement des données, avec un lien vers votre politique de confidentialité.

Testez le formulaire vous-même, sur téléphone, avant chaque campagne : un formulaire qui n'envoie rien est l'erreur la plus coûteuse et la plus discrète.

Pourquoi la vitesse change-t-elle le résultat ?

Une page lente fait partir des visiteurs que vous avez déjà payés : sur une page d'atterrissage, le coût d'un clic perdu est direct. La mesure et la correction sont traitées à part : voir pourquoi votre site est lent. Pour une landing page, gardez ce principe : peu d'images et légères, un seul script de suivi par outil indispensable, pas de vidéo qui se lance seule.

Comment soigner l'affichage sur mobile ?

Selon Statcounter, le mobile représente 60,3 % de l'usage d'internet au Bénin en septembre 2026 (38,65 % pour l'ordinateur) : le téléphone est l'écran principal de vos visiteurs. Concevez la page d'abord pour l'écran étroit, puis adaptez-la à l'ordinateur.

  • Le titre, la promesse et le bouton sont visibles sans défiler.

  • Le texte se lit sans zoomer, les boutons se touchent sans erreur du pouce.

  • Pas de pop-up qui couvre l'écran.

  • Le bouton d'appel ou WhatsApp déclenche directement l'application.

Ouvrez la page sur un vrai téléphone d'entrée de gamme, en 4G moyenne : c'est ce que vivent beaucoup de vos visiteurs.

Pourquoi retirer le menu et les distractions ?

Chaque lien de sortie offre au visiteur une porte pour quitter la page avant d'avoir agi. Retirez le menu de navigation, les liens vers vos réseaux sociaux, les bannières et tout bloc étranger à l'offre. Conservez le logo (non cliquable), les mentions légales en pied de page et le bouton. Une page qui veut tout dire ne convainc personne : posez-vous la question pour chaque ligne, et supprimez celle qui n'aide pas à décider.

Comment tester deux versions de la page ?

Le test A/B montre la moitié des visiteurs à la version A et l'autre moitié à la version B, puis compare le nombre de conversions.

  1. Choisissez une hypothèse (« un titre qui parle du délai convertit mieux »).

  2. Ne changez qu'un élément à la fois : titre, bouton, image ou longueur du formulaire.

  3. Répartissez le trafic au hasard et simultanément, jamais une version cette semaine et l'autre la semaine suivante.

  4. Attendez assez de conversions avant de conclure : quelques dizaines de visites ne prouvent rien.

  5. Gardez la gagnante, notez le résultat, testez l'élément suivant.

Avec peu de trafic, un test rigoureux n'est pas possible : corrigez alors les points évidents de cette liste et mesurez avant et après, sur une durée identique.

Quel taux de conversion espérer ?

Selon la page d'Unbounce sur les taux de conversion moyens des landing pages (mise à jour le 4 mars 2025), le taux de conversion médian est d'environ 6,6 % au quatrième trimestre 2024, tous secteurs confondus. Cette mesure repose sur 41 000 landing pages, 464 millions de visiteurs et 57 millions de conversions. Unbounce considère qu'un taux de 10 % ou plus est « bon » en général, tout en précisant que la définition varie beaucoup d'un secteur à l'autre.

Lisez ce chiffre avec prudence : c'est une médiane (la moitié des pages fait moins), il porte sur les pages analysées par Unbounce, une entreprise nord-américaine, et rien n'indique qu'il reflète le marché béninois ; enfin, une « conversion » dépend de l'action choisie (un clic sur WhatsApp ne vaut pas une vente). Votre vrai repère est votre propre taux avant et après chaque modification, pour la même source de trafic.

Quelles erreurs font fuir les visiteurs ?

  • Plusieurs objectifs sur la même page (acheter, s'abonner, suivre la page, lire le blog).

  • Un titre qui ne reprend pas la promesse de l'annonce.

  • Un bouton noyé dans le contenu ou nommé « Envoyer ».

  • Des preuves fabriquées, ou absentes alors que le visiteur hésite.

  • Un formulaire trop long ou qui ne fonctionne pas sur mobile.

  • Une page lourde, testée seulement sur ordinateur et connexion rapide.

  • Aucun suivi : sans mesure des visites et des conversions, impossible de savoir ce qui marche. Pour la visibilité de la page dans Google, voir les 7 erreurs qui tuent votre référencement.

Si vous préférez confier la construction, contactez Richard SALANON ; la landing page démarre à 150 000 FCFA (environ 229 €), le détail est sur la page du service.

Questions fréquentes

Quelle différence entre une landing page et une page d'accueil ?

La page d'accueil oriente vers plusieurs destinations pour plusieurs publics. La landing page vise un public et une action, sans menu.

Combien de boutons d'action mettre ?

Une seule action, donc un seul type de bouton. Vous pouvez le répéter si la page est longue.

Une landing page améliore-t-elle mes publicités ?

Elle évite de payer des clics qui arrivent sur une page non pertinente. Le gain exact dépend de votre offre : mesurez-l'avant et l'après plutôt que de croire une promesse chiffrée.

Quelle longueur doit avoir une landing page ?

Celle qu'il faut pour lever les doutes. Une offre simple et peu chère tient sur un écran ou deux ; une offre chère ou nouvelle demande plus de preuves et d'explications.

Faut-il un nom de domaine propre pour une landing page ?

C'est préférable : une adresse à votre nom rassure davantage qu'un sous-domaine d'un outil gratuit, surtout pour une demande de contact ou un paiement.

Peut-on faire une landing page sans publicité ?

Oui. Elle sert aussi dans un message WhatsApp, une signature d'e-mail ou un lien de profil, partout où vous voulez une action précise.

Que préparer avant de faire créer une landing page ?

Votre offre en une phrase, vos avis et réalisations réels, vos visuels et l'action unique attendue. Le texte et les preuves demandent plus de temps que l'intégration. Le délai de Richard SALANON est donné sur devis.

Sources

  • Unbounce, taux de conversion moyens des landing pages (mise à jour du 4 mars 2025), consultée le 7 octobre 2026

  • Statcounter Global Stats, part des plateformes au Bénin (septembre 2026), consultée le 7 octobre 2026

title: Animations without GSAP: what 111 free components use instead
description:
I'm Florent, a front-end dev. I build Kodza, a free library of UI components in plain HTML, CSS and JS. 111 of them so far: a menu that swings the page open like a trapdoor, cards that stack as you scroll, a carousel you can throw.

Zero dependencies. Not "lightweight". Zero.

The question I get most: "So what do you animate with?" The honest answer is boring. The browser already ships an animation engine, a pinning system and a frame loop. Here is how each one does the job, with code taken from the components (trimmed a little).

1. Long sequences: the Web Animations API

Press Menu on Trapdoor Menu and the page tips back on its bottom edge. Each link rises from its mask as the edge uncovers it, a hairline draws in above it, the image uncovers. A couple dozen animations, one timeline.

element.animate() gives you keyframes, easing, delay and duration per element. What it doesn't give you is a timeline. The trick: give every animation the same total length with endDelay. They all start together and end together, so you can drive them as one.

// steps: [element, keyframes, { delay, duration, easing }]
const total = Math.max(...steps.map(([, , o]) => o.delay + o.duration));

const sequence = steps.map(([el, frames, o]) =>
  el.animate(frames, { ...o, fill: 'both', endDelay: total - o.delay - o.duration })
);

Closing is the same timeline played backwards, a bit faster:

sequence.forEach((animation) => {
  animation.updatePlaybackRate(-1.6);
  animation.play();
});
await Promise.all(sequence.map((animation) => animation.finished));

Press Menu again halfway through the opening, and it turns around from where it is. No second timeline to keep in sync.

Two details that helped:

  • updatePlaybackRate() rather than setting playbackRate: the speed changes without a jump, even for animations running on the compositor.
  • The pseudoElement option animates ::before and ::after directly. The menu's cross is two pseudo-elements, so no extra spans in the markup: 
cross.animate(
  [{ transform: 'rotate(0deg)' }, { transform: 'translateY(3.25px) rotate(45deg)' }],
  { delay: 200, duration: 600, easing: 'cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)', pseudoElement: '::before' }
);

2. Pinning: position: sticky

Sticky Cards stacks cards as you scroll. Each one sticks a little below the previous, and the card being covered steps back and darkens.

The stacking is CSS. No pin spacer, no scroll handler holding things in place, nothing to recompute on resize:

.kodza-stack__card {
  position: sticky;
  top: calc(var(--kz-stack-top) + var(--i, 0) * var(--kz-stack-offset));
}

The script sets --i on each card, then measures how much each one is covered to scale and darken it. That's the only job left for JavaScript. If it never runs, the cards still stick and stack.

3. Inertia: a spring in twenty lines

Carousel is a native scroll-snap carousel first. On top of it: buttons, and mouse drag you can throw. The glide is a critically damped spring, solved in closed form and sampled in requestAnimationFrame. No physics library.

// From `from` (moving at `velocity` px/s) to `to`
const spring = (from, to, velocity, omega, onFrame, onDone) => {
  const x0 = from - to;
  const b = velocity + omega * x0;
  const start = performance.now();
  let raf = 0;
  const step = (time) => {
    const t = Math.max(0, (time - start) / 1000);
    const decay = Math.exp(-omega * t);
    const x = to + (x0 + b * t) * decay;
    const v = (velocity - omega * b * t) * decay;
    const done = (Math.abs(x - to) < 1 && Math.abs(v) < 30) || t > 3;
    onFrame(done ? to : x);
    if (done) onDone();
    else raf = requestAnimationFrame(step);
  };
  raf = requestAnimationFrame(step);
  return () => cancelAnimationFrame(raf);
};

It's a formula of time, not a step-by-step simulation, so a slow frame doesn't change where it lands. From rest, it eases in and out. Started at the speed of your release, it keeps your hand's momentum, then settles on the slide where the throw would have ended.

4. The part nobody puts in the demo: cleanup

Animating is the easy part. The hard part is a WordPress theme that swaps content with Ajax, a page router, or React mounting everything twice in strict mode.

Every Kodza component mounts the same way: one instance per root, and everything it starts is tied to one AbortSignal.

function mount(root, signal) {
  window.addEventListener('resize', onResize, { signal });
  const observer = new IntersectionObserver(onView);
  observer.observe(root);
  signal.addEventListener('abort', () => observer.disconnect());
}

Two events drive it, the same in every component:

document.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('kodza:destroy', { detail: { root: oldContent } }));
// swap the content
document.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('kodza:init', { detail: { root: newContent } }));

kodza:destroy aborts the signal (listeners, observers, timers and loops stop) and puts the original markup back. kodza:init starts whatever is inside the new root. That's how the same files run in a static page, a theme with Ajax navigation, Swup or a React app.

And every component reads prefers-reduced-motion before it moves anything. Reduced motion is not a setting, it is a person.

What GSAP still does better

GSAP is excellent and battle-tested, and its plugins (SplitText, MorphSVG, Draggable) solve problems the platform doesn't solve yet. If your project already loads it, keep it.

But for a menu that opens, cards that stack and a carousel you can throw, the platform covers it. One less script to load, version and update, and the component you copy works without a package manager.

Try it

All 111 components are free, with the code on each page: kodza.dev

  • Trapdoor Menu
  • Sticky Cards
  • Carousel

Your AI assistant can fetch them too. In Claude Code:

claude mcp add -t http kodza https://kodza.dev/api/mcp

Then ask for a component in plain words. Cursor and VS Code work too, setup on kodza.dev/docs.

What's the last animation you reached for a library to do? I'm curious which ones the platform still can't handle.

title: Perceptual Color Systems in JavaScript: OKLCH Conversion and WCAG 2.1 Contrast Auto-Fix
description:
Design systems built on cylindrical hsl(h, s, l) math consistently run into the same perceptual flaw: human vision does not perceive equal lightness across hues. In HSL, pure yellow (hsl(60, 100%, 50%), #FFFF00) and pure blue (hsl(240, 100%, 50%), #0000FF) both report a lightness of 50%. Yet their WCAG 2.1 relative luminances are 0.9278 and 0.0722 respectively—meaning white text is illegible on yellow (1.07:1) while passing AAA on blue (8.59:1).

Below is the mathematical implementation for converting sRGB colors into Björn Ottosson's perceptual OKLCH color space, evaluating WCAG 2.1 luminance contrast, and automatically solving for the nearest accessible foreground lightness—all in zero-dependency JavaScript.

(If you want to drop these functions directly into a Node.js or browser project, the open-source package sunasty-color-math and the online Sunasty Color Picker implement the full pipeline client-side.)

1. Transforming sRGB to Perceptual OKLCH

Converting an 8-bit sRGB triplet $(R, G, B \in [0, 255])$ into oklch(L C h) requires four deterministic steps:

  1. Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF): Undo sRGB gamma compression to obtain linear-light RGB channels in $[0, 1]$.
  2. LMS Cone Response Matrix: Map linear sRGB into approximate human cone responses $(l, m, s)$.
  3. Cube-Root Non-Linearity: Apply $\sqrt[3]{x}$ to model perceptual lightness compression, then project into Oklab $(L, a, b)$.
  4. Polar Coordinate Conversion: Convert Cartesian $(a, b)$ into Chroma $C = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ and Hue angle $h = \text{atan2}(b, a) \cdot \frac{180}{\pi}$. 
function srgbChannelToLinear(c) {
  const v = Math.max(0, Math.min(255, c)) / 255;
  return v <= 0.04045 ? v / 12.92 : ((v + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4;
}

export function rgbToOklch(r, g, b) {
  const lr = srgbChannelToLinear(r);
  const lg = srgbChannelToLinear(g);
  const lb = srgbChannelToLinear(b);

  const l = 0.4122214708 * lr + 0.5363325363 * lg + 0.0514459929 * lb;
  const m = 0.2119034982 * lr + 0.6806995451 * lg + 0.1073969566 * lb;
  const s = 0.0883024619 * lr + 0.2817188376 * lg + 0.6299787005 * lb;

  const l_ = Math.cbrt(l);
  const m_ = Math.cbrt(m);
  const s_ = Math.cbrt(s);

  const L = 0.2104542553 * l_ + 0.793617785 * m_ - 0.0040720468 * s_;
  const a = 1.9779984951 * l_ - 2.428592205 * m_ + 0.4505937099 * s_;
  const bVal = 0.0259040371 * l_ + 0.7827717662 * m_ - 0.808675766 * s_;

  const C = Math.sqrt(a * a + bVal * bVal);
  let h = (Math.atan2(bVal, a) * 180) / Math.PI;
  if (h < 0) h += 360;

  return {
    L: Number(Math.max(0, Math.min(1, L)).toFixed(2)),
    C: Number(C.toFixed(2)),
    h: C < 0.004 ? 0 : Math.round(h),
  };
}

When you rotate the hue $h$ in oklch(L C h) while holding $L$ constant (for example, L = 0.62), every generated badge or chart series maintains uniform perceived brightness.

2. Computing WCAG 2.1 Contrast Ratios and Automatic AA Lightness Adjustment

Under WCAG 2.1 Success Criterion 1.4.3, normal body text requires a luminance contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, while large text (18pt+ or 14pt+ bold) and UI graphics (including QR codes and icons) require at least 3.0:1:

$$\text{Contrast Ratio} = \frac{L_{\text{lighter}} + 0.05}{L_{\text{darker}} + 0.05}$$

where relative luminance $Y$ is weighted by the CIE 1931 photopic luminosity function:

$$Y = 0.2126 \cdot R_{\text{lin}} + 0.7152 \cdot G_{\text{lin}} + 0.0722 \cdot B_{\text{lin}}$$

When a designer picks a muted brand accent—such as Slate 400 (#94A3B8) on a white surface (#FFFFFF), which yields 2.56:1—we can automatically compute the closest accessible shade that preserves the original hue and saturation while meeting 4.5:1:

export function relativeLuminance(r, g, b) {
  return (
    0.2126 * srgbChannelToLinear(r) +
    0.7152 * srgbChannelToLinear(g) +
    0.0722 * srgbChannelToLinear(b)
  );
}

export function computeContrastRatio(fgRgb, bgRgb) {
  const lum1 = relativeLuminance(fgRgb.r, fgRgb.g, fgRgb.b);
  const lum2 = relativeLuminance(bgRgb.r, bgRgb.g, bgRgb.b);
  const brightest = Math.max(lum1, lum2);
  const darkest = Math.min(lum1, lum2);
  const rawRatio = (brightest + 0.05) / (darkest + 0.05);

  return {
    ratio: Number(rawRatio.toFixed(2)),
    aaNormal: rawRatio >= 4.5,
    aaLarge: rawRatio >= 3.0,
    aaaNormal: rawRatio >= 7.0,
  };
}

By stepping lightness downward when the background luminance exceeds 0.18 (or upward on dark surfaces), autoFixContrastForAA('#94A3B8', '#FFFFFF', 4.5) converges in under 50 iterations to #596B82 (4.56:1), preserving the cool slate hue (215deg).

3. Practical Verification Across UI Components and Scannable Graphics

Color math does not stop at CSS custom properties; it directly impacts visual regression testing and optical decoding:

  • Interactive Token Inspection: Use the Sunasty Color Picker (or the open-source Chromium MV3 extension) to sample any viewport pixel, inspect its HEX, HSL, OKLCH, and nearest Tailwind CSS token, and run one-click WCAG AA auto-fixes.
  • Visual Regression Auditing: When migrating a legacy HSL palette to perceptual OKLCH tokens or compressing UI assets, verify pixel-level deltas side-by-side in the Sunasty Image Compare split-view inspector.
  • Optical Contrast for QR Matrices: Custom-branded QR codes frequently fail to scan on mobile cameras when designers style the foreground modules with low-contrast pastels. Maintaining at least a 3.0:1 luminance ratio (and testing low-contrast binarization against the Sunasty QR Scanner) ensures reliable decoding across both hardware laser scanners and browser camera feeds.

title: 'TikiTaki: two-dimensional swipe navigation in TypeScript, without runtime dependencies'
description:
Most swipe interfaces move along one axis. But what if each vertical section also contains its own horizontal collection?

Think of a portfolio with projects arranged by category, a fullscreen catalog, or a gallery where each row tells a different story.

I’m building TikiTaki, an open-source TypeScript library for this kind of navigation: swipe vertically between rows and horizontally between items.

The core has zero runtime dependencies, with separate adapters for React, Vue, Svelte, and Angular.

Try the live demo · GitHub · npm

The grid does not have to be rectangular

Rows can contain different numbers of items:

const grid = [['A1', 'A2', 'A3'], ['B1'], ['C1', 'C2']];

The navigation rules are deliberately predictable:

  • Swipe left or right to move within the current row.
  • Swipe up or down to change rows.
  • A successful vertical transition always opens the first item.
  • An unavailable transition preserves the entire current position.
  • One gesture moves at most one neighboring cell.

For example:

A3 → swipe up → B1
B1 → swipe up → C1
C1 → swipe left → C2
C2 → swipe down → B1
B1 → swipe down → A1

Returning to a row does not restore its previous column. This makes vertical navigation independent of the lengths of neighboring rows.

A minimal integration

Install the core package:

npm install tikitaki

Give the engine a dedicated container with explicit dimensions:

<div id="swipe-view" style="width: 100%; height: 100dvh"></div>

Then create the engine after the container exists:

import { createSwipeEngine } from 'tikitaki/dom';

const container = document.querySelector<HTMLElement>('#swipe-view');

if (!container) {
  throw new Error('Missing swipe container');
}

const engine = createSwipeEngine({
  container,
  grid: [['A1', 'A2', 'A3'], ['B1'], ['C1', 'C2']],

  renderCell(item) {
    const element = document.createElement('article');
    element.textContent = item;

    return element;
  },

  onPositionChange(position, previous) {
    console.log('Navigation:', previous, '→', position);
  },

  onError(error) {
    console.error('Swipe interaction failed', error);
  },
});

Items can be objects rather than strings. Your renderer decides how to turn each item into content.

When the owning view is removed, release the engine:

engine.destroy();

Gestures and programmatic navigation

Pointer Events handle mouse, touch, and pen input. After an initial movement threshold, the gesture locks to one axis.

A transition can commit by distance or velocity. An insufficient gesture returns to the current cell, while dragging against a boundary applies resistance.

You can also navigate from application controls:

const moved = await engine.navigate('up');

console.log(moved); // Whether the transition committed

Or jump directly to a valid position:

await engine.goTo({ row: 2, col: 1 });

Commands are not queued while the engine is busy. Navigation can resolve false, for example, when a boundary prevents movement or another transition is active.

The demo also supports vertical mouse-wheel navigation.

Framework components need their own lifecycle

One important architectural decision was keeping framework rendering outside the core.

A React or Vue component cannot simply be converted into an HTMLElement. It needs to remain connected to its framework’s rendering tree and lifecycle.

TikiTaki provides separate adapter packages:

@tikitaki_gagarinbefree/react
@tikitaki_gagarinbefree/vue
@tikitaki_gagarinbefree/svelte
@tikitaki_gagarinbefree/angular

Install only the adapter your application needs. The core does not import any of these frameworks.

The repository includes examples for all four, plus a plain JavaScript demo.

Rendering and testing

The engine mounts the current cell and the necessary neighboring cells rather than rendering the entire grid.

Movement uses requestAnimationFrame and CSS transforms. Navigation, gesture recognition, and DOM rendering are separate modules.

The project includes unit and integration tests, strict TypeScript checks, and browser tests running in Google Chrome with desktop input and touch emulation.

It is still an early project. Chrome is the current browser target, and testing on a physical Android device remains pending. Touch emulation does not replace that validation.

What would you build with it?

TikiTaki is available under the MIT license.

I’d appreciate feedback on two things:

  • Where would two-dimensional swipe navigation be useful in your application?
  • What would make the integration easier for your framework?

You can explore the live demo, read the integration documentation, or open an issue.

If you try it in a project, I’d love to hear what worked and what got in the way.
