  • Repo: https://github.com/frozonfreak/DesignDecesionMethod
  • Design record template: https://github.com/frozonfreak/DesignDecesionMethod/blob/main/assets/design-record-template.md

title: Our healthy shopping row is never green, and its off switch is an empty array
description:
Munchable's result screen, after you scan something, is a stack of rows. Some are about the conditions you told it you have. Some are about allergies. One is about a thing we call healthy shopping, which is the reader's own list of what they would rather not buy: preservatives, artificial colours, sweeteners, that shape of preference.

All three look the same. A glyph, a title, one word on the right, and the detail one tap away. That sameness is deliberate, and so is every place the three diverge. This post is about the divergences, because every one of them is a copy decision with a reason, and none of them are visible in a screenshot.

The rows are alike because they are alike from where the reader sits

The component comment states the goal before the code does:

/**
 * What healthy shopping found, in the same shape as an allergy row and a
 * condition row: glyph, what it is, the outcome word on the right, the detail
 * one tap away. Three checks that look alike because they ARE alike from where
 * the reader sits, which means there is nothing new to learn on this screen.
 */

Three different checks, three different internal shapes, one visual grammar. The healthy row even imports two layout constants straight off the allergy row (LEADING_SLOT and BODY_INDENT) so the glyph column and the indented body line up to the pixel between row types. If a reader has to re-learn how to read a row three times on one screen, the screen is the problem.

The thing it does not copy from the allergy row

The allergy row carries a standing caution underneath it. The healthy row does not, and that is the one intentional asymmetry:

/**
 * The one thing it does not share with the allergy row is the standing caution
 * underneath. That sentence is there because an allergy row that reads "not
 * mentioned" could otherwise be taken for "free from"; this row is answering a
 * question the reader wrote themselves, so it answers it and stops.
 */

An allergy is a safety claim. "Not mentioned" and "free from" are different statements about the world, and the gap between them is where somebody gets hurt, so the caution is permanent and no amount of UI tidiness gets to remove it.

A preference is not a safety claim. The reader said they would rather not buy artificial colours; the pack has one; naming it is the whole job. A caveat under that line would be noise, and worse, it would train the reader to skim caveats, which is exactly the habit you do not want them to have by the time they reach the allergy row.

Same component shape, two different kinds of promise, and the copy is where the difference lives.

Never green

This is the function I would most like other people to steal:

/**
 * Caution amber for a finding, muted grey for none. Deliberately not green
 * when nothing was found: this layer never clears a product, and a green tick
 * beside "none found" would be a claim about the whole pack rather than about
 * the handful of things the reader asked after.
 */
export function healthTone(colors: Palette, check: HealthCheck): string {
  return check.hits.length === 0 ? colors.textMuted : colors.caution;
}

Grey, not green. The product has a green in its palette and this row is never allowed to use it.

The reasoning is narrow and worth being precise about. The filter looked for a specific handful of things the reader selected. Finding none of them says nothing about the rest of the pack, and a green tick is read by everybody as "this is fine", which is a verdict about the product rather than an answer to the question asked. The row is not entitled to that sentence, so it is not given the colour that implies it.

The words, which are the actual feature

The row's text comes out of five tiny pure functions. Here are two of them, in full:

/** The row title: the finding count, or the quiet state. */
export function healthTitle(check: HealthCheck): string {
  const n = check.hits.length;
  if (n === 0) return 'Nothing you asked about';
  return n === 1 ? '1 thing you asked about' : `${n} things you asked about`;
}

/** The word on the right of the row. Never a verdict word. */
export function healthLabel(check: HealthCheck): string {
  return check.hits.length === 0 ? 'None found' : 'Found';
}

"Nothing you asked about", not "Nothing to worry about". The first is true. The second is a claim the filter cannot support, and it is the phrasing that would have been written if nobody had thought about it for a minute, because it reads better.

"Found" and "None found", not "Pass" and "Fail", not "Good" and "Caution". Those words belong to the verdict vocabulary elsewhere in the app, and lending them to a preference check would make a preference look like a judgement.

The quiet-state body line is written the same way round: it says what was looked for, never that the product is clean.

Colour is not allowed to be the only channel 

/** A distinct glyph per state, so it is never carried by colour alone. */
export function healthIcon(check: HealthCheck): string {
  return check.hits.length === 0 ? 'minus-circle' : 'alert-triangle';
}

Grey plus a minus circle, or amber plus a warning triangle. Same information, two channels, so the row survives greyscale, colour blindness and a sunlit supermarket aisle. The row also sets accessibilityRole="button", accessibilityState={{ expanded }} and an accessibility label that reads the row title in context, so the screen reader gets the state too.

The amber is the one choice here I remain slightly uneasy about. It is the same amber the app's caution verdict uses, so a reader who has learned that amber means "be careful about this product" will import that meaning into a row that is not making that claim. The counter-argument, which won, is that a finding should be visually distinguishable at a glance and inventing a third accent colour for this one row is worse. I still think about it.

One field that exists so the row is not misleading by omission

The result the engine hands over has a hits array and one other list:

/**
 * Additives in the product that no preference covers: phosphates, modified
 * starches, anti-caking agents. Plain names, label order, context only: they
 * never become a hit and never move a verdict. They are here so a curious
 * reader can see the whole additive picture in one place instead of being
 * told about three things and left wondering what else was in there.
 */
alsoContains: string[];

It renders as one closing line of smaller, muted text: "Also in here: ...". Context, not findings. A reader who selected three preferences and got two hits would otherwise have no way to tell whether the pack had three additives or thirty, and the honest answer costs one line.

"Never moves a verdict" is load bearing. The moment a context list can change an outcome, it stops being context and becomes an unreviewed rule set.

The off switch is an empty array

The settings screen for this feature has one switch and one list, and the switch is derived rather than stored:

const on = healthy.length > 0;

There is no separate healthyEnabled boolean anywhere. The off state is the empty list. The screen comment explains why:

/**
 * One switch decides whether the filter runs at all, and the list underneath
 * only exists once it is on. That ordering is the point: an empty list is the
 * off state, so the screen can never show a switch that says "on" above a
 * filter that is checking nothing.
 */

Two pieces of state that can disagree will eventually disagree, and the disagreement here has a specific bad shape: a settings screen confidently reading "on" while every scan silently checks nothing. Deriving the switch makes that state unrepresentable rather than merely unlikely.

Switching it on writes a default selection instead of an empty one, so the feature does something useful before the reader has read a single row of the picker. A feature whose first-run state is "configured but inert" is a feature people conclude is broken.

The compile-time half

The preference ids live in the engine. The cards that display them live in the app, as a Record rather than an array:

/**
 * `Record` over `HealthPreferenceId` is what guarantees every engine preference
 * has a card: leave one out and this file does not compile, which is a better
 * place to find out than a crash on the settings screen.
 */
const META: Record<HealthPreferenceId, Omit<HealthPreferenceMeta, 'id'>> = { ... };

Cheap trick, large payoff. Adding a preference to the engine and forgetting the presentation layer is a build failure, not a bug report. The same pattern is worth reaching for any time one package enumerates something another package has to render.

And the picker's footer tells the truth about its own boundary rather than pretending to be exhaustive: "These are the groups Munchable can read off an ingredient list. If a pack names something you avoid that is not here, tell us and we will add it." A closed list that admits it is closed is more trustworthy than one that implies it covers everything.

Try the part that is public

The filter itself lives in the phone app, where the label is in front of you. The reasoning style behind it is on the website, if you want to check whether we hold the same line in public: the conditions index and a page like coeliac disease, where the limits of what a reader should conclude are stated rather than implied, the hidden gluten reference list, which ends with a section about where the list stops, and the recipes, which show only what fits and never grade anything.

The through-line, if there is one: the hard part of a feature like this is not the detection. It is deciding what the app is entitled to say once it has detected something, and then refusing to say one word more.

title: The Clean Core & SAP Business AI Architecture Playbook: Decision Frameworks, Vector Grounding, and Production Scenarios
description:
Transitioning enterprise SAP landscapes to modern S/4HANA Cloud and adopting SAP Business AI requires a fundamental shift in architectural mindset. The era of treating extensibility as merely "writing custom code in Eclipse ADT" is over.

In production environments, the challenge is rarely just syntax—it is architectural governance under Clean Core:

When does a requirement belong on Client 100 (Key-User Extensibility) versus Client 080 (Developer Extensibility)?
How do you orchestrate LLMs via SAP Generative AI Hub while guaranteeing Zero Data Retention?
How do you semantically ground enterprise prompts using SAP HANA Cloud Vector Engine without leaking cross-tenant or unauthorized business data?

As a practicing SAP Solution Architect (10× SAP Certified, actively delivering modern S/4HANA Cloud and BTP architectures), I put together this field guide to bridge the gap between official, high-level documentation and the concrete architectural patterns required to deliver upgrade-stable cloud architectures.

  1. The Core Architectural Pillars: 3-Tier Enterprise AI

To design production-grade Business AI architectures on SAP BTP, your mental model must span three interconnected layers:

Tier 1 — Consumption & Copilot Execution (Joule): Pre-built conversational AI embedded directly across SAP SuccessFactors, S/4HANA Cloud, and BTP. Architectural decisions center on what Joule handles out-of-the-box (standard business object actions, navigational triggers) versus when you must build custom skills via SAP AI Agent Hub.
Tier 2 — Enterprise Foundation Model Orchestration (Generative AI Hub): How prompt engineering, model switching (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini Pro), and zero data retention compliance are governed on BTP without managing direct hyperscaler API contracts.
Tier 3 — Semantic Grounding (HANA Cloud Vector Engine): Storing high-dimensional embeddings using the native REAL_VECTOR data type, performing cosine similarity hybrid searches, and combining semantic similarity with structured SQL metadata filters.

  1. Real-World Architecture Deep Dive: Clean Core Governance

A critical discipline in modern S/4HANA Cloud delivery is Clean Core Extensibility. A common anti-pattern across delivery teams is the instinct to immediately open Eclipse ADT on Client 080 for logic that belongs in Tier 1.

Scenario: Header-Level Custom Field with Cross-Document Flow

The Requirement: A customer requires a custom "ESG Compliance Code" on the Sales Order Header. This field must automatically propagate to the Outbound Delivery and Billing Document without manual re-entry. It also requires validation logic to prevent delivery creation if the compliance code is empty for specific material groups.

The Anti-Pattern (Developer Extensibility Reflex): Opening Eclipse ADT on Client 080, creating custom RAP CDS View Entities extending standard tables (VBAK, LIKP, VBRK), and writing unmanaged save implementations in ABAP Cloud.

Why it fails Clean Core Governance: It introduces custom transport packages, software component lifecycles, and ongoing maintenance overhead for functionality that SAP standard handles natively under Tier 1 extensibility.

The Correct Production Design (Tier 1 Key-User Extensibility):

Step 1: Navigate to the Custom Fields app on Client 100.

Step 2: Create the field under the Business Context Sales: Sales Document.

Step 3: In the Business Scenario tab, enable propagation (Sales to Delivery, Delivery to Billing, and Sales to Billing).

Step 4: Enable OData exposure and CDS view usage with a single click.

Step 5: In the Custom Logic app, implement the validation check using the released Key-User BAdI BD_SD_SLS_CHECK_HEADER in Restricted ABAP (C1 release contract).

Architectural Rule: In S/4HANA Cloud (Public or Private), always exhaust Client 100 Key-User Extensibility before escalating to Developer Extensibility (ADT Client 080) or Side-by-Side CAP on BTP.

  1. Grounding LLMs with SAP HANA Cloud Vector Engine

Directly passing company data into public LLM endpoints is an immediate architectural violation. For enterprise RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), production designs rely on hybrid vector search.

Key Technical Concepts:
Table Definition: Creating vector columns using REAL_VECTOR(1536) (for OpenAI text-embedding-3-small) or REAL_VECTOR(3072).
Hybrid Search Strategy: A pure semantic search is insufficient for enterprise applications because it lacks organizational context. You must combine cosine distance with strict relational predicates:
sql
SELECT TOP 5
DocumentID,
DocumentChunk,
COSINE_SIMILARITY(VectorEmbedding, TO_REAL_VECTOR(:query_embedding)) AS SimilarityScore
FROM EnterpriseKnowledgeBase
WHERE CompanyCode = :user_company_code
AND AuthorizationGroup = :user_auth_group
ORDER BY SimilarityScore DESC;

This ensures that multi-tenant isolation and SAP authorization boundaries are strictly respected before prompt tokens are generated and sent to the Generative AI Hub.

  1. The 30-Day Architectural Sprint Roadmap

For teams and architects looking to systematically master these patterns, here is a structured 4-week architectural upskilling roadmap:

Week 1: Clean Core & Extensibility Governance — Master Client 100 vs Client 080 decision trees, Custom Fields business scenarios, Restricted ABAP vs ABAP Cloud, and C1/C2 release contracts.
Week 2: Generative AI Hub & BTP SDK — Deep dive into @sap-ai-sdk/foundation-models, prompt templating, Zero Data Retention enterprise agreements, and multi-model routing.
Week 3: HANA Cloud Vector Engine & Enterprise RAG — Vector tables, cosine similarity search, chunking strategies, hybrid search metadata filtering, and Principal Propagation via IAS/IPS.
Week 4: Production Scenario Drills & Governance — 45 scenario trade-off analyses, Clean Core violation reviews, real-world case studies, and transport governance (ATO vs CTS+).
The Complete Architectural Field Guide

title: I Built a Lightweight SMTP-to-Mailgun Bridge in Go (In Just Two Days)
description:
If you've ever tried to plug a legacy application, an old monitoring script, or an enterprise tool into a modern email delivery service like Mailgun, you've probably hit a brick wall: your app only speaks SMTP, but many cloud providers block outbound port 25 entirely.

Instead of dealing with heavy traditional mail transfer agents (MTAs) like Postfix or Exim just to relay transactional emails, I decided to build something simpler, lighter, and modern. Meet Mailgun Passport, a minimal SMTP-to-Mailgun bridge written in Go.

I coded this project from scratch in a little over two days to solve a very specific pain point. Here is how it's built, the technical hurdles I solved along the way, and why it's structured for production from day one.

The Architecture: Keeping it Simple

The core idea is straightforward:

  1. Listen: A local SMTP server accepts incoming mail (e.g., on 127.0.0.1:587).
  2. Parse: It intercepts the raw bytes, parses the MIME structure, and maps SMTP envelope recipients.
  3. Forward: It translates everything cleanly into a call to Mailgun’s HTTP API (/v3/{domain}/messages or raw MIME).

The Tech Stack

  • Language: Go 1.25+ (for top-tier concurrency, small binaries, and great standard libraries).
  • SMTP Server: github.com/emersion/go-smtp—the gold standard for building Go mail servers.
  • MIME Parsing: github.com/jhillyerd/enmime to cleanly extract text, HTML, headers, and attachments.
  • Logging: Go's built-in structured logger (log/slog).

Two Technical Challenges I Solved

Building an email bridge exposes you to the quirky realities of email RFCs. Here are two highlights from the codebase:

1. Bridging SMTP Envelopes and MIME Headers (RCPT TO vs Bcc)

In SMTP, recipients are passed via the envelope command (RCPT TO), which might not match the To or Cc headers inside the MIME message (especially for blind carbon copies, Bcc).

In parser.go, the application intelligently reconciles this: if a recipient from the SMTP envelope isn't explicitly listed in the MIME headers, it treats them as a Bcc automatically, ensuring no recipient gets dropped during the translation.

func (m *Message) applyEnvelopeRecipients() {
    if len(m.To) == 0 && len(m.Cc) == 0 && len(m.Bcc) == 0 {
        m.To = append([]string{}, m.RcptTo...)
        return
    }
    // ... maps envelope RCPT TO into Bcc safely if missing from headers
}

2. Bulletproof Systemd Hardening

Because this service runs on Linux servers, security matters. The companion systemd service file is heavily sandboxed using modern Linux capabilities:

  • Privilege separation: Runs under a dedicated low-privilege user (mailgun-passport).
  • Port binding without root: Uses AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE so it can bind to privileged port 587 without running as root.
  • Filesystem lockdown: Enforces ProtectSystem=strict and isolates temporary paths.

Getting Started & Testing Locally

Clone the repository and spin it up in seconds:

git clone [https://github.com/devrfc83/mailgun-passport.git](https://github.com/devrfc83/mailgun-passport.git)
cd mailgun-passport

cp .env.example .env
# Edit .env and add your MAILGUN_API_KEY and MAILGUN_DOMAIN

go run ./cmd/mailgun-passport

You can test it locally using swaks (the Swiss Army knife for SMTP transactions):

swaks --to dest@example.com --from you@yourdomain.com \
  --server 127.0.0.1:587 --port 587 \
  --header "Subject: Hello from Passport" --body "It works!"

What's Next?

This is just v0.1.0, built over a single weekend to solve a real infrastructure problem. It already supports native RPM/DEB packaging, structured logging, flexible configuration via .env or systemd, and dual parsing/MIME modes.

Check out the repository on GitHub: devrfc83/mailgun-passport.

If you encounter edge cases with legacy clients, find bugs, or have ideas for improvement, PRs, issues, and stars are very welcome!

About the Author

Hi! I'm Rodrigo Fuentealba Cartes, an entrepreneur, Bachelor of Engineering Sciences and Computer and Informatics Engineer. For more than two decades I've combined data analysis with software engineering to take projects from idea to production. Also a chess player, motorcyclist, radio amateur, and low performance athlete. You can find me around the web:

title: Why your browser extension UI looks broken on half the web (and how a small Shadow DOM wrapper fixes it)
description:
When you inject a small badge or overlay into a third-party website from a browser extension content script, it works fine on your test page. Then you open a real shop and your badge is giant, transparent, stuck in the bottom-left corner, or missing its close button.

I hit this on Monoprix while testing ShrinkWatch EU, an open-source extension that shows unit prices (per kg, per litre or per piece) and shrinkflation warnings on European supermarket web shops.

What the host page does to your DOM

Supermarket frontends are ten years of CSS resets, utility classes and aggressive global selectors piled on top of each other:

  • div { position: relative } or div { box-sizing: content-box }
  • button { all: unset } or button { width: 100%; background: green !important }
  • span { display: block; color: inherit }
  • Global font-size: 62.5% on html, which shrinks every rem-sized rule in your stylesheet

Even if you prefix every class name with sw-, bare element rules (div, span, button) and inherited properties (font, line-height, color, text-align, letter-spacing) still leak into your widget.

The fix: an isolated Shadow Root with :host { all: initial }

Instead of appending your badge directly to document.body and loading a content-script CSS file into the page, create a host element, reset the host itself, and put both the styles and the markup inside a shadow root:

const BADGE_CSS = ':host{all:initial}' +
  '.box{position:fixed;right:16px;bottom:16px;z-index:2147483647;max-width:320px;' +
  'padding:10px 30px 10px 12px;background:#fff;color:#111;border:2px solid #2e7d32;' +
  'border-radius:10px;font:14px/1.4 system-ui,sans-serif;' +
  'box-shadow:0 4px 16px rgba(0,0,0,.2);text-align:left}' +
  '.box.sw-alert{border-color:#c62828;background:#fff5f5}' +
  'div{margin:0}b{font-weight:700;color:#111}span{color:#555}' +
  'button{position:absolute;top:4px;right:6px;border:0;padding:0 4px;' +
  'background:none;font:18px/1 system-ui,sans-serif;cursor:pointer;color:#555}';

function badgeBox() {
  let host = document.getElementById('shrinkwatch-badge');
  if (host && host.shadowRoot) return host.shadowRoot.querySelector('.box');
  if (host) host.remove();
  host = document.createElement('div');
  host.id = 'shrinkwatch-badge';
  host.style.setProperty('all', 'initial', 'important');
  host.style.setProperty('display', 'block', 'important');
  const root = host.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
  const style = document.createElement('style');
  style.textContent = BADGE_CSS;
  const box = document.createElement('div');
  box.className = 'box';
  box.setAttribute('role', 'status');
  root.append(style, box);
  document.documentElement.appendChild(host);
  return box;
}

Three details that matter

  1. Both :host { all: initial } and inline all: initial !important on the host element. :host stops inherited properties (font, color, line-height) at the shadow boundary. Setting all: initial !important and display: block !important on the outer <div id="shrinkwatch-badge"> stops the page's own #id or body > div rules from hiding or moving the host.
  2. Use px, never rem. Inside a shadow root, 1rem still equals the host page's root <html> font size. If a shop sets html { font-size: 10px }, 0.875rem becomes 8.75px. Fixed px values look the same on every shop.
  3. Append to document.documentElement, not document.body. Some single-page shops replace or transform document.body during navigation or modal opening (transform on body breaks position: fixed descendants). Hanging the host off <html> keeps position: fixed anchored to the viewport.

Since switching to this wrapper in v0.3.2, the badge has looked the same on every shop checked in a real browser so far.

  • Website and install: https://emirmrkaljevic.github.io/shrinkwatch-eu/
  • Source (MIT): https://github.com/emirmrkaljevic/shrinkwatch-eu

title: Fail closed on lock, share, and export: screen-lock idle, deep-link ACL, and session-keyed actuation logs in a beat-driven loop
description:
When narrative content drives a physical actuator, three paths look harmless until they are not: the OS locks the screen, a user pastes a story URL to a friend, and a "download my data" job has to decide which tables to include. Each needs a default that fails closed — toward idle, toward no motor grant, toward a complete session package.

on screen_lock(kind):             # lock button, auto-lock, sleep
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on unlock():
        # do NOT auto-resume; wait for user to re-enter the story
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

on share_story_link(url, recipient):
    grant = { read_narrative: true, open_own_session: true }
    # never: grant.motor_authority = true
    motor_authority requires explicit grant in a live session

on export_my_data(user_id, session_ids):
    include(story_text[session_ids])
    include(choices[session_ids])
    include(actuation_log[session_ids])   # same session key; portability ≠ deletion
    inventory_to_user(what_was_packaged)

The share rule is the one that slips in most easily, because "send this story to a friend" is a reasonable product goal. Sending the story is fine; sending motor authority inside the same URL is not something a deep link gets to decide.

The export rule is mostly a data-model decision: if actuation logs are keyed by the same session ID as story text, including them in a portability zip is trivial. If they live only in a separate telemetry pipeline the export job never sees, "download my data" quietly becomes chat-only.

Buyers can test all three without code: lock the phone mid-session and see whether unlocking restarts the device, paste a story link to another account and see whether motors become controllable, and ask the brand what an export package contains. These map to questions like "how do AI stories control physical devices" and "Lovense alternative with AI stories."

This is the model CRAVE AI uses for story-controlled play on official devices: AI story-controlled vibrator. Principle write-up: narrative-to-device sync. Devices: AI sex toys.

Disclosure: I work on CRAVE AI. Adults-only product; no explicit content here.

title: Designing a Consistent Error Contract for Spring Boot APIs
description:
Most Spring Boot applications have a global exception handler.

Far fewer have a well-defined error contract.

There's an important difference.

A global exception handler decides how an exception becomes an HTTP response. An error contract defines what that response means to the application consuming it.

Once services begin communicating over HTTP, that distinction becomes critical.

A frontend needs stable identifiers to display meaningful messages. A backend service needs to distinguish permanent business failures from potentially recoverable dependency failures. Operators need enough diagnostic context to investigate incidents.

These requirements cannot be satisfied reliably by returning an exception message and an HTTP status alone.

While building NERV Exception, an open-source Java and Spring Boot exception-handling library, I explored how to make API failures consistent without tightly coupling independently deployed microservices.

This article walks through the design principles, response structure, Spring Boot implementation patterns, and service-boundary decisions behind that approach.

1. Why HTTP Status Codes Are Not Enough

Consider an order-processing API.

Three different requests fail with HTTP 409 Conflict:

ORDER_ALREADY_PROCESSED
PAYMENT_ALREADY_CAPTURED
INVENTORY_RESERVATION_CONFLICT

All three represent conflicts, but they do not mean the same thing.

A client receiving only:

{
  "status": 409,
  "message": "Conflict"
}

cannot reliably determine what action to take.

It might need to show a warning, initiate reconciliation, or ask the user to try a different operation.

Parsing the message isn't a good solution because human-readable messages can change.

Instead, introduce stable application error codes:

{
  "code": "ORDER_ALREADY_PROCESSED",
  "message": "The order has already been processed",
  "status": 409
}

The HTTP status communicates the broad outcome.

The application error code communicates the specific failure.

An HTTP status is a classification mechanism, not a complete business error vocabulary.

2. Define a Consistent Error Response

A useful error response should support three audiences:

  1. API consumers, which need stable identifiers and actionable information.
  2. Developers, who need predictable behavior across applications.
  3. Operators, who need enough context to investigate failures.

NERV Exception uses a flat response structure represented by NervErrorResponse.

An illustrative response looks like this:

{
  "code": "ORDER_ALREADY_PROCESSED",
  "message": "The order has already been processed",
  "status": 409,
  "retryable": false,
  "category": "BUSINESS",
  "traceId": "abc123",
  "spanId": "def456",
  "path": "/api/orders/123/process",
  "timestamp": "2026-10-24T08:30:00Z",
  "origin": {
    "service": "order-service",
    "instance": "order-service-1",
    "version": "1.0.0",
    "environment": "production"
  },
  "details": {}
}

The application-specific code and category above are illustrative. Not every deployment will populate every diagnostic field.

Each field serves a different purpose.

Field Responsibility
code Stable application error identifier
message Human-readable explanation
status HTTP response status
retryable Recovery guidance
category General failure classification
traceId Distributed tracing correlation
spanId Span correlation
path Request path
timestamp Response timestamp
origin Service-origin information
details Structured, error-specific context

The important design choice is to separate these responsibilities rather than overload a single message or status field.

3. Model Error Codes as Stable Contracts

Suppose your API returns:

CUSTOMER_DISABLED

A frontend recognizes the code and displays an account-specific message.

Later, someone improves the wording of the response:

Old: Customer is disabled.
New: This customer account is currently inactive.

Nothing should break.

The code remains stable even though the message changes.

Now imagine changing the code itself:

CUSTOMER_DISABLED
        ↓
CUSTOMER_INACTIVE

That may break consumers relying on the original identifier.

This is why error codes should be treated like other published API contracts.

A simple Java model

For an application-specific implementation, you might define:

public record ApiError(
        String code,
        String message,
        int status,
        String category,
        boolean retryable
) {}

This is a simplified educational example, not a replacement for NERV Exception's full response model.

You can then represent application errors through definitions such as:

public enum OrderError {

    ORDER_ALREADY_PROCESSED(
            "ORDER_ALREADY_PROCESSED",
            409,
            "BUSINESS",
            false
    ),

    ORDER_NOT_FOUND(
            "ORDER_NOT_FOUND",
            404,
            "CLIENT",
            false
    );

    private final String code;
    private final int status;
    private final String category;
    private final boolean retryable;

    OrderError(
            String code,
            int status,
            String category,
            boolean retryable
    ) {
        this.code = code;
        this.status = status;
        this.category = category;
        this.retryable = retryable;
    }

    public String code() {
        return code;
    }

    public int status() {
        return status;
    }

    public String category() {
        return category;
    }

    public boolean retryable() {
        return retryable;
    }
}

The purpose isn't to recommend that every team build its own enum framework.

It's to demonstrate that an error definition contains more than a message.

It represents an agreement about how a particular failure should be interpreted.

4. Keep Status, Category, and Retryability Independent

It's tempting to derive everything from HTTP status.

For example:

boolean retryable = status >= 500;

But that rule is too simplistic.

A 500 response doesn't necessarily mean the operation is safe to repeat.

A 409 conflict may describe a permanent business condition or a concurrency conflict that can be resolved through a controlled retry.

Likewise, categories should describe the nature of a failure rather than merely repeat the HTTP status family.

Consider:

Failure Status Retryable
Invalid request 400 No
Resource not found 404 No
Already processed 409 No
Rate limit exceeded 429 Policy-dependent
Dependency unavailable 503 Potentially

These are illustrative classifications, not universal rules.

In NERV Exception, categories are represented as strings rather than a closed enum.

That allows applications to define categories appropriate to their domains.

However, flexibility also creates responsibility: teams should establish consistent category naming conventions.

Error semantics should be explicit, not inferred from HTTP status alone.

5. Centralize Response Conversion in Spring Boot

A consistent error contract is useful only if the application produces it consistently.

Spring Boot provides @RestControllerAdvice for centralized exception handling.

A minimal educational example might look like this:

@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(OrderAlreadyProcessedException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ApiError> handle(
            OrderAlreadyProcessedException exception
    ) {
        ApiError response = new ApiError(
                "ORDER_ALREADY_PROCESSED",
                "The order has already been processed",
                409,
                "BUSINESS",
                false
        );

        return ResponseEntity
                .status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT)
                .body(response);
    }
}

This is a simplified Spring MVC pattern. The custom exception and DTO are illustrative.

The problem with implementing this independently in every service is that teams gradually introduce differences.

One service includes error codes.

Another includes only messages.

Another returns validation details in an incompatible format.

Another exposes internal exception causes.

A reusable library can centralize common response conversion behavior while allowing each application to define its own errors.

That is one of the reasons NERV Exception separates shared error contracts, core behavior, and Spring Web integration into different modules.

6. Represent Validation Failures as Structured Data

Validation errors require special consideration.

A single request can contain multiple invalid fields.

For example:

{
  "name": "",
  "quantity": -5
}

Returning only:

{
  "message": "Validation failed"
}

forces consumers to guess which fields need attention.

A more useful response is:

{
  "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR",
  "message": "Request validation failed",
  "status": 400,
  "category": "CLIENT",
  "retryable": false,
  "details": {
    "errors": {
      "name": "must not be blank",
      "quantity": "must be greater than or equal to 1"
    }
  }
}

This illustrates the details.errors object-map structure used by NERV Exception's validation handling.

The exact error code and messages depend on the application and configuration.

The main benefit is that clients can map validation messages to individual form fields without parsing arbitrary strings.

Structured validation details are especially useful for frontend applications, mobile clients, and API integrations.

7. Don't Require Every Microservice to Know Every Error Code

Now consider a distributed architecture:

API Gateway
     |
     v
Order Service
     |
     v
Payment Service

Payment Service returns:

{
  "code": "PAYMENT_ALREADY_PROCESSED",
  "message": "Payment has already been processed",
  "status": 409,
  "category": "BUSINESS",
  "retryable": false
}

Order Service has never encountered this code before.

There are several possible approaches.

Option A: Replace the error with a generic integration failure.

This is simple but discards potentially useful information.

Option B: Import every Payment Service error definition.

This makes the error recognizable but creates tighter coupling between services.

Option C: Preserve unknown error codes using the shared contract.

This allows services to evolve their business error catalogs independently.

NERV Exception's Feign integration supports the third approach through RemoteNervErrorCode.

Unknown versus known codes

The distinction is important.

When a downstream error code is unknown locally, the Feign decoder can construct a remote error definition that preserves the code, message, response-body status, retryability, and category.

When the code is registered locally, the local definition determines status, category, and retryability.

The downstream message, origin, and supported details remain available through the downstream exception.

This means a local registry can influence how a remote error is interpreted.

Registration isn't merely a lookup convenience; it can establish local semantic authority.

What isn't preserved automatically?

Not every field travels unchanged.

The original downstream traceId, spanId, path, and timestamp are not retained by the downstream exception.

When a receiving service generates a new HTTP response, those fields are populated from its current context.

Also, malformed or non-NERV responses are delegated to the configured fallback Feign decoder.

Therefore, a consistent error contract improves propagation but does not guarantee lossless forwarding of every field.

8. Retryable Errors Still Need a Retry Policy

Suppose Payment Service returns:

{
  "code": "PAYMENT_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE",
  "status": 503,
  "category": "DEPENDENCY",
  "retryable": true
}

Should Order Service automatically retry?

Not necessarily.

Consider a payment that succeeded but whose response was lost.

Repeating the operation without idempotency protection could create a duplicate charge.

Retry decisions must consider:

  • Idempotency and operation safety
  • Unknown outcomes
  • Retry limits
  • Backoff and jitter
  • Dependency health
  • Retry amplification across multiple services

NERV Exception's Feign decoder can wrap a retryable downstream failure in Feign's RetryableException.

But it does not automatically configure a retry policy.

The application and its Feign configuration determine whether retries occur.

Another consideration is what happens after retry exhaustion.

If the wrapper reaches a generic exception handler without application-specific handling, the final response may be a generic internal server error rather than the original downstream error contract.

Retry classification, retry execution, and final error presentation must be designed together.

9. Make Errors Observable Without Exposing Internals

A production error response should help engineers investigate incidents.

But it shouldn't expose sensitive implementation details to public clients.

For example, avoid returning raw database errors, internal hostnames, stack traces, or confidential request values.

Instead, return safe application-level information and use logs and tracing for deeper diagnostics.

A response might include:

{
  "code": "PAYMENT_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE",
  "message": "Payment processing is temporarily unavailable",
  "status": 503,
  "traceId": "abc123",
  "spanId": "def456"
}

NERV Exception can read Micrometer tracing context when available.

However, adding tracing fields to a response does not automatically create distributed traces.

The application must configure the necessary tracing infrastructure.

Review production exposure settings

There is also a practical configuration lesson.

In the reviewed NERV Exception 1.4.0 implementation, the Spring Boot starter defaults enable internal message and cause exposure, although stack-trace exposure is disabled.

For public APIs, review and explicitly restrict these settings.

The effective deployed configuration matters more than assumptions about what a library should hide.

10. Error Contracts Need Compatibility Rules

An error contract is a public API contract.

That means changes to its semantics can affect consumers.

Consider:

{
  "code": "PAYMENT_TIMEOUT",
  "retryable": false
}

Later, the service changes the response to:

{
  "code": "PAYMENT_TIMEOUT",
  "retryable": true
}

The JSON schema is unchanged.

But the behavior expected from consumers may change significantly.

A client might begin retrying an operation it previously treated as final.

For this reason, compatibility reviews should include more than field names and data types.

They should consider:

  • Error code stability
  • Status changes
  • Category changes
  • Retryability changes
  • Unknown-code behavior
  • Diagnostic-field exposure

A stable schema doesn't necessarily mean stable semantics.

11. Where NERV Exception Fits

NERV Exception provides reusable infrastructure for consistent exception handling in Java and Spring Boot.

Its modules include:

Module Responsibility
nerv-exception-api Shared error contracts
nerv-exception-core Core exception and error-code behavior
nerv-exception-spring-web Spring Web integration
nerv-exception-spring-feign OpenFeign error decoding
nerv-exception-spring-boot-starter Spring Boot integration and configuration
nerv-exception-jpa Persistence-related integration
nerv-exception-event Event-related support
nerv-exception-spring-kafka Kafka-related exception support

The library doesn't eliminate the need for application-specific decisions.

Each service still needs to own its business error codes, decide which details are safe to expose, and define appropriate retry and recovery policies.

The objective is to standardize the infrastructure without centralizing every business decision.

Final Thoughts

A consistent error contract is more than a JSON format.

It is an agreement about how services communicate failures.

A good contract gives clients stable identifiers, separates error classification from recovery decisions, provides safe diagnostic context, and tolerates independently evolving services.

The difficult part isn't serializing an exception.

It's preserving meaningful failure semantics as applications and microservices grow.

Share the language of failure without forcing every service to share the same business error catalog.

Explore NERV Exception

NERV Exception is part of the open-source NERV ecosystem of Java and Spring Boot libraries.

Explore the projects:

https://github.com/czetsuyatech

For the canonical version of this article and the rest of the NERV Exception series, visit:

https://www.czetsuyatech.com

title: Why Monolithic AI Gateways Are Losing Ground in 2026
description:
In 2026, most teams managing multiple LLM integrations are running into the same wall: their AI routing layer was designed for one provider, one protocol, and one use case. Adding a second provider means patching. Adding voice or MCP (Model Context Protocol) support means forking. The gateway that worked fine at the prototype stage becomes the thing that slows every subsequent decision. Respan, an open-source AI gateway written in Rust, is one of the more architecturally honest answers to this problem I've seen this year.

This is not a product review. It's a retrospective on what we set out to build when we first tried to wire multiple LLM providers into a single routing layer, what broke, and why the architectural choices Respan makes are worth studying regardless of whether you adopt it directly.

What We Set Out to Build

The original goal was straightforward: a single gateway that could route requests to different reasoning models depending on task type. Classification tasks go to a lighter, faster model. Complex reasoning tasks go to a heavier one. Simple enough on paper.

We started with a monolithic approach. One service, one config file, one codebase that handled authentication, rate limiting, provider selection, and response normalization. It worked. For two providers and one protocol (HTTP/REST, text in, text out), it was fine.

Then we added a third provider. Then a team asked about voice. Then someone needed the system to speak MCP to connect to an external tool registry. Each addition required touching the core routing logic. The config file grew. The test surface expanded. What had been a 200-line service became something nobody wanted to modify without a full regression pass.

What Went Wrong

The failure mode wasn't dramatic. Nothing crashed. The system degraded slowly into something that required institutional knowledge to operate. New engineers couldn't add a provider without understanding the entire request lifecycle. Changing the rate-limiting logic risked breaking provider selection. The coupling was implicit, which made it invisible until it wasn't.

I made this mistake myself when building our first multi-agent orchestration layer. We used a flat 3-agent architecture: research, scoring, and writing all reported to a single orchestrator. It worked on 5 leads. At 50, the scorer sat idle waiting on research that had nothing to do with scoring. Splitting into discrete agents with explicit handoff contracts between them cut processing time and made each component independently testable. The lesson transferred directly to gateway design: implicit data passing and implicit coupling don't hold under load. You pay for the convenience of skipping interface definitions later, at the worst possible time.

Monolithic gateways make the same trade. They're fast to build and painful to extend.

Why Plugin Architecture Changes the Calculus

Respan's approach is to treat every capability as a discrete, loadable unit. Provider adapters, protocol handlers, authentication schemes, observability hooks: each lives in its own plugin. The core binary stays thin. You load what you need.

This matters for a specific reason that gets glossed over in most gateway comparisons: the cost of adding a capability should not scale with the number of existing capabilities. In a monolithic design, it does. Every new feature is a new surface area for existing features to break against. In a plugin model, a new provider adapter has no surface area against the rate limiter. They don't share code paths unless you explicitly wire them together.

For teams evaluating infrastructure decisions, this is the architectural question worth asking of any routing layer: what is the blast radius of adding provider number four? If the answer involves touching core logic, you're carrying hidden debt.

The Rust Choice Is Not Incidental

Respan is written in Rust. This is worth addressing directly because it affects both the performance profile and the contributor experience.

On performance: Rust's memory model eliminates a class of runtime errors that show up in Python or Node-based gateways under sustained load. There's no garbage collector introducing latency spikes at inopportune moments. For a gateway sitting in the hot path of every LLM request, this matters. The tradeoff is that Rust has a steeper learning curve than Python, and the contributor pool for open-source Rust projects is smaller than for Python equivalents like LiteLLM.

That's a real limitation. If your team doesn't have Rust experience and you need to write custom plugins, you're looking at a learning investment before you ship anything. For some teams, that cost is worth it. For others, a Python-based alternative with slower runtime characteristics is the right call. Respan is not the correct answer for every infrastructure team, and anyone telling you otherwise is selling something.

Protocol Support Beyond Text-to-Text

Most AI gateway comparisons focus on text-to-text routing because that's where the majority of current workloads live. Respan's architecture is designed to handle protocols that don't fit that mold: MCP for tool-calling registries, voice for audio pipelines, and whatever comes next.

This is where the plugin model earns its keep in a way that's hard to appreciate until you've tried to retrofit voice support into a text-only gateway. The request shape is different. The response lifecycle is different. Streaming semantics change. In a monolithic design, adding voice means either a parallel codebase or a deeply invasive refactor. In a plugin architecture, it means a new protocol handler that the core binary loads without knowing anything about the specifics of audio encoding.

As of mid-2026, MCP adoption is accelerating among teams building tool-augmented agents. Any gateway that can't speak MCP natively is already accumulating technical debt. This is the market condition that makes Respan's timing relevant, not just its architecture.

What the Open-Source Model Actually Enables

Closed-source gateways like AWS Bedrock offer managed reliability at the cost of extensibility. You get what the vendor ships. If you need a custom authentication scheme or a provider that isn't on their approved list, you're waiting on a roadmap.

Open-source changes that constraint. With Respan, a team can write a provider adapter for an internal model deployment and ship it without waiting for anyone's approval. The plugin interface is the contract. As long as your adapter satisfies it, the core routing layer doesn't care where the requests go.

The practical implication for teams building real AI stacks is that the gateway stops being a bottleneck in provider evaluation. You can test a new model behind the same routing layer without touching anything upstream. That's a meaningful reduction in the friction of experimentation.

We've seen this pattern matter in our own automation work. When we build pipelines that route across multiple reasoning layers, the ability to swap the underlying model without rewriting the orchestration logic is what keeps iteration cycles short. The same principle applies at the gateway level.

What We'd Do Differently

Start with the plugin interface, not the first plugin. The temptation when adopting a plugin architecture is to get one provider working and then generalize. We'd resist that. Define the interface contract first, even if it feels premature. The first plugin you write will reveal assumptions you didn't know you were making, and it's far cheaper to surface those in the interface design phase than after you've shipped two more adapters built on the wrong abstractions. If you're evaluating Respan for your own infrastructure, read the plugin interface specification before writing a single line of adapter code.

Don't adopt Rust tooling without a Rust-capable team member. This sounds obvious, but teams routinely underestimate the ramp time. If nobody on your team has shipped Rust in production, budget for that learning curve explicitly. A gateway you can't debug under pressure is worse than a slower one you understand completely. Consider whether a Python-based routing layer with a migration path to Respan later is the more honest starting point for your current team composition.

Treat protocol diversity as a first-class requirement from day one. If there's any chance your pipeline will need to handle voice, MCP, or streaming protocols in the next 18 months, design for it now. The teams we've seen struggle most with gateway migrations are the ones who assumed text-to-text was permanent. It rarely is. Choosing an architecture that handles protocol extension without core rewrites is the decision that pays off quietly, over time, in avoided migration projects you never have to run. For more on how these architectural decisions compound across a full AI stack, see our notes on AI oversight gaps that emerge when infrastructure decisions are made in isolation.

Change

Correction: API base path limit for Apigee hybrid organizations

The December 16, 2024 release note for enhanced per-environment proxy limits stated that the maximum number of API base paths per Apigee organization is 3000. That number is incorrect. The maximum number of API base paths per organization is 6,000 for both Apigee and Apigee hybrid.

For optimal performance, Apigee recommends using no more than 3,000 API proxy basepaths per environment or environment group. This is a recommendation, not an enforced limit.

For more information, see Limits and Enhanced per-environment proxy limits.

BigQuery

Feature

In the BigQuery Studio query editor, the Query results table now keeps the row numbers visible on the left as you scroll horizontally. This helps you maintain context and track data across wide tables. This feature is generally available (GA).

Feature

For more information, see Create and manage tags for Certificate Manager resources.

Feature

Compute Engine

Feature

Preview: To protect standard snapshots from accidental or malicious deletion, Compute Engine retains deleted snapshots in the recycle bin for three days before permanently erasing the snapshots.

For more information, see Retain deleted resources in the recycle bin.

Data Studio

Feature

Bulk styling

You can customize all series, dimensions, or metrics at once, or select an individual item to style it separately. Styles that you set for an individual item override styles that you set for all items.

For more information, see the Line chart and combo chart reference, Time series reference, and Table reference.

Feature

Connect to PostgreSQL (Private IP)

You can connect Data Studio to PostgreSQL databases on Cloud SQL by using a private IP address. Private IP connections keep your database traffic on a private network instead of the public internet.

For more information, see Connect to PostgreSQL.

Support for MySQL 5.6 and 5.7 in the MySQL connector is ending:

  • Creating new data sources that connect to MySQL 5.6 or 5.7 won't be possible after February 26, 2027.
  • Data sources or reports that use MySQL 5.6 or 5.7 might not properly load data after February 26, 2027.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.10.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Impact-aware PR delta scanning: Added --diff and --staged flags to cm find to audit modified pull request hunks and 1-hop neighbor files while suppressing pre-existing vulnerabilities.
  • SARIF report export and CI gating: Added SARIF v2.1.0 export (--format sarif, --output) and severity-based CI gating (--fail-on) to cm report to integrate scan results into CI/CD pipelines and code scanning tools.
  • Adaptive hybrid deep scanning: Added --deep and --deep-workers flags to cm find to combine deterministic file pruning, parallel package-batched analysis, and post-triage verification for higher vulnerability recall and precision.
  • Custom workspace directory: Added support for the CM_HOME environment variable to override the default ~/.codemender directory for configuration, local state (state.db), backups, and artifacts.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Required build and test validation (build.command) to succeed during cm fix before marking a patch as applied and a finding as fixed.
    • Stabilized vulnerability fingerprints across multiple scans and bound cm verify directly to the target finding ID to prevent duplicate findings.
    • Restored the configured session model automatically when reconnecting to an active session with cm session resume.
    • Updated cm verify to add .exploit to .gitignore before execution so cancelled verification sessions do not leave untracked proof-of-concept scripts.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Feature

GKE ambient networking is now available in Preview through an allowlist.

GKE ambient networking provides a simplified, sidecarless deployment model for a service mesh with Layer 4 capabilities. By moving proxy functionality to node-level components integrated into GKE Dataplane V2, ambient networking reduces resource overhead, eliminates workload restarts for proxy updates, and simplifies mesh lifecycle management.

The Preview release supports single-cluster Layer 4 mesh capabilities using the Gateway API, which includes mutual TLS (mTLS), service discovery, Layer 4 traffic management, and Layer 4 telemetry.

Announcement

Advanced reporting dashboards 6.14

We've released version 6.14 of the advanced reporting dashboards.

Feature

Two new tables in the Real-time Queue Monitoring - Calls dashboard: Today's Scheduled Calls and Upcoming Scheduled Calls

We've added two new tables to the Real-time Queue Monitoring - Calls dashboard: Today's Scheduled Calls and Upcoming Scheduled Calls. These tables display pending scheduled calls across your allowed scheduling window, regardless of when they were initially created. The tables provide actionable details for each scheduled call, including the time until the call is due, an overdue flag, and a direct CRM link to the scheduled call. With these tables, you can view your full schedule of pending callbacks to help you plan staffing.

For more information, see Queue monitoring dashboards.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue that caused delays when loading and refreshing real-time agent dashboards.

  • Fixed an issue where the Queue Group and Queue Name filters inflated agent counts by including historical, rather than just current, queue assignments. If you have alerts or thresholds based on the previously inflated counts, update them to reflect the new, accurate counts.

  • Fixed an issue where certain queues were incorrectly mapped or dropped entirely from Queue Group filter results.

  • Fixed an issue where the Is Inbound Call and Is Inbound Chat columns in the Live Agent Data table on the Real-time Agent Monitoring dashboard displayed inverted values, incorrectly showing No for inbound interactions and Yes for outbound. This update also standardizes how interaction direction is defined across all reports, ensuring accurate classification and filtering for API-dialed calls, scheduled callbacks, and direct inbound calls. Additionally, it introduces several enhancements to reporting dashboards to ensure accurate timezone formatting, correct CSAT population by direction, and proper queue time tracking for newer call types.

  • Fixed an issue where the Queue Time column of the Queued Calls tile in advanced reporting displayed inflated wait times for calls that re-entered a queue after being answered or transferred.

  • Fixed an issue where agents performing mandatory after-call work were incorrectly classified as "In-Call" instead of "Wrap-up" on real-time reporting dashboards. You can expect a decrease in active "In-Call" agent counts and a corresponding increase in "Wrap-up" statuses across your live monitoring views. This change only affects dashboard reporting and doesn't affect agent routing or historical data. No action is required.

  • Fixed an issue where the SLA Target on the Real-time Channel Performance dashboards appeared blank for queues with no recent activity or when filters matched no configured queues.

  • Fixed an issue where the Missed Interactions dashboards double-counted declined calls and inflated missed chat volumes by incorrectly including agent response-time alerts. You can expect chat volumes to drop and average missed chat time to rise.

  • Fixed an issue where selecting the Subtotals option for call queue metrics for a Look returned an error.

  • Fixed an issue in downloadable call and chat history reports where French-language calls incorrectly appeared under English queue names.

  • Fixed an issue where scheduled calls disappeared from real-time reporting dashboards 12 hours after their creation, which caused the metric to undercount the total number of upcoming scheduled calls.

  • Fixed an issue where filter options for agent and team data in advanced reporting dashboards weren't correctly scoped to the user's assigned permissions.

  • Fixed an issue where the Agents monitoring page became unresponsive when displaying large numbers of agents, causing significant latency when navigating to other pages.

  • Fixed an issue that caused the following problems with raw data exports:

    • Poor export performance due to inefficient database queries.

    • In the call_recordings export, the url field incorrectly contained a timestamp instead of the actual recording URL.

    The url field now contains the correct recording URL, and the timestamp has been moved to a newly added updated_at field. If you ingest call_recordings data using a fixed schema, update your data mappings to accommodate these changes.

Backup and DR

Security

Note: These fixes and updates are available starting with Backup and DR release 11.0.17.496. These fixes are not rolled out to the 11.0.16 release; we recommend upgrading the backup/recovery appliance to version 11.0.17 to receive these updates.

Security Bulletin – Appliance:

  • Addressed multiple input sanitization vulnerabilities, including SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS), across appliance platform server utilities.
  • Remediated an authorization and validation vulnerability in user management workflows.

Security Bulletin – Host Agent:

  • Strengthened local RPC interface access controls and improved credential isolation between concurrent backup jobs on the Host Agent.
  • Hardened database layer against command injection, path traversal, and unauthorized directory permission modifications.
  • Remediated local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Oracle and SAP HANA host agent environment and profile handling.
  • Improved temporary file creation and link handling across Windows and Linux Host Agents to mitigate symlink race conditions.
  • Addressed buffer overflow vulnerabilities in Linux Host Agent components.

Libraries Bugs (Appliance):

  • Upgraded third-party runtime and application libraries (including Go and Java packages such as Netty and Jackson Databind) on the appliance management server.
  • Updated the Linux kernel and base operating system packages across Backup and DR appliance virtual machine images to mitigate reported vulnerabilities.

Fixed

Note: These fixes and updates are available starting with Backup and DR release 11.0.17.496. These fixes are not rolled out to the 11.0.16 release; we recommend upgrading the backup/recovery appliance to version 11.0.17 to receive these updates.

These issues have been resolved for the Host Agent:

  • Resolved an issue where Oracle ASM backups failed with the error "Failed to create ASM staging disk group".
  • Resolved an issue causing Oracle RAC database restores to fail with error 6407 due to invalid node names in the nodelist.
  • Fixed a PostgreSQL backup failure during snapshot preparation where the database user lacked execute permissions on pg_backup_start.
  • Corrected an issue where the Oracle mount process was unable to locate the undo catalog configuration file.
  • Improved Oracle backup metadata processing to support databases containing a large volume of datafiles.
  • Resolved an issue where discovery of SAP Sybase instances failed when multiple instances were configured under different user accounts.
  • Fixed an issue causing PostgreSQL database discovery to fail during host agent discovery workflows.
  • Resolved an issue that prevented successful discovery of MySQL database applications.

Change

Note: These fixes and updates are available starting with Backup and DR release 11.0.17.496. These fixes are not rolled out to the 11.0.16 release; we recommend upgrading the backup/recovery appliance to version 11.0.17 to receive these updates.

Non-Breaking Changes (Host Agent):

  • Modernized host agent database integration scripts for IBM Db2, MySQL, MariaDB, SAP Sybase IQ, and MaxDB to standard Bash execution for improved stability and security hardening.

Feature

Note: These fixes and updates are available starting with Backup and DR release 11.0.17.496. These fixes are not rolled out to the 11.0.16 release; we recommend upgrading the backup/recovery appliance to version 11.0.17 to receive these updates.

These features are now available for the Host Agent:

Gemini Enterprise: Configure granular access controls for apps and data stores

Administrators can configure granular, resource-level Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to restrict access to specific Gemini Enterprise apps and data stores using the Google Cloud console, the Google Cloud CLI, or the REST API.

Feature

Configure streaming for LLM responses and other traffic

You can now create API Gateway gateways that stream requests and responses instead of buffering them. This Public Preview feature supports incremental response delivery over HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 chunked transfer encoding, Server-Sent Events (SSE), WebSockets, and gRPC bidirectional streaming. A common use is streaming token-by-token responses from a large language model (LLM).

To enable streaming, create a gateway with the --enable-streaming flag. The streaming mode is fixed when you create the gateway and can't be changed later.

For more information, see Configure streaming for LLM responses and other traffic.

API hub now includes Service type, a system attribute that classifies an API as Code, Model, Agent, or Skill. Service type describes what a service is. API style describes how you call it. Use Service type to find and govern your APIs, agents, models, and skills.

Set Service type when you register or edit an API. To show only your agents, filter the API list by Service type, or select the new Agent chip. In the API, use the service_type field.

This feature is Generally Available (GA). For more information, see Supported system attributes.

Feature

AI performance and Tool performance dashboards in API insights

API insights in API hub now includes two dashboards for AI and agent traffic:

  • AI performance reports token usage and model latency for the large language models called through your gateways, with filters for model and provider.
  • Tool performance reports traffic, throughput, payload sizes, and latency for your Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, with filters for MCP server, deployment, and tool name.

For more information, see API insights dashboards.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.17.1

On September 30, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.17.1.

  • For information on upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version v1.17.1.
  • For information on new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release: The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch via the Helm chart automatically updates the images. No manual image changes are typically needed. For information on container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Feature

External Cassandra datastore support

Apigee hybrid v1.17.1 adds support for connecting an Apigee hybrid runtime to a Cassandra datastore that runs in a separate Kubernetes cluster (external datastore mode). In external datastore mode, the runtime cluster runs with cassandra.replicaCount: 0 (no local Cassandra pods) and connects to the remote Cassandra ring using the cassandra.properties.externalHost property (a comma-separated list of remote Cassandra IP addresses) and the optional cassandra.properties.externalEndpointsSync property for dynamic endpoint synchronization.

For more information, see Use an external Cassandra datastore and Configuration property reference.

Change

The Apigee operator's Kubernetes manager role now includes the core endpoints permission.

In v1.17.1, the Apigee operator's manager role is granted the core ("" API group) endpoints resource, with the verbs get, list, watch, create, update, patch, and delete. This role is the namespaced apigee-manager-role Kubernetes Role created by default in the apigee namespace. The operator needs this permission for the external (cross-cluster) Cassandra datastore feature: when a datastore uses an external host, the operator directly manages the Endpoints object of the selectorless Kubernetes Service that fronts it.

This permission is granted to all v1.17.1 installations, whether or not you use an external datastore. It is added to the operator's manager role and is not gated on any configuration property, so security teams that audit operator permissions should expect it after upgrading. Because the grant is on a namespaced Role, the new access is limited to the Apigee namespace and does not extend cluster-wide.

Most installations require no action. The apigee-operator Helm chart defines this role, so running helm upgrade on the apigee-operator chart grants the permission automatically.

If you self-manage the Apigee operator's Kubernetes RBAC, meaning you prevent Helm from creating or updating the operator's Role objects, add the endpoints resource to the existing core ("") API group rule of the apigee-manager-role Role in the Apigee namespace, or append the following rule:

- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["endpoints"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]

If you self-manage the operator's RBAC, add this permission before you upgrade to v1.17.1. If you have already upgraded without this permission, apply the update to your role configuration to ensure proper operator functionality. Without this permission, the operator cannot manage the Endpoints object of an external datastore, so the external datastore feature does not work. If you do not use an external datastore, the operator works without this permission.

Note: The ao.args.disableManagedClusterRoles property does not apply to this change. That property governs only ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding objects, whereas this permission is added to a namespaced Role.

Bug ID Description
565753858 Fixed an issue where the apigee-mcp-server controller dropped pod-level volumes configured on the mcpServer component (such as fwi-token volumes when Federated Workload Identity is enabled), causing ReplicaSet creation to fail.
565072374 Fixed an issue where VerifyJWT policies using a JWKS uriRef could return steps.jwt.NoMatchingPublicKey on the first request after the 5-minute JWKS cache TTL expired when the identity provider rotated keys. The cache now refreshes synchronously upon expiration.
564969400 Fixed an issue where variables initialized from an empty <Value/> element in AssignMessage (AssignVariable) were not treated as empty strings when referenced in message template functions such as replaceAll.
563557547 Fixed an issue where EventFlow (Server-Sent Events) could coalesce multiple events into a single policy invocation under burst traffic on the http-adaptor datapath, producing malformed SSE responses.
560372165 Fixed a synchronizer readiness-gate deadlock that could leave a Message Processor on an older contract revision and return 404 ApplicationNotFound for newly deployed standard proxies.
560130499 Fixed a security issue by hardening the JavaCallout policy sandbox.
558888960 Fixed an issue in distributed tracing where the target URL was omitted from outbound target request span attributes after a request-flow policy step executed.
