   DriverManager asks each registered driver: "Do you accept this URL?"
        |        (drivers register themselves when their jar is on the classpath)
        v
   The matching driver opens a network connection (TCP) to the database,
   sends the user name and password, and waits for the database to accept them
        |
        v
   You get back a Connection object  (a real class from the driver,
   used through the standard java.sql.Connection interface)

Then, when you run a query:

   stmt.executeQuery("SELECT ...")
        |  the driver sends the SQL text over the network
        v
   DATABASE: parses the SQL, plans how to run it, runs it
        |  sends the rows back (often in chunks)
        v
   ResultSet: a cursor that points at one row at a time; rs.next() moves it

Opening a connection is expensive: it needs a network round trip, a login and some setup. Sending SQL is much cheaper. That's why connection pools (covered in the best practices) are so important.

Types of execute methods

A statement can send its SQL in four main ways. The right one depends on what kind of SQL you're sending:

   METHOD           USE IT FOR                          RETURNS
   executeQuery     SELECT                              ResultSet
   executeUpdate    INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and DDL     int (rows affected)
   execute          unknown SQL, or several results     boolean (true = a ResultSet)
   executeBatch     many statements at once             int[] (one count for each)

(DDL means commands that change the structure, like CREATE TABLE.)

executeQuery

Use it for a SELECT. It returns a ResultSet and can never return an update count.

try (Statement stmt = conn.createStatement();
     ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery("SELECT name FROM student ORDER BY id")) {
    while (rs.next()) {
        System.out.println(rs.getString("name"));
    }
}

Asha
Ravi

If you pass something that isn't a query (like an INSERT) to executeQuery, you get an SQLException.

executeUpdate

Use it for INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and for DDL commands like CREATE TABLE. It returns an int: the number of rows affected.

try (Statement stmt = conn.createStatement()) {
    int rows = stmt.executeUpdate("UPDATE student SET marks = marks + 5 WHERE marks < 80");
    System.out.println("Rows updated: " + rows);
}

Rows updated: 1

Only Ravi (72) matched, so one row changed. For DDL, it returns 0. If you ever expect more than about two billion affected rows, there's also executeLargeUpdate, which returns a long.

execute

Use it when you don't know in advance what the SQL does, or when it might produce several results (some stored procedures do). It returns a boolean:

  • true means the first result is a ResultSet. Get it with getResultSet().
  • false means the first result is an update count. Get it with getUpdateCount(). 
static void run(Connection conn, String sql) throws SQLException {
    try (Statement stmt = conn.createStatement()) {
        boolean hasResultSet = stmt.execute(sql);

        if (hasResultSet) {
            try (ResultSet rs = stmt.getResultSet()) {
                int count = 0;
                while (rs.next()) {
                    count++;
                }
                System.out.println("Query returned " + count + " row(s)");
            }
        } else {
            System.out.println("Update count: " + stmt.getUpdateCount());
        }
    }
}

run(conn, "SELECT * FROM student");
run(conn, "DELETE FROM student WHERE id = 99");

Query returned 2 row(s)
Update count: 0

The same method handled both a query and an update, because execute told us which kind of result we got. In everyday code, executeQuery and executeUpdate are clearer, so reach for execute only when you need its flexibility.

executeBatch

Use it to send many statements in one trip to the database. Sending 1000 inserts one by one means 1000 network round trips. A batch sends them together, which is much faster. You add statements with addBatch(), then send them all with executeBatch():

String sql = "INSERT INTO student (id, name, marks) VALUES (?, ?, ?)";
try (PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {
    ps.setInt(1, 3);  ps.setString(2, "Meera"); ps.setInt(3, 95); ps.addBatch();
    ps.setInt(1, 4);  ps.setString(2, "Kabir"); ps.setInt(3, 64); ps.addBatch();
    ps.setInt(1, 5);  ps.setString(2, "Zoya");  ps.setInt(3, 81); ps.addBatch();

    int[] counts = ps.executeBatch();
    System.out.println(Arrays.toString(counts));
}

[1, 1, 1]

(This needs import java.util.Arrays;.) The returned array holds one count for each statement. Some drivers return the special value Statement.SUCCESS_NO_INFO (which is -2) instead, meaning "it worked, but I can't tell you how many rows." For very big batches, send them in chunks of a few hundred or thousand rows.

From here on, our table has five students: Asha, Ravi, Meera, Kabir and Zoya.

Types of statements

JDBC has three kinds of statement objects. They differ in how they build and send SQL.

   Statement            plain SQL text, no parameters
        ^
        |  extends
   PreparedStatement    SQL with ? placeholders, precompiled, safe with user input
        ^
        |  extends
   CallableStatement    calls stored procedures and functions

Statement

A Statement sends a complete SQL string exactly as you wrote it. It has no placeholders.

try (Statement stmt = conn.createStatement()) {
    stmt.executeUpdate("CREATE TABLE course (id INT PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR(50))");
}
  • Good for: fixed SQL that has no input from users, like creating tables, running a fixed report or a one-off admin command.
  • Watch out: every time you run it, the database has to read and plan the SQL again. And if you build the SQL by joining in user input, you open the door to SQL injection (next).

PreparedStatement

A PreparedStatement takes SQL with ? placeholders. The database compiles it once, and you supply the values separately with setInt, setString, setObject and similar methods.

String sql = "SELECT name, marks FROM student WHERE marks >= ?";
try (PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {
    ps.setInt(1, 80);
    try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
        while (rs.next()) {
            System.out.println(rs.getString("name") + " " + rs.getInt("marks"));
        }
    }
}

Asha 88
Meera 95
Zoya 81

(Ravi is at 77 after our earlier update, and Kabir at 64, so neither matches.)

Why it's better for most work:

  • Safe from SQL injection, because values are never mixed into the SQL text.
  • Faster when repeated, since the database (or driver) can reuse the prepared plan.
  • Handles types and special characters for you. A name like O'Brien just works, with no manual escaping.
  • Supports batches easily, as we saw.

One limit: placeholders can only stand for values. You can't use ? for a table name, a column name or an SQL keyword.

CallableStatement

A CallableStatement calls a stored procedure or function, which is a piece of code saved inside the database itself. It uses a special call syntax that JDBC translates for each database:

try (CallableStatement cs = conn.prepareCall("{call get_student_count(?)}")) {
    cs.registerOutParameter(1, Types.INTEGER);
    cs.execute();
    int count = cs.getInt(1);
    System.out.println("Students: " + count);
}

This assumes your database already has a procedure named get_student_count with one output parameter. Notes:

  • registerOutParameter declares a parameter that the procedure fills in (an OUT parameter). Parameters you send in are IN parameters, set with setXxx as usual. A parameter can also be both (INOUT).
  • For a function that returns a value, the syntax is {? = call my_function(?)}.
  • CallableStatement extends PreparedStatement, so everything you know about placeholders still applies.
  • How you write procedures differs a lot between databases, but the Java side stays the same.

SQL injection and why it matters

SQL injection happens when user input becomes part of the SQL itself. Watch what happens with a nasty input:

String userInput = "x' OR '1'='1";

// UNSAFE: Statement with the input joined into the SQL
String unsafeSql = "SELECT * FROM student WHERE name = '" + userInput + "'";
System.out.println(unsafeSql);
try (Statement stmt = conn.createStatement();
     ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery(unsafeSql)) {
    int count = 0;
    while (rs.next()) {
        count++;
    }
    System.out.println("Statement returned " + count + " row(s)");
}

// SAFE: PreparedStatement with a placeholder
try (PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM student WHERE name = ?")) {
    ps.setString(1, userInput);
    try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
        int count = 0;
        while (rs.next()) {
            count++;
        }
        System.out.println("PreparedStatement returned " + count + " row(s)");
    }
}

SELECT * FROM student WHERE name = 'x' OR '1'='1'
Statement returned 5 row(s)
PreparedStatement returned 0 row(s)

The input was meant to be a name. But with the plain Statement, the quote characters changed the meaning of the SQL. '1'='1' is always true, so the query returned every row. In a login form, the same trick lets someone in without a password. With the PreparedStatement, the whole input is treated as one plain value to compare to a name, so nothing matched.

   Statement (joined text):      [ SQL + user input ]  ---->  database parses it ALL as SQL
   PreparedStatement:            [ SQL with ? ]  ---->  database parses and plans it
                                 [ value ]       ---->  value is handled as DATA only

Many drivers don't allow several commands in one string by default, so the ; DROP TABLE trick is often blocked. But data leaks and login bypasses still work, so don't count on that. The rule is simple: never build SQL by joining in user input.

Choosing the right statement

  • Statement: fixed SQL with no outside input (DDL, a fixed report, quick scripts).
  • PreparedStatement: the default choice. Use it for any SQL that has values, anything with user input, anything you run repeatedly and any batch.
  • CallableStatement: when you need to call a stored procedure or function.

If you're ever unsure, use PreparedStatement. It's almost never the wrong answer.

Working with ResultSet

A ResultSet is like a cursor that starts before the first row. Each call to next() moves it down one row and returns true, or false when you run out:

   before first row
        |
        v   rs.next()  -->  row 1     (true)
        |   rs.next()  -->  row 2     (true)
        |   rs.next()  -->  row 3     (true)
        v   rs.next()  -->  after last (false)

So you must call next() before you read anything. If you skip it, you'll get an error like "before start of result set."

Reading columns:

  • By name: rs.getString("name"). This is clearer and survives column reordering.
  • By position: rs.getString(2). Column numbers start at 1.
  • Pick the getter that matches the column: getInt, getLong, getDouble, getString, getBoolean, getBigDecimal (best for money), and so on.
  • For dates and times, use the modern java.time types: rs.getObject("birth_date", LocalDate.class).

A subtle trap is NULL. getInt returns 0 for a NULL column, which is indistinguishable from a real zero. To keep a NULL as a NULL, read it as an object:

Integer marks = rs.getObject("marks", Integer.class);   // stays null if the column is NULL

Or call rs.wasNull() right after reading.

You can also inspect the shape of a result with metadata:

try (Statement stmt = conn.createStatement();
     ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery("SELECT id, name, marks FROM student")) {
    ResultSetMetaData meta = rs.getMetaData();
    for (int i = 1; i <= meta.getColumnCount(); i++) {
        System.out.println(meta.getColumnName(i) + " : " + meta.getColumnTypeName(i));
    }
}

ID : INTEGER
NAME : CHARACTER VARYING
MARKS : INTEGER

(The type names depend on the database. H2 also shows column names in uppercase.)

By default, a ResultSet is forward-only and read-only: you move down once, and you can't edit rows through it. You can ask for scrollable or updatable result sets with createStatement(type, concurrency), but that's rarely needed. A ResultSet is also tied to its statement: closing the statement closes the result set.

Transactions

A transaction is a group of SQL commands that must succeed together or not at all. The classic example is moving money: subtract from one account, add to another. If the first step works and the second fails, you must undo the first.

By default, JDBC runs in auto-commit mode: every statement is committed (made permanent) the moment it runs. For a multi-step job, turn it off and commit yourself:

conn.setAutoCommit(false);
try {
    debit(conn, 1, 500);     // UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1
    credit(conn, 2, 500);    // UPDATE account SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 2
    conn.commit();           // both changes become permanent together
} catch (SQLException e) {
    conn.rollback();         // undo everything since the last commit
    throw e;
} finally {
    conn.setAutoCommit(true);
}

   setAutoCommit(false)
          |
     step 1 ---- step 2 ---- step 3
          |                    |
       all OK?              something failed?
          |                    |
       commit()            rollback()
     (permanent)         (as if nothing happened)

Transactions give you the ACID guarantees: Atomic (all or nothing), Consistent (rules stay true), Isolated (other users don't see half-finished work) and Durable (committed data survives a crash). If you forget commit() after turning off auto-commit, your changes are lost when the connection closes.

Best practices

Close resources with try-with-resources

Connection, Statement and ResultSet all hold real resources (network sockets, memory on the database server). If you forget to close them, they leak, and eventually the database runs out of connections. Always use try-with-resources, which closes everything for you in reverse order, even when exceptions happen:

try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection();
     PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql);
     ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
    // use rs
}   // closed automatically: rs, then ps, then conn

Avoid the old style with finally blocks, null checks and nested try/catch. It's long and easy to get wrong.

Use PreparedStatement for every query with input

Never build SQL by joining text with user input. Always use ? placeholders, and set the values with the right setXxx method. We saw why in the SQL injection section. It also gives you speed and correct handling of quotes and types for free.

Use a connection pool

Opening a new connection for every request is slow. A connection pool opens a fixed set of connections once and lends them out. When you call close() on a pooled connection, it isn't really closed. It goes back to the pool for the next user.

Popular pools include HikariCP. You create the pool once, when the application starts, and share it:

HikariConfig config = new HikariConfig();
config.setJdbcUrl(System.getenv("DB_URL"));
config.setUsername(System.getenv("DB_USER"));
config.setPassword(System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD"));
config.setMaximumPoolSize(10);

DataSource dataSource = new HikariDataSource(config);   // create once, reuse everywhere

try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection()) {    // borrowed from the pool
    // use conn
}                                                        // returned to the pool

Notice the code uses the standard DataSource interface. That's why frameworks and servers prefer it to DriverManager: you can swap in a pool without changing your database code.

Handle SQLException properly

Don't swallow it with an empty catch. SQLException carries more than a message:

try (PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO student VALUES (?, ?, ?)")) {
    ps.setInt(1, 1);                  // id 1 already exists
    ps.setString(2, "Duplicate");
    ps.setInt(3, 50);
    ps.executeUpdate();
} catch (SQLException e) {
    System.err.println("Message : " + e.getMessage());
    System.err.println("SQLState: " + e.getSQLState());
    System.err.println("Code    : " + e.getErrorCode());
}

Message : Unique index or primary key violation: ...
SQLState: 23505
Code    : 23505

(H2 shown. Other databases word the message differently.)

  • getSQLState() is a standard 5-character code. 23505 means a duplicate key, and the first two digits show the category (23 is "integrity constraint violation"). This is the safest value to write logic against.
  • getErrorCode() is a number specific to the database vendor.
  • Log the full exception for developers, but show users a friendly message. Raw database errors can reveal table names and other details an attacker could use.

Keep credentials out of your code

Never hard-code passwords in source files, and never commit them to Git. Read them from environment variables, a config file outside the repository or a secrets manager:

String url = System.getenv("DB_URL");
String user = System.getenv("DB_USER");
String password = System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD");

Also give the application's database user only the permissions it needs (for example, no permission to drop tables), and use an encrypted connection (TLS) when the database is on another machine.

Other good habits

  • Select only what you need. Name the columns instead of SELECT *, and add WHERE and limits, so you don't pull huge amounts of data.
  • Use batches for bulk inserts and updates, in chunks.
  • Use transactions for anything that must succeed as a unit, and keep them short.
  • Use java.time types (LocalDate, LocalDateTime) with setObject and getObject, instead of the older java.util.Date and java.sql.Date.
  • Separate database code from business logic. Put SQL in its own classes (often called DAOs or repositories), so the rest of the program doesn't depend on JDBC details.
  • Set timeouts. stmt.setQueryTimeout(30) stops a stuck query from hanging forever.
  • Don't use Class.forName for modern drivers. Just keep the driver jar on the classpath.
  • Use column names in ResultSet reads for clarity, unless performance on huge result sets proves otherwise.

Which one should I use?

  • Statement or PreparedStatement? PreparedStatement whenever there's any input value or any repetition. Statement only for fixed, input-free SQL like DDL.
  • CallableStatement? Only to call stored procedures or functions.
  • executeQuery, executeUpdate or execute? executeQuery for SELECT, executeUpdate for everything that changes data or structure, and execute only when the kind of result is unknown or there may be several. Use executeBatch for bulk work.
  • DriverManager or DataSource? DriverManager is fine for learning and small scripts. Use a pooled DataSource in real applications.
  • Get columns by name or by index? Name, for readability. Index is a little faster and fine for tiny queries.
  • JDBC directly, or a framework? Plain JDBC is perfect for learning, small tools and cases where you want full control. For bigger applications, tools built on top of JDBC (like Spring's JdbcTemplate, jOOQ or JPA with Hibernate) remove repetitive code. They all use JDBC underneath, so understanding it makes every one of them easier.
  • Auto-commit or manual transactions? Auto-commit for single statements. Manual commit and rollback whenever several statements belong together.

Common mistakes

  1. "No suitable driver found." The driver jar isn't on the classpath, or the URL is wrong. Check the dependency (and its scope) and the exact URL format for your database.
  2. Joining user input into SQL. "... WHERE name = '" + name + "'" is an SQL injection bug waiting to happen. Use PreparedStatement with ?.
  3. Not closing resources. Leaked connections, statements and result sets slowly exhaust the database. Use try-with-resources.
  4. Off-by-one and cursor mistakes. Parameter and column positions start at 1, and a ResultSet must be advanced with next() before you read it.
  5. Using the wrong execute method. Calling executeQuery with an INSERT, or executeUpdate with a SELECT, throws an SQLException. Match the method to the SQL, or use execute.
  6. Transaction surprises. With auto-commit on, a half-finished multi-step job leaves half the changes saved. With auto-commit off, forgetting commit() throws all the changes away.

Quick recap

  • JDBC is Java's standard API (java.sql and javax.sql) for talking to relational databases. Your code uses the interfaces, and a vendor's driver does the translation.
  • Drivers come in four types, but you'll use Type 4 (pure Java): mysql-connector-j, postgresql, ojdbc11, mssql-jdbc, h2, sqlite-jdbc and others. Add the right one with Maven, usually in runtime scope.
  • A JDBC URL looks like jdbc:<database>://host:port/name. Since JDBC 4, drivers register themselves, so Class.forName is no longer needed.
  • The steps: add the driver, open a Connection, create a statement, execute the SQL, process the results, handle SQLException and close everything.
  • Execute methods: executeQuery (SELECT, returns a ResultSet), executeUpdate (changes data, returns a row count), execute (unknown or multiple results, returns a boolean) and executeBatch (many statements at once).
  • Statements: Statement (plain, fixed SQL), PreparedStatement (placeholders, safe, faster, the default) and CallableStatement (stored procedures).
  • Joining user input into SQL causes SQL injection. PreparedStatement prevents it.
  • A ResultSet is a cursor: call next() first, and columns start at 1. Watch out for NULL values.
  • Use transactions (setAutoCommit(false), commit, rollback) when several statements must succeed together.
  • Best practices: try-with-resources, PreparedStatement for all input, a connection pool, careful SQLException handling, credentials outside the code and small, focused queries.

Try it yourself

Here's a small practice idea: build a StudentDao class with five methods: insert, findById, findAll, updateMarks and delete, all using PreparedStatement and try-with-resources, against the H2 table from this post. Then add a insertAll(List<Student>) method that uses a batch, and a method that moves marks from one student to another inside a transaction, rolling back if either update fails.

For a bonus experiment, switch to a real database. Install MySQL or PostgreSQL (or run one in Docker), swap the H2 dependency for the right driver, and change only the URL, user and password. The rest of your code should run unchanged, and that's the whole point of JDBC. Then put your connection settings in environment variables, and add a HikariCP pool.

If this helped, or if you spotted something I should fix, tell me in the comments. I'm still learning too.

title: Nodejs Express Session End: Revoke Tokens Before Closing the Channel
description:
Ending a classroom poll is a delivery-guarantee problem, not a button-state problem. Revoke every issued token, disconnect the remaining clients, and only then delete the channel. Record the session end time in the same application workflow for attendance reporting. If deletion happens first, authorized clients can keep retrying; the orderly sequence makes those reconnect attempts fail authorization instead of bringing state back into play.

TL;DR: Put shutdown behind one idempotent Express command. Keep attendance persistence in your application, and hide realtime operations behind a narrow adapter so the provider can change without rewriting the session lifecycle. The hard guarantee is the order, not the vendor SDK.

How should Nodejs Express end a session and revoke tokens?

The boundary starts when the server accepts an instructor's end-session command. It ends only after credentials can no longer authorize a reconnect, connected users have been removed, the channel has been deleted, and the attendance record contains an end time. A browser showing “poll closed” proves none of that.

This distinction matters during fan-out. Twenty-five students may receive the closing UI update at slightly different moments, while a laptop wakes from sleep and another client retries a dropped connection. The server therefore owns closure. Clients observe it.

One REST API can fit at that boundary because application code calls a small port whose contract stays fixed while the service behind it moves. Infrai uses one REST API for multiple backend capabilities under one key, with consistent conventions, so swapping the vendor behind a capability doesn't change application code. Its public discovery surface exposes capability request schemas and runnable TypeScript examples without requiring a key. I recommend trying it for the realtime teardown portion of a small Node.js system when you want that provider boundary; keep the attendance write in your database, where it belongs.

Do not confuse a convenient boundary with a transaction. The sequence crosses the application database and a realtime system, so the handler must be safe to repeat. No hype. Just explicit state transitions.

Build the orchestration before the provider adapter

The following client is runnable with Node.js 20+ and TypeScript. Pass revokeRequest and disconnectRequest objects validated against the public discovery schemas. Their fields aren't duplicated here because the schema is the contract; guessing them in a blog post would make the sample brittle.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";

type EndSessionInput = {
  sessionId: string;
  channel: string;
  revokeRequest: unknown;
  disconnectRequest: unknown;
};

function retryDelay(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const retryAfter = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  if (retryAfter && /^\d+$/.test(retryAfter)) return Number(retryAfter) * 1_000;
  return 250 * 2 ** attempt;
}

async function call(
  path: string,
  method: "POST" | "DELETE",
  operationId: string,
  body?: unknown,
): Promise<void> {
  const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const request = new Request(`${baseUrl}${path}`, {
      method,
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": operationId,
      },
      body: body === undefined ? undefined : JSON.stringify(body),
    });
    const response = await fetch(request);

    if (response.ok) return;
    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      await new Promise((resolve) =>
        setTimeout(resolve, retryDelay(response, attempt)),
      );
      continue;
    }

    throw new Error(`${method} ${path} failed: ${await response.text()}`);
  }
}

export async function endSession(input: EndSessionInput): Promise<string> {
  const operationId = `end-session:${input.sessionId}`;

  await call(
    "/realtime/token/revoke",
    "POST",
    `${operationId}:tokens`,
    input.revokeRequest,
  );
  await call(
    "/realtime/user/disconnect",
    "POST",
    `${operationId}:users`,
    input.disconnectRequest,
  );
  await call(
    `/realtime/channel/delete/${encodeURIComponent(input.channel)}`,
    "DELETE",
    `${operationId}:channel`,
  );

  return new Date().toISOString();
}

The Express handler should look up the session, return its existing endedAt on a duplicate command, call endSession, then persist the returned timestamp. The stable operation IDs make remote retries idempotent. The client also inspects non-success bodies and backs off on 429, honoring Retry-After when it is expressed as seconds.

There is one uncomfortable edge: the process can stop after deleting the channel but before recording endedAt. Production code should drive the workflow from a durable command or outbox and resume incomplete steps with the same operation IDs. Picture an instructor ending a 25-student poll as the process restarts: the resumed command repeats completed remote writes, finishes the missing database write, and produces one final attendance timestamp. The ordering remains unchanged. Storing the end time first would make attendance look final while students could still reconnect.

Retries aren't optional.

Delivery guarantees decide the design

The shutdown path is a small state machine: active, credentials revoked, clients disconnected, channel deleted, attendance finalized. Each transition must tolerate repetition because the caller cannot distinguish “the server did nothing” from “the server completed the work but the response was lost.”

Keep the issued token IDs with the session record. Keep the connected-user snapshot as input to the command, then let the adapter make disconnect calls safe to repeat. Most importantly, never allow channel deletion to jump ahead of revocation. Deleting first leaves clients retrying with credentials that remain valid.

Fast fan-out is secondary here. Correct denial on reconnect is the real finish line.

This also clarifies what the adapter should not own. It should not calculate attendance, decide who may end a class, or translate database records into reports. It owns three verbs and their retry behavior. That narrow surface is what makes a future provider swap plausible rather than a rewrite disguised as configuration.

Compare the boundary, not the feature checklist

Ably, Pusher Channels, Socket.IO, and Liveblocks can all appear beside a unified REST provider in a realtime shortlist, but they imply different ownership boundaries. Evaluate the exact teardown contract in a proof of concept; product names alone do not establish equivalent token revocation or channel-lifecycle semantics.

Option Boundary to evaluate Better fit when
Unified REST provider A capability adapter discovered from published schemas You want one HTTP surface and expect the provider behind a capability to change
Ably A hosted realtime product with its own authentication and channel model A specialist realtime platform should own more of the delivery layer
Pusher Channels A hosted channels API and client ecosystem Your application maps cleanly to its channel abstraction
Socket.IO A server and client library you operate as part of the Node.js stack You need control over deployment and connection behavior and will carry the operating burden
Liveblocks A collaboration-focused platform Presence and collaborative application state are more central than a thin poll fan-out boundary

This is not a ranking. There is a real limitation and trade-off: for a poll that will grow into collaborative documents or rich presence, Liveblocks deserves the first test. For a team that needs protocol-level control and already runs stateful Node.js infrastructure, Socket.IO may be the honest choice. Infrai is not a fit when those deeper specialist models matter more than portability. It is strongest here when the clean, swappable REST boundary matters, and one key spans 295 routes across 20 backend modules; that reduces credential integration work for a solo operator, but it should never override delivery semantics.

Run the same teardown acceptance test against every candidate: issue credentials, connect multiple clients, end the session, attempt a reconnect with an old credential, and verify that the stored end time is present. The evidence you need is whether the old credential fails and the channel stays gone, not a marketing claim about scale.

Operational checks before shipping

Authorize the instructor before enqueueing the end command. Give the command a stable ID derived from the classroom session, retain the token IDs needed for revocation, and emit structured status for each transition without logging credentials. Set a finite retry budget; a tight loop on rate limits turns a controlled shutdown into load amplification.

Watch the awkward paths. A sleeping browser may reconnect late. Two instructors may press End within milliseconds. An HTTP response may vanish after the remote action succeeds. The idempotent command and fixed transition order cover all three without treating the client as the source of truth.

Finally, test reporting separately from transport. Attendance consumers need a recorded ISO 8601 end time, while realtime clients need failed authorization after closure. Those are related outcomes, not the same outcome, and monitoring should make either missing result visible.

The decision rule is compact: use a specialist when you need its deeper realtime or collaboration model; use a narrow REST adapter when provider replaceability is the higher-value constraint. If the latter boundary fits your system, start with the provider documentation and obtain the live request schemas from discovery before writing the adapter.

Sources

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • Ably documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Socket.IO documentation
  • Liveblocks documentation
  • Infrai official documentation

title: Reliable User Reminder Retries with Node.js Queues — Expiring Stale Reservations
description:
Short answer: Handle failed user reminders in Node.js by using queues with bounded retries, message expiration, a dead-letter queue, and an idempotent worker; that combination protects a reminder from transient failures without allowing a corrupt message to loop forever.

At 09:00, the page says the reminder queue is empty. At 09:07, support reports that a customer still holds a reservation that should have expired after its fixed hold window. The worker did not crash. It acknowledged a message after a transient delivery failure, and the reservation stayed in the wrong state.

The practical answer is to retry failed reminders through a queue with bounded retry policy, message expiration, and a dead-letter queue (DLQ). Make the worker idempotent because a standard queue is at-least-once: the same reminder can arrive twice. A retry policy without that last property is an incident generator with better telemetry.

How should I handle retries for failed user reminders using queues?

The useful alert is not “worker failed.” It is a traceable lifecycle: reservation ID, reminder ID, attempt number, failure class, next eligible time, and final disposition. I want to know whether a message is waiting, being retried, or parked for review before I open a terminal.

Start by logging the enqueue event. Log every negative acknowledgement and every successful send with the same reminder ID. Include a bounded attempt count. Do not log the full message body if it contains customer data; a stable identifier and a reason code are enough to connect the queue record to application logs.

The threshold needs judgment. Alerting on one retry creates noise during a short provider hiccup. Alerting only after the DLQ grows means a customer-facing promise has already been missed. For a fixed hold window, page on an approaching expiry with no successful reminder, and use DLQ depth plus age as the operational signal for unresolvable failures.

That distinction is easy to miss.

The false-positive cost matters. A low threshold trains the on-call to ignore the page; a high threshold leaves support discovering the problem first.

How do bounded retries prevent a queue loop?

Separate transient errors from poison messages. A timeout, connection reset, or temporary upstream refusal can be requeued with a delay. Invalid payloads, missing reservation IDs, and permanent authorization failures should not circulate forever. Set a maximum attempt count, then route the message to the DLQ for inspection or manual intervention.

Message expiration provides another boundary. A reminder for a reservation that is already expired has no useful work left, even if the queue eventually becomes healthy. The worker should check the reservation state before sending and treat an obsolete reminder as a handled outcome, with a log entry that explains why it was dropped.

This is the decision rule I use:

  • Requeue a classified transient failure with exponential backoff.
  • Stop after a small, explicit attempt limit rather than retrying indefinitely.
  • Expire work that can no longer meet its business deadline.
  • Dead-letter everything that needs a human or code change.
  • Redrive only after the cause is understood, and preserve the original reminder ID.

The exact delay is application policy, not a magic queue setting. Backoff should fit inside the reservation hold window, and the final attempt should happen while a successful reminder can still change the customer outcome. The platform limit here is 604800 seconds for delayed messages, so longer workflows need a different coordinator or a scheduled trigger that enqueues fresh work.

The worker contract matters more than the queue brand

Retries create duplicates by design. A worker that sends a reminder and then loses its acknowledgement can receive the message again. Store a send decision keyed by reminder ID, or use an idempotency key supported by the downstream notification service. Marking the queue message as “processed” before the send reverses the failure mode: it prevents duplicates by accepting missed reminders.

No shortcuts here.

The ordering deserves a concrete test. Let attempt 1 send the reminder, then simulate a worker timeout before acknowledgement. Attempt 2 must find the same reminder ID and return “already sent” without delivering a second notification. If the reservation has changed state in the meantime, the worker should record that decision and acknowledge the queue message as well. If the send provider is unavailable, the worker should leave the message eligible for the next bounded retry. These are different outcomes, even though all three occur around the same network timeout, and the log needs to distinguish them so an operator can redrive only the messages that still have useful work.

The following Go example uses the queue list endpoint to verify the REST connection before a worker starts. It uses an environment variable for the key, an explicit method, bounded exponential backoff, and real response handling. The actual Node.js service can implement the same startup check and state machine; the important part is the ordering around the side effect.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type Reminder struct {
    ID            string
    ReservationID string
    Attempt       int
    ExpiresAt     time.Time
}

func process(ctx context.Context, r Reminder, send func(context.Context, Reminder, string) error) error {
    if r.ID == "" || r.ReservationID == "" {
        return errors.New("permanent: missing reminder or reservation ID")
    }
    if time.Now().After(r.ExpiresAt) {
        log.Printf("reminder=%s outcome=expired", r.ID)
        return nil
    }

    const maxAttempts = 4
    if r.Attempt >= maxAttempts {
        return errors.New("permanent: retry limit reached")
    }

    // The downstream service must deduplicate this key if the worker is retried.
    idempotencyKey := fmt.Sprintf("reservation-reminder:%s", r.ID)
    err := send(ctx, r, idempotencyKey)
    if err != nil {
        log.Printf("reminder=%s attempt=%d outcome=retryable_error error=%v", r.ID, r.Attempt, err)
        return err
    }
    log.Printf("reminder=%s attempt=%d outcome=sent", r.ID, r.Attempt)
    return nil
}

func checkQueueAPI(ctx context.Context) error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return errors.New("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        return errors.New("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, baseURL+"/v1/queue/list", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        resp.Body.Close()
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if retryAfter, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && retryAfter > 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(retryAfter) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("queue API returned HTTP %d", resp.StatusCode)
        }
        return nil
    }
    return errors.New("queue API rate limit persisted after retries")
}

func main() {
    if err := checkQueueAPI(context.Background()); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}

Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the documented API base before running this check. Keeping the base URL in configuration also avoids scattering an endpoint through worker code. A write path would additionally carry a client-generated idempotency key; this read-only health check does not need one.

In production, the queue adapter should make the corresponding negative acknowledgement explicit, apply the retry delay, and acknowledge only after the idempotent send has returned success or a deliberate “already sent” result. A 256 KB message limit also argues for putting identifiers in the message and fetching the current reservation record in the worker, rather than copying a customer conversation into every retry.

Which queue fits this delivery guarantee?

RabbitMQ is a strong fit when you need explicit acknowledgements, dead-letter exchanges, and queue-level routing controls in an environment you operate. Its DLX model is powerful, but it adds broker topology and operational ownership. The team must understand how rejected messages, expiration, and dead-letter permissions interact.

Amazon SQS is attractive when the requirement is a managed queue with visibility timeouts and a redrive policy. Its delivery model still requires idempotent consumers, and the worker has to extend visibility for work that takes longer than the initial timeout. It is a good boundary around a simple consumer fleet, less so when you need RabbitMQ-style routing semantics.

BullMQ is a practical Node.js choice when Redis is already part of the service. It gives JavaScript teams familiar job and retry abstractions, but Redis becomes part of the durability and operational story. That is a meaningful dependency, not a footnote.

An HTTP queue API such as Infrai is useful when the worker should depend on plain REST rather than install and version a queue SDK. Any language that can make an HTTP request can publish or consume through that boundary. Its public discovery surface is self-describing, which can reduce the friction of checking request and response contracts before wiring a Node.js worker. It remains the wrong tool for DAG orchestration, fan-out joins, or replay through multiple Kafka-style consumer groups; those requirements deserve a system designed for them.

Here is the trade-off in one view:

Option Integration Fits this reminder workflow when Main limitation
RabbitMQ Broker protocol and client libraries You need explicit acknowledgements, DLX routing, and broker control You own topology and broker operations
Amazon SQS Managed cloud API and SDKs You want a managed queue with visibility timeouts and redrive policy Routing semantics are narrower, and idempotency is still the consumer's job
BullMQ Node.js library over Redis Redis is already a durable part of the service Redis becomes part of the queue reliability story
Temporal Workflow SDKs The process needs durable orchestration, timers, and multi-step state It is a larger workflow platform than a reminder queue
Infrai Plain REST A language-neutral API avoids another SDK and the surrounding backend already uses its single key It has no DAG or join primitive, no Kafka-style replay, and delayed messages are limited to 7 days

The REST option also concentrates integration on one credential and one billing relationship across a broader backend surface. That can remove operational paperwork when a team needs queues alongside other backend capabilities, but it is not a reason to force every workflow into one queue abstraction.

The choice follows the failure boundary, not the feature checklist. Pick RabbitMQ for routing control, SQS for a managed cloud queue, BullMQ for a Redis-backed Node.js application, or a REST queue when a language-neutral integration surface removes real deployment friction. In every case, preserve the same consumer contract.

The instrumentation change that closes the loop

Track three timestamps: scheduled, first attempted, and completed or dead-lettered. Track attempt count and a reason category, not just an exception string. A useful dashboard can then answer two different questions: “Are transient failures recovering?” and “Are reminders aging past their business deadline?”

Keep retention long enough for an investigation, but do not confuse retention with replay. Messages are removed after acknowledgement, and this queue model does not provide Kafka-like replay or multiple consumer groups. If an audit trail is required, write an application event separately before acknowledging the message.

For a longer operation, let a cron task trigger queue work and let workers consume it. A cron execution is capped at 900 seconds, so it should not hold a reservation cleanup loop open while waiting for downstream notifications. Also remember that a paused cron does not backfill missed triggers; a separate reconciliation check is needed if missed schedules affect the business deadline.

The runbook should end with a controlled redrive: inspect the DLQ, correct the payload or dependency, redrive a bounded batch, and watch successful and duplicate-send metrics. Never turn a DLQ into an automatic infinite retry lane. That only moves the page.

Reliable reminder retries are a small state machine: pending, retrying, sent, expired, or dead-lettered. The queue supplies delivery mechanics. The worker supplies the business guarantee. Once those responsibilities are explicit, the on-call signal points to a decision instead of a symptom.

Further reading

  • RabbitMQ dead letter exchanges
  • BullMQ retrying failing jobs
  • Amazon SQS visibility timeout
  • Amazon SQS message deduplication and exactly-once processing
  • Temporal durable execution

title: Heroku is in sustaining engineering mode now, and that's a different kind of risk than a price increase
description:
On February 6, 2026, Heroku’s chief product officer Nitin T Bhat published a short post titled “An Update on Heroku,” announcing that the platform was moving to what Salesforce calls a sustaining engineering model. The post is specific about what that means in practice: Enterprise Account contracts will no longer be offered to new customers, and the engineering focus going forward is “stability, security, reliability, and support,” with an explicit statement that this comes “rather than introducing new features.” Existing customers, the post says, see no immediate change: pricing, billing and day-to-day service stay the same, and existing Enterprise contracts continue to be honored and can renew. Salesforce’s own framing for the shift is that it’s redirecting product and engineering investment toward “areas where we can deliver the greatest long-term customer value,” specifically enterprise AI products, which is the actual business reason behind the change, stated plainly rather than inferred.

This is a different kind of story than the pricing changes other platforms have made this year, and it deserves to be treated differently. A price going up or a bandwidth allowance getting cut is a cost question: run the numbers, decide if the new number still works. Software that stops moving forward is a different, slower-moving kind of risk, and it’s worth being precise about what it actually changes day to day, rather than reaching for either “nothing to worry about” or “Heroku is dead,” neither of which is accurate.

What does “sustaining engineering” actually mean for Heroku users?
The term itself isn’t exotic. It’s a recognized mode in long-lived commercial software: a product that’s past its growth phase gets a smaller, dedicated team whose job is keeping it running correctly, patched and secure, without the team that would normally be building what’s next. Heroku’s own post is careful to say this isn’t a shutdown notice. Apps already running stay running. Pipelines, teams, and the existing add-on ecosystem are explicitly called out as unaffected. Billing doesn’t change for customers paying by credit card through the dashboard. None of that is spin; it matches what sustaining engineering means everywhere else it’s used, and Heroku’s wording avoids overstating or understating it.

What the post does confirm, directly, is the part that matters for anyone planning around Heroku for the next few years: no new features. Not “fewer” features, not “a slower cadence,” the stated posture is that new capability development is not what the team is doing anymore. Combined with no new Enterprise contracts for new customers, the practical read is that Heroku the product, as of February 2026, is not something a team should expect to keep up with developments in the broader platform space on. Whatever the buildpack ecosystem looks like in two years, whatever regions get added to competing platforms, whatever managed-database feature becomes standard elsewhere, Heroku’s answer to all of it is very likely “that’s not something we’re building,” because the team whose job that would have been isn’t doing that job anymore.

What that costs in practice, for a team still on it today
For a team with a stable app, modest growth, and no plans to add new kinds of workloads, this genuinely might not matter for a long while. The post is honest that existing functionality keeps working, and “stability, security, reliability and support” is a real commitment, not an empty one, assuming Salesforce holds to it. Security patches for the existing buildpack stack, bug fixes for existing features, these are explicitly still in scope.

The exposure shows up in a few specific, foreseeable places. New framework or language runtime support is the first: a team that adopts a new version of a framework, or a language runtime Heroku hasn’t already built support for, has no reason to expect Heroku to add it, because that’s new feature work by definition. New regions are the second: infrastructure expansion is product development, and a company in sustaining mode has no stated reason to build new regions, which matters for any team whose latency requirements or compliance needs change over the life of the product. The third, and the one that compounds quietly, is responsiveness to bugs that aren’t security-critical: “stability and reliability” covers keeping existing behavior correct, but a non-critical bug that’s inconvenient rather than dangerous is exactly the kind of issue a smaller, maintenance-focused team reasonably deprioritizes, because that’s what a shrunk roadmap is for. None of these are catastrophic on their own. Together, over two or three years, they describe a platform that quietly falls further behind the part of the category that’s still actively built, while continuing to run correctly for exactly the workload it already supported on the day of the announcement.

Why this is a structural risk specific to renting the whole stack
The deeper point isn’t about Heroku specifically, it’s about what it means to depend entirely on one company’s product roadmap for your own infrastructure. On a fully managed platform, a customer has no path to keep the parts of the service they value moving forward if the vendor’s own priorities change. There’s no server to patch yourself, no infrastructure layer underneath the product that the customer still controls, the entire thing is the vendor’s roadmap, and when that roadmap gets reprioritized, every customer’s future capability gets reprioritized along with it, with no way to opt out short of leaving the platform entirely.

That’s the specific risk sustaining engineering represents, and it’s worth being fair about why Salesforce made the call: a 2026 enterprise software company redirecting investment toward enterprise AI is a rational business decision given the market, and Heroku, nearly two decades old, is a mature product with a well-known shape rather than a growth bet. Nothing about the decision is reckless or dishonest, the announcement itself is unusually direct about what’s changing and why. The risk isn’t that Salesforce did something wrong. It’s that any customer fully inside one company’s managed stack has no lever to pull when that company’s internal priorities shift, because the infrastructure was never theirs to begin with.

What a BYO-server model changes about this specific risk
A platform that runs on servers the customer owns can’t fully eliminate this risk, the control-plane software itself is still built by a company with its own roadmap and its own priorities that could shift. But it changes what’s actually at stake if that happens. The server itself, a plain Linux box at DigitalOcean, Hetzner or Vultr, running an ordinary Docker container behind a standard reverse proxy, doesn’t go stale because the control plane’s roadmap changes. If Railyard stopped shipping new features tomorrow, the apps already deployed keep running on infrastructure the customer already owns and controls directly over SSH, with no dependency on Railyard’s continued development to keep serving traffic. The worst case for a customer in that scenario is losing access to a dashboard and some automation convenience, not losing the infrastructure the app actually runs on, because that infrastructure was never the vendor’s to begin with.

That’s the structural answer to “what if the company behind my platform deprioritizes it,” and it’s a meaningfully different answer than anything available to a customer on a fully managed platform. It doesn’t require Railyard, or any BYO-server platform, to promise it will never happen here; it requires the architecture to make the consequence survivable if it does, which is a guarantee a rented stack can’t offer no matter how well-run the vendor is.

The honest takeaway
Heroku’s February 2026 announcement isn’t a crisis for anyone running on it today, and it isn’t dishonest or poorly communicated, if anything it’s a more direct statement than most companies give when deprioritizing a mature product. The actual lesson is about the category of risk itself: a team that depends entirely on a managed platform is also, by construction, depending entirely on that one company’s internal roadmap decisions staying aligned with the team’s own needs indefinitely, with no fallback if they stop being aligned. That’s a real structural property of renting the whole stack, independent of how good or bad any particular vendor’s intentions are, and it’s worth weighing on its own terms, separately from whatever the current pricing or feature set looks like on the day a team signs up.

FAQ
When did Heroku enter sustaining engineering mode? Heroku’s chief product officer, Nitin T Bhat, announced the shift on February 6, 2026, in a post titled “An Update on Heroku.”

Is Heroku shutting down? No. Existing apps, pipelines, teams and add-ons keep working, and credit-card customers see no change to pricing or billing. Sustaining engineering means no new features and no new Enterprise contracts for new customers, not a shutdown.

Will Heroku add new features or regions? The announcement is explicit that new feature development is not the team’s focus going forward, which also means new regions and new framework or runtime support shouldn’t be expected.

Is this a bigger risk than a price increase? It’s a different kind of risk. A price increase is a cost question you can calculate once. A platform that stops moving forward is a risk that compounds slowly over years, as the rest of the category keeps shipping and a frozen platform doesn’t.

Sources
Heroku: “An Update on Heroku,” by Nitin T Bhat, Chief Product Officer, published February 6, 2026, Heroku and Salesforce’s own primary announcement
DeployHQ: “Heroku Enters Sustaining Engineering Mode: What It Means and When to Consider Alternatives”, analysis of the practical implications
DevClass: “Heroku future in doubt as Salesforce freezes features to focus on AI”, independent coverage of the February 2026 announcement
Railyard’s own how it works page for details on running apps directly on infrastructure you control

See how Railyard specifically compares for a team evaluating a move: Compare Railyard to Heroku, or see how Railyard runs on servers you own.

title: From ImportError to Video: Bringing Looking Ahead to Windows
description:
Looking Ahead's 1.3B image-to-video example stopped on my Windows machine before inference started:

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'fcntl'

The machine had an RTX 5090. FlashAttention 4 was installed. Neither was enough to get past the import.

My fix, TencentARC/Looking-Ahead PR #2, was merged on October 23, 2026 (UTC). With the patch, the tested 1.3B example produced 80 frames at 768×432 on Windows 11, using PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention fallback.

The change spans six files. The interesting part is how three separate assumptions had to be removed before the fallback actually worked end to end.

Why I wanted to run Looking Ahead

Looking Ahead is a video-generation research project from researchers at Nanjing University, Tencent ARC Lab, and Zhejiang University.

Its method, Future Chunk Prediction (FCP), addresses a shortcut in autoregressive video training: neighboring video chunks can be similar enough that a model relies on local continuity without learning much about how a scene evolves.

FCP adds auxiliary training branches that predict more distant future chunks from the current chunk's intermediate features, without seeing the intervening chunks. Those branches are removed at inference. The authors report improvements in physical consistency; the project page explains the method and shows their comparisons.

The released code includes 1.3B and 5B models. Its documented test environment was Linux with an NVIDIA H200. My contribution makes the tested Windows inference path accessible through the upstream code. It does not change FCP, retrain the model, or establish Windows support for every configuration.

That is why this merge matters to me: the compatibility fix now lives in the research repository, where the next person trying the model can receive it.

1. Installed does not mean importable

The attention modules used is_flash_attn_4_available() before importing flash_attn.cute.

In the tested environment, that availability check reported the installed package. Importing it still failed: its quack dependency imported fcntl, a Unix-specific module unavailable on Windows.

The merged code attempts the import and treats an ImportError as an unavailable optional backend:

FLASH_ATTN_4_AVAILABLE = is_flash_attn_4_available()
if FLASH_ATTN_4_AVAILABLE:
    try:
        import flash_attn.cute
    except ImportError as exc:
        FLASH_ATTN_4_AVAILABLE = False
        warn_flash_attention_fallback(type(exc).__name__, str(exc))

Both attention modules receive this handling. A shared helper logs the selected backend and reports each distinct import failure once.

The warning explicitly says that performance and numerical results may differ. That matters because a run that silently switches backend is harder to reproduce or compare.

The helper receives the exception type and message as strings. It does not cache the exception object and its traceback just to deduplicate a warning.

This check establishes importability, not a guarantee that every subsequent kernel call will work on every device. It also catches ImportError specifically; it does not convert arbitrary runtime failures into silent fallbacks.

2. Cross-attention bypassed the fallback

Getting past the import exposed the next problem.

The code already had an attention() function that selected between FlashAttention 4 and PyTorch SDPA. But cross-attention called the FA4-only flash_attention() directly. Removing FA4 from the environment therefore avoided the import error while leaving an assertion waiting later in the run.

The relevant change is small:

- x = flash_attention(q, k, v, k_lens=context_lens)
+ x = attention(q, k, v, k_lens=context_lens)

Now cross-attention uses the same backend-selection boundary.

There is a semantic condition behind that edit. In the call path covered by the PR, context_lens is None, so the fallback computes full attention. The SDPA branch does not implement arbitrary variable-length padding masks. Routing a masked attention call through it would need additional work.

When FA4 is available, the dispatcher forwards the same arguments to the existing FA4 implementation.

The general lesson is to trace the callers. An optional backend is only optional if the execution paths that need it actually pass through the fallback.

3. Model loading had its own Unix dependency

The remaining fcntl dependency was outside attention.

The project stages base-model files and checkpoints into a local cache, using fcntl for file locking. The default staging path brought the same platform assumption back into the run.

The patch makes the import optional in both loading utilities. If fcntl is unavailable, staging is skipped and the model or checkpoint is loaded from its original path.

This preserves the underlying operation—reading the weights—without pretending that the Unix locking mechanism exists. It also avoids adding a new cross-platform lock implementation for a cache optimization.

On systems where fcntl exists, the existing staging path remains available. On systems where FA4 imports successfully, that attention path remains available too.

What the Windows run established

The PR records the following setup:

  • Windows 11 and RTX 5090.
  • Python 3.12 and PyTorch 2.10.0+cu128.
  • Other package versions from the project's uv.lock.
  • FCP 1.3B EMA checkpoint, sailboat example, seed 42, and a five-second duration request.

Before the patch, the run stopped at import. With the patch and SDPA, it produced 80 frames at 768×432, with 209 seconds of sampling, 231 seconds for the whole run, and 16.4 GiB peak allocated GPU memory.

One detail belongs beside those results: all reported runs used load_diffusion_pretrained=false. The PR explains that the EMA checkpoint strictly replaces every backbone weight, so the base DiT initialization does not determine the final output. This was not a claim that every model file or loading step could be omitted.

These numbers describe one tested example and environment. They are not an end-to-end validation of training, every checkpoint, or every GPU.

Preserving FA4 and comparing SDPA are different checks

The fallback needed to work, but the original fast path also needed a regression check.

For a controlled experiment, I made FA4 importable using triton-windows and a test-only no-op fcntl module. That shim is not in the PR and is not an installation recommendation—it does not provide real file locking.

With FA4 available, the original branch and the patched branch produced bit-identical decoded frames. That comparison checks whether the patch changed the existing FA4 path.

Comparing SDPA against FA4 answers a different question. On the same example, the first conditioning frame was identical, while frame PSNR was 33.5 dB on average and 31.6 dB at minimum. The generated results were not bit-identical.

FA4 sampling took 154 seconds, versus 209 seconds for SDPA. The fallback made the example runnable with a measurable speed tradeoff. It did not reproduce FA4's exact numerical output.

These are comparisons recorded in the PR's validation notes, not new experiments performed for this article.

The 5B follow-up found the next boundary

I also checked the 5B model with the paper-fan example and documented the result in a follow-up comment.

Sampling completed: 30 latent frames in 231 seconds, with 24.3 GiB peak allocated GPU memory.

The immediately following VAE decode did not fit in the same process on the tested 32 GB GPU / 64 GB RAM machine. The generator and both KV caches remained on the GPU; Windows commit charge passed 104 GiB, and I stopped the run.

Decoding those saved latents separately took 8.2 GiB and 11 seconds. That result points to a phase-lifetime and memory-management problem, beyond the portability fix in this PR.

So the precise outcome is: the 1.3B example completed end to end; the 5B example completed sampling, with decode checked in a separate process. The merge does not include a solution for the combined 5B memory peak.

What I would carry into the next portability fix

This patch connected three things: optional-backend detection, the callers that select that backend, and the platform-specific optimization in model loading.

For another research implementation, I would follow the same checks: attempt the optional import, trace every caller, verify that the fallback preserves the required attention semantics, log the selected path, and test the complete workload. A successful import is only the beginning.

The merged changes are small enough to read alongside the model's setup and inference instructions. FCP and the released models are the research authors' work; my contribution is getting this tested inference path through Windows without replacing the existing FA4 path.

Have you encountered an “optional” dependency that turned out to be mandatory through a different call site?

Drafted with AI assistance from the merged diff, project documentation, and recorded PR validation results. Merge commit: 15f90becc4d37f4f8c74cb0c868b6d855a7c605d.
