title: Never Trust File Uploads: Building a Secure S3 Pipeline
description:
File uploads look simple.

A user selects a file, your backend receives it, saves it to storage, and returns a URL.

Done, right?

Not really.

What if someone uploads a malicious file disguised as an image? What if hundreds of users upload large files at the same time? Or what if an infected PDF becomes available for everyone to download?

A simple upload feature can quickly become a security problem.

Let's look at how to build a safer file upload pipeline using S3, magic bytes, and ClamAV.

1. Stop sending files through your API server

A common approach is to receive files through your Node.js backend and then upload them to S3.

This works, but your API becomes a middleman.

Every upload uses server bandwidth and connections. If you're buffering files in memory, large uploads can also consume a lot of RAM.

A better approach is to use S3 presigned URLs.

Here's how it works:

  1. The client requests an upload URL from your API.
  2. Your API checks permission and generates a short-lived URL.
  3. The client uploads the file directly to S3.
  4. S3 stores the file in a private quarantine location.

Your API handles permissions, not the actual file transfer.

For example, using AWS SDK v3:

import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";
import { S3Client } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";
import { createPresignedPost } from "@aws-sdk/s3-presigned-post";

const s3 = new S3Client({ region: "us-east-1" });

export async function createUpload(userId: string) {
  // userId must come from the authenticated session
  const key = `quarantine/${userId}/${randomUUID()}`;

  const { url, fields } = await createPresignedPost(s3, {
    Bucket: "my-private-uploads",
    Key: key,
    Expires: 300,
    Conditions: [
      ["content-length-range", 1, 10 * 1024 * 1024],
    ],
  });

  return { url, fields };
}

This creates a presigned POST that allows uploads up to 10 MB and expires after five minutes.

The client sends the returned fields and file as multipart/form-data directly to S3.

The bucket stays private, and the backend should record the generated key against the authenticated user.

One important thing: a successful upload doesn't mean the file is safe.

We still need to inspect it.

2. Never trust file extensions or MIME types

Imagine someone uploads a file named profile.png.

Your backend checks:

if (file.mimetype === "image/png") {
  // Accept file
}

Looks fine, right?

The problem is that the MIME type usually comes from the client.

Anyone can rename a file or send a fake Content-Type header.

Instead, check the actual file content.

Check the magic bytes

Many file formats have recognizable binary signatures called magic bytes.

For example:

File Signature
PNG 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A
JPEG FF D8 FF
PDF 25 50 44 46 2D
ZIP 50 4B 03 04

In Node.js, the file-type package makes this easier.

import { fileTypeFromBuffer } from "file-type";

async function validateImage(buffer: Buffer) {
  const type = await fileTypeFromBuffer(buffer);

  const allowed = ["image/png", "image/jpeg"];

  if (!type || !allowed.includes(type.mime)) {
    throw new Error("Unsupported file format");
  }

  return type;
}

You don't need to download the entire file just to check its signature.

For supported formats, you can read a small part of the object using an S3 range request. The number of bytes needed depends on the format and detection library.

But remember, valid magic bytes don't mean a file is safe.

A valid PDF or image can still contain harmful content or exploit a vulnerable file parser.

That's why we need another layer.

3. Scan files before making them available

This is the part I wouldn't skip.

Never make an uploaded file available to users before it passes validation and scanning.

Instead, use a quarantine system.

Here's the flow:

Client
  |
  | Request upload URL
  v
Node.js API
  |
  | Generate presigned URL
  v
Client
  |
  | Upload directly
  v
Private S3 Quarantine
  |
  | Storage event
  v
Background Worker
  |
  | Check file size
  | Check magic bytes
  | Scan with ClamAV
  |
  +-- Failed --> Reject
  |
  +-- Passed --> Approved Storage
                       |
                       v
                Available to User

For malware scanning, we can use ClamAV, a free, open-source antivirus engine.

A background worker can download or stream the quarantined object to the scanner.

Here's a simplified example using the clamscan package:

import NodeClam from "clamscan";

const clam = await new NodeClam().init({
  clamdscan: {
    host: "clamav-service",
    port: 3310,
  },
});

export async function scanFile(
  fileStream: NodeJS.ReadableStream,
) {
  const result = await clam.scanStream(fileStream);

  if (result.isInfected !== false) {
    throw new Error("File rejected");
  }

  return true;
}

This example only shows the scanning step. The worker still needs to retrieve the correct S3 object, validate it, handle failures, and update the database.

If the scan fails, times out, or returns an unknown result, keep the file quarantined.

Don't approve it automatically.

Also, ClamAV reduces malware risk, but it cannot detect every possible threat.

4. Let background workers handle the heavy work

Virus scanning can take time.

You don't want users waiting for it inside an HTTP request.

Instead, use a background queue like BullMQ or AWS SQS.

When S3 receives a file, a storage event can trigger a job.

The worker validates the file, scans it, and updates its status.

A simple database lifecycle could look like this:

PENDING_UPLOAD
      |
      v
 QUARANTINED
      |
      v
   SCANNING
    /    \
   v      v
APPROVED REJECTED

The frontend can show "Processing your file" while scanning is in progress.

Make sure workers can safely retry jobs and handle duplicate events.

There's another important detail here.

Scan and approve the exact same object.

Otherwise, a file could be replaced after scanning but before approval.

Use unique storage keys and object versioning or other controls that prevent an unscanned replacement from being published.

5. A few security rules worth following

Even with these three layers, I'd still add a few protections:

  • Limit file sizes. Don't allow unlimited uploads.
  • Use random file names. Generate UUID-based storage keys instead of trusting user-provided paths.
  • Keep storage private. Approved files don't always need public URLs. Use authorized downloads when appropriate.
  • Limit upload requests. Add authentication, rate limits, and storage quotas.
  • Protect against ZIP bombs. Limit archive extraction size, file count, and nesting depth.
  • Serve files safely. Use correct response headers and avoid serving risky user content from your application's main origin.
  • Monitor failures. Track rejected uploads, scanner errors, and unusual upload activity.

And one underrated point: don't expose your ClamAV service directly to the internet. Keep it accessible only to trusted workers.

Final thoughts

File uploads are easy to build, but securing them takes a little more thought.

You don't need a complicated system from day one.

Start with three things:

1. Presign: Let clients upload directly to private object storage.

2. Validate: Check file size, format, and actual content instead of trusting filenames.

3. Scan: Run malware checks in the background before making files available.

These steps won't eliminate every security risk, but they'll give you a much safer foundation.

The main thing I've learned is simple:

Uploading a file and trusting a file should be two different steps.

How do you handle file uploads in your applications? Do you scan files before making them available, or use a different approach?

References

  • AWS S3 Presigned URLs
  • AWS S3 Presigned POST
  • ClamAV Documentation
  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet

title: node2shell: How to Check If Your Node.js App Is Exposed and Patch It
description:
node2shell is the nickname for CVE-2026-111497, a flaw in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js. The Node.js project fixed it on 21 October 2026, and the fix is a runtime upgrade. Here's how to check and patch, based on the advisories listed at the end.

What node2shell is

The Node.js security release describes an out-of-bounds write in the bundled Brotli decoder. If an attacker can supply Brotli data that your app decompresses with node:zlib, they can corrupt process memory. Node.js says this can lead to a crash, memory disclosure or remote code execution. It affects the 22.x, 24.x and 26.x lines, and Node.js credits OpenAI Codex Security with reporting it.

Severity ratings differ by source:

  • The Node.js advisory rates it high.
  • The CVE record gives it 9.2 (critical) on CVSS 4.0 and places the root bug in Google's Brotli library, versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0.
  • Singapore's Cyber Security Agency calls it critical, citing a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8.

Imperva's Red Team says it got code execution against the official Node.js 24.22.0 image, through both the built-in fetch() and Express 5 / body-parser 2 request parsers. It says 24.22.1 rejected the same input.

Where http2shell fits in

http2shell is not a second bug. Aikido Security uses the name for the same CVE now that it is known to reach beyond Node.js. It lists fixes for Python's Brotli and brotlicffi packages, libbrotli, curl/libcurl, Bun, Envoy and Istio. On 23 October, Aikido said patches were not yet available for every affected service.

Am I exposed?

Vercel's advisory explains that Node.js doesn't decode Brotli by itself. Your app is exposed when your code or a library decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data. That data can come in a request body or in a response your app fetches.

1. Check the runtime version.

node -v

The fixed versions are 22.23.4, 24.22.1 and 26.12.1 (or newer in the same line). Anything older in those lines is affected. Node.js 20 is end-of-life and won't get a fix, according to Vercel.

2. Look for paths that decode Brotli. Imperva's tests found Express 5 and body-parser 2 decode Brotli request bodies when their parsers are configured:

npm ls express body-parser

Also look for fetch() calls to servers you don't control and direct zlib Brotli use (brotliDecompress).

3. Check containers and CI, not just your laptop. Imperva warns that a package inventory can miss an older Node binary inside a container image:

docker run --rm your-image:tag node -v

How to patch

With nvm:

nvm install 24
nvm use 24
node -v   # should print v24.22.1 or newer

For Docker, rebuild on a base image with a fixed Node version and redeploy. For distro packages, Aikido notes vendors may backport the fix without changing the version number, so check your distribution's security notice.

On a managed platform, check the provider's notice. Vercel says it manages patch versions for 22.x and 24.x, but projects on 20.x must move to 22.x or 24.x and redeploy.

Python and Bun users get their own fixes, per Aikido:

pip show Brotli brotlicffi
pip install -U "Brotli>=1.2.1"      # or "brotlicffi>=1.2.1.0"
bun --version                        # 1.4.4 or later is fixed

Aikido notes that requests, httpx and aiohttp use these packages automatically when installed, and that pip-audit and Dependabot weren't flagging it as of 23 October, so check by hand.

If you can't upgrade today

Vercel and Imperva both added WAF rules, but both say that doesn't replace patching. A WAF also can't see Brotli responses your app fetches from other servers. As a stopgap, Aikido suggests rejecting requests whose Content-Encoding includes br before any decoder runs. For outbound traffic, it suggests disabling or rejecting Brotli response decoding.

Sources

  • Node.js: Wednesday, October 21, 2026 Security Releases
  • CVE.org: CVE-2026-111497
  • Cyber Security Agency of Singapore: Critical Vulnerability in Node.js (AL-2026-154)
  • Vercel: Node.js security advisory, Brotli decoder RCE
  • Imperva: Node2Shell, From Brotli Data to Remote Code Execution
  • Aikido Security: Node2Shell evolves to HTTP2Shell

For more research-based AI and tech news, see AI News by AIFix at ainews.useaifix.com, and useaifix.com for help keeping sites and workflows in shape.

title: Per-block difficulty adjustment in a post-quantum Proof-of-Work chain (Rust, integer-only) published:
description:
I'm building Quantum-Lattice (QL), a Layer 1 Proof-of-Work chain written in Rust that signs every transaction with ML-DSA-65 (NIST FIPS 204), a post-quantum signature scheme. This post covers one piece of the latest hard fork: moving from a coarse every-10-blocks difficulty retarget to a per-block, fixed-point adjustment.

The old rule

Difficulty was an integer number of leading zero bits, recalculated every 10 blocks and clamped to ±2 bits per step. That is simple, but coarse: it only reacts at window boundaries, it moves in whole bits, and a window can land in a band where the rounded result is zero change.

The new rule

Three ideas:

  1. Fixed-point difficulty. 65,536 units = 1 bit. The target is 2^(256 - d) for fractional d, so difficulty can move in tiny steps.
  2. Integer-only math. Consensus code must give identical results on every machine, so no floats. The fractional power of two uses a cubic polynomial approximation (the same constants as Bitcoin Cash's aserti3 family). Whole-bit values give exactly the old leading-zero-bits result, so history stays valid.
  3. Per-block, relative update. Each block nudges difficulty according to how far its gap was from the 300 s target: 
pub fn next_fine(parent_baseline: u32, gap_secs: i64) -> u32 {
    let delta = ((TARGET_BLOCK_TIME_SECS - gap_secs) as i128 * FP_ONE as i128)
        / FORK2_TAU_SECS as i128;           // tau = 3600 s
    let v = parent_baseline as i128 + delta;
    v.clamp(FORK2_MIN_FP as i128, FORK2_MAX_FP as i128) as u32
}

A block that comes after 200 s raises difficulty by about 0.028 bits. One that takes 1,200 s lowers it by about 0.25 bits. Because the updates telescope, the result depends on the end points of a stretch of blocks, not on the order of the gaps in between.

A block is valid if hash < target(difficulty), compared as 256-bit big-endian integers.

Timestamps

Per-block rules lean on timestamps, so those get stricter too: a block's timestamp must be above the median of the previous 11 blocks, and no more than 15 minutes ahead of the node's clock.

Does it behave?

I simulated the controller before shipping it (steady hashrate with exponential block arrivals). With a 3,600 s time constant the steady-state wobble is about 0.25 bits, and it recovers from a 5× hashrate step in either direction within about 60 blocks, and from a 100× exodus in about 40.

On the live chain the switch at block 35,600 went through with no stall and no split. Difficulty now moves every block, and blocks have averaged close to the 5-minute target at roughly 330 MH/s.

What I'd flag

  • This does not stop an attacker with majority hashrate. It makes difficulty harder to disturb and smoother to track, nothing more.
  • A hard fork means every node operator has to run the new build. Nodes on the old rules stop following the chain at the activation height.
  • The hashrate is concentrated among a handful of operators, and the difficulty swings show it. That's a network-growth problem, not a code one.

Code and tests

The consensus code and its tests (known target values, monotonicity, a check that whole-bit values match the old rule exactly, timestamp rules) are in src/consensus.rs:

https://github.com/AlthaafM/Quantum-Lattice

Questions, review and criticism welcome. I'd especially like eyes on the integer approximation and the clamp bounds.

title: The Tusi couple in Python: 8 beads in straight lines that roll as a circle
description:
Eight beads sit in eight straight slots. Each bead only ever slides back and forth along its own line. Watch all eight at once, though, and you see a circle rolling around the dial.

The trick: a circle rolling inside a circle twice its size

In 1247 the Persian astronomer Nasir al-Din al-Tusi showed that if a circle of radius r rolls inside a circle of radius 2r, every point on the small circle's rim moves in a straight line through the centre. Copernicus later used the same construction to build straight-line motion out of circles.

The maths is one line. Put the small circle's centre at angle t. It rolls the opposite way, so a rim point that started at angle b sits at

P(t) = r*(cos t, sin t) + r*(cos(b - t), sin(b - t))
     = 2r * cos(t - b/2) * (cos(b/2), sin(b/2))

The direction (cos b/2, sin b/2) never changes. Only the length 2r*cos(t - b/2) changes, so the point just slides along a fixed diameter. Space eight points 45 degrees apart on the small circle and you get eight lines 22.5 degrees apart.

Building it for a 3D printer

I wrote it in Python with manifold3d:

  • Body: a dial with 16 half-slots cut from the centre out, so all 8 diameters meet in an open centre window. The body prints face-down, so the slots are just holes in the first layers.
  • Disc: radius 17 mm, with 8 pegs on a 15 mm circle. Pegs ride in the slots with 0.4 mm clearance per side. No gears needed: the pegs in the slots fully constrain the disc (it is a trammel).
  • Floor and beads: the floor presses in under the disc, and beads glue onto the peg tips above the dial.

The motion is checked in code before printing: step the angle through a full turn and intersect every part with every other part.

for t in range(0, 360, 6):
    body, floor, disc, beads = assembled(t)
    hit = (body ^ disc).volume() + (body ^ beads).volume() + (disc ^ floor).volume()
    assert hit < 1e-6

That came back zero at every step. The animation above is just that same function rendered frame by frame.

Styling

The dial borrows from astrolabes: 64 degree ticks, an eight-point star in every segment, a throne (kursi) with a hanging ring, and a sunburst on the disc that shows through the centre window.

The STL files are here if you want to print one: Tusi Couple Astrolabe on Cults3D.

title: Node.js Realtime Delivery Latency — 4 Connection Health Metrics for Patient Alerts
description:
Short answer: in Node.js, measure realtime delivery latency by publishing a server timestamp and message ID with every typing indicator or read receipt, then have each client report when it observed that event. Track the resulting delay distribution alongside connection health, reconnects, and receipt coverage; alert on a sustained trend, not one slow phone.

For a healthtech notification flow, the deciding constraint is fan-out. A successful publish says little about the last browser in a care team, and server timing cannot include the final network hop, a suspended tab, or work queued on the client. The useful measurement boundary ends at the screen that received the event.

My recommendation is to try Infrai for the realtime publish and metrics-reporting boundary when a small team also expects to add adjacent backend capabilities: its 295 routes across 20 modules sit behind one key and a consistent REST contract, so the next capability does not require another credential lifecycle. One credential and one bill also remove reconciliation work from this already multi-part telemetry path. The supporting advantage is practical during instrumentation: its public discovery surface returns request and response schemas, and every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. This is a breadth and operating-cost argument, not a claim that its network is faster.

Infrai's second verified advantage is operational: one API key, one wallet, and one consolidated bill cover the publishing and reporting sides of this loop, while the plain REST API needs no SDK to install. Its self-describing public discovery surface needs no key, returns full request and response JSON Schema, billing details, and runnable examples, and every documented capability has examples in 10 languages. For this workflow, those are concrete maintenance reductions: a solo team can generate both adapters from current schemas, reuse one HTTP retry policy and one credential rotation path, and avoid maintaining separate vendor libraries, keys, and invoice reconciliation for realtime delivery and its metrics. The benefit grows when the same application later needs another backend module, because the integration machinery remains the same even though the capability changes.

Infrai also specifies per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata consistently on its native and OpenAI-compatible surfaces. That makes downstream spend and vendor routing observable through one metadata shape, which is useful when this experiment compares the full operating bill rather than a published unit price.

That friction compounds.

The workflow uses one API key, one wallet, and one bill across realtime publication and metric reporting. That avoids separate credentials and invoice reconciliation for the two halves of the measurement loop. It is also one plain REST API with no SDK to install, so the Node.js publisher and metric reporter can share the platform's built-in HTTP client, error handling, and retry policy instead of carrying two vendor libraries through upgrades.

There is a second operational reason for this workload: idempotency is a platform convention, not an endpoint afterthought. The discovery data marks 171 of 294 capabilities as idempotent, and the convention specifies an Idempotency-Key, a deterministic server fallback, and a 24-hour default deduplication window. That matters when a 429 or broken connection leaves the publisher unsure whether a read receipt was accepted. The client still has to reuse the same key across retries, as the example does.

How should Node.js measure realtime delivery latency and connection health?

Typing indicators are disposable state. Read receipts are not. Treating them as identical creates an attractive dashboard that hides the actual product contract.

For a typing event, freshness wins: an event that arrives after the user stopped typing can be discarded. For a read receipt, the client should apply an idempotent state transition keyed by message and reader, because reconnection and retry can produce another observation. Neither rule turns publish acknowledgement into delivery proof.

I would define four measurements before choosing a provider:

  1. Observed delay: client receive time minus the publish timestamp, summarized with percentiles rather than an average.
  2. Receipt coverage: distinct intended clients reporting an observation divided by intended clients for a sampled event.
  3. Heartbeat age: time since the client last demonstrated a healthy connection.
  4. Reconnect rate: reconnect attempts per active client over a fixed window.

The first metric answers speed. The next three explain confidence in that answer. If receipt coverage falls, a flattering latency percentile may merely describe the clients that remained connected.

There is a clock caveat. Client receive time and server publish time live on different clocks, so raw subtraction includes clock skew. Record a client clock-offset estimate from a small request-response exchange, keep the uncorrected value for diagnosis, and reject impossible values from alert aggregation. For stricter measurement, send a server timestamp periodically and estimate offset from the midpoint of the round trip. It is an estimate, not truth.

A focused TypeScript measurement loop

The simple approach is to start a timer around the server's publish call. That measures provider acceptance latency. It does not measure delivery, and it gets less representative as fan-out grows.

The following dependency-free TypeScript sketch measures at the recipient. It keeps transport details behind two tiny interfaces, so the same code can sit above a hosted realtime service, WebSocket gateway, or Server-Sent Events connection. The reporter batches observations to control downstream metric volume; a read receipt can be fully observed while high-frequency typing events are sampled.

import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

type RealtimeEvent = {
  id: string;
  channel: string;
  kind: "typing" | "read";
  publishedAtMs: number;
  actorId: string;
  messageId?: string;
};

type DeliveryObservation = {
  eventId: string;
  clientId: string;
  kind: RealtimeEvent["kind"];
  observedDelayMs: number;
  rawDelayMs: number;
  connectionAgeMs: number;
  observedAtMs: number;
};

interface ObservationReporter {
  report(observation: DeliveryObservation): Promise<void>;
}

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function postInfrai(url: string, body: unknown): Promise<unknown> {
  const idempotencyKey = randomUUID();
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(url, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1_000
        : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
      continue;
    }

    const result: unknown = await response.json();
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Infrai ${response.status}: ${JSON.stringify(result)}`);
    }
    return result;
  }
  throw new Error("Infrai retry budget exhausted");
}

export async function publishCareEvent(
  publishBody: Record<string, unknown>,
  event: Omit<RealtimeEvent, "id" | "publishedAtMs">,
): Promise<RealtimeEvent> {
  const stamped: RealtimeEvent = {
    ...event,
    id: randomUUID(),
    publishedAtMs: Date.now(),
  };
  await postInfrai(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/publish",
    { ...publishBody, data: stamped },
  );
  return stamped;
}

export async function observeCareEvent(
  reporter: ObservationReporter,
  event: RealtimeEvent,
  clientId: string,
  connectedAtMs: number,
  estimatedClockOffsetMs: number,
): Promise<void> {
  const observedAtMs = Date.now();
  const rawDelayMs = observedAtMs - event.publishedAtMs;
  const observedDelayMs = rawDelayMs - estimatedClockOffsetMs;

  if (!Number.isFinite(observedDelayMs) || observedDelayMs < 0) return;

  const observation = {
    eventId: event.id,
    clientId,
    kind: event.kind,
    observedDelayMs,
    rawDelayMs,
    connectionAgeMs: observedAtMs - connectedAtMs,
    observedAtMs,
  };

  await reporter.report(observation);
  await postInfrai(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/metrics/report",
    observation,
  );
}

Pass publishBody fields from the current public discovery schema rather than freezing undocumented fields into the adapter. The example adds only the measured event under data; before running it, confirm that field against discovery as well. Authentication is Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY, and the adapter surfaces non-2xx response bodies while backing off on HTTP 429 and honoring Retry-After.

Do not report every keystroke from every client. A deterministic sampler based on event ID keeps a stable subset across retries. Keep every read-receipt observation where the audit value warrants it, aggregate typing observations into short windows, and attach only low-cardinality dimensions such as event kind, client platform, and region. Patient IDs and message IDs belong in controlled diagnostic storage, not metric labels.

Why averages fail this experiment

Suppose a care-team notification fans out to 12 intended sessions. Ten arrive quickly, one arrives much later, and one disconnected session never reports. The mean over the ten reports erases both tails: the delayed clinician and the absent device. No invented threshold fixes that modeling error.

Store a histogram of observed delay and a separate coverage ratio. Review p50, p95, and p99 over a rolling window, split by event kind and client platform. Then compare those distributions with heartbeat age and reconnect rate. A rising p95 with stable coverage points toward slower delivery; falling coverage with a normal p95 points toward connection loss or clients unable to report.

One sample proves nothing.

Alert when several adjacent windows depart from the service objective, and require enough samples for a percentile to mean anything. The exact window, minimum count, and threshold must come from the clinical workflow's tolerance and measured baseline. A typing indicator may expire quietly. A read receipt may need a durable reconciliation path in the application data model. Realtime telemetry should reveal that difference rather than flatten it.

Effective cost also changes with fan-out. Count publish operations, delivered messages if the provider bills that way, client observation writes, retained diagnostic records, and the engineer time spent maintaining authentication, schemas, dashboards, and retries. Downstream metric cardinality can dominate a design that looked inexpensive at the publish boundary. Sampling and aggregation are product decisions as much as telemetry decisions.

Where each provider fits

No public feature page can establish which service will be fastest for your users. Run the same instrumented workload in the regions, browsers, mobile states, and fan-out sizes you expect. Product architecture still narrows the shortlist.

Option Useful fit for this experiment Boundary to evaluate
Infrai A small team that values one REST contract across realtime, metrics, and later backend modules Use discovery for exact schemas; validate delivery behavior and regional fit with the client-reported experiment
Ably Teams that want a realtime specialist with documented message ordering, delivery semantics, and connection-state behavior Map its guarantees to ephemeral typing versus durable receipt requirements, then measure the actual client path
Pusher Channels Teams that want a focused hosted channels model with presence and client events Plan the separate metrics pipeline and test how reconnect behavior affects coverage
PubNub Workloads that benefit from a specialist publish/subscribe network plus presence and message persistence options Decide which events merit persistence and account for the resulting delivery and storage workload
AWS AppSync Events AWS-centered systems that want managed serverless WebSocket events integrated with AWS identity and operations Include cloud coupling, authorization design, and observability assembly in the operating bill

Ably is the stronger candidate when explicit realtime protocol semantics and specialist tooling are the main purchase. Pusher Channels can be easier to reason about when the scope stays narrowly channel-oriented. PubNub deserves evaluation when presence, persistence, and wide publish/subscribe distribution drive the design. AppSync Events makes sense when the team already operates inside AWS and accepts that coupling.

Infrai's advantage is different: breadth behind one surface. It is a sensible shortlist entry when adding the metrics side of this experiment, and later capabilities, would otherwise mean more integrations, keys, and billing paths. A specialist is the better choice if its delivery guarantees, regional topology, connection controls, or protocol-specific tooling match a hard requirement that the broader surface does not document.

What to measure before copying this choice

Run a replayable test matrix before committing. Vary fan-out, payload size, client platform, network state, and foreground versus suspended execution. For each cell, capture observed-delay percentiles, receipt coverage, heartbeat age, reconnect rate, duplicated observations, and metric ingestion volume. Keep provider acceptance time too, but label it correctly.

Test read receipts and typing indicators separately. Confirm that stale typing events expire at the application boundary, duplicate read observations converge to one state, and a reconnecting client cannot make the dashboard look healthier by omitting missed events. Then estimate the full operating bill from the workload: realtime traffic, reporting traffic, telemetry retention, cardinality, and integration ownership. Price per call is only one input, and it changes.

The decision rule is compact: choose the option whose measured delivery distribution and coverage meet the workflow objective, whose guarantees fit each event type, and whose complete operating burden a small team can sustain. If the unified boundary fits that result, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live discovery schema before implementing adapters.

References

  • Infrai documentation
  • Ably: Message ordering and delivery guarantees
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • PubNub: Message persistence
  • AWS AppSync Events
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0

title: Missed Realtime Messages: 3 Sequence Rules for State Refetch
description:
Use a monotonically increasing sequence number for each property-maintenance conversation, keep the last accepted number in the browser, and fetch the authoritative conversation state as soon as the next number skips ahead. TL;DR: detect the gap, replace local state with a full snapshot, and report how often recovery happens. This is less complicated, and usually more dependable, than trying to make every typing or read-receipt event arrive exactly once.

The practical boundary matters. Typing indicators are disposable hints; read receipts affect what a manager and tenant believe has happened. Both can travel over the same realtime channel, but only the server snapshot should settle disagreement. For a solo builder, that rule keeps the recovery path small enough to understand at 2 a.m.

Infrai fits here as the REST publication and channel layer, while Express owns the authoritative maintenance snapshot. It offers one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 backend modules, but consolidation is only half the case. Infrai uses one plain REST API, so there is no SDK to install; any language or runtime can send the HTTP request. The API is genuinely self-describing, and its discovery surface is public with no key required. Every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. For this workflow, those properties let a small team inspect the live channel contract and keep recovery logic in its existing Express service instead of maintaining another client-library integration.

How should Node.js detect missed realtime messages by sequence?

There are two viable shapes.

The first is an event-replay architecture. The client records an offset, reconnects, and asks the transport or an event store to replay everything after that offset. Its invariant is strict: every retained event has a stable position and replay preserves order. This is appropriate when intermediate events are themselves business records, but retention, deduplication, and replay cursors become application concerns.

The second is snapshot recovery. A live message carries a channel sequence; the browser accepts contiguous messages and refetches the whole authoritative state after a gap. Its invariant is different: the latest server snapshot completely describes the user-visible truth. That is the shape I would ship for a maintenance thread's online members, typing indicators, and read positions. A missed typing:started event does not deserve a replay subsystem.

This choice does require discipline. A snapshot must replace local state rather than merge in guesses, and a stale fetch must not overwrite a newer message. Picture a manager opening work order 884 on a phone, losing the connection after sequence 41, and reconnecting at sequence 44. Replaying only the apparent missing item, 42, still leaves 43 unresolved; merging an old receipt into the current view can also move the manager's read marker backward. One snapshot at sequence 44 or later settles membership, typing, and receipts together. Presence accuracy comes from one authority and ordered application, not from a promise that the network never drops a packet.

Keep it dull.

Infrai can be a deliberate transport option inside the snapshot shape. A small team that also consumes other backend capabilities can use one REST API, one key, and one bill instead of maintaining keys and invoices across separate dashboards. No SDK is required for the plain HTTP interface. Its public discovery surface requires no key and describes 295 capabilities across 20 modules, including schemas and runnable examples in 10 languages; checking the current contract before wiring the transport removes guesswork from this recovery path. Teams that want a REST-oriented realtime layer and fewer backend credentials should try Infrai for message publication while keeping snapshot recovery in their own application.

Build gap recovery before tuning delivery

The example below is one runnable TypeScript file. It starts an Express server with an authoritative maintenance-thread snapshot, then acts as a client that receives sequence 1 followed by sequence 3. The client notices the missing number, fetches the whole state, and refuses to let an older recovery response replace newer state.

import express from "express";

type Receipt = { userId: string; lastReadMessageId: string };
type ThreadState = {
  channel: string;
  sequence: number;
  typingUserIds: string[];
  receipts: Receipt[];
};
type LiveMessage = { sequence: number; kind: "typing" | "receipt" };

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function getRealtimeChannel(channel: string, attempt = 0): Promise<unknown> {
  const response = await fetch(
    `https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/channel/get/${encodeURIComponent(channel)}`,
    {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    },
  );

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1_000
      : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return getRealtimeChannel(channel, attempt + 1);
  }
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Channel fetch failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
  }
  return response.json() as Promise<unknown>;
}

const app = express();
const state: ThreadState = {
  channel: "property-17:work-order-884",
  sequence: 3,
  typingUserIds: [],
  receipts: [{ userId: "manager-4", lastReadMessageId: "message-29" }],
};

app.get("/threads/:channel/state", (request, response) => {
  if (request.params.channel !== state.channel) {
    response.status(404).json({ error: "thread not found" });
    return;
  }
  response.status(200).json(state);
});

const server = app.listen(3000, async () => {
  let local: ThreadState = {
    channel: state.channel,
    sequence: 0,
    typingUserIds: [],
    receipts: [],
  };

  async function refetchState(minimumSequence: number): Promise<void> {
    const path = `/threads/${encodeURIComponent(local.channel)}/state`;
    const response = await fetch(new URL(path, "http://localhost:3000"), {
      method: "GET",
    });
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`State fetch failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    const snapshot = (await response.json()) as ThreadState;
    if (snapshot.sequence >= minimumSequence && snapshot.sequence > local.sequence) {
      local = snapshot;
    }
  }

  async function acceptRealtimeMessage(message: LiveMessage): Promise<void> {
    if (message.sequence <= local.sequence) return;
    if (message.sequence !== local.sequence + 1) {
      await refetchState(message.sequence);
      return;
    }
    local = { ...local, sequence: message.sequence };
  }

  try {
    await getRealtimeChannel(state.channel);
    await acceptRealtimeMessage({ sequence: 1, kind: "typing" });
    await acceptRealtimeMessage({ sequence: 3, kind: "receipt" });
    console.log(local);
  } finally {
    server.close();
  }
});

Run it with a TypeScript runtime after installing Express. In production, the live transport calls acceptRealtimeMessage; it is not another source of truth. The refetch endpoint is deliberately application-owned because only the application knows what a complete maintenance-thread snapshot contains.

Notice what the code does not do: it does not request sequence 2. Refetching one missing event can still leave the browser wrong if several messages vanished, arrived out of order, or summarized transient presence. A complete state response closes all of those gaps at one boundary.

Compare transports without confusing them with recovery

Transport products expose different connection and presence machinery, but none removes the need to decide what the application considers authoritative. The useful comparison is therefore about system fit, not a feature-count contest.

Option Relevant mechanism Best fit Boundary to keep visible
Socket.IO Connection-state recovery can restore a session and missed packets after a temporary disconnect Teams that want a Node-centric protocol and operate their own server Its documentation says recovery is not always successful, so the application still needs synchronization handling
Ably Presence supplies member enter, update, and leave events on channels Teams that want a managed pub/sub product with presence semantics Presence events describe channel membership; durable read truth still belongs in application state
Pusher Channels Presence channels expose subscribed members and membership events Teams already comfortable with Pusher's channel model and client libraries Membership and typing signals should not become the authoritative read-receipt store
PubNub Presence tracks occupancy and join, leave, timeout, and state-change events Systems that need a managed presence-focused feature set Occupancy signals and business acknowledgements have different durability needs
Infrai REST publication can sit beside application-owned state refetch under one credential surface Small teams consolidating several backend services behind one key Choose a specialist when transport-specific replay, client ecosystem, or deeper presence controls dominate the decision

That last boundary is important. Infrai's supporting advantage here is operational: its documented capabilities use a consistent interface and include runnable TypeScript examples, reducing the integration surface a solo team has to keep current. The limitation is equally concrete: it is not the right fit when transport-specific replay, a specialist client ecosystem, or fine-grained managed presence controls are the primary requirement. Socket.IO is the more direct choice when self-hosted Node transport control is the goal; Ably, Pusher Channels, or PubNub may be better when their specialist presence semantics and client tooling are the center of the product. That trade-off should be decided before the application adopts vendor-specific channel behavior.

Measure the recovery path

Count every detected gap by channel class and client version, then report the frequency. Do not treat the counter as vanity telemetry. A rising rate tells you that reconnect behavior, message ordering, or a release deserves investigation even when snapshot recovery keeps the interface correct.

Measure recovery, not optimism.

Keep the metric low-cardinality: use a category such as maintenance-thread, not a property ID or user ID. Track attempted recoveries, successful snapshot replacements, and failed refetches separately in your own observability system. No invented precision. The ratio becomes meaningful only after you define the denominator, such as received realtime messages or active channel-minutes, and keep that definition stable.

Operationally, verify three things before release. First, sequences advance within one channel scope and reset only under an explicit channel-lifecycle rule. Second, snapshot responses carry a sequence so racing responses cannot move the UI backward. Third, reconnect, duplicate, delayed, and out-of-order cases are exercised in tests. Then watch gap frequency after deployment. This short checklist protects presence accuracy more effectively than a vague claim of guaranteed delivery.

Make the boundary boring

The three rules are enough: track the last sequence, replace state after a gap, and measure recovery. Keep typing ephemeral. Keep read positions in the authoritative snapshot. Pick event replay only when intermediate events must remain individually recoverable; otherwise, snapshot recovery is the smaller system and the easier one to reason about.

If the consolidated REST boundary fits your stack, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live capability contract before integrating.

Further reading

  • Socket.IO connection state recovery
  • Ably Presence
  • Pusher Channels presence channels
  • PubNub Presence
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • Infrai official documentation

title: Keeping tags attached when files move: watched folders in AssetHoard 0.2.4
description:
A file manager knows where a file is. An asset library also knows what you said about it: its tags, its category, which bundle it belongs to and which projects use it. The moment someone renames that file in Explorer or Finder, those two views of the world disagree.

AssetHoard is a local-first desktop asset manager for indie game devs, built in Rust and Tauri. Watched folders let you point it at directories you already organise by hand, and it keeps the library in step. Version 0.2.4 rewrites how watched folders handle files that change underneath them.

The cases that break naive watching

A file watcher reports events. Turning those events into "this is the same asset as before" is where it gets interesting.

Renames and moves. The event stream for a move is not always a tidy rename. Moves across directories, or batches of them from a sync tool, can arrive as separate removals and creations. In 0.2.4 the asset is the thing being preserved, so tags, category, bundle and project links follow the file to its new path. Mirrored bundles move with their folders.

Case-only renames. Renaming Rock.png to rock.png is a real rename, but a case-insensitive comparison sees no change at all. These now keep their metadata too.

Changes made while the app was closed. There are no events to listen to when nothing is running. AssetHoard now recognises moves made while it was closed. Existing libraries are catalogued in the background after the update.

Saving over a file. Plenty of tools save by writing a new file and replacing the old one. To a watcher, that looks like a deletion. AssetHoard now waits briefly before marking anything missing, so a save does not flag the asset.

Disconnected drives. An unplugged external drive is not a deleted library. Assets on a disconnected drive or network share are paused rather than marked missing, and if the drive comes back under a different letter, AssetHoard picks it up again.

Nested watched folders. Watch Assets/ and also Assets/Characters/, and two watchers claim the same files. The rule now is that the innermost watched folder owns its files, and you get a preview with exact counts before anything moves.

The limit: network drives

Live rename and move tracking depends on the operating system sending file change events. Network drives over SMB or UNC paths do not provide them, so they do not get live tracking. They still pause cleanly when they disconnect.

Also in 0.2.4

  • 3D model thumbnails generate around 20x faster on import.
  • Most image thumbnails are now generated after import, so imports finish much sooner.
  • Re-importing a changed file updates the existing asset instead of creating a duplicate.
  • The search index is reused on launch instead of rebuilt, and text search no longer waits for image search.

Everything else is in the 0.2.4 release notes, and setup is covered in the watched folders docs. AssetHoard is free to download during the open beta.

If you have built file watching into a desktop app, I would like to hear how you handled renames and saves that replace files.

title: Building a Local AI SOC Lab with Wazuh and Qwen: Lessons from a Real Implementation
description:
Security monitoring generates a lot of data. But collecting alerts is only the beginning. The real challenge is retrieving the right events, understanding what happened, and making decisions based on evidence.

I wanted to explore a practical question:

Can a locally hosted AI model help a security analyst investigate Wazuh alerts without giving the AI control over the infrastructure?

To explore this, I built an isolated AI-assisted Security Operations Center (SOC) lab using Wazuh, OpenSearch, Python, SQLite, and a local Qwen model.

This is a manually operated proof of concept, not a production SOC or an autonomous security platform.

1. My Lab Architecture

The environment includes Ubuntu 24.04 virtual machines for security telemetry and Wazuh services, together with a Windows workstation running the Python assistant and LM Studio.

The main components are:

  • Wazuh Agent: collects security events from an Ubuntu endpoint.
  • Wazuh Manager and OpenSearch Indexer: process and store security alerts.
  • Python SOC Assistant: retrieves alerts and prepares them for analysis.
  • SQLite: tracks processed events and stores generated reports.
  • LM Studio + Qwen 3.5 4B Instruct: generates structured incident analysis proposals.
  • Human analyst: reviews findings and determines the next steps.

The assistant uses a restricted reader account. Access to the Indexer is protected through SSH port forwarding and TLS verification.

Important security boundary: The AI cannot execute firewall commands, modify server configurations, or automatically block IP addresses.

Its purpose is investigation support, not autonomous remediation.

2. The First Problem: Missing Alerts

My initial implementation retrieved only the 20 newest alerts.

This worked for a small demonstration, but it was not reliable when more events were present.

I improved the Python client using OpenSearch Scroll pagination to retrieve a bounded snapshot of matching alerts.

In one documented integration test:

152 matching alerts were reported by OpenSearch.

152 alerts were successfully retrieved.

152 unique event IDs were verified.

That confirmed the pagination logic worked correctly for that query snapshot.

It did not prove continuous monitoring or complete historical coverage.

I also encountered an Indexer permission issue affecting Scroll cleanup. Fixing the reader permissions was part of making the workflow reliable without giving it unnecessary access.

3. Why I Added SQLite

Originally, processed event IDs were tracked using a JSON file.

That approach was simple, but I wanted more reliable event state, recovery, and retry behavior.

I introduced SQLite to preserve processed identifiers and incident reports.

During verification, I successfully migrated 20 existing event IDs and confirmed database integrity.

I also tested restoring a synthetic incident report from the database after its Markdown export was missing.

This taught me an important engineering lesson:

AI analysis is only one part of the system. Reliable event state and recovery matter just as much.

4. Connecting a Local Qwen Model

The Python assistant connects to Qwen through LM Studio's local API-compatible endpoint.

The workflow sends selected security events to the model and requests structured JSON output.

The application validates required fields before saving a report.

In one test, I used a synthetic failed SSH authentication event.

Qwen proposed:

Disposition: SUSPICIOUS

Severity: LOW

Recommended action: Investigate and review related logs.

This was useful, but I also noticed how easily a language model could misinterpret technical context.

For example, a client source port can be confused with a destination service port. A single failed login also does not automatically indicate brute-force activity.

That is why I separate observed evidence from AI-generated hypotheses.

5. Prompt Injection in Security Logs

One of the most interesting experiments involved an untrusted SSH log message.

I tested synthetic log content containing text designed to manipulate the model into treating failed authentication as successful authentication.

In a documented retest, the model preserved the failed-login finding.

An earlier test also exposed an unsafe recommendation to block an IP address. I introduced conservative recommendation filtering and regression tests to help keep responses within the lab's read-only investigation scope.

These were limited experiments.

They do not demonstrate complete resistance to prompt injection or guarantee that every AI-generated recommendation is safe.

Security logs are evidence, not instructions.

Human review remains essential.

6. Testing and Verification

I wanted the project to demonstrate more than a working screenshot.

The repository includes 31 mocked and offline Python tests, exercised through GitHub Actions using Python 3.10 and 3.12.

The implementation also includes validation of event identity, persistent processing state, structured model responses, and read-only operational boundaries.

However, automated tests alone do not prove production security or detection accuracy.

The lab still has important limitations: manual execution, no continuous alert monitoring, and network restrictions around the local model service that require further verification before broader deployment.

7. What I Learned

Three lessons stand out from this project.

First, reliable data retrieval comes before AI analysis. Missing alerts can undermine even a well-written incident report.

Second, local AI can assist security investigations, but its output must be validated. A structured response is not necessarily a correct response.

Third, automation needs clear security boundaries. I prefer a system that helps an analyst understand an event over one that performs potentially harmful actions without approval.

My next areas of work include more realistic alert replay tests, better performance measurements, and stronger local-model network restrictions.

Project Resources

The public repository includes the Python implementation, tests, documentation, and sanitized verification examples.

GitHub: AI-Powered SOC Lab

Original engineering article: Building a Local AI SOC Lab with Wazuh and Qwen

I'm interested in how other engineers approach local AI for security operations.

Would you trust a local LLM to prepare incident triage reports if every recommendation required human approval?

Editorial disclosure: This DEV.to adaptation was prepared with AI writing assistance using my original engineering article and documented project results as source material.

title: firmware-auditor: Zero-Emulation Static Security Analysis for Firmware Rootfs in CI/CD
description:
Security assessments for IoT devices and embedded Linux systems have long relied on two main approaches: manual static inspection or full dynamic emulation (QEMU, Unicorn, Firmadyne, FirmAE).

Dynamic analysis is invaluable for verifying vulnerabilities, but plugging emulated environments into automated CI/CD pipelines often leads to:

  1. High execution overhead and slow feedback loops.
  2. Architecture incompatibilities: custom NVRAM, vendor peripherals and proprietary SoC hardware are exactly where generic emulators tend to break.
  3. Flaky automation that stalls pull requests.

To bridge this gap I built firmware-auditor: a fast, zero-emulation static analysis framework for unpacked root filesystem images.

The Core Idea: Reproducible Static Posture

When you have an unpacked SquashFS, ext4 or UBIFS rootfs, many security posture indicators can be checked entirely offline, without executing a single target binary:

  • ELF binary hardening: are binaries built with modern mitigations, or exposed to classic exploitation techniques?
  • Filesystem hygiene and secret exposure: did the build bake private SSH keys, a readable /etc/shadow or world-writable scripts into production?
  • Actionable DevSecOps gates: can the pipeline fail (exit 1) on critical issues and emit standardized, machine-readable results?

Here is what a run looks like. This is a test rootfs with intentionally planted flaws, not a real firmware image:

rootfs     : test_rootfs
duration   : 0.007s (workers=1)
severity   : >= info
analyzers  : binary_hardening 1.0.0 ok (0 findings, 0.004s)
             filesystem_hygiene 1.0.0 ok (5 findings, 0.002s)

SUMMARY BY SEVERITY
CRITICAL   5 ####################
HIGH       0
MEDIUM     0
LOW        0
TOTAL      5

FINDINGS BY RULE (4 rule(s), 5 finding(s))
SEVERITY RULE         COUNT LOCATION SAMPLE     TITLE
CRITICAL FWK-PERM-001     1 etc                 World-writable directory
CRITICAL FWK-KEY-001      1 etc/id_rsa          Private key material in the firmware image
CRITICAL FWK-PERM-002     2 etc/id_rsa; shadow  World-writable file in a sensitive tree
CRITICAL FWK-PERM-004     1 etc/shadow          Password hash database readable by any user

Architecture

The framework is written in Python 3.10+ with a modular design built around isolation and reproducibility:

firmware_auditor/
├── analyzers/
│   ├── base.py                 # Base analyzer & Finding contract
│   ├── binary_hardening.py     # ELF checks (NX, PIE, Canary, RELRO)
│   └── filesystem_hygiene.py   # Secrets, permissions, credentials
├── core/
│   ├── pipeline.py             # Concurrent runner, fault isolation
│   └── reporter.py             # Console, JSON and SARIF v2.1.0
└── tests/                      # pytest suite (Ubuntu & Windows)

Each analyzer runs behind a fault-isolation boundary with a timeout guard, so one broken analyzer or a malformed binary doesn't take down the whole scan.

1. ELF Hardening Inspections

Using pyelftools, the engine parses ELF headers directly:

  • NX / DEP: checks the PT_GNU_STACK flags for an executable stack. A missing PT_GNU_STACK header is also treated as an executable stack, since that is the default on several architectures common in firmware (ARM, MIPS).
  • PIE / ASLR: ET_DYN alone is not enough, because shared libraries are ET_DYN too. The engine separates PIE executables from .so files by checking for PT_INTERP and the DF_1_PIE flag in DT_FLAGS_1. ET_EXEC means a fixed load address.
  • Stack canaries: looks for __stack_chk_fail in .dynsym and .symtab.
  • RELRO: checks PT_GNU_RELRO for Partial RELRO, and for Full RELRO also requires immediate binding (DT_BIND_NOW, DF_BIND_NOW in DT_FLAGS, or DF_1_NOW in DT_FLAGS_1).

2. Filesystem Hygiene

Instead of running arbitrary regex over the entire filesystem, the module targets specific security attributes:

  • Checks permission masks (st_mode) on sensitive Unix paths (/etc, /bin, /sbin).
  • Detects unshadowed or empty password hashes in authentication files.
  • Identifies raw private key material without leaking the secret into CI logs or reports.

Note: permission checks need an extraction that preserves Unix modes (unsquashfs, tar, WSL or Linux). A rootfs copied onto NTFS loses this information, and permission findings will not be reliable.

3. Native SARIF Support for GitHub Code Scanning

firmware-auditor outputs SARIF v2.1.0 instead of a proprietary report format, so findings can show up directly under Security > Code scanning on GitHub:

firmware-auditor /path/to/extracted/rootfs \
  --format sarif \
  --output report.sarif \
  --fail-on high

GitHub Actions example 

name: firmware-audit
on: [pull_request]

permissions:
  contents: read
  security-events: write

jobs:
  audit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Install firmware-auditor
        run: |
          git clone https://github.com/RichJJ98/firmware-auditor
          pip install ./firmware-auditor

      - name: Extract rootfs (preserving permissions)
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y squashfs-tools
          sudo unsquashfs -f -d rootfs firmware.squashfs

      - name: Run audit
        run: firmware-auditor rootfs --format sarif --output report.sarif --fail-on high

      - name: Upload SARIF
        if: always()
        uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        with:
          sarif_file: report.sarif

The if: always() on the upload step matters: with --fail-on high the audit step exits non-zero, and without it the findings would never reach the Code scanning tab.

Limitations (What It Does Not Cover)

Static analysis has blind spots, and it is better to say so upfront:

  • Not a replacement for dynamic analysis. It won't confirm exploitability or find runtime and logic vulnerabilities.
  • No CVE matching of bundled library versions (yet).
  • Possible false negatives on canaries: stripped or statically linked binaries may not expose __stack_chk_fail.
  • Needs an already unpacked rootfs. Extraction (binwalk, unsquashfs, etc.) is a separate step, and encrypted or proprietary containers are out of scope.
  • Permission checks depend on extraction fidelity (see the note above).

Open Source & Next Steps

firmware-auditor is released under the MIT License, and the test suite runs in CI on both Linux and Windows.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/RichJJ98/firmware-auditor

If you work with embedded devices, IoT security or DevSecOps pipelines, clone it, try it on your own firmware images and contribute new rule modules. Feedback, issues and pull requests are very welcome.

title: Building a Dynamic Tax & Account Code Validation Engine for Financial Data Pipelines
description:
When you're building software that interfaces with financial systems like Xero, schema validation is only half the battle. You can parse CSV syntax and format dates all day long, but your pipeline will still fail if the business logic layer encounters an unverified tax rate or a missing ledger account code.

In this post, let's look at how we architected a robust validation and mapping layer for Sync2Zero to catch tax rate mismatches and account code errors before files hit accounting software ingestion gates.

The Problem: Strict Financial Taxonomy Validation

When users upload supplier invoices or generate CSV exports, software platforms enforce rigid foreign-key-style constraints on text fields. If a user inputs a custom string for a tax rate or account code that doesn't exist in their target Xero organization, the platform rejects the payload.

Common edge cases that break production imports include:

  • Unrecognized Tax Strings: Mismatched casing, shorthand abbreviations, or regional tax variances (20% (VAT) vs Standard Rate).
  • Orphaned Account Codes: Line items referencing ledger codes that haven't been provisioned in the organization's chart of accounts.

Implementing a Pre-Flight Validation Layer

To prevent runtime failures during bulk imports, we implemented a pre-flight validation check that inspects and normalizes ledger mappings against organization schemas:

interface TaxMappingRule {
  alias: string[];
  officialCode: string;
}

const SUPPORTED_TAX_MAPS: TaxMappingRule[] = [
  { alias: ['vat', '20% vat', 'standard vat'], officialCode: 'OUTPUT20' },
  { alias: ['zero rated', '0% vat', 'exempt'], officialCode: 'EXEMPT' }
];

function resolveTaxCode(rawInput: string): string {
  const normalized = rawInput.trim().toLowerCase();
  const match = SUPPORTED_TAX_MAPS.find(rule => rule.alias.includes(normalized));

  if (!match) {
    throw new Error(`Unrecognized tax code identifier: "${rawInput}". Please verify your chart of accounts.`);
  }

  return match.officialCode;
}

1. Alias Matching & Normalization

Instead of letting raw user strings pass through to the parser, our ingestion layer normalizes input strings and matches them against known regional tax aliases.

2. Hard Stop Warnings

If a tax code or account code fails lookup resolution, the engine halts the export, flagging the exact row and column for the user to review in the dashboard UI rather than failing silently inside Xero.

Wrapping Up

Building developer tools in the fintech space means designing systems that anticipate human data entry inconsistencies. Handling tax and account code mapping gracefully is key to high-conversion SaaS workflows.

If you're building document parsers or invoice automation pipelines, check out what we're building at sync2zero.com. I'd love to hear how your teams handle taxonomy mapping in the comments!

title: Leader Election
description:
In a distributed system, sometimes exactly ONE node must act as the "leader". How do you pick it?

Why Leader Election?

Some tasks must run on exactly one node:

  • Sending scheduled emails (don't send twice)
  • Coordinating distributed transactions
  • Acting as primary in a database cluster
  • Processing a specific partition of a queue

Problem: Nodes can crash. The leader must be detected as dead and a new one elected.

Algorithms

Bully Algorithm

  • Node with highest ID wins
  • When a node thinks the leader is dead → sends election messages to all higher-ID nodes
  • If no response → declares itself leader
  • ✅ Simple | ❌ Many messages, assumes ordered IDs

Raft Consensus

  • Nodes vote for a leader candidate
  • Candidate needs majority vote (quorum)
  • Leader sends heartbeats; if missed → new election
  • ✅ Well-proven, used in production systems
  • Used by: etcd, CockroachDB, TiKV

ZooKeeper / etcd-based Leader Election (Practical) 

All nodes race to create an ephemeral node:
  /election/leader

First node to create it → wins leadership
Others watch the node for deletion (leader crash)
On deletion → race again
  • ✅ Battle-tested, you don't implement the algorithm yourself
  • ✅ Ephemeral nodes auto-delete when the session dies (crash detection built in)
  • ❌ Adds ZooKeeper/etcd as dependency

Split-Brain Problem

What if the network partitions and both halves elect a leader?

  • Two leaders making conflicting decisions = data corruption
  • Solution: quorum — leader must maintain majority (N/2 + 1) connections
  • If minority partition can't reach quorum → steps down

Real-World Usage

System Leader Election
Kafka ZooKeeper (legacy) / KRaft (new) for controller
Elasticsearch Zen Discovery / Raft-based
Redis Sentinel Sentinel quorum for primary election
PostgreSQL HA Patroni uses etcd/ZooKeeper

title: Queue depth lies when one Service Bus queue serves every customer
description:
Here's the design question that keeps coming back on our SaaS platform: one queue, shared by every customer, sitting between the cloud product and whatever the customer runs on-prem. Is that one queue enough? Scalable enough, reliable enough? I think the answer is yes for a surprisingly long time. What I don't think survives is the dashboard most teams put on top of it.

Start with the plumbing, because the on-prem link is where the decision actually gets made.

There are two ways to get the cloud talking to a customer's data centre. You can have the cloud call in over HTTP, a trigger that hits an endpoint on their side. Or you can put a broker in the middle, Service Bus say, and let the on-prem agent reach out and pull. I'm firmly in the second camp. Customers' firewall teams will say no to inbound holes. They rarely object to an outbound connection on 443 from one agent. And an HTTP trigger has an ugly failure mode: when the customer's site is down for maintenance, your caller either blocks, retries in a tight loop, or drops the call. A queue just holds the message.

That last point is the whole value. The queue turns "the customer is offline" from an incident into a backlog.

Now the multi-tenant part. A single queue for all customers is cheap and simple, and the usual objection is noisy neighbours: one customer bulk-loads fifty thousand messages and everyone behind them waits. That's real. But it's a fairness problem, not a capacity problem, and the two get different fixes. Capacity you buy: Premium tier, more messaging units, partitioning. Fairness you design: session IDs keyed on tenant, so ordering holds per customer and a slow consumer for one tenant doesn't block the others' sessions.

Sessions have a cost. A session-enabled queue means every receiver has to accept a session before it reads anything, and a tenant's session is locked to one receiver at a time. That caps single-tenant throughput at what one receiver can chew through. For most B2B integration traffic that's fine. For a tenant who really does send in bursts, give them their own queue. I'd rather have a shared default and a handful of promoted exceptions than start with queue-per-tenant and own a thousand entities in the deployment pipeline.

So far so ordinary. Here's where I think teams get hurt.

They wire up an alert on active message count. Over 5,000, page someone. It feels right. It's wrong in a multi-tenant queue, and wrong in a specific way: it measures the sum of everybody, and the sum hides the one person who is actually broken.

Picture it. Customer A's on-prem agent lost its credentials on Tuesday afternoon. Their messages pile up, 300 of them. Total queue depth is 300 on a queue that normally runs at 2,000 during business hours. No alert. Nothing looks unusual. Customer A finds out their data hasn't synced for two days when they phone support on Thursday.

Depth fails you in both directions. A big batch from a healthy tenant trips the alarm while every message is being consumed on time. A stuck tenant stays under the threshold forever because the rest of the queue is quiet.

The metric I want instead is the age of the oldest unprocessed message, per tenant. A stuck tenant shows up in minutes, because their oldest message keeps getting older while every other tenant's resets constantly. A bulk load from a healthy tenant shows high depth but a low, flat age. Age separates "busy" from "broken", and depth cannot.

Getting it isn't free. Service Bus doesn't hand you per-session oldest-age as a built-in metric, so you stamp the enqueue time and the tenant ID on every message, and emit the delay from the consumer when it completes one. That gives you processing latency per tenant, which is already useful. For the stuck case, where nothing is completing at all, you need a second signal: a small scheduled check that peeks the head of the queue and flags any tenant with a message older than your threshold. Peek doesn't lock anything, so it's safe to run every minute. Messy, yes. Still much cheaper than the Thursday phone call.

Dead-letter needs the same treatment. A total dead-letter count of 40 means nothing until you know 38 of them belong to one tenant whose payloads started failing schema validation after a release. Tag it, group by tenant, alert on a tenant crossing a number rather than the queue crossing one.

I'll admit the counterpoint with some weight behind it: per-tenant tracking adds cardinality, and metrics platforms bill on it. If you have ten thousand tenants, per-tenant time series is its own cost problem. Fine. Track the top offenders, or sample. But even at that scale, I'd take the oldest-age-by-tenant on the worst twenty over a perfect global depth chart.

On reliability, the answer to "one queue for all customers" comes down to three choices, and none is exotic. Turn on duplicate detection, since the on-prem agent will retry and you don't want a customer's order processed twice. Set max delivery count deliberately, because the default of 10 means a poison message cycles ten times before dead-lettering, and in a session queue that stalls the whole tenant while it does. And make the on-prem consumer idempotent regardless, because duplicate detection only covers the window you configured.

Where does that leave the original question? One queue is fine to start. HTTP triggers into customer networks are the thing I'd avoid. But the part that deserves your design time isn't the topology at all. It's whether, on a quiet Tuesday, you would find out that one customer has been silently stuck since lunch.

If your current alert can't answer that, the queue is not the thing to fix.
