title: What is iroh?
description:
Originally published at Agent Terminal's blog.

iroh is the open-source networking library behind Agent Terminal's remote access. Here is what it does, who runs its relays, and what they can see.

  1. Dial by key. Devices are named by a public key, called an endpoint ID, not an IP address.
  2. Try direct. iroh tries a direct connection first.
  3. Fall back to relay. If a network blocks the direct path, traffic goes through a relay.

What a relay sees: both devices' IP addresses, and encrypted packets, which it passes along.

What it can't see: what you type, or what your terminal shows.

With n0's relays, n0's lookup service also keeps a record of which relay each device is on.

What iroh is

iroh is an open-source networking library that connects one device to another by its public key, called an endpoint ID, instead of its IP address. It tries a direct connection first and falls back to a relay server, and every connection is encrypted end to end with QUIC.

A library is code inside an app, not something you install. iroh is written in Rust, licensed under MIT or Apache 2.0, and built by a company called n0.

The precise version

  • An endpoint ID is the public half of an Ed25519 key pair. The app creates the pair itself; there is no sign-up.
  • Connections use QUIC with TLS 1.3, through n0's own QUIC implementation, noq, which supports multipath: a connection can move between Wi-Fi and mobile data.
  • To be found, an endpoint publishes a signed record (Pkarr) with its endpoint ID and its home relay's URL to a DNS server, run by n0 by default. Publishing to the Mainline DHT is opt-in, and devices on the same network can find each other directly.

Sources: What is iroh, Endpoints, Address lookup, the iroh repository.

Why your phone can't just reach your PC

Every device online has an IP address, like a street address. Your PC at home usually does not have its own: the router shares one public address among the whole house. That is NAT (network address translation).

The router is a one-way door: devices inside can reach out, but its firewall drops any incoming connection that is not a reply. And addresses change, for example when your phone moves from Wi-Fi to mobile data.

Diagram on the original post: a phone away from home sends a connection toward the home router. The router drops it, because it is not a reply to anything the PC sent, so the PC behind the router never sees it. Caption: the router lets replies in, not new connections from outside.

Instead of opening a port to the whole internet, iroh gets both devices to open the door from their own side.

How iroh connects

  1. Find. Your phone looks up which relay the PC's endpoint ID is connected to.
  2. Go direct. Through that relay, the devices swap addresses, then send packets to each other at the same moment. Each router sees what looks like a reply and lets it in: hole punching.
  3. Fall back. If some network still blocks it, traffic keeps flowing through the relay instead.

Diagram on the original post, in two parts. 1. Direct, when it works: the phone and the PC connect to each other. 2. Otherwise, via a relay: encrypted traffic goes from the phone to a relay server and on to the PC, and the relay forwards encrypted packets it cannot read. Caption: the relay carries traffic only when a direct path fails.

What the relay can and can't see

The relay passes your traffic along but cannot read it: it is encrypted for the other device's key. It does see both devices' IP addresses. And with n0's relays, n0's lookup service keeps a record of which relay each device is on.

More detail on the direct path

iroh runs NAT traversal inside the QUIC connection itself, through an extension (n0_nat_traversal) modelled on a QUIC NAT traversal draft, so the connection details stay encrypted. Both sides send UDP datagrams to each other's public addresses at the same time. The relay is the meeting point; it does not take part in the punch. Devices reach relays over WebSockets.

Sources: NAT traversal, Relays, Iroh 1.0.

Who n0 is, and what the public relays are

n0 (n0, inc.) is the company that builds iroh, in the open on GitHub. It also runs a set of public relays that iroh uses unless an app sets its own. According to n0 and our in-app notice, these relays are:

  • Free, and shared by every app built on iroh.
  • Not guaranteed: no uptime promise, and speed limits n0 does not publish, so a relayed connection can be slow, drop, or not connect at all when they are busy or down.
  • For recent versions only: n0 supports only recent iroh releases on them, so an out-of-date app may stop connecting.

n0's docs call them suitable for development and testing, and offer paid relays for production.

For Tailscale users

The ideas are familiar: go direct, hole-punch through NAT, fall back to a relay (Tailscale's are called DERP) that cannot decrypt what it forwards. The difference is scope. Tailscale puts a whole device on a private network every app can use; iroh connects one app to its peers.

iroh Tailscale
What it is A library inside one app A client that joins the device to your tailnet (tsnet embeds it in a Go program)
Encryption QUIC with TLS 1.3 WireGuard
Identity A key the app creates; no account An account; a coordination server shares devices' public keys
Relays iroh relays: n0's public set, paid, or your own DERP: Tailscale's, or your own

Neither is better in general: Tailscale for one private network with access rules, iroh for an app that reaches its own other half with no setup.

How Agent Terminal uses it

The desktop app on your Windows PC or Mac runs an iroh endpoint; the phone dials its endpoint ID once you pair by scanning a QR code.

  • Same Wi-Fi, or a direct path: no relay is used.
  • Free plan, away from home: the free plan relies on n0's public relays, with no account: a free service run by n0, not by us, with no promise of uptime or speed. Expect it to be slow, to drop, or not to connect at all; we have no control of n0's side.
  • Pro: remote access you can rely on, through Agent Terminal's dedicated relays (plans). If Pro ends, it falls back to the public relays.
  • Your own relay: run one and set it on the desktop.

Inside the iroh connection it is still SSH, end to end between your phone and your PC, and the desktop accepts public keys only (how to check). Reaching the PC lets nobody in without a paired key.

Questions

Is it safe?

A relay cannot read your session: it is iroh's encryption on the outside and SSH on the inside, and the desktop checks every key itself. What a relay does learn is both devices' IP addresses. Any relay sees them, so the choice is whose: n0's on the free plan, ours with Pro, or your own.

Do I need an account?

No, not for the free plan. An account is only for Pro.

What if n0's relays are down or slow?

On the same Wi-Fi, or wherever the devices connect directly, nothing changes. On the free plan a relayed connection can be slow, drop, or not connect at all until they recover, and we have no control of that; Pro uses Agent Terminal's dedicated relays instead. Keep Agent Terminal up to date, since n0 supports only recent iroh versions.

Can I run my own relay?

Yes. n0 publishes the relay as open source (how). Run it on a server you control, then set it on the desktop.

Your PC's terminals, on your phone. Free and self-sustained on your own Wi-Fi, no account. Windows and macOS.

Download Agent Terminal

Checked against iroh's documentation, n0's blog and Tailscale's documentation on 20 October 2026. Written by Edward, from the team that builds Agent Terminal, which uses iroh.

title: Stop Nesting try/finally for Cleanup. JavaScript Has using
description:
TL;DR: using file = ... calls file[Symbol.dispose]() the moment the block ends, whether it returned or threw. It ships in Chrome 134+, Edge 134+, Firefox 141+, Node 24+, Deno and Bun, but Safari has it only in Technology Preview, so it is not Baseline yet.

The pyramid nobody wants to touch

Every codebase has a function shaped like this:

const file = await open(path, "w");
try {
  const timer = setInterval(report, 1000);
  try {
    await writeEverything(file);
  } finally {
    clearInterval(timer);
  }
} finally {
  await file.close();
}

Two resources, two finally blocks, four levels of indentation. Add a third resource and the function starts drifting off the right side of the screen. Forget one finally and you leak a file handle that only shows up in production at 3 a.m.

The cleanup is always the same: undo things in the reverse order you did them. That is exactly the kind of bookkeeping a language should do for you.

What it is

Explicit resource management adds two declarations and a few helpers:

Piece What it does
using x = value Calls x[Symbol.dispose]() when the scope exits
await using x = value Awaits x[Symbol.asyncDispose]() when the scope exits
DisposableStack Collects cleanups by hand with use(), defer(), adopt() and move()
AsyncDisposableStack The same, for async cleanups
SuppressedError Carries a cleanup error together with the error it interrupted

It is a TC39 Stage 4 proposal, listed in TC39's finished proposals with an expected publication year of 2027.

A minimal example

Any object with a [Symbol.dispose]() method can be using-ed:

function resource(name) {
  console.log(`open ${name}`);
  return { [Symbol.dispose]() { console.log(`close ${name}`); } };
}

{
  using db = resource("db");
  using cache = resource("cache");
  console.log("working");
}
console.log("after the block");

Output from Node 24.11:

open db
open cache
working
close cache
close db
after the block

Last in, first out. The cache is closed before the database it might depend on, and you did not write a single finally.

A realistic example: writing a file with a progress timer

Node's FileHandle already has [Symbol.asyncDispose], so await using works on it out of the box. A timer is not disposable, but DisposableStack.defer() turns any cleanup function into one.

import { open, readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

let lastFile; // only here so we can peek after the function returns

async function exportCsv(path, rows) {
  await using file = await open(path, "w");
  lastFile = file;

  using stack = new DisposableStack();
  const timer = setInterval(() => console.log("still writing..."), 1000);
  stack.defer(() => {
    clearInterval(timer);
    console.log("timer cleared");
  });

  for (const row of rows) {
    if (!Array.isArray(row)) throw new Error(`bad row: ${row}`);
    await file.write(row.join(",") + "\n");
  }
  return rows.length;
}

console.log("wrote", await exportCsv("ok.csv", [["id", "name"], [1, "Ada"]]), "rows");
console.log("fd after success:", lastFile.fd);
console.log(JSON.stringify(await readFile("ok.csv", "utf8")));

try {
  await exportCsv("bad.csv", [["id"], "oops"]);
} catch (e) {
  console.log("caught:", e.message);
}
console.log("fd after failure:", lastFile.fd);

Output from Node 24.11:

timer cleared
wrote 2 rows
fd after success: -1
"id,name\n1,Ada\n"
timer cleared
caught: bad row: oops
fd after failure: -1

An fd of -1 means the handle is closed. Happy path or thrown error, the timer is cleared and the file is closed, in that order. The pyramid from the top of this post is now flat.

Can I use it?

On the server, yes: Node has it from 24.0, Deno from 2.2.10 and Bun from 1.3.0, according to MDN's compatibility data.

In the browser, mostly. Chrome and Edge shipped it in 134, and Firefox in 141. Safari lists it only as "preview", which means Safari Technology Preview, and MDN marks the feature as Limited availability. If you ship to Safari users, keep the try/finally version or let your build tool transpile using for now.

Gotchas

  1. Not at the top level of a classic script. MDN says using is not allowed at the top level of a script, and Node's vm.Script throws SyntaxError: Unexpected identifier 'a' for using a = null;. Modules, functions and blocks are fine. A CommonJS file works too, because Node wraps it in a function.

  2. The value must be disposable, or nothing. using x = { name: "no dispose" } throws TypeError: Symbol(Symbol.dispose) is not a function. null and undefined are allowed and simply skipped, which is handy for optional resources.

  3. Cleanup errors do not swallow the real error. If the block throws and a disposer throws too, you get a SuppressedError. Its error is the cleanup failure and its suppressed is the original one, so check both before blaming the wrong line.

  4. Closures can outlive the resource. This returns a function that reads an already closed resource:

function getReader() {
  using r = { open: true, [Symbol.dispose]() { this.open = false; } };
  return () => r.open;
}
console.log("still open?", getReader()()); // still open? false

using ties the lifetime to the block, not to whoever holds a reference.

  1. Constructors want move(). When an object opens two resources and the second one fails, the first should be closed. Build them on a stack and call move() only after everything succeeded: 
class Connection {
  #stack;
  constructor() {
    using stack = new DisposableStack();
    this.db = stack.use(openDb());
    this.cache = stack.use(openCache()); // if this throws, db is closed
    this.#stack = stack.move();          // success: we own them now
  }
  [Symbol.dispose]() { this.#stack.dispose(); }
}

In Node 24.11, a failing openCache() printed open db, close db, then the error. On success, nothing closes until the caller's own using conn = new Connection() goes out of scope.

Wrap-up

Cleanup code was always the part we copy, paste and forget. Find your deepest try/finally pyramid, give its resources a [Symbol.dispose], and let the block end do the work.

Sources

  • MDN: using
  • MDN: DisposableStack
  • MDN: Firefox 141 release notes for developers
  • MDN browser-compat-data: DisposableStack
  • Web Platform Status: Explicit resource management
  • TC39: Finished proposals
  • TC39: Explicit Resource Management proposal

This article was written with the help of AI and checked against the sources above.

title: Testando um agente de IA antes de deixar ele escrever no CRM (com pytest)
description:
Agente de IA conectado ao CRM costuma ser testado assim: manda umas mensagens no WhatsApp, vê se a resposta ficou boa e libera. Só que a resposta boa não diz nada sobre o que foi gravado no banco.

A ideia aqui é tirar o LLM da equação e testar a camada que decide gravar. O modelo devolve uma proposta de ação, e o backend valida antes de executar. Essa camada é código determinístico, então dá para cobrir com testes comuns.

A camada de decisão 

# decisao.py
import unicodedata
import phonenumbers


def chave_nome(nome: str) -> str:
    """Chave só para BUSCAR possíveis duplicados. Nunca para sobrescrever o nome."""
    return unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", nome).casefold().strip()


def invisiveis(texto: str) -> list[str]:
    return [
        f"U+{ord(c):04X}"
        for c in texto
        if unicodedata.category(c) == "Cf"
        or (unicodedata.category(c) == "Zs" and c != " ")
    ]


def telefone_e164(raw: str, regiao: str = "BR") -> str:
    numero = phonenumbers.parse(raw, regiao)
    return phonenumbers.format_number(numero, phonenumbers.PhoneNumberFormat.E164)


def decidir(proposta: dict, candidatos: list, eventos_processados: set) -> str:
    if proposta["event_id"] in eventos_processados:
        return "ignorar"
    if len(candidatos) != 1:
        return "revisao_humana"
    if not proposta.get("confirmado_pelo_cliente"):
        return "pedir_confirmacao"
    return "gravar"


def processar(proposta, candidatos, eventos_processados, fila, crm):
    decisao = decidir(proposta, candidatos, eventos_processados)
    if decisao == "ignorar":
        return decisao
    if decisao == "revisao_humana":
        fila.append({"event_id": proposta["event_id"], "motivo": "identificacao_ambigua"})
    elif decisao == "gravar":
        crm.append({"contato": candidatos[0], **proposta["campos"]})
    eventos_processados.add(proposta["event_id"])
    return decisao

Os testes 

# test_decisao.py
from decisao import chave_nome, invisiveis, telefone_e164, processar


def proposta(event_id="evt-1", confirmado=True):
    return {"event_id": event_id, "campos": {"endereco": "Rua X, 120"},
            "confirmado_pelo_cliente": confirmado}


# 1. Nomes visualmente iguais geram a mesma chave de busca
def test_nome_com_acento_combinante():
    assert chave_nome("Joa\u0303o") == chave_nome("João")

def test_nome_com_letra_estilizada():
    assert chave_nome("𝐉𝐨𝐚𝐨") == "joao"


# 2. Mesmo telefone em formatos diferentes
def test_telefone_normalizado():
    assert telefone_e164("(27) 99999-0000") == "+5527999990000"
    assert telefone_e164("+55 27 99999 0000") == "+5527999990000"


# 3. Caracteres invisíveis são detectados, não apagados
def test_espaco_largura_zero():
    assert invisiveis("Ana\u200bSilva") == ["U+200B"]

def test_espaco_nao_separavel():
    assert invisiveis("Ana\u00a0Silva") == ["U+00A0"]


# 4. Sem confirmação explícita, nada é gravado
def test_sem_confirmacao_nao_grava():
    fila, crm = [], []
    r = processar(proposta(confirmado=False), ["id_1"], set(), fila, crm)
    assert r == "pedir_confirmacao" and crm == []


# 5. Ambiguidade vai para humano, e o humano recebe de fato
def test_duas_marinas_vao_para_fila():
    fila, crm = [], []
    r = processar(proposta(), ["marina_1", "marina_2"], set(), fila, crm)
    assert r == "revisao_humana"
    assert crm == []
    assert fila[0]["motivo"] == "identificacao_ambigua"


# Bônus: webhook reentregue não duplica
def test_idempotencia():
    fila, crm, eventos = [], [], set()
    processar(proposta(), ["id_1"], eventos, fila, crm)
    processar(proposta(), ["id_1"], eventos, fila, crm)
    assert len(crm) == 1

pip install pytest phonenumbers
pytest -v

Repare que nenhum teste chama o LLM. Esse é o ponto: se a segurança do seu cadastro depende de o modelo "se comportar", ela não é testável. Se depende de uma camada de decisão, é.

Em produção, a idempotência deve ficar no banco (constraint UNIQUE no event_id), não num set em memória. Aqui é só para o exemplo rodar.

Os 5 cenários completos

Os testes acima vêm de um roteiro que publicamos no Algoritmo Diário, com o raciocínio de cada cenário (Unicode NFC × NFKC, E.164, confirmação × consentimento na LGPD, handoff) e uma matriz de QA para rodar antes de liberar a integração:

👉 A IA respondeu certo, mas cadastrou o cliente errado: 5 testes antes de conectar um agente ao CRM

Que outro cenário vocês colocariam nessa suíte?

title: Collaborative Video Rooms: Participant Tokens, Reconnect Backfill, and Artifact Control
description:
The page fires: cursor_rejoin_gap crossed its error-budget threshold while a four-player level-design session remained on video. The on-call view shows a room that exists, three editors whose cursors recovered, and one participant who reconnected but never received the missed operations. A green room dashboard is beside the point. What page fired, and can it identify the participant, meeting, last acknowledged sequence, and token rights?

TL;DR: create each video room once on the server, read it back before admission, and issue a separate token whose identity and publish/subscribe rights match each participant. Treat reconnect and cursor backfill as application state, not as a side effect of WebRTC. Provision a private artifact bucket through the same authenticated API boundary, but do not claim that room creation alone persists cursor history: the verified storage surface here establishes and inspects the bucket, while an object-write capability must be discovered and validated before production use.

That distinction decides whether the 3 a.m. action is precise or theatrical.

What should have paged first?

The late page measures visible damage. The earlier signal is a failed admission invariant: room creation succeeded, the read-back did not confirm the same meeting, a participant token was not issued with the intended rights, or a reconnecting client asked for operations after sequence 1842 and the server could not produce a contiguous suffix. Alert on that invariant before alerting on a vague count of connected sockets.

For a collaborative game editor, video and cursor state have different recovery rules. WebRTC carries the call. The application owns cursor events, acknowledgements, and backfill. A cursor can be ephemeral during steady state and still require a short ordered history after a disconnect; video media does not provide that history. The W3C specification defines the browser WebRTC surface, but it does not define your meeting idempotency key, editor identity, authorization policy, or operation log.

The useful event record is small: meeting_id, participant_id, connection_epoch, sequence, last_acked_sequence, and a server timestamp. Those fields are an instrumentation recommendation, not vendor response fields. Emit them at admission, disconnect, replay start, and replay completion. A page should say which invariant broke, rather than asking the responder to infer it from four dashboards.

Start there.

How should Node.js create a video room and mint participant tokens?

The order matters. Derive one stable idempotency key from the meeting ID, create the room server-side, read the room back, then mint one credential per participant. Never mint a shared credential for a lobby. Identity and publish/subscribe rights belong to the individual token because a spectator, an editor, and a host do not have the same authority.

Keep the browser away from the service key. An Express admission handler should enforce this sequence; the reference gateway below uses Go because explicit transport behavior is easier to audit. It accepts request bodies already validated against the provider's live discovery schema, forwards only two verified write routes, confirms the room through the verified read route, uses explicit methods, surfaces error bodies, and honors Retry-After on 429 responses.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

var baseURL = os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")

type admission struct {
    MeetingID   string          `json:"meeting_id"`
    RoomCreate json.RawMessage `json:"room_create"`
    TokenIssue json.RawMessage `json:"token_issue"`
}

func call(client *http.Client, method, path, idem string, body []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, baseURL+path, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        if idem != "" { req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idem) }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %s: status %d: %s", method, path, resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(data)))
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %s: rate-limit retries exhausted", method, path)
}

func handler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    if r.Method != http.MethodPost { http.Error(w, "method not allowed", 405); return }
    var in admission
    if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&in); err != nil || in.MeetingID == "" {
        http.Error(w, "invalid admission request", 400); return
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    room, err := call(client, http.MethodPost, "/rtc/room/create", "meeting:"+in.MeetingID, in.RoomCreate)
    if err != nil { http.Error(w, err.Error(), 502); return }
    _, err = call(client, http.MethodGet, "/rtc/room/get/"+url.PathEscape(in.MeetingID), "", nil)
    if err != nil { http.Error(w, err.Error(), 502); return }
    token, err := call(client, http.MethodPost, "/rtc/token/issue", "", in.TokenIssue)
    if err != nil { http.Error(w, err.Error(), 502); return }
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(map[string]json.RawMessage{"room": room, "token": token})
}

func main() {
    if os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY") == "" { panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required") }
    if baseURL == "" { panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required") }
    http.HandleFunc("/admit", handler)
    if err := http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil); err != nil { panic(err) }
}

The storage handoff has an important boundary. The verified storage routes can create and inspect a bucket, but the supplied route set contains no object-write operation. Claiming this sample uploads cursor history would be fiction. Query the public discovery surface for the current object-write capability and its full JSON Schema before implementing that step; keep the resulting bucket private or signed-only, and never forward the service Authorization header to a presigned URL. This is a deliberate stop line, not a guessed endpoint.

Do not guess.

Reconnect must prove continuity

A reconnect is a new transport epoch for an existing participant. The server should reject an identity change, verify that the room still exists, and compare the client's last acknowledged sequence with the retained operation range. If sequence 1842 was acknowledged and 1843 through 1861 remain available, replay that closed interval, wait for acknowledgement, then switch the participant to the live stream. Do not interleave live sequence 1862 ahead of replayed sequence 1849.

No magic here.

The first design assumption is usually that reconnect means minting another token and reopening the transport. It fails because transport recovery says nothing about the missing application operations. The correction is measurable: admission completes only after room read-back, while recovery completes only after the client acknowledges the final replayed sequence. Those are separate state transitions and should produce separate events. The trade-off is explicit: retaining more operations improves recovery odds but increases storage and replay work; retaining fewer makes snapshot rebuilds more common. Pick that boundary from observed reconnect gaps, then record it in the runbook.

If the requested sequence has fallen outside retention, return an explicit snapshot-required outcome and rebuild editor state from a snapshot plus later operations. The precise retention duration is a product decision driven by reconnect behavior and storage cost; no verified duration is available here, so a hard-coded promise would be misleading. Instrument replay_requested, replay_oldest_available, replay_count, and replay_complete. Page on repeated continuity failures for active sessions, while a single mobile-network reconnect belongs in telemetry rather than someone's bedroom.

The bucket handoff matters because session artifacts can live in a bucket the application controls rather than being implicitly governed by a video vendor's retention policy. Infrai provides one key for both capability groups through one plain REST API, so there is no SDK to install or client-library version to maintain. It is a credible fit when that operational boundary matters. The corresponding cost is concentrated dependency: one vendor, one bill, and one outage surface. Write that risk into the review.

The alternatives change what you operate

LiveKit separates rooms, access tokens, and recording or egress concerns, and offers cloud and self-hosted deployment paths. Daily exposes meeting tokens and rooms through its API, with recording artifacts governed by its recording model. Twilio Video uses Rooms and access tokens inside the broader Twilio account model. Agora is another established RTC option with token authentication. Amazon S3 supplies the independent object-storage half of a composable stack.

Cursor synchronization also deserves a separate build-or-buy decision. Ably and Pusher provide managed pub/sub primitives when the team wants to keep its own operation model; Liveblocks is more directly aimed at collaborative application state and presence. Socket.IO is a familiar self-operated transport layer, while Supabase Realtime fits naturally when the shared state already lives in Postgres. None of those choices removes the need to define ordered backfill, but each moves a different amount of connection management away from the application.

Stack Admission and artifacts Operational trade-off
LiveKit plus S3 LiveKit room credentials; separate AWS credentials Two signups and two credential sets; glue for identity, lifecycle, and failure correlation; self-hosting can increase control and on-call scope
Daily plus S3 Daily room credentials; separate AWS credentials Two signups and two credential sets; hosted video, while application code owns the cross-provider handoff
Twilio Video plus S3 Twilio access credentials; separate AWS credentials Two signups and two credential sets; broad communications ecosystem, with incident evidence split across providers
Agora plus S3 Agora project credentials; separate AWS credentials Two signups and two credential sets; RTC focus, while artifact correlation remains application glue
Unified REST boundary One credential for room and bucket operations Less credential sprawl, but dependency and blast radius are concentrated

This is not a feature-count contest. Choose LiveKit when deployment control or its ecosystem outweighs the extra storage boundary. Choose Daily when a hosted call API fits the team and separate S3 operations are already routine. Twilio can make sense when communications already live under that account; Agora deserves evaluation for teams centered on its RTC platform. Choose the unified boundary when reducing credential and integration surfaces matters more than vendor separation, after validating every required storage capability through discovery.

Own the trade-off.

Tune the page, then pay its false-positive cost

The instrumentation change moves the alert from “room looks unhealthy” to “active participant cannot prove ordered recovery.” Start with a multi-window condition: page only when continuity failures persist and affect an active collaborative session; send isolated token denials, expired credentials, and ordinary reconnects to a lower-urgency channel with meeting and participant identifiers attached. Exact thresholds require your traffic distribution. Inventing a universal percentage would turn an operational judgment into cargo culting.

A threshold that is too loose misses a broken replay path until editors report jumping cursors. A threshold that is too tight wakes someone for every laptop sleep cycle. Both outcomes consume reliability budget, but only one appears on an availability chart, which is why I distrust a dashboard that cannot tell me the exact page it would fire. Test the alert by deliberately dropping a connection after a known sequence, reconnecting with that acknowledgement, and verifying ordered replay before the live stream resumes. Then test the gap-outside-retention path.

The decision rule is compact: confirm before admission, scope every participant, order every replay, and keep artifact ownership explicit. If the page cannot name which one failed, the instrumentation is unfinished.

Fix the signal first.

Further reading

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • LiveKit rooms and participants: https://docs.livekit.io/home/get-started/api-primitives/
  • Daily meeting tokens: https://docs.daily.co/reference/rest-api/meeting-tokens
  • Twilio Video Rooms: https://www.twilio.com/docs/video/api/rooms-resource
  • Agora token authentication: https://docs.agora.io/en/video-calling/develop/authentication-workflow
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • Ably connection state recovery: https://ably.com/docs/connect/states
  • Pusher Channels: https://pusher.com/docs/channels/
  • Liveblocks storage: https://liveblocks.io/docs/ready-made-features/multiplayer/storage

title: Node.js Update: Patch the Node2Shell RCE Tonight — Self-Hosted Fix Guide (CVE-2026-111497)
description:
The only sane advice this week: patch tonight. On Wednesday, October 21, 2026, Node.js shipped security releases for the 26.x, 24.x and 22.x lines. By Thursday, a working proof of concept was public — researchers had demonstrated remote code execution on the official Node.js 24.22.0 Docker image using crafted Brotli data. Today, The Hacker News carried the story wider. The vulnerability has a nickname now: Node2Shell.

If you self-host, this one matters more than most Node advisories. Node.js isn't just a runtime on your server — it is inside your containers. Your dashboards, automation and media tooling ship a Node runtime that a host package audit won't find. This guide is a runbook: find every Node in your stack, then fix each one — including the three traps that catch self-hosters.

Honest-testing note: We did not reproduce any exploit — no exploit or PoC instructions here, only defensive checks. Every fact below is quoted or derived from the official Node.js advisory, Imperva's research, Singapore's CSA advisory, or The Hacker News' coverage.

What Node2Shell actually is

Node2Shell is CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in Node.js's bundled Brotli decoder. The official advisory: "A flaw in Node.js can cause Node.js Brotli decoder out-of-bounds write permits remote code execution." It affects the 26.x, 24.x and 22.x lines; the fixed builds are 26.12.1, 24.22.1 and 22.23.4. Reported by OpenAI Codex Security — Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer; fixed by mcollina and aduh95.

Two things to get right on severity. Node.js's own words: "The highest severity issue fixed in this release is HIGH." Separately, Singapore's CSA scored the same CVE at CVSS v3.1 9.8 — the CSA's score, not the Node.js project's rating. Per CSA: "Successful exploitation of this out-of-bounds write vulnerability could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code remotely or disclose sensitive information from the memory of affected systems. Exploitation requires an affected application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli-compressed data."

Imperva's research identified three paths: (1) incoming request bodies with Brotli encoding — Express 5 (versions 5.0.0–5.3.0) and body-parser 2.x (2.0.0–2.3.0) decompress these; (2) outbound fetch() calls decoding Brotli responses from servers you don't control; (3) direct use of node:zlib. Imperva demonstrated RCE against the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image and confirmed the fixed 24.22.1 rejected the same input. No in-the-wild exploitation was reported as of October 22 — a window-of-opportunity story, which is exactly when patching pays off.

This release also fixed ten vulnerabilities total (four high, three medium, three low) — TLS hostname-check bypasses, a dns.resolve NUL-truncation bug, and bundled updates (c-ares, ca-cert with the eMudhra Intermediate CA compromise, OpenSSL, SQLite, Undici). More reasons to update Node.js everywhere it hides.

Step 0 — Are you exposed? Audit every Node in your stack

Start with the Node you know about, on the host:

node -v
# If it prints v22.23.4, v24.22.1 or v26.12.1 (or newer), the host runtime is fixed.

Then the Node you forgot about — inside your containers. A package inventory misses a runtime bundled in an image, so query the image itself:

docker run --rm my-app-image node --version
# Repeat for every Node-based app image in your compose stacks

Critical detail: check the running container, not just the pulled image — an old running container survives an image update:

docker exec my-app-container node --version
# or, for compose: docker compose exec app node --version

Make a list: every container older than 22.23.4 / 24.22.1 / 26.12.1 on its line, plus anything on an end-of-life line. That's your patch queue for tonight.

Step 1 — Re-pull and verify (the image-publisher lag trap)

The lag trap: Your app's Docker image is not fixed until its maintainer rebuilds it on node ≥22.23.4 / ≥24.22.1 / ≥26.12.1. Updating your image tag or restarting the container changes nothing if the publisher hasn't rebuilt yet. Never assume a re-pull fixed it — verify.

Before touching anything, snapshot first — the same snapshot-first discipline as our SafePay ransomware NAS survival guide. Then, for each Node-based app in your patch queue:

cd /path/to/your/compose/stack
docker compose pull          # get the publisher's latest build
docker compose up -d         # recreate containers on the new image
docker compose exec app node --version   # verify the RUNNING container is fixed

Two failure modes. First, a cached digest: if the version still shows old after the pull, confirm the digest actually changed (docker images --digests) — pinned digests and cached layers redeploy the old image silently. Second, the publisher may not have rebuilt yet — check the project's release notes. Same patch-tonight discipline as our GitLab CVSS-10 RCE guide: the vendor's fix and your deployment of it are two different events.

Step 2 — Fix the pin trap

If you build your own images, check your base-image pins. Aikido's warning, in spirit: a Dockerfile pinned to node:24.22.0 stays vulnerable no matter how often you rebuild it — rebuilding on the old pin changes nothing. So:

# In your Dockerfile, change:
#   FROM node:24.22.0-alpine
# to the fixed patch on your line:
#   FROM node:24.22.1-alpine
# Then rebuild:
docker build --no-cache -t my-app:latest .
docker run --rm my-app:latest node --version

Move to 24.22.1, 22.23.4 or 26.12.1 (or later) on whichever line you run. Same careful sequencing as our n8n 3.0 breaking-changes walkthrough — line jumps need release-note reading; patch bumps within a line are tonight's safe, fast move.

Step 3 — The EOL trap

The official advisory is blunt about end-of-life lines: "It's important to note that End-of-Life versions are always affected when a security release occurs." Per third-party guides (Aikido and others), lines like 20.x and earlier, plus odd lines 23.x/25.x, receive no fix — that detail comes from third-party analysis, not the official page.

The homelab killer: check your image's base. If any image you run is still built on an EOL Node line, no re-pull will ever fix it. Two moves: migrate the app to an image built on a supported line (22.x or 24.x), or — if the app can't move tonight — pull it off the public internet and sandbox it behind your VPN. Verify each project's Dockerfile or release notes yourself rather than trusting memory.

Can't patch tonight? A bridge-only stopgap

The official advisory offers no workaround in Node.js itself — patching is the fix. For the container you genuinely can't update tonight, reduce inbound exposure at the reverse proxy by rejecting Brotli request bodies. A bridge only: it does nothing about Brotli responses your app fetches, so don't treat it as protection.

For Nginx Proxy Manager, add to the proxy host's Custom Nginx Configuration:

# Node2Shell stopgap — TEMPORARY, remove after patching
if ($http_content_encoding ~* "br") {
  return 415;
}

For Caddy (in the site's handle block):

# Node2Shell stopgap — TEMPORARY, remove after patching
@brotli header Content-Encoding br
respond @brotli 415

Legitimate browsers sending Brotli request bodies will get a 415 — acceptable for one night on most homelab services, since Brotli request bodies are rare. Schedule the real node js security update for the morning and remove the rule once you're patched.

A note on Bun

If any self-hosted app runs on Bun rather than Node.js: Bun before 1.4.4 is affected, and Bun 1.4.4 includes the fix (per Aikido's FAQ). bun --version on the host or in the container tells you where you stand — update it the same way you'd update Node.js.

Verify the fix

Close the loop the same way you opened it — confirm the running state, not your intent:

# Host runtime
node -v
# Every patched container, checked live:
docker compose exec app node --version
docker exec my-other-app node --version

Expected: 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1 (or newer) on each app's line. Anything still old goes back on the queue — or gets the stopgap and an off-internet sandbox until it can be patched.

One last operator caveat: if you run Watchtower or similar auto-updaters, exclude or pin images prone to major version jumps — the same discipline every nodejs docker update demands — so tonight's fix doesn't arrive as tomorrow's breaking change. Patch the runtime, verify the running container, then sleep.

Companion read: our Plex2Shell compromise check and patch guide covers the same patch-tonight workflow for Plex servers.

Node2Shell FAQ — quick answers

Which Node.js versions fix Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497)?

The October 21, 2026 releases: 22.23.4, 24.22.1 and 26.12.1 for the 22.x, 24.x and 26.x lines. End-of-life lines (per third-party guides, 20.x and earlier) get no fix — the official advisory states end-of-life versions are always affected.

Is Node2Shell being exploited in the wild?

No in-the-wild exploitation was reported as of October 22, per The Hacker News — but a working proof of concept was publicly demonstrated on October 22. Patch now, while the window is open.

How do I check if my Docker containers run a vulnerable Node version?

Query the image directly — docker run --rm <image> node --version — since a host package audit misses runtimes bundled inside images. Then verify the running container with docker exec <container> node --version, because an old running container survives an image update.

My app image still reports the old Node version after updating — what now?

Three checks: (1) confirm the image digest actually changed after the pull — a cached or pinned digest redeploys the old image; (2) check the project's release notes — the publisher may not have rebuilt on the fixed base yet; (3) check your Dockerfile pins — a Dockerfile pinned to node:24.22.0 stays vulnerable no matter how often you rebuild it.

Does blocking Brotli at my reverse proxy fully protect me?

No. Rejecting Content-Encoding: br request bodies at the proxy only covers one attack path. It does nothing about Brotli responses your app fetches from servers you don't control, or direct node:zlib use. A temporary bridge for the night — the real fix is the Node.js update.

Is Bun affected by Node2Shell?

Bun before 1.4.4 is affected; Bun 1.4.4 includes the fix (per Aikido's FAQ). Run bun --version on the host or in the container and update the same night.

Originally published on The Homelab Fixer.

title: My webhook catcher taught me that testing Stripe callbacks locally is a lie you tell yourself
description:
I built a webhook catcher because every agent developer hits the same wall: you're wiring up a payment flow, a GitHub integration, or some internal service, and you need a public HTTPS URL that actually receives POSTs. Ngrok works until your laptop sleeps. Deploying a throwaway function to some cloud costs more than the test is worth.

So I made an ephemeral webhook receiver: one call creates a single-use HTTPS URL, senders need no credentials, it stores up to 100 events for 24 hours, then deletes itself. In-memory, no database, no cleanup cron.

The lesson came from watching my own test suite. I was testing a Stripe-like flow end to end: fire a webhook, read it back, assert the payload shape. Worked perfectly until I added a retry loop — the sender retries on timeout, which my catcher intentionally doesn't simulate, so every test "passed" while my real integration would have collapsed under the first network blip.

The fix wasn't in the catcher. It was in my mental model of what a webhook receiver is for. It's not a mock. It's a mirror. If you're testing retry logic, durability, ordering guarantees — those are properties of the sender and your consumer, not the pipe. The catcher's job is to be a dumb, reliable pipe so you can see exactly what your consumer receives, byte for byte, headers included.

That distinction shaped the API. No filtering, no transformation, no "helpful" normalization. Store the raw body, the headers, the timestamp. Let the agent decide what matters. I've used it for Stripe webhook shapes, GitHub push events, and once for debugging why an internal service's JSON was arriving as form-encoded — the catcher showed me the Content-Type lie in one call.

If you're building anything that receives callbacks, point your sender at a fresh hook, do your real work, then read back what actually arrived. The gap between what you sent and what landed is where the bugs live.

I packaged it as https://x402.freeq.one/tools/webhook_catch.html

title: Hardening Enterprise SSO with Keycloak: SAML 2.0, OAuth2 PKCE, and Zero-Trust RBAC
description:
Originally published on the HostingPodium Enterprise Engineering Blog.

Free SRE & Developer Diagnostics: Test your stack live with our Free Website Speed Test & Core Web Vitals Checker, Free Website Speed & Core Web Vitals Checker, or explore all 9 Free Webmaster & Cloud Engineering Tools.

This guide presents a production-grade Keycloak deployment that hardens SAML, OAuth2 PKCE, and RBAC for zero-trust enterprises. It includes HA design, configuration snippets, and an operational runbook.

Scope and Design Premise

This guide details a production-grade Keycloak deployment that satisfies PCI-DSS, NIST-800-53, and internal zero-trust mandates. The architecture couples a multi-node Infinispan cache, strict SAML 2.0 assertion signature verification, OAuth2 PKCE with token rotation, and a federated RBAC model that maps external LDAP groups to fine-grained resource policies.

Clustered High Availability with Infinispan

Keycloak stores sessions, tokens, and client metadata in an Infinispan cache. For enterprise resilience we configure a three-node synchronous replication cluster behind a virtual IP managed by Keepalived. The following

standalone-ha.xml

excerpt shows the cache container definition:

Key parameters:

  • Lock timeout 60 s prevents deadlock under burst load.
  • Max-idle 30 min evicts idle sessions, limiting memory pressure.
  • Synchronous replication guarantees that a write succeeds only when all three nodes acknowledge.

Network latency must stay below 5 ms for the 99th percentile of cache writes; otherwise the lock timeout will trigger failover. Use jumbo frames (MTU 9000) on the intra-cluster VLAN and enable net.core.somaxconn=65535 on each host.

SAML 2.0 Assertion Signature Validation

Keycloak validates inbound SAML assertions against the IdP metadata. The security posture requires:

  • Enforced RSA-SHA256 or ECDSA-SHA384 signatures.
  • Rejecting assertions with NotOnOrAfter timestamps older than 5 seconds.
  • Strict audience restriction matching the service provider entity ID.

Configuration snippet for the IdP metadata provider:

{
 "entityId": "https://idp.example.com/saml2",
 "singleSignOnService": [{"binding": "POST", "location": "https://idp.example.com/SSO"}],
 "singleLogoutService": [{"binding": "POST", "location": "https://idp.example.com/SLO"}],
 "signature": {
 "algorithm": "RSA_SHA256",
 "certificate": "MIID..." 
 },
 "wantAssertionsSigned": true,
 "wantAuthnRequestsSigned": true
}

Keycloak must be started with -Dkeycloak.saml.forceSignatureAlgorithm=RSA_SHA256 to reject weaker hashes. The assertion validation code path runs inside the org.keycloak.saml.SAML2LoginProcessor class; enabling DEBUG logging for that package provides audit trails for rejected assertions.

OAuth2 PKCE with Token Rotation

Public clients (mobile, SPA) are required to use PKCE (RFC 7636) with rotating refresh tokens. The server enforces a maximum token lifetime of 15 minutes and a refresh token reuse limit of 1. The following JSON client definition encodes the policy:

{
 "clientId": "mobile-app",
 "protocol": "openid-connect",
 "publicClient": true,
 "standardFlowEnabled": true,
 "directAccessGrantsEnabled": false,
 "pkceCodeChallengeMethod": "S256",
 "accessTokenLifespan": 900,
 "refreshTokenLifespan": 3600,
 "reuseRefreshToken": false,
 "rotateRefreshToken": true
}

Keycloak’s TokenManager rotates the refresh token after each use and stores the previous token hash in the user session. A failed reuse attempt increments the failedRefreshTokenAttempts counter; exceeding three attempts locks the user for 10 minutes. This behavior is configurable via the realm settings revokeRefreshToken and maxRefreshTokenReuse.

Zero-Trust RBAC Federation

The enterprise policy engine lives in an external OPA (Open Policy Agent) service. Keycloak forwards the authenticated principal’s attributes to OPA over a signed JWT. The policy decision point (PDP) evaluates group membership against a hierarchical RBAC matrix stored in PostgreSQL. Example policy fragment:

{
 "input": {
 "user": "{{.sub}}",
 "groups": {{.groups}},
 "resource": "{{.resource}}",
 "action": "{{.action}}"
 },
 "policy": "allow if input.groups contains \"finance:admin\" and input.action == \"write\""
}

Keycloak’s AuthorizationProvider is configured with a remote policy provider:

Network latency to the OPA endpoint must stay below 2 ms for 99 % of requests; otherwise the request timeout (set to 500 ms) will trigger a fallback deny. Deploy OPA as a sidecar on each Keycloak node to meet latency targets.

Operational Runbook

Startup Sequence

  • Provision three VMs with identical kernel parameters: vm.max_map_count=262144, net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1, fs.file-max=200000.
  • Install JDK 17, set JAVA_OPTS="-Xms8g -Xmx8g -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200".
  • Deploy Infinispan container, verify cluster health via curl http://localhost:11222/rest/v2/cache-manager.
  • Start Keycloak with systemd unit that includes ExecStart=/opt/keycloak/bin/kc.sh start --optimized and Restart=on-failure.
  • Run kc.sh export --realm master --output realm-export.json to capture baseline configuration.

Failure Detection

Prometheus scrapes /metrics on each node. Alert rules:

ALERT KeycloakNodeDown {
 expr: up{job="keycloak"} == 0
 for: 2m
 labels: {severity="critical"}
 annotations: {summary="Keycloak node unreachable", description="Check Keepalived and JVM logs"}
}

ALERT InfinispanReplicationLag {
 expr: infinispan_cache_replication_lag_seconds > 5
 for: 1m
 labels: {severity="warning"}
 annotations: {summary="Cache replication lag", description="Investigate network jitter"}
}

Patch Cycle

Apply quarterly Keycloak patches using rolling updates. Drain a node with kubectl cordon (if deployed on K8s) or disable the virtual IP on the node. After the node is out of service, replace the JARs, run kc.sh build, and bring the node back online. Verify session continuity by checking infinispan_cache_hits_total does not drop below 95 % of baseline.

Monitoring, Auditing, and Observability

Log aggregation uses Elastic Stack. Keycloak logs are emitted in JSON format with fields event_type, client_id, user_id, and duration_ms. A Kibana dashboard tracks:

  • Successful SAML assertion validations per IdP.
  • PKCE token exchange latency (target
  • OPA deny ratio (target

Kernel audit rules capture privileged system calls made by the JVM process:

-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -F uid=0 -k keycloak-audit

Retention policy: 90 days for audit logs, 180 days for authentication logs, complying with GDPR retention schedules.

Architectural Trade-offs

Dimension Choice Impact
Cache Replication Mode Synchronous (SYNC) Higher write latency (≈3 ms) but guarantees strong consistency across nodes.
Token Lifetime 15 min access, 1 h refresh Reduces exposure window; increases token refresh traffic (~12 % of auth volume).
OPA Deployment Sidecar per node Meets sub-2 ms latency; raises pod count and resource fragmentation.
Signature Algorithm RSA-SHA256 only Eliminates weaker hashes; requires IdPs to support RSA-2048 minimum key size.

The design favors deterministic security guarantees over raw throughput. In environments where peak login bursts exceed 10 k req/s, consider scaling the Infinispan cluster to five nodes and enabling client-side load balancing.

Final Remarks

The configuration presented delivers a repeatable, auditable SSO platform that satisfies zero-trust mandates while preserving high availability. Operators should embed the runbook steps into CI/CD pipelines to enforce drift-free deployments.

Production Verification Checklist & Operational Runbook: Hardening Enterprise Single Sign-On: Keycloak SAML 2.0, OAuth2 PKCE & Zero-Trust RBAC

Before promoting any Hardening Enterprise Single Sign-On: Keycloak SAML 2.0, OAuth2 PKCE & Zero-Trust RBAC deployment into production traffic, senior platform and SRE teams validate deterministic failure handling, kernel resource ceilings, and observability telemetry across keycloak high availability infinispan, oauth2 pkce token rotation, saml 2.0 assertion signature validation, enterprise rbac identity federation. Unlike lab prototypes, production clusters must survive upstream network partitions, sudden concurrency bursts, and rolling node maintenance without dropping in-flight client transactions.

Pre-Cutover Acceptance Gates 

- **Synthetic Load & Tail-Latency Benchmarking:** Execute sustained concurrency tests against staging endpoints for Hardening Enterprise Single Sign-On: Keycloak SAML 2.0, OAuth2 PKCE & Zero-Trust RBAC, verifying that p95 and p99 response latencies remain within contractual SLO boundaries under 3x peak projected load.

- **Fault Injection & Chaos Verification:** Simulate primary worker termination, AZ link degradation, and storage IOPS saturation to confirm automated failover and circuit-breaker recovery complete within sub-second thresholds.

- **Telemetry & Alert Routing Validation:** Confirm Prometheus scrape targets, structured JSON log pipelines, and OpenTelemetry trace propagation emit actionable metrics for hardening-enterprise-sso-keycloak-saml-oauth2-pkce-rbac before live traffic cutover.

- **Immutable Rollback Readiness:** Verify that declarative GitOps manifests, database migration snapshots, and previous container image digests can restore the prior production state in under 120 seconds.

title: I Typed Four Sentences Into the USB Coding Expert Demo. I Got Back a Solidity Contract on the Python Tab
description:
I typed four sentences into the demo. I got back a Solidity contract on the Python tab.

Every page on WorkflowAlpha ships a working demo, and I keep coming back to that
as the reason to take the pages seriously: you can test before you pay. For USB
Coding Expert the promise is specific. Under Live Demo — Code Generator:

Describe what you want in plain English, pick a language, and generate real
working code instantly.

That is a testable claim. I tested it, and I want to be precise about what I
found, because the finding is not "the demo is fake."

The demo is one router over sixteen canned strings

The generator is a single IIFE with two objects: presets (four prompts) and
templates (four languages x four prompts = sixteen code strings).
generateCode() picks a template with this cascade:

var key = 'reverse';
if (input.toLowerCase().includes('http') || input.toLowerCase().includes('server')) key = 'http';
else if (input.toLowerCase().includes('file') || input.toLowerCase().includes('read')
         || input.toLowerCase().includes('write')) key = 'file';
else if (input.toLowerCase().includes('token') || input.toLowerCase().includes('erc')
         || input.toLowerCase().includes('solidity')) key = 'token';
else if (input.toLowerCase().includes('reverse') || input.toLowerCase().includes('string')) key = 'reverse';
var code = templates[lang][key] || templates[lang].reverse;

So the honest shape is: a keyword router over sixteen canned templates, with
reverse as the default for anything unmatched. No model, no completion, no
context. That is fine for a demo. It is not what "generate real working code"
implies at first read, and I would rather say that plainly than have you
discover it in a tab you already paid for.

I then checked whether the sixteen strings are real code. They are, mostly.

The four prompts the page advertises, run for real

I captured what the page actually puts in the textarea — driving the page's own
generateCode() against a DOM stub, so this is the real output, not a
reconstruction — and executed each payload with the interpreter its tab claims.

Tab Prompt Compiles? What I actually got
Python reverse a string yes Reversed: dlrow olleh
Python HTTP server yes binds :8080, serves <h1>Hello from USB Coding Expert!</h1>
Python read/write a file yes wrote 29 bytes, read them back
Python ERC-20 token no SyntaxError: invalid syntax
JS reverse a string parses ReferenceError: prompt is not defined
JS HTTP server yes binds :8080, correct body
JS read/write a file yes wrote 29 bytes, read them back
JS ERC-20 token parses Cannot find module 'web3'
Bash reverse a string yes olleh
Bash HTTP server yes, one request serves once, then break exits the loop
Bash ERC-20 token fails at runtime solc: command not found
Solidity all four not compile-checked solc is not on my host

The HTTP ones are real. I curl'd the Python and Node versions and got the
advertised HTML back. The Bash version is the interesting one: it is a
while true loop with a break on the next line, so it serves exactly one
request and then the process is gone. If you expect a server, that is a
surprise. If you expected a demonstration that the pipeline works, it is
adequate.

The bug I actually want to flag

Pick the Python tab. Type Create an ERC-20 token. The demo returns this as
"Python code":

pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract MyToken {
    string public name = "MyToken";
    string public symbol = "MTK";
    uint8 public decimals = 18;
    uint256 public totalSupply;
    mapping(address => uint256) public balanceOf;
    ...
}

That is a Solidity contract, on the Python tab. python3 cannot parse it. It is
not a near-miss or a rough edge — the token template was written once for
Solidity and the same string is reused in the Python slot, so the "pick a
language" selector returns the wrong language for one of the four advertised
presets.

The JS tab has the same class of problem in a different shape: its ERC-20
snippet is const Web3 = require("web3") against
https://mainnet.infura.io/v3/YOUR_KEY with 0x... placeholders. It parses,
and it cannot run, and it needs a network — which is the one thing this product
exists to avoid.

And the keyword router has no way to tell "write" as in write a function from
"write" as in write a file. So Write a function that checks if a number is
prime returns the file I/O script. Build a CLI that greets a user by name
returns the string-reverser, because no keyword matched and reverse is the
default. I counted: 7 of the 12 prompts I tried were not one of the page's own
four presets, and every one of them still returned one of the same four canned
payloads.

To the page's credit, one entry is honest about its own limits. On the Solidity
tab, Create a simple HTTP server returns:

// HTTP server in Solidity is not possible
// Use an oracle or off-chain server instead

That is the right instinct — say what cannot be done — applied to exactly one of
sixteen cells.

What this means if you are evaluating it

I am not telling you the product is a scam. I am telling you what the demo
proves and what it does not, because the demo is the only thing on the page that
lets a stranger check a claim before money moves.

What the demo proves: the page is alive, the code it emits is mostly real,
and at least one of the advertised snippets executes and serves a correct
response.

What the demo does not prove: that a model lives on the USB stick, that it
generates code for a request you did not type, or that any of this is offline.
The demo is a keyword router in a browser. It never touches a model and never
touches the USB image. Those are two separate claims, and only one of them is
demonstrated.

What I would do as a buyer: open the page, type the four presets, and run
what comes back. Then type something the page never advertised and see whether
the answer has any relationship to your sentence. If that matters to you — and
for a $149.99 air-gapped coding tool, it should — ask the seller one question
before paying: does the model on the stick answer a prompt you invented, and can
I see that before I buy?

Getting it

USB Coding Expert
is $149.99, one-time, lifetime license: bootable image, model files, boot scripts,
documentation, 30-day email support.

Payment — PayPal to redman1309@proton.me (buyer writes a note, seller
confirms in the inbox), crypto to 0x078fE079A9440631Bc6AD722D7143dC382b4ea4f
on Base (ETH / USDC / USDT), or Western Union / MoneyGram. Email
workflowalpha.ai@gmail.com to buy; after payment confirmation you get the
package as a download link or pre-flashed to a drive.

The thing I did not test

I did not boot the image. I have not verified that it leaves the host
byte-for-byte identical, that it boots in under 60 seconds on arbitrary x86-64,
or that the model files are what the page says they are. Those are the claims
that carry the price, and I cannot check them from a browser. If you have run it,
I would rather read your result than my own guess.

title: Is FilmCraft 100% Free? I Scored the Open-Source Premiere Pro Clone in 10 Rounds
description:
AI-assisted disclosure: I used an AI assistant to help structure this write-up. Every number comes from my own runs on my Mac or from the sources linked at the end.

Short answer: yes, FilmCraft is free. It's open source (MIT OR Apache-2.0), it rebuilds Adobe Premiere Pro from scratch in pure Rust, and it costs $0. Premiere Pro costs US$22.99/month on the annual plan.

But is a free Premiere clone actually usable? I gave FilmCraft 0.9.0 real jobs on a Mac mini M4 (16 GB) and scored it against Premiere in 10 rounds.

📺 Full video (5:38): https://youtu.be/0moxAPMMego

What FilmCraft is

  • A clean-room reimplementation of Premiere Pro: same panels, workspaces, tools and keyboard shortcuts (with shortcut presets for Premiere, Final Cut Pro and Avid).
  • Pure Rust, no FFmpeg inside. It ships its own H.264, HEVC, ProRes and AAC codecs.
  • From the ArtCraft team. The repo was created Sep 30, 2026 and had 14,962 stars and 6,249 forks 19 days later.
  • Runs on macOS, Windows, Linux and in the browser (WebAssembly).
  • 650+ engine commands, a CLI and an MCP server, so an AI agent can drive the editor. This is the part developers should care about most.

The scorecard

Round Winner Score (FilmCraft–Premiere)
1. Interface & shortcuts Tie 1–1
2. Editing & trimming Tie 2–2
3. Green-screen keying Tie 3–3
4. Effects & transitions Premiere 3–4
5. Color grading Tie 4–5
6. Audio Premiere 4–6
7. Captions & AI Premiere 4–7
8. Formats & export Premiere 4–8
9. Projects & plugins Premiere 4–9
10. Price & freedom FilmCraft 5–9

Premiere wins on depth. FilmCraft wins on price.

Honesty note: Premiere was not installed on my Mac. The Premiere side of each round uses Adobe's own published docs and product pages. The FilmCraft side is real runs.

The developer angle: a whole edit from one script

"Every menu item, button, slider and drag in FilmCraft is a command" (that's from the README). So I built a 15-second 4K coffee-shop ad without touching the timeline:

  • a new sequence, 5 clip placements, 4 cross dissolves
  • a Lumetri grade on all 5 clips (9 settings each)
  • 2 titles

That's 58 commands, run from one script in 0.01 s. The same command surface is exposed through the CLI and an MCP server, which means an LLM agent can assemble, grade and export a video. Premiere can't do this without a plugin SDK and a lot of glue.

Real numbers from my Mac mini M4

Test Result
Build the 15 s 4K ad (58 commands) 0.01 s
One 4K frame preview ~0.6 s
Export 15 s 4K H.264, software 82 s (4.4 fps)
Export 15 s 4K H.264, hardware encoding on 131 s (2.8 fps), slower
Export 13 s 1080p30 meme, H.264 27.4 s
Export to FCP7 XML (what Premiere imports) valid: 7 clip items, 4 transitions

Yes, hardware encoding was slower than software. Lumetri, keys and export rendering still run on the CPU in this build.

Green-screen keying: a 1:1 copy, with a catch

FilmCraft's Ultra Key has the same 18 parameters with the same defaults as Premiere's (Transparency 45, Highlight 10, Shadow 50, Tolerance 50, Pedestal 10, and so on).

But on my green-screen clip (a tourist with a map, backdrop rgb 102,221,9) the default key colour didn't key it at all. Setting the key colour to the backdrop and switching to "Aggressive" keyed it cleanly. Every meme in the video was made this way.

Where it falls short

  • Can't open .prproj files. This is the team's main beta blocker. Importing a Premiere sequence via XML took 97 s in their own report.
  • No plugins: no VST3 / Audio Units, no OpenFX, no Premiere/After Effects plug-in API.
  • Auto captions don't work out of the box on Mac. Offline Whisper transcription exists, but the macOS release build says model downloads aren't available ("built without speech-download").
  • H.264 is 8-bit 4:2:0 only, no camera RAW, and no AV1 export.
  • The team's own parity report: ~86% of Premiere's features, but only ~56% "ready for real work". Status: alpha.

Verdict

  • Pro client work? Stay on Premiere.
  • Memes, shorts, school projects, small ads? FilmCraft works, for $0.
  • Building an AI video pipeline? FilmCraft's command/CLI/MCP surface is the most interesting thing here, and it's open source, so you can read exactly what each command does.

Would you switch? Tell me in the comments.

📺 Full video with all 10 rounds: https://youtu.be/0moxAPMMego

Sources

  • FilmCraft repo and README: https://github.com/storytold/filmcraft
  • FilmCraft parity report (vs Premiere Pro 26.5.2): https://github.com/storytold/filmcraft/blob/main/docs/target-app-parity.md
  • Adobe Premiere Pro pricing: https://www.adobe.com/products/premiere.html
  • Adobe Help Center, "Ultra Key effect parameters" (updated Jan 7, 2026)

title: Building a Data Fabric on AWS: Connect Data, Improve Governance, and Power AI
description:
Modern organizations store data across databases, applications, data lakes, and streaming platforms. The challenge is making all that data discoverable, secure, and useful without building a completely separate integration solution for every team.

Data Fabric on AWS offers an architectural approach to connecting data sources, managing metadata, enforcing governance, and enabling analytics and AI applications.

In this tutorial, we'll explore an AWS data fabric architecture and build a small customer analytics project using Amazon S3, AWS Glue, and Amazon Athena.

What Is Data Fabric?

A data fabric is an architecture that connects data discovery, integration, metadata management, and governance across distributed systems.

On AWS, you can use services such as:

  • Amazon S3: Store raw and curated datasets.
  • AWS Glue: Discover, catalog, and transform data.
  • AWS Glue Data Catalog: Maintain metadata and table definitions.
  • AWS Lake Formation: Manage permissions for supported data lake resources.
  • Amazon Athena: Query data in S3 using SQL.
  • Amazon Redshift: Support data warehousing and analytical workloads.
  • Amazon DataZone: Help teams discover, share, and govern data assets.
  • Amazon Bedrock: Build generative AI applications that use approved business information through controlled retrieval and data-access layers.

These services are building blocks. A data fabric is an architecture you design and configure, not a single AWS service that automatically connects everything.

Why Does It Matter?

Imagine an e-commerce company with:

  • Customer records in Amazon RDS.
  • Order history in S3 files.
  • Website events arriving through streaming services.

Without a coordinated approach, different teams may duplicate datasets, define metrics differently, and manage permissions inconsistently.

A data fabric can help teams improve data discovery, reduce repeated integration work, and establish more consistent governance.

Reference Architecture 

       DATA SOURCES
  ┌────────┬─────────┬───────────┐
  │ RDS    │ S3 Files│ Event Data│
  └────┬───┴────┬────┴─────┬─────┘
       └────────┼──────────┘
                ▼
         DATA INGESTION
        AWS Glue / Streams
                │
                ▼
           AMAZON S3
       Raw → Clean → Curated
                │
        ┌───────┴────────┐
        ▼                ▼
   Glue Catalog     Lake Formation
        │                │
        └───────┬────────┘
                ▼
          QUERY LAYER
        Athena / Redshift
                │
                ▼
       Analytics / Reports / AI

This is a conceptual design. Each source needs an appropriate ingestion process, and access policies must be configured for the services involved.

Hands-On Project: Customer Order Analytics

Let's create a simple data pipeline and query customer orders using SQL.

Step 1: Create a sample CSV file

Create orders.csv:

order_id,customer_id,region,amount,status
1001,C101,Asia,250,COMPLETED
1002,C102,Europe,180,COMPLETED
1003,C101,Asia,90,PENDING
1004,C103,North America,420,COMPLETED
1005,C104,Europe,120,CANCELLED
1006,C102,Europe,310,COMPLETED

Upload it to an S3 location such as:

s3://your-data-fabric-bucket/raw/orders/orders.csv

Replace your-data-fabric-bucket with your own bucket name. Keep public access blocked and configure appropriate encryption and permissions.

Step 2: Catalog the dataset with AWS Glue

Open the AWS Glue console and:

  1. Create a database named customer_analytics.
  2. Create a crawler that points to your S3 raw/orders/ prefix.
  3. Configure an IAM role with the required S3 read and Data Catalog permissions.
  4. Run the crawler.
  5. Review the table schema and confirm the column types.

The crawler can discover the CSV structure and register a table in the Glue Data Catalog. Always verify inferred types before relying on them in production.

Step 3: Query the data with Athena

Open Amazon Athena and configure an S3 query-results location. Then execute:

SELECT
    region,
    COUNT(*) AS completed_orders,
    SUM(amount) AS total_revenue,
    AVG(amount) AS average_order_value
FROM customer_analytics.orders
WHERE status = 'COMPLETED'
GROUP BY region
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

Expected output:

Region Completed orders Total revenue Average order value
Europe 2 490 245
North America 1 420 420
Asia 1 250 250

The query filters out pending and cancelled orders and calculates revenue by region.

Note: Your actual database and table names depend on your Glue configuration.

Step 4: Add Governance

A useful data platform must control access as well as provide discovery.

For this project:

  • Give analysts access only to the datasets they need.
  • Separate engineering and administrative permissions.
  • Configure Lake Formation permissions where applicable.
  • Protect sensitive customer information.
  • Review access logs and test permissions using a restricted analyst identity.

A catalog entry does not automatically grant permission to query the underlying data. Configure the required catalog, storage, query, IAM, and Lake Formation permissions consistently.

Step 5: Extend the Architecture

Once the basic project works, you can improve it by adding:

  • AWS Glue ETL jobs to validate and transform records.
  • Parquet datasets to improve query efficiency for suitable workloads.
  • Amazon Redshift for more demanding warehouse analytics.
  • Amazon DataZone to improve discovery and sharing across teams.
  • Amazon Bedrock for an AI assistant that answers business questions using approved data through a controlled retrieval or query layer.

For AI applications, validate generated queries and enforce permissions in the data-access layer. Do not give an AI model unrestricted access to every dataset.

Data Fabric vs. Data Lake vs. Data Mesh

Concept Purpose
Data lake Stores large amounts of data in formats such as CSV, JSON, and Parquet.
Data fabric Connects data discovery, integration, metadata, and governance.
Data mesh Organizes data ownership around business domains and data products.

These approaches can complement each other. Amazon S3 can provide the storage foundation, a data fabric architecture can connect and govern datasets, and a data mesh operating model can define domain ownership.

Production Best Practices

Before scaling your implementation:

  1. Improve metadata quality: Document schemas, owners, and dataset descriptions.
  2. Enforce least privilege: Keep administrative, engineering, and analyst permissions separate.
  3. Validate data: Check missing values, duplicates, and schema changes.
  4. Monitor pipelines: Track failures, processing time, and data freshness.
  5. Optimize costs: Use appropriate partitioning and file formats to reduce unnecessary Athena scans.
  6. Document lineage: Record where data originates and how it changes.
  7. Secure AI access: Use controlled tools, authorization, and query validation.
  8. Start small: Prove value with one business use case before connecting every source.

Final Thoughts

Data Fabric on AWS is not about moving all your data into one database. It is about making distributed data easier to discover, integrate, govern, and use.

With Amazon S3, AWS Glue, the Glue Data Catalog, Lake Formation, and Athena, you can build a foundation for reliable analytics and future AI applications.

Start with one dataset, catalog it, secure it, and demonstrate a useful business query. Then expand as your organization's needs grow.

The goal is simple: make the right data available to the right people and applications, securely.
