                'amount' => $this->total_minor, // integer minor units, not floats
                'currency' => $this->currency,
            ],
            'updated_at' => $this->updated_at->toIso8601String(),
        ];
    }
}

Rules that keep decoders working across releases:

  • Only additive changes within a version. Adding a field is safe; removing, renaming, or changing a type is a new version.
  • Money as integer minor units with a currency code. Dates as ISO 8601 with an offset.
  • Enums as strings, and clients that map unknown values to a fallback case instead of failing the whole decode. Swift: give the enum a raw value and a custom init(from:) that falls back to .unknown.
  • JSON for every error, including 401, 404, 422, 429, and 500. A mobile client cannot do anything useful with an HTML error page.

Laravel decides whether to render an exception as JSON from the Accept header, and mobile HTTP clients do not always send one. Force it for API routes in bootstrap/app.php and render your envelope from the same place:

// bootstrap/app.php
return Application::configure(basePath: dirname(__DIR__))
    // ...routing and middleware...
    ->withExceptions(function (Exceptions $exceptions) {
        $exceptions->shouldRenderJsonWhen(fn (Request $request) => $request->is('api/*'));

        $exceptions->render(function (ApiException $e, Request $request) {
            return response()->json([
                'error' => [
                    'code' => $e->code(),          // stable, machine-readable
                    'message' => $e->getMessage(), // display text, safe to change server-side
                    'fields' => [],
                ],
            ], $e->status());
        });
    })->create();

The code is what the app branches on, so it never changes once shipped. The message is copy you can reword without a release. fields carries per-field validation messages for 422 responses and is otherwise empty, so the client always has one decoder and one error-handling path.

Which authentication should a mobile app use with Laravel?

For a first-party app, use Laravel Sanctum API tokens: one token per device, named after the device, scoped with abilities, and revocable by deleting a row. Reach for Passport only when you need an OAuth2 server for third-party clients. Self-contained JWTs make revocation harder than it needs to be.

Sanctum vs Passport vs JWT for mobile apps

Factor Sanctum tokens Passport (OAuth2) JWT package
Token type Opaque, stored hashed in the database OAuth2 access and refresh tokens Signed, self-contained token
Revoke one device Delete the token row Revoke the token and its refresh token Needs a denylist until expiry
Refresh flow Not built in; use expiry plus re-login or a custom rotate endpoint Built in Provided by the package
Third-party clients Not designed for it Yes, including authorization code with PKCE Not designed for it
Setup and upkeep Low, first-party Higher: clients, grants, keys Moderate, community-maintained
Best fit Your own iOS, Android, Flutter, or React Native app Platforms where partners need delegated access Stateless verification across several services

Issue the token from a login endpoint that takes a device_name, so users can see and sign out individual devices, and a lost phone can be revoked without logging out everything else:

$token = $user->createToken(
    $request->input('device_name'),    // e.g. "iPhone 16 - iOS"
    ['orders:read', 'orders:write'],   // abilities checked per route
    now()->addDays(30),                // per-token expiry
);

return ['token' => $token->plainTextToken];

On both sides of the token lifecycle:

  • Store the token in the platform keystore: the iOS Keychain or Android Keystore-backed storage. Never in UserDefaults, plain shared preferences, or AsyncStorage.
  • Set an expiry. Sanctum tokens never expire unless expiration in config/sanctum.php is set (minutes) or createToken() gets a date. Pair it with a scheduled sanctum:prune-expired so the table does not grow forever.
  • Revoke on risk events. A password change, account recovery, or “sign out all devices” should delete the relevant token rows immediately.
  • Treat a 401 as a state, not an error. The client clears the stored token and returns to sign-in once, rather than retrying in a loop.

For the client side of the same problem, the mobile banking security checklist covers token storage, session handling, and the controls a security review expects in the app.

How do you version a Laravel API so old app builds keep working?

Put the version in the URL, starting at /api/v1 on day one, and only make additive changes inside a version. Ship a public configuration endpoint that returns the minimum supported build, so you can prompt or force an update before you remove anything an old build depends on.

// routes/api.php
Route::prefix('v1')->group(function () {
    Route::get('/app-config', AppConfigController::class);   // public, cacheable
    Route::post('/auth/token', [AuthController::class, 'store'])
        ->middleware('throttle:auth');

    Route::middleware(['auth:sanctum', 'throttle:api'])->group(function () {
        Route::get('/orders', [OrderController::class, 'index']);
        Route::delete('/auth/token', [AuthController::class, 'destroy']);
    });
});

The client sends its platform and build number on every request and checks the configuration endpoint at launch. A Swift version using URLSession:

struct AppConfig: Decodable {
    let minimumSupportedBuild: Int
    let latestBuild: Int
    let updateUrl: URL
}

func fetchAppConfig() async throws -> AppConfig {
    var request = URLRequest(url: URL(string: "https://api.example.com/api/v1/app-config")!)
    request.setValue("ios", forHTTPHeaderField: "X-Client-Platform")
    request.setValue(Bundle.main.object(forInfoDictionaryKey: "CFBundleVersion") as? String,
                     forHTTPHeaderField: "X-Client-Build")

    let (data, response) = try await URLSession.shared.data(for: request)
    guard (response as? HTTPURLResponse)?.statusCode == 200 else {
        throw URLError(.badServerResponse)
    }

    let decoder = JSONDecoder()
    decoder.keyDecodingStrategy = .convertFromSnakeCase
    return try decoder.decode(AppConfig.self, from: data)
}

A deprecation policy that holds up:

  • Log the client build on every request. You cannot retire a version without knowing which builds still call it.
  • Run versions side by side. v2 controllers reuse the same services and models; only the resources and request validation differ.
  • Soft prompt, then hard block. Raise a “recommended update” first, and only raise minimum_supported_build once usage of the old build is negligible by your own numbers, not by the calendar.
  • Return a specific error code, such as client_update_required, from retired endpoints so even a build that predates the update prompt shows something sensible.

Header-based versioning (Accept: application/vnd.example.v2+json) is tidier in theory. In practice a URL prefix is easier to grep in logs, route in a load balancer, and explain to the person writing the Android client.

How should pagination and sync work for offline-first apps?

Use cursor pagination for lists and an updated_since parameter for sync. Offset pagination skips or duplicates rows when data changes between page requests, which happens constantly on a phone with a flaky connection. Cursors are stable, and delta sync means the app downloads only what changed.

$orders = $request->user()->orders()
    ->withTrashed()   // include soft-deleted rows as tombstones
    ->when($request->filled('updated_since'), fn ($query) =>
        $query->where('updated_at', '>', $request->date('updated_since')))
    ->orderBy('updated_at')
    ->orderBy('id')   // tie-breaker: cursor columns must be unique together
    ->cursorPaginate(min($request->integer('per_page', 50), 100));

return OrderResource::collection($orders);

Details that decide whether sync is reliable:

  • Deletions must sync too. Soft deletes with a deleted_at in the resource let the client remove local rows it would otherwise keep forever.
  • The client stores the server’s timestamp, not the device clock, as its next updated_since value. Return it in the response; device clocks drift.
  • Writes are idempotent. Accept a client-generated UUID or Idempotency-Key header on create requests, store it with the row, and return the existing record on a repeat, so a retry after a dropped response does not create a duplicate.
  • Conflicts have a rule decided up front: last write wins, server wins, or a 409 with both versions that the app resolves. Undefined behaviour here turns into data loss.

How do you send push notifications from Laravel?

Send them from queued jobs, never inside the request. Store each device’s push token against the user and platform, dispatch a queued notification, and deliver through APNs for iOS and Firebase Cloud Messaging for Android. For APNs, use token-based authentication with a .p8 signing key rather than a certificate; the key does not expire and works across all your apps. For FCM, use the HTTP v1 API; the legacy API was shut down in 2024 and some older packages still target it.

  • Register tokens on every launch with an upsert endpoint. Push tokens change, and the app is the only party that knows when.
  • Prune invalid tokens when APNs returns 410 or FCM reports UNREGISTERED, otherwise the queue spends its time on devices that no longer exist.
  • Keep payloads small and non-sensitive. Send an identifier and let the app fetch the detail over the authenticated API; lock screens are not private.
  • Separate queues by priority so a bulk marketing send cannot delay a time-sensitive transactional alert.

How should mobile apps upload files to a Laravel backend?

Let the app upload directly to object storage with a short-lived presigned URL, then tell the API the upload finished. Streaming large photos or videos through PHP ties up workers on slow mobile connections. Laravel generates presigned S3 upload URLs, so the API only authorizes and records the file.

['url' => $url, 'headers' => $headers] = Storage::disk('s3')
    ->temporaryUploadUrl(
        'uploads/'.$request->user()->id.'/'.Str::uuid().'.jpg',
        now()->addMinutes(5)
    );

return ['upload_url' => $url, 'headers' => $headers];

A presigned PUT cannot enforce a size limit, so after the app confirms the upload, check the object server-side: Storage::size() against your cap, the real content type from the bytes rather than the extension, and that the key belongs to the caller. Push any processing such as thumbnails onto a queue. Never trust the file type the client claims.

What rate limits does a mobile API need?

At minimum, a general per-user limit for authenticated routes and much stricter limits on login, one-time codes, and password reset. Key limits by user ID when authenticated and by IP otherwise. Mobile carriers put many users behind shared IP addresses, so IP-only limits punish legitimate users.

Laravel’s named rate limiters express this in a few lines. The numbers below are starting points; tune them from your own traffic:

// AppServiceProvider::boot()
RateLimiter::for('api', function (Request $request) {
    return Limit::perMinute(60)->by($request->user()?->id ?: $request->ip());
});

RateLimiter::for('auth', function (Request $request) {
    return [
        Limit::perMinute(5)->by(strtolower((string) $request->input('email')).'|'.$request->ip()),
        Limit::perMinute(20)->by($request->ip()),
    ];
});

The throttle middleware adds Retry-After and X-RateLimit-* headers to the 429 for you; make sure the body is still your error envelope, and make the client honour Retry-After with jittered backoff. A client that retries instantly on failure turns a brief incident into a self-inflicted outage. The OWASP API Security Top 10 lists unrestricted resource consumption and broken authorization among the most common API risks, and both apply directly to mobile backends.

What should you monitor on a mobile backend?

Error rates and latency per endpoint, broken down by app version and platform. A backend change that looks healthy overall can break one older build entirely, and you will only see it if requests carry the client build and your dashboards can filter by it.

  • Request context: client platform, build, and a request ID. Generate the ID in middleware, put it in Log::withContext(), and return it in a response header so support can match an app report to a server log.
  • Error tracking on both sides, with the same request ID visible in app crash reports and server exceptions.
  • Queue health: backlog depth, failed jobs, and job duration. Laravel Pulse or a hosted APM covers the basics; Horizon adds detail if you run Redis queues.
  • Version adoption: requests per build over time, which is the number you need before retiring an API version.

Where does Next.js fit next to a Laravel mobile backend?

Beside Laravel, not in front of the mobile app. Next.js works well for an admin dashboard, marketing site, or web version of the product, consuming the same Laravel API or a separate web backend-for-frontend (see Next.js web development). The mobile app should call Laravel directly through its versioned API.

Adding a Next.js layer between the app and Laravel means two services that must both stay compatible with every installed build. Keep the mobile contract in one place. If you are planning the stack as a whole, my Laravel API backend development service covers the API, admin tooling, and infrastructure together.

What should you build first?

Before the first app release, get the decisions that are expensive to reverse in place: the /api/v1 prefix, the response and error envelope, per-device Sanctum tokens with an expiry, the app-config endpoint with a minimum build, and client build logging. Everything else in this guide can be added later without breaking installed apps. Cursor pagination is the one I would move up the list if the app has any list that grows, because switching from offset to cursor later changes the response shape.

If you are still scoping the product, the mobile MVP playbook covers what to include in a first release, and mobile app development covers the client side. When you want the backend designed and built alongside the app, I offer Laravel backend and API development for mobile apps.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should a mobile app use Laravel Sanctum or Passport?

Use Sanctum when your own first-party app is the only client. It issues revocable per-device tokens with very little setup. Choose Passport only when you need a real OAuth2 server, for example when third-party developers or partner apps must obtain delegated access to your users' data.

How long should a Laravel API keep supporting an old version?

Long enough that almost no active installs still depend on it. Set the window from your own analytics on build adoption rather than the calendar, announce it in-app before removal, and use a minimum-supported-build check so the last stragglers see an update prompt instead of broken screens.

Can Laravel handle real-time features for a mobile app?

Yes. Laravel broadcasting with Laravel Reverb, or a hosted WebSocket service, covers live updates while the app is in the foreground. Push notifications through APNs and FCM still handle the background case, because mobile operating systems suspend open sockets when the app is not active.

Should a mobile app call Laravel directly or go through Next.js?

Call Laravel directly. A mobile client gains little from an extra hop, and every layer is another thing that has to stay backward compatible with old app builds. Next.js earns its place for the admin panel, marketing site, or a web client, not as a proxy in front of the mobile API.

Originally published at puneetpal.dev.

title: Your API Returned 202. Why Does the UI Say Done?
description:
Your export button turns green. The API returned 202. The worker has not produced a file.

That screen may be reporting a success your system has not observed yet.

Here is a hypothetical implementation:

const response = await fetch("/exports", { method: "POST" });
if (!response.ok) throw new Error("Export request rejected");
showToast("Your export is ready");

The last line silently changes the meaning of the response. HTTP 202 means the request was accepted for processing. Processing may be incomplete or may not have started, and it can still fail. A successful HTTP response is insufficient evidence that this particular file exists.

Give the button a job lifecycle

For this export feature, use distinct application states: submitting, queued, running, completed and failed. Add a state for losing the ability to observe the job. That last state matters when the browser loses its connection while a worker continues.

These are proposed product states, not extra meanings assigned to the HTTP status code. Your backend must define how the client observes them: a status resource, events, or another documented mechanism.

An illustrative response contract could be:

{
  "jobId": "export-demo-17",
  "state": "queued",
  "statusUrl": "/exports/export-demo-17"
}

Those field names are specific to the example. HTTP 202 does not automatically supply a status endpoint.

Make each claim depend on evidence

“Request received” can follow acceptance. “Preparing your file” needs a known active job. “Download ready” needs a completed result the user can access.

If a status request fails, keep the job identifier. Show that its state cannot currently be checked and let the user check again. Creating another export immediately can duplicate work and leave two jobs whose results are difficult to distinguish.

Refreshing the page is another useful rehearsal. Does the screen reconnect to the original job, forget it, or start over? Decide that behavior before shipping the optimistic toast.

Test the promise made by the interface

I would use a controlled service with these outcomes:

  • acceptance followed by completion;
  • acceptance followed by worker failure;
  • acceptance followed by a lost status response;
  • page reload while the job is queued;
  • a completed job whose download is no longer available.

For every case, compare the visible message with the state the application actually knows. Include a check that observation failure never becomes a “ready” badge.

The interesting review artifact is a short sequence of observations: accepted response, job state, final result, visible copy. A screenshot of the green toast by itself cannot establish that an export worked.

Which part of your product currently uses “success” for a request that only entered a queue?

title: GBase Database Deployment Planning: Four Tables That Define Your Cluster
description:
The most expensive mistakes in database deployment often happen before anyone runs the installation command.

For GBase Database(GBase 8a), a Shared-Nothing MPP analytical database with columnar storage, node roles, network topology, hardware specifications, and port allocation all affect deployment readiness. If these decisions are left until installation, problems can emerge together when workloads and data volumes grow.

My approach is simple: complete four planning tables before requesting hardware.

1. Network Plane Planning

GBase Database(GBase 8a) uses two network planes for different purposes:

  • Data plane: Connects cluster nodes and carries internal data exchange and cluster communication.
  • Business plane: Handles client access, typically through GCluster nodes.

Separating these traffic paths helps reduce contention and makes network troubleshooting easier.

A deployment might consider 10GbE for internal connectivity, 40GbE aggregation, and 1GbE or higher for external access. These are planning reference points, not universal requirements; actual bandwidth depends on node count, query patterns, concurrency, and workload.

For resilience, dual-NIC active/standby bonding across separate switches can reduce the impact of a single link or switch failure, provided the network and failover configuration are designed correctly.

Document the interface assignments, IP addresses, switch connections, bandwidth requirements, and firewall rules before installation.

2. Cluster Sizing: Plan Around Data Node Count

GBase Database cluster sizing should account for the number of Data nodes, coordinator capacity, management requirements, and expected workload.

The following table illustrates one proposed sizing plan. Confirm these values against the deployment guide for your specific GBase Database(GBase 8a) release before procurement.

Data nodes (D) GCluster nodes GCware nodes
D less than 10 3 3
10 ≤ D less than 30 5 3
30 ≤ D less than 100 7 or 9 3
D ≥ 100 9 or 11 3

The key benefit of a sizing table is consistency. Instead of choosing node counts by intuition, the team can document its assumptions and review the proposed architecture before ordering machines.

The final configuration should also account for query concurrency, availability requirements, and the capacity of each coordinator.

3. Hardware and RAID Configuration

Hardware planning should distinguish minimum installation requirements from production capacity.

The initial specification may include CPU, memory, system disks, data disks, RAID configuration, and network interfaces. For example, 256GB of memory might be a production planning target, while 32GB could be considered a lower reference point for a particular deployment. Neither figure should be treated as a universal requirement without checking the target release and workload.

Likewise, RAID1 for system disks and RAID5 for data disks are possible design choices, not mandatory configurations for every environment.

Before procurement, document:

  • CPU count, core count, and frequency.
  • Memory capacity and expected workload.
  • System and data disk layout.
  • RAID level, usable capacity, and redundancy.
  • Storage growth and backup requirements.

Avoid sizing production systems around the minimum needed to start a service. Query concurrency, memory-intensive operations, and intermediate results can create very different resource demands under load.

4. Port Inventory and Pre-Installation Checks

Port conflicts can delay deployment or prevent services from starting. Record the required ports for each component and validate them against the documentation for your GBase Database version.

The following is an example port inventory to verify for the target environment:

Component or service Port
GCluster 5258
GNode 5050
GCware 5918, 5919
syncServer 5288
GCRecover 6268
Remote management 16066–16166

Run a basic check on every node before installation:

#!/bin/bash

for p in 5258 5050 5918 5919 5288 6268; do
  if ss -H -lnt 2>/dev/null |
     awk -v port="$p" '
       {
         addr = $4
         sub(/^.*:/, "", addr)
         if (addr == port) found = 1
       }
       END { exit !found }
     '; then
    echo "LISTENING: $p"
  else
    echo "No TCP listener found: $p"
  fi
done

free -h
nproc
df -h /data

This script checks for TCP listeners on the listed ports and reports basic system resources. A port with no listener is not necessarily available under every configuration, so also verify firewall rules, service requirements, and other protocol usage where relevant.

Save the results with the machine inventory. Repeat the checks after replacing, reinstalling, or cloning nodes.

Understand the Cluster Roles

A clear deployment plan also identifies what each component does:

  • GCware: Provides cluster consistency services and cluster metadata management.
  • GCluster: Handles SQL parsing, optimization, and distributed execution planning.
  • GNode: Handles data storage and computation.

GCluster and GCware may be colocated in a combined Coordinator node, depending on the deployment architecture.

Symmetric and asymmetric deployment designs offer different trade-offs. Symmetric designs can reduce machine count and simplify infrastructure. Asymmetric designs separate management and data roles, which may improve isolation but require additional resources and operational planning.

Choose based on cluster scale, workload, availability requirements, and the intended failure domains—not simply a preference for one topology.

Verify Operating System Compatibility Early

Operating system compatibility is another procurement prerequisite.

All nodes within a Virtual Cluster must meet the version-consistency requirements of the target GBase Database release. Python dependencies and supported operating system versions can also vary by release.

Before provisioning, confirm the supported distribution, exact OS version, required packages, and Python configuration against the official deployment documentation. Do not assume that a prerequisite documented for one CentOS, RHEL, Kylin, or UOS release automatically applies to another.

These checks are much easier to complete before machines are installed and configured.

A Repeatable GBase Database Deployment Workflow

A practical workflow is:

  1. Complete the network plane design.
  2. Confirm cluster topology and node sizing.
  3. Finalize hardware and RAID specifications.
  4. Validate port allocation and operating system compatibility.
  5. Provision machines and configure networking.
  6. Run pre-installation checks on every node.
  7. Archive the approved tables and check results for future expansion.

This turns deployment planning into a repeatable engineering process rather than a collection of individual experiences.

The takeaway: GBase Database deployment quality is heavily influenced by decisions made before installation. Four well-maintained planning tables can align hardware procurement, network configuration, cluster sizing, and operational readiness.

Which causes more rework in your projects: network design or cluster sizing?

title: TIL: Why GBase Database Separates Data and Business Network Planes
description:
When deploying GBase Database(GBase 8a), network design is more than an infrastructure detail. It directly affects how reliably an MPP cluster exchanges data, executes distributed queries, and serves client requests.

The reason for separating the data plane from the business plane becomes clearer when you look at how the database works.

1. Understand the Two Network Planes

GBase Database(GBase 8a) uses a Shared-Nothing MPP architecture with columnar storage. Data is distributed across nodes, each with its own local storage and computing resources.

When a query involves a large cross-node JOIN, the database may need to exchange substantial amounts of intermediate data between nodes. This traffic travels over the data plane, which must provide connectivity for all participating cluster nodes.

The business plane serves a different purpose: client access.

GCluster acts as the SQL entry point, handling SQL parsing, optimization, and distributed execution planning. Clients typically connect through GCluster rather than connecting directly to every GNode.

Separating these traffic paths makes the network architecture easier to manage and helps isolate internal cluster communication from external application traffic.

2. What Happens When Both Planes Share One Network?

Combining data-plane and business-plane traffic may appear to reduce deployment complexity. However, both traffic types then compete for network resources.

During a busy reporting period, large query results and client requests can consume bandwidth that internal cluster communication also needs. Depending on the workload and network configuration, this contention can increase latency and reduce overall query throughput.

The resulting symptom is familiar: the busier the system becomes, the less predictable its performance feels.

The problem may not be attributable to one SQL statement. Network congestion can affect multiple distributed operations simultaneously.

For GBase Database deployment planning, separating the two planes helps establish clearer traffic boundaries and simplifies troubleshooting.

3. Size Network Bandwidth for the Actual Workload

Network capacity should be based on expected traffic, concurrency, query patterns, and cluster scale—not a single universal number.

For example, a deployment design might consider:

  • Internal network: 10GbE connectivity as an initial design point, subject to workload and node count.
  • Aggregation layer: 40GbE links or higher where traffic modeling indicates that multiple nodes may saturate shared uplinks.
  • Business network: 1GbE or higher, depending on client concurrency, result-set sizes, and application throughput requirements.

These are planning examples, not universal minimum requirements for every GBase Database(GBase 8a) deployment. Benchmarking and traffic estimation should determine the final design.

Analytical queries can return large result sets, so business-plane capacity matters as much as internal data exchange. If client-facing links become saturated, users may perceive the database as slow even when the underlying query execution is performing well.

4. Improve Link Resilience with NIC Bonding

Physical network separation can be combined with NIC bonding to improve link availability.

On Linux systems that use the traditional network-scripts configuration, an active/backup bond may resemble the following example.

# /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-bond0
DEVICE=bond0
TYPE=Bond
BONDING_OPTS="mode=1 miimon=100"
IPADDR=192.168.10.11
NETMASK=255.255.255.0

The physical interfaces are configured as bond members. A simplified example for each member is:

# Example settings for each physical interface
MASTER=bond0
SLAVE=yes

The complete interface files also require the appropriate device names and settings for the operating system and network configuration tool in use.

In this example:

  • mode=1 configures active/backup bonding.
  • miimon=100 checks link status at 100-millisecond intervals.

Active/backup bonding provides link redundancy; it does not combine the bandwidth of both links. Also, link monitoring alone may not detect every upstream switch or end-to-end connectivity failure.

For stronger resilience, connect the two bond members to separate switches and verify that the switch topology, VLANs, and failover behavior are configured correctly. Where possible, consider independent power feeds and avoid sharing a single failure domain across critical network paths.

Note that network-scripts configuration is not supported by every modern Linux distribution. Use the networking tools supported by your target operating system.

5. Make Network Separation Part of Deployment Planning

Before installing GBase Database(GBase 8a), document:

  • Which interfaces and IP addresses belong to each network plane.
  • Which nodes require data-plane and business-plane connectivity.
  • Expected bandwidth and aggregation requirements.
  • Bonding configuration and switch redundancy.
  • Firewall rules, routing, and connectivity validation procedures.

This information should be reviewed before hardware installation, not improvised after the cluster is running.

Final Takeaway

For GBase Database(GBase 8a), network plane separation is an architectural decision that influences scalability, resilience, and distributed query performance.

The data plane supports communication across the cluster. The business plane provides controlled client access. Designing them separately makes traffic behavior easier to reason about and failure boundaries easier to manage.

A reliable MPP deployment starts with a network topology designed for the workload—not simply one that allows every node to connect.

title: TIL: Check Ports Before Deploying GBase Database(GBase 8a)
description:
A port conflict can turn a straightforward database installation into hours of troubleshooting. One of the simplest ways to avoid this is to scan every node before deploying GBase Database(GBase 8a).

During a deployment for a large government analytics platform, a pre-installation check revealed that two machines still had an old instance occupying port 5258. Replacing the machines before installation helped the team avoid troubleshooting the conflict during deployment.

The lesson: port verification should be part of your GBase Database deployment checklist, not an afterthought.

1. Understand the ports before deployment

GBase Database(GBase 8a) uses three main component types:

  • GCware: Provides cluster consistency services and metadata management.
  • GCluster: Handles SQL parsing, optimization, and distributed execution planning.
  • GNode: Handles data storage and computation.

The deployment plan should document the required ports for each component. The following ports are used in the environment described here; verify them against the documentation for your specific GBase Database release and configuration.

Component or service Port
GCluster 5258
GNode 5050
GCware 5918, 5919
syncServer 5288
GCRecover 6268
Remote management 16066–16166

Do not treat this table as a substitute for version-specific configuration documentation. Record each port's component, purpose, communication direction, and firewall requirements.

2. Scan for port conflicts on every node

An old database instance or another service may already be listening on a required port. Discovering this before installation is much easier than diagnosing a service that fails to start afterward.

On Linux systems with ss, run:

for p in 5258 5050 5918 5919 5288 6268; do
  if ss -H -lntp 2>/dev/null |
     awk -v port="$p" '
       {
         addr = $4
         sub(/^.*:/, "", addr)
         if (addr == port) found = 1
       }
       END { exit !found }
     '; then
    echo "LISTENING: port $p"
  else
    echo "No TCP listener found: port $p"
  fi
done

This checks for TCP listeners on the specified ports. It does not prove that a port is available for every protocol or configuration, and insufficient permissions may hide process details.

For further investigation, use:

sudo ss -lntp
sudo lsof -nP -iTCP:5258 -sTCP:LISTEN

Replace 5258 with the port you need to investigate.

Important: A port scan identifies current listeners, not every possible future conflict. Check the intended service configuration and repeat the scan after reinstalling or cloning a machine.

3. Check system resources at the same time

Port availability is only one part of GBase Database deployment readiness. A quick resource check can reveal other potential issues before installation.

free -h
nproc
df -h /data

These commands report memory, available CPU cores, and filesystem capacity for /data. Adjust the filesystem path to match your planned data directory.

Compare the results across nodes. Inconsistent resources or insufficient disk space can undermine an otherwise successful installation.

4. Include firewall rules and remote management ports

A deployment may succeed while remote access fails later because the firewall rules are incomplete.

The remote management range deserves particular attention. Confirm which ports the selected release actually requires, which hosts need access, and which firewall rules must be applied. Avoid opening an entire port range indiscriminately; follow the product's requirements and your organization's security policy.

Document the rules before deployment and coordinate with the network team so that connectivity can be verified systematically.

5. Make port checks part of automated provisioning

For a small deployment, checking ports manually may seem sufficient. For a cluster with many Data nodes, repeatable checks are more reliable than memory.

A practical GBase Database deployment checklist should include:

  • [ ] Verify required ports on every node.
  • [ ] Investigate unexpected listeners and identify their owning processes.
  • [ ] Confirm firewall rules and communication paths.
  • [ ] Compare CPU, memory, and disk capacity across nodes.
  • [ ] Repeat the checks after machine replacement, reinstallation, or cloning.
  • [ ] Save the results with the deployment records.

Automating these checks in a provisioning pipeline makes the results reproducible and easier to audit.

Final takeaway

A few minutes of pre-installation verification can prevent avoidable deployment delays. The larger the GBase Database(GBase 8a) cluster, the more valuable it becomes to standardize checks across every node.

Check the ports before you install—not after a service refuses to start.

How does your team handle port validation during database deployment: manual checks, automated scripts, or a dedicated infrastructure checklist?
