title: Node.js Report Scheduling: Combining Cron Jobs with Worker-Based Long-Running Tasks
description:
A cron process should create one durable scheduling record and exit. A worker queue should own report generation, subscriber fan-out, retries, and delivery state. That boundary keeps a slow daily shipment report from turning a timer into an accidental job runner, while still leaving room to choose latency or cost deliberately.

Short answer: run the scheduler at a fixed time, claim the day with an idempotency key, enqueue one report job, and let workers split the resulting shipment update into subscriber-sized deliveries. The scheduler needs a small timeout. The report worker needs a lease, bounded concurrency, durable progress, and a clear rule for permanent failure.

The concrete case here is a fintech operation that sends a daily shipment-status report by email to many subscribers. Report generation may scan a large event range; the final update may fan out to thousands of recipients. The report is one logical job, but delivery is many independently retryable jobs. Treating those as one unit is the first design mistake.

How should I combine a cron job trigger with a worker-based queue?

The clock is not a guarantee that work happened. It is only a request to start work. This combining of a cron trigger with worker-based execution is useful because the two components have different failure boundaries. I define these invariants before choosing a queue library or storage engine:

Keep it boring.

The queue is the boundary.

  • At most one report run is active for a tenant and report date, unless an operator explicitly starts a replacement.
  • A worker may execute a job more than once, but a subscriber must not receive an unbounded number of copies because of a retry.
  • A generated report is retained long enough for delivery retries, and its status is observable without reading worker logs.
  • One slow subscriber cannot hold the report-generation lease forever.
  • A failure has a category: retryable, permanent, or awaiting operator action.

The identifier should be derived from stable business data, such as tenant_id + report_date + report_type, rather than from the scheduler attempt. Otherwise two timer invocations create two valid-looking reports. A uniqueness constraint at the persistence boundary is more convincing than a promise that the cron process will never overlap.

Here is the decision record I use for the critical path:

Boundary Option Latency benefit Cost or failure trade-off
Timer to queue enqueue one run key Low scheduler overhead Requires durable deduplication
Report to delivery fan out child jobs Slow recipients are isolated More queue records and state transitions
Retry policy bounded exponential delay Absorbs short outages Delays visibility of a bad dependency
Result storage immutable artifact plus status row Delivery can resume Retention and access controls become explicit work

This is a latency-versus-cost decision, not a contest between cron and queues. More parallel delivery reduces wall-clock time but increases connection pressure, provider calls, and duplicate-delivery exposure.

Why should cron stop before the report is finished?

A timer process has a narrow responsibility: determine the intended run, record it, and publish a message. It should not wait for a database scan, render a large attachment, or send email. A long-lived cron invocation makes timeout semantics ambiguous: did the process die before enqueueing, after enqueueing, or after the work completed but before acknowledging it? Those are long-running tasks, so the trigger should return before the expensive work begins.

A generic Node.js scheduler can hand the durable parts to a queue client like this. The interface is intentionally abstract; the important detail is the stable key and the separation between schedule time and execution time.

from datetime import date


def schedule_daily_report(store, queue, tenant_id: str, run_date: date) -> None:
    run_key = f"shipment-report:{tenant_id}:{run_date.isoformat()}"

    created = store.insert_run_if_absent(
        key=run_key,
        tenant_id=tenant_id,
        report_date=run_date,
        status="queued",
    )
    if created:
        queue.publish(
            topic="report.generate",
            key=run_key,
            payload={
                "run_key": run_key,
                "tenant_id": tenant_id,
                "report_date": run_date.isoformat(),
            },
        )

The insert and publish operations need a defined relationship. If they cannot share a transaction, use an outbox record in the same transaction as the run row, then have a small publisher relay unsent outbox records. That adds storage and a relay, but it closes the gap where the run exists and the message does not. A queue's acknowledgement alone cannot repair that gap.

How do workers survive retries and partial fan-out?

The report worker claims a run with a lease, reads the required event range, writes an immutable artifact, and records the artifact checksum or version. It then creates delivery jobs keyed by (run_key, subscriber_id). The fan-out step is a state transition, not a loop whose progress lives only in memory.

I use a lease such as 15 minutes only when the report can make progress or renew it; a fixed lease that outlives the worker's real liveness delays recovery. A reaper can return expired work to the queue, but it must not assume that an expired lease means the old worker stopped. The delivery write needs its own idempotency key, and the email boundary needs an explicit duplicate policy because a process can lose its acknowledgement after sending.

def deliver_one(store, mailer, delivery_id: str) -> None:
    delivery = store.claim_delivery(delivery_id, lease_seconds=900)
    if delivery is None:
        return

    if delivery.status == "sent":
        return

    try:
        mailer.send(
            recipient=delivery.recipient,
            artifact_ref=delivery.artifact_ref,
            idempotency_key=delivery.idempotency_key,
        )
        store.mark_sent(delivery_id)
    except TemporaryDependencyError as error:
        store.release_for_retry(delivery_id, reason=str(error))
    except PermanentDeliveryError as error:
        store.mark_failed(delivery_id, reason=str(error))

The code cannot make an external email provider transactional with the database. That is a real failure boundary. If the send succeeds and the process crashes before mark_sent, a retry may send again. The practical answer is to use provider-supported idempotency where available, or make the message tolerate duplicates and expose the duplicate risk to operations. Claiming exactly-once delivery without controlling both sides is a misleading label.

Which failure modes deserve a separate alarm?

A queue depth alarm is not enough. A growing queue can mean a report scan is slow, delivery is throttled, or workers are repeatedly receiving poison messages. Those require different actions.

Track schedule lag, time from run creation to artifact completion, fan-out count, retry age, lease expirations, permanent failures, and delivery-provider responses. Keep the run key in every log and metric. The useful question at 09:30 UTC is not “are workers up?” but “which tenant and report date cannot reach a terminal state, and at which boundary?”

Security belongs in the same record of decisions. A report worker that fetches a callback URL, attachment, or remote logo must validate the destination and restrict network access; an attacker should not be able to turn report generation into a server-side request forgery primitive. The OWASP guidance distinguishes allowlisting approaches for trusted destinations from broader controls, and the right choice depends on whether destinations are fixed or user-supplied.

Do not let retries amplify that risk. A permanent validation error should move to a review state, not be retried every minute. Conversely, a transient database connection failure should not be marked permanent merely because the first attempt exceeded a short worker timeout.

When is a single scheduled worker enough?

A queue with separate generation and delivery jobs has a price: more rows, more instrumentation, more deployment coordination, and more operational states. For one tenant, a small report, and a recipient list that fits comfortably inside the execution budget, one scheduled worker can be the better design. It should still persist a run key and an outcome; simplicity does not remove the need for recovery.

Choose the split when report duration is variable, subscribers have uneven delivery behavior, or a missed retry has business consequences. Choose the simpler worker when the work is short, the recipient set is small, and the team can inspect and replay one run without reconstructing hidden progress. My decision rule is to buy parallelism only where it removes a measured bottleneck or isolates a failure boundary. Otherwise it is operational interest on a system that has not earned the complexity.

The durable architecture is therefore modest: a timer creates intent, an outbox protects publication, a worker materializes one report, and child jobs make fan-out independently recoverable. Latency improves through controlled concurrency; cost stays visible through queue volume, storage retention, and provider calls. The design is credible because it names what it cannot guarantee.

References

  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457

title: Day 23 of My React.js Learning Journey 🚀 | JSX and Components
description:
Today, I learned about JSX in React, component-based architecture, and the two types of React components: class components and functional components. I also got introduced to Hooks and the useState Hook.

1. What Is JSX?

Today, I learned about JSX in React, component-based architecture, and the two types of React components: class components and functional components. I also got introduced to Hooks and the useState Hook.

JSX stands for JavaScript XML. It is a syntax extension for JavaScript that allows us to write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript code.

Although JSX looks similar to HTML, it follows some different rules.

Example

`function App() {
return <h1>Hello, React!</h1>;
}

export default App;`

Here, JSX allows us to write

markup directly inside a JavaScript function.

Important: JSX lets us create our own React components, such as . It does not allow us to invent arbitrary HTML tags and automatically make them work.



  1. React's Component-Based Architecture

React uses a component-based architecture. This means we can divide a user interface into small, reusable components.

For example, an e-commerce website can contain:

  • Navbar component
  • Product component
  • Cart component
  • Footer component

Example

`function Welcome() {
return

Welcome to React!

;
}

function App() {
return (





);
}

export default App;`

Here, the Welcome component is reused twice inside the App component.

3. What Is the Root in React?

`jsx
`import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import App from './App.jsx';

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(

);
``

Here:

  • document.getElementById('root') finds the HTML element with the ID root.
  • createRoot() creates a React root.
  • .render() displays the App component inside that element.

4. Types of React Components

There are two commonly discussed types of React components.

Class Components

`Class components use JavaScript classes and extend React.Component.
import { Component } from 'react';

class Welcome extends Component {
render() {
return

Hello, React!

;
}
}

export default Welcome;`

Class components are still supported, but they are less commonly used in new React code.

Functional Components

Functional components are JavaScript functions that return React elements.

`function Welcome() {
return

Hello, React!

;
}

export default Welcome;`

Functional components are the preferred approach for most new React components.

5. What Are Hooks?

Hooks are special React functions that let functional components use React features such as state.

useState() — manages state.

6. What Is useState?

useState is a React Hook that allows a component to store information and update its UI when that information changes.

Example: Like Button 👍

import { useState } from 'react';

function LikeButton() {
const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);

return (


Likes: {likes}

  <button onClick={() => setLikes(likes + 1)}>
    Like 👍
  </button>
</div>

);
}

export default LikeButton;`

`What I Learned Today

  • JSX stands for JavaScript XML.
  • JSX lets us write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript.
  • React uses reusable components to organize user interfaces.
  • React has class components and functional components.
  • Functional components and Hooks are commonly used in modern React development.
  • useState manages state and helps update the UI.
  • The React root is where React renders and manages the application UI.

title: RBAC Is Not Enough for Sensitive Investigation Workflows
description:
At first, an anonymous reporting system looks like a fairly ordinary CRUD application.

Someone submits a report.

An administrator receives it.

Evidence gets attached.

The case moves through a few statuses.

Eventually, someone closes it.

You can model that with roles:

reporter
investigator
admin

And permissions:

reporter      -> create report, read own case
investigator  -> read cases, add notes
admin         -> read everything, manage users

Simple.

Until the first sensitive case arrives.

Imagine an employee reports their own manager.

That manager happens to be an administrator.

Should admin still mean:

can_read_all_cases = true

Obviously not.

And that's where the authorization model starts getting much more interesting.

The problem is no longer:

What role does this user have?

It becomes:

What is this user's relationship with this specific case?

Role-based access is only the first layer

RBAC works well when permissions mostly follow organizational roles.

A billing employee sees billing information.

Support sees tickets.

Administrators configure the system.

Sensitive investigations introduce another dimension: context.

A user can be perfectly authorized to investigate reports in general and still be forbidden from accessing one particular report.

For example:

can_access_case =
    has_investigator_role
    && !is_subject_of_case
    && !has_conflict_of_interest

That is already different from standard RBAC.

Now imagine another situation.

An HR director is allowed to access investigations.

But the case mentions their spouse.

Or their direct report.

Or their own department.

The role didn't change.

The context did.

This is why systems that deal with sensitive cases often need some combination of:

  • role-based permissions;
  • case-level permissions;
  • explicit exclusions;
  • conflict-of-interest rules;
  • temporary assignments;
  • auditable overrides.

"Admin" stops being a sufficient security model very quickly.

Case access and identity access should not be the same permission

Another mistake is treating a report as one indivisible object.

Suppose the report contains:

case
├── allegation
├── attachments
├── reporter identity
├── internal notes
├── interviews
├── investigation findings
└── resolution

Does everyone who can access the case need to see every field?

Usually not.

An investigator may need to read the allegation but not know the reporter's identity.

Someone reviewing evidence may need attachments but not internal interview notes.

A compliance lead may need to approve the final decision without seeing unnecessary personal information.

So instead of:

can_view_case

you start needing permissions closer to:

can_view_report
can_view_reporter_identity
can_view_evidence
can_view_internal_notes
can_add_evidence
can_interview
can_assign_case
can_close_case

This matters for privacy, but it also changes your domain model.

The reporter's identity should not just be another field conveniently returned by:

GET /cases/:id

If identity deserves stronger protection, model it that way.

Different storage.

Different access policy.

Different audit trail.

Possibly different encryption boundaries.

The data model should reflect the sensitivity model.

Anonymity is not a boolean

Developers are often tempted to model anonymity like this:

{
  "anonymous": true
}

But anonymity is not really a property of the report.

It is a property of the entire system around the report.

You can remove the name field and still collect:

  • IP addresses;
  • analytics identifiers;
  • session metadata;
  • authentication information;
  • reverse-proxy logs;
  • device fingerprints;
  • email notifications containing sensitive context.

The UI may tell the user:

Your report is anonymous.

Meanwhile the infrastructure may know exactly where it came from.

That doesn't necessarily mean those systems are malicious.

It often means nobody modeled anonymity as an architectural requirement.

For sensitive reporting, a better question is:

Which pieces of information could allow us to identify this person, and do we actually need them?

That's data minimization as an engineering decision, not just a privacy-policy sentence.

Anonymous follow-up creates another design problem

If you don't know who the reporter is, how do you ask them another question?

You still need conversations like:

Can you tell us approximately when this happened?

or:

Do you still have the original file?

Traditional messaging assumes identity.

Anonymous reporting can't.

One pattern is to issue an opaque credential when the report is created:

report_id
access_token

The reporter stores that credential and uses it to return later.

Something conceptually like:

POST /reports

201 Created

{
  "report_id": "RPT-8FH2K",
  "access_token": "<opaque-secret>"
}

The token is not an account.

It doesn't need an email address.

It simply proves that whoever holds it is allowed to access the reporter-facing side of that specific case.

That lets the system provide bidirectional communication without forcing identity.

But then more questions appear:

  • Can the token be recovered?
  • Can administrators see it?
  • Should it be stored hashed?
  • Can it be rotated?
  • What happens if it is leaked?
  • How long does it remain valid?

The apparently simple requirement "allow anonymous follow-up" becomes an authentication design problem.

Evidence needs history, not just storage

Attachments are another deceptively simple feature.

The product requirement may begin as:

Users can upload evidence.

So you create:

attachments

and store files somewhere.

But once those files may influence an investigation, the system needs to answer more questions.

Where did this file come from?

When was it uploaded?

Was it replaced?

Who downloaded it?

Did anyone modify its metadata?

Was it deleted?

If it was deleted, why?

A useful evidence record might look more like:

Evidence
--------
id
case_id
original_filename
storage_key
content_hash
submitted_at
submitted_by
source_type
status

And then every important operation becomes an event:

EVIDENCE_UPLOADED
EVIDENCE_VIEWED
EVIDENCE_DOWNLOADED
EVIDENCE_MARKED_IRRELEVANT
EVIDENCE_RESTRICTED

Notice what is missing:

EVIDENCE_SILENTLY_DISAPPEARED

For sensitive systems, destructive CRUD operations deserve suspicion.

Sometimes the better model is not:

DELETE FROM evidence
WHERE id = ?;

but something closer to:

status = discarded
discard_reason = duplicate
discarded_by = investigator_42
discarded_at = ...

The original remains protected according to retention rules, while the investigation history remains understandable.

Whether you need immutable storage, hashing, signed records or stronger chain-of-custody controls depends on the system.

But auditability should be designed before you need it.

Your audit log is security infrastructure

Most applications have logs.

That doesn't automatically mean they have an audit trail.

An application log might say:

GET /api/cases/381 200

An investigation audit trail should answer something more useful:

actor: user_827
action: viewed_reporter_identity
case: case_381
timestamp: ...
reason: assigned_investigator

Those are different things.

For highly sensitive operations, I want to know:

  • who performed the action;
  • which case it affected;
  • what kind of data was accessed;
  • when it happened;
  • whether the action was authorized;
  • when relevant, why it happened.

And the audit system itself needs protection.

If administrators can rewrite the audit trail, it isn't much of an audit trail.

Investigation state is richer than open/closed

Another place where domain complexity leaks into the software is case status.

The naive model:

open
closed

doesn't tell you much.

So maybe you add:

new
triage
investigating
resolved
closed

Better.

But eventually you discover that workflow state and investigation outcome are different concepts.

A case might be:

workflow_status = closed

while its outcome is:

outcome = inconclusive

That matters because an inconclusive report is not the same thing as a false report.

A more expressive model separates them:

workflow_status:
  new
  triage
  investigating
  awaiting_information
  decision_pending
  closed

outcome:
  substantiated
  partially_substantiated
  unsubstantiated
  inconclusive

Why care?

Because software shapes behavior.

If your UI forces investigators to choose only:

true
false

you are embedding an oversimplified policy into the product.

Your enum is making an organizational decision.

Conflicts of interest belong in the domain model

This is another thing I initially thought belonged entirely to company policy.

It doesn't.

Suppose Alice is normally an investigator.

A report arrives involving Alice.

The system should not rely on another administrator remembering:

Oh, we probably shouldn't assign that one to Alice.

The conflict should be representable.

For example:

CaseParticipant
---------------
case_id
user_id
relationship

relationships:
  reporter
  subject
  witness
  investigator
  reviewer
  conflicted

Now authorization can use domain information.

Conceptually:

def can_access_case(user, case):
    if not user.has_permission("investigate"):
        return False

    if case.has_conflict(user):
        return False

    return case.is_assigned_to(user)

Real systems will be more complex.

But the important point is this:

conflict of interest stops being a note in a policy PDF and becomes something the application can enforce.

That's a much stronger guarantee.

Overrides should be possible — and uncomfortable

Eventually someone will need emergency access.

Maybe every normal investigator is conflicted.

Maybe a legal hold requires access.

Maybe an incident needs escalation.

Hard-coding "never" into authorization rules can make a system unusable.

But the opposite is also dangerous:

super_admin = god_mode

A useful pattern is controlled break-glass access.

For example:

override requires:
- elevated permission
- explicit reason
- re-authentication
- audit event
- optional second approval

You are not making the action impossible.

You are making it deliberate and visible.

That difference matters.

Sensitive workflows make generic admin panels dangerous

A lot of SaaS products are built around the idea that the customer administrator owns everything.

For many products, that's reasonable.

For sensitive reporting systems, it can be exactly the wrong assumption.

The person who bought the software may not be entitled to inspect every report.

The company owner may be the subject of a report.

The account administrator may work in the department being investigated.

So tenant ownership and data access cannot automatically mean the same thing.

This is one of those cases where traditional B2B SaaS assumptions start breaking.

The customer owns the workspace.

That does not necessarily mean every customer administrator should be able to read every piece of information inside it.

The hardest requirements often appear after POST /reports

When we first think about a reporting system, it's natural to focus on intake.

The form.

Validation.

File uploads.

Anonymous submission.

Those are visible.

They are easy to put on a roadmap.

But most of the difficult engineering decisions happen afterward:

submit
  ↓
triage
  ↓
conflict detection
  ↓
assignment
  ↓
evidence collection
  ↓
restricted interviews
  ↓
decision
  ↓
follow-up
  ↓
retention

Every arrow hides authorization decisions.

Every box contains potentially sensitive data.

And every shortcut can affect whether users trust the system.

That's why I no longer think of anonymous reporting as a form with a back office.

It's a context-sensitive authorization system wrapped around an investigation workflow.

The form is just where the data enters.

A few questions I now ask much earlier

If I were designing another sensitive workflow from scratch, I'd ask these before choosing the database schema:

Can someone be authorized globally but forbidden from one specific case?

Is identity access separate from case access?

Can sensitive information disappear without leaving a trace?

Can users communicate without revealing their identity?

Can the system represent conflicts of interest?

What happens when normal authorization rules need an emergency override?

Do our statuses reflect the real domain, or just make the UI convenient?

If those questions arrive late, changing the architecture becomes much more painful.

If they arrive early, they shape a much better system.

AI assistance disclosure: AI was used during drafting and editing. The technical concepts and product decisions were reviewed by the author before publication.

Conceptual illustration of a sensitive reporting workflow. AI-generated.

title: One-Time Token passwordless Login in spring security
description:
The Password Paradox:

  • Create a password strong enough to protect state secrets.
  • Forget it instantly.
  • Click 'Forgot Password?'
  • Go through the 5-step authentication ritual.
  • Try to set a new password, only to hear: 'You cannot use a previous password.'

Meanwhile, Chrome is hoarding 47 saved passwords like a digital dragon, yet none of them unlock the one page you actually need right now. 😅"

And just when you think you’ve finally cracked it, the system hits you with:

Your new password must contain at least one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter, one number, one special character, one emoji of existential dread, and the blood of a virgin spreadsheet… and still not be the same as any of the 47 passwords Chrome already knows.

This is one of the reasons passwordless authentication is becoming an attractive approach to modern application security. Instead of asking users to remember yet another password, what if we could authenticate them using a short-lived, one-time token sent to a trusted channel, such as their registered email address?

Setting Up Spring Security

To get started with One-Time Token (OTT) passwordless authentication, we need to add the appropriate Spring Boot dependency to our project.

Depending on the application's requirements, we can use either of the following dependencies:

Option 1: Spring Boot OAuth2 Authorization Server

implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-oauth2-authorization-server")

Option 2: Spring Boot Security

implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-security")

For this implementation, we will use spring-boot-starter-oauth2-authorization-server, as it provides the Spring Authorization Server functionality built on top of Spring Security.

Note: The choice of dependency depends on the application's architecture. If you only need to implement OTT authentication in an existing Spring Security application, spring-boot-starter-security may be sufficient. The authorization server starter is more appropriate when you are building an OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect authorization server.

We invented passwords to protect our data, then made them so complicated that we need another password to recover the first one. Maybe the biggest security vulnerability was asking humans to remember everything! 😅

And here’s the best part: Spring Security makes implementing passwordless authentication much easier than remembering all those passwords! 😄

Instead of reinventing the authentication wheel, we can leverage Spring Security’s built-in One-Time Token (OTT) support and focus on integrating it into our application.

In other words, let Spring Security handle the authentication plumbing while we focus on building features users actually care about.

“Why make users jump through password-reset hoops when Spring Security can help them log in with a one-time token? Less password drama, more actual development!” 🚀

Configuration 

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) {
        http
        .oneTimeTokenLogin(Customizer.withDefaults());
        return http.build();
    }

}

How does it work?

When we enable oneTimeTokenLogin() with its default configuration, Spring Security automatically provides the necessary login pages:

One-Time Token Submission Page: The DefaultOneTimeTokenSubmitPageGeneratingFiltergenerates a default page where users can submit their one-time token to complete authentication.

You enable .oneTimeTokenLogin(Customizer.withDefaults()), start your Spring Boot application, and expect passwordless authentication to work out of the box.

Instead, Spring greets you with a familiar Java experience: a long stack trace and an UnsatisfiedDependencyException. 😅

org.springframework.beans.factory.UnsatisfiedDependencyException: Error creating bean with name 'org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.configuration.WebSecurityConfiguration': Unsatisfied dependency expressed through method 'setFilterChains' parameter 0: Error creating bean with name 'defaultSecurityFilterChain' defined in class path resource [web/security/SecurityConfig.class]: Failed to instantiate [org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain]: Factory method 'defaultSecurityFilterChain' threw exception with message: A OneTimeTokenGenerationSuccessHandler is required to enable oneTimeTokenLogin().
Please provide it as a bean or pass it to the oneTimeTokenLogin() DSL.

Token Delivery
Usually a custom OneTimeTokenGenerationSuccessHandlermust be implemented, responsible for delivering the token to the end user.

@Component
public class OneTimeTokenSenderHandler implements OneTimeTokenGenerationSuccessHandler {
    @Override
    public void handle(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response, OneTimeToken oneTimeToken) throws IOException, ServletException {
         String tokenValue = oneTimeToken.getTokenValue();
        // Send the token to the user
        IO.println("One-Time Token generated: " + tokenValue);
    }
}

Customising the OTT Login Page with Angular

When we enable One-Time Token authentication using:

.oneTimeTokenLogin(Customizer.withDefaults())

Spring Security generates default pages for initiating the OTT login process and submitting the token. This is convenient for getting started, but production applications often require a customised login experience that matches the application's branding and frontend architecture.

For example, if our frontend is built with Angular and Angular Material, we probably want users to see our own login component rather than a default Spring Security page.

Fortunately, Spring Security allows us to customise the login page through the loginPage() method in the OTT DSL.

** Configure Spring Security**
We can configure a custom login page and provide a OneTimeTokenGenerationSuccessHandler to handle successful token generation.

.oneTimeTokenLogin(ott ->
                        ott.loginPage("/login")                     .tokenGenerationSuccessHandler(oneTimeTokenSenderHandler)
                );

Here:

loginPage("/login") specifies the custom OTT login page.

tokenGenerationSuccessHandler(oneTimeTokenSenderHandler) defines what happens after Spring Security successfully generates a one-time token. For example, our handler can deliver the token to the user by email.

Important: The login page configuration and token delivery are separate concerns. Customising the login page does not automatically configure email delivery or redirect the user to the Angular application.

<form
      #loginForm="ngForm"
      class="mt-8"
      action="/ott/generate"
      method="POST"
      (ngSubmit)="onSubmit(loginForm)"
    >
      <input type="hidden" name="_csrf" [value]="csrfToken" />
      <div class="flex flex-col">
        <div class="flex flex-col space-y-2">
          <mat-label>Email</mat-label>
          <mat-form-field appearance="outline">
            <input
              name="username"
              type="email"
              matInput
              placeholder="Enter your email"
              required
              email
              #username="ngModel"
              [(ngModel)]="model.username"
              autofocus
            />
            <mat-icon matPrefix>mail</mat-icon>
            @if (username.invalid && (username.dirty || username.touched)) {
              <mat-error>
                @if (username.errors?.['required']) {
                  <span class="text-sm">Email is required</span>
                }
                @if (username.errors?.['email']) {
                  <span class="text-sm">Please enter a valid email</span>
                }
              </mat-error>
            }
          </mat-form-field>
        </div>
      </div>
      <button
        mat-flat-button
        type="submit"
        class="mt-5 w-full font-medium text-base text-white py-3 px-4"
        [disabled]="loginForm.invalid"
      >
        Sign in
      </button>
    </form>

The important detail is the form's endpoint:

action="/ott/generate"

Spring Security processes this request to generate a one-time token. The form submits the user's email address using the username parameter, which is the expected parameter name in the default OTT configuration.

Because this is a POST request, CSRF protection must also be handled correctly. The hidden CSRF field is one way to submit the token, provided the Angular application obtains a valid CSRF token from the backend.


public class SpaCsrfTokenRequestHandler implements CsrfTokenRequestHandler {
    private final CsrfTokenRequestHandler plain = new CsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler();
    private final CsrfTokenRequestHandler xor = new XorCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler();

    @Override
    public void handle(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response, Supplier<CsrfToken> csrfToken) {
        /*
         * Always use XorCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler to provide BREACH protection of
         * the CsrfToken when it is rendered in the response body.
         */
        this.xor.handle(request, response, csrfToken);
        /*
         * Render the token value to a cookie by causing the deferred token to be loaded.
         */
        csrfToken.get();
    }

    @Override
    public @Nullable String resolveCsrfTokenValue(HttpServletRequest request, CsrfToken csrfToken) {
        String headerValue = request.getHeader(csrfToken.getHeaderName());
        if (StringUtils.hasText(headerValue)) {
            return (StringUtils.hasText(headerValue) ? this.plain : this.xor).resolveCsrfTokenValue(request, csrfToken);
        }

        // Fallback to form parameter
        String paramValue = request.getParameter(csrfToken.getParameterName());
        if (StringUtils.hasText(paramValue)) {
            return (StringUtils.hasText(paramValue) ? this.plain : this.xor).resolveCsrfTokenValue(request, csrfToken);
        }

        return null;
    }
}

Redirecting the User After Token Generation

Once Spring Security successfully generates the one-time token, the next step is to deliver it to the user and redirect them to a page where they can enter the code to complete authentication.

To achieve this, we can implement OneTimeTokenGenerationSuccessHandler and delegate the redirect to Spring Security's RedirectOneTimeTokenGenerationSuccessHandler.

public class OneTimeTokenSenderHandler  implements OneTimeTokenGenerationSuccessHandler {
    private final OneTimeTokenGenerationSuccessHandler redirectHandler = new RedirectOneTimeTokenGenerationSuccessHandler("/ott/validate");

    @Override
    public void handle(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response, OneTimeToken oneTimeToken) throws IOException, ServletException {
        String tokenValue = oneTimeToken.getTokenValue();
        // Send the token to the user
        IO.println("One-Time Token generated: " + tokenValue);
        this.redirectHandler.handle(request, response, oneTimeToken);
    }
}

Conclusion

One-Time Token passwordless authentication provides a practical alternative to traditional password-based login. By combining Spring Security's built-in OTT support with a custom Angular frontend, we can create a login experience that is straightforward for users while retaining the security controls provided by the Spring Security framework.

The implementation requires only a few key pieces: enabling oneTimeTokenLogin(), configuring a custom login page, implementing a token-generation success handler, delivering the token securely, and providing a page where users can submit it.

Of course, passwordless authentication is not automatically secure just because passwords are no longer involved. Token expiration, single-use enforcement, rate limiting, CSRF protection, and secure delivery remain essential.

The real advantage is that we can reduce password-related friction without having to build an authentication system from scratch.

And perhaps the best part? Users can finally stop asking, “Was my password Spring@123, Spring@1234, or Spring@12345?” 😄

Let Spring Security handle the authentication. Let Angular handle the experience. And let your users get on with what they came to do. 🚀

title: Scientific_fastapi: How I Organize Reproducible Scientific Computing Through an API
description:
Author: Artem — Artem7898

A scientific algorithm usually starts as a research script or notebook. While one person runs the calculations, parameters can be changed directly in the code and results saved manually. Once other users become involved, additional requirements emerge: validating input, managing concurrent tasks, recovering from failures, and understanding exactly how a result was produced.

With scientific_fastapi, I am developing infrastructure for this transition. The project connects a Python computational core, an HTTP API, background task execution, and scientific artifact storage. In this article, I describe the architecture of v2.0.0, its capabilities, and practical applications.

The central idea is to make each computational run an identifiable, verifiable unit. Every run should have input parameters, an identifier, an execution state, a result, and enough information to investigate how that result was obtained.

This is particularly important for scientific services. A number returned by an API gains meaning through the model description, units, assumptions, and uncertainty estimate that accompany it.

From Request to Result

FastAPI provides the HTTP layer. It accepts requests and validates parameters before computation begins. Inputs follow a strict schema: unknown fields, unsupported values, and invalid numeric inputs are rejected. Additional limits control the computational workload and the number of accepted tasks.

Long-running calculations execute in the background. Once a request is accepted, the client receives HTTP 202 Accepted, a task identifier, and a URL for checking its status. The client can then poll for updates:


pending → running → completed
                  → failed
                  → cancelled

This contract works for notebooks, web interfaces, and other services. A client submits parameters and waits for the result without keeping an HTTP connection open throughout the calculation.

I separate the architecture into four responsibilities:

  • The API validates requests and exposes task states.
  • The computational core implements the scientific model.
  • The background execution mechanism manages tasks and execution attempts.
  • Artifact storage preserves results and run descriptions. This separation allows scientific functions to be tested independently of HTTP and reused in research scripts.

A Scientific Model for Testing the Infrastructure

The current reference computational core is a two-dimensional model of independent particle velocities governed by an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck thermostat. Its identifier is ideal-gas-ou-v1.

The model has analytical properties that make it useful for validating the numerical implementation. It supports investigating temperature relaxation, the statistics of random realizations, and the relationship between uncertainty and particle count.

Calculations use reduced units:

m = k_B = 1

At a constant thermostat temperature, the exact transition for a velocity component is:

a = exp(-dt)
v_next = a * v + sqrt(T_bath * (1 - a²)) * ξ

Here, ξ is an independent standard normal random variable. The relaxation rate in this expression is one. This transition corresponds to the solution of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process over the specified time interval.

The physical meaning of the model also defines its scope. It describes the velocities of independent particles. Full molecular dynamics would require positions, interactions, forces, and an appropriate integrator. Temperature and time are expressed in reduced units; conversion to kelvin or femtoseconds requires a separate physical justification.

What Reproducibility Means in This Project

Reproducibility in scientific_fastapi combines several mechanisms.

Random numbers come from a local PCG64 generator with an explicitly specified seed. A run does not depend on the process-wide random number generator state. This makes it possible to reproduce numerical results with identical parameters in a consistent computational environment.

Dependencies are fixed in uv.lock. Installation and build checks use the locked versions, and the build tools are pinned as well. Export to the PEP 751 format is available for sharing an environment specification.

Each scientific run saves a JSON description and its final state in NPZ format. The artifacts record parameters, numerical results, the model version, and information about the random number generator and environment. SHA256 checksums allow the consistency of the saved files to be verified.

As a result, an output can be connected to a specific set of conditions: which parameters were used, which model performed the calculation, and which files belong to that run.

An identical seed alone does not guarantee bitwise equality across different libraries, hardware, and computational backends. Verifying reproducibility requires considering the complete computational context.

I also tie uncertainty estimates to the specific model. In the reference calculation, the uncertainty concerns temperature estimated from a final snapshot of independent particles. Integrating a different algorithm requires its own justification of uncertainty.

Recovering from Failures During Computation

An in-memory backend is available for local use. Redis supports shared task state and task recovery.

The Redis backend stores task states and execution information. A worker acquires a task for a limited period and periodically confirms that it is still running. If those confirmations stop, the task can be recovered and assigned to another execution attempt.

This uses at-least-once delivery: a calculation may execute again after a failure. The project therefore distinguishes between two identifiers:

  • task_id identifies the user’s task.
  • attempt_id identifies a specific execution attempt. Artifacts from different attempts are stored separately. An additional ownership check protects result publication from an outdated worker.

This is particularly useful when an application restarts or loses its Redis connection. If an integrated algorithm performs external actions, such as modifying another database, the possibility of repeated execution must be handled separately.

Deployments with multiple API instances also require shared artifact storage. Redis coordinates tasks, while access to result files is addressed at the deployment level.

Observing the Service

For a computational system, it is useful to distinguish between time spent waiting and time spent calculating. A slow response may originate in the queue, the computational core, or the storage infrastructure.

scientific_fastapi therefore provides an optional OpenTelemetry integration. It connects the HTTP request, task enqueueing, and computation, including context propagation into worker threads. Metrics capture waiting time, execution duration, and task outcomes.

MLflow can be enabled for experiment tracking. It allows run parameters and artifacts to be recorded in a dedicated tracking system.

Redis, MLflow, observability tools, notebook tools, and research dependencies are provided through optional extras. Users can select the components their scenario requires while keeping the core dependency set small.

Where the Project Can Be Applied

The first application is teaching computational physics and statistical modeling. The reference model can be used to study relaxation, random realizations, and changes in statistical uncertainty. The same computational code can serve an educational interface, a notebook, and automated checks.

The second is preparing reproducible computational experiments. The research pipeline saves results, figures, and a manifest containing checksums. This helps connect a published figure to its input parameters and verify that the data can be regenerated in a consistent environment.

The third is a shared computational service for a research group. Multiple users submit tasks over HTTP, track their status, and retrieve results through a common contract. This is useful when people need to access the same computational code from different client tools.

The fourth is a foundation for an API around a custom scientific algorithm. The reference core can be replaced with a validated solver, experimental data processing, or a scientific machine learning model. Task management, observability, and artifact storage provide a foundation for this work. Each new core still needs an input contract, resource requirements, and scientific validation methods.

The fifth is controlled comparison of execution approaches. The project includes benchmarks for NumPy, threads, processes, Numba, and JAX. Comparisons use a fixed workload, check numerical consistency, and separate warmup from repeated measurements.

For me, such benchmarks are tools for choosing an implementation for a particular task. Small arrays may be dominated by overhead; other workloads may be limited by data transfer or compilation costs. Free-threaded Python likewise requires measurements on the selected computation: changing the GIL configuration alone does not determine overall performance.

What This Approach Provides

In v2.0.0, checks cover the scientific model, HTTP contract, Redis task recovery, artifact isolation, and optional integrations. CI validates Python 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14, installation of the built wheel, and container behavior after restart. Releases are published after successful checks for the corresponding commit, with a wheel, source distribution, and SHA256SUMS attached.

I see scientific_fastapi as a foundation for scientific services with clearly defined responsibilities between the computational model and its infrastructure. The model determines the physical and mathematical meaning of the result. The infrastructure handles request validation, controlled execution, data preservation, and the ability to investigate how that result was produced.

This approach becomes useful when other people begin using scientific code. It helps turn an individual algorithm into a tool for collaborative work while preserving the ability to validate and develop the computation itself.

Source code and setup instructions are available in the scientific_fastapi repository. The project is distributed under the MIT license.

title: Your Rate Limiter Works Until You Deploy a Second Server
description:
A rate limiter can work perfectly in development and still fail in production.

You test it locally, send too many requests, and receive a 429 Too Many Requests response. Everything looks fine.

Then you deploy your Node.js application with two instances behind a load balancer.

Suddenly, users can send more requests than your limit allows.

The problem isn't necessarily your rate-limiting algorithm. It's where you're storing the request counts.

The Problem With In-Memory Rate Limiting

Consider this Express middleware:

const requests = new Map();

function rateLimiter(req, res, next) {
  const key = req.ip;
  const now = Date.now();
  const windowMs = 60_000;
  const limit = 10;

  let record = requests.get(key);

  if (!record || now - record.start >= windowMs) {
    record = {
      count: 0,
      start: now,
    };
  }

  record.count++;
  requests.set(key, record);

  if (record.count > limit) {
    return res.status(429).json({
      message: "Too many requests",
    });
  }

  next();
}

This simplified fixed-window limiter allows up to 10 requests per IP address per minute in a single process.

But what happens when your application runs on two servers?

Imagine the load balancer distributes requests like this:

  • Server A receives 10 requests.
  • Server B receives another 10 requests.
  • Each server maintains its own Map.

Both servers see only 10 requests. Neither rejects the requests.

Your intended limit was 10 requests per minute, but the user managed to send 20.

With more instances, the discrepancy can become even larger.

The key issue is that each process has its own memory.

An in-memory counter is not shared across Node.js processes, containers, or separate application instances.

Why This Matters in Production

This becomes especially important when rate limits protect:

  • Login and password-reset endpoints
  • Public APIs with usage quotas
  • Expensive database queries
  • AI or third-party API calls that cost money
  • Endpoints vulnerable to automated abuse

A rate limiter that works only within one process may provide weaker protection than you expect.

There is another problem: when a process restarts, its counters disappear. Scaling, restarting, or replacing instances can therefore change the effective limit.

A Better Approach: Use Redis

Redis gives multiple application instances access to shared state.

Instead of keeping request counts in a local Map, each instance updates a shared counter.

A simplified Redis fixed-window implementation might look like this:

async function rateLimiter(req, res, next) {
  try {
    const key = `rate-limit:${req.ip}`;
    const limit = 10;
    const windowSeconds = 60;

    const count = await redis.incr(key);

    if (count === 1) {
      await redis.expire(key, windowSeconds);
    }

    if (count > limit) {
      return res.status(429).json({
        message: "Too many requests",
      });
    }

    next();
  } catch (error) {
    next(error);
  }
}

Here, redis represents an already configured Redis client.

Now both servers use the same counter. If Server A processes six requests and Server B processes five, the shared count reaches eleven, so the eleventh request is rejected.

However, this example illustrates the idea rather than providing a complete production-ready implementation.

There is still a subtle problem

The counter increment and expiration are separate commands.

If the process fails between INCR and EXPIRE, the key might remain without an expiration. That could cause requests to be rejected indefinitely.

For production use, execute the counter update and expiration logic atomically, for example with a Redis Lua script or an appropriate atomic Redis operation.

You should also decide what happens when Redis becomes unavailable. Failing open allows requests through but weakens protection; failing closed preserves the limit but can make an endpoint unavailable. The right choice depends on the endpoint and its risk.

Redis Doesn't Automatically Make Every Rate Limiter Correct

Using shared storage solves the per-instance counter problem, but other design decisions still matter.

1. Choose the right algorithm

A fixed-window limiter is easy to implement, but it can allow bursts around window boundaries.

For example, a client might send 10 requests just before a window resets and another 10 immediately afterward.

Depending on your requirements, a sliding-window counter, sliding log, or token bucket may provide better behavior.

2. Identify clients correctly

Using req.ip requires careful proxy configuration.

If Express trusts forwarded headers from untrusted clients, an attacker might spoof their apparent IP address. Configure trust proxy according to your actual infrastructure rather than enabling it blindly.

For authenticated APIs, you may want to rate-limit by user ID, API key, IP address, or a combination of these.

3. Set limits by endpoint

A public read endpoint and a password-reset endpoint do not have the same risk profile.

You might allow more requests for inexpensive reads while applying stricter limits to authentication or resource-intensive operations.

4. Consider an existing library

For many Express applications, using a maintained rate-limiting library with a Redis-compatible store is safer than implementing every detail yourself.

A library can handle important concerns such as response headers, window behavior, storage integration, and configuration. You still need to verify that its algorithm and failure behavior match your requirements.

How to Test Your Rate Limiter

Don't test only one request at a time against your local development server.

A more useful test plan includes:

  1. Send more requests than the configured limit and verify that excess requests receive 429.
  2. Send requests through multiple application instances and confirm that the shared limit is enforced.
  3. Verify that the counter resets or expires as intended.
  4. Test concurrent requests, not just sequential requests.
  5. Simulate Redis failures and confirm the intended fail-open or fail-closed behavior.
  6. Test forwarded IP headers using your actual proxy configuration.

For production systems, also monitor rejected requests and storage errors. A rate limiter that silently fails can be difficult to diagnose.

The Real Lesson

Rate limiting is not just about counting requests. It is about maintaining consistent state across the infrastructure that processes those requests.

An in-memory counter can be perfectly reasonable for a single-process prototype. But once an application scales horizontally, local state is no longer enough for a globally enforced limit.

Before deploying a rate limiter, ask yourself one question: does every server agree on how many requests this client has made?

If the answer is no, your limit might not be the limit you think it is.

Have you implemented rate limiting in a production application? Did you use Redis, a gateway, or another approach?

title: Unified LLM API for Multi-Provider Chatbot Fallback: Automatic Failover for CRM Actions
description:
For an edtech in-app chatbot that turns sales-call notes into CRM actions, a unified LLM API gives a multi-provider fallback path with automatic failover. Keep the frontend speaking one request shape, validate the returned action object, and retry only when the failure is transient. The provider choice is an implementation detail; the CRM contract is not.

My decision rule is practical: pick the route that passes the same structured-output test across normal calls, rate limits, and provider outages. A unified API is a strong fit when that test matters more than provider-specific features. Direct provider clients remain the better choice when you need a model's newest native capability or strict regional control.

Measure the contract, not the vibes.

For this exact routing problem, Infrai is a candidate in the experiment rather than a conclusion. Its public discovery surface describes capabilities, request schemas, response schemas, billing, and runnable examples, so the team can inspect the integration before wiring the chatbot to it. The useful question is still whether its route passes the CRM action contract during fallback.

What is the bill actually made of?

For this workflow, the bill is mostly tokens, not the HTTP request itself. A transcript, a few CRM field definitions, and the model's JSON response make up the recurring input and output volume. If the product sends the full call transcript on every follow-up, input tokens dominate quickly; if it asks for a verbose explanation beside the action object, output tokens become the avoidable part.

That gives the experiment a useful first change: retain a compact call summary and the unresolved action state, then send those with the next user turn instead of replaying every prior message. Count tokens before choosing a cheaper model. tiktoken is useful for OpenAI-family estimates, but provider tokenization differs, so treat the result as a planning signal rather than a universal meter.

There is a retention trade-off here. I would stop keeping raw transcript text in the chatbot state after the CRM action has been accepted, retaining the audit reference and normalized fields instead. That reduces repeated context, but it makes a bad extraction harder to investigate. The remedy is an explicit retention policy and a redacted review sample, not pretending that deletion has no operational cost.

Should a unified LLM API handle multi-provider chatbot fallback?

Use a small fixed corpus before making a routing decision. Ten sales calls is enough to expose malformed dates, missing owners, multiple courses, and a customer who changes their mind mid-call. For each case, ask for exactly one JSON object with lead_status, course, next_action, owner, and follow_up_at; reject unknown keys and require null when the transcript does not support a value.

The pass criteria should be mechanical:

  • The response parses as JSON and contains every required key.
  • No value contradicts the transcript, including a guessed follow-up date.
  • A retry after a simulated 429 returns one action, not two CRM writes.
  • Switching the selected model does not require a frontend change.
  • A provider failure is visible in server logs with a request identifier, while the user receives a useful retry state.

The last two criteria separate fallback from blind repetition. Chat completion retries are safe only while the CRM write is still pending. Once an action is published, give it a client-generated idempotency key and make the consumer deduplicate it. A standard queue is at-least-once delivery; treating it as exactly once is how duplicate follow-up tasks reach admissions staff.

Here is a minimal leg of that experiment using an OpenAI-compatible client. The prompt is deliberately strict, and validation happens before any CRM call. The code does not claim that a different model will produce equivalent results; it records the result so the team can compare them.

import json
import os
import time

from openai import OpenAI


def extract_action(transcript: str, model: str = "auto") -> dict:
    client = OpenAI(
        api_key=os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"],
        base_url="https://api.infrai.cc/v1",
    )
    prompt = (
        "Return only one JSON object with these keys: lead_status, course, "
        "next_action, owner, follow_up_at. Use null when unsupported.\n\n"
        f"Sales call transcript:\n{transcript}"
    )

    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            response = client.chat.completions.create(
                model=model,
                messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
            )
            content = response.choices[0].message.content
            action = json.loads(content)
            required = {
                "lead_status", "course", "next_action", "owner", "follow_up_at"
            }
            if set(action) != required:
                raise ValueError("CRM action keys do not match the contract")
            return action
        except Exception as error:
            status = getattr(error, "status_code", None)
            if status != 429 or attempt == 3:
                raise
            retry_after = getattr(error, "headers", {}).get("retry-after")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
            time.sleep(delay)

    raise RuntimeError("unreachable")

For a discovery probe, the boundary is explicit and easy to inspect:

import os
import requests


response = requests.get(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/models",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"},
    timeout=20,
)
response.raise_for_status()
print(response.json())

In production, put the CRM write behind a queue and make the worker idempotent. Keep the chatbot response independent from the eventual write, because a model retry and a CRM retry are different failure domains. That distinction catches more real defects than adding another provider to a diagram.

That is the trap.

Which provider boundary fits the workflow?

Infrai belongs in the routing leg of this experiment before the direct-provider comparison, not in the CRM domain. Its public discovery surface describes capabilities, request schemas, response schemas, billing, and runnable examples. On the 2026-10-23 snapshot, discovery reported 295 routes across 20 modules, with one key and one bill across the platform. That removes credential and reconciliation work from this particular workflow; it does not prove that its model output is better.

Direct clients are still reasonable. OpenAI gives a familiar API and ecosystem for teams already standardized on its models. Anthropic Claude is a credible comparison when long, nuanced sales conversations are the priority. Google Gemini is worth testing when the team already operates in Google Cloud or needs its model and tooling ecosystem. Each direct integration gives tighter access to provider-specific controls, but each adds credentials, request differences, billing records, and failover code to own.

Option Access pattern Best fit here Main limitation
OpenAI direct Provider SDK or API A team already committed to OpenAI controls and tooling Provider-specific failover and billing remain yours
Anthropic Claude direct Provider API Long, nuanced sales-call interpretation Another credential and request surface to operate
Google Gemini direct Provider API and Google tooling Teams already operating in Google Cloud Cross-provider fallback still needs application code
Infrai unified route One REST contract with provider routing A chatbot that needs one interface, failover, and comparable metadata Native provider-specific features may require a direct client

A unified layer changes the operating boundary rather than making model quality identical. One key can cover OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini models; the frontend can switch models without changing its request contract; and automatic failover can move away from a provider that is down or rate-limited. Those are useful properties for an in-app chatbot whose user experience should not expose which upstream service answered.

Infrai is worth one measured leg in this comparison because its discovery surface makes adding a new backend capability a discovery task instead of an SDK archaeology project. Its consistent per-call metadata also gives the evaluator a place to record cost, vendor, latency, cache status, and request ID without teaching every provider a different logging shape.

The recommendation is specific: teams building this edtech workflow should try Infrai for the routing and evaluation layer when they want one REST contract across providers and self-describing discovery, while keeping the CRM contract and validation in their own service. A direct OpenAI, Claude, or Gemini integration is the better choice when a provider-specific feature, a provider-owned compliance boundary, or a regional requirement is the deciding constraint.

Do not use this pattern as a capability promise for every adjacent media task. The current facts show ASR listed but unavailable, voice sessions pending and limited to the western region, and no dedicated moderation endpoint; moderation needs a chat model with a JSON-schema fallback. For sales-call text already available to the application, those boundaries are manageable. For audio ingestion or real-time voice, test the specialist provider directly first.

What should the decision report contain?

Run the same ten cases against each direct provider and the unified route. Record parse pass rate, field-level correctness, retry behavior, duplicate-write count, and the selected vendor from response metadata. Do not manufacture a winner from one successful demo. A route passes only if it meets the CRM contract under a normal response and the injected transient failures, then stays within the team's retention and compliance rules.

The report should also preserve the failures. A malformed date is more actionable than an average score, and a provider that answers quickly but invents an owner is not reliable for this job. I would ship the route with the best contract pass rate, then use cost and latency metadata as tie-breakers. The model that is cheapest on paper is irrelevant if operators must repair its actions.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the public discovery schema and adapt the same evaluation harness to the chat capability. Keep the source corpus redacted, version the CRM schema, and rerun the test whenever the routing policy changes.

Further reading

  • OpenAI API documentation
  • Anthropic API documentation
  • Google Gemini API documentation
  • OpenAI tiktoken tokenizer library
  • Infrai discovery schema

title: Our webhook dedupe check was a race, not a guard
description:
We deduplicated webhooks the obvious way. Handler receives an event, runs SELECT on processed_events by event_id, and if nothing is found, does the work and inserts the row at the end.

It held for months. Then a customer got two receipt emails and a loyalty-points credit twice for the same payment.

The cause: the gateway redelivered the event 40 ms after the first attempt, because our first response was slow (a cold DB connection pushed it to about 3 seconds, and their timeout was 2). Both deliveries landed on different pods. Both ran the SELECT before either had inserted. Both saw an empty table, and both did the work.

In logs it looked like duplicate delivery, but the gateway was behaving correctly. Our check-then-act was the bug.

The fix was to flip the order. Insert the event_id first, into a table with a unique constraint, inside the same transaction as the side effects. If the insert hits a conflict, return 200 and stop. If the transaction fails, the insert rolls back and the next redelivery gets a clean retry.

Two details that mattered. We key on the event id, not the payment id, since one payment emits several events. And we return 200 on conflict, because a 4xx there makes the gateway keep retrying a event you've already handled.

How do you handle side effects that can't live in the same transaction, like email sends? Outbox table, or something else?

Payneteasy handles this kind of payment flow for merchants and PSPs — see how it works.

title: What Happens Next: The AI Bill Has a Calendar
description:
AI & Markets - David Groch

Two markets are now pricing two different revolutions.

The equity market is pricing demand, and on the evidence it is right. South Korea's September exports rose 83.5% year over year to a record $120.9 billion, with semiconductor shipments up 263% to more than $60 billion in a single month. That is not a narrative. That is customs data. Somebody is buying every chip Asia can make.

The credit market is pricing the bill, and on the evidence it is also right. Five-year credit default swaps hit records across the AI complex this month: Oracle at 322 basis points, up from 144 in January; Broadcom at 136; Nvidia at 101; Meta at 108; SpaceX at 226; CoreWeave near 1,090, which is distressed territory by any definition. Converted into the market's own arithmetic, Oracle's spread implies roughly a 23% five-year default probability, Broadcom's about 12%, Nvidia's about 8%. AI-linked companies have issued an estimated $466 billion of debt in 2026, against $101 billion in the same period of 2025. Weekly trading in CDS on the seven biggest AI names went from under $2 billion in July to over $9 billion in September.

One honest caveat before the calendar: an implied default probability is not a forecast. Part of the widening is mechanical, because equity managers buy CDS as a cheap hedge and hedging demand widens spreads on its own. Oracle is not going bankrupt at a 23% rate in any world a credit analyst would sign. What the spreads actually say is narrower and more useful: the price of insuring the buildout has multiplied, the marginal buyer of AI debt now demands to be paid for duration and doubt, and the next round of funding will not be priced like the last one. That is the story. And unlike most market stories, this one has dates.

Next week: the pincer

Monday, October 26. Celestica reports after the close, with its investor day on Tuesday. This is the margin canary. Celestica is a contract manufacturer with thin EMS margins and enormous hyperscaler exposure, and the one serious bear case on the name is simple: when AI hardware margins compress, they compress for the assembler first. The Street is unanimously bullish (average target near $474 against a $262 stock), which means the print has to be clean, not good. A margin wobble here is the first company-level confirmation that the buildout's economics are squeezing the supply chain. The same morning, the first big SpaceX lockup tranche (up to 328 million shares) becomes tradable, a week after the stock rose 8% on earnings and fell 9% on profit-taking and unlock fears. Supply meets a story stock.

Wednesday, October 28. The week's hinge, and it is a pincer. At 2:00 p.m. ET the FOMC decides. The Reuters poll of 100 economists is as close to unanimous as polls get: 94 expect a hold at 3.75% to 4.00%, and all 100 expect a hike in December. The risk is not the decision, it is the language, because Chair Warsh has dropped forward guidance and publicly distanced himself from the committee's own projections. Two hours later, Microsoft and Alphabet report. Their earnings are no longer really about earnings. Meta already showed the template: beat on revenue, guide above consensus, and lose 7% anyway because the capex line moved. What Microsoft and Alphabet say about 2027 spending is the referendum on whether Meta's repricing was one company's problem or the sector's.

Thursday, October 29. September PCE and the first Q3 GDP print land before the open (consensus: core PCE 3.1% year over year, headline 3.6%), and Amazon reports after the close. A hot core print with a December hike already unanimous is the stagflation-lite combination: it validates the CDS move and pushes the terminal-rate debate from one more hike to two. A soft print is the only scheduled event all week that can actually relieve the credit market.

Next month: the report cards

November 3 brings the US midterms, which matter here for one reason: energy and industrial policy are now market variables, and oil above $110 with the Strategic Petroleum Reserve at its lowest since 1982 (282.7 million barrels) is a political fact as much as an economic one.

November 2 to 12 is the cluster that decides whether the CDS story stays a hedge or becomes a verdict. The leveraged end of the buildout reports in a ten-day window: Cipher Mining on November 2, Core Scientific on November 5, CoreWeave around November 9, Nebius around November 10, TeraWulf in the same stretch. Read these reports for one line only: the funding line. Bank of America's preview of CoreWeave is the template of the whole moment. The bank rates the stock a buy with a $140 target, forecasts Q3 revenue of $3.66 billion (up 168%), cites a $129 billion backlog, and then estimates the company needs roughly $20 billion of additional funding, with $12.5 billion of capex in the quarter alone. Even the bull case is now written as a financing story. Backlog is not the question anymore. The coupon is.

November 18 is Nvidia, the last and largest report of the season, and throughout the month Meta's $25 billion New Mexico judgment accrues interest at 15% a year, roughly $10 million a day, which is its own kind of calendar: every week of appeal is a week the settlement price argument changes.

Just past the horizon, December holds the two dates that could close the loop: the FOMC meeting where 100 of 100 economists expect the hike, and December 9, when Micron's $35 billion buyback authorization becomes usable. The largest memory maker becoming a structural buyer of its own stock is the equity market's best scheduled answer to the credit market's question.

Three ways this resolves

The bill gets paid quietly. Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon hold or trim their capex guides to something the cash flow can carry, the neoclouds fund at tolerable rates, and CDS spreads tighten into year-end. Signpost: Oracle CDS back under 250 basis points and a CoreWeave funding deal at single-digit rates. In this world the October repricing was a tantrum.

The slow bleed. Guides go up again, the Fed hikes in December with two more on the table, and equities de-rate gradually toward where credit already is. No crash, no capitulation, just a multiple that shrinks while the spending does not. Signpost: bank stocks, already on their longest losing streak since 2008 (six straight weeks for the KBW index), keep sliding while the indexes hold up on a narrowing group of names.

Something breaks at the weak end. A funding deal fails, or prices at the mid-teens yields where CoreWeave's bonds already flirt, and the question stops being about one neocloud's balance sheet and becomes about who else financed the same way. Signpost: any postponement or pulled deal in the November cluster, or CoreWeave CDS pushing through 1,200 basis points. This is the only scenario where the Asia story and the credit story collide, because the chip demand is real, and real demand financed badly is exactly how the last buildout ended: the fiber got lit, the carriers did not survive it, and the cables outlived the companies that laid them.

The demand is not the debate. The price of money is. And for once, the market has published the schedule on which it will argue: October 28 for rates, October 28 and 29 for capex, November 2 to 12 for the leveraged end, December for the bill itself. Watch the calendar, not the commentary.

Facts and sources (checked October 23, 2026): CDS levels and implied probabilities, Morgan Stanley research via the Financial Times and Financial Gurkha (October 19-20), Mott Capital via TalkMarkets (October 19). AI-linked issuance $466B and CDS weekly volume, Morgan Stanley via FT. Korea September exports, Reuters and MOTIE customs data (October 1). FOMC expectations, Reuters poll of 100 economists (October 16-20). PCE and GDP consensus, Morningstar week-ahead (October 23). Earnings dates: Microsoft and Alphabet October 28, Amazon October 29 (company notices via Admiral Markets, Reuters, Zacks); CoreWeave around November 9 (Zacks estimate, company date not formally announced); Nebius around November 10 (StockAnalysis estimate); Nvidia November 18 (TradeStation calendar, estimated); Core Scientific November 5 (company). CoreWeave funding estimates and $140 target, Bank of America (October 22). SPR level 282.7M barrels, DOE data via Reuters (October 19). KBW Bank Index six-week losing streak, Bloomberg via TradingView (October 20). Celestica consensus and targets, Seeking Alpha. Implied default probabilities are model outputs that depend on recovery-rate assumptions; they are not forecasts.
