title: Batch Process Multiple Documents with a Summarization API — Tenant Cost Controls
description:
Short answer: use a tenant-aware batch to process multiple documents for summarization, preserve one accounting record per document, and retry only operations with a clear idempotency boundary.

Support-ticket summarization is a small data pipeline, not a loop around a summarization endpoint. For a developer-tools team, the useful unit is a tenant-aware batch: collect a bounded set of documents, normalize them, submit work with an idempotency key, record usage before the result is displayed, and make partial failure visible. The summary is only one output. The other is an accounting trail that explains which tenant consumed which amount of work.

That ordering matters. If I let a retry create a second charge-shaped event, or if I attach usage to the worker instead of the tenant, triage gets faster while the bill becomes impossible to explain. I would rather lose one optional summary than lose the ability to answer, "Which customer caused this usage, and can we reproduce the count?"

The ledger is the boundary.

Keep it boring.

It also forces a useful compromise: source text can expire while hashes and usage records remain available for reconciliation.

What is the bill actually made of?

The dominant term in a multi-document job is usually the amount of text sent for processing, not the number of Python function calls. The exact accounting unit depends on the runtime contract, so treat usage as a measured value returned by the processing system or a deliberately defined estimate. Do not infer it from document count. Five short tickets and five exported logs are both five documents, but they are not the same workload.

For each document, keep the tenant identifier, document identifier, content hash, input measurement, output measurement when available, processing status, and request id. A batch record stores requested, accepted, completed, and failed counts plus aggregate usage. The raw text belongs in controlled storage; the cost ledger does not need to duplicate it.

Here is a deliberately boring manifest. Boring records are easier to audit six weeks later.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Iterable


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Document:
    tenant_id: str
    document_id: str
    text: str
    content_hash: str


def build_manifest(documents: Iterable[Document], batch_id: str) -> dict:
    items = []
    for document in documents:
        if not document.text.strip():
            continue
        items.append({
            "batch_id": batch_id,
            "tenant_id": document.tenant_id,
            "document_id": document.document_id,
            "content_hash": document.content_hash,
            "status": "pending",
        })
    return {"batch_id": batch_id, "items": items}

I keep the manifest and usage event longer than the generated prose, subject to privacy and contractual requirements. That lets a later investigation reconstruct what was attempted without keeping every customer sentence forever. Deleting source text makes content-level debugging harder, so the retention policy needs an owner and a reason.

How can a batch process multiple documents through a summarization API?

A batch worker should not treat the input array as a transaction. One malformed export, timeout, or rate-limit response should move one item to a retryable or terminal state while the rest continues. The batch summary should say so plainly.

I model item states as pending, running, succeeded, retryable, and failed. Each transition includes an attempt number and timestamp. A retry is allowed only when the previous attempt is known to have ended without a committed result, or when an idempotency key protects the boundary. Otherwise, a network ambiguity can produce duplicate summaries and duplicate ledger events. Three attempts is a policy choice in the example, not a guarantee from the runtime.

import time
from collections.abc import Callable


def process_batch(items: list[dict], summarize: Callable[[str], dict],
                  max_attempts: int = 3) -> list[dict]:
    results = []
    for item in items:
        for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):
            item["attempt"] = attempt
            item["status"] = "running"
            try:
                response = summarize(item["text"])
                item["status"] = "succeeded"
                item["usage"] = response.get("usage")
                item["summary"] = response["summary"]
                break
            except TimeoutError:
                item["status"] = "retryable"
                if attempt < max_attempts:
                    time.sleep(2 ** (attempt - 1))
            except ValueError as error:
                item["status"] = "failed"
                item["error"] = str(error)
                break
        results.append(item)
    return results

This example leaves concurrency out on purpose. Add a worker pool only after measuring service limits and tenant fairness. A global concurrency setting can let one large tenant occupy every slot while smaller tenants wait. Per-tenant quotas, a shared queue, and a maximum batch size make behavior explainable. Add jitter to production backoff so workers do not retry on the same schedule. The limitation is deliberate: this worker is unsuitable as a complete queue, scheduler, or cost allocator without durable state around it.

The first version I would ship has one summary per document. Combining documents can reduce request overhead, but it weakens attribution: a bad result becomes harder to map to a source ticket, and one oversized document can prevent the whole group from completing. Grouping is an optimization, not the default correctness boundary.

Which question should the operational record answer?

The useful question is not only "did the API return 200?" It is "can support explain this result and this usage to one tenant?" A successful transport response can still contain an unusable payload, a truncated result, or no usage information. Validate the response schema, cap accepted output length, and store the request id beside the result.

Emit structured events such as summary.requested, summary.completed, and summary.failed. Include tenant id, batch id, document id, attempt, status, and measured usage where available. Do not put ticket text in ordinary logs. Large payloads make the signal difficult to scan and create a privacy problem.

A dashboard should show batches by status, failures by reason, latency by document size, and usage by tenant. The last view is the decision axis. An aggregate total hides noisy neighbors; a tenant view makes an unexpectedly expensive integration visible before the monthly report becomes a surprise.

If a worker times out after the remote operation accepted the request, local state is uncertain. Mark it unknown, reconcile it using the request id, and do not silently classify it as a free failure. Treating uncertainty as zero is how cost reports drift.

What belongs in the deployment and test boundary?

Tests should cover decisions, not only the happy-path parser. Feed the worker an empty document, duplicate content hash, malformed response, timeout after acceptance, and a tenant that reaches its quota. Assert both item state and ledger event. A unit test that checks only summary misses the failure that matters to finance and support.

Use deterministic fixtures for summarization responses. Keep a small integration test for authentication, request serialization, response validation, and usage extraction. Production customer text does not belong in a test fixture.

Before release, set limits for document size, batch size, retries, queue age, and retained source content. These are policy settings, not magic constants scattered through workers. Include effective values in batch metadata so an operator can distinguish a code change from a changed limit.

The API boundary also needs bounded timeouts, explicit non-success handling, and correlation identifiers. WebRTC is not a summarization protocol, but MDN's WebRTC API documentation illustrates the useful lifecycle principle: model distinct objects and states instead of treating a network operation as one opaque call. Apply that to the backend batch: request, processing state, result, and cleanup are separate points.

The retention choice is product behavior

A support-triage system is judged by the speed of the first useful answer, but it is operated by people who handle privacy requests, tenant disputes, and unreliable networks. Keep what the next investigation needs. My default is a manifest, hashes, state transitions, usage records, and a pointer to controlled source storage; raw text expires according to policy.

That choice costs diagnostic detail. If a summary looks wrong after the source expires, the team may prove which document was processed but not recreate its wording. Indefinite content retention creates a different risk. The right answer is a written retention period, an access audit, and a redaction path.

The practical decision rule is simple: batch only work that can share a failure policy and an accounting boundary. Preserve per-document identity when transport groups requests. Report measured usage to the tenant that submitted the document. Reconcile ambiguous outcomes. Make partial completion a first-class result.

That is how a summarization API becomes useful infrastructure for support triage: the prose helps the queue, while the ledger makes the system operable.

Further reading

  • MDN, WebRTC API: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebRTC_API
  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • OpenTelemetry, Logs Data Model: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/logs/data-model/

title: I built a static site generator in Rust because Astro felt slow
description:
Most frameworks feel slow to me. I was using Astro for my blog, and even Astro, which is supposed to be fast, felt slow. Then one day it hit me: why not write a really fast static site generator in Rust, the language that makes everything fast?

That's how agno started. It's a single 4.2 MB binary with no Node.js and no bundler.

Performance blew past my expectations. On the same corpus, cold builds are 3.9-12.8x faster than Hugo and 16.7-185x faster than Astro. I tested it with up to 10,000 posts, and the speed never let me down, it kept surprising me. The full methodology and caveats are in the README.

It has everything I personally need, but that is not the finish line for me, and I'm still working on it.

You can try it with cargo install agno.

Repo: https://github.com/agnogad/agno

title: OpenAI Claude Gemini Chatbot API Comparison: Quality, Latency, and Tenant Boundaries 2026
description:
Short answer: for an OpenAI, Claude, or Gemini chatbot API comparison, choose Claude 3.5 Sonnet for quality or GPT-4o-mini for speed and budget; decide only after checking each tenant’s region, retention, deletion, and processor boundaries.

The boundary comes first.

Claude 3.5 Sonnet is the safest default when conversational quality decides the outcome; GPT-4o-mini is the practical choice for a budget-conscious tenant with acceptable quality. For a healthtech chatbot that helps score candidates against a job rubric, however, the model ranking is only half the architecture. Region, retention, deletion, and processor boundaries decide whether the comparison is safe to operate per tenant.

The useful design keeps candidate data inside an explicit tenant boundary, sends the smallest possible rubric-scoring context to a provider, and records cost and latency metadata beside the tenant request. In practice, that means separating the candidate record from the prompt assembly service, allowing only the rubric fields approved for the tenant, attaching the request ID to cost telemetry, and giving deletion a path through every retained copy rather than trusting a dashboard toggle. Streaming improves perceived performance. It does not answer where data is processed or how it is deleted.

Infrai is relevant here as a plain REST layer with one key and one bill: it can expose consistent request metadata while the tenant service keeps ownership of sensitive records. Its public discovery surface is self-describing, so a team can inspect a capability before wiring it into the path.

What decision are you actually making?

The first decision is not “which model is smartest?” It is “which processor may see which fields, in which region, for how long?” A recruiter’s transcript can contain names, employment history, accommodation information, or other sensitive details even if the prompt calls it a rubric.

I would record four invariants in the architecture decision record:

  • The tenant owns the source record and its deletion request. Model prompts and responses receive a request identifier, not an uncontrolled copy of the tenant database.
  • Region is an allow-list decision. A model name is not proof of residency.
  • Retention has an owner and an expiry path. A streaming response can be displayed without becoming a permanent transcript.
  • Processor boundaries are explicit. A gateway can standardize transport and telemetry, but it cannot grant a specialist provider’s contractual residency or deletion guarantee.

Those invariants make cost visibility useful. Per-call cost, vendor, latency, cache status, and request ID should be attributable to the tenant without copying candidate content into the billing system.

Should OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini power your chatbot API?

Claude 3.5 Sonnet has the highest conversational quality of these choices and typically takes 2-3 seconds. GPT-4o-mini gives good quality with the fastest responses, typically 1-2 seconds, and fits budget-conscious deployments that can accept that quality level. Gemini 1.5 Pro also gives good quality, with competitive pricing, but is slightly slower than GPT-4o-mini. All three support streaming, which helps a recruiter see progress while a longer explanation is generated.

That comparison does not establish any provider’s residency, retention, deletion, or processor terms. Check those against the tenant’s policy and the provider’s current documentation and contract. Treat them as a release gate.

Option Conversational quality Typical latency Boundary implication Good fit
Claude 3.5 Sonnet Highest of these choices 2-3s Verify region and retention terms before sending candidate context Explanations where natural dialogue is the priority
GPT-4o-mini Good 1-2s, fastest of these choices Lower spend does not remove processor review High-volume chat where acceptable quality is enough
Gemini 1.5 Pro Good Slightly slower than GPT-4o-mini Enable only after processing and deletion terms fit the tenant Teams that prefer its quality and pricing position
A REST gateway such as Infrai Depends on the selected model Measure with the tenant’s prompts Can centralize routing and per-call metadata; it cannot create a specialist provider’s contract Teams that want one HTTP integration and an auditable cost boundary

The gateway is an integration decision, not a privacy waiver. Infrai’s useful angle here is a plain REST API: a backend can make HTTP requests without installing or versioning an SDK. Its documented interfaces expose per-call cost, vendor, latency, cache-hit, and request-ID metadata, while one key and one bill reduce credential and reconciliation work across a tenant workflow. That can reduce adapter code needed to attribute a request to a tenant.

The limitation is important: Infrai cannot create a specialist provider’s contractual residency, retention, or deletion guarantee. If those terms are mandatory and unavailable at the gateway boundary, use the specialist provider directly.

For this workflow, I recommend trying Infrai for model routing and cost observation when the team wants one REST integration and tenant-level request metadata; keep provider-specific region, retention, and deletion review as a separate approval. If a tenant requires a specialist provider with a contractual guarantee the gateway cannot supply, use that provider directly or choose a gateway with the required controls.

How do you keep the critical path auditable?

Separate content storage from decision telemetry. The tenant service should retain the rubric, candidate record, and final decision according to its own policy. The inference layer should receive a minimized prompt and return a response. The billing record can retain tenant ID, model, vendor, latency, cost, and request ID while excluding candidate text.

A discovery check is useful before enabling a model or route. It asks what the service currently declares instead of baking a route list into application code. This example uses a verified discovery path and deliberately does not invent a payload for cost comparison.

import json
import os
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

DISCOVERY_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery"


def get_discovery():
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        DISCOVERY_URL,
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"},
        method="GET",
    )
    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=10) as response:
                if response.status != 200:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"discovery failed: HTTP {response.status}")
                return json.load(response)
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
                raise RuntimeError(f"discovery failed: HTTP {error.code}: {detail}") from error
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt)


discovery = get_discovery()
capabilities = discovery.get("capabilities", [])
compare = next(
    (item for item in capabilities if item.get("path") == "/v1/ai/cost/compare"),
    None,
)
if compare is None:
    raise RuntimeError("the cost comparison capability is not declared")
print(json.dumps({"path": compare["path"], "available": compare["available"]}))

The code keeps candidate content out of discovery and telemetry. It also treats a rate limit as a scheduling event, not an invitation to tight-loop. The same discipline belongs around the actual chat call: stream to the UI, enforce a tenant timeout, redact logs, and make a consumer idempotent if a retry can create a durable scoring record.

What should be rejected?

Reject the design that sends the full candidate database to every model and relies on a vendor dashboard to explain tenant spend later. It fails deletion in two directions: the source record can disappear while a copied prompt remains elsewhere, and the billing trail can accidentally become a second store of sensitive content. It also makes a per-tenant cost anomaly hard to distinguish from a prompt-size problem.

Do not treat one latency number as a quality decision. GPT-4o-mini’s 1-2 second range is attractive for an interactive screen, but a recruiter may value the more natural Claude 3.5 Sonnet response enough to accept 2-3 seconds. Gemini 1.5 Pro remains reasonable when its quality and pricing position fit the tenant. These are starting points, not a benchmark for your rubric. Test the exact chatbot prompts, redaction rules, streaming behavior, and tenant accounting before committing.

The rejected design has one valid use case: a low-risk prototype with synthetic candidate records and no production tenant data.

Even then, make the boundary visible so the prototype does not quietly become the production path.

For a production healthtech flow, the clean boundary is simple: the tenant service owns sensitive records and deletion; the selected model provider processes minimized inference context under approved terms; the gateway, if used, owns transport normalization and cost metadata. No layer should claim a guarantee it does not control.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai discovery documentation and validate the current capability declaration before wiring a tenant into the path.

References

  • Infrai discovery: ai.batch.submit request/response schema
  • MDN: Using Server-Sent Events
  • NIST Privacy Framework
  • OWASP: Logging Cheat Sheet

title: Por que texto estilizado vira quadradinho (tofu): fallback de fontes e Unicode
description:
Você cola um nome em negrito cursivo no perfil, ele aparece perfeito no seu celular, e um amigo avisa que só vê uma fileira de quadradinhos. Nada está errado com o texto. O problema é que o aparelho dele não tinha como desenhar aqueles caracteres. Este post explica o porquê e mostra duas armadilhas de código que costumam aparecer junto.

O que é o "tofu"

O quadradinho vazio é chamado de tofu, porque lembra um bloco de tofu. Ele não é um caractere que você digita. É um sintoma de renderização: o sistema pediu uma forma (glyph) para aquele caractere em todas as fontes disponíveis, não achou nenhuma e desenhou um substituto. A família de fontes Noto, do Google, foi nomeada justamente com esse objetivo, "no tofu".

Texto estilizado não é fonte

Os geradores de "letras diferentes" não instalam fonte nenhuma. Eles trocam cada letra comum por outro caractere Unicode que parece negrito, cursivo ou gótico:

const normal = "Ghost";
const estilizado = "𝓖𝓱𝓸𝓼𝓽";

console.log(normal.length);       // 5
console.log(estilizado.length);   // 10
console.log([...estilizado].length); // 5

A maior parte desses estilos vem do bloco Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols (U+1D400 a U+1D7FF), criado para notação matemática. Como cada letra estilizada está fora do plano básico do Unicode, em JavaScript ela ocupa duas unidades UTF-16. Por isso .length devolve 10 e não 5.

Armadilha 1: contar caracteres com .length

Se o seu formulário tem limite de caracteres (um nick de jogo, por exemplo), .length conta unidades UTF-16 e vai dizer que 𝓖𝓱𝓸𝓼𝓽 tem 10. O spread [...texto] conta pontos de código e dá 5. Mas ainda existe um terceiro caso: marcas combinantes, como as do texto "zalgo" ou de um acento decomposto.

const seg = new Intl.Segmenter("pt-BR", { granularity: "grapheme" });

const contar = (t) => ({
  utf16: t.length,
  codepoints: [...t].length,
  graphemes: [...seg.segment(t)].length,
});

Num texto de teste com 6 letras e 13 marcas combinantes empilhadas sobre elas, utf16 e codepoints devolvem 19, enquanto graphemes devolve 6, que é o que a pessoa enxerga. Escolha a contagem que combina com a regra do seu produto e deixe o limite claro para o usuário.

Armadilha 2: pilha de fontes sem fallback

O navegador percorre a lista de font-family até encontrar uma fonte que tenha o caractere. Se a lista termina cedo, sobra o tofu. Termine sempre com uma família genérica:

body {
  font-family: Inter, system-ui, sans-serif;
}

Com sans-serif no fim, o sistema ainda pode usar a fonte de reserva dele para os caracteres que a sua fonte principal não cobre. Isso não garante que todo caractere apareça em todo aparelho, mas reduz muito o problema. E atenção: font-family não "estiliza" texto Unicode estilizado. São caracteres diferentes, não a mesma letra com outra fonte.

Acessibilidade

Leitores de tela podem ler caracteres estilizados pelos nomes longos que o Unicode dá a eles, o que atrapalha quem usa esse recurso. Mantenha em texto comum o que é importante, como nome, data, endereço e link, e use o estilizado só como enfeite.

Checklist rápido

  • Termine a pilha de font-family com sans-serif ou system-ui.
  • Conte caracteres com [...texto] ou Intl.Segmenter, não com .length.
  • Teste a página em um segundo aparelho, de preferência um Android mais antigo.
  • Não coloque informação importante só em texto estilizado.

Se quiser um lugar para ver esses estilos em ação e testá-los em outro celular, eu mantenho um gerador gratuito em português chamado Letra Diferente.

Para saber mais

  • Fallback font (em inglês): como o sistema escolhe uma fonte substituta.
  • Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols (em inglês): o bloco por trás de muitos estilos de negrito e cursivo.
  • Intl.Segmenter no MDN (em inglês): contagem de grafemas em JavaScript.

title: Benchmarking Expo Router Navigation: Memory Footprint and Frame Drop Analysis Under Deep Stack Depth
description:
Benchmarking Expo Router Navigation: Memory Footprint and Frame Drop Analysis Under Deep Stack Depth

When migrating a multi-tenant dashboard from React Navigation to Expo Router's file-based routing, we hit a silent performance cliff at 42 nested routes. Navigation animations dropped from 60fps to 38fps, and memory usage spiked by 140MB on Android mid-range devices. This benchmark isolates the breaking point.

Test Topology

Environment:

  • Expo SDK 52, React Native 0.76
  • Test devices: Pixel 5 (Android 13), iPhone 12 (iOS 17)
  • Profiling: React Native Performance Monitor + Android Studio Memory Profiler
  • Load harness: Automated UI test cycling through 10/25/50/75 nested (tabs) and [id] dynamic routes

Route Structure:

app/
  (auth)/
    login.tsx
  (dashboard)/
    _layout.tsx
    index.tsx
    [tenant]/
      settings/
        [section]/
          [subsection]/
            index.tsx  // Depth = 6 levels

Metric Comparison Table

Route Depth Avg Navigation Time (ms) Memory Delta (MB) Frame Drops (per transition) UI Thread CPU (%)
10 routes 68 +22 0 14
25 routes 105 +58 2 28
50 routes 187 +142 9 51
75 routes 312 +229 18 73

Root Cause: Expo Router's useSegments() hook re-renders the entire layout tree on each navigation event. At 50+ routes, the reconciliation overhead compounds with TailwindCSS class recalculation in nested _layout.tsx components.

Production CSS Mitigation Pattern

The breakthrough came from isolating TailwindCSS utilities into static stylesheet references instead of dynamic className props in deeply nested layouts.

Before (Dynamic Classes):

// app/(dashboard)/_layout.tsx
export default function DashboardLayout() {
  const segments = useSegments();
  const isSettingsActive = segments.includes('settings');

  return (
    <View className={`flex-1 ${
      isSettingsActive ? 'bg-slate-50' : 'bg-white'
    }`}>
      <Slot />
    </View>
  );
}

After (Static Stylesheet + Conditional Mounting):

import { StyleSheet } from 'react-native';

const styles = StyleSheet.create({
  container: { flex: 1 },
  settingsBg: { backgroundColor: '#f8fafc' },
  defaultBg: { backgroundColor: '#ffffff' },
});

export default function DashboardLayout() {
  const segments = useSegments();
  const isSettingsActive = segments.includes('settings');

  return (
    <View style={[
      styles.container,
      isSettingsActive ? styles.settingsBg : styles.defaultBg
    ]}>
      <Slot />
    </View>
  );
}

Result: Navigation time at 50 routes dropped from 187ms to 94ms. Frame drops reduced from 9 to 3 per transition.

Container Query Optimization for Tab Bar

Expo Router's (tabs) layout triggers re-renders when switching between tab screens. Using CSS container queries to scope tab indicator animations prevents layout thrashing:

// app/(dashboard)/(tabs)/_layout.tsx
import { Tabs } from 'expo-router';
import { Platform } from 'react-native';

export default function TabsLayout() {
  return (
    <Tabs
      screenOptions={{
        tabBarStyle: Platform.select({
          ios: styles.tabBarIOS,
          android: styles.tabBarAndroid,
        }),
        tabBarActiveTintColor: '#3b82f6',
        tabBarInactiveTintColor: '#64748b',
      }}
    />
  );
}

const styles = StyleSheet.create({
  tabBarIOS: {
    height: 88,
    paddingBottom: 34,
    borderTopWidth: 0,
    elevation: 0,
    shadowOpacity: 0.1,
    shadowRadius: 8,
  },
  tabBarAndroid: {
    height: 64,
    elevation: 8,
    borderTopWidth: 1,
    borderTopColor: '#e2e8f0',
  },
});

Key: Static StyleSheet objects bypass TailwindCSS runtime parsing. Measured 18% reduction in UI thread CPU usage during tab switches.

Accessibility Focus Trap Fix

Deep navigation stacks broke screen reader focus when modal routes overlaid tab navigators. The issue: <Slot /> doesn't forward accessibilityViewIsModal to child screens.

Fix (Modal Route Layout):

// app/(dashboard)/settings/_layout.tsx
import { Slot } from 'expo-router';
import { View } from 'react-native';

export default function SettingsLayout() {
  return (
    <View
      accessible={true}
      accessibilityViewIsModal={true}
      accessibilityLabel="Settings panel"
      style={{ flex: 1 }}
    >
      <Slot />
    </View>
  );
}

Wrapping <Slot /> in an accessible container with accessibilityViewIsModal ensures VoiceOver and TalkBack trap focus within the modal context.

Production Threshold

Adopting Expo Router's file-based navigation makes architectural sense for:

  • Apps with ≤40 route files in production bundle
  • Teams prioritizing type-safe routing over maximum flexibility
  • Projects where navigation state persists across app restarts (URL-driven state)

When to revert to React Navigation:

  • Dynamic route generation from API responses (e.g., CMS-driven navigation)
  • Apps requiring custom transition animations beyond presentation: 'modal'
  • Route stacks exceeding 60 nested levels (at which point, rearchitect your IA)

The 50-route inflection point isn't arbitrary—it's where JavaScript bundle size intersects with native bridge serialization overhead. Below that threshold, Expo Router's DX benefits outweigh the performance tax.

title: Cloud Computing Made Simple: Understanding IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS
description:
Introduction

Have you ever wondered how apps like Netflix, Gmail, and Spotify work without you having to install or manage complicated servers?

The answer often involves cloud computing.

Cloud computing allows you to use computing resources over the internet instead of owning and maintaining all the physical hardware yourself.

But when you explore cloud computing, you will quickly encounter three terms: IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS.

They sound complicated, but the ideas behind them are surprisingly simple.

Let's break them down using everyday examples, real-world services, and one analogy that makes the differences easy to remember.

First, What Is Cloud Computing?

Before discussing IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS, let's understand cloud computing.

Imagine you want to watch a movie. You don't need to build a cinema, buy all the equipment, and hire people to operate it. You can simply subscribe to a streaming service and watch the movie over the internet.

Cloud computing works similarly.

Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services over the internet instead of requiring you to own and manage all the physical equipment yourself.

These services can include:

  • Servers that run applications.
  • Storage for files and photos.
  • Databases that store information.
  • Platforms for developing software.
  • Applications you can use directly through a browser.

Cloud providers such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud offer many of these resources.

The important thing to understand is that not every cloud service gives you the same level of control or responsibility.

That brings us to IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS.

1. IaaS — Infrastructure as a Service

IaaS gives you access to computing infrastructure, such as virtual servers, storage, and networking, without requiring you to purchase the physical hardware.

Think of it as renting an empty apartment.

The building, electricity connections, and basic infrastructure are provided for you. However, you are responsible for furnishing the apartment and making it suitable for your needs.

With IaaS, the cloud provider manages the physical infrastructure, while you manage much of the software running on it.

What are you responsible for?

Depending on the service, you typically manage:

  • The operating system.
  • Your applications and code.
  • Application configuration.
  • Many security settings and software updates.
  • The data and software you deploy.

The provider manages the physical servers, data center, and underlying infrastructure.

Real-world examples

  • Amazon EC2: Rent virtual servers to run your applications.
  • Azure Virtual Machines: Create and manage virtual machines in Microsoft's cloud.
  • Google Compute Engine: Run virtual machines on Google Cloud.

When would you use IaaS?

Imagine you are building a website that needs a customized server environment.

You want to choose the operating system, install specific software, configure the server, and control how your application runs.

IaaS gives you that flexibility without requiring you to buy a physical server.

In simple terms: IaaS gives you the building blocks, and you decide how to use them.

2. PaaS — Platform as a Service

PaaS provides a platform for building, testing, deploying, and running applications without requiring you to manage the underlying servers and operating systems yourself.

Think of it as renting a fully equipped kitchen.

The kitchen already has an oven, refrigerator, worktops, and cooking equipment. You don't need to install everything before you start cooking.

You can focus on preparing the meal instead of managing the kitchen infrastructure.

With PaaS, developers can focus more on writing and improving code while the provider handles much of the underlying platform.

What are you responsible for?

Typically, you focus on:

  • Writing application code.
  • Building application features.
  • Managing application data.
  • Configuring the application.
  • Testing and improving your software.

The provider manages much of the underlying infrastructure and platform, including the operating system and runtime environment.

The exact division of responsibilities depends on the service.

Real-world examples

  • Google App Engine: Build and run applications without managing the underlying servers.
  • Azure App Service: Host web applications and APIs using a managed platform.
  • Heroku: Deploy applications using a platform that handles much of the infrastructure management.

When would you use PaaS?

Imagine you are developing an online shopping application.

You want to write the code, connect a database, and deploy the application without spending your time configuring virtual machines and maintaining operating systems.

PaaS can simplify that process.

In simple terms: PaaS gives you a ready-to-use platform so you can focus on building your application.

3. SaaS — Software as a Service

SaaS provides a complete software application that you can use over the internet.

Think of it as ordering a meal at a restaurant.

You don't buy the kitchen, install the equipment, or prepare every ingredient yourself. You simply order your meal and enjoy it.

SaaS works similarly. The provider operates and maintains the software, and you use the finished application.

What are you responsible for?

As a typical user, you mainly manage:

  • Your account and access permissions.
  • Your settings and preferences.
  • The information you enter or upload.
  • How you use and share data within the application.

The provider manages the application and its underlying infrastructure, although your organization may still have important security and data-management responsibilities.

Real-world examples

  • Gmail: Send and receive emails through a web-based service.
  • Microsoft 365: Use applications and collaboration tools such as Word and Excel.
  • Salesforce: Manage customer relationships and sales activities.
  • Dropbox: Store, synchronize, and share files.

When would you use SaaS?

Imagine you need to send emails, collaborate with colleagues, or manage customer information.

You don't want to develop an email system or maintain the servers behind a customer management application.

You simply want software that works.

SaaS lets you use an existing application without building and maintaining it yourself.

In simple terms: SaaS gives you the finished product, ready to use.

One Kitchen Analogy to Remember Them All

Let's imagine you want to prepare a meal.

There are three ways you could approach the task.

IaaS: Rent the kitchen infrastructure

You rent a kitchen with the essential infrastructure in place.

You choose and install the equipment and decide how to organize the cooking environment.

This resembles IaaS because you get the infrastructure but retain significant control over what runs on it.

PaaS: Use a fully equipped kitchen

You walk into a kitchen where the equipment is already installed and ready to use.

You bring your recipe and ingredients, then focus on preparing the meal.

This resembles PaaS because the platform is ready, allowing you to focus on building and running your application.

SaaS: Order a prepared meal

You order a meal from a restaurant.

Someone else manages the kitchen, equipment, and cooking process. You simply enjoy the finished meal.

This resembles SaaS because you use a complete application instead of building or maintaining it yourself.

Here's the easiest way to remember the difference:

  • IaaS: You manage more of the environment.
  • PaaS: You focus on building the application.
  • SaaS: You use the finished application.

IaaS vs. PaaS vs. SaaS: What's the Difference?

Feature IaaS PaaS SaaS
Full name Infrastructure as a Service Platform as a Service Software as a Service
What you get Computing infrastructure Application development platform Complete software application
Main focus Infrastructure and configuration Building and deploying applications Using software
Control High over virtual infrastructure Focused on the application Primarily application settings and usage
Server management Mostly your responsibility at the operating-system level and above Mostly handled by the provider Handled by the provider
Coding required Depends on what you build Usually required to build applications Usually not required to use the software
Example Amazon EC2 Azure App Service Gmail
Best suited for Teams needing infrastructure control Developers wanting to simplify deployment Individuals and businesses needing ready-made software

The main difference is how much you manage yourself versus how much the cloud provider manages for you.

Generally, IaaS offers more control, PaaS reduces infrastructure management, and SaaS provides a complete application.

Remember that these are general patterns. Actual responsibilities vary by service.

Are There Other Cloud Service Models?

Not at all!

IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS are the three traditional cloud service models, but cloud computing also offers many other specialised services.

Think about it this way: sometimes you need to rent an entire kitchen, sometimes you need a kitchen where you can prepare your own meals, and sometimes you simply want to order food.

But what if you only need storage, a database, or someone to perform one specific task?

Cloud computing works similarly. You can access specific resources and capabilities without having to manage everything yourself.

Here are some other cloud service models worth knowing.

1. FaaS — Function as a Service

FaaS lets you run small pieces of code in response to events without managing servers directly.

For example, imagine users upload photos to your application. You want each photo to be resized automatically.

A function could run whenever a new photo is uploaded.

Examples:

  • AWS Lambda
  • Azure Functions
  • Google Cloud Run functions

FaaS is commonly associated with serverless computing. Serverless doesn't mean there are no servers; it means the provider manages much of the server infrastructure for you.

2. DBaaS — Database as a Service

DBaaS provides a managed database so you don't have to handle all the setup, maintenance, backups, and infrastructure yourself.

For example, an online store needs to store customer details, orders, and product information. A managed database service can handle much of the database administration.

Examples:

  • Amazon RDS
  • Azure SQL Database
  • Google Cloud SQL

3. STaaS — Storage as a Service

STaaS provides storage over the internet so you can save and retrieve files or data without maintaining your own storage infrastructure.

For example, a company might store backups, images, videos, and documents in cloud storage.

Examples:

  • Amazon S3
  • Azure Blob Storage
  • Google Cloud Storage

4. NaaS — Network as a Service

NaaS provides networking capabilities through cloud-based services.

Businesses can use it to connect offices, manage network access, or establish secure connections without building and managing every networking component themselves.

Examples of related offerings include cloud-managed networking and network security services.

The precise features depend on the provider and service.

5. AIaaS — Artificial Intelligence as a Service

AIaaS lets businesses and developers use AI capabilities through hosted services and APIs rather than building and operating every AI component themselves.

For example, a developer might add text analysis, image recognition, or a generative AI chatbot to an application.

Examples:

  • Amazon Bedrock
  • Azure AI services
  • Google Cloud's Vertex AI

These additional models describe particular capabilities offered as services. They can overlap with IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS rather than forming one mutually exclusive list.

Which Cloud Service Model Should You Choose?

The right choice depends on what you want to accomplish.

Choose IaaS if:

  • You need substantial control over your computing environment.
  • You want to configure virtual machines and operating systems.
  • You have the skills and resources to manage your software environment.

Choose PaaS if:

  • You want to build and deploy applications.
  • You want to spend less time managing servers.
  • You prefer a managed platform for development.

Choose SaaS if:

  • You need a ready-to-use application.
  • You don't want to build the software yourself.
  • You want the provider to manage most of the application's underlying technology.

For many organizations, the answer isn't just one model. A company might use SaaS for email, PaaS to host an application, and IaaS for workloads that need more control.

Conclusion

Cloud computing becomes much easier to understand when you stop focusing on the acronyms and start thinking about what you receive and what you are responsible for managing.

Remember the kitchen analogy:

  • IaaS: You get the kitchen infrastructure and manage more of the environment.
  • PaaS: You get a kitchen ready for your work and focus on creating the meal.
  • SaaS: You order the finished meal and simply use the service.

Once you understand that distinction, it becomes easier to recognize the different cloud services you encounter in real projects.

You don't need to memorize every cloud product. Start by asking one simple question:

"Am I renting the infrastructure, building an application on a platform, or using software that's already built?"

That question will help you identify the model in many everyday situations.

What about you? Have you used IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS in a project? Share your experience in the comments. I will love to hear which model you find most useful!

title: Getting Started with Clojure
description:
Introduction

Clojure is a functional programming language and dialect of the Lisp programming language, which means it use prefix notation for all its expressions, which runs on the Java Virtual Machine (JVM).

From Clojure's website: https://clojure.org

Clojure is a dialect of Lisp, and shares with Lisp the code-as-data philosophy and a powerful macro system. Clojure is predominantly a functional programming language, and features a rich set of immutable, persistent data structures. When mutable state is needed, Clojure offers a software transactional memory system and reactive Agent system that ensure clean, correct, multithreaded designs.

Clojure is a compiled and JVM-hosted language. It's compiler translates Clojure forms into JVM bytecode, which is then executed by the JVM. It also provides REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) support, this allows us to interactively evaluate Clojure expressions.

How Clojure code executes

Clojure code is executed in the following steps:

  • Clojure source code
  • Clojure Reader (Reads source into Clojure forms)
  • Clojure Compiler (Compiles Clojure forms into JVM bytecode)
  • JVM Execution (Executes the compiled bytecode)

Environment Setup

For compiling Clojure code, there are two popular ways to do this:

  1. Using Leiningen (Build and project management)
  2. Using Clojure CLI (Official command-line tool)

Using Clojure CLI

In the case of Clojure CLI, the project is configured manually, unlike Leiningen.

  • Creating a new project using Clojure CLI

In the case of Clojure CLI, new projects are created manually by setting up the folder structure and deps.edn files.

Folder structure for a Clojure CLI project typically looks like this:

where the project is configured using Clojure CLI deps.edn

  • running the project using Clojure CLI 
clojure -M -m hello-world.core
  • running the REPL using Clojure CLI 
clojure -M

Using Leiningen

  • creating a new project using Leiningen 
lein new app hello-world

Folder structure for a Leiningen project typically looks like this:

where the project is configured using Leiningen (project.clj)

  • Running the project using Leiningen 
lein run
  • Running the REPL using Leiningen 
lein repl

Language Basics

  • Data Types Clojure supports several fundamental data types.
Type Example Description
Integer 42 Whole number without a decimal point
Float/Double 3.14 Numeric value with a decimal point
String "Hello" Text enclosed in double quotes
Boolean true, false Logical values representing true or false
Nil nil Represents the absence of a value
Keyword :name Named identifier commonly used as a key in maps
Symbol user-name Name used to refer to a value, function, or other entity
Character \A Represents a single character 
(type 42)
;; => java.lang.Long
(type 12.09)
;; => java.lang.Double
(type "Hello")
;; => java.lang.String
(type :name)
;; => clojure.lang.Keyword
(def name "Vinayak")
(type name)
;; => java.lang.String

Difference between Keyword vs String vs Symbol:

;; Keyword
;; Define a map 
(def user {:name "Vinayak" :age 28})
;; Use
(println (:name user))
;; => "Vinayak"
(println (:age user))
;; => 28
(type user)
;; => clojure.lang.PersistentArrayMap
(type :name)
;; => clojure.lang.Keyword

;; String
(def name "Vinayak")
(println name)
;; => "Vinayak"
(type name)
;; => java.lang.String

;; Symbol -> represent a name literally
(type 'name)
;; => clojure.lang.Symbol
  • Variables

In Clojure, variables are immutable by default. Which means once a value is assigned, it can not be changed.

(def name "vinayak")
;; Try to change name directly
(set! name "vinayak sharma")
;; Execution error (IllegalStateException) at user/eval1577 (REPL:1).
;; Can't change/establish root binding of: name with set

But we can Re-definition using def again:

(def name "vinayak")
(def name "vinayak sharma")
(println name)
;; => vinayak sharma

Defining array

(def numbers [1 2 3 4 5])
(println numbers)
;; => [1 2 3 4 5]
(type numbers)
;; => clojure.lang.PersistentVector

Defining the map

(def user {:name "Vinayak" :age 28})
(println user)
;; => {:name "Vinayak", :age 28}
(type user)
;; => clojure.lang.PersistentArrayMap
  • Operators 
(+ 10 5) ;; => 15
(- 10 5) ;; => 5
(* 10 5) ;; => 50
(/ 10 5) ;; => 2

(= 10 10) ;; => true, this is different from assignment
(not= 10 5) ;; => true
(< 5 10) ;; => true
(>= 10 10) ;; => true

(and true true) ;; => true
(or false true) ;; => true
(not true) ;; => false

In Clojure, arithmetic operation support multiple arguments. For example:

(+ 1 2 3 4) ;; => 10
(* 2 3 4) ;; => 24
(- 10 1 2) ;; => 7
(/ 100 2 5) ;; => 10

  • Compound Data Types

    • Vector: Ordered collection, efficient indexed access.
    • List: Ordered collection, efficient sequential access.
    • Map: Stores key-value pairs.
    • Set: Stores unique values.

  • Functions

In Clojure, functions are defined using the defn macro. Here is an example:

;; Define a function
(defn add [a b] 
    (+ a b))

;; Call the function
(add 10 20)
;; => 30

Quick Reference

Syntax Meaning
fn Creates a function
[name] Defines a function parameter
(str ...) Combines values into a string
#() Shorthand syntax for an anonymous function
% Represents the first argument in #()
%1 Represents the first argument in #()
%2 Represents the second argument in #()
%& Represents the rest of the arguments in #()

Fundamentals

  • Conditionals

  • Loops

When to use what?

Construct Purpose
doseq Perform side effects for each item in a collection.
for Generate a sequence of results.
map Transform every item in a collection.
reduce Combine items into a single result.
loop/recur Implement custom iterative logic using recursion without growing the call stack
  • Atoms in Clojure: values are immutable by default. Atoms allow storing a value that can change over time or creates a mutable reference. 
(def age (atom 25))
(println @age)
;; => 25
(println age)
;; #object[clojure.lang.Atom 0x3a14182a {:status :ready, :val 25}]
(reset! age 30)
(println @age)
;; => 30

Increase the value using a swap!

(def age (atom 25))
(swap! age inc)
(println @age)
;; Output: 26
  • Sequences
Function Purpose Example
first Get the first item (first '(10 20 30)) → 10
rest Get remaining items (rest '(10 20 30)) → (20 30)
seq Get a sequence view (seq [1 2 3]) → (1 2 3)
map Transform every item (map inc [1 2 3]) → (2 3 4)
filter Select matching items (filter even? [1 2 3 4]) → (2 4)
count Count items (count '(10 20 30)) → 3
  • Map & Records
  • Map: Maps are flexible key-value structures. 
(def user
    {:id 101
    :name "Vinayak"
    :role "Engineer"})

(:name user)
;; => "Vinayak"

(assoc user :age 28)
;; => {:id 101, :name "Vinayak",
;; :role "Engineer", :age 28}
  • Records: Records are fixed-schema key-value structures. 
(defrecord Employee [id name department])

(def emp
    (->Employee 101 "Vinayak" "Engineering"))

(:name emp)
;; => "Vinayak"

(assoc emp :location "Bangalore")
;; Returns a new record-like value with the extra key
  • Destructuring: Destructuring extracts values from collections and binds them to local names. 
;; Vector destructuring
(let [[a b c] [1 2 3]]
    (println a b c))
;; => 1 2 3

(let [[a b c] [10 20 30]]
    (+ a b c))
;; => 60

;; Map destructuring
(let [{:keys [id name]} {:id 101 :name "Vinayak"}]
    (println id name))
;; => 101 "Vinayak"

;; Destructuring function arguments
(defn greet [{:keys [name]}]
    (str "Hello, " name))

(greet {:name "Vinayak"})
;; => "Hello, Vinayak"
  • Exception Handling

Clojure uses try, catch, and finally for exception handling.

(try
    (/ 1 0)
    (catch ArithmeticException e
    (println "Caught exception:" (.getMessage e)))
    (finally
    (println "Finally block executed")))

Using throw

(defn withdraw [balance amount]
    (if (> amount balance)
    (throw (ex-info "Insufficient funds"
                    {:balance balance
                        :amount amount}))
    (- balance amount)))

More on Clojure

  • Namespaces

Namespaces organize code into logical modules and prevent naming conflicts.

(ns my-app.core)


(ns myapp.payments)

(defn process-payment [amount]
    (str "Processing payment: " amount))
(process-payment 100)
;; => "Processing payment: 100"

Requiring namespaces in Clojure is done using the require function within the ns macro.

(ns my-app.core
    (:require [myapp.payments :as payments]))
  • Macros

Macros allow to extend the language by transforming code before it executes. Functions operate on values at runtime, whereas macros operate on code at compile-time.

defmacro: Used to define a macro.

(defmacro macro_name [condition & body]
    `(if (not ~condition)
        (do ~@body)))

(macro_name false
    (println "This will be printed"))
;; => "This will be printed"

Understand the Syntax

Syntax Meaning
defmacro Defines a macro
Backtick


``| Syntax-quotes a code form |
|~| Unquotes and inserts a form |
|~@` | Splices a sequence of forms into another form |

  • Watchers: A watcher observes changes to a reference type and runs a callback when its state changes. Watchers can be attached to atoms, refs, and agents.

clojure
(def balance (atom 100))

(add-watch balance :audit
    (fn [key reference old-value new-value]
    (println "Balance changed:"
        old-value "->" new-value)))

(reset! balance 200)
;; Prints a message about 100 -> 200

Note: fn is used to create an anonymous function

  • Agents: An agent manages state through asynchronous actions.

clojure
(def counter (agent 0))
(send counter inc)
(await counter)

@counter
;; => 1

send schedules an action on an agent's thread pool. await waits for actions dispatched before the call to finish.

Atom vs Agent in Clojure

Feature Atom Agent
State update Synchronous Asynchronous
Update operation swap!, reset! send, send-off
Read state @atom @agent
Main use Independent shared state Asynchronous state updates

Note: Atoms are suitable for managing independent shared state, while agents are ideal for handling asynchronous state updates.

  • Reference Values

Clojure provides several reference types for managing state, especially when concurrency is involved.

  • Atoms

clojure
(def x (atom 10))
(swap! x inc)
@x
;; => 11
  • Agent

clojure
(def counter (agent 0))
(send counter inc)
(await counter)
@counter
;; => 1
  • Ref

clojure
(def r (ref 0))
(dosync
    (alter r inc))
@r
;; => 1
  • Var

clojure
(def ^:dynamic *my-var* 42)
*my-var*
;; => 42

title: Syntax Comparison of ES5 vs ES6
description:
Basically, I was revising JavaScript fundamentals. While doing that, I had a curious thought that led me to write content on it. And this is a common topic roaming all over the internet.

## Demo Data
const users = [
{ id: 1, name: "Rafi", age: 22, role: "intern" },
{ id: 2, name: "Nila", age: 17, role: "student" },
{ id: 3, name: "Sami", age: 28, role: "developer" },
{ id: 4, name: "Tina", age: 31, role: "developer" },
];

## ES6 functional expression using template literals

// Option A: Print each user using .forEach()
users.forEach(u => console.log(`${u.name} (${u.age})`));

// Option B: Create a new array of strings using .map()
const names = users.map(u => `${u.name} (${u.age})`);
console.log(names);

## ES5 functional expression

// Option A: Print each user using .forEach()
users.forEach(function(u) {
  console.log(u.name + " (" + u.age + ")");
});

// Option B: Create a new array of strings using .map()
var names = users.map(function(u) {
  return u.name + " (" + u.age + ")";
});
console.log(names);

This Code could be a responsible way to set a vision of understanding ES5 & ES6.
