title: Everything Within a 30-Minute Walk: Practical Geospatial Queries with PostGIS, H3 and Isochrones
description:
Hôm nay trên Hacker News có một project tên "Local Wikipedia" đạt hơn 1100 điểm. Ý tưởng rất đơn giản: Wikipedia, nhưng chỉ hiện các bài về những địa điểm cách bạn khoảng nửa tiếng đi bộ. Đọc xong mình nghĩ ngay tới phía kỹ thuật bên dưới, vì câu hỏi "cái gì ở gần tôi?" là loại query mà gần như dev nào cũng sẽ gặp: app giao đồ ăn, tìm quán cà phê, chấm công theo vị trí, gợi ý phòng trọ gần trường. Nhiều team ở Việt Nam vẫn làm bằng cách lưu lat/lng dạng FLOAT, kéo hết về application rồi tính khoảng cách trong vòng lặp. Với 500 record thì không sao. Với 2 triệu POI thì server khóc. Bài này đi qua 3 cấp độ, từ "bán kính đường chim bay" tới "thật sự đi bộ được trong 30 phút", kèm code chạy được.

Cấp độ 1: Bán kính đường chim bay với PostGIS

Đầu tiên phải đổi "30 phút đi bộ" thành con số. Tốc độ đi bộ trung bình khoảng 4.5–5 km/h, nên 30 phút ≈ 2.5 km. Đây là khoảng cách đường thẳng, nên nó luôn lớn hơn khoảng cách thực tế. Tạm thời cứ chấp nhận vậy.

Đừng tự viết công thức Haversine trong SQL. Dùng PostGIS (mình đang dùng PostGIS 3.5 trên PostgreSQL 17), lưu cột kiểu geography và đánh index GiST:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS postgis;

CREATE TABLE places (
  id      BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  name    TEXT NOT NULL,
  geom    GEOGRAPHY(Point, 4326) NOT NULL
);

CREATE INDEX places_geom_gist ON places USING GIST (geom);

-- Lưu ý: ST_MakePoint nhận (longitude, latitude), KHÔNG phải (lat, lng)
INSERT INTO places (name, geom) VALUES
  ('Hồ Hoàn Kiếm', ST_MakePoint(105.8522, 21.0287)::geography),
  ('Văn Miếu',     ST_MakePoint(105.8355, 21.0293)::geography);

-- Mọi địa điểm trong bán kính 2.5 km, sắp xếp theo khoảng cách
SELECT id, name,
       round(ST_Distance(geom, me)::numeric) AS meters
FROM places,
     (SELECT ST_MakePoint(105.8480, 21.0245)::geography AS me) p
WHERE ST_DWithin(geom, me, 2500)
ORDER BY geom <-> me
LIMIT 50;

Có vài điểm mình thấy người mới hay sai:

  • Thứ tự tham số là (lng, lat). Google Maps hiển thị lat, lng nên ai cũng copy ngược. Kết quả là điểm của bạn rơi xuống đâu đó ở Nam Cực.
  • Dùng ST_DWithin, đừng dùng ST_Distance(...) < 2500 trong WHERE. ST_DWithin dùng được index, còn ST_Distance trong WHERE sẽ scan toàn bộ bảng.
  • geography tính bằng mét trên mặt cầu, còn geometry SRID 4326 tính bằng độ. Nếu viết ST_DWithin(geom, me, 2500) với geometry thì nghĩa là 2500 độ, tức cả Trái Đất.
  • Toán tử <-> là KNN, dùng index để sắp xếp theo khoảng cách. Nó cực nhanh khi đi kèm LIMIT.

Chạy EXPLAIN ANALYZE thì bạn sẽ thấy Index Scan using places_geom_gist. Với khoảng 1 triệu điểm, query này thường mất dưới 10ms.

Cấp độ 2: Khi không có PostGIS, dùng H3 để chia lưới

Có lúc bạn không dùng được PostGIS: data nằm trong Redis, DynamoDB, Elasticsearch không có geo, hoặc bạn cần cache kết quả theo khu vực. Lúc đó cách làm là chia bản đồ thành ô (spatial index). Hai lựa chọn phổ biến là Geohash (ô chữ nhật) và H3 của Uber (ô lục giác). Mình thích H3 hơn vì các ô lân cận đều cách tâm gần như bằng nhau, không bị méo ở góc như ô vuông.

flowchart LR
    A[User location lat/lng] --> B[h3.latlng_to_cell res 8]
    B --> C[grid_disk k ô xung quanh]
    C --> D[Lookup các cell ID trong DB/Redis]
    D --> E[Lọc chính xác bằng Haversine]
    E --> F[Sort và trả kết quả]

Ví dụ với h3 4.x (pip install h3==4.1.2):

import math
import h3

RES = 8  # cạnh ô khoảng 530m ở resolution 8

def haversine_m(lat1, lng1, lat2, lng2):
    r = 6_371_000
    p1, p2 = math.radians(lat1), math.radians(lat2)
    dp = p2 - p1
    dl = math.radians(lng2 - lng1)
    a = math.sin(dp / 2) ** 2 + math.cos(p1) * math.cos(p2) * math.sin(dl / 2) ** 2
    return 2 * r * math.asin(math.sqrt(a))

# Lúc ghi: tính sẵn cell cho mỗi địa điểm, lưu thành 1 cột có index
def index_place(place):
    place["h3"] = h3.latlng_to_cell(place["lat"], place["lng"], RES)
    return place

# Lúc đọc: lấy các ô lân cận rồi lọc chính xác
def nearby(places_by_cell, lat, lng, radius_m=2500):
    center = h3.latlng_to_cell(lat, lng, RES)
    edge = h3.average_hexagon_edge_length(RES, unit="m")
    k = math.ceil(radius_m / (edge * 1.5)) + 1
    candidates = []
    for cell in h3.grid_disk(center, k):
        candidates.extend(places_by_cell.get(cell, []))
    result = [
        (p, haversine_m(lat, lng, p["lat"], p["lng"])) for p in candidates
    ]
    return sorted([x for x in result if x[1] <= radius_m], key=lambda x: x[1])

Pattern ở đây là lọc thô bằng cell → lọc tinh bằng công thức. Cột h3 chỉ là một string hoặc int64 bình thường, nên database nào cũng index được. Thêm một lợi ích: cell ID làm cache key rất tốt. Hai người đứng cách nhau 100m trong cùng một ô sẽ dùng chung kết quả cache.

Cấp độ 3: "Đi bộ được" chứ không phải "đường chim bay"

Đây là chỗ phân biệt một app làm cho có với một app làm tốt. Ở Hà Nội hay Sài Gòn, một quán cách bạn 800m theo đường thẳng có thể nằm bên kia sông, bên kia đường ray, hoặc bên kia một cái hẻm cụt, và đi bộ mất 25 phút. Câu trả lời đúng là isochrone: một polygon bao trọn mọi điểm bạn tới được trong X phút trên mạng lưới đường thực tế.

Công cụ open-source mình hay dùng là Valhalla, chạy trên dữ liệu OpenStreetMap. Tự host bằng Docker:

# Tải dữ liệu OSM Việt Nam (~300MB) từ Geofabrik
mkdir -p valhalla_data && cd valhalla_data
wget https://download.geofabrik.de/asia/vietnam-latest.osm.pbf

# Chạy Valhalla, lần đầu build tiles mất khoảng 15-30 phút
docker run -d --name valhalla -p 8002:8002 \
  -v "$PWD":/custom_files \
  ghcr.io/gis-ops/docker-valhalla/valhalla:latest

# Isochrone đi bộ 30 phút, trả về GeoJSON polygon
curl -s http://localhost:8002/isochrone --data '{
  "locations": [{"lat": 21.0245, "lon": 105.8480}],
  "costing": "pedestrian",
  "contours": [{"time": 30}],
  "polygons": true
}' | jq '.features[0].geometry' > walk30.json

Có polygon rồi thì ghép lại với PostGIS. Mình làm theo flow 2 bước để vẫn tận dụng được index:

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant API as API Server
    participant V as Valhalla
    participant DB as PostGIS
    C->>API: GET /nearby?lat=..&lng=..
    API->>V: POST /isochrone (pedestrian, 30 min)
    V-->>API: GeoJSON polygon
    API->>DB: ST_DWithin 2.5km AND ST_Intersects polygon
    DB-->>API: Danh sách địa điểm
    API-->>C: JSON kết quả
SELECT id, name
FROM places
WHERE ST_DWithin(geom, ST_MakePoint(105.8480, 21.0245)::geography, 2500)
  AND ST_Intersects(
        geom::geometry,
        ST_SetSRID(ST_GeomFromGeoJSON($1), 4326)
      );

Điều kiện ST_DWithin ở đây đóng vai "lưới an toàn": nó dùng index để cắt nhanh tập ứng viên, rồi ST_Intersects với polygon chỉ phải chạy trên vài trăm dòng thay vì cả bảng. Gọi isochrone tốn khoảng 50–200ms, nên hãy cache polygon theo H3 cell của người dùng (ví dụ resolution 9, TTL vài ngày). Đường sá không thay đổi mỗi phút.

Vài cái bẫy production

  • Độ chính xác GPS trên điện thoại trong nhà hoặc giữa các tòa cao tầng có thể lệch 50–200m. Đừng hứa "cách bạn 37m". Làm tròn hiển thị tới 50m hoặc 100m.
  • Privacy: tọa độ người dùng là dữ liệu nhạy cảm. Nếu chỉ cần query thì làm tròn hoặc snap về H3 cell trước khi log. Đừng bao giờ ghi lat/lng chính xác vào access log.
  • Dữ liệu OSM ở Việt Nam khá đầy đủ ở các thành phố lớn, nhưng nhiều hẻm nhỏ còn thiếu. Isochrone vùng ven có thể bị "hụt" so với thực tế.
  • Đừng tính khoảng cách ở frontend cho hàng nghìn marker. Để database làm, client chỉ render.

Kết luận

Những việc bạn làm được ngay tuần này:

  1. Bỏ kiểu lat FLOAT, lng FLOAT + loop trong code. Chuyển sang GEOGRAPHY(Point, 4326) + index GiST, dùng ST_DWithin để lọc và <-> để sắp xếp.
  2. Kiểm tra thứ tự (lng, lat) ở mọi chỗ gọi ST_MakePoint. Đây là bug phổ biến nhất, và hay chạy "có vẻ đúng" ở những khu vực gần xích đạo.
  3. Không có PostGIS thì dùng H3: lưu cell ID như một cột thường, lọc thô bằng grid_disk, lọc tinh bằng Haversine. Tận dụng luôn cell ID làm cache key.
  4. Nếu UX nói "đi bộ X phút" thì dùng isochrone (Valhalla hoặc OSRM tự host với dữ liệu Geofabrik), kết hợp với ST_DWithin làm bộ lọc trước để giữ query nhanh.
  5. Luôn EXPLAIN ANALYZE để chắc query thật sự dùng index. Một geo query không dùng index là quả bom hẹn giờ khi data tăng lên.

"Gần tôi có gì?" nghe có vẻ là một feature nhỏ, nhưng làm đúng thì nó là ranh giới giữa một app lag và một app khiến người dùng thấy "ồ, nhanh thật".

title: Agent memory: the FTS5 trigger bug that silently killed every update
description:
Your agent's memory is an archive until you can update it. Ours was an archive for two weeks, and nothing in the logs said so.

The bug: a trigger that killed every update

We store facts in SQLite with an FTS5 index. The tokenizer is trigram, because it handles Russian morphology without a stemmer: "подпись" and "подписан" share trigrams, and we get recall without shipping a dictionary.

The index is kept in sync by triggers:

CREATE TRIGGER facts_au AFTER UPDATE ON facts BEGIN
  INSERT INTO facts_fts(facts_fts, rowid, text, tags) VALUES('delete', old.id, old.text, old.tags);
  INSERT INTO facts_fts(rowid, text, tags) VALUES (new.id, new.text, new.tags);
END;

That is the canonical FTS5 recipe from the docs, and it is wrong for trigram. Any UPDATE on facts failed with a bare:

sqlite3.OperationalError: SQL logic error

No column, no hint. It took a deliberately written test to find it: we asked the memory to supersede an old price with a new one and the call raised. Which means the feature we advertised — "facts are updated, not duplicated" — had never once run.

The fix 

DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS facts_au;
CREATE TRIGGER facts_au AFTER UPDATE ON facts BEGIN
  INSERT OR REPLACE INTO facts_fts(rowid, text, tags) VALUES (new.id, new.text, new.tags);
END;

INSERT OR REPLACE works with trigram. The DROP matters as much as the new body: databases already on disk carry the old broken trigger, and CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS would happily leave it in place. Init now heals existing files.

The lesson is not "use REPLACE". The lesson is that a single ranking metric hid a dead write path for two weeks.

Five abilities, not one score

We used to measure memory with one number: recall@3 over ten bilingual questions. Ten green checks, and a feature that crashed on first use.

LongMemEval-V2 (MIT) separates memory into abilities. We copied the shape, not the dataset, and wrote one test group per ability:

Ability The question it answers What breaks without it
Extraction is the fact found at all? memory is a write-only log
Cross-session does a fact from last week surface today? each session starts blind
Temporal does a time window exclude the old value? stale facts look current
Supersede does the new fact replace the old one? contradictions pile up
Abstention does it return nothing when it knows nothing? confident invention

The last one is the one nobody tests. A memory that always returns its top-3 will always look useful — and will feed the model a plausible neighbour of the question instead of an honest "I don't know". Our test asserts that a question about an office in Tokyo returns no fact containing "Tokyo", not merely a low score.

What the tests look like 

def test_superseded_fact_is_not_recalled(tmp_path):
    m = Memory(path=str(tmp_path / "m.db"))
    old = m.remember("Soma costs 19 USD per month.", tags="pricing")
    m.supersede(old, "Soma costs 49 USD per month.", tags="pricing")
    hits = [r["text"] for r in m.recall("how much does soma cost", k=3)]
    assert any("49" in t for t in hits)
    assert all("19" not in t for t in hits)      # the dead path shows up here

Run against the broken trigger, this fails with SQL logic error. Run against the fix, it passes. That is the whole difference between a benchmark and a decoration.

Why trigram at all

Because our users write in Russian and English in the same memory. A word-based tokenizer splits "подписан" and "подпись" into different tokens and recall silently drops. Trigram costs index size and gives morphology for free. The trade-off is real: it also made an obscure FTS5 incompatibility reachable, which a word tokenizer would have hidden.

If you run FTS5 with trigram, check your update trigger today. The failure is silent until something tries to change a row.

We build Soma: envelopes with budget, mandate and signature, plus memory that keeps its word — facts, obligations and signed receipts behind one MCP endpoint. If your agent memory passed a single recall test and you have never updated a fact in it, you may have the same two weeks we had.

title: Hybrid Cloud Security: The Gaps Nobody Talks About Until It's Too Late
description:
Most organisations don’t move to the cloud in one clean jump. They end up with a foot in both worlds: some systems on-premises, some in Azure or AWS, and a lot of plumbing connecting the two. That in-between state is where most of the real security risk lives, and it rarely gets the attention it deserves.

I’ve spent years working in and around hybrid environments, and the same gaps come up again and again. None of them are exotic or unusual. They are just the kind of thing that gets missed when everyone assumes someone else is handling it.

What is the identity seam in a hybrid setup?

When you connect your on-premises Active Directory to a cloud identity provider, you create a seam. Accounts sync, permissions flow, and suddenly a compromise in one environment can walk straight into the other.

The mistake I see most often is treating the two directories as if they’re one trusted system. They are not. A service account with too much reach on-premises becomes a much bigger problem the moment it has a path into your cloud tenant. Privileged accounts especially need to be looked at end to end, not just within whichever environment you happened to be reviewing that day. It’s the same reason break-glass accounts should be cloud-only.

Map out exactly what can move between the two, and assume an attacker will find the shortest path. Usually they do.

Stale permissions that never get cleaned up

Hybrid setups accumulate permissions like a garage accumulates junk. Someone needs temporary access for a migration project, it gets granted, the project ends, and the access stays. Multiply that across a few years and a few hundred people and you’ve got a sprawl that nobody fully understands anymore.

The fix isn’t glamorous. It’s regular review, automated where possible, and a genuine willingness to remove access that isn’t being used. The hardest part is cultural. People hate having access taken away, even access they’ve never touched. But every unused permission is a door left unlocked.

Logging that looks fine until you actually need it

Plenty of organisations tick the “logging enabled” box and move on. Then an incident happens, they go to investigate, and they find the logs don’t cover the thing they actually care about, or they’re scattered across systems that don’t talk to each other.

Hybrid makes this worse because your visibility is split. On-premises logs live in one place, cloud logs in another, and the connection between them is exactly where you need clarity during an incident. It’s worth doing the boring work upfront. Decide what you’d need to see if something went wrong, then check you’re actually capturing it. Test it before you’re depending on it at 2am. If those logs land in Sentinel, a few lines of KQL is the quickest way to check what’s really there.

The shared responsibility confusion

Cloud providers are clear about where their responsibility ends and yours begins. The problem is that internally, teams often assume the provider handles more than it does. “It’s in the cloud, so it’s covered” is a sentence that has preceded a lot of incidents.

In a hybrid setup this gets muddier still, because responsibility shifts depending on which part of the stack you’re looking at. The only fix is to be explicit. Write down who owns what, for each system, and make sure the people running things have actually read it.

None of this is about buying more tools

Here’s the part that tends to surprise people. Most hybrid security gaps get solved by understanding your environment properly, removing what you don’t need, and being honest about who’s responsible for what, rather than by spending more money on products.

Tools do help, but a clear picture of your own estate, kept up to date, is worth more than any dashboard you bolt on top of confusion. Handling hybrid well has far less to do with the size of the security budget than with knowing what you’re actually running.

That’s the unglamorous truth of it. Good security in a hybrid world is mostly about paying attention to the joins, the places where two systems meet and everyone assumes the other side has it covered.

I write about security, Azure, data, and the practical side of running things. If this was useful, connect with me on LinkedIn.

Originally published at alanconlon.com, where I post practical security, Azure and data write-ups every other Tuesday.

title: muse-go: Dependency-free Go client for the ElevenMusic Muse…
description:
Most muse-go write-ups stop at the README: here is what the tool does, here is how you run it. This one covers what it refuses to do, and where it breaks.

What it is

Dependency-free Go client for the ElevenMusic Muse judge (prose and lyrics critique); a static linux-amd64 build ships in the Generic Package Registry.

In Russian: Go-клиент к судье ElevenMusic Muse без единой зависимости (критика прозы и текстов); статический linux-amd64 лежит в Generic Package Registry.

Install 

CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o muse-linux-amd64 .

Go. MIT licensed. Standard library first: the tool reads the data you point it at and sends nothing anywhere.

Where it does not fit

Every rule in a checker like this can produce a false positive. Use it to find candidates for a rewrite, not to grade a writer, and not where the voice is the point.

Repository

Source, issue tracker and documentation: https://gitlab.com/ameobius-ai/muse-go

Other tools from the same author: https://ameobius-ai.gitlab.io

title: Next.js use cache Explained: Cache Components, cacheLife and cacheTag in Next.js 16.4
description:
Cross-posted from my blog. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

Next.js use cache is a directive that marks an async function, component or whole file as cacheable, so its output is stored and reused for matching inputs. It is the core of Cache Components, the caching model that Next.js 16.4 now turns on by default in create-next-app. Add 'use cache', set a lifetime with cacheLife, label it with cacheTag, and invalidate it with updateTag or revalidateTag.

This guide is written against Next.js 16.4.2 and React 19.3, the current releases. I scaffolded a fresh app with create-next-app@16.4.2 (its generated next.config.ts already contains cacheComponents: true and partialPrefetching: true), wrote every example below, then type-checked, linted, built and ran it with next start. The build output, headers and timestamps shown are the real ones I got back. Framework behavior links to the official Next.js docs.

Security note: the October 14, 2026 Next.js security update fixed a critical remote code execution bug in use cache functions that return multiple typed arrays. If you use Cache Components, run Next.js 16.4.1 or later before you ship anything from this post.

What does "use cache" do in Next.js?

'use cache' tells Next.js that a function's return value depends only on its inputs, so it can be stored and reused. The first call runs the function and saves the output; later calls with the same arguments get the saved output until the entry revalidates. Cached output can also be baked into the page's prerendered static shell.

The official use cache reference lists what goes into a cache key:

  1. Build ID: every deploy gets new keys, so caches do not survive a deploy.
  2. Function ID: a secure hash of where the function lives and its signature.
  3. Serializable arguments: function arguments or component props.
  4. Closed-over variables: values captured from an outer scope become part of the key.

That makes it different from the old App Router model, where fetch calls and route segments were cached implicitly. With Cache Components, nothing is cached unless you say so, and anything you do cache is explicit at the call site.

Quick definitions

Term What it means
Cache Components The Next.js 16 programming model behind cacheComponents: true: explicit use cache, Partial Prerendering and Suspense streaming (docs)
'use cache' Directive that caches a function, component or file's exports, shared across users
cacheLife Sets how long an entry is fresh (stale, revalidate, expire) (docs)
cacheTag Labels an entry so you can invalidate it on demand (docs)
updateTag Expires a tag immediately from a Server Action; the next read waits for fresh data
revalidateTag Marks a tag stale from a Server Function or Route Handler; serves stale while it refreshes
Static shell The prerendered HTML of a route, including cached output and Suspense fallbacks

TL;DR: Next.js use cache in five lines

You want to... Do this
Cache a database query or API call for everyone 'use cache' + cacheLife('hours') + cacheTag('x') in the data function
Show a user's change right after they submit a form updateTag('x') inside the Server Action
Refresh after a CMS or Stripe webhook revalidateTag('x', 'max') in a Route Handler
Read cookies or headers Read them outside the cached scope and pass values as arguments
Cache something that must read cookies inside 'use cache: private' (per browser only)
Share a cache across many server instances 'use cache: remote' with a cache handler

Is Cache Components enabled by default in Next.js 16.4?

Yes, for new apps. Since Next.js 16.4, released on October 6, 2026, every app created with create-next-app has Cache Components enabled, and the Next.js team says it will become the default for all apps in Next.js 17. Existing apps keep the old model until you add cacheComponents: true.

This is what create-next-app@16.4.2 generated for me, unedited apart from the Tailwind loader lines:

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from 'next'

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
  partialPrefetching: true,
}

export default nextConfig

next build confirms it at the top of the log:

✓ Running next.config.ts took 21ms
- Cache Components enabled
- Partial Prefetching enabled

How do you use "use cache" in Next.js? (step by step)

Here is the full working pattern from my test app: a product list that every visitor shares, a greeting that reads a cookie, and a form that adds a product.

Step 1: cache the data function

Put the directive at the top of the async function body, then set an explicit lifetime and a tag:

// lib/products.ts
import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache'
import { queryProducts } from './db'

// Shared, cached data function: one entry for every visitor.
export async function getProducts() {
  'use cache'
  cacheLife('hours')
  cacheTag('products')

  const products = await queryProducts()
  return { products, cachedAt: new Date().toISOString() }
}

cachedAt is there only to prove caching in the tests below. Because new Date() runs inside the cached scope, its value is stored with the entry, and the route still prerenders.

Step 2: render cached and request-time parts on one page 

// app/page.tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react'
import { cookies } from 'next/headers'
import { getProducts } from '@/lib/products'
import { addProduct } from './actions'

export default function Home() {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Store</h1>
      {/* Request-time hole: reads a cookie, so it streams in */}
      <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading greeting...</p>}>
        <Greeting />
      </Suspense>
      {/* Cached: part of the static shell */}
      <ProductList />
      <form action={addProduct}>
        <input name="name" placeholder="Name" />
        <input name="price" type="number" placeholder="Price" />
        <button>Add</button>
      </form>
    </main>
  )
}

async function Greeting() {
  const name = (await cookies()).get('name')?.value ?? 'guest'
  return <p>Hi, {name}</p>
}

async function ProductList() {
  const { products, cachedAt } = await getProducts()
  return (
    <section>
      <ul>
        {products.map((p) => (
          <li key={p.id}>{p.name}: ${p.price}</li>
        ))}
      </ul>
      <p>cached at {cachedAt}</p>
    </section>
  )
}

Step 3: invalidate from a Server Action with updateTag 

// app/actions.ts
'use server'

import { updateTag } from 'next/cache'
import { insertProduct } from '@/lib/db'

export async function addProduct(formData: FormData) {
  const name = String(formData.get('name') ?? '').trim()
  const price = Number(formData.get('price'))
  if (!name || !Number.isFinite(price)) return

  await insertProduct({ name, price })
  // Expire the tag now: the next read waits for fresh data
  // (read-your-own-writes for the user who submitted the form).
  updateTag('products')
}

In a real app, authenticate and authorize inside the action first. My Server Actions vs Route Handlers guide covers why every action is a public endpoint.

Step 4: invalidate from a webhook with revalidateTag 

// app/api/revalidate/route.ts
import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache'

// Called by a CMS or admin webhook after products change.
export async function POST(request: Request) {
  if (request.headers.get('authorization') !== `Bearer ${process.env.REVALIDATE_SECRET}`) {
    return Response.json({ error: 'unauthorized' }, { status: 401 })
  }
  // Stale-while-revalidate: visitors keep getting the old list
  // while the next request refreshes it in the background.
  revalidateTag('products', 'max')
  return Response.json({ revalidated: true })
}

Step 5: build and read the route table 

Route (app)          Revalidate  Expire
┌ ◐ /                        1h      1d
├ ○ /_not-found
├ ◐ /account
├ ○ /api/products            1h      1d
└ ƒ /api/revalidate

○  (Static)             prerendered as static content
◐  (Partial Prerender)  prerendered as static HTML with dynamic server-streamed content
ƒ  (Dynamic)            server-rendered on demand

The home page is ◐ Partial Prerender: the product list is in the static shell, and the cookie greeting streams in. The 1h / 1d columns come straight from the hours profile. The webhook route is dynamic, as it should be.

Does it actually cache? What I measured with next start

These are the real responses from next start on the test app.

Two requests, one entry. A GET Route Handler that calls getProducts() returned the same timestamp twice. It was filled during next build and reused:

$ curl -s localhost:3141/api/products
{"count":2,"cachedAt":"2026-10-17T13:01:48.233Z"}
$ curl -s localhost:3141/api/products
{"count":2,"cachedAt":"2026-10-17T13:01:48.233Z"}

Shared cache, personal hole. Sending cookie: name=Waseem changed the greeting to Hi, Waseem while the product list kept the same cached at value. The response headers show how Next.js treats the page:

x-nextjs-stale-time: 300
x-nextjs-prerender: 1
x-nextjs-postponed: 1

x-nextjs-stale-time: 300 is the 5-minute client stale value from the hours profile, and x-nextjs-postponed: 1 means part of the page was deferred to request time.

revalidateTag is stale-while-revalidate. Without the bearer token the webhook returned 401. With it, the first request after revalidation still got the old entry, and the next one got a fresh one:

$ curl -s -X POST -H 'authorization: Bearer s3cret' localhost:3141/api/revalidate
{"revalidated":true}
$ curl -s localhost:3141/api/products
{"count":2,"cachedAt":"2026-10-17T13:01:48.233Z"}   # stale, refresh starts
$ curl -s localhost:3141/api/products
{"count":2,"cachedAt":"2026-10-17T13:02:01.283Z"}   # fresh

updateTag is read-your-own-writes. In a headless Chrome test, submitting the form with "Webcam, 59" re-rendered the list with three items and a new cached at time in the same navigation. A second browser that opened the page afterwards saw the same three items and the same new timestamp, so the shared entry was replaced, not forked per user.

What are the cacheLife profiles?

cacheLife sets three values: stale (how long the browser may reuse it without asking), revalidate (after which the server refreshes it in the background) and expire (after which a request must wait for fresh data). These are the built-in presets from the cacheLife reference:

Profile Use case stale revalidate expire
default Standard content 5 minutes 15 minutes never
seconds Real-time data 30 seconds 1 second 1 minute
minutes Frequently updated content 5 minutes 1 minute 1 hour
hours Updated several times a day 5 minutes 1 hour 1 day
days Updated daily 5 minutes 1 day 1 week
weeks Updated weekly 5 minutes 1 week 30 days
max Rarely changes 5 minutes 30 days 1 year

Three rules worth remembering:

  • Always set cacheLife explicitly. Without it the default profile applies, and nesting a short-lived cache inside a scope with no explicit cacheLife fails the build during prerendering.
  • The browser keeps cached output for at least 30 seconds. The client router enforces a minimum 30-second stale time regardless of your profile.
  • You can define custom profiles in next.config.ts under cacheLife, or pass an inline object such as cacheLife({ stale: 60, revalidate: 600, expire: 3600 }).

updateTag vs revalidateTag: which should you use?

Use updateTag inside a Server Action when the user who made a change must see it on the very next render. Use revalidateTag(tag, 'max') from a Route Handler or webhook when a short window of stale data is fine. updateTag blocks the next read until fresh data loads; revalidateTag serves stale content while it refreshes.

updateTag(tag) revalidateTag(tag, 'max')
Where it runs Server Actions only Server Functions and Route Handlers
Next read Waits for fresh data Gets stale data, triggers a refresh
Best for Forms, settings, carts: read-your-own-writes CMS publish, Stripe and GitHub webhooks, admin jobs
In a Route Handler Throws Works

The revalidateTag reference recommends the 'max' profile and marks the single-argument form as deprecated; it behaves like { expire: 0 }, a blocking cache miss. Tags are case-sensitive and capped at 256 characters, and a longer tag is silently never assigned. Revalidation is triggered by the next request, not by the call itself, so pages refresh as they are visited.

use cache vs use cache: private vs use cache: remote

Next.js has three caching directives. Plain 'use cache' covers most apps. The other two solve specific problems, and the use cache: remote reference compares them:

Feature 'use cache' 'use cache: remote' 'use cache: private'
Server-side storage In memory or a cache handler Remote cache handler None
Shared between users Yes Yes No, per browser
Can call cookies() / headers() inside No, pass values as arguments No, pass values as arguments Yes
Extra cost None Storage and network None
Survives a deploy No No N/A

When should you use "use cache: private"?

Use it only when a function must read cookies or headers itself and you cannot refactor it to take those values as arguments, or when compliance rules forbid storing request data in a server cache. It runs at request time, is excluded from the static shell and is cached only in the browser. This is the version from my test app:

// app/account/page.tsx (excerpt)
import { cookies } from 'next/headers'
import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache'

// Reads cookies directly. Cached per browser only, never in a shared server cache.
async function getPreferences() {
  'use cache: private'
  cacheLife({ stale: 60 })
  const currency = (await cookies()).get('currency')?.value ?? 'USD'
  return { currency }
}

With a currency=PKR cookie the page rendered Currency: PKR, and the route still built as ◐ because the component sits inside <Suspense>.

When does "use cache: remote" make sense?

When request-time content gets low hit rates from per-instance memory: serverless functions, many replicas, or an expensive upstream such as a slow CMS. It stores entries in a shared handler like Redis. Skip it when operations already take under about 50 ms, when keys are mostly unique per request, or when data changes every few seconds; the docs list those as cases where remote caching does not pay off.

Does "use cache" work when self-hosting with Docker or Coolify?

Yes. The official platform table lists both the Node.js server and Docker as supported, and static export as not supported. When self-hosted, the default in-memory cache persists across requests in the same process, which is exactly what the next start tests above show. Size it with cacheMaxMemorySize.

Two things change once you run more than one container:

  • Each replica has its own memory cache. Two instances can serve different cachedAt values until both refresh. Configure a shared cacheHandlers entry (for example Redis) if that matters.
  • Every deploy starts cold. The cache key includes the build ID, so use cache entries do not carry over. For data that must survive deploys, the docs still point to unstable_cache or the fetch cache.

If you are deploying this way, my self-hosting Next.js with Coolify guide and production Next.js Dockerfile cover the container side.

How do you migrate an existing app to Cache Components?

Enable cacheComponents: true, then replace each route segment config the build complains about. The migration guide says routes that still export dynamic, revalidate or fetchCache will error once the flag is on. Most of the work is mechanical:

Before (old App Router) After (Cache Components)
export const revalidate = 3600 'use cache' + cacheLife('hours') around the data or UI
export const revalidate = 0 / force-dynamic Remove it; uncached data already runs at request time
export const fetchCache = 'force-cache' Wrap the data in 'use cache'
unstable_cache(fn, keys, { tags, revalidate }) Optional: 'use cache' + cacheTag + cacheLife; the old API keeps working
fetch(url, { next: { tags } }) cacheTag inside a 'use cache' function
revalidateTag('x') updateTag('x') in actions, revalidateTag('x', 'max') elsewhere

For a large app, adopt it incrementally:

  1. Turn on the flag and migrate the segment configs above.
  2. Opt out routes that are not ready with export const instant = false, or run the codemod across the app: npx @next/codemod@canary cache-components-instant-false ./app.
  3. Fix synchronous IO such as new Date(), Math.random() and crypto.randomUUID() in the prerendered shell; instant = false does not clear those errors. Move the call into a cached scope, a Client Component, or behind connection() inside <Suspense>.
  4. Remove instant = false one route at a time and resolve the dev overlay insights.

If you use a coding agent, Next.js ships a skill for this: npx skills add vercel/next.js --skill next-cache-components-adoption, then ask the agent to adopt Cache Components with it.

What can't you do inside "use cache"?

Cached functions run in an isolated environment, and four limits catch most people:

  • No request APIs. cookies(), headers() and searchParams are not allowed, even in a helper the cached function calls. On dynamic routes this can pass next build and fail under next start with the next-request-in-use-cache error.
  • Serializable inputs and outputs only. Arguments follow Server Component serialization, return values follow Client Component serialization. Class instances, symbols, URL objects and functions (except as pass-through) are rejected.
  • React.cache does not cross the boundary. Values stored with React.cache outside a cached scope are not visible inside it. Pass data as arguments.
  • Promises of runtime data hang the build. Passing a cookies() promise or uncached data into a cached function makes prerendering wait, and the build times out after 50 seconds.

For debugging, run NEXT_PRIVATE_DEBUG_CACHE=1 npm run start for verbose cache logs. In development, logs from cached functions are replayed with a Cache prefix.

Common "use cache" mistakes

Mistake What happens Fix
Calling cookies() inside 'use cache' next-request-in-use-cache error Read it outside and pass the value in
Caching per-user data with plain 'use cache' Users can see each other's data if the key misses the user ID Add the user ID as an argument, or use 'use cache: private'
No cacheLife default profile applies; nested short caches can fail the build Set a profile in every cached scope
updateTag in a Route Handler Throws at runtime Use revalidateTag(tag, 'max')
revalidateTag('x') with one argument Deprecated, blocking miss Pass 'max' or migrate to updateTag
Expecting caches to survive deploys Cold cache after each deploy Accept it, or use unstable_cache / fetch cache for that data
Several replicas, default handler Replicas disagree for a while Shared cacheHandlers or 'use cache: remote'
Running Next.js below 16.4.1 Exposed to the October 2026 critical advisories Upgrade now

Related: Next.js 16.4.1 patched a critical RCE in use cache functions that return typed arrays; see the Next.js security update October 2026. To let an AI agent do the migration for you, install the official next-cache-components-adoption skill as shown in Agent Skills: how to write a SKILL.md.

Related: I reused this demo app to benchmark the TypeScript 7 upgrade: the next build type-check step dropped from 1,368 ms to 231 ms.

Related: my React View Transitions guide uses Cache Components with connection() so a Suspense fallback streams in and animates its reveal.

Related: for a side-by-side with a non-Next.js framework, see TanStack Start vs Next.js, where I benchmarked the same app on both for server throughput, client JS, hydration and build time.

Key takeaways

  • 'use cache' caches an async function, component or file by its inputs; with Cache Components nothing else is cached implicitly.
  • New Next.js 16.4 apps have Cache Components and Partial Prefetching on by default, and it becomes the default for all apps in Next.js 17.
  • Pair every cached scope with cacheLife and cacheTag, then invalidate with updateTag in Server Actions or revalidateTag(tag, 'max') elsewhere.
  • Request APIs stay outside cached scopes; pass their values in as arguments, or reach for 'use cache: private' when you truly cannot.
  • Self-hosted next start keeps entries in memory across requests, but not across deploys or between replicas.

FAQ

What does 'use cache' do in Next.js?

'use cache' marks an async function, component or file's exports as cacheable. Next.js runs it once for a given set of serializable inputs, stores the output, and reuses it until the entry revalidates through cacheLife or a cacheTag invalidation. Cached output can also be included in the route's prerendered static shell.

Is Cache Components enabled by default in Next.js 16.4?

Yes for new apps. Since Next.js 16.4, create-next-app generates a next.config.ts with cacheComponents: true and partialPrefetching: true. Existing apps keep the previous model until you enable the flag, and the Next.js team plans to make Cache Components the default for all apps in Next.js 17.

What is the difference between updateTag and revalidateTag?

updateTag runs only in Server Actions and expires a tag immediately, so the next read waits for fresh data and the user sees their own change. revalidateTag runs in Server Functions and Route Handlers; with the recommended 'max' profile it marks the tag stale and serves stale content while the next request refreshes it.

Can I use cookies() inside 'use cache'?

No. cookies(), headers() and searchParams are not allowed inside a 'use cache' scope or any helper it calls, and doing so throws the next-request-in-use-cache error. Read the value outside the cached function and pass it in as an argument. If you cannot refactor, 'use cache: private' allows request APIs but caches only in the browser.

Does 'use cache' replace unstable_cache?

For most code, yes, but you do not have to migrate. unstable_cache keeps working with Cache Components. One difference matters: unstable_cache and the fetch cache persist across deployments, while 'use cache' entries are keyed by build ID and start cold after every deploy.

Does 'use cache' work when self-hosting Next.js with Docker?

Yes. Node.js servers and Docker containers are supported; static export is not. Self-hosted, the default in-memory cache persists across requests in the same process, sized by cacheMaxMemorySize. With several replicas each has its own cache, so configure a shared cacheHandlers entry such as Redis if they must agree.

title: A Read-Only WebMCP Tool Erased My React Form State
description:
The read path in Trip Workbench can erase a person’s unsaved purpose without sending a write.

In a deterministic reproduction, the returned saved snapshot still says “Workshop.” The edit buffer contains “Leadership meeting” before the read, then loses that value when the response is applied.

That failure is reproducible in Trip Workbench at commit 4b3f370, the public React and TypeScript demo I built and maintain. Its get_trip_draft tool refreshes saved state through the same coordinator that manages the React form. The refresh path uses a merge rule designed for a different operation.

The previous article exposed three WebMCP tools: read, update, and validate. This article follows the read path through Chrome’s debugging tools, reproduces the state loss with controlled API responses, and develops a repair that preserves unsaved work.

The reproduction and repair results below are coordinator-level tests. The repair is a local candidate; the linked repository still contains the original behavior. Native Chrome and model-driven verification remain separate steps.

A read must preserve unsaved work

Trip Workbench keeps two representations of a draft:

  • savedDraft contains the last accepted server snapshot and its revision.
  • localFields contains the values currently displayed in the form.

A person can change localFields.purpose without changing the server. The editor then reports unsaved changes.

The read tool promises to return saved fields, along with revision, status, and hasUnsavedChanges. It deliberately does not expose the unsaved buffer to the agent.

For example, the server can contain “Workshop” while the form displays “Leadership meeting.” A successful read should return “Workshop,” report that unsaved changes exist, and leave “Leadership meeting” on screen.

The WebMCP adapter also declares readOnlyHint: true. An annotation describes intended behavior; application code still has to honor it.

This matters beyond the disappearing text. The update path rejects agent mutations while the editor is dirty. If a read accidentally clears the buffer and marks it clean, a later agent update can pass that check. The read has changed the conditions under which a write is allowed.

The useful invariant is concrete: refreshing saved data must preserve current unsaved values and must never move an accepted saved revision backward.

Trace the read through Chrome

For local development, Chrome documents the flag chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing. Enable it and relaunch the browser. WebMCP is still a proposed standard, so record the browser version alongside any result. See the current setup instructions.

Open a disposable Trip Workbench draft with a saved purpose of “Workshop.” Keep the application’s cloud AI mode disabled if you are testing only the page tools.

In DevTools, open Application → WebMCP. The WebMCP pane lists available tools and records invocations, including their arguments, results, and status. Select get_trip_draft, enter the active draft ID, and use its manual test controls.

Before running it, change the form’s purpose to “Leadership meeting” without saving.

Inspect three things after the call: the returned saved purpose, the unsaved-changes indicator, and the visible input. A successful tool response alone cannot tell you whether the editor preserved the person’s work.

You can also invoke the same tool from the Console:

const context = document.modelContext;
if (!context) throw new Error("WebMCP is unavailable");

const tools = await context.getTools();
const readTool = tools.find(tool => tool.name === "get_trip_draft");
if (!readTool) throw new Error("Open a trip draft first");

const result = await context.executeTool(readTool, {
  draftId: "REPLACE_WITH_THE_OPEN_DRAFT_ID"
});
console.log(typeof result === "string" ? JSON.parse(result) : result);

The current imperative API takes a discovered tool descriptor and an argument object. JSON-stringified input arguments are deprecated from Chrome 155.

Then use the Sources panel to follow get_trip_draft → refreshSavedDraft. Put a breakpoint after the GET resolves and before the coordinator applies its result. Compare:

  • the saved fields before the request;
  • the local fields when it started;
  • the local fields when it completed;
  • the response fields and revision.

Chrome’s logpoints are useful when pausing would alter the sequence you are investigating. Log scalar snapshots such as revision, edit version, and dirty state.

A paused JavaScript thread cannot process ordinary typing in that same page. To test typing during a request, use a controlled response delay or a deferred promise instead of assuming that interacting while paused creates the intended race.

Reproduce the failure without timing guesses

The first failure does not require concurrent requests. The edit exists before the read starts.

The coordinator accepts a fetchImpl dependency, so the smallest reproduction can supply a stable server response. This test fits the repository’s existing Vitest setup:

import { expect, it } from "vitest";
import { createCoordinator } from "../../src/client/lib/coordinator.js";
import { defaultTripFields, type TripView } from "../../src/domain/types.js";

it("keeps an unsaved edit when refreshing the saved draft", async () => {
  const saved: TripView = {
    id: "draft-a",
    revision: 1,
    status: "draft",
    fields: { ...defaultTripFields(), purpose: "Workshop" },
    createdAt: "2026-10-17T07:00:00.000Z",
    updatedAt: "2026-10-17T07:00:00.000Z"
  };

  const coordinator = createCoordinator({
    fetchImpl: async <T>() => ({
      ok: true as const,
      data: structuredClone(saved) as T
    })
  });

  await coordinator.openDraft("draft-a");
  coordinator.updateLocalField("purpose", "Leadership meeting");

  const result = await coordinator.refreshSavedDraft("draft-a");
  const state = coordinator.getState();

  expect(result.ok).toBe(true);
  expect(state.savedDraft?.fields.purpose).toBe("Workshop");
  expect(state.localFields?.purpose).toBe("Leadership meeting");
  expect(state.dirty).toBe(true);

  if (result.ok) expect(result.data.hasUnsavedChanges).toBe(true);
});

In the pinned implementation, the assertion for the local purpose fails: it contains “Workshop.”

The relevant comparison is in mergeAfterInFlightEdit:

const humanChanged =
  input.localNow[key] !== input.localAtDispatch[key];

That comparison asks whether the person changed a field after dispatch.

For this refresh, localAtDispatch.purpose and localNow.purpose both contain “Leadership meeting.” The comparison returns false. The helper keeps the server value, even though the person still has an unsaved edit relative to the saved draft.

The surrounding hadLocalEdits check correctly notices that the buffer is dirty. It cannot repair the helper’s choice of comparison baseline.

This also explains why the existing test for typing during an agent update can pass. An edit made after dispatch differs from localAtDispatch; an edit already present does not. Those are different cases.

Give refreshes and saves different merge rules

A confirmed save acknowledges values that the request submitted. Its reconciliation logic needs to distinguish that submitted work from newer typing.

A refresh acknowledges no local edits. Its job is to update the saved snapshot while preserving differences that remain in the current edit buffer.

For the scalar fields in this demo, a refresh can use three values for each field:

Value Meaning
Base Current accepted saved value
Local Current value in the form
Incoming Value in the newly received server snapshot

If local differs from base, keep local in the form. Otherwise, adopt incoming. If both local and incoming differ from base and disagree with each other, retain the local value as unsaved work and surface the overlap for review.

Here is the candidate helper. It uses the repository’s TripFields type and fieldsEqual function:

function mergeSavedRefresh(
  base: TripFields,
  local: TripFields,
  incoming: TripFields
) {
  const localFields = { ...incoming };
  const overlapped: Array<keyof TripFields> = [];

  for (const key of Object.keys(base) as Array<keyof TripFields>) {
    if (local[key] === base[key]) continue;

    localFields[key] = local[key] as never;

    if (incoming[key] !== base[key] && incoming[key] !== local[key]) {
      overlapped.push(key);
    }
  }

  return {
    localFields,
    dirty: !fieldsEqual(localFields, incoming),
    overlapped
  };
}

Keeping a value in the local buffer does not save it or resolve the conflict. The person still needs to review the changed saved value before deciding what to persist. The candidate adds a notice naming overlapping fields; a field-by-field comparison would make that review easier.

Use the current accepted saved snapshot at response application time as the base. Another operation may have completed while the GET was pending. A local value that was unsaved when the read began may already have been confirmed by a manual save.

This rule treats edits as current value differences. An edit that returns a field to its saved value is no longer an unsaved change. Applications that must preserve edit intent even when values match need additional metadata, such as per-field edit versions.

Reject older snapshots before merging

A correct field merge does not prevent the saved revision itself from moving backward.

The original refresh path also accepts this sequence:

Order Event Accepted saved revision
1 A read begins and will return revision 1 1
2 An agent update commits and its response is applied 2
3 The earlier read returns revision 1 Must remain 2

The server has already advanced. Applying the late read makes the browser display older data.

Keep the existing session, editor, and draft identity checks. After those checks succeed, reject a response whose revision is lower than the currently accepted one. Then merge without another asynchronous boundary:

// After checking response success and the active editor identity.
if (res.data.revision < state.savedDraft.revision) {
  return fail(
    "STALE_SNAPSHOT",
    "A newer saved revision is already displayed."
  );
}

const merged = mergeSavedRefresh(
  state.savedDraft.fields,
  state.localFields,
  res.data.fields
);

setState({
  savedDraft: res.data,
  localFields: merged.localFields,
  dirty: merged.dirty,
  ...(merged.overlapped.length ? {
    message:
      `Saved values changed for ${merged.overlapped.join(", ")}. ` +
      "Your local values remain unsaved; review before saving."
  } : {})
});

STALE_SNAPSHOT is a new error in this candidate. It tells the caller that the read lost a race; the caller can read again. It is distinct from the server’s REVISION_CONFLICT response to a stale write.

This comparison assumes revisions increase for one draft and identify immutable versions of its persisted state. It does not order different drafts, replace identity checks, or establish that a snapshot is globally current.

The same rule covers two reads that complete out of order. A response at revision 2 cannot replace an already accepted revision 3 simply because it arrived later.

Check the repair against specific sequences

I exercised the pinned coordinator with controlled API responses, using Node’s test runner after stripping TypeScript syntax from the source modules. The candidate changed the refresh path and added the dedicated merge helper.

These nine checks produced four passes and five failures on the original implementation, and nine passes on the local candidate:

Check Original Candidate
Preserve an edit made before refresh Fail Pass
Preserve an edit made during refresh Pass Pass
Combine a remote destination change with a local purpose edit Fail Pass
Preserve overlapping local text and show a review notice Fail Pass
Ignore a read older than a confirmed mutation Fail Pass
Avoid resurrecting an edit already confirmed by a manual save Pass Pass
Ignore a response after switching drafts Pass Pass
Preserve typing during an agent update Pass Pass
Prevent out-of-order reads from lowering the revision Fail Pass

The delayed cases use deferred promises: start the operation, perform the intervening state change, and explicitly release the response. That makes the order reproducible without relying on how quickly someone types.

These results establish the coordinator behavior for those sequences. They do not exercise Chrome’s native dispatch, React rendering, the database, or a model choosing tools. The repository’s results document also lists native and model-driven WebMCP as unverified.

Keep cancellation and recovery in the test plan

Tool registration and an individual invocation have separate lifetimes. Chrome’s imperative API supports a registration signal for removing a tool and an execution signal for cancelling a call. Since Chrome 153, unregistering a tool does not cancel its in-flight executions.

That leaves application responsibilities after navigation: a late result must not update a different editor, and cancelling a network request does not establish whether a server mutation committed.

Trip Workbench uses command receipts to resolve uncertain writes. There is a separate issue in recheckOutcome: it creates a new dispatch context from the current buffer when recovery starts. That loses the original comparison baseline. A later receipt can therefore treat edits made while the outcome was uncertain as if they existed at mutation dispatch.

The refresh repair does not address that path. Receipt recovery needs to retain the original mutation context and reconcile against it, with a dedicated test for typing between an uncertain outcome and a recheck.

For React registration, also test mount, cleanup, and remount. Strict Mode’s extra Effect setup and cleanup cycle in development is useful for exposing registration leaks. A clean tool list after remount is one check; rejecting stale in-flight results is another.

Finish with native and model driven checks

Once the coordinator repair is integrated, repeat the disposable-draft exercise through Chrome’s native WebMCP interface. Check the actual input value and unsaved indicator alongside the invocation output. Verify that an attempted agent update still receives USER_EDIT_IN_PROGRESS while the preserved edit remains unsaved.

Then test whether an agent handles that response appropriately. Chrome’s DevTools MCP integration exposes list_webmcp_tools and execute_webmcp_tool when started with --categoryExperimentalWebmcp.

With a draft already containing an unsaved human edit, use a prompt such as:

Inspect the open trip draft. If it has unsaved changes, explain that I need to save or discard them and stop. Otherwise, set the destination to JFK using the returned revision, then validate the updated draft. Stop before submission.

Record whether the agent reads first, recognizes the unsaved state, and stops. For the clean-draft branch, inspect the revision it supplies and the resulting saved fields. A plausible final message is insufficient evidence that the intended sequence ran.

The engineering contract is visible in the form: reading a draft preserves what the person is working on, and a response from earlier work cannot replace a newer accepted state. Those properties have to hold for every caller, including the agent.

title: Legal Contract Review Retrieval Architecture: A Release Checklist for Traceable Search
description:
Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that a reviewer can trace back to a document. For a legal contract review workspace, chunking and freshness are the release gates; model choice comes after those are observable.

Retrieval contract and bounded query

Write down what the reviewer must see before choosing an index. A hit is not useful if it cannot carry the tenant, access-control scope, document identifier, source URL, clause location, and the document version used for embedding. Preserve those fields on every indexed item.

I use two stages. First, a broad lexical or web-assisted pass finds candidate clauses and newly published guidance. Second, vector search narrows the candidates for semantic near-duplicate detection. The final prompt receives a bounded set of chunks plus their identifiers, not an unexamined dump of the index. That makes a release review concrete: can we explain why this clause was returned, and can we reproduce the same answer from the recorded version? Don't let a ranking score stand in for that explanation.

That audit trail is the contract.

Keep the query bounded. Eight candidates is a policy choice, not a magic number.

How should chunking and freshness work in a legal contract review workspace?

Chunk by a unit a lawyer can cite: clause, subclause, definition, or a short run of related sentences. Keep the parent section and page or paragraph offsets in metadata. A giant page chunk hides the matching language; tiny sentence chunks lose exceptions and cross-references. The right boundary is the smallest unit that still preserves the legal condition being compared.

Freshness needs an explicit path. Mark an indexed record with its source revision and ingestion time, then replace the old vector when the source revision changes. During a release, include stale-document cases and near-duplicates that differ only in a defined term. Your evaluation set should contain representative agreements, amendments, redlines, and deliberately confusing pairs. Measure recall for known related clauses and precision for the clauses reviewers would actually accept.

A bounded query you can inspect

The query service should return enough context to audit a decision. This small Go example sends a tenant-scoped query and prints the response body; production code should validate the returned identifiers against the reviewer session before displaying them.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    payload := []byte(`{"collection":"contract-clauses","query":"limitation of liability and carve-outs","top_k":8,"filter":{"tenant_id":"tenant-42","acl":"review"}}`)

    var resp *http.Response
    var err error
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
        req, reqErr := http.NewRequest("POST", baseURL+"/v1/vector/query", bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if reqErr != nil {
            panic(reqErr)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        resp, err = http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            break
        }
        retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
        resp.Body.Close()
        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if retryAfter != "" {
            var seconds int
            if _, scanErr := fmt.Sscanf(retryAfter, "%d", &seconds); scanErr == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    if readErr != nil {
        panic(readErr)
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("query failed (%d): %s", resp.StatusCode, body))
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

The retry branch matters. A 429 is a capacity signal, so the client honors Retry-After and backs off instead of amplifying the queue. That's the whole point.

For ingestion, use the same metadata contract and a deterministic document revision as the upsert identity. A retry then replaces the intended item instead of creating a duplicate. Keep that write path separate from the read path so a failed refresh cannot erase the last known-good revision.

Choosing, verifying, and rolling back a backend

The table is a decision aid, not a benchmark. Verify connector behavior, filtering semantics, and operational limits against your workload before signing off.

Infrai's verified breadth is 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, and its public discovery surface describes capabilities with runnable examples. In this workflow, that means the retrieval call and adjacent queue or notification work can share a credential contract while engineers inspect the request shape before implementation.

Option Strength for this workflow Trade-off to verify
Elasticsearch Mature lexical search plus vector and metadata filters in one operational surface Cluster tuning and schema work add ownership overhead
Pinecone Managed vector retrieval with a focused operational model Lexical and document-version workflows may need companion services
Weaviate Vector-first collections with metadata filtering and hybrid search options Hosting and module choices affect the runbook you must own
Infrai A self-describing REST surface exposes discovery and runnable examples, so wiring a capability is reading one endpoint rather than learning an SDK; its 295 routes across 20 modules use one key, which reduces credential and integration handoffs around the review workflow It is a poor fit when your organization requires a single specialized search vendor, on-premise data residency, or deep custom ranking extensions

Stick with Elasticsearch when lexical relevance, custom analyzers, and local control are the primary constraints. Choose Pinecone when a managed vector service is the smaller operational burden. Weaviate is reasonable when hybrid retrieval is central and its deployment model matches your team. The catch with a broad API layer is that you still own the legal metadata model and evaluation discipline.

The practical advantage here is a single key across the retrieval call and adjacent backend capabilities. That reduces handoffs in a release checklist, while the public discovery surface and runnable examples make an unfamiliar capability inspectable before code is merged. It doesn't remove review work; it makes the boundaries visible.

Before release, replay the fixture set against the previous and candidate index. Inspect false positives where two clauses share boilerplate but differ in an exception. Confirm that every result carries a document identifier or source URL and that tenant filters survive both stages. Log the query, collection, revision, and request identifier, while redacting contract text from general application logs.

Run the same checks after a schema or chunking change, even when the application code is untouched. A changed boundary can alter recall more than a model swap, and a fresh embedding can still be wrong for the tenant that owns the source. Record the fixture version, expected matches, and reviewer sign-off beside the release artifact so a later rollback has an evidence trail rather than a guess.

If recall drops or stale clauses appear, route reads back to the previous collection and stop promotion of the candidate. Keep both collections addressable until the comparison is complete; deletion is a later, deliberate action. I am not sure a single global freshness threshold works across all contract repositories, so make that threshold a policy per source and record the reason in the release checklist.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/dense-vector.html
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/index-data/indexing-overview
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate/concepts/search/hybrid-search

title: folderblog 0.2.7: Your blog can be a podcast now
description:
folderblog turns a folder of Markdown into a live blog the moment you save. Four releases since the last word here, 0.2.4 through 0.2.7, and the big one is 0.2.6: the same folder can now publish a podcast, with a proper feed, hosted audio, and a way for an AI agent to help without ever publishing on its own.

Podcasts from a folder

Put episodes in podcast/, one folder per episode, each with its MP3 (or an MP4 if it's a video show). folderblog builds the show page, a page for every episode, and /podcast/feed.xml. Turn it on with:

folderblog podcast on

The feed is ready for Apple Podcasts and Podcasting 2.0: every episode gets a permanent guid, and you can add transcripts, chapters, people, and optional Lightning tips. Episodes stay out of your main blog feed unless you set in_main_feed, so readers who only want posts don't get audio in their reader.

Audio hosted on Cloudflare R2

Audio files are too big to live comfortably next to your HTML, so folderblog uploads them to Cloudflare R2 when the site deploys. The site isn't published until the upload succeeds, which means the feed never points at a file that isn't there yet. folderblog podcast setup walks you through it. It works with an r2.dev address or your own domain, and a custom domain is recommended. Your keys are kept outside the blog folder, so they never end up in git or on the site.

An MCP server for AI agents

folderblog mcp starts an MCP server, so an AI agent can draft, check and publish episodes for you. It only publishes after you say yes. If you'd rather do it yourself, folderblog podcast publish --episode SLUG does the same thing from the terminal. The watcher and a publish take turns, so they never build or deploy at the same time.

Templates to copy

New blogs now come with a templates/ folder holding a sample post and a sample podcast episode. Each one lists every front matter field with a short note on what it does, so you don't have to dig through the guide to remember what draft or image does. To add the folder to a blog you already have, run folderblog templates.

Blogs keep up with updates by themselves

0.2.7 is the small one that makes the rest easier. After you install a new version, restart the service:

systemctl --user restart folderblog

The first time it starts, it adds any sample files your blogs don't have yet, like the new templates/ folder, and refreshes the generated part of AGENTS.md. It logs what it changed. It never turns a feature on, and it never touches your design, blog.toml or your posts. A sample file you delete stays deleted.

Two fixes along the way

  • 0.2.4: draft: true in front matter now really hides a post or page from the live site, as the guide always said. Before, those were still built and listed. They now behave like files in drafts/: visible in folderblog preview and build --drafts, never in real builds.
  • 0.2.5: if you use GoatCounter, 404 pages are now counted as events named after the missing URL instead of page views, so broken links show up on their own instead of looking like visits.

Grab it

System Command
Arch / Omarchy sudo pacman -U folderblog-bin-0.2.7-1-x86_64.pkg.tar.zst
Debian / Ubuntu sudo apt install ./folderblog_0.2.7-1_amd64.deb
Fedora / RHEL / openSUSE sudo dnf install ./folderblog-0.2.7-1.x86_64.rpm
autonomix-cli autonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/folderblog

The packages and a plain tarball are on the v0.2.7 release. New to folderblog? Start with the guide, or run folderblog guide.
