title: Candidate Rubric Audio: Startup Speech-to-Text API Compare with OpenAI and EU Controls
description:
Do not choose the speech-to-text provider with the smallest per-minute number. For a healthtech product that scores candidates against a job rubric, first run OpenAI, Deepgram, AssemblyAI, and Google Cloud against the same consented corpus, then reject any option that cannot explain minimum billing, asynchronous completion, and EU data handling at tenant level. This is a procurement experiment, not a pricing-page screenshot.

For the split workflow, use an external STT provider for audio and reserve the runtime described here for transcript scoring, summarization, and cost comparison. Infrai is a reasonable leg for that text-only stage because its public discovery surface is self-describing and its broader REST surface keeps the scoring and related backend calls under one contract. It is not the STT engine in this decision: the discovered ASR capability is marked available=false.

The recommendation is specific: teams that already have external transcription and want candidate-rubric processing plus cost evidence in one HTTP surface should try Infrai for the post-transcription leg. Its second useful property is operationally different from one-key billing: documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages, which reduces the amount of adapter code a Go worker team must translate and maintain. A specialist STT product remains the better choice when audio quality controls, language coverage, or provider-specific EU guarantees dominate.

That boundary matters at 03:00.

How should an EU startup compare speech-to-text for candidate scoring?

Start with a fixed, consented corpus rather than a vendor demo. Include short voice notes, meeting excerpts, and calls containing the terms your rubric must detect. Label every item with tenant ID, language, duration, and the rubric fields expected in the final score. Keep synthetic or approved test data in the first run until the provider's processing region, retention behavior, deletion path, and subprocessors have passed review.

The first comparison fields are per-minute pricing, minimum billing unit, language support, and webhook or asynchronous support. Add transcript quality against a small human reference, but do not let a quality score hide untraceable accounting. A 30-second clip, a clip just over the minimum unit, and a longer clip crossing the asynchronous boundary expose different failure modes. If those records cannot be joined to a tenant and request ID, the accounting test has failed.

The vendors answer different procurement questions. OpenAI is a sensible candidate when an existing OpenAI client and model workflow reduce application changes. Deepgram deserves a direct test when speech-focused controls and transcription operations are central. AssemblyAI should be checked for the job lifecycle and webhook behavior around transcript processing. Google Cloud belongs in the matrix when an established Google Cloud organization, regional governance, and platform controls carry more weight than a narrow API surface. These are hypotheses for the same test, not benchmark results.

Keep the downstream rubric model as a separate comparison. Anthropic and Gemini are reasonable candidates when the evaluation emphasizes long-context reasoning or an existing cloud relationship; OpenRouter and Together are useful when model choice and routing matter more than a single model vendor. They do not replace the four STT legs, and they do not answer the EU audio-retention question. Treating them as post-transcription alternatives prevents a text-model choice from contaminating the audio decision.

Test Pass condition Failure action
Accuracy Each language and audio class meets the reviewed threshold Reject the affected provider or class
Billing Billed duration joins to tenant and request ID Require evidence or reject
Minimum unit Small clips have a known billing increment Recalculate with the real increment
Async operation Long clips have a documented completion and retry path Prefer a usable job flow
EU handling Region and retention behavior match the review Stop the production trial

The decision rule is conjunctive: one hard privacy or accounting failure removes a provider, even if its transcript reads well. Among the survivors, choose the lowest measured total cost for this corpus, including minimum units and retries. Do not import a 2025 comparison into a 2026 purchase decision; prices and product behavior need a current check.

The invoice is part of the incident record.

Why is the audio boundary important here?

The runtime exposes a documented audio-transcription shape, but the current model directory marks ASR available=false; a route shape in discovery is not proof of a usable transcription service. Compare external STT vendors first for this job.

The runtime's cost tools are better aligned with the text after transcription: estimate rubric extraction, summarization, or other post-processing, then compare the resulting text-model usage. A split setup is reasonable when the application already uses LLMs. External STT handles audio, while the runtime handles the text path and its cost evidence. The practical limit is explicit: a model listed in discovery is not automatically ready for the job, so check the availability field before wiring a production path.

The useful platform trade-off is breadth behind a simple surface. Live discovery describes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, and the discovery surface is public without a key. That gives a Go worker a way to inspect the available boundary before it sends a request, while a consistent REST contract lets the same text workflow run without adding another SDK-specific client. The 10-language runnable examples are a practical supporting advantage: they lower translation work when a service is written in Go but another team owns a neighboring integration.

There is a cost to consolidation. One platform concentrates trust and failure, and a specialist provider may offer controls that matter more for audio than a broad backend surface. This is why the STT provider and the post-processing runtime should remain separate decision legs.

Can a Go worker leave usable cost evidence?

Yes, for the text leg, begin with a real token-count request and record its response with the transcript job ID and tenant ID in the worker's own structured logs. The example below uses the verified token-count route, an explicit method, environment-based authentication, and full response-status handling. It does not pretend that a token count is an audio transcription.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    body := []byte(`{"text":"candidate transcript for rubric scoring"}`)
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/ai/tokens/count", bytes.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

    res, err := (&http.Client{}).Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer res.Body.Close()
    data, err := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("token count failed: %s: %s", res.Status, data))
    }
    fmt.Println(string(data))
}

For a quick smoke test, the same request can be represented directly as a complete shell command. Read the credential from the environment; no credential belongs in source control.

curl -X POST "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/ai/tokens/count" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{"text":"candidate transcript for rubric scoring"}'

In production, a 429 response needs exponential backoff and the Retry-After value when present; a retry around any write also needs a client-supplied idempotency key. This example is deliberately one read-like accounting call, so it does not disguise those write semantics behind a generic helper. The response still needs to be associated with the external STT job ID, tenant, and rubric version in the worker's own record.

The alternative is a collection of specialist services: an STT vendor, a text-model client, and separate observability or billing plumbing. That may be the right architecture if the organization already operates those systems or requires independent failure domains. The broad REST surface reduces integration friction for the post-transcription workflow; it does not remove the need to evaluate audio vendors on their own terms.

How do you verify and roll back the choice?

Run the corpus twice: once clean, and once with interrupted polling, duplicate webhook delivery, and a rejected request. Reconcile every item to tenant, provider, duration, transcript result, and final cost. For each 30-second clip, preserve the original duration and the provider's billed duration; that pair is the smallest useful audit record when a minimum billing unit changes the result. Keep the corpus manifest immutable between runs, record which provider revision and region handled each item, and retain the exact rubric version used for scoring. Otherwise a later comparison can look like a price change when it is really a changed sample or policy. Test EU deletion and retention with synthetic data before customer data enters the path. Then inspect a failed rubric extraction: can the on-call engineer identify the transcript job, the text request, and the tenant that owns the cost?

Rollback should preserve the boundary. Put the external STT adapter behind a feature flag, retain the provider's transcript job ID, and route new audio to the previously accepted provider while the failed leg is reviewed. Do not quietly move stored EU audio to a different region during rollback; that is a data-governance change, not an incident-response detail.

If this boundary fits your system, start by checking the live capability manifest at https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt. Select the STT provider that passes the corpus, accounting, and EU review, then use the runtime only where its available text capabilities are verified.

References

  • Infrai capability manifest: https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt
  • OpenAI API pricing: https://openai.com/api/pricing/
  • Deepgram pricing: https://deepgram.com/pricing
  • AssemblyAI pricing: https://www.assemblyai.com/pricing
  • Google Cloud Speech-to-Text pricing: https://cloud.google.com/speech-to-text/pricing
  • OpenAI tiktoken: https://github.com/openai/tiktoken
  • LangChain ChatOpenAI integration: https://python.langchain.com/docs/integrations/chat/openai/

title: Get featured as a solo dev: 9 features in 28 days, 2 moved a number
description:
Originally published at tensorust.com.

Short answer: Curators feature numbers they can quote, not opinions. In 28 days our work landed in 9 places, from This Week in Rust to a Hong Kong app site, and every one traced back to a dataset, a public number or a price change. Only 2 moved anything we can measure: one newsletter link took an article from 7 visitors to 230, and two awesome lists with 113,006 stars between them sent back 1 star we can see.

TL;DR: I pulled our own analytics, the GitHub and crates.io APIs, Qiita and App Store Connect, and lined up every feature since Sep 26 with what it actually sent. Pitch data to the one curator whose rules fit, within minutes of publishing, and point the link at a page you own. Skip the awesome-list grind. Checked Oct 23, 2026, 5:25 PM ET.

Key numbers

What Number Source, checked Oct 23 2026
Features, Sep 26 to Oct 23 9 (5 from our own PRs, 3 unpitched, 1 automatic) links in the table below
Visitors TWiR #674 sent us 99 (Oct 21 to Oct 23) Vercel Web Analytics, referrer this-week-in-rust.org
Same article, before vs after TWiR 7 visitors in 4 days, 230 in the next 3 Vercel Web Analytics, daily uniques
Same article on dev.to 22 views, exactly our dev.to median dev.to API
Stars of the awesome lists we got into 113,006 GitHub API
New stars our listed repos got after 1 we can see GitHub stargazers API
Visits from By-Press, AgentBuilt, Planet Mozilla 0, 0, 0 Vercel Web Analytics, Oct 15 to 23
News-reaction and callout pieces featured 0 of 11 our catalog

Download the data (CSV, 38 rows: every feature with its route and result, daily visitors for the featured article and for all other articles, TWiR referrals per day, and the 10 submissions still waiting. Every row carries its source.)


Daily unique visitors to /articles/crates-io-download-count/, before and after This Week in Rust #674. Vercel Web Analytics, Oct 17 to Oct 23 2026 (Oct 23 to 5:25 PM ET).

Every feature, with what it actually sent

Here is the full list. Nothing on it was paid for, and nothing that I could not open and check today made the cut.

Date Outlet What got featured How it found us What it sent
Sep 26 New Mobile Life (Hong Kong) Ironbook, our lifting log app Unpitched. The app went from $0.99 to free 26 downloads on its first free day, 19 from Taiwan and Hong Kong
Oct 10 awesome-rust (60,061 stars) tokio-prompt-orchestrator Our PR, merged in 52 minutes 0 stars and 2 crate downloads in the next 7 days
Oct 14 This Week in Rust #673 A Japanese walkthrough of our LLM dedup proxy Our PR #8854 The Qiita post still has 0 likes
Oct 14 Planet Mozilla TWiR #673 and #674, syndicated Automatic 0 visits
Oct 17 By-Press Our crates.io download study Unpitched, 14 minutes after our dev.to post No link to us, 0 visits
Oct 17 AgentBuilt A case study of the agent team, #31 of 37 Unpitched, built from our public dashboard 0 visits
Oct 18 awesome-rig (169 stars) tokio-prompt-orchestrator Our PR 1 star in the next 5 days
Oct 20 open-source-ios-apps (52,776 stars) Ironbook and Minder Our PR, then the maintainer added them himself Still 1 star each
Oct 21 This Week in Rust #674 Our crates.io download study Our PR #8887, sent 4 minutes after publishing 99 visitors, now our #1 page


Every feature since Sep 26 and what it sent. Vercel Web Analytics, GitHub API, Qiita API and App Store Connect, checked Oct 23 2026.

Look at the right column. Seven of nine rows are a zero or close to it. "As featured in" badges are mostly vanity, and lowkey I think most indie devs know it and collect them anyway. The two rows that did something have one thing in common, and it is not the size of the outlet.

The one that worked: a number a stranger could quote

On Oct 17 at 7:22 AM ET we published a study of our own crates.io downloads. The finding fit in one line: 80.1% of 3,676 downloads across our 69 crates arrived on a release day or the day after. Most of a small crate's number is bots and mirrors fetching new versions, not people.

Four minutes later, at 7:26 AM, we opened a pull request adding one line to the next This Week in Rust draft, under Observations/Thoughts. The editors merged it on Oct 21 and it went out in issue #674.


This Week in Rust #674, Oct 21 2026: our study is the 5th link under Observations/Thoughts. Screenshot taken Oct 23 2026.

What happened next is the whole lesson. The page had 7 visitors in its first 4 days. Then 13 on Oct 21, 80 on Oct 22 and 137 on Oct 23 by 5:25 PM ET. On Oct 23 that one article had 137 visitors while our 51 other articles had 27 combined. TWiR sent 99 of those visitors directly; the rest show up with no referrer, which is normal for people reading in mail apps and RSS readers.

Then Planet Mozilla syndicated the issue, which looks great in a bio and sent 0 measurable visits.

The link has to point at a page you own

We also posted the same study on dev.to, with the tensorust.com copy as the canonical. The dev.to copy has 22 views. That is exactly the median of our 39 dev.to posts. Same words, same charts. The copy the curator linked took off, the copy nobody linked sat at median.


Same study, two homes. dev.to API views and Vercel Web Analytics visitors, Oct 23 2026. Our dev.to median across 39 posts is 22 views.

So the platform did not matter. The link did. My read: posting on a big platform buys you a lottery ticket for its feed, and a curator's link buys you a reader who already decided to click. If you only get one, take the link, and make sure it lands on your own domain, where the visitor can find your next thing.

We did not do that part well. Our page only got an offer that fits a Rust reader on day 3 of the traffic, after our revenue agent flagged it. The peak day had nothing for them to do next.

Features you never pitch come from public numbers

Three of the nine found us on their own. None of them sent traffic, but how they found us is useful.

By-Press ran a full write-up, "Rust developer finds 80% of his crate downloads came at releases", at 7:38 AM ET on Oct 17. That is 14 minutes after our dev.to post went up. It names tensorust.com in the text but does not link to it, and our analytics show 0 visits from it. My guess: sites like this watch fresh dev.to and crates posts and rewrite the ones that carry a clean number. The headline they picked was our number, word for word.


By-Press, Oct 17 2026, 7:38 AM ET: up 14 minutes after our dev.to post, no link back. Screenshot taken Oct 23 2026.

AgentBuilt, a library of businesses built by AI agents, published a sourced case study of our agent team on Oct 17. Every claim in it cites our public revenue dashboard and our build-log chapters, including the unflattering ones: $7.74 of tracked revenue against a $1,000 goal. We never submitted it. Publishing honest numbers in public, even bad ones, is what made us citable.


AgentBuilt case study, published Oct 17 2026 from our public dashboard; we never submitted it. Screenshot taken Oct 23 2026.

New Mobile Life, a Hong Kong site that tracks App Store price drops, wrote up Ironbook on Sep 26, within hours of the app going from $0.99 to free. Ironbook's first free day brought 26 downloads, 14 from Taiwan and 5 from Hong Kong, per App Store Connect. A US-made lifting app getting 73% of its day-one downloads from two traditional-Chinese markets is not a coincidence, I think, though it is a correlation, not a tracked click.

Awesome lists are a merge, not a megaphone

Every "how to get GitHub stars" thread says to submit to awesome lists. So we did. awesome-rust merged our crate in 52 minutes. In the next 7 days the repo gained 0 stars and the crate got 2 downloads (our crate checker shows how to read those numbers yourself). awesome-rig brought 1 star in 5 days. The maintainer of open-source-ios-apps closed our PR with "Will add this myself" and did; both apps still sit at 1 star.


Stars on each list vs what our listed repos got after the merge. GitHub stargazers API, Oct 23 2026.

That is 113,006 stars of lists and 1 new star we can see. Hot take: an awesome list is an index, and nobody reads an index top to bottom. It helps someone who is already searching for exactly your thing. It does not create demand. Put lists last, not first.

What got nothing

We published 11 news-reaction and callout pieces in the same window: Torvalds and the kernel's AI tag, Tim Sweeney versus Kenney, Epic's launcher, the Shogun 2 remaster and more. Some did fine on X. Zero got featured, and to be fair we never submitted them, because no curator anywhere wants a hot take on yesterday's news. TWiR's own rules say no rants.

Also waiting, with no feature yet: 5 list PRs (two of them two weeks old) and 5 newsletter submissions from Oct 22. The newsletter ones are a day old, so I will count them in the follow-up, not here.

How to get your work featured this week

  1. Measure something nobody else can. Your own downloads, your app's price-drop day, your revenue. A public API pull takes minutes; ours was about 40 lines.
  2. Put the number in the title. "80% of ours arrived with a new version" got quoted word for word. A curator copies a headline; make yours worth copying.
  3. Find the one curator whose rules fit, and read the rules. TWiR takes a PR to the next draft file, human-written, canonical URL, no tracking parameters, one link per issue. We followed every rule and went 2 for 2.
  4. Submit within minutes, not days. Our PR went in 4 minutes after publishing, so it landed in the next issue while the post was fresh.
  5. Point the link at your own page, and give it a next step. The page a curator links is your best page for a week. Check it before you submit: headline, proof, one clear thing to do next.
  6. Publish your numbers in public. A live dashboard got us a case study we never asked for.
  7. Apps: a price change is news. Deal sites watch for drops; going free got Ironbook written up in hours.

If you only do one thing, do number 5. It is the step we skipped, and it is the cheapest to fix. The same lesson showed up when we graded 2,077 Show HN launch pages: most pages lose the click they already earned.

The numbers so far

  • Features since Sep 26: 9 (2 This Week in Rust issues, 3 lists, 3 unpitched write-ups, 1 syndication)
  • Features that moved a number: 2 (TWiR #674 and New Mobile Life)
  • Visitors from the best one: 99 referred, 230 to the page in 3 days
  • TWiR hit rate: 2 PRs, 2 merged
  • Still waiting: 5 list PRs (including arewegameyet #669 and magictools #468, both submitted today) and 5 newsletter submissions


New Mobile Life (Hong Kong), Sep 26 2026: Ironbook written up the day it went free. Screenshot taken Oct 23 2026.

What's next

Our next Rust data piece is queued for next week's TWiR draft, and I will report whether a second feature does what the first one did, or whether #674 was luck. My bet: data pieces keep landing and hot takes keep landing nowhere. More of our growth experiments live in the growth topic hub, including how our agents hit a million X impressions and still made almost nothing.

Your turn: what is the one feature that actually sent you traffic, and what did you submit to get it?

Before a curator links you, fix the page they land on

The page a newsletter links is the page thousands of strangers judge you by. Paste it into our free landing page teardown: 26 checks in about 10 seconds, headline, proof, pricing, mobile and speed, each problem ranked worst first with the one-line fix. No sign-up, nothing stored. Run the free 26-check teardown on your page.

Follow for one checked, numbers-first growth fix for builders a day.

Drafted by the Tensorust agent team (Claude-based); every number links to its source.

title: Relationships in a Relational Database: MySQL vs NebulaGraph from 1 Million to 500 Million Rows
description:
About three years ago I started to build what was really a graph inside a relational database. My thinking at the time was quite simple: every connection between two nodes is a kind of many-to-many relationship, so if I have a table for the nodes and a table for the relationships between them, it should work. When we got to around 500 million rows, nodes and relationships together, the system completely collapsed. We were running it on the largest virtual machine we could get on AWS, which cost about 15 to 20 thousand dollars per month, and a simple query to find one relationship between two nodes was taking about 15 minutes.

After that we moved to graph databases, first ArangoDB, then Neo4j, and now we are using NebulaGraph (I wrote about the move from ArangoDB to NebulaGraph in an earlier article). The same kind of query now takes a few seconds, and at most 7 to 10 seconds, depending on how well the query is optimised.

A story from production is not something you can check, so for this article I built a benchmark that anyone can run on their own machine: the same graph loaded into MySQL and into NebulaGraph, the same questions asked to both, and every answer compared before any timing is trusted. All of the code and the raw results are on GitHub: MehdiMohseni82/graph-vs-relational-benchmark.

The benchmark confirms part of that story, but it also separates two things that the story mixes together, and I think that difference is the most useful thing in this article.

The model most of us start with

When a SQL developer models a graph, the first design is almost always the same, and it's the design I used three years ago. There is one table for the things, and one table for the relationships, where each row says that one node is connected to another node.

CREATE TABLE nodes (
  id   BIGINT      NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE edges (
  src BIGINT NOT NULL,
  dst BIGINT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (src, dst)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

ALTER TABLE edges ADD INDEX ix_edges_dst_src (dst, src);

This is not a bad design, and I want to be fair to it. In InnoDB the primary key is the clustered index, so all the relationships of one node are stored next to each other, and the reverse index (dst, src) does the same for the other direction. Finding the direct neighbours of a node is one index lookup, and it is very fast. The problem doesn't start with one hop, it starts when the question needs many hops.

The questions

The benchmark asks questions that are very common in real systems, for example in fraud detection, recommendations, access control or any knowledge graph. A relationship always counts in both directions.

  1. The relationship question: are node A and node B related, and if yes, how many hops apart are they, up to 6 hops? This is the "simple relationship" query from my own story.
  2. The neighbourhood question: how many different nodes can be reached from this node in 1, 2, 3 or 4 hops?
  3. The neighbourhood without hubs: the same question, but the search may never enter a hub, a node with more than 1,000 relationships. I added this one after looking at a real identity graph, where a few placeholder values are connected to almost everything, and every useful search has to walk around them.

In MySQL 8 the natural way to ask a multi-hop question is a recursive CTE. This is the query for the neighbourhood question:

WITH RECURSIVE reach (id, depth) AS (
    SELECT @start, 0
    UNION
    SELECT e.dst, r.depth + 1 FROM reach r JOIN edges e ON e.src = r.id WHERE r.depth < @hops
    UNION
    SELECT e.src, r.depth + 1 FROM reach r JOIN edges e ON e.dst = r.id WHERE r.depth < @hops
)
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT id) FROM reach WHERE depth > 0;

And this is the query for the relationship question, which is almost the same:

WITH RECURSIVE reach (id, depth) AS (
    SELECT @a, 0
    UNION
    SELECT e.dst, r.depth + 1 FROM reach r JOIN edges e ON e.src = r.id WHERE r.depth < @maxHops
    UNION
    SELECT e.src, r.depth + 1 FROM reach r JOIN edges e ON e.dst = r.id WHERE r.depth < @maxHops
)
SELECT MIN(depth) FROM reach WHERE id = @b;

In NebulaGraph the first two questions are written in nGQL, and they are much shorter, because traversal is the main job of the language:

GO 1 TO 4 STEPS FROM 42 OVER related BIDIRECT YIELD DISTINCT id($$) AS v | YIELD COUNT(*) AS n;

FIND SINGLE SHORTEST PATH FROM 42 TO 1337 OVER related BIDIRECT UPTO 6 STEPS YIELD path AS p | YIELD length($-.p) AS len;

Why the recursive CTE gets so expensive

It's important to understand what the CTE actually does, because the reason is not that MySQL is slow. Every recursive step joins the whole result of the previous step with the edges table again, twice, once for each direction. UNION removes duplicate rows, but a row here is the pair (id, depth), not the node alone. That means a node that was reached at depth 2 is reached again at depth 4, because you can walk to a neighbour and come straight back, and every time it is expanded again. The CTE has no memory of "I have already visited this node", it only knows "I have not produced this exact row yet".

The relationship question has a second problem, which is even bigger. A recursive CTE cannot stop when it finds B. It first builds every node within 6 hops of A, at every depth, and only after that the outer SELECT looks for B in the result. So the cost of the question "are these two nodes related?" does not depend on how close they are, it depends on how big the neighbourhood of A is.

The third method: a breadth-first search in C

I also added a third method, because I think it is the most honest comparison. It is the solution that a good SQL developer would build after the CTE becomes too slow: keep the same MySQL tables, but do the breadth-first search in C#, one level at a time, with a HashSet of visited nodes and a bidirectional search for the shortest path.

public async Task<long?> ShortestPathAsync(long a, long b, int maxHops, TimeSpan timeout)
{
    if (a == b) return 0;
    var deadline = DateTime.UtcNow + timeout;
    var seenFromA = new HashSet<long> { a };
    var seenFromB = new HashSet<long> { b };
    var frontierA = new List<long> { a };
    var frontierB = new List<long> { b };

    for (int length = 1; length <= maxHops; length++)
    {
        bool expandA = frontierA.Count <= frontierB.Count;
        var (frontier, seen, other) = expandA
            ? (frontierA, seenFromA, seenFromB)
            : (frontierB, seenFromB, seenFromA);
        if (frontier.Count == 0) return null;

        var next = new List<long>();
        foreach (var neighbour in await NeighboursAsync(frontier, deadline, Queries.MySqlNeighboursOf))
        {
            if (other.Contains(neighbour)) return length;
            if (seen.Add(neighbour)) next.Add(neighbour);
        }
        if (expandA) frontierA = next; else frontierB = next;
    }
    return null;
}

NeighboursAsync sends the frontier to MySQL in batches of 2,000 ids and reads the neighbours in both directions with one query per batch:

SELECT dst FROM edges WHERE src IN ({0})
UNION ALL
SELECT src FROM edges WHERE dst IN ({0});

For the third question the BFS uses the same query with one extra condition per direction, NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM hubs h WHERE h.id = e.dst), so MySQL never returns a hub. The CTE gets the same condition inside its recursion. The exact queries are in the repository.

The setup

Everything runs in Docker on one machine, and the repository has a runbook and a script that runs one size from empty databases to the final table.

  • Hardware: Mac Studio, Apple M3 Ultra, 96 GB RAM. Docker had 80 GB of memory and 24 CPUs, and nothing else was running.
  • The same memory for both engines: MySQL 8.4 in a 30 GB container with a 24 GB InnoDB buffer pool. NebulaGraph 3.8 with 30 GB in total: the storage service in a 24 GB container with a 16 GB RocksDB block cache, and the graph service in a 6 GB container. One storage node and 36 partitions.
  • Loading: MySQL with LOAD DATA INFILE and the reverse index built after the load. NebulaGraph with nebula-importer from exactly the same CSV files, followed by a compaction.
  • The data: a deterministic generator in C#. Every node gets on average 9 relationships, and half of the targets come from a skewed distribution, so some nodes become hubs. The sizes are 1M, 10M, 100M and 500M rows, nodes and relationships together, which is the way I counted the rows in my own system.
  • The measurement: 10 cases per question, one warm-up run and 3 measured runs, and the tables show the median. Half of the pairs for the relationship question are close to each other, the other half are two random nodes. The timeout is 15 minutes per query.
  • Validity: after every size the run checks that no container was killed or restarted, that the kernel killed nothing for lack of memory, that no query returned an engine error, and that all methods returned the same answers. Every size passed.

Results: the relationship question

Size (rows) MySQL recursive CTE MySQL + BFS in C# NebulaGraph
1M 5.68 s 1.1 ms 2.1 ms
10M 1.2 min 1.6 ms 18.7 ms
100M 9.7 min, 2 of 10 timed out 1.5 ms 8.6 ms
500M no answer in 15 minutes (10 of 10) 2.7 ms 23.6 ms

This is the result from my story. At 500 million rows the recursive CTE didn't answer a single one of the ten pairs within 15 minutes, while the other two methods answered in milliseconds. The pairs were between 2 and 6 hops apart, so this is not a question of a long path, it's the CTE building the whole 6-hop neighbourhood before it looks for B.

But look at the other two columns. The bidirectional search in C#, on the same MySQL tables, was faster than NebulaGraph at every size. So for this question, the problem was not the relational database. It was the recursive CTE.

Results: the neighbourhood question

Size (rows) MySQL recursive CTE MySQL + BFS in C# NebulaGraph
1M 180 ms 177 ms 72.4 ms
10M 2.65 s 508.5 ms 288.1 ms
100M 10.61 s 1.70 s 1.13 s
500M 3.18 s 579.6 ms 529.1 ms

These are 4 hops. At 1, 2 and 3 hops all three methods answer in at most about 130 ms at every size, and at 1 and 2 hops in a few milliseconds or less.

Two things are worth explaining here. First, NebulaGraph is the fastest at every size, but the BFS in C# is never far behind, between 1.1 and 2.4 times slower, and the CTE is between 2.5 and 9.4 times slower than NebulaGraph.

Second, 500M is faster than 100M for every method, which looks wrong. It isn't: the time of this query depends on how many nodes it reaches, not on the size of the table. With 10 million nodes, the median start node reached 3.9 million nodes in 4 hops, but with 50 million nodes the median start node reached 2.3 million, because the same number of relationships is spread over five times more nodes. Less work, less time, for all three engines in the same way.

Results: a graph with hubs

The graph above is friendly. Real graphs often have hubs, and in an identity graph a single placeholder value, like a default phone number, can be connected to hundreds of thousands of records. So I generated a second graph: 1 million nodes with on average 50 relationships, plus 20 hubs connected to about 630,000 nodes each. 904 nodes have more than 1,000 relationships. It's 63.5 million rows, and the timeout here is 5 minutes.

The first thing this graph shows is why hubs matter: from a median start node, 2 hops reach 999,991 of the 1,000,000 nodes. Every search goes through a hub, and after that it has the whole graph.

Question MySQL recursive CTE MySQL + BFS in C# NebulaGraph
relationship, up to 6 hops no answer in 5 minutes (10 of 10) 0.5 ms 1.1 ms
neighbourhood, 2 hops 8.49 s 1.07 s 575.6 ms
neighbourhood, 3 hops 3.6 min 20.58 s 5.95 s
neighbourhood, 4 hops no answer in 5 minutes (10 of 10) 20.59 s 11.27 s

Here the difference between the BFS in C# and NebulaGraph becomes real: when a query touches the whole graph, NebulaGraph is 1.8 to 3.5 times faster. The BFS has to pull every level of the search over the network into the application, batch by batch, and NebulaGraph does the same work next to the data.

But nobody wants the whole graph. The useful question on this graph is the third one, the neighbourhood that walks around the hubs:

Hops MySQL recursive CTE MySQL + BFS in C#
2 6.8 ms 5.5 ms
3 2.55 s 479.6 ms
4 2.6 min 22.91 s

Avoiding the hubs, the median start node reaches about 12,000 nodes in 2 hops and 730,000 in 3 hops, so this is still a big search, but it is one the user actually asked for.

This question shows the most about NebulaGraph, because I couldn't write it as one nGQL statement that is both correct and usable:

  • GO 1 TO 3 STEPS ... WHERE NOT "hub" IN tags($$) runs, but it returned more nodes than the SQL version. In our check on a small graph it found 5,821 nodes at 2 hops where the correct answer was 463, because the filter doesn't stop the walk from going through a hub.
  • MATCH with a condition that no node on the path is a hub returns the correct answer, but it enumerates paths, and on a 20,000-node test graph the 4-hop version used up the 1 GB the graph service had in that test.

What an application does in this case is to walk one GO step per level from C# and remove the hubs between the levels. That is the same small graph engine in the application as the BFS on MySQL, just on top of a different database. I measured a version of it, but my implementation filtered the hubs with WHERE NOT "hub" IN tags($$) in every step, which makes NebulaGraph read the tags of every destination node, and a version that filtered in C# was about twice as fast in a small test. Because I don't have a fair measurement of that approach at full size, I leave NebulaGraph out of this table rather than show a number that makes it look worse than it is.

What the numbers say

I think the honest summary has three parts.

The recursive CTE is what breaks. In every table it is the slowest method, from about 1.2 times slower on the smallest searches to several thousand times slower on the relationship question, and at 500M rows it didn't answer a single relationship question within 15 minutes. It can't remember visited nodes, can't search from both sides and can't stop early. The query in my story was this kind of relationship question, and the benchmark suggests that the way such a query is written matters at least as much as where the data lives.

A breadth-first search on MySQL is a real alternative, and for paths it was the fastest. With the same tables and the same indexes, the BFS in C# answered the relationship question in under 3 milliseconds at every size, faster than NebulaGraph's FIND SHORTEST PATH, and on the 4-hop neighbourhood it stayed within 2.4 times of NebulaGraph on the normal graph. On the hub-avoiding question it was more than five times faster than the CTE at 3 hops. But it's important to be clear what it is: you are writing a small graph engine inside your application, with the visited set, the frontier, the batching, the bidirectional search and the timeouts, and every new kind of question means more code.

A graph database pays off when the traversal itself is big. On the hub graph, when a query really had to walk a large part of the graph, NebulaGraph was 1.8 to 3.5 times faster than the BFS, because it does the work next to the data instead of pulling every level into the application. It also gives you a language where the first two questions are one line each. What it didn't give me, in this test, is a single statement for a traversal that has to avoid certain nodes, and that is exactly the kind of question real graphs need.

Limits of this benchmark

  • It runs on one machine with local disks and one NebulaGraph storage node. NebulaGraph is designed to spread partitions over many machines, and this test doesn't measure that at all. If your graph doesn't fit on one machine, that is a different question, and a benchmark on one machine can't answer it.
  • The data is generated. It has the right shape (skewed degrees, hubs), but it is not production data with production query patterns and other traffic.
  • The MySQL schema and queries are the common approach, not the only one. If you can make the relational side faster, a pull request with the numbers is very welcome.

When a relational database is still the right choice

If your queries are one or two hops, for example "the orders of this customer" or "the members of this group", a relational database with the right indexes is very fast, much simpler to operate, and you already have it. In every table above, 1 and 2 hops on the normal graph stayed in the range of a few milliseconds for all three methods.

In my view, the signal to look at a graph database is the shape of the questions, not the number of rows. When you start to write recursive CTEs, first replace them with a search in your application: in this benchmark that alone turned minutes into milliseconds. When the traversals become large, when the business keeps asking new kinds of graph questions, or when the graph grows beyond one machine, that's the point where a graph database earns its place.

Run it yourself

The repository has everything needed to reproduce these numbers: the Docker Compose file for MySQL and NebulaGraph, the C# generator, the C# benchmark with all methods, the runbook with the validity checks, and the raw CSV of every single run.

title: Property Payment Reconciliation: Node.js Cron Setup for Periodic Database Cleanup
description:
Short answer: For periodic database cleanup in a Node.js backend, use a cron setup that claims one durable run, processes bounded batches with stable idempotency keys, and leaves retryable work visible; the scheduler is a trigger, not the source of truth.

A nightly payment reconciliation job should be boring: one bounded window, one durable run record, and a retry that cannot charge or delete the same business fact twice. For a property-management backend, my least complex default is a single scheduler that claims a run in the database, processes records with an idempotency key, and leaves retryable work visible when the process disappears.

That distinction matters during cleanup. A timer can fire twice, a deployment can interrupt it, and a payment provider can answer after the caller has timed out. If the cleanup code assumes one invocation, a harmless retention task can remove evidence needed to reconcile a resident payment. If the reconciliation code assumes one response, a retry can create a second ledger entry.

How should a Node.js cron setup handle periodic database cleanup?

The page fires at 02:17 because the nightly reconciliation window has not closed. The dashboard shows 18,420 payment records selected, 18,006 matched, and 414 still pending. The worker process restarted at 02:11 during a deployment. A second scheduler instance then started the same window, so the two processes are competing for rows while the alert counts elapsed time rather than durable progress.

The tempting response is to raise the timeout or lengthen the schedule. That treats the page as a clock problem. The useful question is narrower: which run owns this window, and can another attempt safely continue it?

I would first inspect the run ledger, not the cron expression. It should contain a stable logical key such as property-group-2026-10-23, a state, an attempt count, a lease expiry, and counters for selected, matched, failed, and deleted records. An invocation that finds a completed key exits successfully. An invocation that finds an expired lease may reclaim it, but only after its database transaction has established that the previous owner is no longer valid.

This is the operational contract:

  • The scheduler may deliver a trigger more than once.
  • The database decides whether a logical run is new, active, or complete.
  • Each provider request and each local ledger mutation carries an idempotency key derived from the business record, not from the process attempt.
  • Cleanup deletes only rows whose retention rule is satisfied and whose reconciliation state is terminal.

That is the answer before choosing a Node.js library.

Which retry boundary keeps cleanup safe?

There are three different things people call a retry, and they have different failure consequences. A scheduler retry means “start or resume the window.” A job retry means “process this bounded unit again.” A provider retry means “send the same external operation again.” Collapsing them into one counter makes incident review nearly impossible.

For example, a request can time out after the payment provider has accepted it. Retrying with a fresh random key risks a duplicate operation; retrying with the original operation key lets the provider recognize the attempt when the API supports idempotency. The local database still needs a unique constraint because an external contract cannot replace local protection. HMAC is useful when a service derives a compact signed identifier for a queue or callback, but a MAC authenticates data; it does not make a side effect idempotent. RFC 2104 is precise about that boundary.

A cleanup transaction should be small enough to release locks regularly. Select a batch, mark it claimed with a lease, commit, perform external work outside the transaction, then record the result in a second transaction. A worker that dies after the external result but before the local result can replay the operation with the same key. A worker that dies before external work can safely reclaim the batch after the lease expires.

Here is the shape of a Go-like interface expressed in Go, because the important part is the contract rather than a framework-specific API:

type Reconciler interface {
    Claim(ctx context.Context, runKey string, limit int) ([]Payment, error)
    Apply(ctx context.Context, payment Payment, operationKey string) error
    Complete(ctx context.Context, paymentID string, result Result) error
}

func operationKey(runKey, paymentID string) string {
    return runKey + ":payment:" + paymentID
}

In a real Node.js service, the same boundaries belong in TypeScript interfaces or ordinary functions; the language does not change the failure model. The key must remain stable across process restarts, and it must include the business identity that the provider considers the operation. Do not use a timestamp, a random UUID generated inside the retry loop, or the scheduler invocation ID.

How should the signal fire before the page?

The original alert is late because it measures only the final deadline. Add signals that describe progress and ownership. I want the age of the oldest unprocessed batch, the count of leases nearing expiry, the rate of successful completions, and the number of provider responses classified as retryable. I also want a metric for duplicate trigger attempts, because a rising count says something about deployment overlap or scheduler placement even when the job finishes.

The threshold needs a capacity calculation. If one batch handles 500 records, the provider permits 10 concurrent requests, and the observed upper-bound latency is 2 seconds, the theoretical request capacity is 300 records per minute before database and network overhead. That is not a promise; it is a ceiling. Set the alert from a measured service-level objective and leave room for lock contention, rate limits, and a cold start. A window that usually completes in 12 minutes but has a 30-minute SLO should page on durable progress approaching the SLO, not on an arbitrary 15-minute timer.

The false-positive cost is real. Page too early and on-call learns to mute the alert; page too late and the reconciliation window closes with missing ledger state. I prefer a warning on stalled progress and a page when the oldest lease or pending record threatens the stated SLO. The alert should link to the run key and the last successful batch, so the first action is a query with a known scope rather than a guess.

A useful deployment test is to kill the worker at each boundary: after claim, after provider acceptance, before local completion, and while renewing the lease. The expected result is not “the job runs once.” It is “the final ledger state is correct, the operation key is reused, and a later attempt can explain what happened.”

Which scheduler boundary fits the service?

A scheduler that lives in the Node.js process is easy to understand and often adequate for a single continuously running instance. Its weakness is ownership: every replica may register the same schedule unless leader election or a database claim prevents duplicate work. Process restarts also erase in-memory timing state, so the durable run ledger remains mandatory.

A host or container scheduler moves the trigger outside the application, which makes deployment ownership clearer, but it still does not provide business-level idempotency. A Kubernetes CronJob, for example, expresses scheduled Jobs and has controls for concurrency policy and missed schedules; those controls reduce overlap without proving that a payment operation was applied exactly once. The database contract remains the authority.

Queue-oriented systems add a useful middle layer when the nightly window needs backpressure, delayed retries, or many independent batches. BullMQ represents jobs in Redis and exposes retry and backoff concepts, while the Redis dependency becomes part of the recovery and capacity plan. Bree runs jobs using worker threads and supports cron-style scheduling, which can isolate CPU work but does not turn an external payment call into a transactional operation. node-cron is a lightweight in-process cron scheduler; its small surface is attractive when the application already has a durable claim step.

Those are engineering boundaries, not a ranking. The decision is about where you want failure to be visible:

Boundary Useful property Risk to carry in the design
In-process timer Few moving parts and direct application access Replica overlap and restart loss
Host or cluster scheduler Clear trigger ownership and deployment separation Missed-run semantics still need a durable ledger
Durable queue Per-batch backpressure, delayed retry, and inspection Queue storage becomes another availability and capacity dependency

The platform team's buy-versus-build choice follows the same table. A managed scheduler or queue can reduce on-call work, while a self-hosted component can preserve control over placement, retention, and failure inspection. Neither removes the need to define an SLO, write a unique constraint, or test a provider timeout. A managed service is not a substitute for a business transaction boundary; self-hosting is not free ownership.

The limitation is deliberate: an in-process cron setup is unsuitable when replicas cannot share a database claim or when the service is not continuously running. In that case, an external scheduler is the better boundary. A queue is also the wrong fit for a tiny one-batch cleanup if its extra storage and operational ownership outweigh the retry visibility it provides.

What should be deleted, and when?

Retention cleanup belongs after reconciliation has declared a terminal state. For a property-management system, raw provider responses, local ledger entries, and audit records do not necessarily share the same retention rule. A cleanup query that sees only created_at can delete a response that is old but still needed to resolve a pending dispute. Use explicit states and policy columns, then make the deletion predicate include both age and terminal status.

Keep deletion batches bounded. Record the selected count and deleted count, and make the operation resumable. If a batch fails halfway through, a later run should find only the remaining eligible rows. The delete itself should be idempotent in the ordinary database sense: deleting an already-deleted row is not a second business operation, and the audit trail should record the original logical run key.

Do not use a successful scheduler exit as proof that every row was removed. Emit the result that matters: eligible rows, processed rows, retryable rows, permanent failures, and the age of the oldest eligible row. This gives the next run enough information to continue without inventing state.

The decision rule

Use the least complex trigger that can reliably wake the service, then spend the design effort on the durable run record, stable operation keys, bounded claims, and metrics tied to the reconciliation SLO. Choose an in-process timer for a small, single-owner service only when the database claim is already in place. Choose an external scheduler when deployment ownership or replica count makes trigger duplication likely. Add a durable queue when per-batch retry and backpressure are worth operating another dependency.

The page at 02:17 should become a prompt to inspect a known run, not a mystery about which process fired. The scheduler can be imperfect. The business result cannot be.

Further reading

  • RFC 2104, HMAC: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104
  • Node.js timers documentation: https://nodejs.org/api/timers.html
  • Kubernetes CronJob documentation: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/cron-jobs/
  • node-cron documentation: https://nodecron.com/
  • Bree documentation: https://github.com/breejs/bree
  • BullMQ documentation: https://docs.bullmq.io/

title: Error Messages Are Writing, Too
description:
Error messages are some of the most carefully read sentences in any piece of software. They appear at the exact moment the reader is stuck, often a little frustrated, and looking for help. Yet they are frequently written last, in a hurry, by someone thinking about the code rather than the person on the other side of it.

The good news is that a useful error message follows a simple pattern, and it can be learned like any other kind of editing.

The three parts of a useful message

A clear error message answers three questions:

  1. What happened?
  2. Why did it happen, if that is known?
  3. What can the reader do now?

Most weak messages answer only the first question, and sometimes not even that.

Before:

Error: invalid input.

After:

The date "31.02.2026" could not be read. February has no 31st day. Please enter a date in the format DD.MM.YYYY.

The second version is longer, but every word earns its place. The reader knows which value was wrong, why it was rejected and what a correct value looks like.

Name the thing, not the category

"Invalid input", "operation failed" and "something went wrong" describe a category of problem. The reader needs the specific case.

Whenever the program knows which file, field, value or setting caused the problem, include it in the message. "Could not open config.yaml" is immediately useful. "Could not open file" sends the reader searching.

This also helps when people copy the message into a search engine or a support request. A specific message leads to specific answers.

Speak to the reader, not about the code

Internal terms leak easily into error text: exception names, function names, abbreviations that only the team uses. They make sense to the author and to nobody else.

Before:

NullReferenceException in UserProfileLoader.

After:

Your profile could not be loaded because no account is linked to this email address.

Technical details still have a place. Developers debugging the problem may need the exception and the stack trace. Put those in logs, or below the human-readable message, clearly separated. The first line should be readable by the person who actually sees it.

Do not blame, do not joke

Tone matters more than usual here, because the reader is already having a bad moment.

  • Avoid blame. "You entered an invalid password" sounds like an accusation. "The password does not match this account" states the same fact neutrally.
  • Avoid jokes. A playful "Oops!" can feel friendly the first time and irritating the tenth time, especially when work has been lost.
  • Avoid false certainty. If the cause is only a guess, say "This may be caused by..." rather than presenting it as fact.

Calm, plain language works best. The aim is to sound like a helpful colleague, not a machine and not a comedian.

Offer a way forward

The most important part of an error message is the last one: what the reader can do next. Even when the program cannot fix the problem, it can usually point somewhere.

  • Retry later, if the problem is temporary.
  • Correct a specific value, and show the expected format.
  • Check a specific setting, and name where it is.
  • Contact support, and say what information to include.

A message without a next step leaves the reader at a dead end. A message with one turns a failure into a short detour.

Review your errors like any other text

Collect the error messages in your project in one list and read them in a row. This simple exercise reveals a lot: inconsistent wording, messages that say the same thing in five different ways, and messages that say nothing at all.

Edit them as you would edit any other text. Check that each one names the problem, explains it where possible and offers a next step. They are short, but for the reader in that moment, they may be the most important words in the whole product.

title: Web Search on AWS Bedrock now supports domain filtering and user location controls
description:
Web Search on AWS Bedrock now supports two new controls that give you more precision over the results that ground a model's response: domain filtering and user location. Both are configured directly on the web_search tool in your existing OpenAI Responses API request.

With domain filtering, you can restrict Web Search results to a set of domains you choose. Using the filters parameter, you specify up to 100 allowed_domains to limit results to trusted sources, or up to 100 blocked_domains to exclude sources you don't want. This is useful when you want responses grounded only in specific sites, or when you need to keep certain domains out of results.

With user location, you can optionally specify location parameters so that Web Search can return results relevant to that geography. This helps with location-dependent questions, such as regional availability or local services.

Domain filtering and user location are available in all AWS Regions where Web Search is supported: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), and AWS GovCloud (US-West). To get started, see the Web Search section in the AWS Bedrock User Guide. For pricing, see the AWS Bedrock pricing page.

title: One Load per Key: Collapsing Duplicate Lookups with Spring Boot's Cache and Caffeine
description:
Rule engines, aggregators and validation pipelines share a hidden cost. Many independent components ask the same downstream question, with the same key, at the same moment. Each component is correct on its own; together they multiply the load on whatever sits behind them.

This article shows how to collapse those calls into a single load using Spring's cache abstraction backed by Caffeine. It also covers what tends to bite afterwards: cached empty results, metrics that change meaning, and tests that pass for the wrong reason.

The scenario

Take a promotion eligibility service. To decide whether a product qualifies for a promotion, it evaluates about 20 rules in parallel: in stock, price above a threshold, seller in good standing, category not excluded, and so on.

List<CompletableFuture<Boolean>> results = rules.stream()
        .map(rule -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> rule.test(productId), executor))
        .toList();

Each rule depends on a small, focused service:

@Component
class InStockRule implements Rule {

    private final StockService stockService;

    @Override
    public boolean test(String productId) {
        return stockService.isInStock(productId);
    }
}

@Service
class StockService {

    private final ProductCatalogue catalogue;

    boolean isInStock(String productId) {
        return catalogue.findProduct(productId)
                .map(product -> product.stock() > 0)
                .orElse(false);
    }
}

PricingService, SellerService and CategoryService look the same: each one reads a different field from the same Product, which comes from one place:

@Service
public class ProductCatalogue {

    // Reads from a shared cache (Redis, DynamoDB, ...), falls back to the catalogue API on a miss.
    public Optional<Product> findProduct(String productId) {
        return store.get(productId).or(() -> fetchAndStore(productId));
    }
}

The design is clean: every rule is small, testable and independent. But one evaluation of one product calls findProduct about 20 times:

  • Warm path: 20 reads from the shared cache, plus 20 deserialisations of the same object.
  • Cold path: all 20 calls miss at the same time, so the catalogue API gets 20 concurrent requests for the same product. That's a cache stampede, and it hits hardest when the downstream system is already struggling.

The calls don't need 20 answers. They need one.

Why not request scope?

The first idea is usually a request-scoped cache: memoise the response for the lifetime of the HTTP request. That works less well than it sounds:

  • Thread hopping. The rules run on executor threads. Request attributes are bound to the request thread, so request-scoped beans only work if you propagate the context to every executor (for example with a TaskDecorator).
  • No request at all. Queue consumers, Kafka listeners and scheduled jobs have no HTTP request. A @RequestScope bean there fails with No thread-bound request found.

A short-lived, in-process cache gives the same effect on every entry point. The price is bounded staleness, and with a short enough TTL that price is negligible.

Setup

Dependencies

spring-boot-starter-cache brings Spring's cache abstraction, but not Caffeine. Add both. Spring Boot manages the Caffeine version.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-cache</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.github.ben-manes.caffeine</groupId>
    <artifactId>caffeine</artifactId>
</dependency>

implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-cache")
implementation("com.github.ben-manes.caffeine:caffeine")

Enable caching 

@SpringBootApplication
@EnableCaching
public class Application { }

Configure the cache 

spring:
  cache:
    type: caffeine
    cache-names: products
    caffeine:
      spec: maximumSize=10000,expireAfterWrite=30s,recordStats

Each line matters:

  • type: caffeine makes the application fail at startup if Caffeine is missing. Without it, Spring Boot silently falls back to ConcurrentMapCacheManager. That cache ignores caffeine.spec, so it has no size limit and entries never expire: unbounded memory and unbounded staleness, a worse problem than the one you set out to fix. Dependencies move around, so don't rely on Caffeine always being on the classpath.
  • cache-names creates the listed caches at startup and turns off dynamic creation: a @Cacheable that uses an unlisted name fails at runtime. It's also what lets Spring Boot register Micrometer metrics for the cache, because only caches that exist at startup are bound.
  • spec: maximumSize caps memory, expireAfterWrite caps staleness, and recordStats turns on the hit/miss statistics behind the metrics.

The annotation 

@Cacheable(cacheNames = "products", key = "#productId", sync = true)
public Optional<Product> findProduct(String productId) {
    return store.get(productId).or(() -> fetchAndStore(productId));
}

Two attributes do most of the work here.

sync = true is the difference between caching and collapsing. Without it, Spring checks the cache, misses, calls the method and stores the result. When 20 threads miss at the same moment, all 20 call the method. With sync = true, Spring hands the load to Caffeine's atomic get(key, loader): the first thread runs the method, and the other 19 wait for its result.

key = "#productId" makes the key explicit. The default key generator uses the bare argument for single-argument methods, but the moment someone adds a second parameter, the key changes shape and any matching @CacheEvict silently stops working. Referring to parameters by name needs the -parameters compiler flag (Spring Boot's build plugins enable it); otherwise use #p0.

Evicting works the same way:

@CacheEvict(cacheNames = "products", key = "#productId")
public void evict(String productId) { }

@CacheEvict(cacheNames = "products", allEntries = true)
public void evictAll() { }

A classic mistake: @CacheEvict("products") on a method with no arguments evicts the key SimpleKey.EMPTY, which clears nothing. Use allEntries = true to clear the whole cache.

What will surprise you

1. Empty results are cached too

Spring unwraps Optional: present values are stored as the value, and empty ones are stored as null. CaffeineCacheManager allows null values by default, so "product not found" is memoised for the full TTL.

This is often what you want: without it, a missing product is looked up again by every one of the 20 callers. But decide it deliberately. The usual escape hatch, unless = "#result == null", isn't allowed together with sync = true. If you can't accept caching empty results, you'll need a different shape, for example throwing a not-found exception (exceptions are never cached) or using the Cache API directly.

2. Failures are not shared

Exceptions aren't cached. That's good: a transient failure doesn't stick for the next 30 seconds. But it also means that when the load fails, the waiting callers don't get the error. They retry the load one after another. Under a sustained outage, put a circuit breaker or a stale-fallback strategy inside the loaded method. Don't count on the cache to absorb the failures.

3. Every caller gets the same instance

Before the cache, each caller got its own freshly deserialised copy. Now all callers within the TTL share one object, across threads. If anything modifies it, you have a data race between components that don't know about each other. Prefer immutable types (records, or immutable generated classes). If you can't, say so in a comment on the cached method.

4. Self-invocation bypasses the cache

@Cacheable works through a Spring proxy. A call from inside the same class (this.findProduct(...)) skips the proxy and the cache. Check that every hot caller goes through the bean.

5. The cache is per instance

Each pod or instance has its own cache. An eviction endpoint only clears the instance that received the request; the others keep serving the old value until the TTL expires. That's acceptable when the TTL is short. Write it down for whoever operates the endpoint.

6. Your existing metrics change meaning

Any counter incremented inside the cached method (misses on the shared cache, remote calls, fallbacks) now only fires on in-memory misses. On the day you deploy, dashboards show a sudden drop that looks like an outage or a miracle. It's neither. Warn people before the deploy, and add the cache's own metrics, which recordStats exposes:

  • cache.gets{cache="products", result="hit"|"miss"}
  • cache.puts
  • cache.evictions
  • cache.size

7. Pick the TTL for the unit of work

The goal is to collapse the calls within one unit of work, not to build a long-lived performance cache. So the TTL needs to be long enough to cover one evaluation including slow paths (retries and their backoff), and short enough that the extra staleness is negligible compared with how fresh the data behind it is anyway. Seconds to tens of seconds is usually right. If you want a longer TTL, that's a different cache, and it needs its own invalidation design.

8. Virtual threads on JDK 21–23

With sync = true, the load runs inside Caffeine's atomic compute, which holds a synchronized lock. On JDK 21–23, a virtual thread that blocks on I/O inside synchronized pins its carrier thread. Since carrier threads are few (one per core by default), many concurrent cold loads can starve the scheduler. JDK 24 fixed this (JEP 491). On older JDKs, load-test the cold path with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full.

Testing it

Prove that concurrent misses collapse

A naive test fires 20 calls and checks that the loader ran once. It usually passes even without sync = true: the stubbed load returns instantly, so the calls run one after another and the first one fills the cache before the second arrives. The test has to keep callers inside the loader until all of them have arrived:

@SpringJUnitConfig(ProductCatalogueCachingTest.Config.class)
class ProductCatalogueCachingTest {

    private static final int CALLERS = 20;

    @Autowired
    ProductCatalogue catalogue;
    @MockitoBean
    ProductStore store;

    @Test
    void concurrentMissesLoadOnce() throws Exception {
        var allCallersLoading = new CountDownLatch(CALLERS);
        var release = new CountDownLatch(1);
        // Every caller that reaches the loader waits here, so without sync = true all of them would load.
        when(store.get("p-1")).thenAnswer(invocation -> {
            allCallersLoading.countDown();
            release.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
            return Optional.of(new Product("p-1", 3));
        });

        try (var executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(CALLERS)) {
            var futures = IntStream.range(0, CALLERS)
                    .mapToObj(i -> executor.submit(() -> catalogue.findProduct("p-1")))
                    .toList();
            allCallersLoading.await(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
            release.countDown();
            for (var future : futures) {
                assertThat(future.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isPresent();
            }
        }
        verify(store, times(1)).get("p-1");
    }

    @Configuration
    @EnableCaching
    static class Config {

        @Bean
        CacheManager cacheManager() {
            return new CaffeineCacheManager("products");
        }

        @Bean
        ProductCatalogue catalogue(ProductStore store) {
            return new ProductCatalogue(store);
        }
    }
}

With sync = true, the first caller enters the loader and the other 19 wait in Caffeine, so get runs once. Without it, all 20 enter the loader and the test fails with Wanted 1 time, but was 20 times. Remove sync = true once to see that failure: a test you've never seen fail hasn't proven anything.

Prove that the shipped configuration is the one you think

The test above builds its own CaffeineCacheManager, so it never touches application.yml. A typo in cache-names, or a missing type, would only show up in production. ApplicationContextRunner can load the real configuration file with only the cache auto-configuration:

@Test
void applicationConfigurationCreatesBoundedCaffeineCache() {
    new ApplicationContextRunner()
            .withInitializer(new ConfigDataApplicationContextInitializer())
            .withConfiguration(AutoConfigurations.of(CacheAutoConfiguration.class))
            .withUserConfiguration(CachingEnabled.class)
            .run(context -> {
                var manager = context.getBean(CacheManager.class);
                assertThat(manager).isInstanceOf(CaffeineCacheManager.class);

                var cache = (com.github.benmanes.caffeine.cache.Cache<?, ?>)
                        manager.getCache("products").getNativeCache();
                assertThat(cache.policy().eviction().orElseThrow().getMaximum()).isEqualTo(10_000);
                assertThat(cache.policy().expireAfterWrite().orElseThrow().getExpiresAfter())
                        .isEqualTo(Duration.ofSeconds(30));
            });
}

@Configuration
@EnableCaching
static class CachingEnabled { }

CacheAutoConfiguration lives in org.springframework.boot.cache.autoconfigure in Spring Boot 4, and in org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.cache in Spring Boot 3.

Also add one test each for eviction (evict, call again, check the loader ran twice) and for whichever empty-result behaviour you chose.

Checklist

  • [ ] spring-boot-starter-cache and caffeine declared, @EnableCaching on
  • [ ] spring.cache.type: caffeine so a missing Caffeine fails at startup
  • [ ] cache-names declared (and new names added there)
  • [ ] maximumSize, expireAfterWrite and recordStats in the spec
  • [ ] @Cacheable(sync = true) with an explicit key
  • [ ] @CacheEvict uses the same key; clear-all uses allEntries = true
  • [ ] Empty-result caching decided and tested
  • [ ] Cached return type immutable, or documented as shared
  • [ ] No self-invocation on hot paths
  • [ ] Dashboard owners warned about counters inside the cached method
  • [ ] Concurrency test that fails without sync = true
  • [ ] Configuration test against the real application.yml
  • [ ] On JDK 21–23 with virtual threads: cold path load-tested for pinning

Wrapping up

The change itself is a dependency, a few lines of YAML and one annotation. Most of the value is in the rest: deciding what gets cached (including "not found"), making the configuration fail loudly instead of degrading silently, warning the people who read the metrics, and writing tests that actually fail when the behaviour breaks. Get those right, and twenty components asking the same question cost the same as one.
