title: 84% of abandoned v0 apps run a known-exploited Next.js
description:
A field note on what happens to AI-built apps after the builder walks away, measured on October 21, 2026, the day Next.js 15 left security support.

Of 274 abandoned v0-built apps whose Next.js version we could read, 231 (84%) declare a version inside the React2Shell range, the remote code execution flaw CISA has listed as actively exploited since December 5, 2025. 226 of them run the exact same version: Next.js 15.2.4. Only 3 run Next.js 16, and none runs the current patched release.

The date matters for a second reason. Next.js 15 was released on October 21, 2024, and the Next.js support policy keeps a major in Maintenance LTS for two years. Since October 21, 2026, the policy sends security fixes to Next.js 16 only. That leaves 271 of the 274 apps on a major outside its support window, on top of the 231 already in a known-exploited range.

This note explains how we measured it, why so many apps landed on one version, what the numbers do and do not prove, and what to do if one of these apps is yours.

1. What we measured

We wanted apps that were generated by an AI builder, deployed, and then left alone. v0 makes that population easy to find without guessing: projects it syncs to GitHub carry a recognizable notice in their README. We searched public GitHub repositories with that notice, created between January and August 2025, whose last push was before October 1, 2025, and that list a live homepage. That gave 398 apps, each untouched for more than a year.

For each one we fetched the homepage and the JavaScript files it links, exactly what any visitor's browser downloads. An App Router build of Next.js declares its own version in that code (a line of the form window.next = { version: "15.2.4", appDir: true }), and that self-reported version is what we recorded. We sent no exploit, no crafted request and no login attempt, and we are not publishing any app's address.

Result Apps
Sampled (v0 notice, created Jan to Aug 2025, no push since Sep 30, 2025) 398
Still serving a page 304
Next.js version readable from the served code 274
Version inside the React2Shell range (CVE-2025-55182, on CISA KEV) 231
On Next.js 14, out of support since October 2025 39
On Next.js 15, out of support since October 21, 2026, already patched for React2Shell 1
On Next.js 16, the only supported major 3
On the current patched release (16.4.2) 0

The other 94 apps were gone or unreadable: 69 answered 404 (a deleted deployment), 7 answered 402 (a paused Vercel project), and the rest timed out, no longer resolved, or ran a build whose version we could not read.

2. Why one version dominates: the exact pin

The concentration on 15.2.4 is not a coincidence, and it is not about people choosing an old version. We opened the package.json of sampled repositories, and the generated projects of that period declare "next": "15.2.4" with no range operator. An exact pin means a fresh install, a rebuild or a redeploy all produce the same 15.2.4 forever. Nothing upstream can move the app forward. Only a person editing that line can.

That turns a normal software habit into a trap. In a hand-maintained project, an exact pin is a deliberate choice somebody revisits. In a generated project, it is a snapshot of the day the model wrote the file, and the builder who accepted it usually never opened package.json at all. The 35 apps on 14.2.16 show the same pattern from an earlier template: one version, pinned, frozen.

Then the builder moved on. Every app in this sample was created in a burst of experimentation in 2025 and has not received a single commit in over a year. The deployment kept running anyway, because hosting a small app costs nothing and nobody turns it off. The app outlived the attention of the person who made it, and the version it was generated with became its permanent version.

3. What React2Shell is, and what the numbers do not prove

CVE-2025-55182, known as React2Shell, is unauthenticated remote code execution in React Server Components, which the Next.js App Router uses. It affects every Next.js 15 release line and 16.0 until that line's patch (15.2.6 for the 15.2 line), and CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on December 5, 2025. Its one precondition, the App Router, is stated on the same line as the version we read, which is why a version in range is a meaningful signal and not a guess.

It is still not proof that any of these apps can be compromised today, and we want to be precise about why:

  • Most of these apps sit behind Vercel's firewall. 266 of the 274 are hosted on vercel.app, where Vercel deployed firewall rules against React2Shell for every project. Vercel itself says those rules cannot guarantee protection against all possible variants of an attack and that upgrading is the fix, and researchers have found ways around some WAF defenses. A firewall rule is a mitigation in front of vulnerable code, not a patch to it.
  • The version is self-reported. It is what the served code declares, which is the version that was built. We did not test whether the flaw can be triggered, and we will not.
  • The sample is v0 projects on public GitHub. Builders who kept their repositories private, or who used other tools, are not in it. We think the mechanism (exact pins plus abandonment) generalizes, but the 84% figure describes this population.

What the numbers do show is the gap between how long an AI-built app keeps running and how long anyone maintains it. The fix for React2Shell has existed for more than ten months, and 84% of this population never received it.

4. The second problem started on October 21

Even the apps outside the exploited range are not in a safe place. Next.js 14 left its support window in October 2025, and 37 of the 39 apps on it run a version below the fix for the March 2025 middleware authorization bypass, which matters for any app that checks sign-in in middleware.

Since October 21, 2026, Next.js 15 joins it. The October 14 security release, two critical fixes and one high, was the last that 15.x was owed under the support policy. Vercel has made exceptions for severe flaws before (it shipped 14.2.35 in December 2025, after 14 had left support), but an exception only helps an app that installs it. A pinned, abandoned app misses every patch equally: the ones that ship for its line and the ones that never will.

5. If one of these apps is yours

The cheapest fix is often the right one. An app you no longer use should not be running. Delete the deployment or pause the project, and the exposure is gone along with everything else it might hold (an API key in its code, a database it still talks to).

For an app you want to keep:

  • Upgrade Next.js to 16. The official upgrade guide covers the breaking changes, and a codemod handles most of them. A generated app is usually small enough that this takes minutes, not days.
  • Replace the exact pin with a range ("next": "^16.4.2"), so a rebuild picks up patch releases.
  • Turn on automated dependency updates (Dependabot or Renovate) in the repository, so the next advisory arrives as a pull request instead of as nothing.
  • Check what the live app actually serves, not what you remember deploying.

MacroCyber reads the Next.js version an App Router site serves and flags it when it falls inside a range CISA lists as exploited, as a signal to verify, alongside the AI-era exposures it was built for (open Supabase and Firebase databases, leaked AI keys, exposed MCP servers). You can scan any site free, or give your coding agent the same check with our MCP server so it can scan what it just deployed and confirm its own fix. If your app runs on Supabase, the Supabase exposure check covers the other common way abandoned AI-built apps leak.

6. Method details

  • Population: public GitHub repositories whose README carries v0's sync notice, found through GitHub's repository search, one query per creation month from January to August 2025, restricted to repositories last pushed before October 1, 2025 and listing a homepage. Four repositories that had been pushed after that date by the time we read them were excluded.
  • Reading: one GET of the homepage and of the Next.js JavaScript files it references, with a user agent naming MacroCyber, on October 21, 2026. The version is the one the App Router runtime declares in the served code.
  • Matching: versions were matched with the same advisory table the MacroCyber scanner uses, so the article and the product cannot disagree.
  • Publication: aggregate figures only. No app is named.

This note reflects data read on October 21, 2026. Versions, hosting protections and support dates change, so check the current Next.js advisories before acting on any single figure.

Originally published on macrocyber.co. Written with AI assistance from data we collected on October 21, 2026, and checked against it.

title: Where can I get free credits to test LLM inference
description:
DigitalOcean gives new customers a free \$5 credit, with no credit card required, through its Managed Agents free trial. The credit covers inference on DigitalOcean-hosted models plus the agent runtime and tools around them. It's sized for testing, and Managed Agents is in Public Preview.

Key takeaways:

  • New DigitalOcean customers get \$5 in free credit, no credit card required, to test inference through Managed Agents.
  • Trial inference runs on DigitalOcean-hosted models such as Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, and DeepSeek V4 Flash. Frontier models like Claude and GPT bill at list price.
  • Credit drains as you use compute, storage, and tools, so pause idle sessions and watch your balance.

What the free credit covers

Managed Agents pairs Harness Runtime, which runs agent sessions in isolated Firecracker microVMs, with Action Gateway, which gives agents governed access to 16,000+ tools through one MCP endpoint. It integrates natively with the Inference Engine, so inference tokens, agent execution, and tool use come together in one place.

Refer to the Agent Droplets pricing page for more details about the trial offer, as well as details for paid Pro (\$50 per month) and Team (\$200 per month) plans.

Which models you can test

The trial's inference is built around models DigitalOcean hosts, including Kimi K3 and GLM 5.3. For scale, as of October 2026, the DigitalOcean-hosted GLM-5.3 Flash lists at \$0.15 per million input tokens and \$0.50 per million output tokens on the Inference pricing page. Frontier models like Claude and GPT are also available through DigitalOcean without a provider key of your own, billed at list price and outside the Agent Droplets plan discounts. If you bring your own provider key, that provider bills you directly.

DigitalOcean's Agent Droplets announcement estimates the free trial at roughly 4.5M tokens of inference.

How to start

Sign up as a new customer, open Managed Agents in the control panel, and start the trial. The Harness Runtime docs include a quickstart that launches an agent with one doctl command, and the launch post reports supported harnesses like OpenCode and Codex CLI.

What to watch while you test

Usage draws down your balance as agents run, and Harness Runtime has no per-session or per-product spend limit. Some Action Gateway tools, like Exa web search and web fetch, are prepaid and metered per call. Serverless inference is prepaid too, so access is suspended when credits and balances run out.

To save credits, pause sessions you aren't using. Pausing stops CPU and memory charges, though retained checkpoints still accrue storage fees. Current rates are on the Harness Runtime pricing page.

LLM inference free credits FAQ

Is there an inference provider with a free tier?

DigitalOcean offers new customers a free trial with \$5 in credit through Managed Agents, no credit card required. It's a starter credit for new customers rather than an ongoing free tier, and it covers inference on DigitalOcean-hosted models, runtime, storage, and tools.

Where can I run inference for an AI app and bill it all through one invoice?

Managed Agents integrates with the DigitalOcean Inference Engine, so inference on DigitalOcean-hosted models, agent compute, storage, and tool calls bill together. Models you reach with your own provider key are billed by that provider.

How do I cap inference billing to avoid surprise costs from runaway agents?

Harness Runtime has no per-session or per-product spend limit, and usage draws down your prepaid balance. Pausing a session stops CPU and memory charges, and auto-pause handles idle sessions, though retained checkpoints still accrue storage fees. Monitor usage closely on autonomous workflows.

References & further reading

  • Start with the Managed Agents product page for trial terms.
  • The launch post and the Agent Droplets announcement explain the architecture and the trial.
  • Worth bookmarking: the Agent Droplets pricing page for plan comparisons.
  • The Harness Runtime pricing page lists compute and storage rates. Worth checking directly before you build.
  • The Inference pricing docs have per-model token rates and prepaid billing rules.
  • Learn more about Harness Runtime and the Inference Engine.

title: Why We Don’t Always Need Kafka: High-Throughput Background Queues in Spring Boot with Redis & Virtual Threads
description:
By Gaurav Kumar Yadav • Canonical URL: https://gaurav10610.github.io/oxmq/guide/spring-boot.html

Every engineering team eventually hits this architectural crossroads:

"Our application needs background workers for payment processing, report generation, webhooks, and email notifications. What should we use?"

Too often, the default answer is: "Let's spin up Apache Kafka."

Three months later, the team is wrestling with partition rebalances, consumer group lag, broker ZooKeeper/KRaft quorum tuning, and high AWS MSK bills—all for a workload that just needed reliable task retries, sliding-window rate limiting, and parent-child task workflows.

If you don't need petabyte-scale append-only event streaming with weeks of historical replay, Kafka is often the wrong tool for task queues.

In this article, we’ll explore how to build a modern, high-throughput distributed background processing engine in Spring Boot 3+ using Redis, Java 21 Project Loom Virtual Threads, and OxMQ—the Virtual Thread-native Java alternative to BullMQ.

The Distributed Task Queue Dilemma in Java

In Node.js, developers have BullMQ—a battle-tested Redis queue that executes Lua scripts for atomic state transitions, supports delayed scheduling, sliding-window rate limiters, and parent-child DAG flows, with instant visibility via the open-source Bull-Board Web UI.

In Java, teams typically faced frustrating trade-offs:

  1. In-Memory ExecutorService: Fast, but loses all tasks on crash or pod restart. No distributed lock or cluster coordination.
  2. Spring @Scheduled & DB polling (db-scheduler, shedlock): Great for simple crons, but database table polling collapses under 5,000+ jobs/s and creates high DB CPU contention.
  3. Redisson Queues: Opaque Lua implementations, no parent-child DAG orchestration, and no out-of-the-box monitoring UI.
  4. Kafka / RabbitMQ: Heavy operational overhead, lack of native token-bucket rate limiting per tenant, and complex delayed job retries (dead-letter exchange looping).

This is why we built OxMQ.

Architecture: How OxMQ Works

OxMQ executes BullMQ’s official 49 battle-tested Lua scripts directly inside Redis. This guarantees:

  • 100% Atomic State Transitions: No race conditions between workers claiming tasks.
  • Polyglot Cross-Talk: A Node.js microservice can push jobs that Java workers consume, and vice-versa.
  • Instant Bull-Board Web UI: Point the open-source Bull-Board dashboard at your Redis instance to inspect queues, pause workers, and review failed jobs with zero Node.js code. 
flowchart TD
    Client["Spring Boot 3 Producer\n@Autowired OxmqQueue"] -->|queue.add / addBulk| Redis[("Redis / KeyDB / Valkey Cluster\n49 BullMQ Lua Scripts")]

    subgraph OxMQCluster ["Distributed OxMQ Worker Pods (Loom Virtual Threads)"]
        W1["Worker Pod 1\n500 Virtual Threads\n(~1 KB Heap/task)"]
        W2["Worker Pod 2\n500 Virtual Threads\n(~1 KB Heap/task)"]
    end

    Redis -->|Atomic Dequeue\nmoveToActive.lua| W1
    Redis -->|Atomic Dequeue\nmoveToActive.lua| W2

    W1 -->|AIMD Dynamic Yield / Cooldown| CloudAPI["External Cloud / Partner API\n(HTTP 429 Sentinel)"]
    W2 -->|AIMD Dynamic Yield / Cooldown| CloudAPI

    Redis -.->|Real-time Metrics| BB["Bull-Board Web UI\nQueue Depths & Latencies"]
    Redis -.->|Prometheus Exporter| Grafana["Grafana Dashboards\nThroughput & JVM Heap"]

1. Project Loom Virtual Threads: The Concurrency Breakthrough

Before Java 21, running 500 concurrent worker threads meant allocating 500 MB to 1 GB of OS stack memory (each platform thread takes ~1 MB). When workers blocked on slow network calls (e.g. Stripe API, OpenAI, or database transactions), underlying OS carrier threads sat idle, wasting CPU cycles.

With Java 21 Project Loom:

  • Virtual Threads are managed by the JVM, consuming only ~1 KB of heap memory each.
  • When an OxMQ worker blocks on network I/O, the JVM unmounts the virtual thread, freeing the carrier thread to execute other jobs.
  • On benchmark tests, OxMQ sustains 800+ concurrent workers on a strictly flat 35 OS threads under realistic 10ms I/O delays.

2. Spring Boot 3 Declarative Setup

Getting started in Spring Boot takes under 2 minutes:

Step 1: Add Dependency 

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.gaurav10610</groupId>
    <artifactId>oxmq-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
    <version>1.7.0</version>
</dependency>

Step 2: Configure application.yml 

oxmq:
  redis:
    uri: redis://localhost:6379
  namespace: billing-service # Multi-tenant context isolation
  worker:
    concurrency: 50           # 50 Virtual Threads on Java 21+

Step 3: Produce Jobs 

@Service
public class PaymentService {

    @Autowired
    private OxmqQueue<PaymentRequest> paymentQueue;

    public void processPayment(String orderId, double amount) {
        // Enqueue with exponential backoff & memory retention
        paymentQueue.add("charge-customer",
            new PaymentRequest(orderId, amount),
            JobOptions.builder()
                .attempts(5)
                .backoff(Backoff.exponential(1000)) // 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s
                .keepJobs(KeepJobs.builder().count(5000).build()) // Prevent Redis RAM bloat
                .build()
        );
    }
}

Step 4: Consume Jobs Declaratively 

@Component
public class PaymentWorker {

    @OxmqListener(queue = "billing-service:charge-customer", concurrency = 50)
    public PaymentResult handlePayment(Job<PaymentRequest> job) throws Exception {
        PaymentRequest req = job.getData();

        // Report progress in real-time to Redis & Bull-Board
        job.updateProgress(50);

        return paymentGateway.charge(req.getOrderId(), req.getAmount());
    }
}

3. Handling Cloud Throttling: The AIMD Adaptive Rate Limiter Plugin

In modern microservices, external APIs (Microsoft Graph, Stripe, Shopify) enforce dynamic quotas and return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header.

OxMQ provides native Enterprise Interceptor Plugins to solve this:

  1. RateLimitSentinelPlugin: Automatically catches HTTP 429, extracts Retry-After, and engages a distributed Redis lockout across all cluster pods. Upcoming jobs defer without burning retry attempts.
  2. AdaptiveRateLimiterPlugin: Uses TCP-style AIMD (Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease) to tune concurrency dynamically:
    • On HTTP 429: Immediately halves capacity (L(t+1) = max(L_min, ⌊L(t) × 0.5⌋)).
    • On clean execution: Additively increases capacity (L(t+1) = min(L_max, L(t) + 25 RUs)). 
@Bean
public JobInterceptor adaptiveRateLimiter(RedisClient redisClient) {
    return AdaptiveRateLimiterPlugin.builder()
        .minLimit(25)
        .maxLimit(250)
        .dampingWindowMs(60_000) // Freeze upgrades during recovery to prevent flapping
        .redisClient(redisClient)
        .build();
}

4. Performance Benchmarks: 10,001-Node DAG Trees

In benchmark stress tests executing massive 10,001-node parent-child DAG dependency trees:

  • Resolution Throughput: 2,645.1 jobs/sec (resolved in 3.78s).
  • Peak Ingestion Rate: ~3,250 nodes/sec (saturating Redis TCP buffer).
  • Redis Memory: Asymptotically stabilizes at ~904 Bytes per node (~8.68 MB for 10,001 jobs).
  • Virtual Thread Overhead: Flat 35 OS carrier threads.

Full benchmark code and reproduction scripts are open-sourced in the repo.

5. Instant Bull-Board Web UI Integration

You can spin up the open-source Bull-Board dashboard in Docker in seconds:

docker run -d -p 3000:3000 \
  -e REDIS_HOST=localhost \
  -e REDIS_PORT=6379 \
  felixmosh/bull-board

Open http://localhost:3000 to immediately inspect queue depths, pause/resume workers, trigger manual retries, and review JSON stack traces.

Conclusion & Resources

If you’re building distributed background processing in Java and want high performance without Kafka-level operational baggage:

  • Project Repository: github.com/gaurav10610/oxmq
  • Official Documentation: gaurav10610.github.io/oxmq
  • Maven Central: io.github.gaurav10610:oxmq:1.7.0
  • License: 100% Free & Open Source (Apache 2.0 / MIT)

⭐ If you find OxMQ helpful, star the project on GitHub and let us know your feedback!

title: Railway alternatives in 2026: six options compared, and when to switch
description:
The best Railway alternatives in 2026 are Ownkube, Render, Fly.io, Northflank, DigitalOcean App Platform and Coolify. Ownkube is the closest swap if your worry is the bill: you load a prepaid wallet, apps draw it down per minute, and credit you do not spend rolls over. Render suits steady services with fixed prices, Fly.io suits apps spread across continents, and Coolify suits people happy to run their own server. Railway is still one of the nicest ways to ship a container, so this post also covers when to stay.

Our picks

If you want Pick
A bounded bill and a full stack (Postgres from $4, a cache from $2) Ownkube
A few steady, busy services at flat prices Render
Low latency for users on several continents Fly.io
Kubernetes power without running Kubernetes Northflank
To run the server yourself Coolify
To stay next to your existing DigitalOcean resources DigitalOcean App Platform

The Railway alternatives at a glance

Prices are approximate list prices from each provider's pricing page, as of October 2026. They move, so read the table as the shape of each model.

Alternative Billing model Smallest service Managed Postgres Best for
Ownkube Prepaid wallet, metered per minute or a flat box per app Metered from cents, or a Spark 1 box at $5 a month Yes, from $4 a month Personal software and small teams who want a bounded bill
Render Workspace plan plus flat instances, postpaid $7 a month (0.5 CPU, 512 MB) Yes, from $6 a month Steady services with predictable line items
Fly.io Per-second machines, postpaid $2.19 a month (shared-cpu-1x, 256 MB) Yes, managed from $38 a month Global, multi-region apps
Northflank Per-second compute, postpaid $2.70 a month (0.1 shared vCPU, 256 MB) Yes Teams that want Kubernetes power without running it
DigitalOcean App Platform Flat container tiers, postpaid $5 a month Yes, from $15.15 a month Teams already on DigitalOcean
Coolify Free software, you pay for the server Whatever your server costs You run it Developers happy to operate the box

Render, Fly.io, Northflank and DigitalOcean keep Railway's postpaid model and change the pricing shape. Coolify moves the platform onto a server you run. Ownkube changes the billing direction: you load a wallet first and usage draws it down. For Render and Northflank in more depth, see Railway vs Render vs Northflank.

Why people look for a Railway alternative

The reasons show up on the invoice or in the roadmap, rarely in the demo.

The postpaid surprise bill. Railway meters usage by the second and bills it after the fact. That works when someone watches the dashboard daily. It bites when a test service runs all month, or a traffic spike meters against a card faster than an alert reaches you.

Credit that resets each month. Railway's plans include a monthly usage allowance scoped to the cycle. A quiet month does not bank credit you can spend later.

The old free plan is gone. What remains is about $1 of credit a month after a one-time trial credit. For a lot of side projects, the free plan was the reason to be there.

The roadmap is moving upmarket. Like most of the category, Railway is building for Pro and Enterprise buyers. That is a healthy move for the company, and it puts the one-developer project further from the center of the roadmap.

The alternatives, one by one

Ownkube

Ownkube is a cloud for personal software. You deploy web apps, workers, cron jobs, Postgres and a Valkey cache onto Ownkube Compute with no cloud account to set up. Connect a GitHub or GitLab repo (a Dockerfile is optional) or pick an app from the Marketplace, and it gets an *.ownkube.app hostname with TLS.

Billing is a prepaid wallet. Pay as you go starts with a $5 top-up; Personal ($5 a month) and Team ($20 a month) load that much credit each month and raise the limits. Usage draws the wallet down per minute, and unused credit rolls over and never expires. Each app either meters CPU and memory on actual use (about $18 per vCPU and $4.50 per GiB a month) or sits on a flat box (Spark from $5, Core from $58). Databases run on boxes from $4 a month plus $0.25 per GB of storage, caches from $2. For the full-stack math, we priced a web app, Postgres and a cache on seven platforms.

Idle web apps, databases and caches can sleep. A sleeping app meters nothing, a sleeping database bills only its storage, and the next request wakes it. You can also set a monthly budget that either emails you or pauses everything.

The trade-offs: two regions today (Mumbai and Germany), no GPU, and custom domains are not on Ownkube Compute yet, so apps use their *.ownkube.app hostname. When an app later has to run inside your own or a customer's AWS account, the same app ships there with no rewrite, and its logs, metrics and health checks come with it.

Render

Render bills a workspace plan (from $0, Pro at $25 a month) plus a flat price per instance. A 1 CPU, 2 GB service is $25 a month whether it idles or not, which is easy to forecast and expensive for mostly idle apps. Its free instances spin down after 15 minutes idle, and free Postgres expires after 30 days. See Render pricing explained.

Fly.io

Fly.io runs Machines in many regions and bills them per second while they run. It is the strongest pick when latency on several continents matters. Managed Postgres starts around $38 a month, which changes the math for small apps. See Fly.io pricing explained.

Northflank

Northflank bills compute per second and offers GPU, job runners and an option for platform teams to run it in their own cloud. It is closer to a Kubernetes control panel than a quick-start platform, which is the point for teams that want that power.

DigitalOcean App Platform

App Platform has flat container tiers from $5 a month and managed databases from about $15. It fits best when your Droplets, Spaces and databases already live on DigitalOcean.

Coolify

Coolify is free, open-source software that turns a server you rent into a small platform. You pay only for the server, and you also patch it, back it up and debug it at 2am. See the self-hosted PaaS comparison.

Railway vs Ownkube

Ownkube Railway
Pricing structure Metered, or a flat box, chosen per app Metered usage, per second
Billing method Prepaid wallet the plan loads and usage drains Plan credit, then postpaid to your card
Credit rollover Unused wallet credit rolls over and never expires Monthly allowance resets each cycle
Entry plan Pay as you go from a $5 top-up; Personal $5 a month $5 plan with $5 of usage
Managed Postgres Database box from $4 a month plus $0.25 per GB Metered like any other service
Idle apps Sleep and meter nothing; databases bill only storage Optional sleep for serverless services
At zero balance Apps pause with data kept, resume on top-up, deleted after 7 days paused Billing continues on the card
Custom domains Not on Compute yet Yes
GPU No Yes

Railway figures are approximate, as of October 2026.

When to stay on Railway

Stay if developer experience is what you value most. Railway's onboarding, templates and project graph are among the best in the category, and Ownkube's dashboard is younger. Stay if you need GPU workloads or a custom domain on every app today. Stay if your bill is steady and someone already watches it.

A quick checklist before you switch

  • Price the whole app (web, worker, Postgres, cache, egress), not the web process alone.
  • Check where your users are and whether two regions cover them.
  • List the domains you serve today and whether an *.ownkube.app hostname works for now.
  • Export the database with pg_dump and test a restore before you cut over.
  • Decide whether you want a hard ceiling on spend or an alert.

FAQ

Is there a Railway free tier?

Railway's free plan is about $1 of credit a month after a one-time trial credit. Ownkube Compute has no free tier: Pay as you go starts with a $5 top-up, and that credit never expires.

Does Railway credit expire?

Railway's plan credit is scoped to the billing cycle and resets. Ownkube's wallet credit rolls over to the next month and never expires. More in does Railway credit roll over or expire.

Railway vs Ownkube cost: which is cheaper?

On compute alone the two are close: Railway's per-second CPU lands near Ownkube's metered CPU, and Ownkube's memory rate is lower. The gap opens with the database and cache. Take a 1 vCPU / 1 GiB web app, a 1 GiB / 10 GB Postgres and a small cache: that lands around $44 to $56 a month on Railway against roughly $27 on Ownkube. Treat those as illustrative (approximate, as of October 2026) and run your own sizes on the homepage calculator.

Can I move from Railway without a Dockerfile?

Yes. Ownkube builds straight from a GitHub or GitLab repo with automatic build, and uses your Dockerfile when there is one.

Reference: for the side-by-side breakdown, see Ownkube vs Railway in the docs.

Where Ownkube fits

Move off Railway when the postpaid meter or the monthly reset is what costs you. Stay if polished onboarding, GPU or custom domains matter most today. Ownkube is built for personal software and small teams: ship in seconds, load a wallet instead of exposing a card, and keep the credit you do not spend. Deploy my first app.

title: Heroku alternatives in 2026: five options compared, with real dyno math
description:
The best Heroku alternatives in 2026 are Ownkube, Render, Railway, Fly.io and DigitalOcean App Platform. Ownkube is the closest swap if you want the Heroku workflow (push a repo, get a URL, add Postgres) at a lower total: the small production stack priced below comes to about $178 a month on Heroku and about $57 on Ownkube. Render is the most Heroku-like in pricing shape, Railway has the fastest setup, and Fly.io suits apps spread across continents. Heroku is still a good place to be for some teams, so this post also covers when to stay.

Our picks

If you want Pick
The Heroku workflow, Postgres and a cache, at a lower full-stack total Ownkube
Fixed instance prices that read like a dyno price list Render
The fastest setup and a big template catalog Railway
Low latency on several continents Fly.io
To stay next to your existing DigitalOcean resources DigitalOcean App Platform
Salesforce integration and the add-on marketplace you already use Stay on Heroku

The Heroku alternatives at a glance

Prices are approximate list prices from each provider's pricing page, as of October 2026.

Alternative Billing model Smallest always-on service Managed Postgres Cache Best for
Ownkube Prepaid wallet, metered per minute or a flat box per app Metered from cents, or a Spark 1 box at $5 a month From $4 a month plus $0.25 per GB Valkey from $2 a month Personal software and small teams
Render Workspace plan plus flat instances $7 a month (0.5 CPU, 512 MB) From $6 a month Key Value from $10 Steady services
Railway Metered per second Whatever it uses, from cents Metered service Metered service Fast setup
Fly.io Machines per second $2.19 a month (256 MB) Managed from $38 a month Bring your own Global apps
DigitalOcean App Platform Flat container tiers $5 a month From $15.15 a month Managed, priced separately DigitalOcean users
Heroku Flat dynos plus add-ons Basic dyno, $7 a month (512 MB) Essential-0 from $5 a month Key-Value Mini $3 Salesforce-centric teams

Why people look for a Heroku alternative

Memory per dollar. A Standard-1X dyno is $25 a month for 512 MB, and Standard-2X is $50 for 1 GB. The same $25 buys 2 GB on Render. Once a team runs a few web dynos and workers, that ratio becomes most of the bill.

There is no free tier. The cheapest dyno is Eco at $5 a month, and it sleeps after 30 minutes of inactivity. Basic at $7 stays up.

Add-ons add up. Logging, search, monitoring and the cache are each a separate add-on with its own price. A real app collects several.

The roadmap is quiet for small teams. New work at Heroku centers on Salesforce and enterprise buyers, which leaves small apps further from the middle of the roadmap.

The alternatives, one by one

Ownkube

Ownkube is a cloud for personal software, and it keeps the part of Heroku people liked. You connect a GitHub or GitLab repo, every push builds and deploys, and the app gets an *.ownkube.app hostname with TLS. A Dockerfile is optional. Web apps, workers, cron jobs, Postgres and a Valkey cache sit side by side on one canvas.

Where Heroku sells add-ons, Ownkube includes the basics: logs, CPU and memory metrics, request rates, alerts and rollback to recent builds come with every app. The Marketplace deploys open-source apps such as n8n, Directus, Metabase and Umami with their database already connected.

Billing is a prepaid wallet. Pay as you go starts with a $5 top-up, Personal ($5 a month) and Team ($20 a month) load credit each month, and unused credit never expires. Apps meter CPU and memory per minute on actual use (about $18 per vCPU and $4.50 per GiB a month), or sit on a flat box like a dyno (Spark from $5, Core from $58). Postgres runs on a database box from $4 a month plus $0.25 per GB of storage, with 7-day backups on paid plans. See managed Postgres pricing across eight providers for how that compares.

The trade-offs: Ownkube Compute runs in two regions (Mumbai and Germany), there is no add-on marketplace for third-party services, and custom domains are not on Compute yet. When an app has to move into your own or a customer's AWS account, the same app ships there with no rewrite, and its logs, metrics and health checks come with it.

Render

Render is the most common Heroku replacement because the pricing shape matches: a flat price per instance, plus a workspace plan. You get more memory per dollar, and Postgres scales in smaller steps. See Render vs Heroku.

Railway

Railway meters usage per second and has excellent onboarding and templates. It is a good fit for many small, mostly idle services. See Railway alternatives for its trade-offs.

Fly.io

Fly.io runs Machines in dozens of regions. It is the pick when latency on several continents matters, and its managed Postgres from about $38 a month is the line to check. See Fly.io pricing explained.

DigitalOcean App Platform

Flat container tiers from $5 a month and managed databases from about $15. A sensible move if your other infrastructure is on DigitalOcean.

A small production stack, priced

Two web processes at 1 GB, one 512 MB worker, a Postgres with 4 GB of memory and 20 GB of data, and a small cache. Heroku and Ownkube figures assume the apps run all month; the Ownkube web and worker lines assume an average of a quarter of a vCPU each, since metered CPU follows actual use.

Line Ownkube Heroku
Web 2 apps, metered, about $18 2 x Standard-2X, $100
Worker Metered, about $4 Standard-1X, $25
Postgres DB 4 box $28 plus 20 GB at $0.25, $33 Standard-0, $50
Cache Cache 0.25 box, $2 Key-Value Mini, $3
Total about $57, plus bandwidth about $178

Heroku figures are approximate, as of October 2026. A busier app moves the Ownkube compute lines up; a Core box fixes them at a flat price if you prefer. Run your own sizes on the homepage calculator.

When to stay on Heroku

Stay if your team runs on Salesforce and uses Heroku Connect or the data integrations. Stay if your app depends on several third-party add-ons that would each need a new home. Stay if the bill is small, stable and nobody has time to migrate, since a working app on a known platform is worth something.

A quick checklist before you switch

  • List every add-on and decide where each one goes.
  • Export Postgres with pg_dump and test the restore on the new platform.
  • Copy config vars into environment variables.
  • Check whether a Procfile process maps to a web app, a worker or a cron job.
  • Keep the Heroku app running until the new one has served real traffic.

FAQ

What is the cheapest Heroku alternative?

For a full stack with Postgres and a cache, Ownkube comes out cheapest in our comparison. For a single tiny process, Fly.io's 256 MB Machine at about $2 a month is hard to beat. Price the whole app, since the database and cache are where totals diverge.

Does Heroku have a free tier in 2026?

No. The cheapest option is the Eco dyno at $5 a month, which sleeps after 30 minutes of inactivity. Ownkube Compute has no free tier either: Pay as you go starts with a $5 top-up, and that credit never expires.

Do I need a Dockerfile to move from Heroku?

No. Ownkube builds from your repo with automatic build, the way Heroku buildpacks did, and uses your Dockerfile if you have one. The migration guide walks through each step.

Reference: for the side-by-side breakdown, see Ownkube vs Heroku in the docs.

Where Ownkube fits

Move off Heroku when the dyno and add-on lines cost more than the workflow is worth to you. Stay when Salesforce integration is the reason you are there. Ownkube is built for personal software and small teams: push a repo, get a URL, run Postgres from $4 a month, and keep the credit you do not spend. Deploy my first app.

title: Railway vs Render vs Northflank in 2026
description:
Railway, Render, and Northflank are the three app platforms we see developers put side by side most often in 2026. All three will take a container or a git repo and give you a running URL, so the demo looks the same on every one. The differences that matter show up a month later: on the invoice, in how the bill is calculated, and in what happens when the project you shipped as a side project turns into something you actually depend on.

This post is a buyer's comparison. We'll cover what each platform is good at, how each one prices, and the buyer each one is really built for. Then we'll be straight about where Ownkube fits and where it doesn't. If you're coming from Heroku specifically, our Heroku alternatives guide covers that migration in more detail.

The short version

  • Railway has the best raw developer experience of the three, and it bills purely on metered usage by the second. The catch is that the metered model is postpaid, so a service you forget about keeps spending, and the old free plan has shrunk to about a dollar of credit a month.
  • Render is the most predictable and the most Heroku-like. You pick a fixed instance size and pay a flat rate for it. The catch is that you pay for that instance whether it's busy or idle, and Render is drifting upmarket (a new $499-a-month Scale plan, SSO, SCIM, HIPAA).
  • Northflank is the most powerful and the only one of the three that can run in your own cloud account. It's also the cheapest on raw CPU. The catch is that it still puts Kubernetes in front of you (its own tagline is "making Kubernetes boring"), and it's built for platform teams more than for one developer with a side project.
  • Ownkube is for personal software and small teams: a prepaid wallet so nothing surprises you, a choice of metered or flat pricing per app, and managed Postgres from $4 a month. It's the least suited of the group if you want a single throwaway server or GPU training runs.

The rest of this post is the detail behind that call.

How they price: the structure behind the number

The prices below move, so treat them as the shape of each model rather than a quote. The structural differences are the part that stays true.

Ownkube Railway Render Northflank
Pricing structure Metered or a flat-price box, your choice per app Metered usage, per second Fixed instance sizes + a workspace plan Metered usage per vCPU-hour (fixed plans optional)
Billing method Prepaid wallet the plan loads and usage drains Plan credit, then postpaid to your card Postpaid to your card Postpaid pay-as-you-go
Entry plan Pay as you go (top up from $5), Personal $5/mo, Team $20/mo $5 plan (includes $5 usage) Free workspace, small instance from about $7/mo Free tier, then pay-as-you-go
Free tier None; Pay as you go starts with a $5 top-up that never expires About $1 of credit a month Real, but web services spin down and a free Postgres expires in 30 days A couple of always-on services
Own cloud AWS today, same app with no rewrite No No Yes, multi-cloud
Egress $0.02/GB (Germany) to $0.13/GB (Mumbai), outbound only About $0.05/GB About $0.15/GB over the included amount About $0.06/GB

Three different philosophies sit in that table. Railway meters everything and bills you after. Render sells you a fixed box and bills you a flat rate for it. Northflank meters like Railway but will also run inside your own cloud account. The thing all three share is that the spend is postpaid: the meter runs, or the box exists, and the invoice arrives at the end.

The four things that actually differ

1. Prepaid wallet vs the surprise invoice

This is the difference most people feel first, because it's the one that shows up as a bad morning. Railway and Northflank are postpaid metered, which is the model behind every "I left a service running and got a four-figure bill" story. Render hides the same problem in a different shape: you pay for the instance while it sleeps, so the waste is quiet instead of loud.

Ownkube runs on a prepaid wallet. Your plan loads credit each month (Personal loads $5, Team loads $20), and usage draws it down per minute. When the balance reaches zero, your apps pause and your data stays put until you top up or the next monthly load arrives. Nothing runs up a card you weren't watching. For personal software and small teams, spending being bounded by a number you chose on purpose is worth more than shaving a cent off the per-hour rate.

2. Metered or flat, and you pick per app

Railway only meters. That's great for an app that idles most of the day and painful for a busy one, because the number keeps moving. Render only does fixed sizes. That's predictable and it means you pay for idle. Both models are fine; the problem is that each platform forces one on you for everything you run.

Ownkube lets you choose per deployment. Run a bursty web app metered so an idle hour costs almost nothing, and put a steady worker on a flat Spark or Core box so its price never moves, in the same project, and flip either one later. Metered CPU and memory both bill on what the app actually uses, and an idle web app can sleep, metering nothing until the next request wakes it. Databases and caches are always a flat box (a database box from $4 a month plus $0.25 per GB of storage, a Valkey cache box from $2), because those hold memory and run continuously either way.

3. Where your app is allowed to run

Railway and Render run your app on their infrastructure. For a weekend project that's fine. When a customer's security team asks for the app inside their own cloud account, neither has an answer.

Northflank can run inside your own cloud, and it's a genuine strength: if multi-cloud is your main requirement, give it a serious look. Its own-cloud story is built for platform teams standing up infrastructure. Ownkube starts you on managed compute with nothing to set up, and when an app has to run in your own or a customer's AWS account, the same app ships there with no rewrite, with its logs, metrics and health checks. GCP and Azure are coming soon.

4. Who the platform is actually built for

This one is easy to miss because it hides in the roadmap rather than the pricing page. Railway shrank its free plan and is pushing toward Pro and Enterprise. Render just added a $499-a-month Scale plan with SSO, SCIM, and HIPAA eligibility. Both are healthy moves for those companies, and both point the same direction: upmarket, toward platform and compliance buyers. Northflank was aimed at platform teams from the start.

The developer shipping a real side project, or the team of three that wants to look like a bigger company without hiring for it, is being quietly left behind by two of the three. That's the buyer Ownkube is built for. "A cloud for personal software" is the whole thesis.

An honest note on raw price

If your only question is the lowest possible dollar-per-vCPU, Ownkube is not always the answer, and we'd rather say so than pretend. Northflank's metered CPU works out cheaper than ours per vCPU. Railway's per-second CPU lands close to ours. Where Ownkube wins on the number is memory: our rate per GiB is well under Railway's, and personal software tends to be memory-heavy and CPU-idle, so the app sits on the memory line most of the day. A typical always-on app of that shape comes in under the equivalent Railway bill once you add both lines together.

But raw rate is the wrong thing to optimize for at this size. The money you actually lose on a small platform is the forgotten service that metered all month, the fixed instance that sat idle, or the migration you have to pay for when your app has to move. Structure beats rate at this scale, which is why we lead with the wallet and the full-stack total instead of a price war.

Now price the whole app

The per-vCPU argument misses the point because nobody ships a bare web process. A real app is a web service plus a managed Postgres plus a cache, and that is where the comparison actually lands. Railway, Render, and Northflank all bill the database and the cache as separate line items with a markup over the raw compute. Ownkube meters the app per minute and runs Postgres and the cache on near-cost boxes (a database box from $4 a month plus $0.25 per GB of storage, a Valkey cache box from $2), so the parts that run all day are the parts where we are cheapest.

Price one representative stack: a small always-on web app (1 vCPU, 1 GiB), a managed Postgres (1 GiB RAM, 10 GB), and a small Redis-compatible cache.

Monthly cost, full stack Ownkube Railway Render Northflank
Web app (1 vCPU / 1 GiB, always on) ~$12 ~$18 to $30 ~$25 ~$18
Managed Postgres (1 GiB / 10 GB) ~$11 ~$18 ~$22 ~$14
Cache (small Redis-compatible) ~$5 ~$5 to $8 ~$10 ~$5
Total ~$27 ~$44 to $56 ~$57 ~$37

Treat the numbers as illustrative: competitor plans are mapped to the nearest real tier from their published pricing as of October 2026, and the metered platforms (Railway and Ownkube) move with how busy the app is, so an idle app costs Ownkube less than the figure above and a CPU-hot one costs more. Northflank stays the closest of the three, which is fair: its metered compute is genuinely cheap. The gap comes from the database and the cache. You can run the same comparison with your own sizes on the homepage calculator.

Where Ownkube fits

Pick Ownkube if the following sound like you:

  • You want to ship an app or a database in seconds with no cloud account to set up, and you want the bill to be a balance you loaded.
  • You want to choose predictable flat pricing or pay-for-what-runs metering per app, instead of having one model forced on everything.
  • You may one day need the same app inside your own or a customer's AWS account, with its logs and metrics, and you want that to be a move rather than a rewrite.
  • You're one developer or a small team, and you'd rather the platform handle TLS, managed Postgres, a Valkey cache, autoscaling, logs, metrics, and zero-downtime rollbacks than hire someone to.

Pick something else if you want a single $5 server for a throwaway project (a self-hosted option is simpler, see our self-hosted PaaS comparison), if you need GPU training runs today (Northflank), or if raw dollar-per-vCPU is the only axis you care about (Northflank again).

Reference: For the side-by-side breakdown, see Ownkube vs Render in the docs.

Closing

Railway, Render, and Northflank are all good platforms, and each earns its place: Railway for developer experience, Render for predictability, Northflank for power and multi-cloud. The gap they share for personal software is the invoice model. Two of them can surprise you, and one makes you pay for idle.

Ownkube is the other shape. Ship in seconds on Ownkube Compute with nothing to set up, load a wallet instead of exposing a card, keep the credit you do not spend, and price the whole app instead of the vCPU. Deploy my first app.

title: Managed Postgres pricing in 2026: eight providers compared
description:
Managed Postgres is priced in more ways than almost any other cloud product. Some providers sell a fixed instance with storage on top, some include storage up to a cap, one meters memory by the hour, and one wraps the database in a $25 platform plan. That makes two quotes hard to compare at a glance. This post prices the same two databases on eight providers, using list prices read from each provider's pricing page on 2026-10-13. The numbers match our managed Postgres cost calculator, where you can try any size.

TL;DR

  • For a small database (1 GB of memory, 10 GB of storage), monthly prices run from $9 on Heroku Essential-1 to about $41 on Fly.io Managed Postgres. Ownkube is $10.50.
  • For a mid-size database (4 GB of memory, 50 GB of storage), the range runs from $40.50 on Ownkube to $296 on Fly.io, which has no plan between 2 GB and 8 GB.
  • Heroku's Essential plans are the cheapest small option, with shared memory and a hard 10 GB storage cap on Essential-1.
  • Neon and Railway bill by usage, so a quiet database costs less than the always-on figures here. Fly.io includes high availability in every plan, which is part of why it costs more.

How do providers price managed Postgres?

Four models show up across the eight providers:

  • Fixed instance plus storage. You pick a memory size and pay a flat monthly price, then pay per GB of disk. Ownkube, Render and Fly.io work this way.
  • Fixed instance with storage included. The plan price covers a set amount of disk. Heroku includes storage up to each plan's cap. DigitalOcean includes the low end of a storage range and charges for more in 10 GiB steps.
  • Usage-based. Neon bills compute in CU-hours (one CU is about 4 GB of memory) plus storage. Railway bills memory and CPU by the minute plus volume storage.
  • Platform plan plus compute. Supabase Pro costs $25 a month and includes $10 of compute credit and 8 GB of disk. Larger compute sizes and extra disk add to that.

The storage rate is easy to skim past. It ranges from $0.125 per GB on Supabase to $0.35 per GB on Neon, which matters more as the database grows.

What does a 1 GB and a 4 GB database cost on each provider?

Provider 1 GB memory, 10 GB storage 4 GB memory, 50 GB storage
Ownkube $10.50 (DB 1) $40.50 (DB 4)
Heroku $9.00 (Essential-1, shared memory) $50.00 (Standard-0)
Railway $13.50 (usage) $49.50 (usage)
DigitalOcean $15.15 (1 GiB node) $60.90 (4 GiB node)
Render $22.00 (0.5c-1g) $70.00 (1c-4g)
Neon $22.85 (Launch, 0.25 CU always on) $94.88 (Launch, 1 CU always on)
Supabase $25.25 (Pro + Micro) $80.25 (Pro + Medium)
Fly.io $40.80 (Basic) $296.00 (Launch, 8 GB)

List prices in USD per month, read from each provider's pricing page on 2026-10-13. Railway assumes 0.1 vCPU of average database CPU; each extra 0.1 vCPU adds about $2. Neon is modelled always on. Single instance unless noted. Taxes and bandwidth excluded.

Why is Heroku the cheapest small database?

Heroku Essential-1 costs $9 a month with 10 GB of storage included, and nothing on this list beats it at that size. The trade is in the plan shape. Essential databases run on shared memory with no stated allocation, and storage is a hard cap: Essential-1 stops at 10 GB, and the next step is Essential-2 at $20 for 32 GB. Above that, Heroku moves to the Standard plans, which start at $50 for 4 GB of memory and jump to $200 for 8 GB.

So Heroku is a good fit for a small database that will stay small. Once you need a guaranteed memory size or more than 32 GB of data, the price steps are large. Our Heroku pricing and alternatives guide covers the rest of the Heroku bill.

What do Neon and Railway cost when the database is quiet?

Less than the table shows. Both bill by usage, and the table prices them as if the database runs all month.

Neon scales compute to zero after a period without queries, so a database that serves a few hours of traffic a day pays for those hours plus storage. The always-on figure ($22.85 at 0.25 CU) is the ceiling for that size. Neon also gives you branching, which makes a copy of the database for each pull request.

Railway bills the memory the database process holds and the CPU it uses. Postgres keeps its buffers in memory, so the memory line tends to stay near the allocation. The CPU line is where a quiet database saves money.

On fixed-instance providers, including Ownkube, the price stays the same whether the database is busy or idle.

Why does Fly.io cost more?

Fly.io Managed Postgres includes high availability, backups and connection pooling on every plan, and the $38 Basic price pays for all three. If you need a standby from day one, compare Fly against the high-availability price elsewhere. On Ownkube, for example, each standby bills as another database box plus its own storage, so a primary with one standby costs about twice the single-instance figure.

The plan ladder also matters at the 4 GB size. Fly's plans go from Starter (2 GB) to Launch (8 GB), so a 4 GB requirement lands on the 8 GB plan.

What does Supabase include for $25?

Supabase Pro is a platform plan: Postgres plus authentication, file storage, realtime and edge functions, with $10 of compute credit that covers the Micro size. If you use those features, the $25 buys much more than a database. If you only use Postgres behind your own API, you are paying for the bundle. Our Supabase alternatives post walks through that decision.

How does Ownkube price Postgres?

Ownkube runs Postgres 17 or 18 on database boxes: a flat monthly price for the memory size, plus storage.

  • Boxes: DB 0.5 at $4, DB 1 at $8, DB 2 at $12, DB 4 at $28, DB 8 at $54 and DB 16 at $104 a month.
  • Storage: $0.25 per GB per month from the first GB, on the volume you provision.
  • Backups: on the Personal and Team plans, storage includes 7-day backups with point-in-time restore. Backups are off by default and you turn them on per database.
  • High availability: a primary plus up to two standbys with automatic failover, on Team. Each standby bills as its own database box, and storage bills per replica.

Pay as you go accounts can run databases up to DB 2, with no backups. Personal costs $5 a month, loads $5 of wallet credit, and unlocks every size and backups. Everything draws one prepaid wallet, and unused credit never expires.

A database on Ownkube sits next to your app in the same region, on the same bill. Our guide to adding a managed Postgres database shows the setup, and the Postgres hosting page covers versions and connection details.

When is another provider the better choice?

  • The database is small and will stay small. Heroku Essential is cheaper than Ownkube at 1 GB, as long as shared memory and a storage cap are fine for you.
  • You want branching or scale to zero. Neon is built for that workflow.
  • You need high availability on the smallest plan. Fly.io includes it from Basic. On Ownkube, standbys are a Team feature.
  • You need a region outside Europe and South Asia. Ownkube databases run in the Mumbai and Germany regions today. DigitalOcean, Render and Fly.io cover far more locations.
  • You use Supabase's auth, storage and realtime. Keep Supabase; replacing all of it is real work.

FAQ

What is the cheapest managed Postgres in 2026?

For a 1 GB database with 10 GB of storage, Heroku Essential-1 at $9 a month, followed by Ownkube at $10.50 and Railway at about $13.50. For a 4 GB database with 50 GB of storage, Ownkube at $40.50, followed by Railway at about $49.50 and Heroku Standard-0 at $50. Prices are list prices checked on 2026-10-13.

Is Neon cheaper than Supabase?

It depends on how often the database is busy. Always on, a 1 GB Neon database costs about $22.85 against $25.25 on Supabase Pro. If the database sleeps for much of the day, Neon drops well below that. Supabase includes auth, storage and realtime in its $25, which Neon does not.

Does managed Postgres pricing include backups?

It varies. On Ownkube, 7-day backups with point-in-time restore are included in the storage price on Personal and Team. Fly.io includes backups on every plan, and Render offers point-in-time recovery on paid instances. Check each provider's retention window, since a day of backups and a week of point-in-time restore are very different safety nets.

How much storage should I plan for?

Plan for your data plus its indexes plus room to grow. On Ownkube and Render you pay per GB provisioned. On Heroku a database that crosses its plan's cap needs a plan change, and DigitalOcean adds storage in 10 GiB steps up to each plan's maximum. Our calculator lets you price any storage size.

Where Ownkube fits

Ownkube is a developer platform that runs your app and its Postgres side by side on one prepaid wallet. Database boxes start at $4 a month, storage is $0.25 per GB with 7-day backups included on Personal and Team, and at the 4 GB size priced here it has the lowest list price of the eight providers. Deploy my first app.

title: Matita 0.4.0: 60 new icons, and one number from sketchy to exact
description:
Matita is a set of pencil-style icons for the web, drawn by code. Lines run a little past their ends, box corners cross, circles overlap where the pen closes. 0.4.0 is out today: 60 new icons (200 to 260) and a new setting called wobble that goes from the full sketchy hand all the way down to exact shapes.

If you haven't seen it, the first post explains the engine: [LINK to the first dev.to article]. The short version is that every icon is a line of plotted shapes, and a small deterministic engine adds the pencil habits, so the same name always draws the same way. This post is about what changed.

60 new icons, mostly what people asked for

When I posted the set, the most concrete request in the comments was a medical and science set. So that is the biggest group: 22 icons.

stethoscope, syringe, pill, test-tube, microscope, thermometer, heart-pulse, medical-cross, bandage, radiation, x-ray, dna, atom, brain, tooth, bone, ambulance, hospital-bed, mars, venus, face-mask, pipette.

The other 38 fill everyday gaps: people and files (user-check, file-check, folder-plus, mail-open), tools, devices and places (wrench, hammer, plug, keyboard, cpu, store, car, plane), and things you reach for all the time (timer, calculator, receipt, qr-code, trophy, percent, shuffle, repeat).

Every glyph still goes through the same checks: a contact sheet at 96 px and at 24 px, a bounds check with the stroke included, and a lint. That caught real things. A fingerprint read as wifi at 24 px, so it is not in the set. Six of the new icons (brain, x-ray, microscope, pipette, wrench, car) were drawn twice because the first version did not read: the first brain looked like a butterfly, so it is now a top view with two hemispheres; the first car could have been a bus, so it has a sloped roof and bigger windows now.

Not in this release: Greek letters, a lab coat and a surgeon. I couldn't draw them clearly at 24 px yet. If you need them, say which ones.

Wobble: one number, from sketchy to exact

The part I wanted most is the setting. The sketchy default is the point of the set, but there are places where you want the same icon calmer, or exactly straight.

import { SketchIcon } from '@matita/icons/react';

<SketchIcon name="wrench" />              // the full hand (default, wobble 1)
<SketchIcon name="wrench" wobble={0.4} /> // a calm hand
<SketchIcon name="wrench" wobble={0} />   // exact shapes

)

Plain JavaScript works too, and so do your own glyphs:

import { drawIcon } from '@matita/icons/engine';
import { toSvg } from '@matita/icons';

toSvg(drawIcon('calendar', { wobble: 0 }), { size: 24 });

How it works

Every habit of the pencil in the engine already had an amount: how far a line overshoots its end, how much it bows, how much a point jitters, how far a ring overlaps. Wobble multiplies those amounts:

const K = wobble, S = v => K === 1 ? v : v * K;
const j = a => (r() * 2 - 1) * a * K;          // jitter
const e1 = S(ov) * (.45 + r() * .9);           // overshoot

Two things follow from that. First, at wobble = 1 every expression multiplies by nothing, so the default draws exactly what 0.3.0 drew. I checked it with a hash over 200 glyphs at 6 seeds before and after the change: identical. Second, the random numbers come from the same stream whatever the wobble is, so 0.5 is the same drawing as 1, just calmer, not a different one. Sliding the number looks like one icon relaxing instead of flickering between takes.

At wobble = 0 the engine takes a different path: it stops sketching and draws the shapes as they are plotted. True lines, circles and ellipses as two arcs, arcs, curves, and closed shapes with square corners. There is no jitter left, so an exact icon does not depend on the seed.

Exact icons are also small. An average exact SVG is about 0.47 KB raw (0.26 KB gzipped), against about 0.82 KB (0.45 KB) for the sketchy one. There are ready-made files for all 260 at @matita/icons/exact/<name>.svg, so you can use them without running any code. The pencil variant also works over exact shapes.

Try the slider on matita.dev: there is a Wobble slider and a Perfect button next to the seed, and the copy snippets follow.

Also new on the site

  • matita.dev/changelog/ says when each icon arrived, and the icon browser shows an "Added in" label with a New badge on the latest ones.
  • matita.dev/roadmap/ is the public list of what is shipped, what is being built and what is next. Targets move.
  • matita.dev/llms.txt and matita.dev/icons.json list every icon with the version it arrived in, so an assistant (or a script) can check that a name exists instead of guessing.

Using it 

npm i @matita/icons

React components, plain SVG files, a script tag, a sprite and the Figma file are all there. It is MIT, free for personal and commercial projects, no signup. The Figma file is at https://www.figma.com/community/file/1688850201209755442 <!-- publish the Figma update to 260 icons before posting -->.

What's next

On the roadmap: search by meaning (type "delete", find the bin) targeted for November, and more science glyphs for December depending on requests. title: KubeVirt does not run on Apple Silicon, so I built KubeSilicon
description:
KubeVirt does not run on a Mac with Apple Silicon. It needs KVM, and macOS has no KVM.

I maintain VirtFoundry, a private cloud operator built on KubeVirt. That means every time I wanted to test something that creates VMs, I needed a Linux server. My M5 Pro could run the cluster, but not the VMs.

So I built KubeSilicon: you declare a SiliconVM object, and a daemon on the Mac boots a Linux ARM64 VM with Apple's Virtualization.framework. Pods in your local cluster reach the VM by IP or DNS name.

Watch the 3.5 minute tutorial video (plays in the README).

From-scratch install, 3.5 minutes: kind cluster, install, first VM, SSH, pod to VM, stop/start.

How it works 

 kind (Docker Desktop VM)              macOS host
 ┌──────────────────────┐              ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ SiliconVM objects    │◄─ API watch ─┤ kubesilicond                        │
 │ (CRD kubesilicon.io) │── status ───►│   download + convert image          │
 │                      │              │   cloud-init ISO                    │
 │ pod ──────── ping/ssh ─────────────►│   Virtualization.framework  ──► VM  │
 └──────────────────────┘              └────────────────────────────────────┘

The daemon runs on the Mac, outside the cluster. It watches SiliconVM objects, starts one detached process per VM, and writes status.phase and status.ip back. It also publishes a headless Service, so demo.default.svc.cluster.local resolves from any pod. The daemon can stop or crash and the VMs keep running.

Three commands 

kind create cluster --name kubesilicon
make install CTX=kind-kubesilicon
kubectl --context kind-kubesilicon apply -f examples/vm.yaml

apiVersion: kubesilicon.io/v1
kind: SiliconVM
metadata: { name: demo }
spec:
  cpu: 2
  memory: 2Gi
  disk:
    source: https://cloud-images.ubuntu.com/releases/noble/release/ubuntu-24.04-server-cloudimg-arm64.img
    size: 10Gi
  cloudInit:
    userData: |
      #cloud-config
      users:
        - name: ubuntu
          sudo: ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL
          ssh_authorized_keys: [ssh-ed25519 AAAA... you@host]

In my tests the VM reaches Running in about 6 seconds once the image is cached, and a busybox pod pings it in 1 to 2 ms.

kind, minikube, and others

The daemon only needs two things: the Kubernetes API of your cluster, and a network path between the pods and the VM (the VMs get a NAT address on the Mac, 192.168.64.x).

  • Tested: kind on Docker Desktop. This is the only setup I have validated.
  • Should work, not tested: minikube, Colima, OrbStack, k3d. Anything where the cluster runs in a VM or container on the same Mac and can reach that NAT range.
  • Does not apply: a cluster in the cloud. The VMs live on your Mac.

If you try another one, tell me what happened. I will add it to the validation notes either way.

How it relates to KubeVirt and VirtFoundry

KubeSilicon is not KubeVirt and does not use its CRDs. It has its own kubesilicon.io/v1 API, shaped like KubeVirt's, because KubeVirt's launcher is built around KVM and QEMU.

KubeVirt KubeSilicon
Hypervisor KVM + QEMU Apple Virtualization.framework
Where VMs run Inside pods, on Linux nodes Processes on the Mac, outside the cluster
Guests Linux, Windows, more Linux ARM64 only
Live migration, hotplug, snapshots Yes No
Runs on Apple Silicon No Yes
Maturity CNCF incubating Early, one Mac, one maintainer

KubeVirt is the right choice on Linux servers. KubeSilicon is for the laptop: development, demos, and CI on your own Mac.

VirtFoundry sits one layer above. It gives you tenants, VPCs, IAM, and a UI on top of the hypervisor. Mapping which KubeVirt resources VirtFoundry uses, so it could drive SiliconVM on a Mac, is the idea I want to explore next. It is not built yet.

An honest note on stability

Early on, guests crashed at random: kernel Oops and SIGILL in 3 of 4 boots with Apple's default disk mode. Switching the disk attachment to cached with fsync gave 0 crashes in 9 boots. The sample is small and I do not know the cause below the framework, so treat it as strong evidence, not proof. The numbers are in docs/validation.md.

Limits today

  • One Mac, one worker. Multiple Macs as nodes is a design goal, not a feature.
  • The Service has no ports. Use the VM IP or ping.
  • A VM whose launcher process died is not restarted automatically.
  • Linux ARM64 guests only. macOS guests are out of scope.
  • API v1 in name only. It will change.

Try it

  • Repo: github.com/Matheus-Thurler/KubeSilicon, Apache-2.0.
  • Needs an Apple Silicon Mac, Go, qemu-img, a running kind cluster, and kubectl.
  • Issues and pull requests are welcome, especially reports from other cluster tools.

title: Cron Job Trigger Approach: Combining Worker-Based Queues for 24-Hour Report Generation
description:
Short answer: let the cron-like scheduler create a small, idempotent sweep command, and let a worker queue own the long-running report job. Keep reservation expiry separate from report rendering. The important boundary is not the timer; it is the retry contract. A repeated trigger must enqueue equivalent work, a repeated worker delivery must not send a second email, and a delayed report must never extend a reservation that has already crossed its fixed hold window.

For a B2B SaaS daily report email, I would set the report's schedule and the reservation's expiry policy independently. A 24-hour hold is a business rule, not a queue timeout. The scheduler can wake every 5 minutes, discover due work, and enqueue a stable job key. Workers can then spend minutes on report generation without making the scheduler wait. This combining approach gives the platform team a tractable SLO: for example, 99.9% of due reports accepted within 10 minutes, with report delivery latency measured separately from trigger latency.

That is the whole boundary.

The incident lesson: the timer was innocent

The bounded failure scenario is familiar: a daily sweep starts while yesterday's report is still rendering. The sweep sees the same account again, submits another job, and a retry after a worker timeout submits a third. Meanwhile, a reservation created for a fixed hold window is still eligible in one code path because the renderer copied an old status into its output. The scheduler did what it was asked to do. The missing invariant was elsewhere.

I treat a trigger as a request to reconcile state, never as proof that work has happened exactly once. That distinction survives process restarts, overlapping sweeps, queue redelivery, and a database failover. The durable record needs a business key such as (account_id, report_date), a reservation version or expiry timestamp, and a send state that can be checked atomically. A queue message is a delivery mechanism; it is not the source of truth.

The preventative path is deliberately boring:

  1. Read due report rows using a bounded query and claim them with a lease or compare-and-swap update.
  2. Enqueue a job containing the immutable report key, not a large snapshot of mutable account data.
  3. Let the worker re-read current state, render, and record an idempotency result before acknowledging delivery.
  4. Retry transient failures with a bounded policy; send permanent validation failures to an operator-visible dead-letter path.

The same rule applies to reservation expiry. A sweep may issue expire(reservation_id, expected_version). If the row is already expired, the operation succeeds as a no-op. If its version changed, the worker reloads and decides again. It does not resurrect the reservation because an earlier message arrived late.

How should I combine a cron job trigger with a worker-based queue?

A scheduler should own time and discovery. It should not own report computation, outbound HTTP calls, or email delivery. Its run duration should be predictable enough to fit inside the trigger interval, and its query should be resumable when the due set is larger than one process can inspect. A cursor, a partition key, or a database-side claim can provide that boundary; a loop that loads every account into memory cannot.

A worker-based queue owns the expensive and failure-prone part. It can apply concurrency limits, back pressure, timeouts, and per-tenant fairness while the scheduler remains available for the next sweep. I would make the job payload small and versioned. These are report-generation tasks, so the payload should identify work rather than attempt to carry every input needed to perform it:

package reports

import "time"

type ReportJob struct {
    AccountID  string
    ReportDate string
    Schema     int
    CreatedAt  time.Time
}

func (j ReportJob) Key() string {
    return j.AccountID + ":" + j.ReportDate
}

The identifier is not a magic guarantee. It must be enforced by a unique constraint or an equivalent atomic state transition. If the queue hands the same job to two workers, both may render; only one should be allowed to commit the send decision. Where the email provider cannot offer an idempotency contract, an outbox record and a send ledger reduce duplicates, but they cannot make an external side effect perfectly transactional with the database. That limitation belongs in the design review.

How do retries avoid extending the hold window?

Retry policy needs two clocks. The first is the business deadline: expires_at for the reservation. The second is the operational deadline: how long the report job may be retried before it becomes an incident or a dead-letter item. Mixing them is how a transient queue outage silently changes business behavior.

At each attempt, the worker should compare the current time with the stored expiry and compare the stored version with the job's expected version. The update must be conditional. In SQL terms, the intended shape is an atomic update with predicates for identity, version, and state; the exact syntax depends on the database. A successful update returns one affected row. Zero rows means the worker must inspect current state, not blindly retry the same mutation.

package reservations

import "context"

type Store interface {
    ExpireIfDue(ctx context.Context, id string, version int64) (bool, error)
}

func Expire(ctx context.Context, store Store, id string, version int64) error {
    changed, err := store.ExpireIfDue(ctx, id, version)
    if err != nil {
        return err // The queue may retry a transient storage failure.
    }
    if !changed {
        // Already expired, cancelled, or updated: all are terminal here.
        return nil
    }
    return nil
}

This advice does not apply unchanged to a job whose effect is intentionally cumulative, such as appending an audit event for every attempt. There, the attempt identifier belongs in the event identity and deduplication rules. It also does not remove the need for an email provider's delivery semantics; it only prevents the platform from treating an at-least-once queue as exactly-once execution.

Build or buy: compare the operational boundary

The choice is less about the word cron and more about which failure handling the team is prepared to operate. A managed scheduler plus a managed queue can reduce control-plane maintenance, while a self-hosted scheduler and queue can offer more direct control over persistence, topology, and upgrade timing. Neither choice supplies the reservation invariant automatically.

Decision area Managed components Self-hosted components
On-call load Less scheduler and broker maintenance; provider limits become part of the design More patching, capacity planning, failover drills, and operational ownership
Retry semantics Must verify documented delivery, visibility, and redelivery behavior Can tune behavior deeply, while owning every edge case and upgrade
Lock-in APIs and event formats may become migration constraints Fewer service-specific dependencies, but more internal platform code
Cost model Often tracks executions, retention, or throughput Tracks infrastructure, people, and the capacity headroom needed for bursts
Team fit Useful when the team needs to focus on report logic and SLOs Useful when queue behavior is a core platform capability

I would reject a design that cannot answer three questions in a review: what happens when the sweep runs twice, what happens when a worker acknowledges after the email call but before recording success, and what happens when a reservation changes between enqueue and execution? The answers should be testable state transitions, not an assumption about a vendor's exactly-once label.

Testing the boundary before production

The highest-value tests are not happy-path timer tests. Freeze time and run two scheduler instances against the same due rows. Deliver one job twice. Kill a worker after the external send and before the database commit. Advance the clock beyond expires_at, then deliver a job created before expiry. Verify that the reservation remains terminal and that the report ledger records one logical send decision.

Load tests should vary the due-set size, worker concurrency, report duration, and retry delay independently. A capacity plan that uses only average report duration will fail during the morning burst; reserve headroom for the longest permitted retry backlog and for database claim contention. Alert on age of the oldest due item, queue depth, retry rate, dead-letter count, duplicate-send conflicts, and the percentage of reservations whose expiry transition misses its SLO.

The practical result is a narrow, defensible architecture: a short periodic reconciliation creates durable work, workers perform slow computation, and every state-changing operation is conditional and repeatable. The scheduler provides time. The database provides truth. The queue provides delivery attempts. Keeping those responsibilities separate is what makes a daily report system recoverable when the boring failures arrive. It also makes capacity planning concrete: the trigger path needs headroom for due-row discovery, while the worker path needs headroom for report duration, retries, and the largest expected burst, and those are different resources with different alerts.

The failure is visible sooner.

Sources

  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html
  • https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/
