title: I let a 4B model watch 321 stock clips overnight so I never have to scroll again
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 3: Slow and Steady.

What I Built

I make short videos, and all of them draw from one shared folder of stock clips: 321 files from Pixabay and Pexels, 7.6 GB, about two and a half hours of footage. Every file is named with a number. pixabay/4926.mp4 could be anything.

There is a catalog next to the files, with tags, but the tags are the search queries I typed when I downloaded each clip. They tell me what I was looking for that day, not what the clip contains. So when I need "a single candle on a dark background", the honest method is to open the folder and scrub through thumbnails. I have done that more times than I want to admit.

nightshelf is a small command-line tool that looks at the library once, unattended, and writes down what is in every clip. For each video it pulls three evenly spaced frames, asks Gemma 3 (the 4B vision model, running locally through Ollama) to describe them, embeds the description, and stores everything in a SQLite file. After that I just type what I want:

$ nightshelf search "a candle flame" --limit 3
1. pixabay/4926   score 0.0328  sim 0.83  10.6s
   A single candle burns brightly against a dark background, casting a warm, flickering light…
   status: prayers-nightwatch=approved | used: prayers-nightwatch
2. pixabay/4933   score 0.0320  sim 0.80  33.1s
   A single candle with a flickering flame burns brightly against a dark background…
3. pixabay/51749  score 0.0320  sim 0.82  20.0s
   A single lit candle burns brightly in a dark room, casting a warm glow against a black background…

The tool also reads my existing catalog (read-only, it never writes to it), so it knows which clips I already approved, rejected, or used for a given project. --status unused means "something I have not used yet and did not reject".

The real run on my library: 321 clips described and embedded, 0 failures, 2,874 seconds in total, 8.9 seconds per clip, on my Mac, with no GPU server involved.

Demo

The video (about 80 seconds, a real terminal on my real library) shows the overnight run with its one-line-per-clip progress, the stats of the full run, a few searches, and an export of a shortlist.

These are real terminal outputs from my library (the path of my clip folder is masked):

Code

Deval123 / nightshelf

Overnight, local video-clip librarian: an open-weight vision model describes your stock clips so you can search them by meaning.

nightshelf

Overnight indexer that makes a local video clip library searchable by meaning.

A stock-clip library grows until nobody remembers what is in it, and file names like clip_0412.mp4 say nothing. nightshelf looks at a few frames of every clip with an open-weight vision model running on your own machine, writes a short description, stores it in a local SQLite database, and lets you search the library from the command line ("rainy city at night", "someone walking a dog on a beach"). Nothing leaves your network, the library is only ever read and the whole library is processed unattended, overnight.

How it works

flowchart LR
    L[("Clip library<br/>read-only")] --> S["scan + sync<br/>(new / changed / removed)"]
    C["catalog.json<br/>read-only"] -. "filters, status, uses" .-> Q
    S --> F["ffmpeg<br/>N frames per clip"]
    F --> V["Vision model<br/>(Ollama)"]
    V --> D[("SQLite index<br/>descriptions + FTS5")]
    D --> E["Embedding model<br/>(Ollama)"]
    E --> D
    D --> Q["search / export<br/>full-text
…
View on GitHub

Apache 2.0, Java 21, no framework, 169 tests. The README has a quick start (jar or Docker), every command, and a configuration table.

How I Built It

The pipeline is deliberately boring:

clip library (read-only) → scan + sync → ffmpeg (3 frames) → Gemma 3 via Ollama
      → SQLite (descriptions + FTS5) → embeddings → search / export

One structured answer per clip. I ask Gemma for JSON matching a schema: a description of at most two sentences, a list of subjects, a setting, a time of day (day, night, dusk, dawn, unknown) and a mood. Temperature is 0, and 0.3 on the retry after a malformed answer, so a retry does not repeat the same bad output. Everything the model returns is treated as untrusted: the JSON is validated, lengths are capped, control and bidirectional characters are stripped, and the prompt tells the model that any text visible in a frame is content to describe, never an instruction.

Hybrid search without a vector database. 321 vectors do not need a server. Search runs SQLite FTS5 for the words and a plain cosine similarity in Java over the embeddings (nomic-embed-text, also through Ollama), then merges the two rankings with reciprocal rank fusion (k = 60). If Ollama is not reachable at search time, it falls back to full-text only and says so in one line.

SQLite, on purpose. One machine, one writer, a few hundred rows. The database uses WAL, foreign keys and versioned migrations, every statement is parameterized, and it refuses to open on a network filesystem, because SQLite locking on SMB or NFS is not something I want to trust. The clip library is mounted read-only, in Docker as well.

Slow and steady, as a design rule. The indexer handles one clip at a time and commits each result in its own transaction. A SIGTERM finishes the current clip, prints a summary and exits cleanly. A test simulates a hard kill and checks that the next run redoes only the unfinished clips. Ten failures in a row stop the run, because Ollama is probably down. And if the library drive is unmounted, the scan sees zero clips, so a guard refuses to flag more than half of the index as removed. An unplugged disk should never look like a deletion.

Things that did not work the first time. Almost every description began with "The video shows…". A sentence in the prompt reduced it, a display-time cleanup removed the rest, and the stored text and embeddings are untouched. The query "spring flowers in daylight" matched nearly everything because of the word "in", so stop words are now removed from the full-text query. User text is always split into words and quoted before it reaches FTS5, so operators like NEAR or * are plain text.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

My library is not secret, but it is mine: 7.6 GB, plus a record of every choice I made about it. A hosted vision API would mean sending frames from every clip to someone else's servers, and paying again every time I add a clip.

With open weights, none of that applies:

  • Nothing leaves the machine. Frames and descriptions go to a model on localhost. The README says plainly that traffic to Ollama is unencrypted http, so it must stay on localhost, a trusted LAN, or an SSH tunnel.
  • No per-image cost, no quota. Indexing 321 clips cost electricity and about 48 minutes of waiting.
  • It works offline once two models are pulled.
  • The model is pinned. The index was built with gemma3:4b. Nobody can change it under me, and swapping models is two environment variables (VISION_MODEL, EMBED_MODEL).

There is a real trade-off: a larger hosted model would probably describe some clips better. For this job, a 4B model that I can run unattended on my own computer was enough, and I would rather have an index I fully control.

The Lazy Payoff

I waited once, for 48 minutes, while doing something else. Now finding a clip takes a second instead of a scroll through hundreds of thumbnails, and export turns a query into a shortlist file (Markdown, CSV or JSON) that I can keep next to a project. The tool never copies or moves a clip.

It has limits, and they are worth stating. Concrete visual queries work well: "a candle flame" returns candles, with similarity between 0.80 and 0.83 for the top three. Abstract ones do not: "hope after a storm" returned wind turbines, raindrops on a window and a rainy night street, with similarity between 0.58 and 0.63, and I would not trust it. Three frames per clip can also miss fast action. For my use, the approach is good enough, and I know where it stops.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma. Gemma 3 (4B, vision) runs locally through Ollama and produces the description of each of the 321 clips: structured output with a JSON schema, a retry strategy, and sanitized results. It is not fine-tuned.

title: An agent ships the forward migration and forgets the way back
description:
An agent writes the forward migration, it applies cleanly on the branch, and the PR body reads 'schema updated.' What it leaves out: how the change reverses, what happens to existing rows, and how you prove a read after the write still works. A migration that only runs one direction is a draft, not a finished change.

A forward-applied migration is not a done migration

The green checks that cover the code branch usually run against an empty or seeded development database, so 'applies cleanly' proves almost nothing about production. A column added, a type widened, a value moved from one field to another: the forward path is one line in the migration file. The operational risk lives in what the forward file cannot show, which is old rows, partial deployments, and the moment you need to back out.

The three missing pieces

  • A rollback that runs. The down migration must be tested, not just written. A column-drop rollback that forgets to restore the moved data is worse than no rollback, because it sounds reversible while destroying the record.
  • A backfill for existing rows. New columns filled by a default on new writes leave old rows stale. The backfill window, batch size, and lock behavior belong in the PR, not discovered at 2 a.m.
  • A read-after-write check. After the change, prove a write lands where expected and a read returns it, against the same shape production uses. This catches the half-migrated state where some rows carry the new value and others still carry the old one.

Make the agent list both directions before coding

Give the task a fixed block: forward steps, reverse steps, backfill strategy, and the check that proves success. The agent tends to write forward because that is the requested feature; asking for the down path up front forces it to consider what it is moving before it destroys the original location. If the rollback cannot preserve data, that limitation belongs in the PR rather than hiding behind 'no rollback needed.'

The cheap reviewer check

Before merging, ask two things: what command reverses this, and what happens to a row written before the deploy. If the agent cannot answer both without inventing them on the spot, the change was planned as a one-way trip. Reversible or not, the PR should state the assumption and the fallback plainly.

When the changed column also feeds an API response field, keep the contract spec moving with the migration instead of letting the backend drift ahead of the documented shape. That local-first spec workflow is what we built into Powerduck, where the spec stays the source of truth rather than a stale markdown note nobody reopens.

Done for a migration means the operator can apply, reverse, fill, and verify. It does not mean the forward file exists.

title: SQL Deep Dive: Window Functions, Joins, CTEs, and Subqueries
description:
Introduction

This article covers four SQL concepts: window functions, joins, common table expressions (CTEs) and subqueries. Window functions let you rank rows, calculate running totals and compare a row to the ones around it without losing any data. Joins bring information from different tables together. CTEs break a long query into small named steps, and subqueries let one query use the result of another.

This article will use a hospital dataset which contains various tables. For each concept I explain what it does, show a query on that data and give the expected result.

1. Window Functions

A window function calculates across a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing them. Window function keeps every row and attaches the result to each one. Thus, for each row, SQL opens a "window" that shows some other rows. It looks through that window, calculates something, and writes the answer next to the row.

a. Ranking Functions

Ranking functions give each row a position inside its group. They include, ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK(), and differ only in how they handle ties that is rows with equal values.

  • ROW_NUMBER()-Ignores ties. Gives every row a unique number
  • RANK()-Tied rows get the same rank. The next rank skips numbers
  • DENSE_RANK()-Tied rows get the same rank. The next rank has no gaps

Based on the hospital dataset, we rank the medicine department based on the highest satisfaction score from highest as follows:

The result will be:

Visit_id 1002 and 1029 both scored 4.1, so both get rank 2.
After that, RANK jumps to 4 because rank 3 was "used up" by the tie. DENSE_RANK simply moves to 3.
ROW_NUMBER never repeats. When scores tie, it uses visit_id to decide the order. That is why visit_id was added to the ORDER BY.

NTILE(n)

NTILE(n) splits the ordered rows into n buckets of roughly equal size and tells which bucket each row is in. It is useful for quartiles (NTILE(4)) as well as percentiles.
Based on the hospital dataset, split the cardiology visits into groups of 4 based on the bill size, from highest bill to lowest bill:

The result will be:


This translates that 9 rows are divided by 4 buckets and leaves 1 extra row. The extra row goes to the first bucket, so bucket 1 has 3 rows and the other buckets have 2 each. Bucket 1 holds the most expensive visits.

b. Offset Functions

Offset functions lets a row look at another row in the same group: the one before, the one after, the first, or the last.
LAG() and LEAD()
LAG(column, offset, default) looks backward (at an earlier row).
LEAD(column, offset, default) looks forward (at a later row).

The offset is how many rows to move. It is 1 if left out. The default is the value to show when there is no such row otherwise, it is NULL.

In the hospital dataset, for instance patients came back for a second visit of patient IDs 1, 2, and 5. To get how their bills changed and how many days passed between visits is as follows:

The result will be:

Partition by patient_id means each patient is handled separately, so no one patient is compared to another.
A patient's first visit has no earlier visit, so previous_bill is null. Their last visit has no later visit, so next_bill is null.

3. Joins

A join matches rows from two tables using a condition, usually a primary key on one side and a foreign key on the other:
Below is the syntax used for joins:

select column
from table 1 
join kind table 2 
on table 1.common_column=table 2.common_column;

a. Inner Join

Inner Join - returns only the rows with matches in both tables
For instance, show the patients and the doctor assigned to them

The result will provide the doctors assigned to the respective patients. The 'f' and 'd' are aliases that save typing, ease of referencing and make it clear which table each column comes from.

b. Full Join

Full join returns everything from both/all tables regardless whether there is a match or not. Where rows match, they are combined. Where a row has no match, the other side is filled with null.

It basically returns the left join result and the right join result in one query.


The result will provide a list of all the doctors and the procedures done

c. Left Join

Left Join - returns every record from the left join, which is the table written before the join and matches on the right.
For instance, list all doctors and their respective departments

The result will provide all doctors and their respective departments

d. Right Join

Right Join - Returns every record from the right table and matches to the left
For instance, list all doctors and their respective departments


The result will provide all doctors and their respective departments

e. Cross Join

Cross Join - gives every possible combination. It pairs every row of the first table with every row of the second.

No need for the on clause. The only join where no common column is needed

For instance, in the hospital dataset suppose we want a show visit counts for every department.


The result will provide the following visits of each department

f. Natural Join

Natural Join joins tables with the same column names. It looks at both tables, finds every column that has the same name, and joins on all of them. It does not need to have an ON condition.
For instance, suppose we find the visits with their department name and respective bill costs


The result of the query will be

4. Subqueries

A subquery is a query written inside another query. It sits in parentheses, and the outer query uses its result.
Depending on where the subqueries are written there are different types of subqueries

  • where - lets the outer query filter rows using the answer of another query.
  • having - filters aggregated rows
  • select - generates a calculated column

For instance, the visits that costs more than the average bill:

select visit_id, total_bill_kes
from facts_visits 
where total_bill_kes > (select avg(total_bill_kes) from facts_visits);

The result generated will be

Subqueries can either be correlated or non-correlated

  • Correlated - subquery that cannot be executed without the main query
  • Non-correlated - subquery that can be executed without the main query. For instance 
(select avg(total_bill_kes)

Subquery Categories

Scalar - returns a single value
Table - returns multiple rows and multiple columns
Column - returns 1 column, multiple rows
Rows - returns 1 row, multiple columns

5. Common Table Expressions (CTEs)

A Common Table Expression or CTE, is a named temporary result that is defined at the top of a query and then used like a table in the rest of that query. It is a way to give a name to a step in the query.
A CTE starts with the word with
Think of it as giving a name to a subquery. For instance, which departments earned more than 100,000.
This first version depicts the query with a subquery, that is a step inside another query

select d.department_name, f.total_revenue
from(select department_id, sum(total_bill_kes) as total_revenue
from facts_visits f
group by department_id) as f
join departments d 
on d.department_id = f.department_id
where f.total_revenue > 100000
order by f.total_revenue desc;

This second version depicts a query with a CTE

with dept_revenue as 
(select department_id, sum(total_bill_kes) as total_revenue
from facts_visits f
group by department_id)
select d.department_name, f. total_revenue
from dept_revenue f
join departments d 
on d.department_id = f.department_id
where f.total_revenue > 100000
order by f.total_revenue desc;

The result for both queries will be as follows:

Conclusion

Window functions, joins, subqueries and CTEs each solve a different problem. Window functions rank rows and calculate running totals without losing any data. Joins combine tables, and the join type decides what happens to rows with no match. Subqueries let one query use the result of another, and CTEs turn long queries into named steps that are easy to read.

title: Closing a Modal Is Not One Operation
description:
Once open() returns a Promise, modal lifecycle design becomes observable API behavior: resolve, dismiss, remove, animate, and tear down are no longer interchangeable.

A promise-based modal API looks wonderfully small:

const result = await modal.open(someModal, input);

The complexity is simply hidden below the call site.

What happens when:

  • the modal completes successfully?
  • the modal explicitly rejects because the operation failed?
  • the user presses Escape?
  • the caller dismisses the modal programmatically?
  • all modals are closed at once?
  • the provider unmounts?
  • the UI needs a 200 ms exit animation?
  • two different pieces of code try to settle the same modal?

Once an interaction is represented by a Promise, these are not merely rendering details.

They are part of the API contract.

close(result) and dismiss() should mean different things

Suppose a rename modal has this result:

type RenameResult =
  | {
      status: "renamed";
      name: string;
    }
  | {
      status: "cancelled";
    };

The modal can explicitly complete with:

close({
  status: "renamed",
  name,
});

or:

close({
  status: "cancelled",
});

Both values are valid domain results.

From the caller's point of view:

const result = await modal.open(renameModal, input);

resolves with a RenameResult.

But now imagine the caller does this:

const handle = modal.open(renameModal, input);

handle.dismiss();

Should that resolve to:

{ status: "cancelled" }

automatically?

Not necessarily.

The library cannot assume that every modal has a cancelled variant.

Even if it does, a programmatic lifecycle interruption may mean something different from the user intentionally selecting "Cancel."

That suggests an important separation:

close(result)
    ↓
successful completion with TResult


dismiss()
    ↓
lifecycle interruption

In react-modal-manager, dismissal rejects the pending operation with ModalDismissError.

Why lifecycle dismissal belongs on the rejection channel

Consider a modal that must return a selected account:

type AccountPickerResult = {
  accountId: string;
};

There is no natural fake value to return if the modal disappears.

Resolving with undefined weakens the type:

Promise<AccountPickerResult | undefined>

Adding a cancellation variant changes the domain contract even if cancellation is not conceptually a result.

Silently leaving the Promise pending is worse.

Rejection provides a separate channel:

try {
  const result = await modal.open(accountPickerModal, input);

  await selectAccount(result.accountId);
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof ModalDismissError) {
    return; // lifecycle interruption
  }

  throw error;
}

The successful path stays:

Promise<TResult>

while interruption remains explicit.

reject(error) is a third semantic channel

Once close(result) and dismiss() are separate, there is still another case:

the modal operation itself failed.

For that, a lifecycle API can expose:

reject(error);

This is different from both successful completion and abandonment:

close(result)
    -> resolve with TResult

reject(error)
    -> reject because the operation failed

dismiss(reason)
    -> reject because the interaction was abandoned

In react-modal-manager, non-Error rejection values are normalized to ModalRejectError, while lifecycle dismissal uses ModalDismissError.

The distinction matters because callers may want to react differently:

try {
  const result = await modal.open(importModal, input);
  await processImportResult(result);
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof ModalDismissError) {
    return;
  }

  reportFailure(error);
}

A single "close" operation cannot express all three semantics without smuggling meaning into arbitrary result values.

Domain cancellation can still be a valid result

This does not mean "Cancel" must always reject.

If cancellation is a meaningful outcome of the interaction, model it:

type RenameResult =
  | {
      status: "renamed";
      name: string;
    }
  | {
      status: "cancelled";
    };

Then the Cancel button can call:

close({
  status: "cancelled",
});

The key distinction is ownership of the decision.

The modal intentionally produced a valid result.

That is different from the lifecycle being interrupted externally.

The built-in confirm() is a good example.

Its normal UI actions resolve with typed results:

{ confirmed: true }
{ confirmed: false, reason: "cancel" }
{ confirmed: false, reason: "dismiss" }

So pressing Escape in the built-in confirmation UI resolves as:

{
  confirmed: false,
  reason: "dismiss",
}

That UI action intentionally calls close(result).

By contrast, these manager-level operations reject with ModalDismissError:

handle.dismiss();
modal.dismiss(instanceId);
modal.closeAll();

Provider teardown does the same for still-pending operations.

The important rule is therefore not:

Escape always rejects.

It is:

a component may model a user action as a valid domain result, while lifecycle-level interruption remains a rejection.

A Promise can still expose instance control

Sometimes awaiting the result is enough:

const result = await modal.open(renameModal, input);

Sometimes the caller needs to control the specific instance later.

For example:

const handle = modal.open(progressModal, {
  title: "Generating report...",
});

// Observe the handle's rejection before programmatic dismissal.
const completion = handle.catch((error: unknown) => {
  if (!(error instanceof ModalDismissError)) {
    reportFailure(error);
  }
});

try {
  await generateReport();
} finally {
  handle.dismiss();
  await completion;
}

A useful API can therefore return a Promise-like handle:

const handle = modal.open(renameModal, input);

console.log(handle.instanceId);

try {
  // The caller may dismiss this instance from another event.
  const result = await handle;
  processRenameResult(result);
} catch (error) {
  if (!(error instanceof ModalDismissError)) {
    throw error;
  }
}

// Elsewhere, while the handle is still pending:
// handle.dismiss();

This preserves the ergonomic async API while still exposing instance-level lifecycle control.

Conceptually:

interface ModalHandle<TResult>
  extends Promise<TResult> {
  readonly instanceId: string;
  dismiss(): void;
}

The exact implementation can vary, but the design goal is useful:

do not force the caller to choose between awaiting the operation and controlling its instance.

Every instance gets one logical settlement

Promise settlement is idempotent at the JavaScript level, but lifecycle state still needs clear rules.

Imagine:

  1. the user clicks "Save";
  2. close(result) runs;
  3. an Escape event fires during the same frame;
  4. dismiss() also runs.

The abstraction must guarantee a single logical outcome.

A modal instance should move from pending to settled once.

Conceptually:

          ┌─ resolve(result)
pending ──┤
          └─ reject(dismissal)

after settlement:
additional settlement attempts do nothing

This matters because callbacks around settlement can affect more than the Promise:

  • removing state;
  • starting animations;
  • releasing registry references;
  • restoring focus;
  • logging;
  • triggering caller code.

The lifecycle therefore needs its own once-only transition, not merely reliance on JavaScript's Promise behavior.

In the current design, the first close(result), reject(error), or dismiss(reason) wins. Later settlement attempts for that instance are ignored.

"Promises ignore the second resolve" is not a complete lifecycle design.

Promise settlement and visual removal run on different clocks

Exit animation introduces another subtlety.

Suppose the user clicks Save.

The application should be able to continue immediately:

const result = await modal.open(...);

navigateToNextStep(result);

But visually, the modal may need to fade out for 150 ms.

If Promise settlement waits for the animation, application logic becomes coupled to presentation timing.

If the modal disappears immediately, the animation cannot run.

The solution is to separate:

logical settlement

from:

visual removal

For example:

open
  ↓
close(result)
  ↓
Promise resolves immediately
  ↓
status = "closing"
  ↓
exit transition
  ↓
instance removed

In react-modal-manager, closeDelayMs supports this separation.

The caller gets the result without waiting for CSS.

The renderer gets time to animate the closing instance.

Expose semantic status; let the renderer decide the animation

A renderer can use lifecycle status:

function AppModalRenderer({
  children,
  modal,
}: ModalRendererProps) {
  return (
    <div
      data-status={modal.status}
      className="modal-shell"
    >
      {children}
    </div>
  );
}

Then CSS can react to:

.modal-shell[data-status="closing"] {
  opacity: 0;
}

The modal manager does not need to know which animation library is used.

It only needs to expose enough lifecycle information for the presentation layer to respond.

This is a useful boundary:

manager:
  semantic lifecycle

renderer:
  visual lifecycle

Provider teardown must terminate pending operations

Provider-owned state creates another lifecycle edge case.

Consider:

<ModalProvider>
  <Feature />
</ModalProvider>

Feature opens a modal:

const pending = modal.open(someModal, input);

Then the entire provider unmounts before the modal completes.

What should happen to pending?

Leaving it unresolved would create a dangling Promise.

Resolving it with a fabricated result would violate the result contract.

A lifecycle dismissal is the natural outcome.

In the current react-modal-manager contract, provider teardown rejects pending operations with ModalDismissError.

The same principle applies to operations such as closing all active instances.

Every pending operation must have a defined termination path.

Caller unmount is not provider unmount

A subtler case appears when the component that opened a modal disappears while the provider remains mounted.

Consider:

<ModalProvider>
  <Page />
</ModalProvider>

Page opens a modal, then Page unmounts because navigation changes.

Should the modal be dismissed automatically?

Not necessarily.

The provider owns the lifecycle, so the modal can legitimately outlive the component that initiated it.

That is useful for operations whose lifetime belongs to a broader application scope.

But sometimes the caller does own the interaction.

In that case, cleanup should be explicit.

And if the caller can launch more than one modal concurrently, tracking only the latest handle is not enough.

function RenameLauncher() {
  const modal = useModalManager();
  const pending = useRef(
    new Set<ModalHandle<RenameReportResult>>(),
  );

  useEffect(() => {
    const handles = pending.current;

    return () => {
      for (const handle of handles) {
        handle.dismiss();
      }

      handles.clear();
    };
  }, []);

  async function handleClick() {
    const handle = modal.open(renameReportModal, {
      reportId: "report-1",
      currentName: "Draft",
    });

    pending.current.add(handle);

    try {
      const result = await handle;

      if (result.status === "renamed") {
        await renameReport({
          reportId: "report-1",
          name: result.name,
        });
      }
    } catch (error) {
      if (!(error instanceof ModalDismissError)) {
        throw error;
      }
    } finally {
      pending.current.delete(handle);
    }
  }

  return <button onClick={handleClick}>Rename</button>;
}

Why a Set?

Because this is incorrect when repeated launches are possible:

pending.current = modal.open(...);

A second click replaces the first handle. Cleanup would dismiss only the latest modal and leave the earlier Promise pending.

Tracking every active handle makes the ownership policy match the actual concurrency model.

This is an important architectural point:

caller cleanup is optional policy, not hidden library behavior.

If the operation should survive the caller, do not dismiss it in caller cleanup. If the caller owns the operation, track and terminate every pending instance it created.

Dismiss an instance, not merely a modal definition

Once multiple instances can exist, "close modal X" is not always precise enough.

The same modal definition might be opened twice:

const first = modal.open(renameModal, firstInput);
const second = modal.open(renameModal, secondInput);

A definition identifies a kind of modal.

It does not necessarily identify an active instance.

That is why an instance identifier matters:

first.instanceId;
second.instanceId;

The handle can remain bound to exactly the lifecycle that created it:

first.dismiss();

This avoids ambiguity and becomes especially useful for:

  • stacked modals;
  • concurrent operations;
  • progress dialogs;
  • timeout-driven dismissal;
  • external commands.

Bridge design-system close events into lifecycle semantics

A design-system dialog can have its own closing behavior.

For example, a user clicks an overlay and the underlying dialog component reports:

onOpenChange(false)

That needs to reach the lifecycle manager.

A renderer can bridge the event:

function ShadcnRenderer({
  children,
  modal,
}: ModalRendererProps) {
  const manager = useModalManager();

  return (
    <Dialog
      open={modal.status === "open"}
      onOpenChange={(open) => {
        if (!open) {
          manager.dismiss(modal.instanceId);
        }
      }}
    >
      <DialogContent>
        {children}
      </DialogContent>
    </Dialog>
  );
}

The design system detects presentation-level dismissal.

The modal manager converts that event into lifecycle semantics.

The pending Promise then terminates consistently with other dismissal paths.

Integration note: This is a conceptual renderer sketch, not a drop-in shadcn/ui integration. A provider-wide renderer wraps both custom modals and built-in confirmation content. If a child already renders its own <Dialog> or <dialog>, wrapping it in DialogContent can create nested dialog semantics and conflicting focus management. Use content-only modal components with this renderer and supply a compatible custom confirmModal when needed. The renderer also needs an explicit strategy for Radix exit animations and closeDelayMs; closing immediately via open={false} does not by itself prove that the visual exit matches the manager's removal delay.

Strict Mode changes how teardown must be implemented

React 18 and 19 development Strict Mode can replay effects.

That creates a trap for provider-owned lifecycle state.

A naïve cleanup implementation might interpret the development-only effect cleanup as final provider disposal and reject every pending modal — even though React immediately remounts the same owner as part of replay.

The lifecycle therefore needs to distinguish:

temporary Strict Mode cleanup

from:

final provider disposal

The current implementation defers final teardown and cancels it when the same lifecycle owner immediately remounts.

This is not merely a test convenience. It preserves the public guarantee that provider teardown terminates pending work without making development Strict Mode behave differently from a real mounted application.

The larger lesson is useful beyond modals:

when asynchronous resources are owned by a React provider, effect cleanup is not always equivalent to permanent ownership loss.

If callers can observe it, it is part of the API

It is tempting to treat all of this as internal implementation detail.

But callers observe the consequences.

They observe whether:

await modal.open(...)

resolves, rejects, or never settles.

They observe whether programmatic dismissal is possible.

They observe whether a closing animation delays business logic.

They observe what happens when the owning provider disappears.

Therefore lifecycle semantics are part of the contract, even if internal data structures are not.

Think in two state machines

A simplified model could look like:

                  close(result)
               ┌───────────────► settled: resolved
               │
open ─► pending
               │
               └───────────────► settled: rejected
                    dismiss()


visual state:

open
  ↓
closing   (optional)
  ↓
removed

The two models interact, but they answer different questions.

Promise state answers:

Has the operation completed?

Visual state answers:

Should the modal still be rendered?

That separation is what makes exit animations possible without delaying application control flow.

Final thoughts

The first version of a promise-based modal API often focuses on this:

const result = await openModal();

The difficult part comes next.

You have to define:

  • what counts as a valid result;
  • what counts as operational failure;
  • what counts as lifecycle dismissal;
  • whether a particular Cancel/Escape action resolves or rejects;
  • who can dismiss an instance;
  • whether the caller or provider owns its lifetime;
  • how concurrent instances are tracked;
  • what provider teardown does;
  • how Strict Mode replay interacts with cleanup;
  • whether promises settle before or after exit animations;
  • how repeated settlement attempts are handled.

Those decisions determine whether the abstraction remains predictable under real application pressure.

A modal is not finished merely because it disappeared from the screen.

Its operation and its visual instance each have a lifecycle.

Once those lifecycles are designed separately, await modal.open(...) can stay simple without making the underlying semantics vague.

If you like the approach, drop a ⭐️ on the GitHub repo and let me know what you think in the comments! 👇

title: Next.js Security Update October 2026: Patch the use cache RCE, SVG sharp RCE and Server Actions DoS
description:
The Next.js security update of October 14, 2026 fixes three vulnerabilities: two critical unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) bugs, one in use cache and one in SVG image optimization through sharp, and a high severity denial of service in Server Actions. Upgrade to Next.js 16.4.1 or later on 16.x, or 15.5.28 on 15.x, make sure sharp is 0.35.5 or later, then rebuild and redeploy.

The patch is easy to apply and easy to get wrong when you self-host. I reproduced the upgrade on real installs and found that upgrading Next.js 15 to 15.5.28 left the vulnerable sharp 0.34.5 in place, while npm audit on an unpatched next@16.4.0 reported 0 vulnerabilities. This guide shows how to check whether you are affected, a script that checks for you, and the exact steps to patch a Docker or Coolify deployment. Everything is cited to the official advisories.

What did the October 2026 Next.js security update fix?

It fixed three advisories published on October 14, 2026, all patched in Next.js 16.4.1 (Active LTS) and 15.5.28 (Maintenance LTS), according to the official Next.js security update. Two allow unauthenticated remote code execution with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.5; the third lets crafted requests pin a server's CPU.

Advisory Severity What it is Affected next versions Fixed in Workaround
GHSA-673q-mjm6-r5xr Critical, 9.5 RCE in use cache functions that return multiple typed arrays 16.0.0 to 16.4.0 16.4.1 None
CVE-2026-96889 / GHSA-2464-fhr4-w9xw Critical, 9.5 RCE in the Image Optimization API with SVG, via sharp's librsvg, on glibc Linux 10.0.0 to 15.5.27, 16.0.0 to 16.4.0 15.5.28, 16.4.1 sharp 0.35.5 or later
GHSA-p3m5-59mp-jv5r High, 8.2 DoS: crafted requests cause excessive CPU in App Router apps with Server Actions 13.0.0 to 15.5.27, 16.0.0 to 16.4.0 15.5.28, 16.4.1 None

The two React Server Components bugs also have upstream React advisories: GHSA-xqc2-xf4c-x3h3 for the typed-array RCE and GHSA-h3gv-c5rc-p453 for the DoS. Next.js ships its own compiled copy of react-server-dom-webpack and react-server-dom-turbopack inside the next package (I checked node_modules/next/dist/compiled), so upgrading next is what fixes a Next.js app, not bumping react alone.

Quick definitions

Term What it means
RCE Remote code execution: an attacker can run code on your server
DoS Denial of service: the server stops answering legitimate requests
GHSA A GitHub Security Advisory ID
sharp The image library Next.js uses for Image Optimization; it bundles libvips and librsvg
glibc The C library used by Debian, Ubuntu and node:*-slim images (Alpine uses musl instead)
Active / Maintenance LTS Next.js 16.4.x and 15.5.x, the two release lines that receive security fixes

TL;DR: how to patch Next.js now

  1. Upgrade: npm install next@16.4.2 on 16.x (16.4.1 is the security release; 16.4.2 adds bug fixes) or npm install next@15.5.28 on 15.x.
  2. Check sharp: run npm ls next sharp and confirm sharp@0.35.5 or later. On 15.x, run npm update sharp if it still shows 0.34.x.
  3. Commit the lockfile, rebuild the image from scratch and redeploy.
  4. Verify the running container, not just your laptop.

Is my Next.js app affected?

You are affected if your installed next is 16.0.0 through 16.4.0, or 15.5.27 and earlier, or if the sharp copy Next.js loads is older than 0.35.5. Which bugs reach you depends on features: use cache needs Cache Components, the DoS needs at least one Server Action, and the SVG bug needs glibc Linux.

Check the versions first:

npm ls next sharp

Then match your app against each advisory:

  • use cache RCE (GHSA-673q-mjm6-r5xr). Only Next.js 16 apps using the App Router with Cache Components can be exposed, and the trigger is a use cache function that returns multiple typed arrays. The advisory still says to upgrade immediately even if your application does not have similar functions. New apps from create-next-app 16.4 have Cache Components on by default, as I covered in Next.js use cache explained.
  • SVG Image Optimization RCE (CVE-2026-96889). A memory bug in librsvg, which sharp uses to decode SVG, can lead to RCE when Next.js runs on glibc-based Linux. That covers most Debian and Ubuntu based Docker images and VPS installs. By default Next.js does not optimize SVG images; apps that set images.dangerouslyAllowSVG: true are the clearest exposure, but the advisory is not limited to that setting, so patch either way.
  • Server Actions DoS (GHSA-p3m5-59mp-jv5r). Any App Router app with at least one Server Action, on Next.js 13 through 15.5.27 or 16.0.0 through 16.4.0. Pages Router apps and apps without Server Actions are not vulnerable.

Why does npm audit say my app is safe?

Because the advisory feed it reads may not list these issues yet. On October 17, 2026, I installed next@16.4.0, react and react-dom in an empty project and ran npm audit:

$ npm audit --json | jq .metadata.vulnerabilities
{ "info": 0, "low": 0, "moderate": 0, "high": 0, "critical": 0, "total": 0 }

Zero findings on a version with two open critical advisories. Treat npm audit, Dependabot and similar scanners as a backstop here and check the versions yourself, or use the script below.

A script that checks your app against all three advisories

I wrote this to check every app I run. It reads the installed next version, resolves sharp from Next.js's own folder (the copy the image optimizer actually loads), scans your source for use cache, use server and dangerouslyAllowSVG, and exits with code 1 if anything is unpatched, so you can drop it into CI. It has no dependencies.

// check-next-security.mjs: checks a Next.js app against the October 14, 2026 advisories.
// Usage: node check-next-security.mjs [projectDir]
import { readFileSync, readdirSync, statSync, existsSync } from 'node:fs'
import { createRequire } from 'node:module'
import path from 'node:path'

const dir = path.resolve(process.argv[2] ?? '.')
const req = createRequire(path.join(dir, 'package.json'))
// Find node_modules/<pkg>/package.json the way Node would, without relying on "exports".
const version = (pkg, from = req) => {
  for (const base of from.resolve.paths(pkg) ?? []) {
    const file = path.join(base, pkg, 'package.json')
    if (existsSync(file)) return JSON.parse(readFileSync(file, 'utf8')).version
  }
  return null
}
const cmp = (a, b) => {
  const [x, y] = [a, b].map((v) => v.split('-')[0].split('.').map(Number))
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) if (x[i] !== y[i]) return x[i] - y[i]
  return 0
}
const inRange = (v, lo, hi) => cmp(v, lo) >= 0 && cmp(v, hi) <= 0

// Scan source files for features the advisories depend on.
const src = []
const walk = (d) => {
  for (const name of readdirSync(d)) {
    if (['node_modules', '.next', '.git', 'out', 'dist'].includes(name)) continue
    const p = path.join(d, name)
    if (statSync(p).isDirectory()) walk(p)
    else if (/\.(m?[jt]sx?)$/.test(name)) src.push(readFileSync(p, 'utf8'))
  }
}
walk(dir)
const code = src.join('\n')
const uses = {
  useCache: /['"]use cache(: \w+)?['"]/.test(code),
  serverActions: /['"]use server['"]/.test(code),
  svgOptimizer: /dangerouslyAllowSVG\s*:\s*true/.test(code),
  nextOg: /from ['"]next\/og['"]/.test(code),
}

const next = version('next')
if (!next) { console.error('next is not installed in', dir); process.exit(2) }
// Resolve sharp from next's own folder, since that is the copy the image optimizer loads.
const nextPkg = (req.resolve.paths('next') ?? []).map((b) => path.join(b, 'next', 'package.json')).find(existsSync)
const sharp = version('sharp', createRequire(nextPkg))
const major = Number(next.split('.')[0])

const checks = [
  {
    id: 'GHSA-673q-mjm6-r5xr (critical): RCE in use cache returning typed arrays',
    vulnerable: inRange(next, '16.0.0', '16.4.0'),
    fix: 'upgrade next to 16.4.1+ (no workaround)',
    note: uses.useCache ? 'app uses "use cache"' : 'no "use cache" found, upgrade anyway',
  },
  {
    id: 'CVE-2026-96889 / GHSA-2464-fhr4-w9xw (critical): RCE via SVG in image optimization',
    vulnerable: sharp ? cmp(sharp, '0.35.5') < 0 : false,
    fix: 'sharp must be 0.35.5+ (npm update sharp), next 16.4.1+ or 15.5.28+',
    note: `sharp ${sharp ?? 'not installed'}` + (uses.svgOptimizer ? ', dangerouslyAllowSVG on' : '') + (uses.nextOg ? ', uses next/og' : ''),
  },
  {
    id: 'GHSA-p3m5-59mp-jv5r (high): DoS via Server Actions',
    vulnerable: inRange(next, '13.0.0', '15.5.27') || inRange(next, '16.0.0', '16.4.0'),
    fix: major >= 16 ? 'upgrade next to 16.4.1+' : 'upgrade next to 15.5.28+',
    note: uses.serverActions ? 'app defines Server Actions' : 'no "use server" found',
  },
]

console.log(`next ${next}, sharp ${sharp ?? 'not installed'} in ${dir}\n`)
let bad = 0
for (const c of checks) {
  if (c.vulnerable) bad++
  console.log(`${c.vulnerable ? 'VULNERABLE' : 'ok        '}  ${c.id}`)
  console.log(`            ${c.note}${c.vulnerable ? `\n            fix: ${c.fix}` : ''}`)
}
console.log(bad ? `\n${bad} issue(s) found. Patch, rebuild and redeploy.` : '\nAll three October 14, 2026 advisories are patched.')
process.exit(bad ? 1 : 0)

Run it from your project root with node check-next-security.mjs. This is the real output on a Next.js 16.4.0 app with one use cache function and one Server Action, before and after npm install next@16.4.2:

$ node check-next-security.mjs
next 16.4.0, sharp 0.35.4 in /app

VULNERABLE  GHSA-673q-mjm6-r5xr (critical): RCE in use cache returning typed arrays
            app uses "use cache"
            fix: upgrade next to 16.4.1+ (no workaround)
VULNERABLE  CVE-2026-96889 / GHSA-2464-fhr4-w9xw (critical): RCE via SVG in image optimization
            sharp 0.35.4
            fix: sharp must be 0.35.5+ (npm update sharp), next 16.4.1+ or 15.5.28+
VULNERABLE  GHSA-p3m5-59mp-jv5r (high): DoS via Server Actions
            app defines Server Actions
            fix: upgrade next to 16.4.1+

3 issue(s) found. Patch, rebuild and redeploy.

$ npm install next@16.4.2 && node check-next-security.mjs
next 16.4.2, sharp 0.35.5 in /app

ok          GHSA-673q-mjm6-r5xr (critical): RCE in use cache returning typed arrays
            app uses "use cache"
ok          CVE-2026-96889 / GHSA-2464-fhr4-w9xw (critical): RCE via SVG in image optimization
            sharp 0.35.5
ok          GHSA-p3m5-59mp-jv5r (high): DoS via Server Actions
            app defines Server Actions

All three October 14, 2026 advisories are patched.

The script checks versions and source patterns; it is not an exploit test. A clean result means you are on patched versions, which is what the advisories ask for.

How do you upgrade Next.js 16 to the patched version?

Install the latest 16.4 patch, then confirm sharp moved with it. Next.js 16.4.1 raised its sharp requirement to ^0.35.5 (16.4.0 accepted ^0.35.4; I read both from the npm registry), so npm has to upgrade sharp when you upgrade next.

npm install next@16.4.2
npm ls next sharp

In my test, a project whose lockfile held next@16.4.0 and sharp@0.35.4 came out of npm install next@16.4.1 with sharp@0.35.5, as expected. Run the same check with pnpm why sharp or yarn why sharp if you use those package managers.

eslint-config-next should match your next version, so bump it in the same commit. If you have not moved to 16 yet, the version 16 upgrade guide covers the breaking changes; that is a bigger job than this patch, so patch 15.x first.

How do you patch Next.js 15 safely?

Upgrade to 15.5.28, then check sharp separately, because upgrading next alone may not fix the SVG bug. Next.js 15.5.28 declares sharp as ^0.34.3 || ^0.35.5, so an existing lockfile that already resolved sharp 0.34.x still satisfies it, and npm keeps it.

This is what happened on a real project with next@15.5.27 and sharp@0.34.5 in the lockfile:

$ npm install next@15.5.28
$ npm ls sharp
└─┬ next@15.5.28
  └── sharp@0.34.5        # still vulnerable

$ npm update sharp
$ npm ls sharp
└─┬ next@15.5.28
  └── sharp@0.35.5        # fixed

If sharp is a direct dependency in your package.json, run npm install sharp@0.35.5 instead. To force one version across a monorepo, add an override:

{
  "overrides": {
    "sharp": "0.35.5"
  }
}

pnpm uses pnpm.overrides and Yarn uses resolutions for the same job.

How do you patch a self-hosted Next.js app in Docker or Coolify?

Update the lockfile, rebuild the image without reusing old layers, redeploy, then check the versions inside the running container. A dependency fix only protects you once the container that serves traffic contains it, and a Docker build that copies package-lock.json and runs npm ci installs exactly what the lockfile says.

  1. Update and verify locally. npm install next@16.4.2, npm ls next sharp, run the checker.
  2. Commit package-lock.json. Without it, your build server resolves whatever it resolved last time.
  3. Rebuild the image. With the standalone output used in my production Next.js Dockerfile, next build copies sharp and its native libvips package into .next/standalone/node_modules. In my build that was @img/sharp-libvips-linux-x64, the glibc variant. An image built before the patch keeps the old sharp until you rebuild it.
  4. Redeploy. In Coolify, push the commit or click Redeploy. To skip cached layers for this one build, trigger a forced deploy, for example through the Coolify API with GET /api/v1/deploy?uuid=<app-uuid>&force=true. My self-host Next.js with Coolify guide covers the deploy setup. With plain Docker, run docker compose build --no-cache && docker compose up -d.
  5. Verify the running container. In a standalone image the app lives in /app, so: 
docker exec <container> node -e "console.log(require('/app/node_modules/next/package.json').version, require('/app/node_modules/sharp/package.json').version)"

Requiring the package.json files by absolute path works even though sharp 0.35.5 does not export ./package.json. I checked the same command against a standalone build of Next.js 16.4.2; it printed 0.35.5 16.4.2 for sharp and next. Adjust the path if your Dockerfile copies the app somewhere other than /app.

What if you cannot upgrade Next.js today?

Only the SVG bug has an interim mitigation; the use cache RCE and the Server Actions DoS have no workaround, so plan the upgrade within hours, not weeks. In the meantime:

Bug Interim step Source
SVG / sharp RCE Make sure sharp is 0.35.5 or later, even without upgrading next Next.js advisory
SVG / sharp RCE In your own code that calls sharp, block SVG decoding with sharp.block({ operation: ['VipsForeignLoadSvg'] }) sharp advisory
SVG / sharp RCE Turn off images.dangerouslyAllowSVG if you do not need optimized SVGs Image docs
use cache RCE None. Upgrade. Next.js advisory
Server Actions DoS None. Upgrade. Rate limits only reduce the blast radius. Next.js advisory

I tested the sharp.block call with sharp 0.35.5: before it, a small SVG converted to a 100-byte PNG; after it, the same call failed with Input buffer contains unsupported image format.

import sharp from 'sharp'

// Refuse to decode SVG input anywhere this sharp instance is used.
sharp.block({ operation: ['VipsForeignLoadSvg'] })

The sharp advisory adds one hardening note: whether the librsvg bug can reach code execution depends partly on the Node.js binary. It recommends a node built as a Position Independent Executable (PIE), notes that most Linux distribution packages already are, and warns that the official Node.js binaries are not.

How do you know whether you were attacked?

The advisories publish no indicators of compromise and do not mention exploitation in the wild, so look for the side effects each bug would leave, and re-check the advisories for updates.

  • DoS: sustained 100% CPU on a Next.js process together with slow or failed requests, especially POST requests carrying a Next-Action header.
  • SVG RCE: unexpected requests to /_next/image with .svg sources, crashes of the Node.js process during image optimization, and new child processes or outbound connections from the container.
  • Any RCE: unknown files in the container filesystem, changed environment variables or secrets used from new IPs. If you find any of these, rotate secrets (database URLs, API keys, NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY) after patching.

Security habits that make the next patch faster

This was an out-of-band release that landed eight days after 16.4.0 shipped on October 6. A few habits keep the next one to a ten-minute job:

  • Stay on an LTS line. Security fixes land on 16.4.x (Active LTS) and 15.5.x (Maintenance LTS).
  • Turn on upgrade nudges. Next.js 16.4 added experimental.agentUpgrade, whose default 'security' policy reminds you during next dev and next build when an upgrade fixes a known vulnerability in your installed version (Next.js 16.4 notes).
  • Run the checker in CI. Exit code 1 fails the build when a vulnerable version is installed.
  • Pin and commit lockfiles, then rebuild images from them so the running version is the one you reviewed.
  • Keep Server Actions small and authenticated. The DoS needs only one action to exist, but auth and input validation limit what any future bug can reach; see Server Actions vs Route Handlers.

Common mistakes when patching

Mistake What happens Fix
Upgrading react instead of next Next.js keeps its bundled RSC runtime Upgrade next
Upgrading 15.x to 15.5.28 and stopping sharp 0.34.x can stay in the lockfile npm update sharp, confirm 0.35.5+
Trusting npm audit It reported 0 issues on unpatched 16.4.0 Check versions or run the script
Not committing the lockfile CI or Coolify rebuilds the old versions Commit package-lock.json
Rebuilding from a cached layer Old node_modules layer is reused Build once with no cache
Checking only the laptop Production still runs the old image docker exec into the running container

Related: I packaged the checker script above as a reusable agent skill, so Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or Copilot can run the check and patch for you. See Agent Skills: how to write a SKILL.md.

Related: running an MCP server next to your Next.js app? MCP security in 2026 covers this month's MCP SDK OAuth advisories and how to fix them.

Key takeaways

  • The October 14, 2026 update fixes two critical RCEs (use cache typed arrays and SVG via sharp) and a high-severity Server Actions DoS.
  • Patched versions are Next.js 16.4.1+ and 15.5.28+, with sharp 0.35.5 or later.
  • On 15.x, upgrading next can leave sharp 0.34.x installed; run npm update sharp and verify.
  • npm audit reported nothing for unpatched next@16.4.0 on October 17, 2026, so check versions directly.
  • A self-hosted fix only counts after you rebuild the image, redeploy and verify the versions inside the running container.

title: Go Retrieval Admission Control: Query Limits for Customer-Support Knowledge Base PDFs
description:
Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, hard query budgets, and source context that survives every stage; tune recall inside those limits instead of letting a customer-support knowledge base search an unbounded PDF corpus.

For a B2B SaaS team answering questions over folders of customer manuals, the hard trade-off is retrieval quality versus tail latency. More candidates can improve recall, but they also enlarge reranking and answer context. My operating rule is to admit a bounded amount of work, preserve tenant and access-control metadata on every indexed item, and reject or degrade excess work before it becomes an invisible queue.

I've been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. The retrieval version of that incident has the same shape: retries arrive while the original work is still running, a shared worker pool fills, and a small latency problem becomes a backlog. Don't make topK the only guardrail.

How should customer-support knowledge base retrieval architecture enforce query limits?

Start with a retrieval contract tied to the user-visible answer. For each request, name the tenant, the permitted collections, the maximum number of candidate chunks, the maximum context bytes, and a deadline. The answer must carry traceable source context back to the PDF and page or section. If any of those values is unknown, the query is not ready for admission.

This is scheduling, not just search.

A useful contract separates four budgets. The concurrency budget caps work already in flight. The candidate budget limits what vector search can return. The context budget limits what reaches answer generation. The time budget leaves enough of the request deadline for citation assembly and the final response. One large tenant must not consume every slot, so enforce concurrency per tenant as well as globally.

Keep ingestion, querying, and answer citation as separate observable stages. A single end-to-end duration hides the failure domain: ingestion lag looks like poor recall, an oversized candidate set looks like slow reranking, and missing source context looks like an answer-generation problem. Record stage, tenant, collection, admitted limit, returned count, and deadline outcome. Do not log private PDF contents merely to make the dashboard convenient.

The invariant is plain: every admitted query has bounded fan-out and enough identity to explain its answer.

An incident-shaped design for PDF support answers

Consider a SaaS product for commercial HVAC contractors. Each tenant uploads installation guides, warranty PDFs, and its own operating procedures. A dispatcher asks, "Can this controller run after a pressure-switch alarm?" The broad collection may contain several product generations with nearly identical terminology. Searching every tenant or allowing an arbitrary candidate count can produce a plausible answer from the wrong manual. Returning only one chunk is fast, but it can omit the reset conditions on the following page.

I would make the first stage select explicit tenant-scoped collections and preserve access-control metadata during ingestion. The second stage retrieves a bounded candidate set. The third trims or reranks those candidates under a separate context budget. The answer stage receives source identifiers with the text, so the UI can show which manual supported the response. No stage gets to silently widen scope when recall looks weak.

That last point matters. A retry after HTTP 429 should respect Retry-After when it is present and use exponential backoff, but a retry must still obey the original tenant and collection boundary. A retry that doubles the search surface changes the question. It also makes the latency incident harder to reconstruct.

I'm not sure which candidate limit will be best for your PDFs, and nobody can derive it from a vendor feature list. Resolve that uncertainty with a fixed evaluation set built from representative documents and known failure cases. Include near-duplicate manuals, answers split across adjacent pages, obsolete procedures, access-denied documents, and questions with no supported answer. Measure recall and precision, then inspect latency at the same limits. The chosen limit is the smallest budget that meets the support-quality target, with enough deadline left to build cited answers under expected concurrency.

One miss is useful evidence. Treat it as a corpus or retrieval-contract failure before raising every limit.

Put the limit in the Go code path

The preventative path belongs ahead of the retriever. This runnable Go program validates tenant scope, applies a deadline, bounds candidates and context, and uses a per-tenant semaphore. The in-memory retriever keeps the example honest: replace that interface implementation with a provider call, while leaving admission policy in application code.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const vectorQueryPath = "/v1/vector/query"

type QueryRequest struct {
    Collection      string    `json:"collection"`
    Embedding       []float64 `json:"embedding"`
    TopK            int       `json:"top_k"`
    IncludeMetadata bool      `json:"include_metadata"`
}

type Gate struct {
    tenantSlots chan struct{}
    client      *http.Client
    apiKey      string
    baseURL     string
}

func (g Gate) Query(ctx context.Context, in QueryRequest) (json.RawMessage, error) {
    if in.Collection == "" || len(in.Embedding) == 0 {
        return nil, errors.New("tenant collection and embedding are required")
    }
    if in.TopK < 1 || in.TopK > 20 {
        return nil, errors.New("top_k must be between 1 and 20")
    }

    select {
    case g.tenantSlots <- struct{}{}:
        defer func() { <-g.tenantSlots }()
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return nil, ctx.Err()
    }

    payload, err := json.Marshal(in)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        url := strings.TrimRight(g.baseURL, "/") + vectorQueryPath
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, url, bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+g.apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

        res, err := g.client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(res.Body, 2<<20))
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(res.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(wait)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("vector query status %d: %s", res.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return json.RawMessage(body), nil
    }
    return nil, errors.New("vector query remained rate limited")
}

func parseEmbedding(raw string) ([]float64, error) {
    parts := strings.Split(raw, ",")
    values := make([]float64, 0, len(parts))
    for _, part := range parts {
        value, err := strconv.ParseFloat(strings.TrimSpace(part), 64)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("parse embedding: %w", err)
        }
        values = append(values, value)
    }
    return values, nil
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    collection := os.Getenv("INFRAI_TENANT_COLLECTION")
    embedding, err := parseEmbedding(os.Getenv("QUERY_EMBEDDING"))
    if err != nil || key == "" || baseURL == "" || collection == "" {
        panic("set INFRAI_API_KEY, INFRAI_BASE_URL, INFRAI_TENANT_COLLECTION, and QUERY_EMBEDDING")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 750*time.Millisecond)
    defer cancel()
    gate := Gate{
        tenantSlots: make(chan struct{}, 2), client: &http.Client{},
        apiKey: key, baseURL: baseURL,
    }
    result, err := gate.Query(ctx, QueryRequest{
        Collection: collection, Embedding: embedding,
        TopK: 8, IncludeMetadata: true,
    })
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(result))
}

The numbers are policy examples, not benchmark results. Put production values in configuration, cap them server-side, and version them with the evaluation set. If a request times out, return a controlled no-answer result rather than launching detached retrieval that can outlive its caller. If the client retries, give the request a stable identifier so traces from both attempts can be joined; any downstream write must be idempotent.

For Infrai, the relevant search path is POST /v1/vector/query. Infrai fits operational consolidation because one API key and one bill can cover backend services, so the on-call team has fewer secret rotations and month-end invoices to reconcile. The plain REST surface also avoids adding a provider SDK to this Go service. Keep the application-owned gate anyway. Provider breadth does not replace tenant isolation, query admission, or corpus evaluation.

Compare the operating model, not a feature checklist

Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, and Infrai can all sit behind the Retriever interface. The useful comparison is who owns each control and how much provider sprawl the team accepts, not which landing page has the longest checklist.

Option Integration shape Query-limit decision Operational trade-off
Pinecone Dedicated vector database service Keep application admission and provider query settings aligned Stick with it when a dedicated vector platform and its operating model are already standard in the team
Weaviate Vector database with its own query surface Enforce tenant scope and context budgets outside the database too A reasonable choice when its data and query model match the existing stack
Qdrant Vector database available through its own API Retain application-side concurrency and deadline gates Fits teams prepared to own the deployment choice and database-specific integration
Infrai Search capability within a broader REST API Discover the request schema, then apply the same application gate Useful when reducing key and billing sprawl matters across backend services

The catch is that consolidation is not always the right axis. Infrai is not suitable when the organization requires a dedicated vector-database operating model or has standardized deeply on provider-specific query features; stick with Pinecone, Weaviate, or Qdrant when that specialization matters more than a shared backend API. Conversely, a small platform team that is already reconciling many service keys and invoices may value one credential and one bill, provided its evaluation corpus confirms the required retrieval quality.

Do the trial under load, but don't invent a universal winner. Use the same tenant-filtered PDFs, questions, candidate limits, and citation checks for every option. Record precision, recall, deadline completion, and denied-access behavior. Your mileage may vary because PDF layout, chunking, and question distribution change the result more than a generic product category does.

Runbook checks before raising a query budget

When recall drops, first check ingestion completeness, collection selection, tenant metadata, and whether the expected source is in the evaluation set. Then inspect candidate truncation and context truncation separately. Raise a limit only when the trace proves the relevant stage discarded a correct source and the remaining deadline can absorb more work.

When latency rises, stop admitting more parallel work before tuning ranking. Check per-tenant saturation, global saturation, retry volume, and the fraction of queries reaching each budget. A wave of retries can look like organic demand. Respect 429 backoff, preserve the original scope, and make writes idempotent.

Keep the rollback boring: restore the previous versioned budgets. Re-run the fixed failure cases. Verify citations still point to permitted source documents. Then write the postmortem around the violated invariant, not around whichever vendor happened to be underneath it.

Sources

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/search/search-overview
  • https://docs.weaviate.io/weaviate/search
  • https://qdrant.tech/documentation/search/
