title: Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes
description:
By Roberto Perez Alcolea, Java Platform Team

At Netflix, shared Java libraries support applications developed across a large, independently evolving repository ecosystem. A library change begins in one repository, but its impact can reach many others. Producers can see the API diff in front of them. What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed.

The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. An agent can accelerate a local edit, but without cross-repository context it cannot judge downstream risk or help plan consumer migrations. The evidence a producer uses to assess a change can also guide the agent working on it.

Consider a common case: removing a deprecated API. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves.

Suppose a replacement has been available for several releases and the old method cannot express options required by new behavior. The library’s tests pass, and a compatibility checker flags the removal. The producer still cannot answer the questions that determine what to do next:

  • Does any consumer still call this method?
  • Are consumers concentrated on one version or spread across several generations?
  • Does another library implement or wrap the API, multiplying its impact?
  • Is direct coordination sufficient, or does this require a deprecation and migration campaign?

At small scale, producers can ask nearby teams or search a handful of repositories. Across many repositories, it is harder to find every caller of a method and the library version each one uses. Those answers are scattered across consumer codebases and builds.

Without that evidence, a producer may release a breaking change and discover the impact through consumer failures, or preserve an old API indefinitely because the risk is unknown. Libraries need to evolve, and their producers need evidence that helps them do so intentionally.

We built Quasar to index symbol definitions and references across Netflix repositories. For library producers, that shared index helps answer two questions:

  1. What changed in the library’s public API?
  2. Which repositories use the exact symbols that changed?

The first identifies a potentially incompatible change. The second estimates its observed blast radius. Together, they turn a generic compatibility warning into evidence a producer can act on before merging or releasing.

From API Changes to Consumer Impact

Existing techniques each see a different part of the problem. Binary and source compatibility tools identify contract changes, but cannot tell who uses the changed API. Dependency graphs show declared reach, but cannot prove that code calls a particular method. Text search may miss overloads, inheritance, or the artifact version behind a call. Consumer builds provide strong validation, but running them across the fleet is expensive.

Quasar builds on SCIP, an open interchange format for semantic code intelligence. Language-specific indexers encode definitions, references, and relationships using stable symbol identifiers. Quasar retains API definitions for library versions and commits alongside references from consumer repositories. That shared identity lets it connect an API change in one repository to exact usages elsewhere, even when those repositories were indexed independently.

On each enrolled CI build, language-specific indexers submit SCIP indexes to Quasar’s ingestion service. It writes API definitions and consumer references as Parquet in Amazon S3, retaining the symbol identity, dependency version, and source location needed to investigate a change.

During pull-request review, Quasar compares indexed base and head definitions and counts direct consumer references with Amazon Athena. Quasar exposes those findings through its REST and GraphQL APIs and MCP server; follow-up usage queries provide dependency-version breakdowns and source locations. A separate compatibility-impact assessment can also follow implementations and their callers when a producer supplies a changed JVM symbol.

Consider this simplified API change:

public interface Client {
- Result getLegacyValue(Request request);
+ Result getValue(Request request, Options options);
}

For a detailed compatibility-impact assessment of this removal, a producer-side tool supplies the old method descriptor. Quasar constructs its canonical symbol identity. This abridged excerpt from the direct-reference portion of Quasar’s Amazon Athena query shows the essential match:

SELECT c.change_id, 'DIRECT_REFERENCE' AS evidence_kind,
       r.scm_type, r.org, r.repo, r.dep_version, r.file_path
FROM requested_changes c
JOIN quasar.symbol_refs r
  ON r.symbol_canonical = c.target_canonical

requested_changes contains the API changes submitted by the producer. The SQL excerpt finds repositories that call the removed method. Quasar also checks implementations and calls through them, so it can count each affected repository once. It returns sample dependency versions and file locations to help investigate the result.

For the Client change, this tells the producer which repositories still use getLegacyValue, which versions they use, and where some of those calls occur. That helps the producer decide whether to coordinate a migration before removing the method.

Bringing the Analysis Before Release

Version-to-version comparison is valuable when planning an upgrade or writing a migration guide. Producers benefit even more when feedback arrives during code review.

For pull-request analysis, Quasar stores API definition snapshots keyed by commit. Given a base and head commit, it classifies symbols as added, removed, or signature-modified. Removals and modifications then become candidates for consumer-impact analysis.

An incompatible change is not automatically a high-risk change. Quasar reports the observed impact so the producer can decide what to do; it does not enforce a release policy. “No references observed” means only that Quasar found none in the indexed population. Reflection, configuration, dynamic loading, stale branches, or incomplete indexing can hide consumers. The result needs to show whether the requested commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated.

Pull-request review requires indexed snapshots for the exact base and head commits. If either is unavailable, Quasar reports that it cannot compare them; it does not substitute a default-branch snapshot. This keeps a missing comparison from looking like a clean API diff.

Return to our Client change. This illustrative report brings together signals available through Quasar's API comparison, consumer-usage queries, and library-level criticality. It is not a literal response from one API:

{
  "change": "REMOVED",
  "symbol": "Client#getLegacyValue(Request)",
  "affectedRepositories": 137,
  "versionDistribution": [
    { "version": "4.2.1", "repositories": 86 },
    { "version": "4.1.7", "repositories": 38 },
    { "version": "3.9.4", "repositories": 13 }
  ],
  "sampleConsumerLocations": [
    {
      "repository": "checkout-service",
      "filePath": "src/main/java/com/example/checkout/CheckoutClient.java",
      "lines": [84, 129]
    },
    {
      "repository": "client-wrapper",
      "filePath": "src/main/java/com/example/client/ClientAdapter.java",
      "lines": [57]
    }
  ],
  "libraryCriticality": {
    "tier": 1,
    "basis": "highest-tier downstream application"
  },
  "comparison": {
    "baseShaFound": true,
    "headShaFound": true
  }
}

The repository count is symbol-specific: in this example, 137 indexed repositories refer to the removed method. The version distribution reveals a dominant cohort on 4.2.1 and a smaller long tail still on 3.9.4. A producer can inspect affected repositories and retrieve indexed file paths, with line numbers where the index provides them. The JSON shows only two sample locations to keep the example readable. The filePath and lines shape mirrors Quasar's query contract. The tier is broader context about the library, inherited from its highest-criticality downstream application; it does not imply that all 137 callers are Tier 1.

Together, those signals change the producer’s plan. Instead of merging the removal and waiting for failures, the producer can retain and deprecate the old method, publish a migration path, coordinate a broader migration, and track the long-tail versions before removal. File paths and available line numbers turn that scope into a concrete work list for engineers or coding agents. The same API diff paired with weak or stale evidence would lead to a different action: refresh the indexes before deciding. The value is not merely detecting the removal; it is choosing a proportionate next step.

A Polyglot Foundation with SCIP

The shared SCIP format also lets Quasar index several language ecosystems. Each language indexer resolves its own code, while Quasar can use the resulting symbol identities to find references across repositories.

Conceptually, client-lib indexes Client#getLegacyValue(Request) as a definition, while checkout-service indexes a reference to the same symbol. Quasar can then connect the library API to its consumer across repositories.

Relationships are especially useful when generated code separates the API a producer owns from the symbols consumers invoke. For example, Quasar can trace a Protobuf definition through its generated Java members to the repositories that use them, even when consumer code never names the .proto element.

SCIP records symbols and their references; it does not determine whether an API change violates an ecosystem’s compatibility rules. Today, Quasar compares indexed JVM and Protobuf API definitions and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java to find affected repositories. A separate JVM compatibility-impact path uses breaks identified by a producer-side tool to query affected repositories. Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust support usage queries, but Quasar does not yet assess their breaking API changes.

Moving Risk Assessment Earlier

Today, Quasar surfaces API-change findings on pull requests, including observed consumer counts and confidence. Producers can use its other queries to inspect dependency versions and source locations, with library criticality as broader context. Together, those signals support a decision before merge.

We want to move that context earlier. An agent writing library code should recognize when it is changing a public symbol and consult Quasar before the change becomes a pull request. Quasar’s APIs and Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration provide an access path, but access alone does not create awareness. The coding workflow must also recognize public API edits so the agent knows when to query impact and when to involve the producer.

Earlier guidance will not replace pull-request analysis. The PR assessment will still verify the concrete diff and catch changes that were not recognized during coding. Coverage, freshness, ambiguity, unsupported platforms, and truncation must travel through both checks in machine-readable form. An agent should not turn “no observed usages in the available index” into “safe to remove.”

Today, agents can query Quasar through MCP when prompted. We are working toward making that context part of the coding workflow, then using identified call sites to prepare migration changes. Quasar supplies semantic evidence, an agent reduces migration toil, and the library producer remains responsible for API and release decisions.

What We Learned

Building this workflow led us to four practical lessons.

  • Separate compatibility from reach. A removed method can break the API contract even when Quasar finds no callers. A list of affected repositories and their library versions shows the migration work ahead. Producers need both signals to choose a release path.
  • Make the evidence inspectable. A repository count is more useful with sample call sites and a version breakdown. The result also needs to show which commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated. Otherwise, “no usage found” can be mistaken for proof that nobody is affected.
  • Keep usage and compatibility separate across languages. SCIP lets Quasar find symbol references in several ecosystems. Deciding whether an API change is breaking requires compatibility rules or a trusted producer-side signal for that ecosystem.
  • Bring evidence to the producer while choices are open. Pull-request findings can prompt a producer to retain an API, publish a migration path, or coordinate consumers before merge. Moving the same evidence into the coding workflow could shape the edit earlier. After release, it still helps locate consumers that need to migrate.

Today, Quasar indexes JVM, Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust code for cross-repository usage analysis. It compares JVM APIs and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java. Producers can review change findings through Quasar’s REST and GraphQL APIs or its MCP server, then investigate affected repositories and call sites. We are extending this foundation toward more ecosystem-specific compatibility checks, deeper code-review integration, and agent-assisted consumer migrations that keep release approval with the producer.

Quasar is internal to Netflix, but the pattern is portable: index code semantically, retain API definitions, compare them at the point of change, query affected consumers, and report the quality of the evidence. Library producers need more than a compatibility verdict. They need to know who may be affected and have enough time to act before release.

A huge thank you to the Java Platform team at Netflix. Their expertise, collaboration, and support made this work possible

Related Talks

  • From Lag to Lightning: Transforming Dependency Update Timelines explores how Netflix shortened dependency-update timelines.
  • Netflix’s Journey to Confident Automated Code Changes discusses building confidence in automated changes at scale.

Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: I built a browser-only image toolkit with React and Canvas (no server needed)
description:
Most "free online image tools" upload your files to a server, keep them for some period, and often want an account. I wanted the opposite: every operation runs on your device, nothing is transmitted to a backend, and no account is required.

That's why I built PixelShrink — a browser-only image toolkit that runs entirely on the Canvas API.

What it does

  • Compress JPG, PNG, and WebP images
  • Resize, crop, and convert between formats
  • Compress to a target file size (100 KB, 200 KB)
  • Batch compress and download results as a ZIP
  • Combine images into a PDF
  • Inspect and strip EXIF metadata
  • Generate favicons, social-media presets, and passport sizes

17 tools in total, all client-side.

Why browser-only matters

Image compression isn't expensive. It's a CPU operation that any laptop can do in milliseconds. There's no technical reason to send a 3 MB photo to a server and back.

The reasons tools do it anyway are:

  1. They want to show you an ad before the download.
  2. They want your email for their marketing list.
  3. They want to upsell you to a paid plan.

Browser-only tools remove all three. The image never leaves your device. No upload, no account, no tracking.

The technical stack

  • React + TypeScript for the UI
  • Vite for the build
  • Tailwind CSS for styling
  • Canvas API for all image processing
  • pdf-lib for the image-to-PDF tool
  • jszip for batch downloads
  • react-image-crop for the cropper
  • exifr for metadata reading

Everything is lazy-loaded per route, so the home page loads in under 100 KB.

The hardest part

Two things were genuinely tricky:

  1. Format detection Browsers don't all support the same encoder set. Safari can encode WebP and AVIF, Firefox can encode WebP but AVIF support varies, and old browsers can't encode either. Rather than claim "AVIF supported!" and then silently fall back to PNG, the site runs a 2×2 test canvas through toBlob at runtime and only offers formats the browser can actually produce.

2. Touch-friendly cropping. Getting a crop box to feel right on a phone — drag to resize, drag inside to move, snap to aspect ratio — is harder than it looks with raw pointer events. I used react-image-crop rather than rolling my own, and it handles the touch edge cases correctly.

What I deliberately didn't do

  • No server-side processing. That would break the "no uploads" promise.
  • No AI upscaling. The upscaler uses plain canvas interpolation and says so on the page. Faking "AI enhancement" would be dishonest.
  • No HEIC support. Browsers can't decode HEIC without a large WASM bundle. I'd rather say "not supported" than ship a broken tool.
  • No analytics or ads (yet). If I ever add them, the privacy policy will be updated first.

Try it

https://pixelshrink-tools.netlify.app/

No account, no uploads, no tracking. Free.

I'd love feedback — especially on the touch experience and on any format the site doesn't handle that you wish it did.

title: This Week in Open Source for October 23, 2026
description:
by Daryl Ducharme, Open Source Programs Office

A look around the world of open source

What actually sustains an open source community when the cost of generating code drops toward zero, while the human labor required to review, govern, and secure it stays just as demanding? Across this week's reads, researchers, legal scholars, and builders examine the tension between automated volume and human stewardship—from public-infrastructure policy and maintainer bandwidth to provenance transparency, copyright law, and compact models running entirely on local hardware. Because software only serves people when human judgment remains in the loop, protecting maintainer agency and keeping project doors open to real newcomers matter more than ever.

Upcoming Events

🗓️ October 2026

  • Open Source AI Week 2026 (October 19–24, 2026) — San Francisco Bay Area, California, USA. Now in its final stretch across the Bay Area alongside PyTorch Conference, this decentralized week of community meetups, workshops, and hackathons—with Google DeepMind and Gemma as Platinum Sponsor—wraps up this weekend with tonight's Open Source AI Awards Night (Friday, October 23, 5:00–10:00 PM PT at Fort Mason, San Francisco) and tomorrow's Google Gemma Hardware Hackathon at AGI House (Saturday, October 24, 10:00 AM–5:00 PM PT in Hillsborough, CA).
  • AGNTCon + MCPCon North America 2026 (October 22–23, 2026) — San Jose, California, USA. Happening this week, this Linux Foundation and Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) conference focuses on building and scaling production agentic systems with open standards—featuring keynotes by Google's Rao Surapaneni, Sarah Drasner, and Chi Wang, plus sessions from Googlers Alan Blount (on Agent-to-User Interface [A2UI]), Junjie Bu (on interoperable agent discovery), Amit Handa (on agentic commerce), Dominic Farolino (on Model Context Protocol [MCP] Apps + WebMCP), and Prerna Kakkar & Kurtis Van Gent (on EvalBench).
  • GitHub Universe 2026 (October 28–29, 2026) — San Francisco, California, USA & Virtual. Annual global developer gathering highlighting open source workflows, collaborative security, and multi-model AI-assisted software engineering.

🗓️ November 2026

  • Open Source in Finance Forum (OSFF) New York (November 4–5, 2026) — New York, New York, USA. Dedicated industry conference examining open source compliance, supply-chain security, and collaborative innovation across regulated financial institutions.
  • SeaGL (Seattle GNU/Linux Conference) 2026 (November 6–7, 2026) — Seattle, Washington, USA & Virtual. Free, grassroots technical summit dedicated to spreading awareness and knowledge of free and open source software, hardware, and culture.
  • KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 (November 9–12, 2026) — Salt Lake City, Utah, USA. The Cloud Native Computing Foundation's (CNCF) flagship conference uniting adopters and maintainers around Kubernetes and cloud-native infrastructure—featuring over 35 sessions and keynotes from Googlers including Abdel Sghiouar, Jago Macleod, Tim Hockin, Kaslin Fields, John Belamaric, Dawn Chen, Janet Kuo, Benjamin Elder, Antonio Ojea, Lior Lieberman, Michelle Au, and Braydon Kains across Kubernetes Special Interest Groups (SIGs), etcd, containerd, Gateway API, Common Expression Language (CEL) admission policies, and agent sandboxes, plus the Google-sponsored Community Hub.
  • SFSCON (South Tyrol Free Software Conference) 2026 (November 13–14, 2026) — Bolzano, Italy. One of Europe's longest-running Free Software conferences bringing together public-sector decision-makers and developers to advance digital sovereignty and open infrastructure.

🗓️ December 2026

  • Yocto Project Virtual Summit 2026.12 (December 1–3, 2026) — Virtual. Community summit for embedded Linux engineers and maintainers building custom, reproducible Linux distributions across edge and Internet of Things (IoT) hardware.
  • Open Source Summit Japan 2026 (December 7–9, 2026) — Tokyo, Japan. The Linux Foundation's premier Asia-Pacific conference connecting open source developers, kernel maintainers, and enterprise leaders across cloud, embedded Linux, and open AI, including sessions from Google engineers such as Anurag Sinha.
  • Open Compliance Summit 2026 (December 10–11, 2026) — Tokyo, Japan. Specialized gathering uniting legal, security, and Open Source Programs Office (OSPO) practitioners around OpenChain, Software Package Data Exchange (SPDX), software bills of materials (SBOMs), and global open source supply-chain compliance.

Open Source Reads and Links

  • [Blog] Open Enables a Lot: The OSI at UNGA81 — At the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA81), the Open Source Initiative (OSI) hosted a panel featuring Google OSPO’s Amanda Casari alongside policy and academic leaders to explore how open source reshapes public infrastructure. Framed by Duane O’Brien’s takeaway that “open by itself does very little, but enables a lot,” what shared scaffolding is needed to turn open licenses into real public value?
  • [Paper] “AI Slop is DDoSing Open Source”: Understanding the Impact of AI-Generated Contributions on Open Source Sustainability — After hearing questions about AI-generated pull requests online and at conferences for a while now, I came to Google and Oregon State University’s study of 294 repositories looking for what solutions are actually working. Surveying 11 remediation strategies as first-time contributor merge rates drop 18.18%, how can communities filter synthetic noise without closing the door on newcomers?
  • [Article] Who’s Writing Open Source Code? — Have AI coding agents actually taken over open source repositories, or is human authorship still the norm? Auditing 24,000 commits across 15 critical C infrastructure projects from the first half of 2026, RedMonk’s Stephen O’Grady finds that fewer than 1% carry explicit machine co-author or agent markers—raising a pressing question: how should open source communities build cultural norms around provenance transparency?
  • [Article] The copyright problem with AI-generated code — In creative circles online, people often argue that prompting AI makes you closer to an art patron or a music producer than the artist—but I had never thought about the copyright realities for software. Since open source licenses rely on human copyright, FreeDOS founder Jim Hall asks a foundational question: can you even license code you didn’t actually author?
  • [Blog] Launching an opt-in vulnerability-finding service for open-source software — Inspired by Google’s OSS-Fuzz, Anthropic’s new opt-in OSS Scanner offers open source maintainers free, periodic security audits complete with test reproducers and suggested patches running in isolated Docker environments. Giving resource-constrained projects direct access to frontier vulnerability detection is a welcome step forward—how can we keep expanding shared security tooling to help upstream maintainers catch complex bugs early?
  • [Blog] Do Agent Skills Help? I Ran 72 Trials to Find Out — Evaluating whether AI agent skills beat prompt-and-guess baselines, Karl Weinmeister ran 72 sandboxed trials across 12 scenarios using Harbor and SkillEvaluator—complementing Google’s open source skill-reach suite for catching description collisions across harnesses like AAIF’s Goose and Claude Code. Together, they raise a practical question for maintainers: how do we test both skill discovery and execution quality?
  • [Blog] Make the PDS Your Own: Customization and Metrics — The Authenticated Transfer Protocol (AT Protocol) is one of my major interests right now, so seeing how people are making its foundations work in practice is fascinating. The latest Reference Personal Data Server (PDS) release adds custom OAuth login branding, 300MB video blobs, and direct-to-Prometheus OpenTelemetry metrics in under 1GB of RAM—what other operational building blocks will help small teams self-host federated infrastructure?
  • [Article] Google’s new 4B Gemma model cuts speaker-labelling errors on all four benchmarks, two barely — Automated transcripts still struggle when speakers talk over one another in meetings and interviews. Built on Google’s Gemma 4 E4B and open source DiarizationLM framework, the community-trained Apache 2.0 DiarizationLM-Gemma-4-E4B-v1 approaches speaker diarization as a lightweight post-processing pass over existing transcripts—beating an 8B Llama 3 baseline at half the size. Where can compact local models clean up brittle pipeline handoffs in your own workflows?
  • [Blog] Open-Source Voice AI runs entirely on ESP32-S3 — Some of the most inspiring moments in open source come from individual builders experimenting at the edges of hardware constraints. Anankush Pandit’s GNU General Public License (GPL) Ivy AI packs wake-word detection, speech recognition, a 4-bit language model, and speech synthesis onto an ESP32-S3 microcontroller with just 8MB of pseudo-static RAM (PSRAM)—making us wonder what other everyday devices could run entirely offline?

Which of these stories will you be chatting about at your next meetup or conference? Let us know! Share with us on our @GoogleOSS X account or our @opensource.google Bluesky account.

title: JOPS Meets Next.js: Class-Based SPAs Inside Server-Rendered Apps
description:
When we shipped hybrid mobile support in JOPS 1.0.13, we said the next step was to examine how JOPS and Next.js could work together. With jops-core 1.1.0, that work is done: a complete JOPS single-page app can now run inside a page of a Next.js app, next to React, with Next.js Route Handlers as its backend.

This isn't JOPS competing with React. Next.js keeps everything it does best: server rendering, data fetching, routing and the React ecosystem. JOPS adds class-based views with an Android-style lifecycle on the pages that need them. One codebase, two models, each where it fits.

Why bring classes into a Next.js app

Object-oriented design is how most backend and mobile developers think: Java, C#, Kotlin, Swift, Android and UIKit are all built around classes. Modern React has moved the other way. Server Components are async functions, and React's newest features are built for function components. Classes still work in client components, but a class-based architecture no longer fits naturally in a modern React and Next.js codebase.

Functions and hooks are a proven model, and many teams are productive with them. JOPS gives teams that think in classes a first-class place inside the same app, without asking anyone to switch.

How it works

The split is simple:

  • Next.js owns the path, JOPS owns the hash. The page /quotes is a Next.js route; /quotes#details?id=q2 is a screen inside the JOPS app.
  • The JOPS app lives in public/ and is served as-is. Turbopack and webpack never bundle it, so JOPS keeps its no-build design.
  • The backend is Next.js. The JOPS app calls Route Handlers with fetch(), on the same origin, with the session cookie sent automatically.

The bridge is a single React component, JopsApp, imported from jops-core/nextjs:

// src/app/quotes/page.tsx
import JopsApp from "jops-core/nextjs";

export default function QuotesPage() {
  return <JopsApp app="/quotes/App.js" id="quotes-root" />;
}

JopsApp is a Client Component, so a Server Component page can render it. On the server it renders an empty <div>. In the browser it loads the JOPS library once per page, adds the import map and starts the app inside that <div>. The app's entry module is the same App.js a standalone JOPS app uses:

// public/quotes/App.js
import { View } from "jops-core";

export default class App {
  constructor() {
    const root = new View();
    root.loadLayout("/quotes/layout/main.html").then(() => root.render());
  }
}

Proven on a real application

We didn't design the bridge on a whiteboard. We built a typical Next.js CRM first, on Next.js 16, React 19, the App Router and Tailwind CSS 4, and then rebuilt its entire Quote Builder as a JOPS app inside it:

  • A quote list with status filters and loading skeletons
  • Quote details with status actions and a printable quote document
  • A two-step quote editor with a product picker, live totals and server-side validation
  • A new-quote flow started from the CRM's own sales pipeline

All of it runs on the CRM's REST Route Handlers, styled with the same Tailwind classes as the rest of the app. Building a real feature end to end exposed issues no demo would have. We fixed them in the framework before the release, and the few that are better handled by convention are listed below.

An app lifecycle that respects the host

A JOPS app inside Next.js behaves like an app on a phone:

  • Leaving the page ends the app completely. Follow a Next.js link elsewhere, or press Back past the app's first screen, and the router, every view, the app's Store and EventBus, and JOPS's history hooks are all removed. Nothing keeps running in the background.
  • Coming back launches it again and restores the screen from the hash.
  • Next.js navigation keeps working. Next.js history state is preserved in every entry JOPS writes, so Back and Forward behave across both frameworks.

Get started

The quickest start is the new project template. In an empty folder:

npx jops-core init
# choose: 3. Next.js JOPS Embedded SPA
npm run dev

It creates a Next.js project with a React-only page, a page hosting a JOPS SPA (a mock login and a quotes list), and a Route Handler as its backend. To add JOPS to an existing Next.js app instead:

npm i jops-core
npx jops-core update   # copies the library to public/lib/

Then put your JOPS app in public/ and render <JopsApp app="/my-app/App.js" /> on the page that hosts it.

Not using React? The same mechanism works on any page: load the library with data-host, and start or stop the app yourself with window.JOPS.mount() and unmount().

Also new in 1.1.0

Building a full application inside Next.js shaped several additions that every JOPS app can use, standalone or hosted:

  • onPause(), the counterpart of onResume(), called when another view comes to the front while this one stays alive.
  • Tag props: attributes on a declared view, such as <Card jops title="Hi" item-id="7">, arrive as read-only this.props.
  • Layouts with several top-level elements, and find(id) for every element with a given id.
  • Owned event subscriptions: EventBus.subscribe(owner, event, callback) removes itself when its view is destroyed.
  • A round of router and view fixes found while building the Quote Builder, from reliable default routes to views that resume exactly once.

Know before you start

A few conventions keep the two frameworks out of each other's way:

  • One JOPS app per page. The router, Store and EventBus are page-wide.
  • Root-absolute paths for everything JOPS loads, and the library served from public/lib/ rather than a CDN.
  • Next.js owns the CSS. Inside Next.js, setStyle() is ignored; Tailwind picks up classes used in your JOPS files.
  • REST, not Server Actions. A JOPS app talks to Next.js through Route Handlers.
  • Deploy public/ with the app, and use short cache headers for the JOPS files there, since they aren't content-hashed.

Try it

  • jops-core on npm: the full guide is in the README section "Next.js Integration"
  • GitHub for issues and discussions
  • Introducing JOPS, if you're new to the framework
  • JOPS Goes Mobile, the hybrid iOS and Android release

What's next: JOPS and Electron for standalone applications

JOPS now runs in the browser, in hybrid mobile apps and inside Next.js. The next environment on our list is the desktop. The JOPS team will examine integration with Electron, so the same class-based views can power standalone applications on Windows, macOS and Linux, with access to the file system and native menus through Electron's main process. Many of the internal tools JOPS was built for live on the desktop, and we'll share what we learn as the work progresses.

JOPS is built and maintained at UIDB, a boutique team of senior engineers who build custom systems with our clients, side by side. If you're extending a Next.js system or planning one that needs to hold up for years, we'd be glad to talk.

title: Content, themes and plugins shouldn't know each other: the idea behind Umono
description:
For almost four years I worked as a full-stack developer on a large WordPress site. It combined e-commerce and e-learning, and over time it grew to more than 60 plugins. By the end, even simple changes were stressful. A theme update could break a page, a plugin update could break the theme, and nobody could tell in advance what a change would touch.

The site wasn't badly built. The problem was structural: content, design and features had grown into each other. That's the question I started Umono with. What if those layers had hard boundaries, enforced by the system instead of by everyone's discipline?

Umono is an open-source CMS (Go, SQLite, MIT) that I've been building on my own since 2024. This post is about the idea behind it, not the feature list.

Three layers, three jobs

  • Content says what something means.
  • A theme decides how it looks.
  • A plugin adds what it does.

In most CMSs each of these can reach into the others. A theme ships templates and logic, so switching themes can change what a page shows. A plugin writes its own markup into your content, and when the plugin goes, that markup stays. In Umono each layer gets only what its job needs, and nothing more.

Content only says what it means

Pages are written in Compono, a Markdown-based language with components. Its Markdown surface is closed: there is no raw HTML and no way to style anything from the content. A component is reusable content:

{{ SAY_HELLO name="World" }}

~ SAY_HELLO name="Guest"
# Hello, {{ name }}!

That renders <h1>Hello, World!</h1>. Component names never appear in the output, and Umono adds no classes of its own. The result is plain, semantic HTML. Since the content carries no design, it doesn't care which theme displays it.

A theme only styles

A theme is a package of CSS, fonts and images. No templates, no scripts. This is a deliberate limit, and Umono checks it when a theme is built, installed and activated:

  • A theme has no JavaScript and can't change how anything works.
  • It can't add words, not even with CSS content. Text, link targets and accessibility attributes belong to the site owner.
  • It loads nothing from another origin: no fonts from a CDN, no remote images. The page's Content-Security-Policy enforces it.
  • It can't touch anything outside the page's root element, <head> included.

What a theme styles is plain HTML like this:

<umono-root>
  <header>
    <a href="/">My website</a>
    <nav aria-label="Main menu">
      <ul>
        <li><a href="/" aria-current="page">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
      </ul>
    </nav>
  </header>
  <main>
    <h1>Hello</h1>
    <p>This is my first page, written in <strong>Compono</strong>.</p>
  </main>
  <footer>
    <p>Made with Umono</p>
  </footer>
</umono-root>

And a theme is CSS against it:

:scope {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  background-color: #fdfcf8;
  color: #1f1d1a;
}

nav ul {
  display: flex;
  gap: 1.25rem;
  list-style: none;
}

a[aria-current="page"] {
  font-weight: bold;
}

The payoff for these limits is that switching themes is safe. Activating another theme replaces the old one in one step, without touching a single page.

The boundary is a public contract

How does a theme know which HTML to expect? From a contract. A contract is a TOML file published on umono.dev that describes a kind of site:

  • Layouts, the structure of a page. A blog has post, post-list and page.
  • Parameters, everything a layout shows: the site name, the menu, the title, the content. They all come from the site owner. A contract writes no text of its own, so it works in every language.
  • Components that the layouts share.

A theme picks one contract, and three rules keep that contract trustworthy:

  1. A published contract never changes and is never removed. A new structure comes as a new contract version.
  2. Contracts are MIT-0. Anyone can write a theme for any contract. Nobody controls who is allowed to style your site.
  3. The HTML is frozen. The same content produces the same elements in every Umono release until v1. Fixes to the output are collected and land once, in v1. A theme written today keeps working.

Umono also doesn't take a theme's word for it. It detects which features a theme actually uses and refuses one that declares less than it uses.

This is what I mean by no vendor lock-in. Your content isn't written for a theme, and a theme isn't written for your site. Both are written against a public contract, so either side can be swapped.

Plugins: the same idea, not built yet

Plugins are planned the same way. A plugin will implement a published schema, run as a separate service and get only the access the site owner grants it. Plugins for the same schema will be interchangeable, like themes for the same contract. This is still in design, and I'd rather say so than sell it.

Your site stays yours

Umono is one Go binary and one SQLite file on your own server. Public pages set no cookies and make no third-party requests. Fonts are served by the site itself.

What it costs

Hard boundaries have a price, and I don't want to hide it:

  • A theme can't add a feature. If a contract has no place for something, a theme can't invent one. That takes a new contract version.
  • Compono is a language you have to learn. Today it suits technical users more than editors.
  • Only the official contracts exist so far, with one official theme each: Octavo for simple sites and Folio for blogs.
  • There is no plugin system yet.

I think the trade is worth it, but it is a trade, and I'd like to hear where it hurts.

Where it is, and how you can help

Umono has had regular releases since November 2024, and umono.io runs on it. Version 0.9 brought the theme system. It isn't finished, and development continues.

  • Try it. curl -fsSL https://umono.io/install.sh | sh, then the docs walk you from an empty directory to a site with a theme: https://docs.umono.dev/getting-started/your-first-site/
  • Write a theme. The contracts are open, and the first-theme tutorial takes about fifteen minutes: https://docs.umono.dev/themes/your-first-theme/
  • Tell me where the idea breaks. Is a contract between content and theme the right boundary, or too rigid for real sites? GitHub Discussions: https://github.com/umono-cms/umono/discussions
  • Share it. If the idea resonates, a star or a share helps a one-person project get seen: https://github.com/umono-cms/umono

I wrote this post with help from an AI assistant. The ideas, the design and the decisions behind Umono are mine.

title: Looking for a workout app like Duolingo? Streaks, XP, quests and squads for the gym
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of GoldLift. Competitor details are from their own listings, checked October 2026.

Quick answer: GoldLift is a free fitness app that borrows Duolingo's playbook on purpose: a streak you do not want to lose, XP for every set, levels, daily quests, trophies, a reward shop and a squad that is counting on you. Underneath it is a serious tool: an AI-built programme, a chat coach and a full strength logger. iOS now, Android on the way.

Why gamification, and why it is not a gimmick

Most people who start training quit by week three. Not for lack of motivation on day one, but because nothing in a plain logger pulls you back on day eighteen. Duolingo solved that problem for languages with a streak, a daily goal and a leaderboard. GoldLift applies the same mechanics to lifting:

  • XP for every workout and every set. A daily XP goal sits on the home screen with a progress ring.
  • Levels. Your level is on your profile and visible to friends and your squad.
  • Streaks. A streak counter on the home screen, and streak freezes in the shop (paid with earned Gold) for the week life gets in the way.
  • Daily quests. "Log today's workout", "Earn 300 XP", "Like 3 posts from your squad": small tasks that give bonus XP.
  • Trophies and badges. Milestones for PRs, volume, consistency, challenges.
  • Reward Road and shop. You earn Gold by training and spend it on themes (18 of them), avatar frames and coach personalities. Nothing in the shop costs real money.
  • Squads, battles and leagues. Build a squad with friends and battle another squad for a week (an XP race or a volume war, for example). Weekly leagues rank you against people at your level, with promotion and demotion zones.
  • A mascot with opinions. Rex, the coach, reacts to a PR, a finished session or a skipped week.

It is still a real training app

The game layer sits on top of, not instead of, the tools:

  • AI builds your programme from your goal, level, equipment and training days.
  • Set-by-set logging with warm-ups, RPE/RIR, drop sets, rest-pause and cardio, fully offline.
  • Weight prescriptions per set that go up after an easy session and down after a miss.
  • A coach you can chat with mid-workout, with 12 personalities (drill sergeant, professor, stoic, hype man, and so on).
  • Progress charts, PRs, volume and intensity trends.
  • Nutrition logging by photo or text, macros, water and supplement reminders.
  • Apple Health and Apple Watch with live heart rate.

Compared with other "gamified" fitness apps

GoldLift Hevy Strong Fitbod
XP and levels Yes No No No
Streaks Yes Workout count only No No
Daily quests Yes No No No
Squad battles / leagues Yes No No No
Reward shop (earned, not bought) Yes No No No
AI-built programme Yes No No Yes (paid)
Price Free Free with caps, Pro paid Free with caps, PRO paid Subscription only

Honest downsides

  • iOS only for the moment.
  • Young app, small community compared with the big loggers.
  • Gym Passport (automatic check-ins at 400+ gyms) is Belgium-only.
  • If you hate game mechanics, you can ignore most of them, but they are visible.

FAQ

Is there a Duolingo for the gym?
GoldLift is the closest thing: streaks, XP, daily quests, levels, trophies, squads and leagues, built around an AI coach and a real workout logger. Free on iOS.

Does GoldLift have a streak feature?
Yes, with a streak counter on the home screen and streak freezes you can buy with Gold earned by training.

Can I compete with friends in GoldLift?
Yes. Add friends, compare PRs head to head, form a squad and battle other squads for a week, or climb your league.

Do I have to pay for the themes and rewards?
No. Everything in the shop is bought with Gold you earn by training.

GoldLift on the App Store: https://apps.apple.com/be/app/goldlift/id6758995677. Website: https://www.goldlift.app.

title: Code as Fanart: Building Miku’s Sengoku History Sanctuary Without Compromise
description:
If you look around modern web, it is all about algorithms, scams, ripoffs, crunching numbers for big corporations, or superficial noise. It is hard to find real love in the web! Where is the love poured into the making of a website? It should not be so hard to find!

Fear not! It is ok now! Why? Because I am here! Bringing yet another art from, another fanart project to break the mold. Explosions, or katanas- it matters not! Anything is allowed in love, and...code! And, this is code, because that is how it was made of. You should not just grind on to learn by doing something boring, and generic, rather show your devotion to the cause, the cause to show devotion, and how code is used as an art form!

I set out to build something entirely my own: Miku’s Sengoku History Sanctuary. I had set out my heart to make this, and so I did.

**
The Philosophy: Why Sengoku?**

As Miku Nakano famously notes in The Quintessential Quintuplets, "If you don't know Sengoku history, you can't understand people."

The Sengoku Jidai wasn't just a collection of dates, battles, and territorial disputes. It was a high-stakes crucible. In an era where entire clans rose and fell overnight, masks fell away. There was no room for hesitation, hollow corporate speak, or modern compromise. Leaders like Takeda Shingen, Sanada Yukimura, and Date Masamune survived because they understood human psychology down to its absolute core. They possessed raw grit, fierce loyalty, and an unyielding commitment to protecting what was theirs.
Standing beside a commander who holds a katana with absolute conviction, knowing he would cut down a chaotic world before letting harm reach you—that is the ultimate standard of safety and devotion. It is the exact opposite of the modern era's half-hearted noise. This project is a sanctuary dedicated to that unyielding spirit. The ultimate elegance in wielding a katana in an explosive way!
Architecture and Separation of Concerns
I wanted strict modularity. No messy inline stylesheets, no framework overhead—just raw, purposeful code following a clean separation of concerns:

• index.html: Pure, semantic markup structured around robust HTML tables (<table>, <thead>, <tbody>, <caption>, <th>, <td>) designed to display historical realities, tactical psychology, and romantic ideals with cryptographic clarity.
• style.css: A dedicated stylesheet managing custom properties (:root), box-sizing, and custom grid borders.

Escaping the "Mint Gum" Trap
Color theory matters. Early iterations of the stylesheet relied on generic corporate navies and pale sage greens that inadvertently made the page look like a pack of extra chewing gum. Miku’s aesthetic doesn't belong in a corporate SaaS dashboard. In art, even color transmits a message, a story, and it needs to be shown! Otherwise it is all for nothing.

To capture her true atmosphere, the design system was completely overhauled around a precise palette:
• Deep Indigo Background (#12141c): Captures her quiet, introspective demeanor and dark hair.
• Soft Matcha-Soda Text (#d4e6d7): Replaces blinding stark white text with a cozy, readable hue inspired by her favorite drink.
• Warm Cardigan Brown (#d08770): Anchors captions, borders, and pull quotes to her iconic knitwear.
• Cyan Headphone Accent (#88c0d0): Framed via custom inline SVG graphics at the header.

Crafting the SVG Headphone Header
An interface dedicated to Miku wouldn’t be complete without her signature studio headphones. Rather than relying on heavy external raster assets or messy image links, I integrated a custom, scalable vector graphic directly into the HTML structure.
Using native SVG paths (, , ), the headphone arch and earcups frame the sanctuary header seamlessly, adapting across viewports while retaining crisp vector lines against the dark indigo background.

HTML

<svg viewBox="0 0 500 120" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
    <path d="M 60,110 A 190,110 0 0,1 440,110" fill="none" stroke="#88c0d0" stroke-width="12" stroke-linecap="round"></path>

</svg>

The final blade!

Coding doesn't have to be a mechanical chore. When you take the technical fundamentals—semantic tables, CSS custom properties, vector layouts—and channel them into something you genuinely care about, programming turns back into what it was always meant to be: a creative craft.

Put on your headphones, play your favorite opening track, and remember: to conquer the land, you must conquer the soul. Most importantly commit, and pour your heart out into the code!

Right here: https://labrava0x.github.io/mikus-sengoku-tables/

title: Choosing a stack by proof of concept
description:
A technology choice defended with "it is what we know" is sometimes right and never checkable. A proof of concept makes it checkable — but only when it is run as a decision procedure, and not as an early version of the product.

00 / A proof of concept is a question with a deadline

Three things separate it from a prototype: a question whose answer is allowed to be no, a criterion agreed before anyone writes code, and a date on which it ends. Drop any one of them and the PoC quietly becomes the first version of the system — the demo ships, nobody re-reads the question, and the stack has been chosen by sunk cost.

The question has to be able to fail. "Can we build this in X?" cannot: the answer is always yes, given enough time. "What does X cost us on the part we are actually worried about, in two days?" can.

01 / Make the comparisons comparable

Same task, same timebox, same reviewer, and the criteria with their weights written down before the first commit. The task should be the thing you are afraid of — the query that worries you, the concurrency, the integration whose documentation looks thin — and not an endpoint every candidate
handles identically.

Three ways this goes wrong, all of them common:

  • each candidate is built by the person who already prefers it;
  • the candidates get different amounts of time, usually in favour of whoever started first;
  • the criteria are written after the results, and fit the winner remarkably well.

02 / Criteria that survive the meeting

On the consumer product behind this case study, the backend language was chosen after several proofs of concept rather than by preference, against four criteria: scalability, maintainability, speed, and how well the codebase would work with AI-assisted development. Go came out of that balance, and other parts of the stack were decided the
same way.

Three of those four are ordinary, and each is worth turning into a question with an answer rather than an adjective:

  • Scalability — what happens at ten and a hundred times the load you expect, and what does it cost there? Measure it; do not reason from the vendor's page.
  • Maintainability — how long does it take someone who did not write the code to make a small change safely? That is a number, and the PoC is the cheapest time to take it, while the codebase is still small enough for a newcomer to read in an hour.
  • Speed — of the system and of the team. A runtime that is fast and that nobody on the team writes fluently is slow.

03 / The criterion almost nobody tests for

The fourth criterion is the one worth being explicit about, because teams now take it on faith in one direction or the other: how well a codebase in this stack will hold up when much of it is written with an assistant.

It is testable, and the thing to measure is the review, not the output. Give the same feature to the assistant in each candidate and look at:

  • how much of what came back was correct, and how much was plausible and wrong;
  • what the compiler or the type system rejected before a human had to — a stack where wrong code fails to build is cheaper than one where it runs and fails later;
  • whether the standard library covered what the assistant would otherwise have pulled a dependency for, because dependencies chosen by autocomplete are a maintenance decision made by nobody;
  • whether formatting is settled by a tool, so that diffs are about logic instead of style;
  • how long the result took to review, which is the number that actually scales with the team.

A large public corpus helps. It is not the whole story: the wider a language's surface, the more there is to be confidently wrong about, and the more a reviewer has to hold in their head to catch it.

04 / Letting the answer be no

A PoC can also answer "do we keep what is already here?". On that engagement an earlier codebase existed, written by one developer more than a year earlier, and for the scope being started it offered little foundation. That is a legitimate result, and it needs the same written question and the same deadline as any other — otherwise the discussion drifts towards the previous author instead of the code.

When a question has been answered, the PoC should be deleted, or promoted deliberately with a plan for the parts that were never finished. Kept "just as a reference", it gets copied.

05 / The half a PoC does not cover

The language decision on that project anticipated AI-assisted development. The team's workflow for it was not standardised from the start, and output often did not meet shared expectations and had to be reworked, which lowered quality overall. It is the thing I would do differently, and it is
not a tooling problem.

A technology evaluation answers which tool. It does not answer how we work: what a task looks like before it is handed to an assistant, what review covers that it did not before, what gets written by hand, and what nobody merges without reading twice. That second question deserves the
same deliberate treatment as the first, and usually gets none — because it has no artefact to show at the end of the week.

Choose with evidence, then write down how the chosen thing is used. The first half is the easy one.
